# BOOK ONE

...things most agreeable to the Christian faith, which the ancients of the Jewish people strove with all their zeal to hide from the nations. Hence, the seventy translators <note>original: *septuaginta interpretes*. These are the scholars who produced the Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> (to speak of them first), as the Talmud testifies, omitted many things when translating for King Ptolemy, and changed many others. This was done so that divine secrets might not happen to become known to the Gentiles, who were at that time unworthy of them. Hence also the **Scribes** <note>Hebrew: *Sophrim* (סופרים)</note> themselves—that is, the scribes or wise men—erased many things from the divine scriptures as if they were absurd, or as if it were a sin to even dream of such things among the nations of the Gentiles. They did this as men who did not yet fully weigh the height of the divine counsel regarding the salvation of the human race. Either they feared that the divine scriptures would be mocked by their own people and by other infidels because of such things, or they suspected that a scandal of impious belief might be generated among the ignorant and simple Jews from such passages. Therefore, it is clear that they made those changes—by which it happened that the Holy Scripture was corrupted—not for the sake of hiding the truth, or from any other evil intent. For in these and almost infinite other places, they did not neglect to reveal the truth to one another, as is clearly evident in the Talmudic books. But it is plainly clear that they acted most wickedly in this, because they dared to act against the command of God. For He spoke thus through Moses in Deuteronomy 4: **You shall not add to the word which I command you, nor shall you take away from it.** <note>original Hebrew: *Lo tosifu al-ha-davar asher anochi metzaveh etchem, ve-lo tigra’u mimenu* (לא תוסיפו על הדבר אשר אנכי מצוה אתכם ולא תגרעו)</note> And again, through Solomon in the 30th chapter of Proverbs, it is said: **Add not to his words, lest he reprove you, and you be found a liar.** <note>original Hebrew: *Al-tosef al-devarav pen-yochiach becha ve-nichzavta* (אל תוסף על דבריו פן יוכיח בך ונכזבת)</note> For that reason Jeremiah, in the prophetic manner, speaking of the future as if it were the past, rebukes the bold deed of these scribes who were to perpetrate such things, with these words in the 8th chapter: **How do you say, "We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us"? But behold, the false pen of the Scribes** <note>Hebrew: *Sophrim* (סופרים)</note> **has worked for a lie.** <note>original Hebrew: *Eichah tomru chachamim anachnu ve-torat Adonai itanu, achen hinneh la-sheker asah et sheker sophrim* (איכה תאמרו חכמים אנחנו ותורת יהוה אתנו אכן הנה לשקר עשה עט שקר סופרים)</note> What kind of lie, or what kind of falsehood the lying pen or quill of the scribes was going to commit, the same prophet expresses in the 23rd chapter, saying: **And you have perverted the words of the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God.** <note>original Hebrew: *Va-haphachtem et-divrei Elohim chayyim, Adonai tzeva’ot Eloheinu* (והפכתם את דברי אלהים חיים יהוה צבאות אלהינו)</note> And again in the 9th chapter he says: **And they will not speak the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies, and have grown weary in acting iniquitously.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-emet lo yedaberu, limdu leshonam davar-sheker, ha’aveh nil’u* (ואמת לא ידברו למדו לשונם דבר שקר העוה נלאו)</note>

->CAPNIO<-
Therefore, so that the truth may be opened to Christians, and the most impudent works of these scribes may come into public knowledge, you would do a useful thing if you brought to light their most unspeakable sacrileges, so rashly committed against the divine writings.

->GALATINO<-
The things which the holy fathers and prophets formerly wrote in the sacred writings as the Holy Spirit dictated, the **Scribes** <note>Hebrew: *Sophrim* (סופרים)</note> themselves—that is, the scribes—corrupted in many ways and wrongly; for which reason they did not fear.

# BOOK ONE

...what a worthlessness, and you have made him expire, says the Lord of hosts. For in that place, <note>original: *uehippachtem othi* (וּתְפַחְתֶּם אֹתִי)</note>, that is, **And you have afflicted me**, was what was written. They, however, wrote <note>original: *uehippachtem otho* (וּתְפַחְתֶּם אֹתוֹ)</note>, that is, **And you have afflicted him**. For the word *othi* which was there signifies "me," but *otho* which they themselves placed there, by changing the letter *yod* into a *vav*, designates "him." <note>The Hebrew letter Yod (י) often indicates the first person "me," while Vav (ו) indicates the third person "him."</note> This is clearly affirmed by **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: *R. Selomo*; this is Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> in his gloss, saying: "And you have made him expire, or you have afflicted him. This is one of the fifteen words of the <term>ticcun sophrim</term> (the correction of the scribes)." Because "and you have made me expire," or "afflicted me," or "vexed me," was what was written. But the writing of the scribes placed "him" instead of "me." Furthermore, the word *uehippachtem* signifies the affliction of the soul. Just as in Job, chapter 11: "And their hope is the affliction of the soul." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. Moreover, that this word *uehippachtem* signifies expiration, or affliction, or vexation, **Rabbi Kimhi** <note>original: *R. Kimhi*; David Kimhi (1160–1235), also known as Radak</note> shows most excellently when he says: "That which is read in Job, chapter 31: 'And I afflicted the soul of its lords.' That also in Malachi, chapter 1, 'and you have afflicted,' signifies labor and vexation, or the affliction and vexation of the soul. For he who has affliction or vexation of the soul is just as if his soul were expired and departed from him." These are his words.

From these things it is clear that the passage in Malachi, chapter 1, which our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate used by the Church</note> has as: **Behold, of labor. And you have puffed at it, says the Lord of hosts**, is entirely corrupted. For which reason, according to the Hebrew truth, it ought to be corrected thus: **Behold, what a worthlessness, and you have afflicted me**, or **you have made me expire, says the Lord of hosts**. **Rabbi Rahmon** <note>Likely a reference to a Midrashic source or a specific rabbi cited in the Zohar</note> puts forward many other things of this kind when he says: "That which is written in the 3rd chapter of the Lamentations of Jeremiah: 'In remembering you will remember, and my soul will sink upon me'—it was originally written as 'your soul upon you.' For that which is now written, 'my soul upon me,' is from the many <term>Ticcun sophrim</term> (corrections of the scribes) which you will find in <term>Berescith rabba</term> <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient collection of Jewish lore and commentary on the book of Genesis.</note>." These are his words.

From which it is evident that what our edition has in the 3rd chapter of Lamentations—"In remembering I will remember, and my soul will sink in me"—is corrupted among the Hebrews as much as among us. For according to this Talmudic tradition it ought to be corrected: **In remembering you will remember, and your soul will sink upon you**. Truly, **Rabbi Moses the Preacher** <note>original: *Moses hadarsan*; an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne</note> on that passage in Genesis, chapter 18: **And Abraham still stood before God**, and in many other places, says this: "And this is a <term>ticcun sophrim</term> (correction of the scribes). For there it was written: **And God still stood before Abraham**." And this is what the masters said in the <term>midras tillim</term> <note>Midrash Tehillim, the ancient commentary on the Psalms.</note> on that passage in Psalm 18: **And you will give me the shield of your salvation**. For there it is said thus:

> "And you have given me the shield of your salvation" [Psalm 18:35]. This speaks of our father Abraham (peace be upon him). Abraham was sitting while the Divine Presence stood before him. Rabbi Berechiah said in the name of Rabbi Levi: Abraham sought to stand up, but the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "Sit, and you shall be a sign for your children; that they shall sit while I stand," as it is said, "God stands in the assembly of God" [Psalm 82:1].

That is, another discourse: **And you shall give me the shield of your salvation.** <note>Psalm 18:35</note> It speaks of our father Abraham, concerning whom it is written: *And Abraham was sitting, etc.*, and the Divine Presence stood before him. <note>referring to Genesis 18:1</note> **Rabbi Berachiah** said in the name of **Rabbi Levi**: Our father Abraham sought to stand up. Just as it is said, *God stood in the assembly or congregation of God.* <note>Psalm 82:1</note> Thus it is written there. It is well known that this was fulfilled when the Apostles, who were the children of Abraham according to the flesh, and the assembly and congregation of God, were sitting, and **Christ** the true God stood before them, washing their feet and wiping them with the towel with which he was girded. <note>A Christian typological interpretation of the Hebrew text, linking Abraham's vision to the Last Supper in John 13.</note> Then (to return to the Talmudic tradition), the aforementioned <note>original: *Midrash Tehillim*; an ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note> continues in the same place, saying:

Why have you set me as a mark against you, so that I am a burden to myself?* For that which is written there, **to myself**, is one of the <term>Tiqqun Soferim</term>, that is, of the corrections of the wise. For previously, **to you** was written. <note>Job originally complained he was a burden to God, which the scribes found irreverent.</note> So also in Job 32: *And they shall condemn God* (or act impiously with God); instead of **God**, they placed **Job**. And also in Ezekiel 8: *Is it a light thing for the house of Judah to commit the abominations which they have done here? For they have filled the land with iniquity, and they return to provoke me, and behold, they put the branch to their nose.* This is a <term>Tiqqun Soferim</term>, that is, a correction of the scribes. For where it says there <note>original: *el apam* (אֶל אַפָּם)</note>, that is, **to their nose**, it was originally written <note>original: *el api* (אֶל אַפִּי)</note>, that is, **to my nose**. <note>The scribes changed "My nose" (God's) to "their nose" to avoid describing God in human physical terms.</note> Furthermore, in Hosea 4: *As they were increased, so they sinned against me; I will change their glory into shame.* This is also a <term>Tiqqun Soferim</term>, a correction of the scribes. Finally, in Jeremiah 2: *And my people have changed its glory for that which does not profit.* This is also a <term>Tiqqun Soferim</term>, a correction of the scribes. For there, **my glory** <note>original: *cheuodi*</note>, and not **its glory** <note>original: *cheuodo*</note>, was written first. These and many other things of this kind are found in the <note>original: *Bereshit Rabbah*; the great midrashic commentary on Genesis</note>. There, Rabbi Johanan said in the name of Rabbi Simeon: "It is better that a single letter be removed from the Law than that the Name of Heaven should be publicly profaned." In these matters, therefore, which they propose in the aforementioned tradition, those texts are best corrected which are read in a flawed and corrupt form among us, as well as among the Hebrews. 

The first of these is Genesis 18, which is held among us as follows: *Abraham, however, still stood before the Lord.* It ought to be corrected to: **God, however, still stood before Abraham.** 

Next is that which is in Psalm 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 18:35</note>, which our edition has as: *And you have given me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand has supported me, and your discipline has corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself shall teach me.* This also should be corrected to: **And you shall give me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand shall strengthen me, and your humility (or your poverty, or your gentleness) shall multiply me (or shall nourish me).** 

Also, that which is read among us in Numbers 11: *Lest I be afflicted by such great evils.* It ought to be amended to: **If I have found grace in your eyes, let me not see Your evil.** <note>The scribe changed "Your evil" (God's punishment) to "my evil/misery" to avoid attributing "evil" to God.</note>

There is also that which we have in Job 7: *What shall I do to you, O guardian of men? Why have you set me contrary to you, and I am become a burden to myself?* It should be corrected to: **What shall I do to you, O guardian of man? Why have you set me as a target against you, so that I shall be a burden upon you?** <note>The scribes changed "a burden upon You" to "a burden to myself" to avoid the image of a human being weighing down God.</note>

Likewise, that which is read among us in Job 32: *But they had only condemned Job.* It should correctly be read: **And they shall condemn God (or act impiously toward God).**

Furthermore, that which we have in Ezekiel 8: *Is it a light thing for the house of Judah to do these abominations which they have committed here? For filling the land with iniquity, they have turned to provoke me. And behold, they apply the branch to my nostrils.* It should be amended to: **Is it a light thing for the house of Judah to have done the abominations they have done here? For they have filled the land with iniquity, and they shall repeat their provocation of me, and they shall be those sending a stench to my nose.** <note>The original Hebrew suggests a more graphic expression of contempt toward God which the scribes softened.</note>

Moreover, that which is among us in Hosea 4: *According to their multitude, so have they sinned against me; I will change their glory into ignominy.* It should be corrected to: **As is their multitude, so they have sinned against me; I will change my glory into ignominy.**

Finally, that which our edition has in Jeremiah 2: *But my people have changed their glory into an idol.* It should be corrected thus: **But my people have changed my glory for that which does not profit.**

<margin>The second way in which the Holy Scripture is altered.</margin>
The second mode of <term>Tiqqun Soferim</term> (that is, the correction of the scribes), as found in certain places of Holy Scripture, is where they left what the Prophets had written and did not change the letters, but presumed to add vowel points differently than the text naturally required. For the Hebrews do not have vowel letters, but use certain points in place of vowels. Therefore, by varying those points, the text is read far differently than what was written, and a far different sense is rendered.

# BOOK ONE. 32

GALATINUS: Moses (as you yourself know best) did not provide vowel points for the Law. This is why the scrolls which the Jews keep with such veneration in their Synagogues are written without points. Nor did any of the prophets add points to their own books. Rather, later scholars added points to the Law, the Prophets, and the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>the 'Holy Writings,' the third section of the Hebrew Bible including Psalms and Proverbs</note>. Some, therefore, say that Ezra was the first to point the sacred volumes. Others, however, affirm that it was not Ezra, but two others who lived after Ezra—one called Ben Naphtali and the other Ben Asher—who first applied points to the sacred letters. This latter opinion is the more common one.

CAPITO: Now, please recount some of those examples that the <term>Scribes</term> <note>original: *Sophrim*</note> corrupted through this kind of change of points in the sacred letters.

GALATINUS: Out of these, one example is found in the second book of Kings, chapter 16 <note>Modern 2 Samuel 16:12</note>. For there, it was originally written among them as follows: *Perhaps the Lord will look upon my humility* (or my *affliction*, or *poverty*, or *gentleness*), *and the Lord will return good to me for his cursing.* But the <term>Scribes</term>, wishing to "correct" this, took the word <term>my affliction</term> <note>Hebrew: בעניי, *be-onyi*</note>, which should naturally be pointed that way—and so pointed signifies "my humility," or "affliction," or "poverty," or "gentleness"—and instead pointed it as <term>in my eye</term> <note>Hebrew: בעייני, *be-eyni*</note>. Because of this, the commentary of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>The famous medieval commentator Rashi (1040–1105)</note> explains this word *in my eye* as referring to "the tears of my eye."

To this, a very similar instance is found in the first chapter of Micah: *I will make all its idols a desolation* (or a *destruction*). And a few verses later: *Over this I will wail and howl. I will go stripped and naked.* And shortly after: *Because its wound is painful and desperate. For it has come even to Judah, it has reached even to the gates of my people, even to Jerusalem. In Geth, do not announce it; in weeping, do not weep. In the house of dust,* <term>I have rolled myself</term> <note>Hebrew: התפלשתי, *hithpallašti*</note> *in the dust.*

That is how it is and was written. However, the Scribes, wishing to correct it, pointed it as <term>roll yourself</term> <note>Hebrew: התפלשי, *hithpallaši*</note>, which is the feminine form of the command "to roll." From these words of Micah, it is clearly held that God was intended to be "involved" in the ground or the dust. It does not matter that the Prophet used the word *I have rolled myself* in the past tense; this is the manner of the prophets, who very often use the past tense for the future to suggest the absolute certainty of a coming event. Hence, regarding that passage in Isaiah 42 (*These things I have done for them*), Rabbi Solomon says in his commentary: "I have done for them, that is, I *will* do for them. For the entire prophetic language speaks of the future as if it were already done." Thus says Rabbi Solomon.

Furthermore, one should not be ignorant of the fact that for this word <term>dust</term> <note>Hebrew: עפר, *aphar*</note>, which refers to moist ground or dust, Abraham also used it when speaking with the Lord. Wishing to express the condition and lowliness of the human body, he said in Genesis 18: *Behold, I pray, I have taken it upon myself to speak to the Lord, I who am* <term>dust</term> <note>Hebrew: עפר, *aphar*</note> (that is, moist earth or dust) <term>and ashes</term> <note>Hebrew: ואפר, *u-eepher*</note>. He said "dust and ashes" so that in the dust, or in

<summary>Galatinus explains that the Hebrew vowel points were not original to Moses but added later by scribes (the Soferim), who allegedly altered the vowels in specific verses (like 2 Samuel 16 and Micah 1) to change the theological meaning. He argues that these "corrections" obscured references to God's future incarnation or humble involvement with humanity.</summary>

->PRIMVS.<-

...or in moistened dust he might express the material principle of man, and in ash his final resolution. What, therefore, does this saying of the Lord in Micah mean, when he says: *In the house for the ground, or from the ground of moistened dust, I have wrapped myself*? <note>Micah 1:10. The author is interpreting the Hebrew place name "Beth-le-Aphrah" literally as "House of Dust."</note> It means nothing else than that he was wrapped—or rather, "I will wrap myself," that is, "I will clothe myself"—in the earthly or fleshly body of a certain virgin. From these things which have been said in this second mode of the <term>Correction of the Scribes</term> <note>original: *Ticcun Sophrim*</note>, two texts are especially corrected, which are held as corrupt both among us and among the Hebrews. The first is that which is found in our edition in the second book of Kings, chapter 16 <note>Modern 2 Samuel 16:12</note>: *If perhaps the Lord may look upon my affliction, and the Lord may return good to me for this day's cursing.* This text, however, must be corrected in this way: *Perhaps the Lord will look upon his own affliction, or his own humility, or his own poverty, or his own gentleness, and the Lord will return good to me for his own curse.* The second text is from Micah, chapter one, which we read as: *In the house of dust, sprinkle yourselves with dust.* This text also ought to be thoroughly corrected as: *In the house toward the ground, or from the dust of the ground, I have wrapped myself, or I have surrounded myself.*

<margin>Third mode of the corruption of scripture.</margin>
Finally, the third mode of the <term>Correction of the Scribes</term> <note>original: *Ticcun Sophrim*</note>, by which the sacred scripture happened to be altered, is when they left what Moses and the Prophets wrote within the text itself, but placed something else in the margin outside, which they call <term>Keri</term> <note>original: קרי, meaning "that which is read"</note>, and what is inside the text they call <term>Ketiv</term> <note>original: כתיב, meaning "that which is written"</note>. This is clearly gathered from the words of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>The famous medieval commentator Rashi (1040–1105)</note> regarding that passage in Deuteronomy 28: *You shall betroth a wife, and another man shall ravish her.* For there, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "The word *isgalenna* <note>original: ישגלנה</note> is a word for the intercourse of a concubine. But the <term>Targum</term> <note>the Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note>, for the sake of courtesy, placed in its stead *iscauenna* <note>original: ישכבנה</note>, that is, 'he shall lie with her.' And this is a <term>correction of the scribes</term> <note>original: *ticcun sophrim*</note>." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. Likewise, the same Rabbi says regarding that passage in Isaiah 36: *And the Rabshakeh said: Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak these words? Is it not rather to the men sitting on the wall, to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?* The gloss of Rabbi Solomon says there: "*Horehem* <note>original: חריהם</note>, that is, 'their dung,' which is the filth coming out from the opening below; but the <term>Scribes</term> corrected this with a beautiful and courtly language, and they wished that *czoatham* <note>original: צואתם</note>, that is, 'their egestion,' should be read." For so the masters decreed, that those things in scripture written discourteously for the sake of shame should be read courtly and politely. Just as in that passage of Deuteronomy chapter 28, where it is written *baapolim* <note>original: בעפולים</note>, that is, "with tumors," they placed in the margin to be read *battechorim* <note>original: בטחורים</note>, that is, "with hemorrhoids" or "dysentery." Likewise, in the same place where Moses wrote *isgalenna* <note>original: ישגלנה</note>, that is, "he shall ravish her," they placed on the outside *iscauenna* <note>original: ישכבנה</note>, that is, "he shall lie with her." Furthermore, in Isaiah chapter 36, where it is written *Horehem*...

...their dung [original: *horehem*], they placed as <term>tz'atam</term> <note>original: *צואתם czoatham*</note>, that is, "their waste." In the same way, where the Prophet wrote <term>sh'tenechem</term> <note>original: *שתינהם sethnechem*</note>, meaning "their urine," the scribes instead placed <term>meimei raglehem</term> <note>original: *מימי רגליהם meme raglehem*</note>, meaning "the waters of their feet." And there are many other examples similar to these. All these points are noted by Rabbi Selomo <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note>. Also, in the ninth chapter of the prophet Hosea, it is written: "For even woe to them, my incarnation from them" <note>Hosea 9:12. The author is arguing the original Hebrew word *be-sari* (my flesh/incarnation) was altered</note>. However, the scribes changed the word <term>be-sari</term>, meaning "my incarnation" or "my flesh," against the very nature of the word itself, and pointed it as <term>be-suri</term>, which signifies "in my departure." I say "against the nature of the word" because <term>be-suri</term>, which is inside the text, is written with the letter *shin* [ש], just as the prophet Hosea had written it. Therefore, <term>be-sari</term> (my incarnation or my flesh) should have been pointed with the vowel *a*, as in <term>basar</term>, meaning "flesh." But <term>be-suri</term>, which they placed on the outside <note>referring to the marginal "Keri" or "read" version</note> and which signifies "in my departure," is written with the letter *samekh* [ס]. Regarding this, Rabbi Selomo, explaining this passage, says: "For also woe to them," namely the fathers, "<term>be-suri</term> is as if it were <term>be-suri</term>, meaning 'in my departure from them.'" And this is one of those instances where a *shin* [ש] is written but a *samekh* [ס] is read. Rabbi Chinhi <note>Likely David Kimhi, known as Radak</note> also says in the *Book of Roots* <note>original: *Seraſcim* / *Sefer Shorashim*</note> that "For also woe to them, <term>be-suri</term>," is written with the letter *shin* and read with the letter *samekh*. All these things are from Rabbi Selomo. Furthermore, from what we have said here regarding this third mode of the <term>Correction of the Scribes</term> <note>original: *ticcun Sophrim*</note>, three specific texts among others are corrected. The first of these is found in the 28th chapter of Deuteronomy, which we have as: "You shall take a wife, and another shall sleep with her." This text, however, according to the Hebrew truth, is to be corrected thus: "You shall betroth a wife, and another man shall violate her" <note>The author argues the scribes used a gentler word for "violate" or "ravish"</note>. The second text is in the 36th chapter of Isaiah, where we read: "And Rabshakeh said: Has my master sent me to your master and to you to speak all these words? And not rather to the men who sit on the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their feet with you?" This text also ought to be corrected as: "And Rabshakeh said, Has my Lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak these words? Is it not rather to the men sitting upon the wall, to eat their own excrement and to drink their own urine?" The third and final text is Hosea 9, which the author of our edition, following the error of the <term>Correction of the Scribes</term>, translated as: "But also woe to them when I shall depart from them." This text, however, must be corrected entirely as: "Because also woe to them, my incarnation—or my flesh—is from them."

**CAPNIO** <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin</note>: I pray you, tell me if there are others of this kind among them.
**GAL.** <note>The persona of Pietro Galatino</note>: There are truly so many that it is almost impossible to name them all. I will, however, tell you a few others out of the many. Nevertheless, I would hope that if it happens that some of these things already mentioned are repeated, it will not be attributed to worthlessness on my part. Indeed, it is hardly possible to report the precise words of those who happened to say the same things (as we must do when arguing against the Jews, lest they deny what we say) without repeating the same point several times.

Therefore, in the book *Sifre* <note>An ancient Jewish legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note>, which is considered highly authentic among them, it is held among other things regarding that passage in Numbers, chapter 10: "Rise up, Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee." Does He who spoke and the world was made have any who hate Him? Rather, the Scripture announces and teaches that whoever hates Israel, it is just as if they hated Him who created the world by His word. And thus He Himself says in Zechariah, chapter 2: "For he who touches you touches the pupil of His eye." Where <term>Rabbi Judah</term> says: "It was not said 'the pupil of His eye,' but 'the pupil of my eye'" <note>original: *pupillam oculi mei*. The argument is that the text originally had God saying "my eye," but scribes changed it to "His eye" to avoid suggesting God has a physical eye</note>. Because it is stated this way in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture was speaking "against the height" <note>original Latin: *Contra sursum*; a euphemism for speaking against God</note>, but the "recent scripture" <note>original: *scriptura recens*; referring to the version corrected by the scribes</note> used a pronoun; that is, it said one thing in place of what had been written. 

It is nearly the same in that passage of Job, chapter 7: "Why have you set me as a mark against you, so that I am a burden to you?" <note>Job 7:20. The author argues the original read "to you" (God), but was changed to "to myself" in many versions</note> Because it is written thus in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture was speaking "against the height" (against God), but the "recent scripture" used a pronoun; that is, it named another thing in place of what had been written. 

Similar to this is also that passage in Ezekiel, chapter 8: "And they are putting a stench to my nose" <note>Ezekiel 8:17. Most versions read "their nose," but the author suggests the original referred to God's nose</note>. Because it is written thus in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture speaks against God, but in its place the "recent scripture" said, "We shall not die." 

Similar to this is that passage in Psalm 106: "And they changed my glory." But in its place, the "recent scripture" said, "their glory." Still similar is that in Numbers, chapter 11: "And if you deal thus with me, kill me, I pray you. If I have found favor in your eyes, let me not see your evil" <note>Numbers 11:15. The author suggests "your evil" (God's) was changed to "my wretchedness" to protect God's reputation</note>. Because it is written thus in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture spoke "against the height," but in its place the "recent scripture" said another thing. 

Moreover, similar to this is Numbers, chapter 12: "Who is as one coming out from our mother's womb, and half of our flesh is consumed." Because it is written thus in the Law, it can be said: the Scripture was speaking "against the height," but the "recent scripture" used a pronoun, which the scribes corrected by putting "his mother" and "his flesh."

This also must be corrected thus: "Are you not from of old, O Lord my God, my Holy One, you who do not die?" <note>The Hebrew text reads "We shall not die," but tradition holds it was originally "You [God] shall not die." Scribes supposedly changed it because suggesting God *could* die—even in the negative—was considered irreverent</note> From all these examples, therefore (as is clearly seen), not only is the sacrilegious audacity of the scribes detected, but the texts of the Holy Scripture themselves are most excellently corrected. This is true not only for them [the Jews], but also for us, who in our editions, both Greek and Latin, have followed the depravations of those same scribes until now.

For he feared the Jews, and showed himself to me as another Nicodemus." Just as he suffered a penury of Jewish masters, so perhaps he also lacked books, and especially the Talmud itself, which the Jews hide because of the secrets of the Messiah [pertaining] to our faith...

## Chapter 9. How one should proceed against the Jews by means of their own scriptures.

### CAPNIO
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style nickname for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous German humanist and Hebraist who appears here as a character in the dialogue.</note>

Since we have been granted the merit of approaching you—you who are inspired by divine power and are able to uncover these secrets, so wonderful and divine, that lie hidden in the Talmudic books of the Jews—we ask you with all earnestness that you not think any of them should be hidden from us. Rather, for the honor of Almighty God himself, for the glory of the most holy Christian Church, for the confirmation of the Orthodox faith, for the salvation of souls, and for the manifestation of Universal truth, do not fail to reveal each one of them to us as we inquire. 

**GALATINUS.** I will indeed try to satisfy your wishes as far as I am able; but if I say anything good, attribute it not to me, but to God, from whom (as Polycrates says) *all good things proceed* <note>original Greek: *πάντα τὰ ἀγαθὰ προέρχονται*</note>. And rightly so. For with Plato as witness, *from the one Good all good things come* <note>original Greek: *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀγαθοῦ πάντα τὰ ἀγαθά*</note>. But whatever is bad, ascribe it to my own ignorance. 

First, therefore, one must know that the sacred Old Scripture contained all the articles of the Christian faith, wrapped in various figures and riddles, covered as if with veils, and sealed with certain seals. This was so that upon the arrival of Christ, the veils and seals having been removed by him, they might be clearly revealed and made public. To the extent that, with truth present, the symbols would cease; with light appearing, the shadows would be driven away; and with the sun now risen, whatever was dark would be rendered clear and bright. Since Christ himself is the truth, the light, and the sun of justice, who (on the authority of John the Evangelist) illuminates every person coming into this world. For which reason he himself said in John, chapter 8: *I am the light of the world; he who follows me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.* <note>original Greek: *ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου, ὁ ἀκολουθῶν ἐμοὶ οὐ μὴ περιπατήσῃ ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ, ἀλλ’ ἕξει τὸ φῶς τῆς ζωῆς*</note> 

However, since the modern Jews are utterly blinded by the impiety of their lack of faith, they twist the right sense of divine Scripture against us and wage war upon us. But we easily convict them through the traditions of the ancient Talmudists, who, in explaining the sayings of the Law and the Prophets, speak more clearly about these very articles. Therefore, so that their falsehood may be more clearly detected and the Universal truth itself may shine forth more brightly, I will do two things in each of these secrets. First, I will bring forward the sayings of the Law and the Prophets themselves—which they strive to pervert with false interpretations and twist back against us—and I will correctly explain them for our purpose by means of their own writings.

# Book Two.

# On the divine trinity and on the divine names through which the trinity of God itself, along with the indivisible unity of essence and its perfections, are best introduced.

## That God is three and one. Chapter 1.

->REUCHLIN,<-
<note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Hebrew. He is referred to by his Greek pseudonym "Capnio" throughout this text.</note>

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial "D" set within a square frame featuring a dense pattern of floral and foliate scrolls. In the center of the letter, a small figure (putto or infant) is depicted holding an object.</image-desc>

**A**mong other things, the more recent Jews especially object to us that, when they hear us confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they claim we worship three Gods and posit a plurality of Gods. This is something we truly abhor far more than they do. For that reason, it behooves you first to prove from the sayings of the Prophets and the testimonies of the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud; Galatinus distinguishes between "ancient" ones who he believes support Christian truth and "modern" ones who do not</note> that God is three and one. 

**GALATINUS.** The Christian religion indeed believes that God is one in the <term>simplicity</term> <note>In theology, "simplicity" means that God is not composed of parts or different substances; He is a single, unified being</note> of His substance and nature. However, it confesses three persons—who are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—whose distinct properties are <term>paternity</term>, <term>generation</term>, and <term>procession</term> <note>These are technical terms describing the relationships within the Trinity: the Father's role as father, the Son being "begotten," and the Holy Spirit "proceeding" from them</note>. It confesses them to be not three in essence nor in nature, but purely one. Therefore, God is indeed three in persons, but one in essence. There is no need to use many words to prove that God is one, nor to linger longer on proving that point. For the unity of God is such a firm and fixed conception of the mind that, by nature, there cannot be anything but one God. Both the Jews and whoever believes in the Law <note>The Torah or the Old Testament</note> all confess and proclaim this. 

**REUCHLIN.** It is enough here, then, if the error of the younger Jews concerning the <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "sacramentum"</note> of the divine trinity is refuted through the opinions of the ancient Jews. 

**GALATINUS.** In a matter so arduous and difficult, their foundation must first be utterly destroyed; then, the falsehood of the interpretations by which they pervert the sacred letters must be condemned. Wishing to avoid wordiness, we shall do both at the same time in this matter, as in many others. The reason upon which they lay the foundation of this error is chiefly that they misunderstand and falsely explain that which is written in the 6th chapter of Deuteronomy: <note>original Hebrew: שמע ישראל יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד</note> "Hear, Israel, God, our God, God is one." <note>This is the "Shema," the central prayer of Judaism. Galatinus translates the divine names (YHWH and Elohim) simply as "God" here to facilitate his argument.</note> Although these words are clear in themselves, yet on account of the word "one," which—

**HOCHSTRATUS.** <note>The Latin text uses "Gostratus," referring to Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican inquisitor and opponent of Reuchlin. For it says: *Hear, Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one* <note>original Greek: *ἄκουε ἰσραὴλ, κύριος ὁ θεὸς σου κύριος εἷς ἐστὶν*</note>. But it is certainly clear that the Hebrew text expresses the truth against the Jews themselves far better than our version, whether Greek or Latin, expresses it. Now, the reason why I have translated it as "God" where our edition (both Greek and Latin) has "Lord" in this place is this: the Hebrew text in that same spot has **YHWH** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note>, which is that <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The "four-letter" name of God. Galatinus argues that this specific name refers to God's essence rather than just a title like "Lord."</note> name of God, which designates God not by His effect, but by His essence. 

But since the divine essence, according to its own proper being, can in no way be conceived by the mind, for that reason it is considered a sacrilege among the Jews for the name itself to be pronounced by the mouth as the letters themselves sound from which it is composed. Therefore, wherever they find this name, they do not dare to utter it at all, but in its place they utter this name **Adonai** <note>original Hebrew: אדני</note>, which is the same as "Lord"; yet the letters of the name itself signify not "Lord," but "God" through His essence. 

The author of both the Greek and Latin editions, therefore, translated the name according to the meaning of its pronunciation [Lord], but omitted the meaning of the writing, which is more important. However, I—to whom it is of the greatest heart to reveal the truth that the Jews deny through their own scriptures—have translated it according to its own proper meaning, so that I might clearly show that God, both three and one, is designated in the aforementioned words. For no other reason did the great Moses place the name of God there three times, except to distinctly suggest the trinity of divine persons. And in the word "one," which he immediately added, he suggests that the three divine persons are not three Gods, but one God. This is (as <term>Damascene</term> <note>St. John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian famous for his defense of icons and his systematic "Exposition of the Orthodox Faith."</note> says) *one essence, one nature, one deity* <note>original Greek: *μία οὐσία, μία φύσις, μία θεότης*</note>. That is: one essence, one nature, one deity. Therefore, the trinity of persons in no way detracts from the unity of the divine nature. 

Furthermore, that in these same words, through the threefold name of God, the three divine persons are designated—namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy <margin>Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai. The exposition of Rabbi Ibba.</margin> Spirit—this the Jews can by no means deny, since Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai, in the book called the **Zohar** <note>original Hebrew: זוהר; the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah. Galatinus frequently cites it to prove Christian doctrines using Jewish mystical sources.</note>, says thus upon this text: 

"Hear, O Israel," says Rabbi Ibba. "This is, O Israel, the ancient **YHWH** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note>, that is, God, who is the beginning of all things, the Ancient of Ancients, the Garden of Roots, and the perfection of all things; and He is called the Father. **Elohenu** <note>original Hebrew: אלהינו, meaning "Our God"</note>, that is 'Our God,' the depth of rivers and the fountain of knowledge which proceed from that Father, and He is called the Son. **YHWH** <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note>, that is, God; this is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both, and is called the Measure of the Voice. He is one, so that one with the other..."

This is clearly evident through Rabbi Menahem Recanati in the book *Zohar* <note>Menahem ben Benjamin Recanati (1250–1310) was an Italian rabbi and Kabbalist; his commentary on the Torah drew heavily on the Zohar.</note> regarding the same text of Deuteronomy. ### Chapter [XX]: Why God did not wish the mystery of the Trinity to be so explicitly handed down in the Old Testament, but reserved it to be revealed in the future through the Messiah.

<margin>
Why the mystery of the trinity was not explicitly handed down under the Old Law.
</margin>
<margin>
The mystery of the trinity was to be explicitly revealed through the Messiah.
</margin>
**GALATINUS.** The people of the Jews (as I do not doubt you know) were extremely prone to idolatry; the entire Old Law was established to avoid this. Therefore, lest they fall into the error of those who worshiped many gods, it was carefully arranged by divine providence that the secret of the divine trinity itself was handed down to them not explicitly, but implicitly. But since idolatry was to be utterly driven out by the Messiah, and the whole world was to be brought back to the worship of one God, for that reason the sacrament of the trinity was reserved for the days of the Messiah, to be revealed explicitly and openly. This is also clearly testified by the entire school of the Cabalists, who assert that the secrets of the divine trinity itself ought to have remained hidden only until the time of the Messiah. At that time, however, when all suspicion of the error of idolatry was to be removed, even the secrets of the divine trinity were to be openly uncovered.

<margin>
Why "Our" is added to the second name of God, and not the first or third.
</margin>
**HOCHSTRATUS.** Since in the previously mentioned words—*Hear, Israel, God, our God, God is one*—the name of God is placed three times, why is it that "Our" is added only to the second name, and not to the first or the third?

**GALATINUS.** That was certainly not done without reason. For from this it is clearly hinted that neither the Father, who is the first person in the trinity, nor the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the same trinity, but only the Son—who is the second person of the same trinity—was to be "ours" through the participation of our humanity. That which is written in Psalm 67 is similar to this: "May God bless us, our God, may God bless us, and let all the ends of the earth fear him." In the fact that "God" is placed there three times, the distinction of the three divine persons is designated. However, in the fact that "Our" is joined only in the second place, it was suggested that only the Son would be "ours" through the assumption of our nature <note>This refers to the Doctrine of the Incarnation—that the second person of the Trinity became human.</note>. Indeed, in the fact that at the end it says "Fear *him*," and not "them," the unity of the persons themselves regarding nature...

### SECOND [BOOK]

...refutation, and toward a clearer expression of Catholic truth, you would do well indeed, my Galatinus, if you were to prove, by reason also strengthened by Hebrew testimonies, the trinity of persons with the unity of the divine essence, without any derogation of that same unity. **GAL.** I shall indeed do so, and certainly as briefly as possible. Would they <note>meaning the Jewish scholars being discussed</note> not, therefore, consider it must be granted that God is in different places? **CAP.** Absolutely. For both the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> affirm this everywhere, and the sacred Scripture asserts it. Especially in what is Psalm 139 among them, which says: <gloss>original Hebrew: אם אסק שמים שם אתה ואציעה שאול הנך אשא כנפי שחר אשכונה באחרית ים : גם שם ידך תנחני ותאחזני ימינך</gloss> **If I ascend to the heavens, you are there; and if I lie down in hell, you are present. If I take the wings of the morning, if I dwell in the furthest part of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.** From these words it is clearly evident that God is everywhere. **GAL.** However, this cannot be verified as being according to different parts of God. For since God is a spirit, and supremely <term>simple</term> <note>In theology, "simplicity" means God is not made of parts; He is a single, unified essence.</note> (as they themselves also say), he lacks all diversity of parts and composition. For in the *Book of Formation*, which they call <gloss>original Hebrew: ספר יצירה Sefer Yetzirah</gloss>, in that place where the ten <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>In Kabbalah, these are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals Himself.</note> are placed—that is, ten incorporeal and abstract numbers, or rather ten incorporeal and secret unities, the first of which is placed as God himself, being the most abstract of all—it is held thus: <gloss>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים חיים ברוך ומבורך שמו של חי העולמים קול ורוח ודבר זה רוח הקדש</gloss> **The Spirit of the living God, or God the Spirit, blessed and praised be his name, who is the life of the ages, voice, spirit, and word: this is the Holy Spirit,** whose beginning (as other books have it) cannot be searched out, and whose end has no limit. So it is said there. Nor would they say that he is in different places successively <note>one after another</note>. For then he would be changeable according to place, which they completely deny, since it can in no way befit God. Since he is eternal, immense, and supremely simple, he cannot be changed according to time, nor according to place, nor according to form. Therefore, they too, just as we do, have asserted him to be entirely immutable. For God himself says in the third chapter of Malachi: <gloss>original Hebrew: אני יהוה לא שניתי</gloss> **I am the Lord, I do not change.** For that reason, it is necessary for them to confess: that God (even if he is one) is entirely, with the truth of his unity, in different places at one and the same time. On which account it is also necessary that they grant this: that the divinity itself (even if it exists as only one in number) is entirely in several persons at once. Now if they grant that first point <note>that God can be in many places at once</note>, why do they deny this second one <note>the Trinity</note>, since one ought to be granted no more than the other? But they certainly cannot deny this at all, since not only do the ancient Talmudists and <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note> (as has already been shown) confess it everywhere, but the divine utterances also testify to it. For wherever in the sacred letters of the Old Testament the essence of the one God is suggested, almost always in the same place the plurality of the three persons is also hinted at. And conversely, in whatever place the trinity of persons is expressed...

# BOOK I

Almost always in the same place, the unity of the divine substance is also explained. This is done so that the trinity of persons is not excluded from the divine nature on account of the unity of the singular God, nor are many Gods believed to exist on account of the trinity of persons. But rather, in the one sense, these three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>A Greek theological term (ὑποστάσεις) referring to the distinct persons of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who share one essence.</note> are believed to be distinct from one another without confusion, while in the other, the unity of God himself is entirely preserved. This is clearly evident in the Song of Moses, in that place where we read: "See that I alone am, and there is no God
<margin>
Deut. 32.
Hebrew

besides me," the Hebrew text has it thus: **ראו עתה כי אני אני הוא ואין אלהים עמדי** <gloss>original Hebrew: Re'u atah ki ani ani hu ve-ein elohim imadi</gloss>. That is: **See now, that I, I, [am] He: and there are no Gods with me.** Where among the Hebrews these three names are placed, which among them are divine: **אני אני הוא** <gloss>original Hebrew: Ani, Ani, Hu</gloss>. Which are interpreted among us as **I, I, Himself**. What then is designated there by these three divine names, if not the plurality and distinction of the three divine persons? And what is suggested by that which is immediately added there, "And there are no Gods with me," unless it is that those three divine hypostases, designated by those three divine names, are not three Gods, but one God? For even if the whole divine essence is in the Father, the whole in the Son, and the whole in the Holy Spirit: since the Father is true and perfect God, from whom are all things; and the Son is true and perfect God, through whom are all things; and the Holy Spirit is true and perfect God, in whom are all things; because that same divine nature is entirely in the three, therefore the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God, who made all things, and from whom, through whom, and in whom all things proceed, subsist, and are given life, and to whom at last all things are brought back. For as that Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" famous for his work on Trinitarian theology.</note>, easily the prince of Greek theologians, says: <note>original Greek: εἷς ἐστιν ὁ θεὸς, ὁ πατὴρ ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα καὶ ὁ υἱὸς δι' οὗ τὰ πάντα. καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐν ᾧ τὰ πάντα, αὐταὶ γὰρ αἱ προθέσεις, τὸ ἐξ οὗ, καὶ δι' οὗ, καὶ ἐν ᾧ, οὐ μὲν τὴν φύσιν τέμνουσιν, ἀλλὰ τὰς τῆς μιᾶς καὶ ἀσυγχύτου φύσεως ἰδιότητας χαρακτηρίζουσιν.</note> **God is one: the Father from whom are all things, and the Son through whom are all things, and the Holy Spirit in whom are all things. For these prepositions—"from whom," "through whom," and "in whom"—do not indeed divide the nature, but characterize the properties of the one and unconfused nature.** How these things come to be, John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century Syrian monk and priest, known for his systematic defense of Christian doctrine.</note> shows, who attempted to explain this mystery no less elegantly than subtly in that book which he inscribed *On the Divine Tradition*, saying thus in chapter 49, among other things: <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς θεότητος μίαν φύσιν ὁμολογοῦμεν, τρεῖς δὲ ὑποστάσεις κατὰ ἀλήθειαν φαμὲν, καὶ πάντα μὲν τὰ φυσικὰ καὶ οὐσιώδη, ἁπλᾶ φαμὲν, τὴν δὲ διαφορὰν τῶν ὑποστάσεων ἐν μόναις τρισὶν ἰδιότησι... [long passage truncated in original]</note> **In the divinity we confess one nature, but we say there are three hypostases in truth. And indeed we say all things natural and essential are simple, but the difference of the hypostases [is] in only three properties: the uncaused and paternal, the caused and filial, and the caused and proceeding. They are joined without departing or being distant from each other, united and yet unconfused with each other—for they are three, though united—and they are divided without distance. For each one subsists by itself, that is, is a perfect hypostasis, and possesses its own property, or rather a different mode of hypostasis, but they are united in essence and natural properties; they do not stand apart, nor depart from the paternal hypostasis, and they are and are called one God.** That is: In the divinity we confess one nature, but we say there are three hypostases, according to the truth. And indeed all things natural and essential, [we say are] simple...

# BOOK

...he says: "And you shall know that the Lord <note>Original: *Deus (tetragrammaton)*, referring to the four-letter divine name יהוה (YHWH).</note> of hosts has sent me to prophesy to you." This cannot be referred to anyone except God being sent—that is, to the Messiah, who was to be sent by God the Father. It is therefore clear enough, both through this prophecy and through the Chaldean translation <note>Original: *Chaldaïcam translationem*, referring to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible used by Jewish scholars.</note> of the prophecy itself, that there is both a God who sends and a God who is sent. For he shows evidently that this one whom he says is to be sent for prophesying is God, from the fact that he immediately says, speaking in his person: "And I will place my divinity in your midst. And you shall know that the Lord <note>Original: *Deus (tetragrammaton)*</note> has sent me to prophesy to you." This same point is also clearly manifested from the fact that in the aforementioned prophecy, that sent God, who must be the Messiah, is called by that most holy name of God, the Tetragrammaton <note>Original: *tetragrammato* יהוה, the sacred name YHWH, which traditional Jewish practice considers too holy to pronounce.</note>, which belongs to God alone.

To prove also that the Messiah is God who is sent, we bring forward the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>Original: מדרש שיר השירים; a traditional Jewish homiletic commentary on the Song of Songs.</note>, that is, the exposition of the Song of Songs by the ancient masters. There, it is read word-for-word as follows: "We will exult and rejoice in you." Rabbi Aben <note>Likely referring to the medieval commentator Abraham Ibn Ezra.</note> explained what was said in the Psalm: "This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it." Rabbi Aben said: "They did not know in whom they should rejoice, whether in the day or in God, until Solomon <note>Latin: *Selomo*</note> came and explained it, saying: 'We will exult and rejoice in you.'" In you—that is, in God, holy and blessed. In you—that is, in your salvation.

This is like a certain noblewoman whose husband the King, her sons, and her sons-in-law set out for a city by the sea. Messengers came and said to her, "Your sons have come." She said, "What is that to me? Or what benefit is that to me? Let my daughters-in-law rejoice." Again they said to her, "Your sons-in-law have come." She said, "What is that to me? Let my daughters rejoice." But when they said to her, "Your husband the King has come," she said, "Behold, surely this is sufficient and perfect joy for me."

So it was to be that the prophets would come and say to Jerusalem: "Your sons shall come from afar" (Isaiah chapter 60). And she said to them, "What is that to me? Let the daughters of Judah exult" (Psalm 97). "And your daughters shall be nursed or cherished at your side" (Isaiah 60). But she said, "What is that to me? Let Mount Zion rejoice" (Psalm 97). But when they said to her: "Behold, your King comes to you, just and having salvation" (Zechariah 9). As it is written in Zechariah 2: "Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst," says the Lord <note>Original: *Deus (tetragrammaton)*</note>. "And many nations shall be joined to the Lord <note>Original: *Deus (tetragrammaton)*</note> in that day, and they shall be my people, and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the Lord <note>Original: *Deus (tetragrammaton)*</note> of hosts has sent me to you." In that hour she said: "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord <note>Original: *Deus (tetragrammaton)*</note>, and my soul shall exult in my God" (Isaiah 61). And this is: "We will exult and rejoice in you," from the first chapter of the Song of Songs.

Thus far the tradition, in which their own faithful antiquity has most elegantly and evidently handed down to the faithless Jews of our time that the Messiah is God. For when, after the parable in the application to the proposal, they prove the coming of God through that passage in Zechariah 9: "Behold, your King will come to you, just and having salvation," along with the rest that follow...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 46, where the author uses Jewish sources to demonstrate that the Messiah possesses a divine nature. # FIRST BOOK.

The ancient Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law and legend.</note> evidently handed down to those who are wise and knowledgeable in the sacred scriptures that the Messiah is God. For these words of Zechariah (as the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, or Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says in that same place) cannot be explained except as referring to the King Messiah. They also confirmed this in a marvelous way when, after the aforementioned words, they immediately added another testimony from the same Prophet. In this, both God sending and God being sent are most excellently expressed. These two are indeed not two Gods, but only one God. For even if there are two in the *middot* <note>Original: מדות (*middot*), meaning "attributes" or "measures." In this context, the author uses it to correspond to the Christian concept of divine "Persons."</note>—that is, in the properties or persons—namely, God sending and God being sent; nevertheless, in the *hayuya* <note>Original: הויה (*hayuya* or *Havayah*), a term used here to mean "essence" or "being," derived from the Hebrew root for "to be."</note>—that is, in the essence—they are only one. Therefore, the Father and the Son, or God and His Word, are not two gods, but one God.

That the Father is the God who sends, and His Word or the Son of God is the God who is sent, is openly gathered from the words of Rabbi Simeon, son of Yochai <note>Simeon bar Yochai, a 2nd-century sage and traditional author of the *Zohar*.</note>, when he says thus at the beginning of the book *Taanit* <note>Original: תענית (*Tahanith*), a tractate of the Talmud concerning fasts. The author specifies the "Jerusalem" version.</note> of the Jerusalem [Talmud]: "Israel migrated to Babylon, and the *Shekhinah* <note>Original: שכינה (*Shekhina*), the divine presence or indwelling of God on earth.</note>—that is, the presence of God—migrated with them." From which there is proof: from that which Isaiah says in chapter 43: "Because of you, I was sent to Babylon." So also it is said in Psalm 107: "He shall send His word and heal them," or "he shall save them and rescue them from their miseries," or "corruptions," or "dispersions." And in Hosea chapter 1, it is also read: "And I will have mercy on the house of Judah. And I will save them in God (the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note>)." This is how Jonathan translated it into Chaldean <note>Original: *Chaldaicè*. Referring to the *Targum Jonathan*, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible. "Chaldean" was a common Renaissance term for Aramaic.</note>: "And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the Word of the Lord <note>Original Aramaic: במימרא דיי (*be-memra d'Adonai*). The 'Memra' or 'Word' is a key concept in the Targums used to describe God's interaction with the world.</note> their God." 

That passage in Daniel is also by no means foreign to the purpose, when he says in chapter 9: "And now, hear, O our God, the prayer of your servant and his supplications, and show your face upon your sanctuary which is desolate, or in your desolate sanctuary, for the sake of the Lord." Where the argument is held: that the Messiah is *Adonai* <note>Hebrew: אדני (*Adonai*), meaning "Lord."</note>, that is, the Lord. Finally, this is most especially to be noted, which is read in Isaiah chapter 48: "Come near to me, hear this. Not from the head—that is, from the beginning—have I spoken in secret. From the time, or from the hour of its being, I was there. And now the Lord God has sent me, and His Spirit." In these words, indeed, not only is the God who sends and the God who is sent shown, but the entire Trinity is also openly and distinctly suggested.

<margin>The heretical exposition of Rabbi Solomon.</margin>
CAPNIO. Rabbi Solomon, in order to extinguish the mystery of the Trinity, says that Isaiah spoke these words about himself, who was on Mount Sinai together with the other prophets at the time the law was given. Whence in the gloss upon this place he says: "Rabbi Tanhuma <note>A 4th-century Palestinian rabbi famous for his homiletic teachings.</note> says that it is held from this place that all the Prophets stood on Mount Sinai. And from this it is that the Prophet speaks of himself when he says: 'From the time of its being'—namely, of that speech which was spoken clearly and not in secret—'I was there'—he who is the giver of the law."

# BOOK [ONE]

Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> also affirms, concerning that passage in Malachi chapter 1, "The burden of the word of the Lord by the hand of Malachi," saying: "Already many days before, this had been delivered into his hands." From this, our masters declared in the supplementary <term>Mechilta</term> <note>A collection of ancient Jewish legal and homiletic interpretations of the Book of Exodus.</note> that all the prophets stood on Mount Sinai when the law was given to Moses, and there the prophecies were delivered to them. <margin>Refutation of the aforementioned heretical interpretation.</margin>
GALATINUS: Among other things, let Rabbi Solomon and his followers hear what is written in the book <term>Mechilta</term>, which for them is a sin to contradict. When commenting upon that passage in Exodus chapter 19, "And they came into the desert of Sinai, and rested, and encamped in the desert," it is said in this manner: "The law was given publicly, in an open place. For if the law had been given in the land of Israel, the Jews would have said to the nations of the world, 'You have no part in it.' But it was given in a traversable desert, publicly, and in an open place, so that whoever wished to receive it might come and receive it." Can it be said that it was given in the night? It teaches that it was not, by that which is said in Exodus 19: "And it came to pass on the third day, when morning had come." Can it also be said that it was given in silence? It teaches that it was not, by what is said in the same place: "And there were voices and lightnings," among other things. Can it still be said that they did not hear the voice? What should be said to this is suggested by that passage of the Psalm: "The voice of the Lord in power, the voice of the Lord in magnificence, the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars of Lebanon," <note>Psalm 29:4-5 (Psalm 28 in the Vulgate numbering).</note> with the rest. Likewise, in the same book, concerning that passage in Exodus 20, "I am the Lord your God," Rabbi Nathan said: "If you should say that the word of God was in secret, does he not say himself in Isaiah: 'I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time that it was, there I was'?" Behold how clearly these two of the ancient Doctors of the Jews assert that those aforementioned words—"From the time that it was, there I was"—were spoken by God. Therefore, Isaiah did not speak them concerning himself, as Rabbi Solomon falsely asserted. From these traditions it is also clearly evident that it is an absurd and entirely false fiction that all the prophets were present on Mount Sinai when the law was given to Moses. The absurdity and falsehood of this fiction is especially evident from this: that neither Moses nor any of the prophets is found to have ever openly mentioned this. Nor, even if they should say that the souls of the prophets without their bodies were present at the giving of the law (which seems to smack of the error of those who say that all souls were created at the same time), could this cloak their madness. For it openly contradicts both the sacred Scriptures and the judgment of their own ancient Doctors. ...first, "nor will I be angry forever with his generations. # BOOK SECOND

<margin>A universal explanation of those same words of Isaiah.</margin>
"Draw near to me," or approach me, "and hear this: I have not spoken in secret from the beginning. From the time it came to be, there I was." <note>A translation of Isaiah 48:16.</note> The meaning is: Approach me through faith and hear what I say. For when I first spoke to Adam and said to him, "Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil," I did not speak in secret or obscurely. However, some—not only among the Hebrews but also among our own [Christian] writers—interpret "from the beginning" to mean the time when God gave the Law to Moses. That this is false is clear not only from what has been said, but especially from the fact that God did not then first speak to the human race, but rather when he commanded Adam not to sin. It follows: "From the time it came to be, there I was"—that is, when Adam was made in time, I was there. "There," meaning in Adam himself, according to the substance of human flesh. HOG. <note>Likely referring to the medieval theologian Hugo of Saint Victor.</note> Our edition [the Vulgate] has it in this place as: "From the time before they were made, there I was." GAL. <note>Pietro Galatino, the author of this work.</note> The author of our edition <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate, St. Jerome.</note> understood this whole discourse as referring to the divinity of Christ. For that reason, he applied everything to his divinity. We, however, following the Hebrew truth <note>A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text as the most reliable source.</note>, accept it as referring partly to the divinity and partly to the humanity of which Christ consists. This is more consistent with the truth, both because the Hebrew letter does not say "before," but *me-et heyotah* <note>original: "מעת היותה"</note>, which means "from the hour that it was"—using a feminine demonstrative, as is clear to those who know the Hebrew letters. Therefore, the text should be explained thus: "From the hour of its being," that is, "From the hour of the creation of the flesh of my mother in the formation of the body of Adam." <note>Galatinus is arguing that the Messiah was "present" in the genetic/spiritual material of the first humans.</note> Thus, the text there speaks not of the divinity, but of the humanity of the Messiah. For if it spoke of divinity, it would have said "before it was made."

<margin>The Kabbalists on the divine name Tetragrammaton and Elohim.</margin>
Furthermore, according to the Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics whose traditions Galatino often attempts to synthesize with Christian doctrine.</note>, the four-letter name of God, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The sacred name YHWH (יהוה).</note>—in place of which they pronounce <term>Adonai</term> <note>Hebrew for "My Lord," used to avoid speaking the sacred name.</note>, which we translate as "Lord"—properly signifies the Father. This is because that name properly implies the divine essence, and the Father is the beginning and origin of the whole divinity. However, <term>Elohim</term> <note>A common Hebrew name for God.</note>, which is translated as "God," properly designates the Son. Now the text says: "And now YHWH Elohim," that is, "The Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit," <note>Isaiah 48:16</note> which is the Holy Spirit. This most evidently shows that the discourse here is not about the divinity of the Messiah, but about his humanity.

<margin>What it means to be "sent" in divine matters.</margin>
For if we follow the doctrine of the Theologians, and especially that of the <term>Subtle Doctor</term> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher.</note> in the 15th [distinction] of the first [book], and <term>Bonaventure</term> <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a Franciscan theologian.</note> in the same distinction, third question: being "sent" in divine matters is nothing other than being manifested as proceeding [from another], and being known to be from someone else; it implies a certain "sub-authority." Consequently, the Son, according to his divinity, can be sent neither by himself nor by the Holy Spirit, but only by the Father. Since he does not have his being from himself or from the Holy Spirit, but only from the Father. Therefore, it is necessary to say—both according to the Hebrew Kabbalists and according to our own Theologians—that the saying, "From the time it came to be," (that is, when it was made in time), is to be understood not of the Messiah’s divinity, but of his humanity.

<meta>This page continues the linguistic and theological analysis of Isaiah 48:16, moving from the identity of the "sender" to a broader discussion of the Trinity. SECOND [BOOK]

the Tetragrammaton <note>original: "tetragrammaton"; the four-letter divine name, YHWH</note>, that is the Father; God, that is the Son; and his Spirit, that is the Holy Spirit, sent me. So that I might be the Redeemer of Israel. In this, three things are to be noted. First, indeed, what the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism</note> maintain: that the name of God, the Tetragrammaton [YHWH], signifies God's mercy, while *Elohim*, which is the same as "God," signifies God's justice. Therefore, when it says here, "the Lord God" or "God [YHWH] God," the conjunction is omitted to designate that, in the sending of the Messiah's humanity, the mercy and justice of God were to be united for the redemption of the human race. According to that verse in Psalm 85: "Mercy and truth have met each other; justice and peace have kissed." The second point is that it does not say "their spirit," meaning of the Father and the Son, but "his spirit." This denotes that the Father and the Son, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, are not two "spirators" <note>Those who "breathe out" the Spirit</note>, but both are only one single spirator of the Holy Spirit itself, a single principle for each. The third and final point is that it does not say, "They sent me," but "He sent me." This is to suggest the unity of the divine essence, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

### *On the distinction and number of the divine persons through their properties. Chapter IV.*

->CAPNIO<-

<margin>GAL.</margin>
I think it will be of no small benefit, both for a clearer manifestation of the truth and for the greater confusion of the modern Jews, if you show that the distinction and number of the divine persons is also maintained among them through their properties. I will do that gladly. That they themselves clearly demonstrate both the number and the distinction of the divine persons through their properties is easily evident first from those things contained in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: "מדרש תילים"; an ancient Jewish homiletic commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, in that place where Psalm 50 says: "The God of gods, the Lord [El, Elohim, YHWH] has spoken and called the earth." For there it is read as follows: "Why is the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, mentioned three times? To teach that by these three names the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, corresponding to the three attributes by which the world was created; and these are Wisdom, Knowledge, and Understanding. Whence is Wisdom? As it is said: 'The Lord [YHWH] by wisdom founded the earth.' Whence is Knowledge? As it is said: 'By his knowledge the depths were broken up.' Whence is Understanding? As it is said: 'He established the heavens by understanding.' And so He says: 'For I the Lord [YHWH] your God am a jealous God.' Behold the three attributes by which the world was created. And likewise the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben say: 'The God of gods, the Lord [El, Elohim, YHWH]; the God of gods, the Lord [El, Elohim, YHWH]; He knows.' And what did they see to say it two times? 'The God of gods, the Lord' by which the world was created; and 'the God of gods, the Lord' by which the Torah was given. Could one have been by itself? No, but both were created together. And so He says: 'Even my hand has founded the earth, and my right hand has spanned the heavens.'" <note>This quote combines several biblical proof-texts (Proverbs 3:19-20, Exodus 20:5, Joshua 22:22) to argue for a triune nature in God's creative action.</note> That is: Why is the name of the Holy and Blessed God mentioned three times? So that you might be taught that by these three names the Holy and Blessed God created the world—

...created, according to the three *Middoth* <note>original: "מידות"; Hebrew for measures, attributes, or properties</note>, that is properties, through which the world was created. These are: Wisdom, science or knowledge, and prudence. From where is Wisdom—if we may add the proof? Just as it is said in Proverbs 3: "The Lord by wisdom founded the earth." From where is science or knowledge? As it is said in the same place: "By his knowledge the depths erupted." From where is Prudence? As it is said above: "He prepared or adorned the heavens with prudence." And because of this, He Himself says in Exodus 20: "For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God." <note>original: "כי אנכי יהוה אלהיך אל קנא"</note> Here are the three properties in place of the three by which the world was created. So also the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben said, in Joshua 22: "God, God, God, God: He knows." <note>The Latin text here repeats "Deus" four times, referencing the Hebrew "El Elohim Yehovah."</note> What did they see, that they should repeat this same thing twice? They said it first: "God, God, God," because by these the world was created. And then they said: "God, God, God," because in these same three the law was given. But could not one of them have created the world alone and separately? By no means; rather, the two others united with Him necessarily created it. These things are in the Talmud. They are placed in almost the same words in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>original: "Rabbi Mosis hadarsan"; a 11th-century scholar from Narbonne</note> upon that verse in Genesis 1: "In the beginning *Elohim* <note>original: "אלהים"; God</note> created heaven and earth." Indeed, all these things agree sufficiently with the Christian faith, with only this exception: that these three divine *Middoth*, that is properties, by which they assert the world was created, they call wisdom, knowledge, and prudence. For if these appear to be several properties in name, in reality they are but one. Nevertheless, elsewhere among them, three properties are found which, according to the orthodox faith, are one God. In the exposition of Rabbi Moses the Preacher on the book of Genesis, upon that passage in chapter 42, "Joseph himself was powerful over the land," it is read that Rabbi Elazar said: "The world was not created except by the word of God, the holy and blessed." As it is said in Psalm 33: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made." <note>original: "בדבר יהוה שמים נעשו"</note> Where also Rabbi Simeon says: "God breathed the spirit of His mouth, and the world was created." As it is said in Psalm 33: "And by the spirit of his mouth all their host." <note>original: "וברוח פיו כל צבאם"</note> This is the tradition. In these, these three—God, His Word, and His Spirit—are placed as having concurred distinctly and openly in the production of the world. But what else are these three than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? For the Word is really distinguished from the one speaking it, and the Spirit from the one breathing it. Therefore, between God the creator of the world, and His Word through which the world was created, and God the breather, and His Spirit in which He produced the world, there must be a real distinction. Since, therefore, there is no "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like being "tall" or "wise," rather than the thing itself</note> in God, as they themselves even concede—since every accident implies imperfection, and in God there can be no imperfection—it follows certainly that neither the Word of God nor His Spirit is an accident. Therefore they are <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: "hypostases"; the Greek term for distinct persons or individual substances existing within the one essence of God</note>, or suppositions, or really distinct persons. And consequently, according to the dogma of the ancient Talmudists, it must necessarily be confessed that there are three persons in God, to whom the three *Middoth*, that is [properties...]
