## BOOK SECOND

...properties are attributed, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These are not three Gods, nor three creators, but one God, and one creator. This is also shown from what immediately follows in that same passage: <note>original Hebrew: כונס כנד מי הים נתן באצרות תהומות; Psalm 33:7</note> *He gathers the waters of the sea as if in a bottle; He places the depths in storehouses.* For in the fact that it speaks in the singular—"gathering" and "placing"—it clearly suggests that the three divine persons, who were meant to be understood by the three aforementioned names, are only one God, the creator of the entire universe. This is very consistent with what is written in 1 John, chapter 5: *There are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. And these three are one.* To this also seems to belong what is found in the *Midrash Coheleth* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes</note>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes, regarding the verse in the fourth chapter which in Hebrew reads: <note>original Hebrew: והחוט המשלש לא במהרה ינתק; Ecclesiastes 4:12</note> *And a threefold cord is not quickly broken.* For there it is said that Rabbi Johanan stated: "Two (namely, a man and a woman) are better than one"—meaning this one by himself, and that one by herself—"and this threefold cord is the holy and blessed God, who visits them both in their children," that is, by giving them children. As for the addition: *It is not quickly broken:* the meaning seems to be that the mystery of the triune and one God is not easily nor quickly unraveled.

### BOOK <note>The header "L I B E R" indicates the continuation of the "Second Book."</note>

...Scripture teaches us to say: *The Ancient Father is his name, and the Child of Old Ages is the name of his son.* <note>original Latin: "Pater senex est nomen eius, & infans senectutum est nomen filij sui." This refers to a mystical interpretation of divine names.</note> Thus far the tradition. In this tradition, God the Father is called "Ancient" for the reason that He neither had a beginning nor will ever have an end. The Son of God, however, is called the "Child of Old Ages" because he was begotten from the Father from eternity and will be begotten for all eternity. Therefore, in this tradition, the Jews possess exactly what their younger generations now deny: namely, God the Father and God the Son, who was born from God from eternity and will never cease to be born throughout eternity. To this also applies that saying of Solomon in the fourth chapter of Proverbs: <note>original Hebrew: כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב נָתַתִּי לָכֶם תּוֹרָתִי אַל תַּעֲזֹבוּ: כִּי בֵן הָיִיתִי לְאָבִי רַךְ וְיָחִיד לִפְנֵי אִמִּי; Proverbs 4:2–3</note> *For I give you good doctrine; forsake not my law. Finally, it is the same in almost all other places. Therefore, here too, this word must be understood as nothing other than the Law. the Son of God was to have a double nature in the Messiah: namely, the divine, by which he was the son to God his Father from eternity, begotten before the ages without a mother; and the human, according to which he is called the Son of Man, born in time from a mother without a father. teachings, warnings, and corrections, by which a human father strives to make his son wise and prudent, he compares the Son of God himself to a father, adapting such teachings, warnings, and corrections to his wisdom as far as possible. Therefore, in the words spoken a little while ago, some refer to the divine nature of the Son of God, and some to the human nature which he was to assume. Both of these are clearly indicated by the words themselves. For when he says: *Hear, O sons, the discipline of a father, and attend that you may know prudence. Because I have given you a good gift or document, that is, a good law.* <note>Proverbs 4:1-2. The author is arguing that the past tense "I have given" implies a divine speaker rather than the historical King Solomon.</note> This cannot be understood as referring to Solomon at all. For if Solomon had been speaking here of his own wisdom, he would have said "I will give," not "I have given," especially since he said, *Hear, O sons, the discipline of a father.* It is necessary, therefore, that this speech be made in the name of him who at some point previously gave the law to the Hebrews. This, however, is God alone. Therefore, this speech is to be referred not to Solomon, but to God. And also that which immediately follows, namely: *Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my father, tender, the only, or unique one among the sons of my mother.* <note>Proverbs 4:2-3.</note> Since this word "because" <note>original: "quia"</note> is causal, it must provide the reason for the preceding clause. It is as if he were saying openly: "This is the reason why you ought not to forsake my law: because I was a son to my father." But if the discourse were about Solomon, no reason would be given for not forsaking his law. For men would not have been obliged not to forsake his law simply because he had been the son of David. But if he had said, "do not forsake my law, because I received it from my father David," then certainly he would have given a reason for not forsaking his law; but it would have had to be known of itself that everything handed down by David himself was right and to be kept—which, however, was not manifest. It is certain, therefore, that Solomon was speaking here not of himself, but in the person of the Son of God.

<margin>Why the Son of God is called tender.</margin>
His law was to be kept for this reason: because he was the Son of God. He also calls himself "tender" <note>original: "tener," often translated as "tender" or "young" in English Bibles, but here interpreted philosophically.</note> for this reason: so that he might not only suggest the tenderness of his immense piety, but also hint at the capacity of his infinite wisdom. For according to the <term>Aristotelian</term> <note>Referring to the philosophy of Aristotle (384–322 BCE).</note> saying in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima." The author refers to a specific medieval commentary (text 49) on Aristotle's work.</note>: *Those with hard flesh are inept in respect to the intellect, but the soft—that is, the tender—are well-suited.* Therefore, to show this excellent disposition of his for receiving the teachings of the father, he said that he was "tender," that is, well-teachable, and rightly most capable of infinite wisdom. But to whom was he tender? *To my father*, he says. It is necessary, therefore, that he speak of such a father who can teach nothing but what is right. This, however, is God alone. Thus, therefore, the words are to be explained: *Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my Father, tender.* This means: because I received those things from my father, who cannot err in teaching, nor could I err in learning, because I was tender, that is, of the best and infinite capacity for receiving it. *And the only or unique one among the sons of my mother*, that is, of the Synagogue, as we explained above. <note>The author views the Messiah as the unique "son" produced by the Jewish community/Synagogue.</note> WHERE the sons or of the sons

For according to the opinion of John of Damascus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD) was a Syrian monk and a central figure in defining Eastern Orthodox theology.</note>, the Son of God himself was to assume human nature in an "atom," that is, in an individual instance. He alone, as a man among all individuals of the human race, was predestined to be the Son of God because of the hypostatic union <note>The "hypostatic union" is the theological term for the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one individual existence.</note> of his divinity. This follows what Paul said in the 1st chapter of Romans: *Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined the Son of God.* <note>Romans 1:3-4.</note> Therefore, most appropriately, he himself says here through Solomon: "I was a son to my father," regarding his divinity; "the only one or unique among the sons of my mother," that is, the Synagogue, regarding his humanity.

<margin>The Synagogue was called the Mother of God.</margin>
Furthermore, that the Synagogue should be called the "mother of God" by reason of the divine incarnation that was to come from her is proved by the sayings of the ancient Talmudists <note>The author uses "Talmudists" to refer to the Jewish sages whose commentaries make up the Talmud and Midrash.</note> in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>original: "Midras scir hascirim"</note>, which is the exposition of the Song of Songs, regarding that saying in the 3rd chapter of the same book: *Go forth and see, O daughters of Zion, King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him.* <note>Song of Songs 3:11. The author interprets this "mother" as the community of Israel/the Synagogue giving birth to the Messiah.</note> As we shall see abundantly in the 25th chapter of the third book.

<term>CAPNIO</term> <note>Capnio is the Greek-style nickname for the famous humanist scholar Johannes Reuchlin.</note>: Although what you have said is as true as it is clear, so much so that the Jews of our age cannot deny it with any slander, yet they, as if most obstinate in the error of their perfidy, in order to escape the truth, flee to another falsehood, saying: Since after these words—*Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my father, tender, and the unique one among the sons of my mother*—these other things are immediately added:

<term>GALATINUS</term> <note>Pietro Galatino, the author, representing himself as the teacher in this dialogue.</note>: It is easy to respond to these.

<margin>Response.</margin>
Since indeed the Son of God was to have a dual nature in the Messiah: namely, the divine nature, by which he was the son to God his Father from eternity, begotten before the ages without a mother; and the human nature, according to which he is called the Son of Man, born in time from a mother without a father. Just as, therefore, there had to be a dual nature in the Messiah, so also there was to be a twin wisdom in him, both having their origin from God the Father. For although the wisdom of the Son in divine matters is one and entirely the same as the wisdom of the Father, yet because the Son is begotten of the Father, therefore just as he had his being eternally from the Father, so also he received from eternity both wisdom itself and everything which he has according to his divinity from the Father. Also the wisdom which he was to have according to his humanity had to take its origin from God himself, who was bound to imbue his soul, from the instant of its creation, with the highest grace and all habits of virtue above all others. Since, therefore, Solomon in this book speaks parabolically and enigmatically about the Son of God, who was to be a man just like one of us, he therefore used parables and enigmas to suggest not only that the wisdom which the Son himself was to receive according to his human nature would emanate from God the Father, but also that the wisdom which he had eternally according to his divinity proceeded from the eternal Father, through...

instructions, warnings, and corrections, by which among men a father strives to make his son wise and prudent, he compares the Son of God himself to a father, fitting such instructions, warnings, and corrections to his wisdom as much as possible. Therefore, regarding the words spoken a little earlier, some refer to the divine nature of the Son of God, and some to the human nature he was to assume. The words themselves clearly indicate both of these. For when he says: *Hear, O sons, the instruction of a father, and attend to know prudence. Because a good doctrine or lesson, that is, a good law, I have given to you* <note>Proverbs 4:1–2. Original Latin: "Audite filij disciplinam patris, & attendite ad cognoscendam prudentiam. Quia doctrinam uel documentum bonum, id est legem bonam tribui uobis."</note>, this cannot be understood as referring to Solomon at all. For if Solomon had spoken here of his own wisdom, he would have said "I will give," not "I have given," especially since he said, "Hear, O sons, the instruction of a father." It is necessary, therefore, that this speech was made in the name of him who had previously given the law to the Hebrews at some time. This is God alone. Therefore, this speech is to be referred not to Solomon, but to God. And also that which follows immediately, namely: *Do not forsake my law, because I was a son to my father, tender, the alone or only one of the sons of my mother.* <note>Proverbs 4:2–3. Original Latin: "Legẽ meam non derelinquatis, quia filius fui patri meo, tener, solus, uel unicus filiorum matris meæ."</note> Since this word "because" <note>original: "quia"</note> is causal, it must provide the reason for the preceding clause. It is as if he were saying openly: "This is the reason why you ought not to forsake my law: because I was a son to my father." But if the speech were about Solomon, no reason would be given for not forsaking his law. For men would not have been obliged to keep his law simply because he had been the son of David. Indeed, if he had said, "Do not forsake my law, because I received it from my father David," then he would certainly have given a reason for not forsaking his law—but it would have to be self-evident that everything handed down by David himself was right and to be observed. Yet that was not manifest. It is clear, therefore, that Solomon was speaking here not of himself, but in the person of the Son of God.

<margin>Why the Son of God is called "tender."</margin>
Whose law was to be observed precisely because he was the Son of God. He calls himself "tender" <note>original: "tenerum"</note> also for this reason: not only to suggest the tenderness of his immense mercy, but to hint at the capacity of his infinite wisdom. For according to the saying of Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima", text comment 49.</note>, those who are "hard of flesh" are inept in terms of the intellect, while those who are "soft"—that is, tender—are well-disposed. Therefore, to show this excellent disposition of his for receiving the lessons of the father, he said that he was "tender," which is to say, well-teachable and rightly capable of infinite wisdom. But "tender" to whom? "To my father," he says. It is necessary, therefore, that he speaks of such a father who can teach nothing but what is right. This is God alone. Thus, the words are to be explained: *Do not forsake my law, because I was a tender son to my father.* That is, because I received those things from my father, who cannot err in teaching, nor could I err in learning, because I was "tender"—that is, possessing the best and infinite capacity for receiving it. And "the alone or only one of the sons of my mother," that is, of the Synagogue, as we explained above. HOG. Where for the sons or of the sons

Which certain others translated as, "before my mother." **GALATINUS.** The word *libne* <note>Hebrew: לבני</note>, which is placed here and written with the letter *beth* <note>ב</note>, signifies neither "in the presence of" nor "before," but properly means the same as "to the sons" or "of the sons." For "before" and "in the presence of" are signified by the word *liphne* <note>Hebrew: לפני</note>, written with the letter *pe* <note>פ</note>. From this it is clearly evident that those who, in this place, translated "in the presence of my mother" or "before my mother" were deceived by the similarity of the words and read *liphne* instead of *libne*. As for what follows, *And he himself taught me*, along with the rest: Christ spoke of this regarding himself when he said in the 8th chapter of John, "As the father taught me, I speak these things" <note>John 8:28</note>. And again, he said, "I always do those things that are pleasing to him" <note>John 8:29</note>. And he says certain other things in the same place which agree with almost the same sentiment. In these passages, he openly shows both that he was taught by the father and that he received from him the mandates of those things which he was to do in the world. Regarding what is also said here, *Keep my precepts*, he reported that he himself had fulfilled this, saying in John 15, "I have kept my father's precepts, and I remain in his love" <note>John 15:10</note>. That which is added at the end, *And live*, he likewise explained concerning himself when he said, "As the father has life in himself, so he has given to the son also to have life in himself" <note>John 5:26</note>. "Live" therefore means, "have life in your own power." Hence he says himself, "I have the power to lay down my soul, and I have the power to take it up again" <note>John 10:18</note>.

### On the Holy Spirit. Chapter VI

->**CAPNIO,**<- <note>Capnio is the Greek-style pseudonym of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), the famous German humanist and Hebraist who is a character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>How the Holy Spirit is named by the Hebrews.</margin> Since you have said enough in the preceding sections concerning the Father and the Son, clearly proving that God is called "Father" in Holy Scripture and that his begotten Wisdom is called the "Son," it now remains for you to discuss something regarding the Holy Spirit in detail. **GALATINUS.** I frequently find the Holy Spirit called "goodness," or "good will," and "charity," or "affection," or "love" by the ancient Jews. This Solomon, therefore—that is, the Messiah—made for himself an אפריון <term>appirion|A Hebrew term from the Song of Songs meaning a palanquin, litter, or bridal carriage</term>, <note>original: "appirion"</note> that is, a bridal chamber or a portable tent, namely his own body. Its interior, namely the heart, was רצוף <gloss>raczuph</gloss>, <note>original Hebrew: "raczuph"</note> that is, paved: or according to another meaning, set on fire, as if with burning coals of love or charity. Since this is the שכינה <gloss>Shekhinah</gloss>, <note>original: "sechina"</note> that is, the divinity, as has been shown through Jewish tradition, it follows that the Messiah, according to his humanity, was to be filled with the Holy Spirit. 

This is excellently suggested by Isaiah, when in chapter 61 he says in the person of the Messiah: רוח אדני יהוה עלי יען משח יהוה אתי <note>Isaiah 61:1</note> That is, *The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me.* Here the Prophet (as Rabbi David Kimhi says in the book *Seraścim* <note>The *Sefer HaShorashim* (Book of Roots), a famous Hebrew grammar and lexicon by the 12th-century scholar David Kimhi, also known as Radak.</note>) spoke in the person of the Messiah. It is just as if the Messiah had said: "Because God anointed me, he sent me to announce the news to the poor or the humble." From these things it is clear that the Holy Spirit is called love or charity, not only because he proceeds from the Father and the Son by way of the will, but also because he is the love with which the Father and the Son love one another.

<margin>What the Holy Spirit is according to the ancient Hebrews</margin>
Therefore, as is gathered from what has been said, those ancient and old fathers of the Jews understood nothing else by the "Holy Spirit" than the third person in the Godhead, produced from eternity by the Father and the Son through a single breathing by way of the will, distinct in reality from them, yet essentially the same as them. For as has been said, even if the three divine persons are really distinguished from one another, essentially they are nonetheless entirely the same.

### Chapter VII. That the three divine persons are one essence, and that each of them is in the other by circumincession. <note>original: "circumincessionem"; this is the Latin theological term for "perichoresis," the idea that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exist within one another.</note>

->CAPNIO,<-

I would wish, for a clearer expression of this Catholic truth and for the greater confusion of the younger Jews, that you would prove through one of their own teachers that the three divine persons are one essence and one nature, and that one is in the other through circumincession.

GAL. Although I could produce many witnesses among them to prove this, lest I be tedious, let it suffice to bring forward one whom the more recent Jews can least contradict: namely, Rabbi Isaac ben Shola <note>Also known as Isaac ibn Sahula, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi and Kabbalist.</note>, a man of great authority among them, who in his commentaries on the Psalter often asserts this very thing, and especially upon that verse of Psalm 111:

<note>original Hebrew: ראשית חכמה יראת יהוה שכל טוב לכל עושיהם תהלתו עומדת לעד</note>
The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; a good understanding have all those who do them. His praise endures forever. <note>Psalm 111:10</note>

This is: The beginning, wisdom, the fear of God, a good understanding to all who do them. His praise remains forever. When he speaks thus:

The wisdom to which he alluded in this verse is the wisdom that is found from "nothing" <note>original Hebrew: "Ayin" (nothingness), referring in Kabbalah to the first Sephirah from which Wisdom (Chokhmah) emanates.</note>; and it is alluded to in the word "In the beginning" <note>original Hebrew: "Bereishit"</note>, meaning "in the house of wisdom." They said: do not read "Beit" <note>meaning the letter 'B' or 'in'</note> but rather "Bayit" <note>meaning "house"</note>, as it is said, "Through wisdom a house is built" <note>Proverbs 24:3</note>. This attribute is concealed and hidden in the depths of the abyss, and stored away and sealed, in the sense of what is said, "It is hidden from the eyes of all living, and concealed from the birds of the air" <note>Job 28:21</note>; and it says, "God understands its way and He knows its place" <note>Job 28:23</note>, meaning that there is no other besides Him who knows the paths engraved within it. And in every place where the Sages enumerated the attributes <term>Sephirot|The ten emanations or attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</term>, they enumerated Wisdom as the first among them, because it is drawn from the Source of Life and is the start of the counting. And they enumerated the second attribute, which is the "Source" and the "Refining," in which it was alluded to that "there is a source for silver" <note>Job 28:1</note>; and it says, "For in the shadow of wisdom is the shadow of silver" <note>Ecclesiastes 7:12</note>. Those who possess wisdom describe this inner attribute by many names: some describe it as "One of Pearls" because all the attributes are chosen within it and it is within them; and some describe it with the term "Nothing" <note>original: "Ayin"</note>, because no hand or thought can grasp it. They relied on this language in the scripture that says "From where [Ayin] shall it come?" <note>Job 28:12</note> and "Where is the place of understanding?" As he said this, you will further know the secret of these things and you will be kept and preserved perfect. Indeed, all the other names attributed to this quality are all directed in this way. In this verse, he alluded to this attribute with the word "beginning," and Wisdom was included. Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said that all the prophets prophesied through a mirror that does not shine <note>original Hebrew: "Aspaklaria she-einah me’irah"; a metaphor for indirect or clouded revelation.</note>, but Moses our Rabbi, peace be upon him, looked through a single mirror that shines <note>original Hebrew: "Aspaklaria ha-Me’irah"; a metaphor for direct, clear revelation of the Divine.</note>, as it is said, "He saw the beginning for himself." <note>Deuteronomy 33:21</note> Furthermore, he added in this verse "the fear of the Lord," and it is the light for the Beginning, as in: "And God has made it so that they should fear before Him." <note>Ecclesiastes 3:14</note> Since the three attributes we have mentioned are called "Faces" <note>original Hebrew: "Panim"; often used to describe the aspects or persons of the Divine.</note> in their entirety, each within the other, he said, "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." And the Wise Man said: "Grace and the fear of the Lord is wisdom." And he said: "Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding." <note>Proverbs 4:5</note> Behold, you have learned that these three crowns are chosen for the crown of perfect unity, and they are mothers to the world from the mothers. And through these, those who come after them see by their means. And they are the utterances—seventy pure utterances that are considered as seven paths in one stalk, full and good. And since they are a strong bond and a law in their totality, all together, he said: "A good understanding for all those who do them," meaning those who aim for them. And it is he who said: "For God has made this day." And he said: "His praise endures forever" regarding the inner attribute we mentioned. And thus he says: "The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever." <note>Psalm 19:9</note> And he said, "She is the praise."

And whenever the wise men enumerated the attributes <note>original: "proprietates"; used here to refer to the Sephirot or divine emanations.</note> of God, they placed **wisdom** as the prince or head, because it is drawn from the fountain of life and is the beginning of all number. And they called that internal attribute the most overflowing vein of ore (which the common people call a mine), and a fountain or emanation was discovered in it; for indeed, there are also flowing veins of silver. And it is said that as is the shadow of wisdom, so is the shadow of silver. <note>Ecclesiastes 7:12.</note> The authors of wisdom, however, have designated this internal attribute by many names. For some named it the **crown** <note>original: "coronam"; referring to the highest Sephirah, Keter.</note>, because the individual attributes are crowned by it, and it by the individuals. Others, however, named it **Nothing** <note>original: "ain" (אין)</note>, because there is no one who can grasp it through imagination (for it is attainable by the intellect alone). And to this alludes what was said: *From where* <note>original: "Meain" (מאין)</note> *shall my help come?* <note>Psalm 121:1. The author is playing on the word "me-ayin," which literally means "from where" but can be read as "from the Nothingness/the Infinite."</note> (*From where* indeed seems to signify something incorporeal, abstract, secret, and intellectual.) 

And if you are fortunate in my sayings, you will know the secrets of the highest mountains, because this attribute is like a light by which all other attributes are crowned in the way of light. Therefore, in this text, notice this attribute in the word **Beginning**, in which wisdom is contained. Thus the doctors said: *All the prophets prophesied in a vision that was not clear; but Moses prophesied in a vision that was lucid and clear.* <note>A common Rabbinic distinction: other prophets saw through a "dark glass," Moses through a "clear glass."</note> As it is said: *And the beginning appeared to him.* <note>Deuteronomy 33:21.</note> There follows, moreover, the **Fear of God**. And this is furthermore a declaration of the **Beginning**. As it is said: *God has acted so that they should fear before His face.* <note>Ecclesiastes 3:14.</note> And these three attributes are called **faces** <note>original: "facies"; translating the Hebrew "Panim," implying the aspects or persons of God.</note>, and they are contained within one another. And for this reason it is said: *The Beginning, Wisdom, and the Fear of God.* And the wise man says: *Truly the fear of God is wisdom.* It is also said: *Possess wisdom, possess prudence.* <note>Proverbs 4:5.</note> 

Behold, you have learned that these three crowns are one crown, united by a most perfect unity. And they are something most choice: the three equal foundations of the world (that is, those by which the world is made firm). And they are ascending lights, surpassing all else that remains, so much so that by their light all things are illuminated. And they are the words of God—pure and precious words—the meaning of the **seven ears of grain on one stalk**, which are full and excellent. <note>Reference to Pharaoh’s dream in Genesis 41.</note> And because they are one strong and inseparable bond, all are grasped as one. As it is said: *A good understanding have all those who do them*—that is, those who strive toward them. ...intrinsic property, which we mentioned. And he also says: *The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.* <note>Psalm 19:9; original Latin: "Timor dei mundus permanet iugiter."</note> And he said: *He is your praise, and He is your God.* <note>Deuteronomy 10:21; original Latin: "Ipse laus tua, & ipse Deus tuus."</note> And understand this. All these things were said by the aforementioned Rabbi. From his words, many excellent points are found that are very much in agreement with our faith and against the Jews of our time, specifically seven points.

And the **first** is that the three properties by which the three divine persons are distinguished, he says (using the words of the Psalmist), are the **beginning**, **wisdom**, and the **fear** of God. And this is indeed correct. For by "beginning" he understands the Father, both because the Father is the first person in the Trinity, and also because he is the beginning and origin of the whole divinity. By "wisdom" he suggests the Son, who is the wisdom of the Father. By the "fear of God," however, he hints at the Holy Spirit, who is not inappropriately called the "fear of God" because of his effect. For he instills the fear of God into the hearts of the faithful into whom he enters, so that they might not be separated by sin from Him to whom they are joined by grace, and lest through sin they lose God Himself, whom they possess dwelling within them through grace. This is also proved by that saying: *God has acted so that they should fear before his face.* <note>Ecclesiastes 3:14; original Latin: "Deus fecit ut timerẽ à facie eius."</note>

The **second** is that he says this wisdom proceeds *from nothing* <note>original Hebrew: "me-ayin" (מאין)</note>, that is, from the supreme and most abstract intellect, which is God; for that Hebrew word *me-ayin* conveys all these meanings. By this he wishes to show that the Son in divine matters is produced by the divine intellect. For a fertile memory, which is nothing other than the intellect having its object present (namely, the divine essence), produces the Word—that is, the Son—who is the generated knowledge and wisdom of the Father.

The **third** is that he says this wisdom is a most abundant vein of ore, in which a fountain or emanation is discovered. By this he clearly wishes to hint that the Son of God is the "art" of the Father, and the Word through whom all things were made.

The **fourth** is that he says this wisdom is like a light, by which all other properties are crowned in the way of light. By this he openly suggests that the Son is light from light, or the light of the world, as the Son himself says in John 8, which illuminates every man coming into this world (John 1).

The **fifth** is that he says these three properties are called **faces**, that is, **persons**, according to the custom of the Greeks, who call persons *prosopa* <note>original Greek: "πρόσωπα" – literally "faces" or "masks," used theologically to mean "persons."</note>.

The **sixth** is that he says these three persons are mutually contained one in another. He is demonstrating that the Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son through a "mutual indwelling," which the Greeks call *perichoresis* <note>term: perichoresis – a theological concept describing the relationship between each person of the triune God.</note>.

The **seventh** is that he says these three crowns are one crown, a unity that is a most perfect unity. By this he clearly shows that the three divine persons are entirely one essence and one nature. He also expressly affirms this in the explanation of the following Psalm, while commenting on that passage of Psalm 112: *The wicked shall see, and shall be angry; he shall gnash with his teeth, and pine away; the desire of the wicked shall perish.* <note>Psalm 112:10; original Hebrew: "רשע יראה וכעס שיניו יחרק ונמס תאות רשעים תאבד"</note> Among other things, he says:

> This verse is similar to the Attribute of Judgment of the depths of the wicked, who kicks against sufferings and gnashes his teeth before the Divine Presence <note>original Hebrew: "Shekhinah" (שכינה) – the indwelling presence of God.</note>, and because of this "the desire of the wicked shall perish." Regarding something similar to this, it is said: "For the Lord your God is a consuming fire" <note>Deuteronomy 4:24</note>, and it says: "A fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him" <note>Psalm 50:3</note>. Behold, there it is in the likeness of what he opened with in the first Psalm, to make known that **everything is one**, and these attributes...

These attributes are His connection; the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His name is blessed. Because of this, He acts within living beings in the measure necessary for them according to their strength, being mingled into the attributes and their timing and with them. But from the perspective of His own essence, everything goes to one place, and all is a perfect unity. These attributes are not limited nor separated; and he who limits or separates one attribute from them, or adds to them or subtracts from them, is called a "cutter of the plantings" <note>original: "קוצץ בנטיעות" (*kotzetz ba-netiot*); a Rabbinic metaphor for heresy, specifically the error of separating divine attributes or powers from the unity of God</note>, and his punishment is as great as that of the "Other" Elisha <note>Elisha ben Abuyah, a 2nd-century scholar who became a famous apostate</note>. However, from these attributes and below is the world of separate things, and although there is no direct proof for this matter, there is a suggestion of it: *And a river went out from Eden to water the garden, and from there it was divided.* <note>Genesis 2:10</note> And if you contemplate what I have hinted to you, you will be worthy of the secret of this verse.

This is to say, this text signifies the nature of the infernal judgment. For the wicked man will kick with his feet and gnash his teeth against the divinity. And for this reason, the desire of the wicked shall perish. Whence it is said: *For the Lord your God is a consuming fire.* <note>Deuteronomy 4:24</note> And furthermore: *A fire shall burn before him, and it shall completely consume those things that are round about him.* <note>Psalm 50:3</note> Behold, he has expressed the meaning of what is contained in the preceding Psalm, to teach that all are one. And these properties which we have commemorated are the name of God, and His name is exalted. And because they operate concerning His creatures according to the property fitting for them according to their power, therefore He Himself is contained in those properties and is numbered with them. But if you consider Him as He is in substance, all things tend toward one place, and all are one unity, perfect in every way. And these properties are not defined nor separated. For if anyone should either define, or separate, or add, or even subtract even one of the said properties, he would rightfully be called a "cutter of the plants," and his punishment would be great, like that of the latter Elisha. Below these properties, however, consists the world of things that are defined and separate. Although we do not have the authority of this thing, except for that which is said: *And a river goes out of paradise to water the garden, and from there it is divided.* <note>Genesis 2:10</note> And if you take heed of those things about which I have admonished you, you will be fortunate in understanding the mystery of this text. Thus far the same Rabbi Isaac ben Shola. From whose two aforementioned expositions, it is clearly shown that the three divine persons are one essence and one nature, and each of them is in the remaining two by *mutual indwelling* <note>original Latin: "circumincessionem"; a theological term (Greek: *perichoresis*) describing the relationship of the persons of the Trinity to one another</note>. Which was to be proven.

[...they] assert that it was so, attempting to draw the scripture itself toward a different meaning, so that they might be able to escape the mystery of the divine Trinity revealed in the creation of man. Therefore, it is now your task to prove through the writings of their own ancient [authorities] that man was made in the image of God, and that the very secret of the divine Trinity is suggested through that same image of God shining within him.

**GALEOTTO:** They can certainly by no means deny that the holy Trinity of God, and His indivisible unity, made man in His own image and likeness. For the text itself is clear, which says in the first [part] of Genesis: *And God said: Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness.* <note>original Hebrew: "ויאמר אלהים נעשה אדם בצלמנו כדמותנו" (*Vayomer Elohim na'aseh adam be-tzalmenu ki-demutenu*)</note> That is, and *Elohim* said—which is to say, "the Gods"—"Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness." And a few [verses] later: *And God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him.* <note>original Hebrew: "ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו בצלם אלהים ברא אתו" (*Vayivra Elohim et ha-adam be-tzalmo be-tzelem Elohim bara oto*)</note> That is, and *Elohim*—the Gods—created man in His own image, in the image of *Elohim*—the Gods—He created him; male and female He created them.

**CAPNIO:** Why did he first use the word that signifies "to make," saying, "Let us make man," and then use the word signifying "creation," saying, "And *Elohim* created man," along with the other things that follow?

**GALEOTTO:** Because the bodies of Adam and Eve were composed from matter, but their souls were truly created from nothing. Therefore, he first used the word that signifies "to make" [from existing material]. Then he used the word for "creation" [from nothing]. The treachery of the Jews of our age can in no way deny that man was made in the image of God, since their ancient [scholars] confess it everywhere. For to bring forward first the testimony of Abraham himself, it is read thus in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A Rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note> upon that [verse] of Psalm 37: *Do not join with the wicked, nor be angry, nor be indignant because of the wicked. Neither be jealous of or imitate those who work iniquity.* <note>original Hebrew: "אל תתחר במרעים אל תקנא בעשי עולה" (*Al tithar ba-mere'im al tikna be-osei avlah*)</note> Our father Abraham said to Melchizedek—who was Shem, the son of Noah, and who was called the priest of the most high God because he offered sacrifice—"By what method, or for what reason, did you come out from the ark?" He replied: "On account of *czedaca* <note>original Hebrew: "צדקה" (*tzedakah*); meaning righteousness or charity</note>, that is, the charity which we performed there." Abraham said to him, "And what kind of charity could you perform there, since no one was there except Noah and his sons? For whom, then, did you perform charity?" He replied to him, "For the wild beasts, the cattle, and the birds. For we did not sleep the whole night, but gave [food] now to this one, now to that one." Abraham therefore said, "If these [men] who performed charity for wild beasts, cattle, and birds received a reward, how much more shall I receive a reward if I perform charity for the children of Adam, who are in the image of the holy and blessed God, and thus I shall be delivered from those who oppose me?" And immediately in 그 hour he performed (it is understood) charity. Just as it is written in Genesis, chapter 18: *And he planted an "essel"* <note>original Hebrew: "אשל" (*eshel*); interpreted here as an orchard, a grove, or an inn for travelers</note>, that is, an orchard or a lodging-place, to receive guests. Next, I will bring forward that which is written in the *Bereshith Ketanna* <note>The "Little Genesis," likely referring to the *Bereshit Rabbati* or a similar Midrashic compilation</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of Genesis. For there it is read thus, word for word: "In the day on which [He] created..."

### THE SECOND BOOK

<term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אלהים (*Elohim*)</note>, that is, the Gods, made Adam in the likeness of <term>Elohim</term>, that is, of the Gods. Rabbi Akiba said: It is written in the 19th chapter of Leviticus, *And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.* A great part of this matter is that you should not say, "Since I have been disgraced, let my neighbor also be disgraced." Rabbi Tanhuma <note>original: תנחומא (*Tanhuma*), a 4th-century Palestinian rabbi known for his haggadic midrashim</note> said: If you do such a thing, know that it is [the Creator] you disgrace. For if you despise him [your neighbor], you despise the one of whom it is written: He made him in the likeness of Elohim, that is, of the Gods. This concludes that tradition.

Let the more recent Jews also hear what is read in the book <term>Mechilta</term> <note>A legal commentary (Midrash Halakha) on the Book of Exodus</note> regarding that passage in Exodus 20: *And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, so that your nakedness may not be exposed upon it.* For so it is said there: "Behold, here is an argument from <term>kal vahomer</term> <note>original: קל וחומר (*kal va-chomer*); a logical principle of 'minor and major'—if a rule applies in a less important case, it must apply in a more important one</note>, that is, from the minor to the major. For if regarding stones, in which there is no knowledge of good and evil, <term>The Place</term> <note>original: המקום (*HaMakom*); a common Rabbinic title for God, signifying that He is the 'place' of the world, containing all things</note>—that is, God (for the Jews are accustomed to call God 'The Place' because He is present everywhere and in every place)—said that you should not walk upon them disrespectfully or disgracefully, how much more does reason demand that you do not walk contemptuously or insultingly toward your neighbor, who is made in the likeness of Him who spoke and the world was created." This is the tradition.

Nor should we overlook what is read in the <term>Bereshit Rabba</term> <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient commentary on the first book of the Bible</note> regarding that first chapter of Genesis: *And Elohim created man in his own image.* The heretics asked Rabbi Semlai <note>original: שמלאי (*Simlai*)</note>: "What is the meaning of the scripture that says, 'And <term>Elohim</term> (the Gods) said: Let **us** make man in **our** image, according to **our** likeness'?" He said to them: "Read what follows: 'And <term>Elohim</term> (the Gods) **created** <note>The author notes that while the subject 'Elohim' is plural in form, the verb 'created' (bara) is singular</note> man.' It is not written 'they created,' but 'He created.'"

Rabbi Hoshaya <note>original: השעה (*hossahaya* in the OCR, likely referring to R. Hoshaya/Osha'ya)</note> said: In the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, created the first man in His own image, the ministering angels were led astray by him and wished to say before him, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God of hosts." **CAPNIO.** Why did he first use the word that signifies 'to make,' saying, "Let us make man," and then use the word signifying 'creation,' saying, "And <term>Elohim</term>—that is, the Gods—created man," along with the other things that follow?

**GALEOTTO.** Because the bodies of Adam and Eve were composed of matter, but their souls were created out of nothing. Therefore, he first placed the word signifying 'to make' <note>Latin: *facere*, corresponding to the Hebrew *asah*</note>, and then used the word for 'creation' <note>Latin: *creatio*, corresponding to the Hebrew *bara*</note>. Therefore, when it is said in Genesis 1: *Elohim*—that is, the Gods—said, "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness." Just as by <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אלהים (*Elohim*). Divine "measures" or attributes.</note> through which they said the world was created—that is, the three divine persons: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. So by the image of *Elohim*—that is, of the Gods—it is necessary to understand the three powers of the soul: memory, intellect, and will, in which the image of the divine Trinity consists. For intellect is formed from memory. Nor is there anything from which the intellect itself is formed except from memory, in the sense that memory is the act of holding knowledge of a thing within oneself. Unless, therefore, knowledge exists in the soul, there is nothing from which the intellect might be formed. But when the intellect extends itself and its knowledge, and receives what is true in the sense of the good and the fitting, immediately from memory and intellect is formed the appetite, which is the will. Therefore, just as intellect is formed from memory, so in divine matters the Son is generated from the Father. And just as the will is formed from memory and intellect extended and, as it were, breathing out the good, so from the Father and the Son, as if from a single breathing principle, the good is breathed out, which is the Holy Spirit. And just as these three powers—memory, intellect, and will—are one soul, so Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. And this is the image of God in which man was created, according to the opinion of the ancient Hebrews.

Although they have not remained silent about other likenesses of God in the soul. For both in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>An ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms.</note> on that passage of Psalm 103: "Bless the Lord, O my soul," and "all my inner parts <note>original: וכל קרבי (*ve-chol keravai*)</note> his holy name." ## On the name of God *Elohim*, and how the divine Trinity is suggested through it. Chapter IX.

<margin>CAPNIO <note>The pen name of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note></margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the beginning of the text, featuring a figure (possibly a saint or scholar) seated and reading within a circular frame with floral corner motifs.</image-desc>
**S**ince for the proof of the mystery of the divine Trinity, nothing is more suitable against the younger Jews <note>Reuchlin uses "younger" or "more recent" Jews to distinguish contemporary Jewish scholars from the ancient "Doctors" or Kabbalists whom he believes secretly held views closer to Christianity.</note>, and nothing more powerful, than the explanation of the divine names, it is therefore now necessary for you to prove that same mystery by explaining the names of God themselves. And first, it is necessary for you to do this through *Elohim* <note>original: אלהים</note>, which is more common than the others. For *Elohim* (as you yourself know) is a plural name, and it signifies what "Gods" signifies among us. Its singular is *El* <note>original: אל</note>, that is, God, or rather *Eloha* <note>original: אלוה</note>, which is also the same as God. Therefore, this name *Elohim*, even if it designates plurality, is nevertheless usually joined with a verb of the singular number whenever it is accepted for the true God in Holy Scripture. Such is that [phrase] in the beginning of the book of Genesis: "In the beginning *Elohim* created the heaven and the earth" <note>original Hebrew: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ (*Bereshith bara Elohim...*)</note>. This is: "In the beginning 'Gods' created <note>singular verb</note> heaven and earth." Where, therefore, our Greek and Latin editions have "God" <note>singular</note>, the "Hebrew Truth" <term>Hebraica Veritas: a scholarly movement to return to the original Hebrew text of the Bible rather than relying solely on the Latin Vulgate</term> says "Gods." This was certainly not done without a great mystery. Because, according to the opinion of Saint Augustine, "the works of the Trinity are undivided on the outside" <note>Latin: *opera trinitatis indivisa sunt ad extra* — a theological principle that while the Trinity has three persons, they act as one in relation to the created world</note>. Therefore, that great Moses, to suggest that all three divine persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—concurred together in the creation of the world, said *Elohim* (that is, "Gods" in the plural) and not *Eloha* or *El* (that is, "God" in the singular). To show, however, that the three persons are not essentially distinguished but are entirely the same—that is, that there is one God and not three Gods—he said *bara* (that is, "he created" in the singular) and not *bareu* (that is, "they created" in the plural). It is established, therefore, that through the name *Elohim* joined with a singular verb, both the Trinity of persons and the unity of the divine essence are excellently designated.

<margin>
The false explanation of the younger Jews.
</margin>
However, the more recent Jews, since they are entirely unable to deny this text, attempt to pervert it with a certain false explanation. For they say that even if this name *Elohim* is plural, it is nevertheless used indifferently in both singular and plural senses, and when it is used for the true God, it is always held as a singular and not a plural. And so they say it is held here, when it is said, "In the beginning *Elohim* created." From this they conclude that since *Elohim* in this place is not held plurally but singularly, we can by no means infer from it that the Trinity of persons is suggested.

<margin>
Refutation.
</margin>
But perhaps they could say these things to those ignorant of Hebrew letters, but not to those who are not entirely lacking in knowledge of them. We, therefore, who are not entirely inexperienced in them, will prove through the Hebrew texts of Holy Scripture and through their own Teachers that they explain this text falsely. For in the *Bereshith Rabbah Ketana* <note>original: בראשית רבה קטנה — literally the "Lesser Genesis Rabbah," a collection of Midrashic commentaries</note>, that is, in the lesser exposition of Genesis on this text, it is read that Rabbi Huna said thus: "If this word had not been written, it would not have been permitted to say: 'And *Elohim* (Gods) created heaven and earth.'" Regarding that passage in Genesis 1 as well: "And *Elohim* (Gods) created Adam in his image, in the image of *Elohim* (Gods) he created him" <note>original Hebrew: ויברא אלהים את האדם בצלמו בצלם אלהים ברא אתו (*Vayivra Elohim et ha-adam...*)</note>, it is read as written: The heretics asked Rabbi Samlai,

How many <note>Latin: *Quot* — catchword for the following page</note>

Reuchlin defends this interpretation against contemporary Jewish grammarians by citing ancient Midrashic sources.</summary>

"How many Gods created the world?" He said to them: "Let me and you seek the answer from the ancient days." In the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>original: "R. Mosis hadarsan" (Moses ha-Darshan), an 11th-century scholar known for his midrashic explanations of the Bible.</note> on the book of Genesis, it is recorded that he responded to them in this way: "Let me and you seek the answer from the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the Torah, the first five books of the Bible.</note>." For it is not written "Gods created Adam" [in the plural], but rather "God [in the plural form] created [in the singular form] Adam." Again they questioned him: "What of that which is written: 'In the beginning God created heaven and earth'?" For it is not written "In the beginning Gods created" [plural verb], but "In the beginning God created" [singular verb]. Rabbi Semlai said: "In every place where you find an objection raised by heretics, you also find its remedy <note>term: "medicamentum" (remedy/medicine). In rabbinic literature, this refers to a scriptural "antidote" or rebuttal to a heretical interpretation.</note> right beside it." Similar to this is what is found in the book of the *Sanhedrin* <note>The Sanhedrin is a tractate of the Talmud dealing primarily with the high court and legal procedures.</note>, in the chapter beginning *Ehad dine mamonoth* <note>original: אחד דיני ממונות; "One of the laws of money," referring to Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1.</note>, that is, "the first of the judgments of wealth," toward the end, where it says that Rabbi Yohanan spoke thus: "Every place from which the Epicureans <note>term: "Epicurei." In Jewish thought, this refers generally to heretics or those who deny divine providence or the authority of the Law.</note> became heretics, its response is found at its side." For where it says, "Let us make man in our image" [plural], there also it is added, "And God <note>gloss: Elohim</note> created [singular] man in his own image." And when it is said in Genesis 11, "Let us go down and let us confound their lips," it is also said in the same place, "And the Lord came down [singular] to see the city and the tower." And where it is written in Genesis 35, "Because there Gods [plural] appeared to him," it is also read in the same place: "And make there an altar to the God [singular] who appeared to you." Likewise in the same place: "And let us arise and go up to the house of God, and I will make there an altar to the God [singular] who heard me in the day of my tribulation." Thus far the tradition.

Many other places besides these are found in the Holy Scriptures in which both the name *Elohim* <note>original: אלהים</note> and certain other names spoken of God are placed in the plural. Indeed, no previous interpreter has translated this manner of speaking about God [as plural], since it seemed highly inconsistent. Therefore, I believe that ancient scripture allowed those forms so that the impiety of the more recent Jews, who deny the plurality of divine persons, might be more strongly refuted. Several of these instances are inserted into the exposition of Genesis ascribed to Rabbi Moses the Preacher. Where it says of the verse, "In the beginning *Elohim*—that is, Gods—created the heaven and the earth," it is said word for word: "The heretics asked Rabbi Semlai <note>original: שמלאי</note>, saying, 'How many Gods created the world?' He responded: 'Let me and you seek this from the Law.' They said to him, 'Behold, it is written in Deuteronomy chapter 4: "What great nation is there that has Gods <note>gloss: Elohim</note> approaching it?" Behold, there are two *reshuyot* <note>term: "ressu ioth" (reshuyot), meaning "authorities" or "principles." In this context, it refers to the "Two Powers in Heaven" heresy.</note>, that is, principles.' He said to them, 'Read the end of the verse: "As the Lord our God in all our calling to *him* [singular]." For it is not written "to them," but "to him."' They said to him, 'Behold, it is written still in the last chapter of Joshua: "You cannot serve the Lord, for he is holy Gods."' He said to them, 'Read the end of the text. For it does not say "Because they are holy Gods," but "Because he is holy Gods [singular pronoun]."' They said to him again: 'Behold, it is written in 2 Samuel chapter 7: "And who is like your people Israel, a unique nation on earth, for whose sake Gods went to redeem."' He said to them, 'Read what is written following it: For it is not written *lahem* <note>gloss: "to them" or "for them" in the plural.</note>, that is, for themselves in the plural, but to redeem—'"

...to him, [using the word] *lo* <note>original: לו (*lo*)</note>, that is, "to him" in the singular. Again they also said to him: "Behold, it is written in Jeremiah, chapter 23: *And you have perverted the words of the living God* <note>original: והפכתם את דברי אלהים חיים (*ve-hpaktam et divrei Elohim hayyim*). In Hebrew, both "God" and "living" are in the plural form.</note>." He said to them: "Read the end of the text. For it is not written 'of the Lords of hosts,' but 'the LORD of hosts, our God' <note>original: יהוה צבאות אלהינו (*Adonai Tzevaot Eloheinu*)</note>." This tradition applies where this name *Elohim* is accepted for the true God, and yet is joined with an adjective in the plural number. This would by no means happen if it were always held in the singular when used for the true God, as they claim. 

Furthermore, similar to this way of speaking about God is what we read written in Hosea, chapter 11: "Ephraim has surrounded me with negation, or a lie, and the house of Israel with deceit. But Judah still rules with God, and is faithful with the holy ones <note>original: ועם קדשים נאמן (*ve-im kedoshim ne'eman*). The word for "holy ones" is plural.</note>." Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>term: Rabbi Solomon (Rashi), the preeminent 11th-century Jewish commentator. Reuchlin frequently cites him to show that even Jewish tradition acknowledges these pluralities.</note> says: "Faithful with the holy ones," that is, with the Holy and Blessed God. 

Nor do I think it should be passed over what is read in the *Midrash Coheleth* <note>term: *Midrash Coheleth*, a rabbinic homiletic commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes, regarding chapter 5: "If you see the oppression of the poor and the taking away of judgment and justice in a city, do not marvel at such a will. For the High One watches over the high one, and there are Higher Ones over them <note>original: וגבהים עליהם (*u-gevohim aleihem*). The word "Higher Ones" is plural.</note>." For there it is said: "If you see the oppressors of the poor and the needy, and justice—that is, the righteous one living forever, multiplying goodness and peace for himself—you should fear the judgment of hell. Because the High One watching over the high one, these are the angels. And the Higher Ones are over them. This is the Holy and Blessed God." 

Moreover, in many places we find this name *Elohim*, when it is used for the true God, coupled with a verb in the plural number. This would not happen at all if, when used for the true God, it were always kept in the singular. And to omit other examples of this kind which are almost infinite, I will bring forward this one which is most relevant to our purpose. For thus it is written in Genesis, chapter 1: "And *Elohim* said: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness <note>original: נעשה אדם בצלמנו כדמותינו (*na'aseh adam be-tzalmenu ki-demutenu*)</note>." 

If, therefore, in this place *Elohim* were held to be singular, He would not have said "let us make," but "I will make." Nor would He have uttered "in our image, after our likeness," but "in my image, after my likeness." However, He said "in our image, after our likeness," and not "in our images, after our likenesses," to indicate the identity of the persons and the unity of the divine essence. For even if the three divine hypostases <note>term: hypostases (singular: hypostasis), a Greek theological term referring to the distinct persons of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) who share one essence.</note> are personally distinguished from one another—since the person of the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another—nevertheless, they are not distinguished essentially, but are entirely the same thing. Since, therefore, this name *Elohim* is accepted here for the true God, and is joined with the verb "let us make" which is uttered in the plural, it is clearly [revealed]...

...it is established that [the name Elohim] is here taken for the true God, not in the singular, but in the plural, to suggest the plurality of the divine persons. <margin>False interpretations of the younger Jews.</margin> However, the younger Jews <note>The author refers to medieval Jewish commentators as "younger" or "later" compared to the ancient biblical authors.</note> try to pervert the truth of this text with certain irrational, even false, distortions. For some say that the reason God spoke in the plural when he was about to create man was because he consulted the heavenly family <note>The "heavenly family" or "heavenly host" refers to the angels.</note>. <margin>Refutations.</margin> Their saying is surely empty and void, as is most evident from the fact that all celestial beings serve God, and he does not need their counsel. Others, however, such as Rabbi David <note>term: Rabbi David Kimhi (Radak, 1160–1235), a famous grammarian and biblical commentator whose work was highly influential on Christian Hebraists.</note> and Rabbi Moses of Gerona <note>term: Nachmanides (Ramban, 1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note>, say in this place that God used this way of speaking because he was then speaking with the earth, since the man he was about to make had to consist of both divine and earthly matter. But this saying is so truly foolish and ridiculous that it needs no refutation. Indeed, it is a ridiculous folly to say that God called upon the earth to be his helper in the creation of man. Finally, some say that, grammatically speaking, in this place the name *Elohim* <note>original: אלהים (*Elohim*)</note> is not joined with the plural verb "Let us make" <note>original: *Faciamus*</note>, but with the verb "He said" <note>original: *Dixit*</note>, which is singular. For the text says, "And *Elohim* [singular verb] said." And later it follows, "Let us make man." This is also worth nothing. For even if *Elohim* is not immediately connected with the verb "let us make," it is nonetheless connected mediately, which is exactly the same thing. For no one other than *Elohim* said, "Let us make man." Furthermore, although here the name *Elohim*, taken for the true God, is coupled mediately and not immediately with a plural verb, it is nevertheless coupled immediately in many other places, as is easily apparent to those who read the Bible written in Hebrew characters. 

However, these and all others who strive to corrupt the meaning of this text are easily refuted by what is found in the *Midrash Koheleth* <note>term: A homiletic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Ecclesiastes.</note>, that is, in the exposition of Ecclesiastes, concerning that which is found in the second chapter: *For who is the man who comes, or enters, after the King, whom they have already made?* <note>original: כי מה האדם שיבוא אחרי המלך את אשר כבר עשוהו (*Ki meh ha-adam she-yavo acharei ha-melekh et asher kvar asuhu*). The Hebrew verb *asuhu* ("they made him") is plural.</note> For it is said there: "After the King—namely the King of kings, the Holy and Blessed God—will you be able to stand?" Moreover, it teaches through this that it must be noted that it is not written "who made him" [singular], but "who made him" [plural]. Because it is written thus in the Law, it can be said that the Holy and Blessed God and his house of judgment made him. If you say because of this, "There are therefore two principles," it does not follow. For has it not already been said in Deuteronomy, chapter 32: *He himself made you, and fashioned, or prepared, or adorned you?* <note>original: *Ipse fecit te...* refers to the singular verb in Deuteronomy 32:6.</note> Thus far the tradition. 

In this tradition, three things are placed that are very worthy of note and highly suited to the proposed matter. The first is that the plural verb "they made" is joined with the singular noun "King" in the creation of man, because when God created man, he spoke in the plural, saying, "Let us make man in our image." Hence the Psalmist said in Psalm 149: *Let Israel rejoice in his makers; let the children of Zion be joyful in their King.* <note>original: ישמח ישראל בעשיו בני ציון יגילו במלכם (*Yismach Yisrael be-osav, benei Tziyon yagilu ve-malkam*). In the Hebrew text, the word for "his maker" (osav) is grammatically plural.</note> That is, let [Israel] rejoice...

# BOOK SECOND

...Israel in his makers, let the sons of Zion exult in their king. <margin>Isaiah says in chapter 54.</margin> Hence also Isaiah says in chapter 54: <note>original: כי בעליך עשיך יהוה צבאות שמו</note> "For your husband is your Maker; the Lord of hosts is his name." That is: Because your masters <note>The Latin text reads "damnatores" (condemners), likely a printer's error for "dominatores" (lords/masters), reflecting the Hebrew *ba'al*.</note> are your makers: God (the Tetragrammaton) of hosts is His name. The second point is when it is said in this tradition: "That the Holy and Blessed God and his House of Judgment made man." Where by "the Holy and Blessed God," the unity of the divine nature is shown; through his "House of Judgment," the Trinity of persons is hinted at. For a "House of Judgment" <note>term: *Beth Din* — a Jewish court. Tradition requires a minimum of three judges to pass a valid legal ruling.</note> was so called among the Jews when at least three together passed a sentence; although it could consist of more, it could not consist of fewer, provided they were always odd in number. Therefore, the House of Judgment of God is nothing other than the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For that reason, in *Bereshith Rabbah* (that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis) regarding what is said in chapter 19: <note>original: ויהוה המטיר על סדום ועל עמורה גפרית ואש</note> "And the Lord <note>original: יהוה — the Tetragrammaton.</note> rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire"—Rabbi Elazar said: "In every place where the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, is placed in Scripture, it always means Himself and His House of Judgment." This same Rabbi also affirms this in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* (that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs), regarding chapter 1: <note>original: לססתי ברכבי פרעה דמיתיך רעיתי</note> "I have compared you, my love, to my mare among Pharaoh’s chariots" <note>or "among Pharaoh's cavalry."</note>. The third point is when it is added in the same tradition that God and His House of Judgment are not two principles of all created things, but only one principle. From this it is clear that the ancient Jewish Doctors did not deny the mystery of the divine Trinity, but only denied multiple principles or multiple gods—which the Christian religion detests no less. Since things are so, it is clearer than light that through the name **Elohim**, the three divine persons must be understood, who, as a single principle, concurred together for the production of all things.

->Antoninus, the ruler of the city of Rome, once requested of our Holy Rabbi that he teach him the truth of the essence of the Name of four letters, the Name of twelve letters, and the Name of forty-two letters. The response: Because you have asked to be taught the truth—meaning the indication of the Name of four letters, the Name of twelve letters, and the Name of forty-two letters—I inform you that these are the secrets of God which ought to be hidden from every person. But because I recognize that you are among the blessed students, and it is a matter consistent with reason to reveal these things to them—since it is not right to hide such things from the people of that province—therefore I inform you that God has no name by which we can attain true recognition. This is because His essence is His name, and His name is His essence. Regarding His essence, we cannot attain any recognition, for with such knowledge we would be equal to Him; except for His name, we cannot attain knowledge. Nevertheless, all His names have a specific indication, because the Name of four letters is more essential to His actions and shows a more complete and essential knowledge according to what we are capable of receiving. From this name, all His other names are joined. According to this, the name is called the *Shem Ha-Mephorash*—not that it is His essential name, but we call it so because it is all that our power can grasp, and we cannot ascend any higher. And you should know regarding the Name of twelve letters and the Name of forty-two, that they are not names where a single word is made of twelve or forty-two letters, but in whichever name it might be, there are many different words that have a single indication.<-

That is, Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome, once requested of the Holy Rabbi <note>original: *Rabbenu Ha-Kadosh* — "Our Holy Rabbi," the title given to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah, who according to legend was a friend of a Roman Emperor named Antoninus.</note> that he should instruct him concerning the truth of what is signified by the Name of four letters <note>The Tetragrammaton: YHWH.</note>, the Name of twelve letters, and the Name of forty-two letters. 
**The Response:** In that you seek to be informed of the truth—namely, what is demonstrated by the Name of four, the Name of twelve, and the Name of forty-two letters—I make it known to you that these are divine mysteries, which ought to be kept secret from all men. Nevertheless, because I recognize you to be well-deserving among scholars, and it is consistent with reason to disclose such things to them—since such things should by no means be hidden from men of this kind—therefore, I make it known to you that God has no name of which we can have knowledge. Since His substance is His name, and vice versa. And just as we can have no knowledge of His substance (since if it were known, we would become like Him), so we cannot have knowledge of His name. Nevertheless, all His names are attributive. And because the Name of four letters is more specific to His operations, and shows a more perfect knowledge of Him, and is more suited to Him (as far as it is possible for us to grasp), and since all His names proceed from this name, therefore this name is called the <term>שם המפורש</term> *Shem Ha-Mephorash* <note>The "Explicit" or "Distinct" Name. This is the name specifically assigned to the most high Creator. Because of this, it is called *Shem Ha-Mephorash* <note>original: "שם המפורש"</note>, which means "the explained name." He means to say that this name itself signifies and reveals the Creator’s substance and His "quiddity" <term>Quiddity: a philosophical term for the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</term> with a perfect and clear revelation. In this name, there is no ambiguity or mixture; that is, there is nothing in this name that is shared between God and His creatures. However, His other glorious names signify ambiguously and with mixture, because they are derived from actions similar to those found in us. Thus, even that name which is spoken in place of the four-letter Name—which is *Adonai* <note>original: "אדני" — Lord</note>—is derived from the word *Adon* <note>original: "אדן"</note>, meaning "Lord." But for the others, such as *Dayyan* <note>original: "דיין"</note>, meaning "Judge," and *Tzadik* <note>original: "צדיק"</note>, meaning "Just," and *Hannun* <note>original: "חנון"</note>, meaning "Gracious," or "Pious and Merciful"—it is obvious that these are common and derived terms. And there is no doubt that this glorious Name—which is not uttered, nor pronounced, nor spoken except in the sanctuary by the sanctified priests of the Lord, and only during the priestly blessing, and then only by the High Priest on the Day of the Fast <note>Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.</note> of glorious sanctification—is that Name in which there is no shared quality between the Creator and anything else. Briefly, I say that the loftiness and excellence of this Name is considered so great, and such great and terrible caution is taken so that no one speaks it, because it signifies the Creator’s substance and essence in such a way that no creature shares in that meaning. Just as our masters asserted, speaking in the person of God: "My Name is unique, or specifically assigned to me." All other names of God signify qualities and other attributes. And when these names of the Creator, derived from His works, were multiplied, it caused the hearts of many sons of Adam to believe that He had many qualities, corresponding to the multitude of works from which those names were derived. For this reason, He promised to give humans understanding that would remove this kind of error from them. ### SECOND BOOK

...He will be called by one name only, which signifies His substance or essence without being derived from any action. It is said in the *Pirke* <note>original: "פרקי" — *Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer*, an 8th-century midrashic work.</note>, that is, the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*: "Before the world was created, there was only the Holy and Blessed God and His Name." Notice how clearly he shows that all these other derived names of God were newly found only after the creation of the world. This is indeed certain, because all of them are named after certain works or effects found in the world. But when you consider God's essence stripped of every operation, He has no derived name at all, but only one alone to designate His essence. 

Now, there is no name among us that is not derived, except for the **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: "τετραγραμματον" — Greek for "four-letter name."</note> יהוה <note>The four Hebrew letters YHWH.</note>. This is the *Shem Ha-Mephorash* <note>original: "שם המפורש"</note>, that is, the name set apart absolutely. Do not believe there is any other but this. Nor should you let your heart be moved by the "brief vanities" of certain writers, or things you may have heard from them or found in their most empty books—certain names of the delirious, composed by them and full of blasphemy, which signify nothing at all. They call these "divine names" and claim that great holiness and purity are necessary to achieve an effect, and that it is possible for a man to perform miracles with such names. A prudent man should not listen to such vanities and insanities, let alone believe them. 

There is no other name called *Ha-Mephorash* <note>original: "המפורש" — meaning "the distinct" or "the explicit."</note>, that is, "set apart," except this glorious name of four letters, which is not read according to its letters <note>This refers to the Jewish tradition of not pronouncing the Tetragrammaton as written, but substituting it with *Adonai*.</note>. They spoke of this clearly with an explanation in the book called *Sifre* <note>original: "ספרי" — an ancient commentary on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</note>, regarding that passage in Numbers, chapter 6: "Thus shall you bless the children of Israel." "Thus" means in this language; "Thus" means with the *Shem Ha-Mephorash*. It was spoken in the Sanctuary as it is written, but in the provinces according to its surrogate pronunciation, which is to say, **Adonai** <note>original: "אדני" — Lord.</note> was said in its place. 

It is also said in the **Talmud** <note>A central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> regarding that same passage in Numbers 6: "Thus shall you bless the children of Israel." "Thus," that is, with the *Shem Ha-Mephorash*, or according to its proper pronunciation. It teaches what is to be said when it states: "And they shall put (or name) my unique name"—namely, the name unique to Me. Behold, it is explained there that the *Shem Ha-Mephorash* is the name of four letters, and that it alone signifies and shows the Creator's substance without any other mixture or secondary meaning. Therefore, the masters said in the person of God: "My name is unique to Me." All these things were said by Rabbi Moses ben Maimon <note>Maimonides.</note>.

**CAPNIO.** <note>The character representing Johannes Reuchlin.</note> Tell me, I pray, this name of four letters, as it is written or as the letters themselves sound—how is it pronounced?

**GALATINUS.** <note>Pietro Galatino, an Italian friar and scholar.</note> Some of our people say this name sounds like *Ioua* in our letters. From this, they say that perhaps the name *Jove* <note>original: "Iouis" — Jupiter.</note> crept in among the ancients. But they are surely very much in error, bringing the blasphemy of such paganism to so holy a name. For these four letters יהוה, if read as they are pointed <note>Referring to the Hebrew vowel points (nikkud).</note>, do not yield *Ioua*; but (as you yourself know best) they produce **Iehoua** <note>This is a very early Latin rendering of "Jehovah."</note>; although the Jews [pronounce it...]
