### What is signified by the name "Messiah," and regarding the two natures and one person of the Messiah. Chapter II.

### CAPNION,

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' featuring a figure and foliage.</image-desc>H**owever**, this is one point among the others that you must strive most of all to prove against the more recent Jews using their own ancient scriptures: namely, that the Messiah was to be truly God, and not merely a true man. **GAL.** I shall attempt to do that with all my strength, and all the more effectively because they deny it so obstinately. In order that the things you are about to say concerning the divinity of the Messiah may be better understood, it is first necessary that you explain what is signified by the name "Messiah."

**GAL.** Just as there are (as has been said) three persons in the Godhead, which—though they are distinguished from one another without separation—are nevertheless united to one another without confusion through a mutual indwelling which the Greeks call <term>perichoresis<note>From the Greek *perichoresis*, meaning "interpenetration" or "mutual indwelling." It describes the relationship between the three persons of the Trinity.</note></term>. So, in the one Christ, we confess there to be three <term>substances<note>In this context, Galatinus uses "substances" to refer to the constituent elements of the incarnate Christ: his divine nature, his human soul, and his human body.</note></term>: namely, divinity, a rational soul, and a human body. These are united without confusion in such a way that they are distinguished inseparably. And just as the three divine <term>hypostases<note>A theological term for "person" or "individual reality," used here to describe the distinct persons of the Trinity who share one essence.</note></term> are one God, so these three—divinity, soul, and body—constitute the one Messiah promised in the Law, who is nothing other than these three. For he is both perfect God and perfect man, subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh. Yet we do not say that he is "composed" of these as a man is composed of soul and body, or as a body is made of the four elements. For that which is "composed" is something different from the parts of which it is made. However, Christ (or the Messiah) is neither something else from those things of which he consists, nor anything other than those very things which are united in him. For as John of Damascus says in the book *On the Tradition of the Orthodox Faith*, in the forty-seventh chapter:

> <note>original: "ἐκ θεότητος καὶ ἀνθρωπότητος θεὸν τέλειον, καὶ ἄνθρωπον τέλειον τὸν αὐτὸν, καὶ ἕνα καὶ λέγεσθαι ἐκ δύο τε καὶ ἐν δυσὶ φύσεσιν ὁμολογούμενον."</note> 
> "From divinity and humanity, the same one is confessed to be and to be called perfect God and perfect man, consisting of and in two natures."

That is, we confess him to be the same person who is both perfect God and perfect man. In Hebrew he is called **משיח** (*Massiah*), in Chaldean [Aramaic] **משיחא** (*Mesicha*), in Greek **χριστὸς** (*Christos*), and in Latin he can be called *Unctus* [Anointed]. John of Damascus proves this same point most beautifully in the same place, saying:

> <note>original: "τὸ χριστὸς ὄνομα τῆς ὑποστάσεως λέγομεν, οὐ μονοτρόπως μὲν ἀλλὰ τῶν δύο φύσεων ὑπάρχον σημαντικὸν, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ἔχρισεν, χρίων μὲν ὡς θεὸς, ὃς ἔχρισε τὸ σῶμα τῇ θεότητι αὑτοῦ, χριόμενος δὲ ὡς ἄνθρωπος, αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐστὶ τοῦτο κἀκεῖνο, χρίσις δὲ ἡ θεότης τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος."</note>
> "We say the name 'Christ' refers to the person, not in a singular way, but as signifying the two natures. For he anointed himself: anointing as God, who anointed the body with his own divinity; and being anointed as man, for he is both this and that. The anointing of the humanity is the divinity."

**CAP.** These things are indeed beautiful. But since the Jews do not...

[...of] our age, who think the Messiah will be a pure human, would deny it. Therefore, it is necessary for you to show these things through their own authentic scriptures. **GALATINUS.** First, let them hear David, speaking thus of the Messiah in Psalm 15 <note>original: "decimoquinto." While the text says 15, the quote that follows is actually from Psalm 45:6-7.</note> according to the Hebrew truth: <note>original Hebrew: כסאך אלהים עולם ועד שבט מישור שבט מלכותך: אהבת צדק ותשנא רשע על כן משחך אלהים אלהיך שמן ששון מחבריך</note> "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of equity. You have loved justice and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." 

Indeed, the Chaldean interpreter <note>The "Chaldean interpreter" refers to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, whom the Jews now frequently have at hand, translated this into the Chaldean language thus: "Your throne, O God, is in the heavens for ever and ever; a strong kingdom is the scepter of your kingdom. And you, O King Messiah, because you have loved justice and hated malice, therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil, or ointment, of joy more than your fellows, or friends." From this Chaldean translation, it clearly appears that the prophet was speaking here about the Messiah. In his words, not only is this name "Messiah"—which is the same as "Anointed"—clearly expressed; indeed, he is called "Messiah" or "Christ" because of this anointing. 

As far as his humanity is concerned, he was to be anointed—both as King and as Priest—with the oil of joy (that is, the anointing of divinity) above his "participants" or "companions"—that is, above all other men who participate with him in the condition of one and the same human nature. Furthermore, the two natures, namely the divine and the human, which were to be <term>hypostatically<note>From the theological term "hypostatic union," referring to the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one individual existence.</note></term> united in him, are most openly suggested. For when he says, "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom," he clearly implies that the one he addresses is God, and thus he openly confesses his divinity. 

But when he says immediately to the same person: "You have loved justice and hated wickedness, therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of joy above your participants or companions," he undoubtedly confesses that the same person is also a man, openly manifesting his humanity. For since there is only one God, it would certainly be a crime to say that He had either a "God" or a "companion" [in the sense of an equal in nature]. 

If the more recent Jews do not believe that the prophet said these things concerning the name "Messiah" and the dual nature (divine and human) brought in through it, let them hear the words of their own ancient Doctors, who spoke more openly about the two natures and the single person of the Messiah. And first, indeed, those things which are read in the *Beressith Ketanna* <note>original: "Bereſſith Ketanna," meaning the "Lesser Genesis," a rabbinic commentary.</note> (that is, in the Lesser Exposition of Genesis) regarding what is said in the twenty-eighth chapter of that book, "And he took of the stones of that place." Also in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: "Midras tillim," a rabbinic commentary on the Psalms.</note> concerning that verse of Psalm 91, "For he has given his angels charge over you." Where it is read literally thus: <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: וכי נחמיה אומר שלש אבנים היו ואמר אם אלהים מיחד שמו עלי בשם שייחד על אבותי יעשו כולם אחד עמד ומצאם כולם לחד שנאמר ויקח את האבן מלמד שנעשו כולם אחד ורבנן אמרו פחות כי שתי אבנים</note> That is, Rabbi Nechmia says:

### BOOK THREE.

Jacob took three stones, and said: "If God unites His name over me, as He united it over my fathers, let them all become one." He stood, and found them all made into one. As it is said in Genesis, chapter twenty-eight: "And he took the stone." <note>The text refers to Genesis 28:11. While the Hebrew text mentions "stones" (plural) at the start and "stone" (singular) at the end, the Midrash explains this as a miraculous merging of the stones.</note> By this word, the scripture teaches that they all became one. But the Masters <note>The Rabbis or Sages of the Talmud.</note> said less, claiming there were two stones. This is from the Midrash. Therefore, whether he took three stones or two—or perhaps first three and then two—in either case the union of the Messiah is perfectly signified. For the union of the two stones signified the union of the two natures: namely, the divinity and the humanity in Christ. The union of the three, however, designated the union of the three substances: namely, the Word, the soul, and the body in the one person of Christ.

This union is also excellently attested by what is said in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, concerning that passage of Isaiah, chapter 23: "And it shall come to pass in that day, and Tyre <note>original: צור (Czor)</note> shall be forgotten for seventy years, according to the days (or according to the days of the King) united." Who is this "united King"? One might say that this is the King Messiah. But the Rabbi said: "This" consists of two—namely, the two natures—and "three generations"—that is, the substances. As it is said in Psalm seventy-one: "They shall fear you with the sun and before the moon, generation and of generation." <note>original: Psalm 71 (modern Psalm 72:5). The Latin "generationem & generationis" reflects a literal rendering of the Hebrew "dor dorim."</note>

The Gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: It is as if he were to say, "O Messiah, of whom it is written 'Before the sun his name is Yinnon' <note>original: ינון (yinnon). In Jewish tradition, Yinnon is one of the names of the Messiah, derived from Psalm 72:17, meaning 'he shall flourish' or 'son.'</note>—that is, 'son' or 'begotten' is his name—the Israelites shall fear you; and 'before the moon'—that is, before the Kingdom of the house of David, which is compared to the moon, as it is written in Psalm eighty-eight: 'Like the moon it shall be established forever.'" <note>Psalm 88 in the Vulgate is Psalm 89:37 in modern Bibles.</note>

Likewise, another gloss by the same author on that passage of Isaiah, "According to the days of the united King," says: "The days of David were seventy years, and I do not know what this sign given here means." Since these things are so, it must be carefully noted how the Talmud, in this aforementioned tradition, says the King Messiah is "united." 

Furthermore, what is even more wonderful is how this Rabbi (who is called "Rabbi" by excellence and is held as the only holy one <note>Referring to Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah, often called "Rabbi" or "Rabbeinu HaKadosh" (Our Holy Rabbi).</note>) indicates what he had received from the fathers regarding the matter and form of the union of the Messiah. He says that "this" <note>original: זה (Ze)</note>—that is, this one, namely the Messiah of whom the preceding discourse speaks; or "this," that is, that which refers to the union of the King Messiah—is "two," namely [God] and man, or the two natures united in the Messiah, the divine and the human. And "three generations" are the three substances of these natures: the Word of God, the rational soul, and the human body. 

He proves this through the prophet, who, addressing the Messiah in the spirit, says in Psalm seventy-one: "They shall fear you"—namely the Israelites, as they themselves explain, or whoever else—"with the sun," namely that [sun] of which it is said in Psalm eighty-three: "The Lord God is a sun and a shield; He will give grace and glory." <note>original Hebrew: שמש ומגן יהוה אלהים חן וכבוד יתן (Psalm 84:11). Galatinus identifies the "sun" here with God's own nature.</note> In this also where he says, "They shall fear you with the sun," he hints at the conjunction of the divinity and humanity of the Messiah. But what he adds, "And before the moon," that is, before the Kingdom...

### BOOK [THREE]

David (as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> explains) or rather the Church, which is compared to the moon, according to what is written in the sixth chapter of the Song of Songs: <note>original: מי זאת הנשקפה כמו שחר יפה כלבנה ברה כחמה</note> "Who is she that looks forth as the morning (or Venus): fair as the moon, bright as the sun?" Next, let them see the Holy Teacher <note>original: "Rabbenum Haccados," referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century redactor of the Mishnah.</note> openly debating this same matter. In the book he named *Gale Razeya* <note>original: גלי רזיא, meaning "The Revealer of Secrets." This is a mystical work often cited by Christian Hebraists.</note>, commenting on that passage of Isaiah chapter nine, "To the increase of his government," <note>original: למרבה המשרה (Lemarbeh ha-Misrah), Isaiah 9:6/7.</note> he says among other things: "Just as the letter *He* [ה] is composed of *Dalet* [ד] and *Vav* [ו], so the King Messiah is composed of divinity and humanity. And as these two—the letter *He* and *He*—are two *Dalets*, and from these proceed two *Vavs*, like two sons who arise from them; so in the substance of the King Messiah are found two sonships, one of which is of divinity, by which he is the Son of God; the other will be of humanity, by which he will be the son of the prophetess, of whom Isaiah spoke in chapter eight: 'And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.' And just as each of these letters *Daleth* and *Vav*, which make up the *He*, is distinct from the other, although both are one letter; so in the Messiah, the substance of divinity will be distinct from the substance of humanity, and vice-versa. These two joined together are the Messiah." Thus says the one whom the Jews call our holy teacher. From these things which have been said, it is therefore manifest that this name "Messiah" implies two natures, namely the divine and the human, and encompasses three things in one person: namely, a human body, a rational soul, and the Word of God.

## Chapter III. What the Word of God is according to the Hebrews, and that the Word of God is consubstantial <note>original: ὁμοούσιον (homoousion), a Greek theological term meaning "of the same substance," famously used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between the Father and the Son.</note> with God.

<margin>The triple Word.</margin>
To prove the divinity of the Messiah, it is necessary above all to say what the ancient Jews thought regarding this Word of God.
**GALATINUS.** Therefore, it must be noted of necessity that just as man has a triple word—namely, that which is written on paper, that which is uttered by the mouth, and that which lies hidden in the mind—it is to this last one that the name "word" most properly belongs, since it is the cause and principle of the others. Indeed, no actions of men would exist unless they were first "spoken" in the mind. For this reason, the saying of a certain Arabic poet is not to be entirely despised when he says: "The word is indeed in the heart, but the tongue was made to be the heart's interpreter." So also according to the Hebrews, God himself—in whose image man was made—is said to have a triple word. For he has the word written in the books of the prophets; he also has the word which is uttered by the mouths of the holy ones and the teachers; concerning which he himself says in the first chapter of Jeremiah: <note>original: הנה נתתי דברי בפיך</note> "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth." He also has the Word in himself, from himself, and not from elsewhere. Concerning which the Psalmist <note>original: "Psalmographus"</note> speaks in Psalm 33:

<meta>catchword: For right [is the word of the Lord]</meta>

->### THIRD [BOOK]<-

<note>original: כי ישר דבר יהוה וכל מעשהו באמונה : אהב צדקה ומשפט חסד : יהוה מלאה הארץ : בדבר יהוה שמים נעשו וברוח פיו כל צבאם</note> "For the word of the Lord is right; and all his works are done in truth. He loveth righteousness and judgment: the earth is full of the goodness of the Lord. By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth." *That is: Because the word of God is upright, and all his works are in faith; loving justice and judgment, the earth is full of the mercy of God. By the word of God the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.* This Word of God, therefore, through which not only the four elements but even the heavens themselves were made, is nothing else than that <term>Reschith<gloss>Beginning</gloss></term>, of which it is written in the first chapter of Genesis: <note>original: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ</note> *That is, in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* For it is established that this "beginning" is nothing other than the begotten wisdom of God, as it is said in the person of that same divine wisdom in the eighth chapter of Solomon’s Proverbs: <note>original: יהוה קנני ראשית דרכו קדם מפעליו מאז</note> *That is: God possessed me as the beginning of his way, before his works, from that time, or before then.* From this it is clear that they are entirely the same thing in reality, though they differ in name: the "beginning" by which the world was created, and the "wisdom" which God possessed. Since what is here called the "beginning of his way" (that is, of his creation) is that very Word of God by which (as was said) the heavens were made. Concerning this, the universal works of God—which Holy Scripture divides into different parts in various places by different names—are gathered together under a single name of power in Psalm 104, which says: <note>original: מה רבו מעשיך יהוה כלם בחכמה עשית</note> *That is: How manifold are your works, O God; you have made them all in wisdom, or through wisdom.* You see, therefore, that whether you say "beginning," or "word," or "hand," or "arm of God," or anything else of this kind, they do not indicate a diversity of things, but only one power and wisdom of God, by which He made all things. It must also be diligently noted that when it is said in the words mentioned a little earlier, "Because the word of God is upright, and all his works are in faith," it is immediately added concerning the same Word, "Loving justice and judgment." This openly suggests that the Word we are dealing with here is a rational substance, and <term>homoousion<gloss>consubstantial</gloss></term>, or of the same substance with God. Indeed, to love justice and judgment is a characteristic proper to a rational and intellectual substance. For that reason, the Word of God itself is frequently called the "eye" or the "eyes of God." For where the Lord says concerning the Jews in the 7th chapter of Ezekiel: <note>original: ולא תחוס עיני עליך</note> *That is: And my eye shall not spare you,* Jonathan, in the <term>Chaldaic translation<gloss>The Aramaic Targum, a paraphrased translation of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term>, says: <note>original: ולא ארחמא במימרי עלוהי</note> *That is: And my Word shall not have mercy upon you.* See how, where the prophet speaking in the person of God placed "my eye," there the Chaldean translator said "my Word." Furthermore, in saying, "And my Word had mercy upon them," it is clearly shown that the Word of God has life, since having mercy is a property of a living thing. And this is what is said in the 1st chapter of John: "That which was made, in him was life." That which is also written in the 24th chapter of Jeremiah: <note>original: ושמתי עיני עליהם לטובה</note> *This...*

In this same way, <term>Jonathan<gloss>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Targum (Aramaic paraphrase) of the Prophets</gloss></term> translated it into <term>Chaldean<gloss>the term used by Renaissance scholars for Aramaic</gloss></term>: <note>original: ואשוי במימרי עליהון לטבתא</note> *That is, And I will place my word upon them for good.* Furthermore, concerning that which the Lord says against them in the opposite sense in the ninth chapter of <term>Amos<gloss>a minor prophet in the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term>: <note>original: ושמתי עיני עליהם לרעה ולא לטובה</note> *This is, And my eyes upon them for evil, and not for good.* Jonathan himself explained this in Chaldean: <note>original: ואישוי במימרי עליהון לבישא ולא לטבא</note> *That is, And I will place my word upon them for evil, and not for good.*

<margin>
How often the Word of God is mentioned.
</margin>

To also suggest the <term>consubstantiality<gloss>the theological doctrine that the Word/Son is of the same essential substance as God the Father</gloss></term> of this Word with God, the very Word of God is sometimes called the "face of God," sometimes the "mouth of God," and sometimes the "hand of God" in the holy scriptures. Indeed, it is called the "face of God" in the fifth chapter of <term>Jeremiah<gloss>one of the major prophets of the Old Testament</gloss></term> when it is said: <note>original: האותי לא תיראו נאם יהוה אם מפני לא תחילו אשר שמתי חול גבול לים חק עולם ולא יעברונהו</note> *That is, Will you not dread my face, says the Lord, who have placed the sand as a boundary for the sea, an eternal decree, which it shall not pass?* Which Jonathan translated into Chaldean as: "Will you not dread before my word, who have placed the sand as a boundary for the sea." Furthermore, that it is called the "mouth of God" is held from what <term>Isaiah<gloss>a major Hebrew prophet</gloss></term> brought forth in the voice of God in the 48th chapter, saying: <note>original: הראשונות מאז הגדתי ומפי יצאו</note> *That is, The former things from then I announced, and they went out from my mouth.* Which Jonathan turned into Chaldean thus: <note>original: קדמיתא מבכיר חויתי וממימרי נפקא</note> *This is, the ancient things from of old I showed, and they proceeded from my word.* Similar to this is what is read in the fifteenth chapter of Jeremiah: <note>original: לכן כה אמר יהוה אם תשוב ואשיבך לפני תעמד ואם תוציא יקר מזולל כפי תהיה</note> *That is, Because of this, thus says God: If you return, I will restore you, or I will make you rest; you shall stand before my face, or you shall stand in my presence. And if you lead out, or extract, the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth.* This also the same Jonathan translated into Chaldean: <note>original: בכין כדנא אמר יהוה אם תתוב ואתיבינך קדמי תשמש ואם תתיב רשיעיא למהוי צדיקיא רעות מימרי תקיים</note> *This is, Because of this, thus says God: If you return, I will restore you, and you shall minister before me. And if you turn the impious so that they become righteous, you will fulfill the pleasure of my word.* Here, where the prophet placed "precious" and "vile," this man [Jonathan] explained them as "righteous" and "impious." And where the former said "mouth of God," the latter translated it as "his word." Finally, that the Word of God is called the "hand of God" is especially evident from what is read in the 48th chapter of Isaiah: <note>original: אף ידי יסדה ארץ וימיני טפחה שמים</note> *That is, My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens with a span.* For Jonathan explains this in the <term>Targum<gloss>an Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</gloss></term> thus: <note>original: אנא במימרי שכללית ארעא ובגבורתי תלית שמיא</note> *That is, By my word also I founded the earth, and in my power or my strength I measured the heavens.* Again, in the 45th chapter of the same prophet, it is said: <note>original: אנכי עשיתי ארץ ואדם עליה בראתי אני ידי נטו שמים וכל צבאם צויתי</note> *That is, I made the earth, and created Adam [man] upon it. My hands stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host.* The translator explained this in Chaldean: <note>original: אנא במימרי עבידית ארעא ואנשא עלה ברית אנא בגבורתי תלית</note> *I by my word made the earth, and created mankind upon it; I by my power suspended...*

# THE THIRD BOOK

<note>original Aramaic: במימרי שמיא וכל חילהון שכללית</note> *That is: By my word I perfected the heavens and all their host.* That is, I by my word, or through my word, made the earth, and created humans upon it. I in my strength stretched out the heavens, and all their powers I confirmed. From all these things which have now been said, it is clearly evident that the Word of God—which is the same as the Wisdom of God, through which He created and perfected the world from nothing—is of the very same substance with God Himself.

<margin>
The heretical exposition of the Jewish views.
</margin>

CAP. <note>Capnio, the dialogue persona representing the scholar Reuchlin</note> The more recent of the Jews, regarding that verse in the 8th chapter of Proverbs, "The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his way," assert that this wisdom—which you have explained as the uncreated Wisdom of God, the Word through which God made all things—is the Mosaic Law. And they say that the Law speaks of itself in that same place, saying: "I love those who love me." Since this is entirely against Catholic truth and is heretical, you ought to refute it using their own authentic scriptures.

GAL. <note>Galatinus, the author’s persona</note> That is certainly of such great absurdity that it requires no refutation. For if the Law of Moses is capable of neither love nor hate—except as other such inanimate things which are written on parchments—how can they say that it says of itself, "I love those who love me"? For to love is a property of a rational nature. Furthermore, if the Law of Moses itself began to be at that time when it took its beginning of existence on Mount Sinai, in what way could it have been with God before the beginning of all things? How could it say of itself, "God possessed me at the beginning of his way, before he made anything," along with the rest of the verses that follow?

Likewise, they say in this place that this word *Kanan* <note>original: קני / קנה</note> is <term>equivocal<gloss>having multiple meanings</gloss></term>, and sometimes signifies "to buy," and sometimes "to possess." And they say it signifies "to possess" in that place where Melchizedek, blessing Abraham, said in Genesis 14: <note>original: ברוך אברם לאל עליון קונה שמים וארץ</note> *That is: Blessed be Abram by God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth.* But here [in Proverbs], they say the word *Kanan* is the same as "to buy." Therefore, one must ask them: If God "bought" heaven and earth and the Law itself, who was the seller of these things? They certainly can assign no one. Therefore, it is shameful even to dream of such things, let alone to speak them. 

Let them cease, therefore, even to think such things, and let them believe according to the ancient traditions of their own Doctors: that Solomon in this place made mention not of the Mosaic Law, but of the very Wisdom of God, through which God fashioned the world. Let them now read what is written in the book <term>Sanhedrin<gloss>a major legal tractate of the Talmud</gloss></term> in the chapter <term>Dine Mamonoth<gloss>meaning "Judgments of Money/Property"</gloss></term>, regarding the 9th chapter of Proverbs: <note>original: חכמות בנתה ביתה חצבה עמודיה שבעה : טבחה טבחה מסכה יינה אף ערכה שלחנה : שלחה נערותיה תקרא על גבי מרומי קרת</note> *This is: Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn out her seven columns, she has slaughtered her victim, she has mixed her wine, and she has also set her table; she has sent her maidens to call from the heights of the city.* 

For there they explain these things thus: "Wisdom has built her house." This is His <term>Middatho<gloss>attribute or property</gloss></term>, that is, the property of the Holy and Blessed God Himself, who created the entire world in wisdom, or through wisdom. Just as it is said in Psalm 103: "How multiplied are your works, O Lord, you have made them all in wisdom." She hewed...

These are Adam the first and Eve. All these things are from tradition. <margin>Proverbs 9 <note>Latin: Sal. 9; referring to the Proverbs of Solomon, chapter 9</note></margin> From these things it is most clearly evident that Wisdom—which built her house, that is, the world—is one of the three *Middoth* <note>Hebrew: מידות; literally "measures," used here to mean divine attributes or properties</note>, that is, the properties of the holy and blessed God, through which they say (as we showed above) the world was established, although they understand "property" much more broadly than we do. However, we have already proved that this property of God—namely, Wisdom, through which God created the world—is exactly the same thing as the Word of God.

### That God is the Word, and the Word of God is God himself.
#### Chapter 4.

### CAPNIO,

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'E' featuring a classical or foliage design, starting the word 'ET'.</image-desc>
EVEN if in the preceding sections you have sufficiently and abundantly proved that the Word of God is of the same substance with God—from which it necessarily follows both that God is the Word and that the Word of God is God himself—nevertheless, so that the very stiff neck of the younger Jews may be further bruised, I beg you to be willing to show more sharply now that God is the Word, and the Word of God is God. 

GALATINUS: That God is indeed the Word is most clearly evident from this: where Isaiah in chapter 45 says, *Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation* <note>Hebrew: ישראל נושע ביהוה תשועת עולמים</note>, that is, Israel shall be saved in God (the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>) with the salvation of ages, or eternal salvation; so the Targum of Jonathan <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> says: *Israel shall be delivered by the Word of the Lord with an eternal deliverance* <note>Aramaic: ישראל אתפריק במימרא דיי פורקן עלמיא</note>. Therefore, where Isaiah said "In God" (the Tetragrammaton)—a name attributed to none but God—there the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translator rendered it "in the Word of God." By this, he openly shows that God is the Word. 

Likewise, where it is said in Hosea chapter 1: *And I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them in the Lord their God* <note>Hebrew: ואת בית יהודה ארחם והושעתים ביהוה אלהיהם</note>, so the same translator turns it into Aramaic: *And upon the house of Judah I will have mercy, and I will deliver them by the Word of the Lord their God* <note>Aramaic: ועל דבית יהודה ארחם ואפריקינון במימרא דיי אלההון</note>. 

Also, that which Isaiah says in chapter 8: *And God added to speak to me yet* <note>Hebrew: ויוסף יהוה ובר אלי עוד</note>, so Jonathan himself translated in Aramaic: *And the Word of the Lord added to speak to me yet* <note>Aramaic: ואוסיף מימרא דיי למלל לי עוד</note>. 

Likewise, what the same prophet said in chapter 41: *Fear not, for I am with you* <note>Hebrew: אל תירא כי עמך אני</note>, so he translated it: *Fear not, for my Word is for your help.* 

Likewise, what is said in the same place: *Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel; I have helped you, says the Lord, and your redeemer the Holy One of Israel.* <note>Hebrew: אל תיראי תולעת יעקב מתי ישראל אני עזרתיך נאם יהוה וגאלך קדוש ישראל</note>

# BOOK THREE

<header>THIRD [BOOK]</header>

This means: "Fear not, you worm, or grub of Jacob, you men of Israel, or you who are of Israel. I have helped you," says God, "and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel." <note>original: "Hoc est, Ne timeas uermis, uel tinea Iacob..." citing Isaiah 41:14</note> Thus he [Rabbi Jonathan] explained it in the Aramaic <term>Chaldaic; an older term for Aramaic, the language of the Targums</term>: "Fear not, tribe of the house of Jacob, seed of the house of Israel, my Word <note>Aramaic: *Memra*</note> is for your help," said God and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel. Furthermore, in the 44th chapter of the same prophet [Isaiah]: "Thus says the Lord your redeemer from the womb, I am the Lord who makes all things, stretching out the heavens *by myself alone* <note>Hebrew: לבדי, *levaddi*</note>," that is, by me alone, "establishing the earth *by that which is with me* <note>Hebrew: מאתי, *meitti*</note>," that is, through him who is with me. Thus he explains it in the Targum: "Thus says the Lord who redeemed you, and who formed you from the womb. I am the Lord, the author of all things, I stretched out the heavens by my Word, or through my Word. I founded the earth by my power or strength." This agrees strongly with that saying of the Evangelist [John]:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

Also that which is said in the ninth chapter of Hosea: "My God will reject or cast them away, because they did not hear him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations." Thus Jonathan explains it in the Targum:

> My God will cast them away, because they did not receive his Word, and they shall be wanderers among the nations.

Since, therefore, in all these places and many others where the prophets placed the name of the Lord or God (the <term>Tetragrammaton; the four-letter sacred name of God, YHWH</term>), the aforementioned Rabbi Jonathan—a man of the greatest authority among them—translated and explained it in Aramaic as "the Word of God," it is plainly consequent that God himself is the Word, and the Word of God is God. Which was to be proven.

->That the Messiah is the Word of God, whom God was to send to heal the whole human race.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter 5.<-

### CAPNIO,

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial N featuring a figure, possibly a scholar or divine, seated among scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
NOW it remains that, for a fuller knowledge of this matter, you show that the Messiah is the Word of God, whom God was to send for the healing of the whole world.

<margin>That the Messiah is of God,</margin>
### GALATINUS,

That the Messiah is the Word of God is most evident from the fact that where David, in the hundred and tenth Psalm, calls the Messiah his Lord, saying: "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand" <note>Hebrew: נאם יהוה לאדני שב לימיני, *Ne'um YHWH l'Adoni shev l'ymini*</note>. There, Rabbi Jonathan in the Aramaic translation says: "The Lord said to his Word, sit at my right hand" <note>Aramaic: אמר יהוה למיימריה הב לימיני, *Amar YHWH l'Memreih*</note>. Certain people object to me at this point, saying it is not so written in the Aramaic translation, which they also deny belongs to Jonathan. To them I respond: it is indeed true that in the Aramaic translation which they have seen, it is not written this way, and that version is not by Jonathan; for it is (as many believe) by Rabbi Joseph the Blind, or (as others would have it) by Rabbi <term>Akilas; likely referring to Aquila of Sinope, a famous translator of the Bible</term>. Which is so...

# BOOK [THREE]

<header>BOOK</header>

"The Lord said through His Word <note>Aramaic: *Memra*</note> to give for greatness the portion which I gave for the study of the Torah." <note>original Aramaic: אמר יהוה במימריה למיתן לירבנותא חלא דיהיבית לאולפן אוריתא</note> Here it says: "Wait at my right hand." <note>original: ימיני אוריך, *yemini orekh*</note> This means: "God said in His Word that He might give me dominion, because I sat to learn the Law; wait at my right hand." Moreover, the translation of Jonathan <note>The *Targum Jonathan*, an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets</note>—which they themselves have not yet seen—states exactly what I have reported. This is clearly evident in the *Book of Collections* <term>Hebrew: *Sefer Kibbutzim*; a compilation of rabbinic sayings</term>, specifically the opinions of the sages. In the passage where it is proved that the Messiah is the one whom David called his "Lord" who would sit at the right hand of God, it says: "This is explained from what they said in the *Midrash Tehillim* <term>The Rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</term> regarding that verse from the Psalms: 'And You gave me the shield of Your salvation, and Your right hand shall support me.' <note>Psalm 18:35</note> Rabbi Judan said in the name of Rabbi Hama: 'In the time to come <note>The Messianic age</note>, the Holy One, blessed be He, will cause the King Messiah to sit at His right hand, as it is said in Psalm 110: The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.' And the Targum of Jonathan ben Uziel explains: 'The Lord said to His Word <note>Aramaic: *Memra*</note>, sit at my right hand.'" So far the tradition.

The same is also confirmed in the same *Midrash Tehillim* regarding that verse in Psalm 2: "I will tell of the decree: The Lord said to me, You are my son; today I have begotten you." For it is said there: "They tell of his mysteries <note>the King Messiah’s</note> in the decree of the Law <note>Torah</note>, in the decree of the Prophets, and in the Writings <note>Hagiographa</note>. In the decree of the Law, it says in Exodus 4: 'Israel is my firstborn son.' In the decree of the Prophets, it says in Isaiah 52: 'Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and lifted up.' And in the Writings, it says in Psalm 110: 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.'" From these traditions, it is clearly shown that the one David predicted would sit at the right hand of God is undoubtedly the Messiah. From this, through the Targum of Jonathan, it is clearly concluded that the Messiah is the Word of God. Therefore, it is not surprising if David called the Messiah himself his "Lord."

"Now, concerning His word, in what shall we believe?" He said to him: "That He might heal them and deliver them from their destruction; and because of their sins, we shall believe in Him and honor Him." He said to him: "Why did it not say, 'He shall send His word and heal *us*', but rather 'and heal *them*'?" "Because it seems to me that he was speaking of specific individuals." He answered him: "You have spoken the truth, for the Word came to heal, but none received it except the individuals whose lives were without intellectual status among the masses—fishermen, servants of the sea. And this is what is meant by: *Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; these have seen the works of the Lord.* <note>Psalm 107:23</note> Those who, by right, were not in a position to receive any intellectual thing due to their coarseness, received the truth of the prophecy and believed in the Lord, and He counted it to him as righteousness." <note>Genesis 15:6</note>

This is: *He will send his word and will heal them, and he will rescue them from their afflictions.* <note>original Latin: "Mittet uerbum suum & sanabit eos, & eripiet eos de plagis eorum." An English translation of Psalm 107:20.</note> Rabbi Samuel Levita says: The Word of God is His messenger <note>original Latin: *nuncius*; can also mean "angel" or "herald"</note>. Concerning which it is written: *Surely my word is like this, like a fire, said God.* <note>original Latin: "Profectò tale est uerbum meum, qualis est ignis, dixit Deus." Referring to Jeremiah 23:29.</note> And this is what was said: *Your word shall come, and we will honor you.* Surely when the Word of God comes, which is His messenger, then we shall honor him. Rabbi Saul said: "Did the prophets not come, and we killed them, and we shed their blood? How then shall we now receive His word? Or for what reason shall we believe him?" Rabbi Samuel answered him: "Because *he will heal them, and he will rescue them from their afflictions*; for the sake of these signs, I say, we shall believe him, and we shall hold him in honor." Then he said to him: "Why (I pray) did he not say, *He will send his word and will heal us*; but said, *and he will heal them*?" He answered: "This is because (as I perceive it) he was speaking of a part, and of some only, but not of all; which is signified, namely according to the property of the Hebrew language, in the word 'Them.'" He said to him: "You certainly speak the truth. For His word came to heal all in general, not only some, and in part. But it was not received except by some individuals, who were reckoned among all to be of a coarser nature, men who were fishermen, and those occupying themselves in the sea. And this is what was said: *Those descending into the sea in ships, doing work in great waters, they have seen the work of God.* <note>Psalm 107:23</note> They indeed, if you consider rightly, did not seem fit to be able to admit anything intellectual, or what pertains to the intellect, on account of the rudeness of their senses. They, I say, received the truth of prophecy and vision, because they believed His word. And this is what is written: *He believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.*" <note>Genesis 15:6</note> From which it is clear, that God was going to send His word, that is, His son, the true Messiah, so that He might heal the whole human race. Yet not all were to be healed, but only those who were to receive Him and believe in Him, and especially simple men <term>Latin: *idiotæ*; referring to those without formal education or high social standing</term> and fishermen, as the apostles were.

BOOK <note>original Latin: LIBER</note>

# That Jesus the Nazarene, the true Messiah, is the Word of God, sent by the eternal Father for the salvation of mankind.
## Chapter VI.

->CAPNIO,<-

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut drop cap 'C' featuring a scholar in a hat seated at a desk with an open book, pointing towards the text.</image-desc> I would like you to prove this conclusion: namely, that our Lord Jesus the Nazarene was the true Word of God, and consequently the true Messiah, sent into the world by the eternal Father for the salvation of men. GALATINUS: So that I may say nothing myself in this place, hear the words of Libertatus Cominetus of Spain (for such is the man's name), recently converted from Judaism to the faith—a man not only exceptionally learned in divine letters, but also skilled in fourteen languages. For he, explaining that passage of the 147th Psalm, *He sends His word and melts them* <note>original Hebrew: ישלח דברו וימסם; Psalm 147:18</note>—that is, *He shall send His word, and it shall heal them; He causes His wind to blow, and the waters flow* <note>original Hebrew: ישב רוחו יזלו מים</note>—speaks thus:

"He sends His word and melts them." He should have said, "He will speak His word," and not "He will send His word," because in regard to a "word," the act of speaking is more appropriate than the act of sending. This is just as it is said: *And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.* <note>Genesis 1:3</note> It does not say "God sent His word to make or create the light," because the language of "sending" is not used unless there is someone sent <note>meaning a distinct person or messenger</note>, just as it says: *Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet.* <note>Malachi 4:5</note> This means that God would send prophets to tell His word and show His wonders. We also see this in the bronze serpent <note>Numbers 21:9</note> which God commanded to be made by the hand of Moses in the wilderness to heal Israel when they looked at it. For it would have been more fitting in those times for Him to heal them by a word alone, so that the people would see His wonders and believe in Him, rather than through that serpent, which might cause doubt in the hearts of the people that it was an act of sorcery—what is today called "the customs of the nation." If He had healed them by a word alone, He would have removed all doubts from their hearts. But what appears to me from this verse is that David prophesied the coming of Jesus, our righteous Messiah <note>term: Messias uerus; "Righteous Messiah" is a common Hebrew messianic title</note>, by saying "His Word." For the truth is that He would be His Word and the proclaimer of His words. And just as speech is not a thing separate from one's essence, so He is not separate from God. This is why it says, "Your Word and His glory shall come," for it should have said "Your Word and Your glory," but rather the appearance of His presence—may He be exalted—and His Word are one thing. For among those who are honored, their speech is honored, and those who honor it honor the speech, for they are inseparable in their essence. And this is the Word which was prophesied to come to heal the sick and revive the dead by speech, and He Himself was the Word, as we see in Jesus our righteous Messiah, who healed by a word and revived several who were sick, and raised Lazarus four days after his death. These things are not appropriate for any except for God. And next to this, it says, "He causes His wind to blow and the waters flow." It seems there is no connection between the healing of bodies and the flowing of water at all. But you must understand how David prophesied the truth by saying "He causes to rest" <note>a play on the Hebrew root Y-Sh-B</note> and not "He will return," meaning that God would cause His Holy Spirit to rest with Him and at His right hand. After this, "waters shall flow," meaning they shall draw holy waters to save His people, which are the cause of our salvation, as it is said: *And you shall draw water with joy from the wells of salvation.* <note>Isaiah 12:3</note> Through these, God is joined to us, as He said: *When you pass through the waters, I am with you.* <note>Isaiah 43:2</note> He did not say "in the seas," but "in the waters," meaning the holy waters. 

This is: *He sends His word and heals them.* It seems it should have been said, "He will speak His word," and not "He will send His word." For indeed, it is more fitting for a word to be pronounced and brought forth than to be sent, which seems to belong to a messenger. And the scripture which says...

<meta>This page continues the speech of Libertatus Cominetus, a Jewish convert to Christianity, who is providing a theological argument to the scholars Capnio and Galatinus. He is explaining why the Messiah is referred to as the "Word" (Verbum) in the Psalms and how this relates to the nature of God's essence and the sacrament of baptism.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

God said, "Let there be light," and there was light <note>Genesis 1:3</note>. However, He did not say, "God sent His word to create the light," because a "sending" <note>original Latin: missio</note> cannot be fulfilled without someone being "sent" <note>original Latin: misso</note>. Therefore it is said elsewhere, *Behold, I send to you Elijah the prophet* <note>Malachi 4:5</note>, indicating that God sends prophets to announce His word and to manifest His wonders.

Because of this, the **bronze serpent** increases the doubt—that object which God commanded to be made by the hand of His prophet Moses, so that the people of Israel might be healed when they looked upon it <note>Numbers 21:8-9</note>. For it seems more reasonable and fitting, especially in those times, that God should have healed the people by His word rather than by the sight of a serpent, a thing which could lead to a suspicion of incantation and magic. And yet, at that time He did not heal by the word. How then does it square with what the prophet says: *He shall send His word, and shall heal them*? <note>Psalm 107:20</note> 

But this is resolved. For as far as I can perceive, David in this place prophesied the coming of **Jesus the Messiah**, our Righteous One, who is rightly called His "Word." But the truth is this: Jesus is the Word of God, and He is the messenger of God's words. And just as the Word of God is not something distinct from the essence of God, so also the Messiah is not entirely distinct from the divine substance. And this is what is written: *Your Word shall come, and we will honor You.* For if the Word were entirely divided from Him, it would have said, "And we will honor it." By these words it is clearly shown that God and the Word of God are one and the same, since they are held as the same: to honor both God and the Word of God, seeing as they are in no way distinct in essence.

And this is the Word about which it was prophesied that it would come to heal the sick and to raise the dead by the word. And indeed, He was to perform all these things by the word. All these things were fulfilled in **Jesus the Messiah**, our Righteous One, by whose works almost innumerable sick people were healed, and Lazarus was raised from the dead, even after the fourth day of his death.

And these things belong to God alone. It agrees with our exposition what immediately follows: *His spirit shall settle, and the waters shall flow* <note>original Latin: "Sedebit spiritus eius," a variation of Psalm 147:18 which usually reads "He causes his wind to blow"</note>. For even if they seem to have no agreement—healing the sick and the flowing of waters—it is nevertheless the truest sense of the prophet. He also, not without mystery, said "His spirit shall settle" and did not say "His spirit shall return," demonstrating that God intended His Holy Spirit to stay <note>original Latin: sedere, literally "to sit"</note> with Him. And he added: *And the waters shall flow*, signifying that the holy waters were to remain for the salvation of His people. 

These waters, indeed, are the causes of our salvation. Just as it is written: *You shall draw waters from the fountain of salvation* <note>Isaiah 12:3</note>. For through the intervention of the holy waters, God is joined with us. As it is written: *When you pass through those waters, I am with you* <note>Isaiah 43:2</note>. And he did not say simply "through waters," but "through **those** waters," demonstrating that he spoke not of just any waters, but of the holy waters, which are the waters of baptism. 

All these things were said by the aforementioned Doctor, the most learned of the Hebrews, recently converted to the truth of the Christian faith. By these things he excellently proves that Jesus the Nazarene...

### CAPNIO,

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a man kneeling or sitting in a field, possibly in prayer or contemplation, with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>Although from what you have said, it follows that the Messiah is the Son of God. For if the Messiah himself is the Word of God, he must undoubtedly also be the Son of God. Nevertheless, so that the stubbornness <note>original: *perfidia*</note> of the Jews of our age may be more and more overcome by their own weapons, you ought to demonstrate more expressly through their scriptures that the Messiah is himself the Son of God. <margin>GALATINUS.</margin> First, that Psalm which begins, *Why do the nations rage* <note>Psalm 2:1</note>, should be set against them. This is interpreted by the ancient Jews as referring to the Messiah, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> testifies, who says of it: "Our masters have interpreted this Psalm concerning the Messiah." Therefore, at the end of the same Psalm, it <margin>reads,</margin> *נשקו בר פן יאנף ותאבדו דרך כי יבער כמעט אפו אשרי כל חוסי בו* <note>original Hebrew: *Nashku bar pen-ye’enaph v’tovdu derekh ki-yiv’ar kim’at appo ashre kol-khose vo*</note>. That is, "Kiss the son, lest he be angry, and you perish from the way. When his wrath is kindled even a little, blessed are all they that put their trust in him." <note>Psalm 2:12</note> To the receiving of this kiss of the Son of God, David was advising the judges of the earth. As is shown by Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a distinguished Spanish Jewish scholar and grammarian</note>. Who, explaining this, says: *נשקו בר* <note>Nashku bar</note>, that is, "kiss the son." Behold, "serve the Lord," is contrary to what he had said above, namely, "against his Messiah." Indeed, the explanation of this word *בר* <note>Bar</note>, is the same as that found in the thirty-first chapter of Proverbs. Where it is said, *מה ברי ומה בר בטני ומה בר נדרי* <note>original Hebrew: *Mah beri u-mah bar bitni u-mah bar nedarai*</note> That is, "What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?" <note>Proverbs 31:2; notably, 'Bar' is the Aramaic word for son, used here in a Hebrew context</note> And thus it is written in this same Psalm, *בני אתה* <note>Beni atah</note>, that is, "you are my son." <note>Psalm 2:7</note> These are the words of the same Rabbi Abraham. In the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note> also, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms on these same words, it is said thus:

> *נשקו בר הוא מה דכתיב. חסד ואמת נפגשו צדק ושלום נשקו . אמר רב משל למלך שכעס על בני המדינה והלכו בני המדינה ופייסו את בן המלך שיפייס את המלך והלך ופייס את האב ופייס את אביו כיון שנתפייס לבנו הלכו בני המדינה לומר הימנון למלך אמר להם לי אתם הימנון לכו ואמרוהו לבני שאלמלא הוא כבר אבדתי את המדינה הוי נשקו בר*

That is, "This is what is written in Psalm 85: *Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.* <note>Psalm 85:10</note> The Rabbi said: This is like a King who was angry with the people of a province. And the people of the province went and pleaded with the King's son to appease the King. The son went and pleased his father. And when the King had been appeased through his son, the people of the province went to give thanks to the King. But the King said to them: To me you [give] thanks..."

# THIRD BOOK.

...you give thanks: Go and give thanks to my son. For if it had not been for him, I would have already destroyed the city. And this is what was said, *Kiss the son*.
<margin>HOG.</margin> Thus far the tradition. Our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate translation used by the Church in the author's time</note> has: *Embrace discipline*. 
<margin>GAL.</margin> Here he has it. The author of our edition, deceived by the ambiguity of words, translated many things quite differently from what the Hebrew truth contains. For although this word בר <note>original Hebrew: *Bar*</note> sometimes signifies son, sometimes discipline or doctrine, sometimes grain, sometimes pure or clean, and sometimes chosen. As Saint Jerome also seems to feel, when in the *Apology against Rufinus* he writes to Pammachius thus: "*Bar* among the Hebrews signifies diverse things. For *Bar* is called son, as in that phrase *Bar-jona*, that is, son of a dove; and *Bartholomew*, that is, son of Ptolemy; and *Barnabas*, that is, son of a prophet; and Bar-chinaeus, and Bar-chiseus, and Barabbas. Also wheat, and a bundle of thorns, and chosen, and pure." These are the words of Jerome. In this place, however, *Bar* is not accepted except for "son," as the aforementioned Rabbi Abraham <note>Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra, a medieval Sephardic scholar</note> accepts in the exposition of this text. And although the Chaldean interpreter <note>The Aramaic translation or Targum</note>, whom the Jews now more frequently have at hand—whether it be Rabbi Joseph the Blind, as some prefer, or Rabbi Akilas, as certain others wish—accepted *bar* in this 
<margin>place for</margin> place for "doctrine," saying: קבילו אולפנא <note>original Aramaic: *Kabbilo ulpana*</note>, that is, "Receive doctrine." Yet it is more correctly and fittingly accepted here as "son" (as we have said). For thus it also favors our faith more (as it has seemed) and agrees more with the exposition of the ancients (as was evident in the traditions mentioned above), and is more consistent with the truth of the literal text. For that which follows, "Lest he be angry," along with the rest, cannot suit anyone except the Son of God alone. From this it is also clear that the interpretation of those who, in order to flee the truth and deny the divinity of the Messiah, translate these same words, 
<margin>נשקו בר</margin> *nassecu bar*, as "worship purely," is not true. Furthermore, that kiss by which the church of the ancients, by kissing the Son of God, also asked to be kissed by him, was nothing other than the instruction and doctrine to be brought forth from the very mouth of God, who had given them the law through the hand of Moses. For which reason (as the ancient Talmudists explained), in the first chapter of the Song of Songs, it said: ישקני מנשיקות פיהו <note>original Hebrew: *Yishakeni minshikot pihu*</note>. That is, "Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth." This means: Let the Messiah, the Son of God, kiss me with the kiss of his mouth—that is, let him instruct and teach me with his own mouth, and let him not despise the touch of my mouth when I shall ask him about the way of salvation. Let him no longer send Moses, who had a heavy tongue. Not Isaiah, who said he was of polluted lips. Not Jeremiah, who said he did not know how to speak because he was a child. But let the Son of God himself, who is the wisdom and power of the Father, come and teach me with his own mouth. By this it is also proved that the Messiah is the Son of God, because God himself says this of him in Psalm 89: הוא יקראני אבי אתה אלי וצור ישועתי : אף אני בכור אתנהו עליון למלכי ארץ : <note>original Hebrew: *Hu yikra’eni avi attah eli vetzur yeshu’ati; aph-ani bekhor ettenehu elyon lemalkhe-aretz*</note>. That is, "He shall call me, 'You are my father, my God, and the strength of my salvation': I also will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."

**CAPNIO.**

Therefore David said before the holy and blessed God: "Because you created the heavens and the earth with your name, I shall attribute those things to your name," saying: *Of the Lord <term>Yahweh</term> <note>The tetragrammaton, the four-letter holy name of God in Hebrew</note> is the*

For the name of God itself is one of the properties of God, with which God himself created the world. This appears even more clearly in the commentaries on Genesis by Rabbi Moses ha-Darshan <note>An 11th-century Jewish scholar from Narbonne, famous for his midrashic explanations.</note>, upon that passage in chapter 41: *And Pharaoh said to Joseph: Without your word, no man shall lift up his hand.* Where, when that verse from Zephaniah is introduced—*To call upon the name of the Lord*—along with others, it is said: "The name of the Lord (the Tetragrammaton) is not mentioned here, except to refer to the King Messiah." Just as it is said in Isaiah, chapter 30: *Behold, the name of the Lord (the Tetragrammaton) comes from afar.* And so on. He teaches the same thing concerning the fathers or concerning God, holy and blessed. Just as it is said in Jeremiah, chapter 31: *From afar the Lord (the Tetragrammaton) appeared to me.* This concludes the tradition. To this also applies what is read in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with legal and messianic matters.</note> in the chapter *Helec*: Rabbi Johanan said, "If you see a generation making itself small and departing, expect the Messiah." Since, therefore, there is no redeemer except God.

And that the Messiah is that redeemer, as will be discussed in the following pages, has been proved (as I judge) quite abundantly both in this and in the preceding traditions: namely, that the Messiah is the name of God, and the name of God is God, and consequently the Messiah himself is God.

### That the Messiah was to be called by the Tetragrammaton, the name of God. Chapter IX.

->CAPNIO,<-

At this point, I would like you to prove that the Messiah was to be called by the name of God, the Tetragrammaton <note>The "four-letter" name of God (YHWH/Yahweh), which was considered so holy in Jewish tradition that it was not pronounced aloud.</note>, through which the divine essence itself is designated.

GAL. To prove this, therefore, I will first bring forward the words of Jeremiah, who says in the twenty-third chapter: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch; and a King shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell in confidence. And this is his name by which they shall call him: The Lord <note>original: "tetragrammaton"</note> our Just One.* <note>The Hebrew text cited here is Jeremiah 23:5-6. The name "The Lord our Righteousness/Just One" (Yahweh Tsidkenu) is the focal point of the argument.</note> The Jews cannot deny that this prophecy is understood to be about the Messiah. First, because the ancient Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> explain it as referring to the Messiah. Furthermore, it is because of the Chaldean translation <note>The Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible used in synagogues when many people no longer spoke Hebrew fluently.</note>, which speaks openly about the Messiah. In this prophecy, not only is the dual nature of the Messiah expressed—both divine and human—but it is also clearly shown that the Messiah himself was to be called by the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, when it is said: *And this is his name, by which they shall call him, The Lord our Just One.* 

CAP. The Jews of our time say that Jeremiah did not say "they shall call," as we have it, but rather "he shall call." For this reason, they assert the sense of these words is this: *This is the name of him who shall call him (namely, the Messiah), "The Lord our Just One."* <note>This is a grammatical dispute. Capnio is pointing out that by changing a single vowel or letter, the subject of the sentence changes from "people calling the Messiah God" to "God calling the Messiah his righteous one."</note> 

GAL. They are plainly lying. By falsely punctuating the letters, they strive to corrupt the text. For from *yikre'u* <note>Hebrew: יקראו</note>, which means "they shall call," they wish to make *yikra* <note>Hebrew: יקרא</note>, which means "he shall call." But it is most evidently clear through almost all the writings of their own ancient predecessors that they are manifest forgers. First, through the Septuagint translators <note>The "Seventy," the famous 3rd-century BCE Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, who translated this passage exactly as our edition has it. Next, through the Targum of Rabbi Jonathan <note>The Aramaic paraphrase of the Prophets attributed to Jonathan ben Uzziel.</note>, who turned these same words into the Chaldean tongue thus: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish for David the Messiah of Justice.* <note>original Aramaic: הא יומין אתן אמר יהוה ואקים לדוד משיח דצדקא</note> And afterward he adds: *And this is his name which they shall call him, The Lord our Just One.* <note>original Aramaic: וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקנו</note> The same prophet also refutes their falsehood in no small way when he says again, in the thirty-third chapter: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will perform the [word...]*

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion regarding the Fall of Man and the nature of Original Sin, specifically transitioning from the biblical account of Eve to the consequences for Adam's descendants.</meta>

# SEVENTH.

(That is, *And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and pleasing to the eyes* <note>original: "Et uidit mulier, quòd bona eſſet arbor ad ueſcendum, & delectabilis oculis" — quoting Genesis 3:6</note>) he filled himself with pride and disobedience, and transgressed the commandment of God, infecting his flesh in such a way that all those descending from him are conceived with that same pride and disobedience, which is the origin of all sins. For this reason, it is called <term>original sin; the inherited state of sinfulness traditionally believed by Christians to be passed from Adam to all humanity</term>, or initial sin. Because of this, people are procreated with lust and unrestrained pleasure, and they are inclined to fulfill their own will, and are subject to sinning and transgressing God's commandment. This is most evident to the senses. For when a man is in the grip of unrestrained lustful desire, the genital member <note>The author uses "superbit" (is proud/swells) to link the physical reaction of the body to the spiritual sin of pride.</note> acts with such pride and proceeds to carry out the desired pleasure that he would not cease from that act even if death were set before him. This is found to be the case in no other limb. For when someone approaches a theft, and before he completes it, he repents of the theft, his feet immediately stop walking and his hands abstain from the robbery according to his will, and they are obedient to his will.

However, as the <term>Master of the Sentences; the 12th-century theologian Peter Lombard, whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of medieval theology</term> says in the 19th distinction of the second book: if the first humans had not sinned, they would have come together in carnal union in paradise without any sin or stain. There, the touch would have been immaculate, and the union would have been without <term>concupiscence; intense desire or lust that defies rational control</term>, and they would have commanded their genital members just like the others, so that they would feel no illicit movement there. And just as we move other limbs of the body toward others without the heat of lust—such as a hand to the head—so they would have used the genital members without the itching of the flesh. For this lethal sickness clung to human limbs as a result of sin. They would have, therefore, fathered children in paradise through immaculate intercourse without corruption.

Hence **Augustine** says in his work *On Genesis*: "Why should we not believe," he says, "that the first humans before sin were able to command their genital members for procreation, just as they use others in any work without the itch of pleasure? For it is not incredible that God made those bodies such that, if they did not sin, they would command those members just like their feet. They would not sow with heat, nor would they give birth with pain. But after sin, they earned that movement which marriage ordains and continence restrains." And the weakness prone to the ruin of shame is received by the honesty of marriage, so that what would have been a duty for the healthy is a remedy for the sick.

From this reasoning, therefore, it is concluded that the **untouched Virgin** was conceived without original sin. For although it is not naturally possible for anyone to be propagated without sin—since the matter is prone to sin due to Adam's infection—nevertheless, the glorious Virgin attained this not by nature, but by grace, so that she might be propagated without sin. Since it was more reasonable and fitting that God should have cleansed the matter from which his mother was to be made, while it was the matter of the maker and before it became the matter of the recipient. For this reason, God took away all bodily lust and unrestrained pleasure from **Saint Joachim** and **Saint Anne**, so that they might generate the immaculate Virgin herself in the same way the first parents would have fathered their children in paradise if they had not sinned.

<margin>Response to the argument of Hogostratus.</margin>
From these points, the solution to the objection of <term>Hogostratus; Jacob van Hoogstraaten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican inquisitor and theologian who often debated the author</term> is clear. Regarding the saying of the blessed Augustine that he brings forward, we say it is indeed true insofar as all humans generated through the sexual intercourse of a man and a woman with bodily lust and pleasure are not free from original sin. But we say our statement is truer still, insofar as the glorious Virgin herself was propagated without unrestrained lust and bodily pleasure. We affirm that this proceeded from divine grace and will, since she was to be His tabernacle, from whose most precious blood the body of Christ, God and man, was to be formed. Therefore, it was necessary that she be the most perfect and purest of all creatures. Augustine himself supports this opinion with his own words; for example, in his book *On Heresies against the Manichaeans*, speaking in the person of Christ, he says: "If my mother could have been defiled when I made her, I could have been defiled when I was born from her." <note>original: "Si potuit inquinari mater mea, cum eam facerem, potui inquinari ego, cum ex ea naſcerer."</note> And in the book *On Nature and Grace*, he says: "Except for the Virgin Mary, concerning whom—for the honor of my Lord—I wish to raise no question at all when sin is discussed." <note>original: "Excepta uirgine Maria, de qua propter honorem Domini mei, cum de peccatis agitur, nullā prorſus uolo facere quæſtionē."</note> In many other places as well, he proclaims her to be immaculate, most pure, and immune from all sin.

### *To the sixth objection of Hogostratus. And that by the merit of the passion of Christ to be shown, the glorious Virgin was redeemed from original sin in a most noble way. Chapter IX.*

## HOGOSTRATUS,

The glorious Virgin was redeemed through the passion of Christ. Otherwise, she herself would have been deprived of so great a good, and Christ would not have stood as the universal redeemer, which is highly unfitting. Therefore, He was also the redeemer and savior of the Virgin herself. She herself confesses this in her song <note>The Magnificat, from the Gospel of Luke 1:46–55.</note>, saying, "And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior." <note>original: "Et exultauit ſpiritus meus in Deo ſalutari meo."</note> However, redemption or salvation presupposes guilt. For one cannot be understood as redeemed and saved except from some fault. Since, therefore, she never had any actual fault, it follows clearly that she must have been redeemed from original sin. For this reason, it follows that she was conceived in original sin.

GALATINUS: Your reasoning is void. For he is equally a redeemer and savior who guards a person so that they do not become a captive, just as he who frees them from <margin>What medicine is.</margin> captivity. In the same way, one is called a doctor who gives a person a rule and order so that they may preserve their health and not fall into sickness, just as much as one who heals the sick. For this reason, <term>Avicenna; Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text in Europe</term> defined medicine as the science by which the dispositions of the human body are known, both from the aspect in which it is healed (or infirmity is removed from it) and the aspect in which health, once possessed, is preserved, and if lost, is recovered. By this same reasoning, we say that he should be called a redeemer and savior who prevents someone from falling into <margin>Twofold redemption.</margin> sin, just as much as he who lifts a person up from sin. From these points, we can say that there is a twofold redemption: "lifting-up" and "preservative."

<meta>catchword: Preserv-</meta>

<summary>This page argues for the Immaculate Conception of Mary, positing that Christ acted as her "preservative redeemer" by preventing her from ever contracting original sin, rather than "lifting" her out of it after the fact.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the Virgin Mary’s exemption from Original Sin. ### SEVENTH [BOOK]

And preservative redemption is far nobler and more perfect than reparative redemption <note>The author uses "sublevativa," literally "lifting up," to describe redemption that rescues someone after they have already fallen into sin.</note>. For just as it is much better to preserve someone from a wound than to apply a remedy after the wound has been received, so it is far nobler and more perfect to preserve someone from sin—so that they do not fall into it—than to free them from sin after they have fallen. Therefore, one who is preserved immune from future sin is redeemed in a nobler and more perfect way, and receives a greater benefit, than one who is snatched away from a sin already committed.

Consequently, preservative redemption is much more excellent and perfect than reparative redemption. All other human beings were redeemed from sin through reparative redemption. But the glorious Virgin alone, among those propagated from a man and a woman, was redeemed by preservative redemption. This is similar to how the good angels were redeemed from sin so that they would not fall with Lucifer, as **John Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was an influential Archbishop of Constantinople and Church Father known for his preaching.</note> excellently concludes. Regarding the immaculate Virgin herself, **Anselm** <note>Saint Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher.</note> says the following in the second book of *Why God Became Man* <note>original: "Cur Deus homo"</note>, chapter 10: "The blessed virgin," he says, "stood in need of redemption and the passion of Christ, not because of sin that was present in her, but because of sin that would have been present, had He not preserved her through a special privilege." <note>original: "Indiguit beata uirgo redemptione, & Chriſti paſſione, non propter peccatum quod inſuerit, ſed propter peccatum quod infuiſſet, niſi ipſemet ex ſpeciali priuilegio eam præſeruaſſet."</note> Furthermore, the very perfection of human redemption necessarily required this.

For there are six modes of redemption. <margin>Six modes of redemption.</margin> The **first** is when someone is redeemed from <term>actual mortal sin; a grave sin committed with full knowledge and consent</term> after they have fallen into it. In this way, sinners who have fallen into mortal sin are redeemed through the <term>Sacrament of Penance; the ritual of confession and absolution</term>. The **second** mode is when someone is preserved from that same mortal sin. In this way the Apostles were redeemed; after they received the Holy Spirit, they never committed a mortal sin. The **third** mode is when someone is redeemed from a <term>venial sin; a minor or "pardonable" sin that does not break one's relationship with God</term> already committed. This is the way the "just" are usually redeemed, who according to the common law of nature cannot entirely avoid venial sin. For as the wise man says, "The just man falls seven times a day, and rises again," which can only be understood as referring to venial sin. The **fourth** mode is when someone is preserved from venial sin itself. In this way **John the Baptist** was redeemed, who (as some believe) was entirely free from venial sin. Because of this, the Church sings of him: "That you might be able to cleanse our lives from even a slight stain of speech." <note>original: "Ne leui ſaltem maculare uitam, famine poſſes." This is a line from the famous hymn "Ut queant laxis" dedicated to St. John the Baptist.</note> The **fifth** mode is when someone is redeemed from <term>original sin; the state of sin inherited from Adam</term> after it has been contracted. In this way, baptized infants are redeemed through the Sacrament of Baptism. Finally, the **sixth** mode is when someone is preserved unharmed from original sin itself. And in this way, the most blessed Virgin alone, among those born of natural propagation, was redeemed. Therefore, unless she had been preserved entirely immune from original sin by the merit of her son's foreseen death, then neither would the human race have been perfectly redeemed, nor would Christ himself have stood as the perfect redeemer of the human race, since he would not have redeemed it in every possible way by which it could be redeemed.

### SEVENTH BOOK.

<margin>Why the Mother of the Messiah died.</margin>
The death and passion of Christ were necessary, since divine justice would not spare the human race without them. Therefore, Christ necessarily had to have a body capable of suffering and mortal. Likewise, since the unstained Virgin was to give birth to a son who was capable of suffering and mortal—who was to be one flesh with her—and since that which is capable of suffering and mortal cannot naturally proceed from that which is incapable of suffering and immortal, she also was necessarily mortal. For this reason, both the mother and the son died. Nevertheless, the blessed Virgin herself was freed from the evils and punishments occurring because of Adam’s sin, which were not necessary for Christ’s passion, since she was entirely immune from original sin. Such things include giving birth with pain—which was given to Eve as a curse—being defiled by menstruation, and being affected by the infirmities arising from sin, of all of which the glorious Virgin was entirely free.

<margin>The Mother of the Messiah, having died, soon rose in glory.</margin>
And because, just as the death and passion of Christ and the untouched Virgin was for the redemption of the human race, as has been said. Thus the resurrection of Christ, notwithstanding that it was necessary for the confirmation of the Catholic faith, had to be necessary, since He was entirely free from original sin. For the same reason, the immaculate Virgin herself rose as soon as she died, and was taken up into the empyrean heaven <note>In medieval cosmology, the Empyrean was the highest heaven, a place of pure light and the dwelling place of God.</note> together with her son, and exalted upon the throne of the heavenly Kingdom, and sitting at the right hand of her son, she reigns most gloriously in both soul and body. And therefore the Psalmist <note>The author of the Psalms, traditionally King David.</note> in Psalm 132, speaking of the resurrection of the son and the mother, says: קומה יהוה למנוחתך אתה וארון עוזך <note>original Hebrew: *Kuma Adonai limnuchatecha ata ve-aron uzecha*</note> That is, *Arise, O Lord, into thy rest: thou and the ark of thy strength.* <note>The "Ark" is here interpreted as a symbol for Mary, who carried the divine presence.</note> Concerning her sitting at the right hand of her son and the glory of her body, the same says in Psalm 45: נצבה שגל לימינך בכתם אופיר <note>original Hebrew: *nitzvah shegal l'iminecha be-kethem Ophir*</note> This is, *The Queen stood at thy right hand in a diadem,* or *golden clothing.* Where, by the golden garment, the heavenly glory and the most excellent glory of the body—which is the clothing of the soul—is expressed.

Hence Anselm <note>Saint Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), known for his ontological arguments and writings on Mary’s purity.</note> says: "It was fitting that the Virgin should shine with a purity than which none greater can be understood under God."
