### Chapter XI. That for the sake of the mother of the Messiah, Israel was called the peculiar people of God.

->CAPNIO,<-

From those things you have said, I believe that the Israelite people, because of the love which God had from eternity toward the mother of the Messiah, were called the peculiar people of God. GALATINUS. You judge most excellently indeed. For so great and so immense was God's love from eternity for the mother of the Messiah, that for her sake He made the Israelite people His own peculiar people, because she was to come forth from them. That Rabbi clearly suggested this, whose authority among the Hebrews is so great that they call him <gloss>Rabbenú Haccados <note>original: רבנו הקדוש</note>, that is, our holy Master</gloss> <note>This refers to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>. For he, in the book which is called <gloss>Gale razeya <note>original: גלי רזיא</note>, that is, Revealer of Secrets</gloss>, in response to the sixth petition of Antoninus the Consul, said this among other things: "As to why Israel was called the peculiar people of God, I will tell you what I found written by Rabbi Simeon son of Jochai in the book titled <gloss>Mechkar hassodoth <note>original: מחקר היסודות</note>, that is, Investigator of Secrets</gloss>, who said: Rabbi Isaiah began his discourse and said, 'Woe to you, Moab! You are lost, O people of Chemosh! He has given his sons into flight and his daughters into captivity' <note>A reference to Numbers 21:29 or Jeremiah 48:46, regarding the downfall of the enemies of Israel.</note>. Woe to them, woe to them, who were called the fathers of the whole world and of the human race, and furthermore the peculiar people of God." And after a few words: "Seeing," he says, "that from Israel was to be cut out a rock without hands, which is the primary rock, from which the Messiah is to be, who will extend his mercies over the whole world, for that reason He wished Israel to be called the father of the whole world and His peculiar people." These are his words. Moreover, Rabbi Nehunias son of Haccana, in <gloss>Beigereth hassodoth <note>original: באיגרת היסודות</note>, that is, the Epistle of Secrets</gloss>, explaining the aforementioned words, says: "This primary rock is the mother of the King Messiah." Therefore, for their declaration, I say that the ancient Doctor believed Israel was called the peculiar people of God for no other reason than because of a certain property hidden from us. This is because every agent acts upon another in one of three ways: either by quantity, or by quality,

<meta>This page continues Book III of Galatinus’s work. The previous page concluded a discussion on the immaculate nature of the Virgin Mary, citing the authority of "Rabbenú Haccados" (Rabbi Judah the Prince). This page applies natural philosophy to explain the divine election of Israel as the lineage for the Messiah’s mother.</meta>

quantity, or by a certain property inherent in itself. That which acts by quantity is, for example, food: if someone takes it beyond measure, they fall into stomach pain; but if they consume less than is required, they fall into <term>consumption <note>original: ethicam, referring to a wasting disease or "hectic" fever often associated with malnutrition in early medical theory</note></term>. That which acts by quality is like fire, which heats, and snow, which cools. One of these is hot by the quality of heat, the other cold by the quality of coldness. Now, heat and coldness are qualities. Finally, that which acts by a **hidden property** <note>In Renaissance science, an "occult" or hidden property was a power inherent in an object that could not be explained by the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry)</note> is like the magnet, which draws iron to itself; or the small stone that the common people call a **turquoise**, which, if someone wears it and falls from a high place, the stone itself is broken if the person's limbs were meant to be broken, yet the wearer remains unhurt. Or like the **amethyst**, which, while it is worn, prevents drunkenness. Or like other small stones and gems having various properties. If anyone asks why they perform such operations, the jewelers respond that these things proceed from their hidden property. They say that the reason for this matter is unknown to them. I, however, say that even if such properties are hidden from us, they are nevertheless known to God, who created the world out of nothing and instilled a specific power into every single thing. Therefore, He knows best why the magnet draws iron. and so it is with each individual thing.

Having established these premises, let us ask the Jews: By which of these operations did God choose the Israelite people, so that they might be His chosen and peculiar people above all nations and peoples? Was it by quantity, quality, or property? If they say by quantity—that is, because of their great number—it is entirely false, since it is written in Deuteronomy, chapter 7: <note>Deuteronomy 7:6-7</note> *The Lord your God has chosen you to be a peculiar people to Himself out of all the peoples who are upon the earth. Not because you surpassed all nations in number was the Lord joined to you and chose you, since you are the fewest of all.* If, however, they respond that it was by quality—that is, because of their holy works—this is likewise false, since it is also written in Deuteronomy, chapter 9: <note>Deuteronomy 9:5</note> *For not because of your righteousness and the uprightness of your heart shall you enter to possess their lands.* Therefore, they must concede that for no other reason did God choose the Israelite people, except because of a **hidden property** that was instilled in them, which was the immaculate mother of the Messiah who was to proceed from them. Just as that ancient Doctor of theirs asserted, whom we have said is called by them <term>Rabbenú Haccados <note>original: רבינו הקדוש</note></term>, that is, **Our Holy Master**.

Therefore, Rabbi Jonathan, son of Uzziel <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel was a famous student of Hillel the Elder, credited with an Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets.</note>, explains these words of Zechariah, *And he shall bring forth the primary stone*, in Aramaic as follows: *And from the very stone the Messiah shall go forth, and his name shall be forever.* <note>original Aramaic: ומפיק אבנא יפוק משיחא ושמיה יהי לעלמיא (*u-mafiq abna yafuq meshicha u-shmeih yehei le-almaya*)</note>. It must be noted, however, that this Zerubbabel is the one of whom Luke writes while weaving the genealogy of the same Virgin through the line of Nathan. He is not the one mentioned by Matthew, who describes Joseph's genealogy through the line of Solomon. For there were two men named Zerubbabel, and two named Shealtiel <note>Latin: *Sealthiéles*</note>, who were the fathers of those two Zerubbabels. This is most clearly evident from the fact that the Zerubbabel of whom Matthew writes was born two generations after the Babylonian exile <note>original: *transmigrationem Babylonis*</note>. For he says: *Josiah begat Jechoniah and his brothers at the time of the Babylonian exile. And Jechoniah begat Shealtiel. And Shealtiel begat Zerubbabel.* 

But the Zerubbabel mentioned by Zechariah and Luke lived before the Babylonian exile. This can be clearly seen from the words of the prophet Haggai, who says in the second chapter: *The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, Governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jozadak, the High Priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying: Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory?* From these words, it appears that this Zerubbabel had seen the House of God <note>the First Temple of Solomon</note> in its original construction, and consequently was born before the Babylonian exile itself. 

Furthermore, the prophecy of Zerubbabel himself occurred during the exile; indeed, he led the people out of that same exile, as is held in the second chapter of Ezra. From these points, it is clearly shown that the Zerubbabel of whom Zechariah and Luke wrote was one man, and the one mentioned by Matthew was another. For this reason, in the genealogy described by Matthew, only eleven generations are placed between Zerubbabel and Joseph. In the genealogy treated by Luke, however, many more are found between Joseph and Zerubbabel, due to the greater span of time that intervened. 

From all of this, it is plainly gathered that the glorious Virgin Mary, the mother of our Savior, existed from the tribe of Judah and the royal lineage of David, and proceeded through the direct line of Nathan, the son of David, which Luke describes so excellently. If anyone should object to what we have said because no mention is made of Saint Joachim, the Virgin's father, in that genealogical sequence: I say that Eli was that same Joachim, who is placed first in the ascending order. For among the Syrians <note>referring here to Aramaic speakers or the Eastern tradition</note>, "Joachim," "Eli," and "Eliakim" are the same name, as Philo the Jew writes. Hence, the father of the Messiah’s mother was called Eli and Joachim, just as Rabbi Haccados <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the compiler of the Mishnah</note> had previously predicted through the revelation of Elijah, as was shown in the premises. And later, Rabbi Haccanas <note>Nehunia ben ha-Kanah, a first-century rabbi</note>, the son of Rabbi Neumia, testified to this most excellently.

as the law commanded both to be raised up. Therefore, if Jacob (as they say) 
took the wife of his deceased brother Eli, he would have given Joseph the name 
not of Joseph, but of Eli, just as the deceased had been called.

I say, therefore, saving better judgment: 
Because spouses were made "one flesh" through true marriage, 
according to that passage in Genesis: *They shall be two in one flesh.* Therefore, the father of one 
spouse was rightly called the father of the other. This is also confirmed 
in the *Bereshith Rabba* <note>Genesis Rabbah, a collection of ancient Jewish interpretations of the book of Genesis.</note> regarding that which is said in Genesis chapter 37, <term>קומו כל בניו וכל בנותיו לנחמו</term> <note>Hebrew: *Kumu kol banav ve-kol benotav le-nachamo*</note>.

## That the mother of the Messiah was to be called Mary. Chapter 14.

For some of their ancients—wonderful to say—were not even ignorant of the very name by which the mother of the Messiah was to be called. Indeed, they predicted she was to be called Mary. That is, "To the multiplying of the empire," or "sovereignty," or "That the empire or sovereignty may be multiplied." These words signify that the Messiah is to be generated by God, who will multiply the empire, and who is the Lord of the entire world. And He shall be born of Mary the Lady. And this is what the text says: <term>למרבה המשרה</term> *lemarbe hamisra*, that is, "To the multiplying of the empire." From these words arises the name <term>מרים שרה</term> *Miriam sara*, that is, "Mary the Lady" <note>Galatinus is using a mystical method of letter manipulation to find Mary's name hidden in the Hebrew text of Isaiah.</note>, in this way: If you take the letters <term>ל</term> (L), <term>מ</term> (M), and <term>ר</term> (R), they form the first part of the word *lemarbe*, which is <term>למר</term> *lemar* [meaning "To the Lord"]. By adding the letter <term>ם</term> (M) from the word *hamisra*, behold, you have <term>מרים</term> *Miriam*, which is Mary. From the word <term>המשרה</term> *hamisra*, what remains is <term>שרה</term> *sara*, which means "Lady" or "Princess," and is written with three letters. Behold, from the phrase *lemarbe hamisra* (to the multiplying of the empire), you get <term>למרים שרה</term> *lemiriam Sara*, that is, "For Mary the Lady." This reveals to us that this Mary is the Lady and Sovereign of the universe, and the Queen of the Heavens. Antoninus said to him: "Why then is the letter <term>י</term> (Yod) divided in..."

two <term>he</term> ה. And why is the letter <term>beth</term> ב placed in the middle of the name <term>Miriam</term> מרים, that is, Mary? Furthermore, the fact that the *Beth* of this word *lemarbe* is placed in the middle of the name מרים (that is, Mary), shows that the mind and every thought of this prophetess is to preserve her virginity. For she will be a virgin in mind and in deed, because through the letter *Beth*, the word <term>bethula</term> בתולה, meaning "virgin," is signified. 

But the "closed" *Mem* of this word *lemarbe*, which carries the numerical value of 277 <note>In Hebrew numerology (gematria), the letters of *lemarbe* (למרבה) add up to 277: L(30) + M(40) + R(200) + B(2) + H(5).</note>, shows that from the hour the prophecy was spoken—"Behold, a virgin shall conceive"—until the birth of the Messiah, exactly 277 years would pass. All these things were said word-for-word by that Doctor of theirs, whom they call "Our Holy Master" <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince.</note>. From these things, the greatest secrets are gathered—secrets that agree with our holy faith, savor of sacred theology, and were unlocked long before Christ was born.

->SEVENTH [BOOK]. 525<-

you would show. **GALATINUS**: That a virgin was to be the mother of the Messiah is something Jewish impiety <note>Galatinus uses "impiety" here in the common 16th-century polemical sense, referring to the rejection of Christian interpretations of the Old Testament.</note> can by no means deny. For this is demonstrated everywhere and most clearly through the Law, the oracles of the prophets, and the testimonies of the ancient Talmudists. First, in **Leviticus chapter 12**, it is plainly stated: <note>original: אשה כי תזריע וילדה זכר וטמאה (*ishah ki tazria ve-yaledah zakhar ve-tame'ah*)</note> "If a woman has received seed and born a male child, she shall be unclean." Since, therefore, naturally no woman can give birth without seed, and yet the text specifies "A woman who has received seed and born a male child," it surely follows that at some time a certain woman was to bear a male child without having received male seed, and she would be clean from all stain. This woman was to be none other than the mother of the Messiah, of whom the prophets later spoke more openly. 

For **Isaiah** says of her in **chapter 7**: <note>original: ויסף יהוה דבר אל אחז לאמר : שאל לך אות מעם יהוה אלהיך... (*Vayosef Adonai daber el Achaz lemor: She'al lekha ot...*)</note> "And the Lord spoke again to Achaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign, or a miracle, from the Lord your God; make your request in the depths, or lift it up on high. And Achaz said: I will not ask, and I will not tempt (or I will not exalt) God. And he (Isaiah) said: Hear then, O house of David! Is it a small thing for you to weary (or trouble) men, that you will also weary my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign, or a miracle. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name <term>Emmanuel</term> <note>Meaning "God with us."</note>." 

Even though these words are so clear that they need no explanation, the Jews of this current time attempt to twist them away from the true sense in many ways. We shall refute their false claims in the following chapter when we respond to their objections. For now, let us hear **Jeremiah**, saying in **chapter 31**: <note>original: ברא יהוה חדשה בארץ נקבה תסובב גבר (*Bara Adonai chadashah ba-aretz, nekevah tesovev gaver*)</note> "The Lord has created a new thing on earth: a woman shall encompass a man (or a strong and powerful one, that is, God)." This is according to the glosses of the ancient Jews, and especially of him whom they call <term>Rabbenu Haccados</term> <note>original: רבינו הקדוש; literally "Our Holy Teacher," referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, in the book he titled <term>Gale Razeya</term> <note>original: גלי רזיא; "The Revealer of Secrets." This is a work Galatinus frequently cites as an ancient source of Christian truth hidden within Judaism.</note>, written at the request of the Roman Consul Antoninus. 

Now, that this "man" is the Messiah, and that he was to be encompassed in the womb through the conception of a virgin—for otherwise no "new thing" would have been created in the world—is clear from what is read in the commentary of **Rabbi Moses Hadarsan** <note>An 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) compilations.</note> on the passage in **Genesis chapter 41**: "And Pharaoh was dreaming." For flesh and blood wounds with a needle or a razor, and heals with a plaster. But the Holy and Blessed God does not possess such an art; rather, with the very same things he wounds, [he heals]..."

Thus far the tradition. From which our proposition is made clear enough. For the "gates" which the Messiah was to defeat were the <term>Limbo of the Fathers</term>, <note>A theological concept referring to the place where the souls of the righteous stayed before the Resurrection of Christ.</note> which, as we said in the preceding book, was called by the Hebrews the "Upper Hell" and the "Gate of Hell," among its other names.

For almost all of them desired to be deflowered, either through husbands or through others. Therefore, only Mary, the most blessed virgin—who alone among all others proposed that she would preserve her virginity forever—deserved to conceive the Messiah. 

This is especially noted in the fact that we read in **Luke, chapter 1**, how she answered the angel: <gloss>How shall this be, since I know not a man?</gloss> Being a Hebrew woman herself, she said "I know not" in place of "I shall not know," following the custom of the Hebrews, who often designate both the present and future tense with one and the same word. **Ezekiel** also very well suggested this virginity of the Messiah's mother when, in **chapter 44**, he brought forth these words: <gloss>And he brought me back the way of the gate of the outward sanctuary... and the Lord said to me: This gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened...</gloss> <note>original: "וישב אתי דרך שער המקדש ויאמר אלי יהוה השער הזה סגור יהיה לא יפתח והוא סגור"</note>

## *Refutation of the objections of more recent Jews who attack the virginity of the Messiah’s mother. Chapter XV.*

---

->CAPNIO,<-

**A**lthough these things are so, the Jews of our own time—desiring to attack the virginity of the Messiah’s mother—do not cease to contradict in many ways that miraculous sign of the virginal conception and birth given by Isaiah and introduced by you. They deem it impossible that a virgin could have conceived and been destined to bear a son. Therefore, they assert that these words of Isaiah, when he said, "The *Alma* <note>original: "Alma concipiet." This refers to Isaiah 7:14. This is despite the fact that their own ancient scholars explained it so, and the Catholic faith affirms that those same words were spoken concerning the glorious Virgin Mary. On this point, they are accustomed to raise several arguments against us. I desire you to respond to them using their own scriptures, so that their "barking" <note>The author uses "latratus" (barking), a common but harsh polemical term of the era for opposing arguments.</note> against the mother of the Messiah may be silenced. First, they argue as follows:

<margin>The first Jewish argument.</margin>
"This sign," they say, "which the prophet gave was a sign of the future liberation of King Ahaz from the two kings who had come against him. <margin>The Solution.</margin>
GALATINUS: It will be easy for us to answer this argument if we first briefly note the history to ensure a true prophetic understanding. At the time when Ahaz was reigning in Judea, two powerful kings—namely those of Syria and Israel—besieged Jerusalem with a massive army, as is written in Isaiah, chapter 7, and the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter 16. <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 16. The Latin Vulgate traditionally titled 1–2 Samuel and 1–2 Kings as 1–4 Kings.</note> Then the Lord God sent Isaiah to Ahaz to warn him not to fear the army of those kings. But Ahaz, being wicked and unbelieving (for he was a worshiper of idols), would not believe the prophet's words. For this reason, the prophet warned him that since he did not believe, he should ask for some sign of his liberation to be performed, saying: "Ask for a sign—or a miracle—from the Lord your God. Make the request deep, or exalt it on high." That is to say: "Ask for a sign of your liberation to occur, whether from the depths of hell through the resurrection of someone dead, or from heaven by the sun standing still, as happened in the time of Joshua." ...since he was impious, refusing to ask for a sign from God, he offered an excuse: that to do so would be to tempt God. For the word נסא <note>original: *anasse* (likely *a-nasseh* from the root *nasah*), meaning to test or tempt, though the author notes a linguistic connection to *nasa*, to lift or exalt</note> which is placed there, signifies both "to tempt" and "to exalt." We must therefore deny what is claimed in the argument—namely, that this sign was given to Ahaz himself. 

As for the second objection—that because Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz, his conception from a virgin could not have been a sign of the predicted liberation from those two

<margin>A sign is twofold: prognostic and rememorative.</margin>
kings—we say that a twofold type of sign is found in Holy Scripture. One is **prognostic**, the other **rememorative**. A **prognostic sign** <term>prognosticum: a sign that predicts or points forward to a future event</term> is indeed one regarding a future event. Such was the sign given to Gideon in the fleece (as told in Judges, chapter 6) indicating a future victory. A **rememorative sign** <term>rememoratiuum: a sign that looks backward to confirm or commemorate a past promise</term> is one regarding a past event. Such was the sign that the Lord gave to Moses in Exodus, chapter 3, saying: וזה לך האות כי אנכי שלחתיך בהוציאך את העם ממצרים תעבדון את האלהים על ההר הזה <note>original Hebrew: "And this shall be a sign unto thee, that I have sent thee: When thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain."</note> This means: "And this shall be a sign for you, that I have sent you. When you have led my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice upon this mountain, giving thanks to me for this mission which is imposed upon you." 

Therefore, the sign of the virgin's conception and birth was **rememorative**, not **prognostic**. Nor does the great distance of time stand in the way, since a rememorative sign looks back to the past across a great distance, just as a prognostic sign looks toward the future. It was certainly fitting for this sign to be given at a great distance, so that Ahaz—who was incredulous toward the word of the prophet—might have a sign as far removed from himself as he was far from believing in his own mind. Yet those who were to descend from him were destined to see it at last. For this reason, the sign was given not to him, but to the House of David.

<margin>The second argument of the Jews.</margin>

Therefore, they say the prophet was not speaking of a virginal conception and birth, but that of a young woman. For if he had been speaking of a virgin’s conception, he would not have said, "Behold, an *alma*" (that is, a young woman), but "Behold, a בתולה *bethula*," which is the specific word for **virgin**.

**GALATINUS.** There are three words among the Hebrews (as you know) that signify nearly the same thing: namely, נערה *Naara*, בתולה *Bethula*, and עלמה *Alma*. For *Naara* only has regard for the girl’s age...

<meta>This page continues the philological defense of the term "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14. While the previous page discussed the nature of the "sign" given to the House of David, Galatinus now shifts to a detailed linguistic analysis of three Hebrew terms—*na’arah*, *bethulah*, and *almah*—to prove that the prophet specifically intended to describe a miraculous virgin birth.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

...signifies a girl or a young woman, whether she is a virgin or has been corrupted. 
<term>Bethula</term> <note>Hebrew: *betulah* (בתולה)</note>, however, having respect only to virginity, signifies a virgin, whether she be a young girl or an old woman. But <term>Alma</term> <note>Hebrew: *almah* (עלמה)</note>, having respect to both—namely, to youth and to virginity—designates both a young woman and a virgin. For this reason, a woman, whether she is a young girl or advanced in years, may be called a *bethula* as long as she is a virgin. Likewise, as long as she is a young girl, she is called a <term>naara</term> <note>Hebrew: *na’arah* (נערה)</note>, whether she is a virgin or has been corrupted. However, no woman can be called an *alma* unless she is both a young woman and an untouched virgin. 

This is clearly indicated by the interpretation of the word itself. For the word **alma** is derived from the verb **alam** <note>Hebrew: *‘alam* (עלם)</note>, which signifies "to hide" or "to conceal," as <term>Rabbi Kimhi</term> <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a preeminent medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note> says in his *Book of Roots* <note>original: *Sefer Shorashim*</note>. This is seen in Psalm 90, where it is said: "You have set our iniquities before you, our hidden sins <note>original Hebrew: *almenu* (עלמנו), from the same root</note> in the light of your countenance." And again in Psalm 44: "He knows the secrets <note>original Hebrew: *ta’alumot* (תעלמות)</note> of the heart." And in Job, chapter 28: "And what is hidden <note>original Hebrew: *ta’alumah* (ותעלמה)</note> he brings forth to light." Likewise in Genesis, chapter 24: "The young woman <note>original Hebrew: *ha-almah* (העלמה)</note> coming out to draw water." All of these, says Rabbi Kimhi, signify hiding and concealment. 

For this reason, among the Hebrews, *alma* signifies a young woman hidden from the gazes of men, concealed, secret, and entirely untouched, about whose modesty and integrity there is no doubt—especially when it is preceded by the article, which in Hebrew is the letter **he** <note>the Hebrew letter 'H' (ה), acting as the definite article "the"</note>. This letter makes the word specific and is often added to things that are either well-known or have been mentioned previously. In the entirety of Holy Scripture, this word **haalma** <note>the virgin</note>, written with the letter *he* or the article, is found in only three places. 

The first is in Genesis, chapter 24, when it is said of Rebecca: "Behold, I stand by the spring of water; and it shall be that the *almah* <note>the virgin</note> who comes out to draw water, and to whom I shall say: Give me, I pray, a little water to drink from your jar." While she was called an *alma*, she was a virgin and untouched, as is clear from the text, which says of her in the same place: "A virgin <note>original: *bethula*</note>, and no man had known her." 

Next, it is found in Exodus, chapter 2, when it is written of Miriam, the sister of Moses: "And the *almah* <note>the virgin</note> went and called the child’s mother." And she too was a young virgin at that time. 

Finally, the third instance is found in Isaiah, in this very passage, as was shown a little earlier. Excepting these three places, nowhere else in the entire Hebrew Sacred Page is this word *haalma* found written with the article. If, therefore, the first two women so named were untouched virgins when they were so called, the same must be held regarding this woman of whom Isaiah speaks. For according to the judgment of the wise, entirely similar cases must receive an entirely identical judgment. On account of this, when the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> came to this passage, they translated *haalma* as "the virgin" with the article prefixed, saying: "Behold, the virgin" <note>original Greek: *idou hē parthenos* (ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος)</note>, and so forth. That it ought to be understood in this way,

<meta>This page continues the linguistic and theological debate from page 531 regarding the specific Hebrew terms used to describe the mother of the Messiah. Galatinus is arguing that the term "almah" used by Isaiah is more precise than "bethulah" because it implies total, miraculous purity.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

...ought to be, is also clear from the fact that the sign given by <term>Isaiah</term> <note>the prophet Isaiah, specifically referencing the prophecy in Isaiah 7:14</note> for the liberation of the city—as <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> says—had to be exceedingly miraculous. But for a young girl to conceive and bear a son, without her virginity remaining, is no miracle at all, since it happens that this occurs naturally every day. Therefore, it must necessarily be said that the sign which the prophet gave them—namely, that a virgin would conceive and bear a son—would be beyond the custom of nature, and would come to pass by the miracle of God alone. Because we are responding to the objection of the Jews: the woman who was to conceive and bear the Son of God had to be both a girl (or young woman) and an entirely untouched virgin. For this reason, in order to imply both, Isaiah said, "Behold, the **almah**" <note>Hebrew: *ha-almah* (העלמה)</note>, which (as has been said) signifies both. He did not say, "Behold, the **bethula**," which designates only one of those things. Furthermore, if he had said "Behold, the **bethula**" <note>Hebrew: *bethulah* (בתולה)</note>, he would not have prefigured the absolute virginity of the mother of the Messiah. For even if **bethula** signifies a virgin, it does not necessarily mean one who is entirely untouched. 

<term>Solomon</term> <note>Rashi</note> clearly shows this when commenting on that passage in Genesis, chapter 24, where it says: "She was a **bethula** (that is, a virgin), and no man had known her." He wished to provide the reason for this phrasing: If the text says she was a **bethula**, why does it add, "and no man had known her"? He says it thus: <note>original Hebrew: בתולה במקום בתולים ואיש לא ידעה למה שלא ברכה לפי שבנות הגוים משמרות עצמן ממקום בתולים ומפסידות עצמן ממקום אחר על כן העיד על זו הפעם שהיתה נקייה מכל</note> "She was a virgin in the place of virginity [the hymen], and no man had known her; that is to say, by an unnatural way. For the daughters of the nations [the heathens] guarded their bodies in the place of virginity, but prostituted themselves in another place <note>a reference to non-vaginal intercourse</note>. Therefore, the text testifies in this instance that she [Rebekah] was clean in every respect." It is clear from this that she was pure in total—that is, entirely unknown and untouched. From these things it is manifest that a **bethula** is not necessarily entirely untouched and unknown, since she could be corrupted against nature and yet be "known" by men. **Alma**, however, signifies one who is entirely untouched, and utterly unknown in both ways. 

<margin>
The third argument of the Jews.
</margin>
To these things the Jews say: If "the **almah**" (*ha-almah*), with the definite article, requires (as you have said) a preceding mention of the person, and if no mention of this virgin—whom you Christians assert would conceive and bear while preserving her virginity—precedes in Isaiah himself or in any other prophet, then it clearly follows that the virgin of whom you speak is not the one Isaiah mentions when he says, "Behold, the **almah** shall conceive and bear a son." By these words, therefore, you have not been able to prove the virginity of the mother of the Messiah.

<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>
GALATINUS: On the contrary, Solomon made mention of that virgin under the name **almah** long before Isaiah, saying in the thirtieth chapter of Proverbs: <note>original Hebrew: שלשה המה נפלאו ממני וארבעה לא ידעתים : דרך הנשר בשמים דרך נחש על-צור דרך אניה בלב-ים ודרך גבר בעלמה</note> "Three things are separated, or distant from me, or are wonders to me, and a fourth I have least of all known: The way of an eagle in the heavens, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship in the heart (or the middle) of the sea, and the way of a man in an **alma**—that is, in a virgin." With these words, Solomon most excellently describes the ways of the Messiah. For beginning from the most recent...

### BOOK SEVEN

->SEVENTH<-

...his final way, that is, from the ascension into heaven, he finally reaches the first, which is his incarnation, which was to come from the Virgin. We should not seek another expositor for these ways than the one whom they call **Rabbenu Haccados** <note>Hebrew: *Rabbeinu HaKadosh*, meaning "Our Holy Master," the title usually given to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note>, that is, our holy Master. For in the book inscribed **Gale razeya** <note>Hebrew: *Galei Razia*, meaning "The Revealer of Secrets." This is a work Galatinus frequently cites as an ancient Rabbinic source, though it is often associated with medieval mystical traditions</note>, in response to the petition of Antoninus, Consul of the city of Rome, who was asking for an explanation of these same words, he says: 

"You have asked a great thing. But because it is said in Proverbs, chapter 11: 'He who withholds grain, the people shall curse him' <note>Hebrew: *mone’a bar yiqbuhu le’om* (מונע בר יקבוהו לאום)</note>, which means he who hides grain—that is, the doctrine or the exposition of the Law—shall be cursed among the peoples. I will tell you a very sublime thing:

The way of an eagle in the heavens is the King Messiah, who after his passion will ascend into heaven. Just as it is said in the ninth chapter of Amos: 'He who builds his ascension in heaven' <note>Hebrew: *ha-boneh ba-shamayim ma'alotav* (הבונה בשמים מעלותיו). Traditionally translated as "He who builds his layers/stories in the heavens"</note>. 

The way of a ship in the middle of the sea: this likewise is the King Messiah, whose life will be tossed like a ship in the middle of the sea. Just as it is said in the thirtieth chapter of Jeremiah: 'Why have I seen every man with his hands on his loins?' <note>Hebrew: *madua ra’iti kol gever yadav al halatzaiv* (מדוע ראיתי כל גבר ידיו על חלציו)</note>. 'Of every man' <note>Hebrew: *gever* (גבר)</note>, that is, of God, who in Hebrew is called **gever**, which means strong or powerful. Since God himself is the strength or power of all. 

And the way of a serpent upon a rock: This is also the King Messiah, who will make himself like the serpent that Moses placed upon a rock <note>A reference to the Bronze Serpent in the wilderness</note>, to lead the children of Israel into the holy land. But Rabbi Iodam said: 'And the way of a serpent upon a rock: This is the King Messiah, who will pass through the rock after he has been buried, and will emerge from it, and it will not be seen where he passed through.' Just as it is said in the thirty-third chapter of Exodus: 'Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand upon the rock. And when my glory passes by, I will set you in a cleft of the rock' <note>Hebrew: *hinneh maqom itti ve-nitzavta al ha-tzur...* (הנה מקום אתי ונצבת על הצור...)</note>. 

And the way of a **gever** (that is, of a man, or one who is strong or powerful) in an **alma** (a young woman or virgin): This too is God loving the daughters of Jerusalem, so that the King Messiah may be generated from one of them. For she shall conceive and give birth, and she shall remain a virgin. Just as it is said in the thirty-first chapter of Jeremiah: 'Because God has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a **gever**' <note>Jeremiah 31:22</note>, that is, a man, strong or powerful—namely, God."

All these things are the literal words of **Rabbenu Haccados**, whom they call our holy Master. Therefore, the way of the **gever**—that is, the strong or powerful man, who is God—in an **alma**—that is, into a virgin—was the incarnation of the Son of God from a virgin. And indeed, Solomon could not fully and perfectly know this way. For in what manner a virgin could conceive without human seed, and enclose the perfect God and man in her womb, and give birth to a son and remain a virgin—neither could Solomon’s intellect fully grasp this, nor could any tongue ever explain it. For which reason he rightly said: "And the fourth I have not known at all." 

Deservedly, therefore, Isaiah says of the mother of the Messiah: "Behold, the virgin (***ha-almah***) shall conceive" <note>Hebrew: *hinne ha-almah hara* (הנה העלמה הרה)</note>; with the letter *he*...

### BOOK SEVEN

<margin>The objection of the younger Jews.</margin>
...that is, with the definite article prefixed, as if speaking of a well-known woman mentioned among the prophets, and of whom Solomon had already made mention. The perversity of the Jews of our age, acting against what has been said concerning the **almah** <note>original: *alma*; the Hebrew term meaning a young woman of marriageable age, which Christians interpreted as "virgin"</note>, still shouting out with mocking and blasphemy, says: "Follow the text you yourselves have introduced! Read further what follows in Proverbs, chapter 30. For you will find it written there immediately: *So is the way of an adulterous woman; she eats, and wipes her mouth, and says: 'I have done no wrong.'*" <note>Hebrew: *ken derekh ishah menafet akhelah u-mahatah piha ve-amerah lo pa’alti aven* (כן דרך אשה מנאפת אכלה ומחתה פיה ואמרה לא פעלתי און)</note>. "Behold," they say, "the **almah** in this place cannot be anything but a corrupted woman, because she is compared to an adulterous woman."

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
To restrain their audacity, it is answered that Solomon’s words in this book are called **Misle** <note>Hebrew: *Mishlei* (משלי), meaning "Proverbs"</note>—that is, proverbs or parables—because they almost always present one thing on the surface but intend another. Otherwise, it would not be a **Massal** <note>Hebrew: *Mashal* (משל)</note>, which means a parable, a likeness, or an example, if it were understood entirely as it sounds. Therefore, we should not take the "way of the adulterous woman" here literally, but as the life and most wicked manner of acting of someone else who imitates the deed of an adulterous woman. 

For this reason, certain ancient Jews understood "the way of an adulterous woman" in this passage to mean the transgression of our first parent <note>Adam</note>. Whence that same man whom we have said is called by them **Rabbenu Haccados** <note>Hebrew: *Rabbeinu HaKadosh* (רבינו הקדוש), "Our Holy Master," Rabbi Judah the Prince</note>, explaining this passage in that same place, says: "*So is the way of an adulterous woman.* Along with the rest, Adam did all this, for he excused himself for his sin and refused to confess it, but said: 'The woman whom you gave to be my companion, she gave to me from the tree, and I ate.' He acted like a harlot who eats and cleans her mouth, contending that she has done nothing wrong. For this reason, it is consistent with reason that the whole world should be punished. And when the time of salvation comes, it is just that God should descend to the underworld and save them." 

And this is what was said in the second chapter of Jeremiah: "Behold, I will enter into judgment with you because you say, 'I have not sinned.'" <note>Hebrew: *hineni nishpat otakh al amrekh lo hatati* (הנני נשפט אותך על אמרך לא חטאתי). Note: Galatinus emphasizes the "judgment" as a dialogue or legal contest</note>. Likewise, in the sixty-sixth chapter of Isaiah: "For by fire shall the Lord be judged." <note>Hebrew: *ki va-esh Adonai nishpat* (כי באש יהוה נשפט). While usually translated as "the Lord will execute judgment," Galatinus uses the passive Latin *iudicabitur* (will be judged) to support a mystical interpretation of God submitting to human conditions</note>. Thus he spoke. 

<margin>The Jews are compared to an adulterous woman.</margin>
However, we can say that by the way of this adulterous woman, the faithlessness of the Jews is also not inaptly designated. To whom it is said by the Lord through Isaiah in the fifty-seventh chapter: "But you, come here, you sons of a sorceress, offspring of an adulterer and a prostitute." <note>Hebrew: *attem qirvu hinnah benei onenah zera menaf ve-tizneh* (אתם קרבו הנה בני עוננה זרע מנאף ותזנה)</note>. Of whom it is also written in the sixteenth chapter of Ezekiel: "Thus says the Lord God to Jerusalem..." and further down: "I was not like a harlot who mocks a gift, but like an adulterous wife who takes strangers in place of her husband." <note>Hebrew: *lo hayiti ke-zonah le-qalles etnan ha-ishah ha-menafet tahat ishah tiqqah et zarim* (לא הייתי כזונה לקלס אתנן האשה המנאפת תחת אישה תקח את זרים)</note>. And after some words in the same place: "And I will judge you with the judgments of adulterous women and those who shed blood, and I will give you the blood of fury and jealousy." <note>Hebrew: *u-shefat-tikh mishpetei no’afot u-shofekhot dam u-netattikh dam hemah ve-qinah* (ושפטתיך משפטי נאפות ושפכות דם ונתתיך דם חמה וקנאה)</note>. And I will judge you in...

### SEVENTH [BOOK]

...by the judgments of adulteresses and those who shed blood, and I will give you over to the blood of fury and jealousy. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the adulterous woman in the aforementioned parable of Solomon is the Jewish synagogue, which eats, and does not cease to eat, that bread most savory to itself, concerning which it is written in Proverbs chapter 20: *Bread of lies is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.* <note>Hebrew: *Arev le-ish lechem shaker ve-achar yimalle fihu chatzatz* (ערב לאיש לחם שקר ואחר ימלא פיהו חצץ)</note>. "Gravel" in this place is nothing other than the eternal punishment of hell. For since gravel is hard, it cannot be chewed, nor consumed, nor swallowed, nor spat out when the whole mouth is full. Thus the punishment of hell <margin>A lie is delightful to the Jews.</margin> is indeed most hard and durable; it can in no way be escaped, nor finished, nor diminished, nor softened by any moisture of tears. Moreover, that the bread of lies is sweet and savory to the Jews is shown most strongly by what is said of them in Jeremiah chapter nine: *And they do not speak the truth; they have taught their tongue to speak lies.* <note>Hebrew: *Ve-emet lo yedabberu limmedu leshonam dabber shaker* (ואמת לא ידברו למדו לשונם דבר שקר)</note>. Likewise, in the fifth chapter of the same: *And though they say, "As the Lord lives," nevertheless they will swear to a lie,* or to falsehood, or to fraud. <note>Hebrew: *Ve-im chai YHVH yomeru lachen lashaker yishave'u* (ואם חי יהוה יאמרו לכן לשקר ישבעו)</note>. Therefore, just as the way of an eagle in the sky, and the way of a serpent upon a rock, and the way of a ship in the heart or middle of the sea, and the way of a man (or a powerful one, that is, of God) into a young woman <note>original: *alma*; referring back to the previous page's discussion on the "virgin" birth</note> were made wonderful and difficult to Solomon, and far distant from his understanding; so too the way of this most wicked adulteress was to him extremely wonderful and very distant from his reason. For how could Solomon’s reason have grasped or contained the immensity of malice, the depth of impiety, and the magnitude of perfidy by which this "adulterous woman" <note>the Synagogue</note> was to condemn to death the just and entirely innocent Messiah, and ask for Barabbas, the seditious murderer, to be released? Or how could the intellect of the same wise man have sufficed to comprehend by what folly, by what insanity, by what lack of mind, or by what diabolical envy stimulated—or by what evil spirit driven—she could reject the true Messiah, who by His word alone gave light to the blind, directed the lame, cured the weak, cleansed the lepers, restored speech to the mute and hearing to the deaf, liberated the demon-possessed, and satisfied many thousands of men with a few loaves? And how could she receive two false messiahs, who had never done any such thing, one after the other as the true Messiah? Namely, **Bencozbam** <note>Simon ben Koziba, known as Bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish revolt against Rome (132–136 AD)</note> before the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and **Barcozbam** at **Bitter** <note>Beitar, the final fortress of the Bar Kokhba revolt</note> not long after the burning of the city. These two, at the very least by their names alone, she ought to have held in horror and suspicion, since both are interpreted as "son of a lie" or "son of falsehood." Rightly, therefore, did Solomon himself, marveling at the height of the four aforementioned ways—that is, the mysteries of the Messiah—and the ingratitude, impiety, and perfidy of this adulterous woman, subjoin these words: *So is the way of an adulterous woman...*

### *That the mother of the Messiah was to conceive the Son of God through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.*
## Chapter XVI.

->CAPNIO,<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap 'H' featuring a landscape scene with foliage and classical ruins or architecture.</image-desc>
Here I would like to know, not without reason, whether the ancient Jews, just as they predicted that the mother of the Messiah would conceive and bear a child as a virgin, also foretold that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit. GALATINUS. That indeed was foretold by the prophets long ago, and expressly explained by the ancient Jewish Doctors. For concerning the prophets, Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Holy Spirit, says in the 8th chapter: <margin>*False interpretation of the Jews.*</margin> *And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.* <note>Hebrew: *Va-ekrav el ha-nevi'ah va-tahar va-teled ben* (ואקרב אל הנביאה ותהר ותלד בן)</note>. CAPNIO. The <term>younger Jews</term> <note>Referring to contemporary medieval Jewish commentators who disagreed with Christian interpretations.</note> explain these words as Isaiah's own approach to his wife for sexual intercourse. Because (as they say) conceiving from him, she bore the prophet's own son. GALATINUS. <margin>*Refutation.*</margin> We shall show from the prophet's own words that they explain those words falsely, and pervert them against the prophet's intention. For neither the immediately preceding words, nor those soon following, support their interpretation; rather, they clearly contradict it. For thus the prophet said before: *And I took for myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest, and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah.* <note>Hebrew: *Ve-a'idah li edim ne'emanim et Uriyah ha-kohen ve-et Zekharyahu ben Yeverekhyahu* (ואעידה לי עדים נאמנים את אוריה הכהן ואת זכריהו בן יברכיהו)</note>. And having set these things before, he immediately brought forth these words: *And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.* And afterward he immediately added: *And the Lord said to me, "Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz."* <note>Hebrew: *Va-yomer YHVH elai kera shemo Maher-shalal-hash-baz* (ויאמר יהוה אלי קרא שמו מהר שלל חש בז)</note>. This means: *Speedily spoil, quickly plunder.* Or: *Call his name, Ready, the spoiler, the hasty, the plunderer.* These things, however...

This is how Jonathan translated it into Chaldean <note>Original: *ואמר יהוה לי קרי שמה איהי למבז ביזה ולמעדי עדא*—Galatinus refers to the Aramaic language of the Targum as "Chaldean."</note>: That is, *And God said to me, Call his name: Swift to plunder the spoils, and quick to take the prey.* These things in no way fit the son of Isaiah. He was to be swift in plundering hell, and quick in taking the prey—that is, in taking away from the devil the prey which he possessed because of the sin of the first man. Our Messiah testified that this was to be fulfilled in himself when he said in Luke chapter 11: *When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his possessions are safe. But when someone stronger attacks and overpowers him, he takes away the armor in which the man trusted and distributes his plunder.* Now, regarding the preceding points, let us ask two questions of the Jews.

<margin>The first question to be asked of the Jews.</margin>
First, for what purpose did the prophet bring in those witnesses? Did he have need of witnesses when approaching his wife for sexual union? 

<margin>The second question.</margin>
For this is a shameful thing even to think, let alone to speak of. Furthermore, who were these witnesses? Namely, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberechiah. It is certain that this Uriah was not that worshiper of idols, as some of our people think, to whom Ahaz wrote letters from Damascus (as read in 2 Kings, chapter 16). Rather, it was the one mentioned by Jeremiah in chapter 26, saying: *There was a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah son of Shemaiah, whom King Jehoiakim killed.* It is also certain that this Zechariah, son of Jeberechiah <note>The Latin says "Barachiae," which is the father of the Zechariah in the Book of the Twelve Prophets, though Isaiah 8:2 names Zechariah son of Jeberechiah.</note>, was the one who is the eleventh among the number of the twelve prophets. Indeed, according to the explanations of the Hebrews, Isaiah is speaking of these men. Yet it happened that these men were born long after Isaiah. From this it is clear that Isaiah uttered those words not in his own person, but in the person of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, before the Holy Spirit approached the <term>prophetess</term> <note>Isaiah 8:3 mentions "the prophetess," which Galatinus interprets here as the Virgin Mary.</note>—that is, that Virgin who was to conceive and give birth to the Savior—so that by His power and cooperation, without the seed of man, she might conceive and bear the Son of God, He ought to have employed these prophets as witnesses for Himself of the future truth. For one of them, namely Uriah son of Shemaiah, predicted many evils that were to come against the Jews and their city, which later befell them in the Babylonian captivity. The other, however—that is, Zechariah son of Jeberechiah—prophesied many and very great goods that would come to them at the arrival of the Messiah. And especially when he said in chapter 2: <note>Original: *רני ושמחי בת ציון כי הנני בא ושכנתי בתוכך נאם יהוה*</note> That is, *Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion. For behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst, says God.* And again in the ninth chapter: <note>Original: *גילי מאד בת ציון הריעי בת ירושלם הנה מלכך יבוא לך צדיק ונושע היא*</note> That is, *Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your King will come to you, the Just One and the Savior himself.* That this is so, as we have explained, is seen most clearly through the <term>Targum</term> <note>An Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Rabbi Jonathan—that is, through the Chaldean translation—which in that place has it thus: *And I took unto me faithful witnesses...*

<margin>Explanation of the aforementioned words of Isaiah.</margin>

She <note>Likely referring to the Synagogue or the Jewish people in this polemical context</note> has eaten the bread of so many lies, and even now never ceases to eat it so greedily. And as if wiping her mouth as if she had done no evil, she does not know how to blush. And this is what is said to her in Jeremiah chapter 3: <note>original: "ומצח אשה זונה היה לך מאנת הכלם"</note> That is, *You have the forehead of a harlot; you refuse to blush.* Since things are thus, notwithstanding the barking oppositions of those who cry out against the virginity of the mother of the Messiah, the aforementioned words of Isaiah are to be explained in this way: *Behold this alma* <term>alma: the Hebrew word 'almah,' which the author argues refers specifically to a "hidden" or "pure" virgin</term>, that is the holy and hidden virgin herself, of whom Solomon made mention long before, shall conceive by divine power and shall bear a son. And the virgin herself, forewarned and instructed by the angel Gabriel and filled with the Holy Spirit, shall call his name Emmanuel, which is the same as "God with us," through which the divine and human natures in the one person of the Messiah are clearly demonstrated. As for the other arguments of the Jews, which they are accustomed to bring against us so that they might pervert the true sense of the prophecy itself, we have already responded more fully in the third book, where we showed that the Messiah was to be called Emmanuel.

## That the mother of the Messiah, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, was to conceive the Son of God. Chapter XVI.

### CAPNIO,

<margin>The false interpretation of the Jews. Refutation.</margin>

Here, not without reason, I would like to know: whether the ancient Jews, just as they predicted that the mother of the Messiah would conceive and give birth as a virgin, also foretold that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit. 
**GALATINUS.** That indeed was foretold long ago by the prophets and expressly explained by the ancient Jewish Doctors <term>Doctors: referring here to the "Chachamim" or the ancient learned sages of the Jewish tradition</term>. For concerning the prophets, Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Holy Spirit, says in chapter 8: <note>original: "ואקרב אל הנביאה ותהר ותלד בן"</note> That is, *And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.* 
**CAPNIO.** The younger Jews <note>Referring to medieval or contemporary Jewish commentators who lived after the rise of Christianity</note> explain these words as being about the withdrawal of Isaiah himself for sexual union <term>concubitus: a formal term for sexual intercourse</term> with his own wife. From which (as they say) she, conceiving from that union, bore the son of the prophet himself. 
**GALATINUS.** We shall show from the words of the prophet himself that they explain these words falsely and pervert them against the prophet's intention. For neither the words immediately preceding nor those soon following support their explanation; rather, they clearly contradict it. For thus the prophet said before: <note>original: "ואעידה לי עדים נאמנים את אוריא הכהן ואת זכריהו בן יברכיהו"</note> That is, *And I took for myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah.* And having stated these things, he immediately brought forth these words: *And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.* And afterward he immediately added: <note>original: "ויאמר יהוה אלי קרא שמו מהר שלל חש בז"</note> That is, *And the Lord said to me, Call his name: Swiftly plunder the spoils, quickly take the prey.* Or, *Call his name: The Ready One, the Plunderer, the Swift One, the Predator.* Now, these things so...

First, for what purpose did the prophet bring in those witnesses? Did he, when approaching his wife for intercourse, have need of witnesses? Indeed, this Holy Spirit—before He approached the prophetess, that is, that virgin who was to conceive and give birth to the Savior, so that by His power and cooperation, without the seed of man, she might conceive and bear the Son of God—ought to have employed these prophets as witnesses of the future truth. For one of them, namely Uriah the son of Shemaiah, predicted many evils to come against the Jews and their city, which later befell them in the Babylonian captivity. But the other, that is, Zechariah the son of Barachiah, prophesied many and great good things to come to them at the arrival of the Messiah. But Isaiah uttered the aforementioned words in the fourth year of King Ahaz (as Rabbi Solomon <term>Rabbi Solomon: Rashi (1040–1105), a famous medieval Jewish scholar whose commentaries are foundational to Jewish study.</term> says). From the fourth year of Ahaz until Jehoiakim, 140 years passed. For all the years that Ahaz reigned were sixteen; when four are subtracted, twelve remain. At the beginning of these twelve years, the aforementioned prophecy of Isaiah was made. Then his son Hezekiah reigned for 29 years; after him, Manasseh for 55; then Amon for two years; afterward, Josiah for 31 years; then Jehoahaz for three months; and after him, Jehoiakim, who killed the aforementioned prophet Uriah, reigned for 11 years. All of these years, taken together, amount to 160 years and three months. From this it is quite clearly manifest that the first witness—namely Uriah, whom Isaiah or the Holy Spirit summoned to himself—was not yet born when he was summoned.

Regarding the second witness, that is Zechariah, no one should doubt this. Since from the fifth year of Ahaz until the second year of Darius, in which he himself prophesied, 250 years passed. Therefore, since these men—such great prophets whom Isaiah, or rather the Holy Spirit through Isaiah, summoned as witnesses when he spoke of the virgin prophetess and her son Emmanuel—were not yet born in the time of Isaiah, it is openly shown to all who have a sound use of reason that the prophetess of whom the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah, saying, *I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son,* had not yet been born either. Consequently, she could not have been Isaiah's wife, as the younger, delusional Jews falsely affirm. <note>The author is engaging in a common medieval polemic, arguing against Jewish interpretations that identify the "prophetess" in Isaiah 8:3 as Isaiah's contemporary wife.</note> But rather, she is that Virgin who, by the intervention of the Holy Spirit, was to conceive and bear the Son of God, whom he had also mentioned a little earlier, saying: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.* From these things it is also clear that this "approach" to the prophetess was to be a spiritual one. Since these things are so, it is clear that this prophetess was none other than the Virgin Mary, who [bore] the Messiah of God...

He did not say: "I will give," but "I have given." And how could this be, since Abraham had not yet fathered any children? It is because God’s word is a deed; therefore He spoke in this way. From this we are also taught that God’s word is a deed when it is said, "I the Lord have spoken, and I have done it." And when did He do it? Only because God’s word is considered a finished deed. Therefore, it is well said, "He has redeemed," even though it was still in the future. This is the tradition. Furthermore, the Commentary <gloss>marginal note: Glossa</gloss> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> on that passage of Isaiah, "These words I have done for them," says this: "I have done," that is, "I shall do." For the entire language of the prophets speaks of the future as if it were already done. From these points it is clear that the objection of the Jews has no weight at all. Since, according to the aforementioned tradition, those words of Isaiah must be understood as: "And I approached," that is "I shall approach the prophetess, and she conceived and bore," that is "and she shall conceive and shall bear a son."

# BOOK

You should also show that she was to be a prophetess herself, by citing some of their ancient authorities who stated this explicitly. GAL. Since much has been said on this matter previously, and more will be said in the following pages, for now let it suffice to hear from that man of the greatest authority among them, whom they call <term>Rabbenu Hakados</term> <note>original Hebrew: רבנו הקדוש; "Our Holy Master." This refers to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah and a central figure in Judaism.</note>, that is, our Holy Master. For he, in the third petition of that book titled <term>Gale Razeya</term> <note>original Hebrew: גלי רזיא; "The Revealer of Secrets." This is a mystical/kabbalistic work often cited by Galatinus, though its historical origins are debated among scholars.</note>, that is, the *Revealer of Secrets*, was asked by Antoninus, a consul of the city of Rome: "Who is that prophetess mentioned by Isaiah when he said in the eighth chapter, *And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son*?" He responded thus: "I have often been left in suspense and anxious over this question. And one day, having entered the cave of the fathers <note>The Cave of Machpelah in Hebron, the traditional burial site of the Biblical patriarchs and matriarchs.</note>, where Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah are buried, so that I might pray there, I found Elijah, whom I questioned. Therefore, I make known to you what I received from him. This prophetess is the mother of the King Messiah, whom the Holy and Blessed God promised He would send to Israel. She is called a prophetess because, by her own prophetic vision, she knows all things from the beginning to the very end—something no other prophet was ever able to know. For she herself is the mistress and teacher of all prophets. And she is that <term>alma</term> <note>The Hebrew word 'almah' (young woman/virgin) is central to the debate over Isaiah 7:14. Galatinus argues here that it specifically denotes a virgin.</note> of whom Solomon spoke in the 30th chapter of Proverbs, *And the way of a man in an alma*, that is, 'And the way of God into a virgin.' Of her, Isaiah also says in chapter 7: *Behold, the alma shall conceive and bear a son.* Concerning her, it is also said in Micah, chapter 5: *And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small...* and after a few words: *Therefore he will give them up until the time when she who is in labor has given birth.* Furthermore, concerning the King Messiah himself, whom this prophetess is to bear, Isaiah said in chapter 9: *A child is born to us, a son is given to us. And the government will be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince, Peace.*" So he said, long before this prophetess was even born. The Jews can by no means deny his words, since they call him "our Holy Master," and his authority (as has been said) is supreme among them.

->*That the mother of the Messiah was to be the seat of God, upon which the divine majesty was to sit. Chapter XIX.*<-

### CAPNIO,

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a detailed landscape with a classical building, trees, and rolling hills.</image-desc>
When Jeremiah, in chapter 17, brought forth these words: <term>A glorious high throne from the beginning is the place of our sanctuary, the hope of Israel, the Lord</term> <note>original Hebrew: כבוד מרום מראשון מקום מקדשנו מקוה ישראל יהוה; Jeremiah 17:12-13.</note>. What does he understand there by the "throne of glory"? For I believe that the "throne of glory" in that passage refers to the glorious Virgin, the mother of the Messiah. Since she is exalted in celestial glory above all the angelic choirs, she is rightly called the "throne of high glory"—that is, the seat of the Most High God upon which the divine majesty sits.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Galatinus and Capnio, moving from the identity of the "prophetess" to the concept of the Divine Throne. Galatinus introduces an argument from Maimonides to establish that the "throne of God" can refer to a physical vessel of His glory, which he then applies to the Mother of the Messiah.</meta>

# THE SEVENTH BOOK.

GALATINUS: You speak rightly, my dear Capnio <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived nickname for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and Hebraist.</note>. So that what you feel may be more clearly explained, I shall bring forward those things which Rabbi Moses ben Maimon <note>Commonly known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> says in the first part of his book *The Guide* <note>original: "More"; referring to the *Moreh Nevukhim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note>, in the ninth chapter. There, explaining in what way a "throne" or "seat" is attributed to God, he says these things among others:

> What a throne signifies is well known. When someone sees one decorated and prepared in the manner of a high priest or ruler, he will assume that a King or some Emperor is going to sit in it. For the throne itself shows the excellence and majesty of the one sitting. By this reasoning, the house of God <note>The Temple in Jerusalem.</note> is called the throne of God, since it shows the dominion and power of Him who reveals His glory and brightness within it. Therefore Jeremiah said: *A throne of glory, set on high from the beginning, is the place of our sanctification.* By the same reasoning, even the heavens are called the throne of God, insofar as they show the strength of the Creator, the mover and moderator of this lower world, and they reveal the influence of His grace. For this reason it was said in the 66th chapter of Isaiah: *The heavens are my throne* <note>original Hebrew: השמים כסאי (ha-shamayim kis’i).</note>. It is as if He were saying: The heavens constantly show my essence, strength, and power, just as a throne suggests the dominion and majesty of him who is worthy to sit in it. This, however, is necessary for one believing in God: not that this throne is a physical body in which God sits—far be it from us to fall into this error! For since we have already proved that God is not a physical being, how shall we say that He requires a physical place or tabernacle? It is certain, however (as we have said), that any place magnified by God with His glory, such as the holy house or the heavens, is called His throne. Nevertheless, when God spoke in a more expansive way in the 17th chapter of Exodus: *Because the hand is upon the throne of the Lord, and the war of God shall be against Amalek from generation to generation.* This is God’s own substance and essence. Nor should it be imagined that this "throne" is a thing distinct from Him, or created by God like His other creatures. For it would follow that God exists within time, and was without a throne before He created it. To say or believe this is the greatest heresy, since it is written in Psalm 102: *But You, O Lord, remain forever; Your throne is from generation to generation* <note>original Hebrew: ואתה יהוה לעולם תשב כסאך לדור ודור (Ve-atah Adonai le-olam teshev, kis’akha le-dor va-dor).</note>. That is: Just as You, O God, are eternal, so also Your throne is eternal. And for this reason it is shown that this throne is not a thing distinct from God. Therefore, this throne—and whatever else signifies the proper essence of God—are not things distinct from Him. Thus far speaks that Egyptian Rabbi Moses.

<margin>Three types of thrones.</margin>
Indeed, from his words, three conclusions are drawn, since he himself brings forward three types of thrones. Two of these are created, but the third is uncreated.

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion is: That the first created throne—which the Teacher himself takes to mean the holy house [the Temple], and says that in it the majesty of the one sitting is recognized because of its excellence—

<margin>The first throne is the mother of the Messiah.</margin>
is nonetheless more rightly understood as the undefiled mother of the Messiah. Because of her perfection and excellence, she was to be the throne of God, in which God Himself was to show His glory and brightness—which is the Messiah, the glory, light, and brightness of the whole world. Because of which it is said...

Having cited Maimonides' view that the Temple or the heavens can be called God’s throne, Galatinus now pivots to argue that these are merely types or shadows of the true throne: the Mother of the Messiah and the person of the Messiah himself.</meta>

# BOOK VII

it was said in the ninth chapter of Isaiah: <note>Isaiah 9:2</note> *The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in the land of the shadow of death, upon them a light has dawned.* <note>original Hebrew: הָעָם הַהֹלְכִים בַּחֹשֶׁךְ רָאוּ אוֹר גָּדוֹל יֹשְׁבֵי בְּאֶרֶץ צַלְמָוֶת אוֹר נָגַהּ עֲלֵיהֶם (ha-am ha-holekhim ba-hoshekh...)</note> That is, "The people who were walking in darkness, have seen a great light. Those who were sitting in the land of the shadow of death, a light has risen over them." For this reason, the words of Jeremiah, when he says, *A throne of glory, set on high from the beginning*, <note>Jeremiah 17:12</note> are not understood to refer to the holy house <note>The Temple</note> which was in Jerusalem. For even if God showed His glory in it, that glory was as nothing in comparison to the glory and brightness which He was to show in the mother of the Messiah. Furthermore, we do not find that the holy house existed from the beginning of the world, whereas it has been proven in the preceding pages that the mother of the Messiah did so exist <note>This refers to the concept of the "ideal" or "predestined" existence of the Virgin Mary before creation.</note>. Moreover, that holy house cannot be called a "throne of glory," since the glorious seat of God ought to be perennial or perpetual, and not vanish away. For whatever God once accepts, He never dismisses. And although two other seats of God, which He Himself claims—namely the heavens and God's own essence—are one perpetual and the other eternal, the Holy House in Jerusalem nevertheless passed away and vanished in destruction. Finally, it follows in the text of Jeremiah: *The expectation of Israel is God.* <note>Jeremiah 17:13</note> But the true expectation and hope of Israel was none other than the Messiah, who was to come forth from his most holy mother. For these reasons, then, it is openly shown that the aforementioned words of Jeremiah must be understood not as referring to the holy house (as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note> thinks), which collapsed along with Jerusalem, but as referring to the mother of the Messiah, just as you yourself so excellently perceive they should be understood. For she herself (as Rabbenus Haccados <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince (c. 135–217 AD), the traditional compiler of the Mishnah. Galatinus is citing a work called *Gale Razeya* (The Revealer of Secrets), a text often used by Christian Hebraists to find Christian mysteries in Jewish tradition.</note> says in the book *Gale Razeya*, in response to the third petition of Antoninus, the consul of the City of Rome) was to be the seat which God constructed, so that the King Messiah might sit in her, to show the glory of His majesty to all mortals.

<margin>The second and third conclusions.</margin>
<margin>The second seat is the humanity of the Messiah.</margin>
Now, the second and third conclusions are that the second seat is created, while the third is uncreated. These two seats of God are the Messiah himself. For his humanity is indeed created, which by the Word of God was made a seat; but his divinity itself is uncreated. That the humanity of the Messiah is called the seat of God is clear through that saying in the 44th Psalm: <note>Psalm 45:6 in modern Bibles; 44 in the Vulgate.</note> *Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever: the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of thy kingdom.* <note>original Hebrew: כִּסְאֲךָ אֱלֹהִים עוֹלָם וָעֶד שֵׁבֶט מִישֹׁר שֵׁבֶט מַלְכוּתֶךָ (kis'akha Elohim olam va-ed...)</note> For just as the glory of their designer is shown from the operation of the heavens—by this argument, namely: whatever is moved, necessarily has a mover and a governor; the heavens are moved, therefore they have a mover and a governor—so from the humanity of the Messiah, on account of his divine operations, it is shown that his "suppositum" <note>A philosophical term meaning the underlying person or individual substance.</note> is God, the founder and governor of the whole world. For just as the heavens show the glory of their mover and the governance of this lower world by means of the influence of His grace, so the humanity of the Messiah shows the magnificence and dominion of the creator and mover of this world, by means of the influence of salvation, which God pours into that humanity.

<margin>The third seat is the divinity.</margin>
The third seat, he says, is the divinity, which is uncreated. For the Father is uncreated, the Son is uncreated, and the Holy Spirit is uncreated.

<summary>Galatinus argues that the "Throne of God" described by the prophets refers primarily to the Mother of the Messiah and the two natures (human and divine) of the Messiah himself, rather than the physical Temple in Jerusalem.</summary>

# SEVENTH.

Now, the meaning of those words which he brings forward—*But you, O Lord, remain forever; your throne from generation to generation* <note>original Latin: "Tu autem Deus in æternum permanes, sedes tua in generationem & generationem." This draws on Psalm 102:12 and Lamentations 5:19.</note>—is this: Just as you, God, are eternal, so your throne, which is your son, is eternal; because the Father is eternal, the Son is eternal, and the Holy Spirit is eternal. Therefore, from the words of <term>Rabbi Moses of Egypt</term> <note>Better known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> himself, it is clearly shown (as we have proved) that the previously mentioned words of Jeremiah—*A throne of glory, set on high from the beginning, the place of our sanctification* <note>Jeremiah 17:12</note>—must be understood as referring to the most blessed mother of the Messiah, who is the throne of the most high God. Moreover, he said, "From the beginning," to show that she was conceived without original sin.

This same point is also most excellently suggested by that which is said in the first chapter of Ezekiel: *And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone; and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it.* <note>Ezekiel 1:26. original Hebrew: וּמִמַּעַל לָרָקִיעַ אֲשֶׁר עַל רֹאשָׁם כְּמַרְאֵה אֶבֶן סַפִּיר דְּמוּת כִּסֵּא וְעַל דְּמוּת הַכִּסֵּא דְּמוּת כְּמַרְאֵה אָדָם עָלָיו מִלְמָעְלָה (u-mi-ma'al la-raqi'a...)</note> Here, Ezekiel prophesied concerning the immaculate mother of the Messiah. For after he had seen the <term>four living creatures</term> <note>The "Hayyot" or tetramorphs in Ezekiel's vision, often interpreted in Christian tradition as symbols of the four Evangelists.</note> and their movement, he says he saw standing above the heads of the creatures in heaven the likeness of a throne, or a royal seat, which is the glorious mother of the Messiah. And soon after, upon this likeness <margin>The Mother of the Messiah is compared to a sapphire.</margin> [appeared the likeness] of a man, who is the incarnate Son of God, or the Messiah. 

Furthermore, he says the appearance of this throne is like sapphire, not only to suggest the glory of this untainted virgin, but also her total purity. For just as the sapphire, though it has its origin from an earthly, opaque, and dark element, is nevertheless transparent and clear from its very beginning; in the same way, the immaculate mother of the Messiah herself, even if she came forth from parents subject to sin, was nevertheless from her own beginning most bright and without the stain of original sin.

Let these things said concerning the immaculate and most holy mother of the Messiah, according to the opinions of the ancient Hebrews, suffice. Now, returning to her son, let us discuss his mysteries.

P

Book Eight.

## On the mysteries of the Messiah which have been fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ

### *That the Messiah, according to the flesh, was to descend from Jacob and the other fathers through a direct lineage.* Chapter 1.

->CAPNIO,<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' containing a small figure, possibly a putto or child, amidst decorative foliate scrolls.</image-desc>

**I** am now about to speak concerning the mysteries of the Messiah, by which the disbelief of the more recent Jews is best refuted. For through these mysteries it is clearly shown that our Lord Jesus Christ was the true Messiah, since in him all those very mysteries of the Messiah foretold by the prophets were perfectly fulfilled <note>original Latin: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," a phrase meaning to the highest degree of precision.</note>. First, you ought to reveal that the Messiah himself was to descend from Jacob and the other patriarchs through a direct line. GALATINUS.

I shall therefore bring forward those things written on this matter in the 24th chapter of Numbers in this manner:
A star has come out of Jacob, and a rod—or scepter—has risen out of Israel, and has struck the corners—or the heights—of Moab, and has destroyed—or scattered—all the sons of Seth. And Edom shall be his possession, and Seir shall be a possession for his enemies, and Israel shall act valiantly. And he shall rule out of Jacob, and shall destroy the remnant—or the remains—from the city. <note>original Hebrew: "דרך כוכב מיעקב וקם שבט מישראל..." (Numbers 24:17-19). This is the famous "Star Prophecy" of Balaam.</note> Where the commentator <term>Solomon</term> <note>Galatinus refers to Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: "From the city—that is, from the famous city of Edom, which is Rome." Regarding the King Messiah, however, it is said, "And he shall rule out of Jacob," along with the rest. For of him it is said in Psalm 72: "And he shall rule from sea to sea." Likewise in Obadiah: "And there shall be no remnant for the house of Jacob" <note>This is likely a reference to Obadiah 1:18, though the context here discusses the destruction of the enemies of Jacob.</note>. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. Furthermore, these words—"A star has come out of Jacob, and a rod (or scepter) has risen out of Israel"—were translated into Aramaic by <term>Rabbi Onkelos</term> <note>The author of the Targum Onkelos, the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah from the 1st or 2nd century AD.</note> as follows: A King shall rise from the house of Jacob, and the Messiah shall be magnified from Israel <note>original Aramaic: "דנח מלכא מיעקב ויתרבי משיחא מישראל" (danach malka mi-yaakov...).</note>. From this Aramaic translation, two things are gathered. First, that this scripture speaks of the Messiah. Second, that the same scripture uses the past tense for the future in the prophetic manner. Moreover, in the commentaries of <term>Rabbi Moses ha-Darshan</term> <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne, France, famous for his "Midrash Bereshit Rabbati."</note> on the book of Genesis, regarding that statement in the 49th chapter of the same book, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah," along with the rest, it is said: "This is what Isaiah said—"
