BOOK EIGHT. 347.

[...Bala]am, "A star shall come out of Jacob," and so forth. And when will this prophecy be fulfilled? "When Shiloh comes," that is, the Messiah. From these things the proposition is clear. That the Messiah was also to come forth from Judah, and subsequently from Jesse, is found in the *Bereshit Ketanna* <note>original: "Beresith קטנה Ketanna," meaning the "Lesser Genesis," a shorter midrashic commentary on the first book of the Bible.</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, upon that saying of Genesis chapter 49: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you." <note>original Hebrew: "יהודה אתה יודוד אחיד" (*Yehudah attah yoducha achecha*).</note> Where it is said: Judah was the fourth born among the tribes; on the fourth day the lights of heaven were created; and of the Messiah it is written in Psalm 88 <note>Modern Bibles usually list this as Psalm 89:36-37.</note>: "and his throne shall be as the sun before me." And from Judah was the Messiah born, according to that saying of Isaiah chapter 11: "And there shall come forth a rod from the stem of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots." This is the tradition.

That he was also to be born from David is found in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The *Midrash Tehillim* is a traditional rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, upon that saying of Psalm 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 16:9.</note>: "Because of this my heart was glad, and my glory rejoiced." <note>original Hebrew: "לכו שמח לבי ויגל כבודי" (*Lachen samach libbi va-yagel kevodi*).</note> Thus it is said: "Rabbi Abhu <note>A prominent scholar of the late 3rd/early 4th century based in Caesarea.</note> said, 'My heart was glad,' namely in the words of the Law, 'and my glory rejoiced,' namely in the King Messiah, who was to come forth from David himself. For concerning him it was said in Isaiah chapter 4: 'For upon all the glory shall be a covering'" <note>original Hebrew: "כי על כל כבוד חפה" (*ki al kol kavod huppah*).</note>, or a bridal chamber. Thus it is said there. Moreover, <term>Rabbi Kimhi</term> <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, was a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical exegete.</note> said that *huppah* <note>original Hebrew: "חפה"</note>, which is used in the words of Isaiah, is the place in which the bride hides herself with the bridegroom. From these things it clearly appears that the Messiah, according to the flesh, was to proceed from Jacob and the other fathers. But since much has been said on this matter in the preceding pages, what we have said now shall suffice.

### That the Messiah was to be born in a new way, that is, without the seed of a man, or from a mother without a father. Chapter 11.

BOOK

###

In the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The *Midrash Tehillim* is a traditional Jewish commentary on the Book of Psalms.</note> on the verse "You are my son; today I have begotten you," <note>original: "במדרש תה' חנני מולך meus es tu. Ego hodie genui te." This refers to Psalm 2:7.</note> it is said:
In the authority of all the Prophets and the Writings <note>Hagiographa</note>, it is said: "From the womb of the morning, yours is the dew of your youth." <note>original Hebrew: "מרחם משחר לך טל" (*me-rechem mishchar lecha tal*). This is a reference to Psalm 110:3.</note> Rabbi Hunna said: Suffering is divided into three parts: one part was taken by the fathers of the world <note>The Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> and every generation; one by the generation of destruction <note>Referring to those persecuted under Roman rule.</note>; and one by the generation of the Messiah. And when his hour comes, the Holy One, Blessed be He, says: "It is upon me to show him as a new creation," and thus it says, "Today I have begotten you." <note>original Hebrew: "אני היום ילדתיך" (*Ani hayom yeladticha*).</note>

That is to say, the matters or mysteries of King Messiah are recounted in the writings of the prophets and the hagiographa <note>The *Hagiographa* or *Ketuvim* is the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. As it is said in Psalm 110: "From the womb, from the morning," or "from the womb of the morning, yours is the dew of your birth." Rabbi Hunna said (or as it is read elsewhere, Rabbi Idi): The tribulations are divided into three divisions. The first was borne by the fathers of the world (namely Abraham and the rest) and all generations. The second was borne by the generation of destruction (namely those who were destroyed by the Romans). The third, however, is for the generation of the Messiah. And when his hour shall come, the Holy and Blessed God will say, "It is upon me," that is, it belongs to me, "to create him as a new creation." And this is what he says: "Today I have begotten you." Thus far the tradition.

In this tradition, there are two points that clearly show that the Messiah was to be conceived and brought forth not like other men, but in a new way. The first is what was said at the end: that God was to create him as a "new creation." The second is what was said a little earlier according to the "Hebrew Truth" <note>original: "Hebraicam ueritatem," a term often used by scholars to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Bible as a standard of accuracy.</note> in that place where we <note>The Latin-speaking Christian church.</note> have the reading: "From the womb before the day-star I begat thee." The Hebrew text says: "From the womb of the morning, yours is the dew of your birth." For the Hebrew text reads in a way that is more in harmony with the truth of our faith. For since it is proven by this tradition that these things were said of the Messiah, nothing else can be reasonably or appropriately understood by the "womb of the morning" than the womb of his most holy mother, literally. She was to conceive and give birth to him by divine power, without the seed of a man, while her virginity remained intact. Just as the morning dawn receives the sun and brings it forth without corruption <note>In this context, "corruption" refers to any physical change, decay, or loss of purity.</note>. All of this is understood through the "dew of birth" of the Messiah from the womb of the morning.

<margin>What the dawn is.</margin>
For the dawn is that part of the sky and earth which appears illuminated in the morning before the sun rises, where the sun comes forth. As soon as it begins to grow light, it is called "dawn" <note>original: "aurora"</note>; but as soon as the sun rises and is seen, it is no longer called dawn.

<margin>What the womb of the dawn is.</margin>
The "womb of the dawn" is said to be that interval between the earth or the sea of our horizon, through which the sun brings itself forth and raises itself, and is seen to rise and ascend.

<margin>What the dew of birth is.</margin>
The "dew of birth" is the first conception of a man in the womb, which is not without reason called "dew." For just as dew is quickly dissolved by the sun, so also the first conceptions of both men and other animals very easily become miscarriages, whereas those of longer duration are miscarried with difficulty.

<margin>The Catholic exposition.</margin>
The meaning, therefore, is this: That just as the pre-existing sun, by itself and without any other bringing it forth, produces itself from the center of the dawn; so the Word of God, through himself and without a generating man, was to receive the first conception of the birth of his humanity from the center of the dawn <note>Here used as a metaphor for the Virgin Mary.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the miraculous birth of the Messiah, transitioning from general prophetic "seed" to a specific linguistic analysis of the "Shiloh" prophecy in Genesis and the meaning of "four generations."</meta>

->### EIGHTH BOOK<-

**"The scepter shall not depart from Judah, etc., until Shiloh comes."** <note>original Hebrew: "לא יסור שבט מיהודה וגו׳ עד כי יבא שילה" (*Lo yasur shevet mi-Yehuda...*)</note> This is: **The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the scribe from the midst of his feet, until Shiloh comes** <note>original Latin: "Non recedet sceptrū de Iuda, & scriba de medio pedū eius, donec ueniat שילה Silo"</note>—that is, his son, specifically the son of the woman. For this is how Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a famous Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> explains this word *Shiloh* in his concordance, under the entry for *Silo*. This was discussed more extensively in the fourth chapter of the fourth book. To clarify this, one must pay attention to a significant distinction the Hebrews make in their grammar (as you yourself well know) between masculine and feminine demonstrations.

For if they intend to say "his son" using the masculine demonstration, they say **Beno** <note>original Hebrew: "בנו"</note>, with the letter *vav* at the end of the word. But if they intend to say "her son" <note>literally: "his son or that one's son," but referring to a female subject.</note> using the feminine demonstration, they say **Bena** <note>original Hebrew: "בנה"</note>, with the letter *he* at the end of the word. Now, although this word **Shiloh** <note>original Hebrew: "שילה"</note> is spoken as a masculine demonstration in pronunciation—whereas it should rightfully have been written *Sila* <note>original Hebrew: "שילא"</note> according to the scribes' convention—it is nonetheless written with the letter *he*, the feminine demonstration. It is pronounced *Silo*. This is the same as "son," namely, of the woman. Thus the text says: **The scepter shall not depart from Judah, and the scribe from the midst of his feet, until the son of that woman comes.**

<margin>The false interpretation of the younger Jews.</margin>
However, to understand what "the son of the woman" signifies, one must note the words written in Genesis, chapter 15: **And in the fourth generation they shall return here.** <note>original Hebrew: "ודור רביעי ישובו הנה" (*Vedor revii yashuvu henna*)</note> These words were spoken by God when he announced to Abraham the Egyptian captivity, which prefigured the captivity of souls in hell. 

Truly, some of the more recent Jewish scholars explain these "four generations" as having been four hundred years, asserting that each of them lasted one hundred years. 
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Their explanation is worthless. For they either calculate these years from the time the prophecy was spoken, or from when the Egyptian captivity itself began. Both are false. If they calculate from the time the prophecy was delivered, they will find that much more than four hundred years passed. But if they calculate from the beginning of the captivity itself, the aforementioned number of years is not completed, since the captivity itself lasted no more than two hundred and ten years.

<margin>Another of their explanations.</margin>
Certain others, and especially **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note>, wish for these four generations to be the father, the son, the grandson, and the great-grandson. 
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Their explanation is even more false than the first. For these four generations must be counted either from the time of the prophecy or from the start of the captivity. If we count them from the time of the prophecy, we find seven generations, not four. These are: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, and Caleb. 
<margin>Rabbi Solomon’s explanation.</margin>
But if we calculate them from the beginning of the captivity itself, as Rabbi Solomon does—counting Judah, Perez, Hezron, and Caleb—there will be fewer than four. 
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
For Judah and his son Perez were born before they entered Egypt, as is clear from Genesis, chapter 45. Therefore, we must see through more subtle investigation what these four generations signify. Thus, it is not yet found to be four generations of men. 

The first was that of **Adam**, who was created without a man or a woman. The second was that of **Eve**, who was created from a man without a woman...
<margin>The fourfold generation of men.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the speaker's (Galatinus) linguistic and symbolic proof that the Messiah would be born specifically from a woman without a male partner. He uses the "four generations" mentioned in Genesis 15:16 as a framework for four types of human production.</meta>

...produced. Therefore, according to the teaching of **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) was the foundational philosopher for medieval logic; the principle cited here is that "the science of opposites is one," meaning understanding one state implies understanding its contrary.</note>, the knowledge of opposites is the same. Once one side of a contradiction is established, it is necessary to establish the other as well. For if "black" is found, "white" must also be found; if "sweet" is discovered, one must also concede that "bitter" is discovered. 

For this reason, it is necessary that, having already established two types of generation, two opposite types must be assigned. The third type of generation—the opposite of **Adam**, who was produced without either man or woman—is the one by which all people are commonly generated from both man and woman. But the fourth generation is given as the opposite of **Eve**, who 
<margin>A universal exposition.</margin>
was formed from a man without a woman: this is the generation by which the **Messiah** was to be born of a woman without a man. Therefore, those previously mentioned words are to be explained thus: *In the fourth generation they shall return here* <note>original Latin: "Generatione quarta reuertentur huc." A reference to God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 15:16.</note>. That is, with the coming of the Messiah’s generation, souls shall be liberated from the captivity of hell and shall return to the heavenly fatherland from which they had been expelled on account of Adam’s sin, with the Messiah himself as their leader. It was because of this generation, therefore, that **Jacob** said: *The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the scribe from the midst of his feet, until the son of that woman comes*—that is, the Messiah, who was called "the son of the woman" because he was to be born of a woman without a man.

### That the Kings of the nations were to come to adore the Messiah, bringing gifts to him. Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a seated figure, possibly a scholar or authority figure, in a classical pose within the letter's counter.</image-desc>
**Since** you have revealed many things in the preceding sections concerning the mysteries that were to occur around the birth of the Messiah—for you have spoken quite abundantly on the time the Messiah was to come, and in what city and in what place he was to be born, and that he should be called by his own name, **Jesus**—it now remains for you to say something from their scriptures <note>Meaning the Hebrew scriptures and commentaries.</note> concerning the **Kings of the nations** who were to come to him at the time of his birth to adore him and offer him gifts. 

**GAL.** I shall speak of that mystery and what the ancient Jews said of it. For in the **Midrash Tehillim** <note>A rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Psalms (Tehillim).</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that which is said in **Psalm 87**: *I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to those who know me* <note>original Hebrew: "אזכיר רהב ובבל ליודעי" (*Azkir Rahab u-Vavel le-yode'ai*)</note>, these things are read: **Rabbi Joses**, the son of Simon, said: *It shall come to pass that the nations of the world shall bring gifts to the King Messiah. As it is said in the fourth chapter of the Song of Songs: "You shall give gifts from the head of Amana."* <note>original Hebrew: "דורונות למלך המשיח שנאמר השוררים מראש אמנה" (*Doronot le-melekh ha-mashiach she-ne'emar ha-shorerim me-rosh amanah*). Galatinus interprets the Hebrew *tashuri* ("look" or "depart") as related to *teshurah* ("a gift").</note> 

It follows in the same Psalm: *The Lord shall record or write in the scripture of the peoples: this one was born there continually.* <note>original Hebrew: "יהוה יספור בכתב עמים זה ילד שם" (*Adonai yispor bi-khtov ammim: zeh yulad sham*). Galatinus adds "continually" (iugiter) to his Latin gloss.</note> This means: from among those peoples who bring gifts to the King Messiah, the Holy and Blessed God shall enroll them with **Israel**. It follows: *This one was born there.* This means: these people shall be just as if they had been born in that very hour. And this is the meaning of: *This one was born there continually.* This is the tradition. For the understanding of this, it must be noted that never in the whole of the old sacred scripture are "peoples" placed in the plural...

That these things were spoken concerning the **Messiah** <term>Messiah: the "Anointed One" or promised redeemer of the Jewish people</term> is clear from what is contained in the **Bereshith Rabba** <note>Genesis Rabbah, an ancient midrashic or interpretive commentary on the Book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of **Genesis**, regarding that which is said in Genesis, chapter 25: *And he sent them away from Isaac his son, while he was still living, to the eastern region.* For there it is said: This is what is written in **Job**, chapter 6: <note>original Hebrew: הביטי ארחות תמא הליכות שבא קוו למו</note> That is, *Look upon the paths of Tema, the ways of Sheba, wait for him* (or them). "Sheba" refers to none other than the sons of **Abraham**, just as it is said in Genesis, chapter 25: <note>original Hebrew: ויקשן ילד את שבא ואת דדן</note> That is, *And Jokshan begat Sheba and Dedan.* 

When **Solomon** <note>The King of Israel famous for his wisdom and the building of the Temple in Jerusalem.</note> had been magnified in his Kingdom, they said, "Perhaps this is the Messiah," and they immediately came to him. Just as it is said in 1 Kings, chapter 10: *And the Queen of Sheba, having heard of the fame of Solomon in the name of God, came to test him with riddles.* Do not read <note>original Hebrew: מלכת שבא</note> *the Queen of Sheba*, but <note>original Hebrew: מלכות שבא</note> *the Kingdom of Sheba*. And what is meant by the phrase "in the name of God"? There were prophets among them who prophesied words to them in the name of the Lord their God, which had been handed down to them and which had come successively to their hands from Abraham. 

And from where is it held that they would come in the days of the Messiah and serve him? From that which was said in **Isaiah**, chapter sixty: <note>original Hebrew: שפעת גמלים תכסך בכרי מדין ועיפה כלם משבא יבאו זהב ולבונה ישאו ותהלות יהוה יבשרו</note> That is, *A multitude of camels shall cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All they from Sheba shall come, they shall bring gold and frankincense, and they shall announce the praises of God (the tetragrammaton).* For this is the King Messiah. Just as it is said in **Jeremiah**, chapters 23 and 33: <note>original Hebrew: וזה שמו אשר יקראו יהוה צדקינו</note> That is, *And this is the name by which they shall call him: God (the tetragrammaton) our just one.* And thus Isaiah says in the sixtieth chapter, *And over you God (the tetragrammaton) shall shine or rise, and his glory shall appear over you. And the nations shall go to your light, and Kings to the brightness...*

## BOOK II

...of your illustration. Thus far the tradition. In this tradition, five things are especially to be noted.

The first of these is that it says that the **Queen of Sheba**, having heard the fame of **Solomon** <note>Solomon: the biblical King of Israel known for his wisdom</note>, came in the name of God to test him with riddles. Assigning a reason for this, the text says: because when Solomon had been magnified in his Kingdom, people had said, "Perhaps this man is the **Messiah**." Regarding the point that one should not read "Queen of Sheba" but rather "the Kingdom of Sheba," an answer is provided to an objection that the younger **Jews** are accustomed to make against us. They falsely attempt to prove that our Christ was not the Messiah because the prophet **Isaiah** said:

> All from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and incense,

but according to the testimony of the **Gospel**, not "all" those from Sheba came to worship Christ, but only a few <note>A reference to the Magi or Wise Men</note>. Here, therefore, they are best refuted by their own **Talmud** <term>Talmud: a central text of Rabbinic Judaism containing discussions on Jewish law and tradition</term>, which says: "Do not read 'Queen of Sheba,' but 'Kingdom of Sheba.'" Since a King represents everyone existing within his Kingdom, the Queen of Sheba herself who came to Solomon represented that entire kingdom. Therefore, since among the Kings who came to worship the newborn Christ there was one king of Sheba who represented all the people of that same kingdom, it was rightly predicted through Isaiah:

> All from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and incense.

It has also been proven in the preceding pages that in Sacred Scripture the word "all" is rarely used to mean every single individual, but rather is frequently used to represent even a very small portion.

Second, it should be noted in the same tradition that he says those from Sheba were to come in the days of the Messiah and serve him. He shows that this was to happen through the aforementioned words of Isaiah.

Third, because he says those people of Sheba were sons of **Abraham**, which he proves by the authority of the Sacred Scripture he cites there. He adds that there was a prophet among them who prophesied words in the name of God—words which had been handed down to them and had come into their hands in succession from Abraham.

Fourth, because in explaining that passage of Isaiah:

> All from Sheba shall come, bringing gold and incense, and they shall announce the praises of God (**the tetragrammaton**).

He says that this God, written with the name **tetragrammaton** <term>tetragrammaton: the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, considered too sacred to be spoken aloud by many traditions</term>, to whom those from Sheba were to offer those gifts and whose praises they would announce, is the King Messiah. He proves this by the testimony of **Jeremiah**, who says:

> And this is the name by which they shall call him: God (**the tetragrammaton**), our just one.

This is (as has been said in previous pages) a name unique to God and attributed to Him alone, indicating the very essence of the Creator. Therefore, no pure creature can be called by that name. From this, it clearly follows that the Messiah is God.

Fifth, that the Gentiles were to go to the name of this Messiah, who is called by the name of God, the tetragrammaton. This agrees perfectly with what **John the Evangelist** says:

> He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world.

And also with what the Church sings in the Creed:

> Light of Light, true God of true God.

Moreover, that the Messiah was to be worshiped as God is found in **Psalm 72**, where it is read as follows:

> <note>Hebrew: מלכי תרשיש ואיים מנחה ישיבו מלכי שבא וסבא אשכר יקריבו</note>
> *The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall bring offerings; the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts.*

This is...

## *That the Messiah was to be recalled from Egypt, to which place he would go after his birth while fleeing Herod. Chapter IV.*

### CAPNIO <note>Capnio: the Greek-style pen name of Johannes Reuchlin, a famous German scholar of Hebrew who appears as a character in this dialogue</note>,

There is yet another mystery that was to occur after the birth of the Messiah: namely, his journey into **Egypt**, and his subsequent return from there into the land of **Israel**. For as the Evangelist relates, after the departure of the Magi kings, when **Herod** was preparing the death of the infant Christ, Christ himself, carried in his mother’s bosom, fled Herod and went into Egypt by angelic warning. And later, after Herod had died, he returned to the land of Israel. I would like to hear from you, therefore, if the ancient Jews who preceded the coming of Christ predicted anything concerning this mystery. 

GALATINUS <note>Galatinus: Pietro Galatino, the author, who speaks as an expert in Jewish tradition</note>: The ancient fathers certainly did not remain silent about the fact that the Messiah, fleeing the persecution of Herod after his birth, would go away into Egypt and would later return by God's command. For it is written in the exposition of the Book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Hadarsan** <term>Rabbi Moses Hadarsan: an 11th-century Jewish scholar from Narbonne known for his allegorical commentaries</term>, concerning that which is said in the fortieth chapter of Genesis: "And behold, a vine was before me" <note>original: והנה גפן לפני</note>, in this manner: "This is Israel, as it is written in the eightieth Psalm: 'You brought a vine out of Egypt'" <note>original: גפן ממצרים תסיע; Psalm 80:8</note>. Another interpretation: "And behold, a vine was before me." This is the King 
<margin>The Messiah is called a vine.</margin> 
Messiah, of whom it is said in the eightieth Psalm: "And the son whom your right hand has planted." <note>original: ובנה אשר נטעה ימינך; Psalm 80:15</note>

### BOOK EIGHT

This is to say: "And prepared," or "perfect that which your right hand has planted," or, "And the vine prepared and arranged." Or, "And the pedestal which your right hand has planted." <note>original: "Et præparata, uel perfice quam plantauit dextera tua... Et abacum quam plantauit dextera tua." These are various ways to translate the Hebrew of Psalm 80:15.</note> Here it must be noted that **chana** <term>chana: a Hebrew word (כנה) which can refer to a plant, a vine, or a base/pedestal</term>, which is placed there, is a noun for a vine that is ordered and well-disposed; it also signifies a pedestal or base. **Chana** is also a verb in the imperative mood from the Hebrew verb **can** <term>can: (כון) meaning to establish, prepare, or make ready</term>, which means to prepare, or to arrange, or to perfect. This **chana**, therefore—that is, the well-disposed and ordered vine—is the King **Messiah** <term>Messiah: the "Anointed One" expected to deliver Israel</term>, who was to be transferred out of Egypt.

To the aforementioned points, much is also contributed by what is written in the book **Berachoth** <term>Berachoth: "Blessings," a tractate of the Talmud dealing with prayers and benedictions</term>, in the chapter beginning **Harroe makom** <term>Harroe makom: "He who sees a place," the ninth chapter of the tractate Berachoth</term>, which means "He who sees the place." For it is said there:

> He who sees in a dream a **Soreka** <term>Soreka: (שורקה) a choice vine branch</term>, that is, a vine-shoot,
> will see or contemplate the Messiah <note>original: "yera sappe" (יראה צפה)</note>, of
> whom it is written in Psalm 80: "You shall transfer a vine from Egypt."

Here it should be noted that the text says "you shall transfer" <note>original: "transferes"</note> and not "you have transferred," as our [Latin] edition has it. Through this, it is clearly evident that the prophet was not speaking about the nation of Israel, but about the Messiah, who was to be called back out of Egypt. This is shown more clearly through the explanation of **Rabbenus Haccados** <term>Rabbenus Haccados: "Our Holy Master," a title for Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</term> in the book which he called **Gale Razeya** <term>Gale Razeya: "The Revealer of Secrets," a mystical work attributed in this period to Rabbi Judah</term>, meaning "The Revealer of Secrets." For in the seventh petition of that same book, it is read that among other things, **Antoninus** the Consul of the City of Rome had asked him: "What is the meaning of that saying in Psalm 80:

> 'You shall transfer,' or 'you shall remove, a vine from Egypt'?"

He answered him: "This is the Messiah." Antoninus said to him: "Is the King Messiah then to be born in Egypt? Was it not said in Micah, chapter 5:

> 'And you, Bethlehem, land of Ephrata, though you are small among the thousands of Ju-
> dah, out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be Ruler in Israel'?"

Rabbenus answered him: "I confess that the King Messiah will be born in Bethlehem. But it says, 'You shall transfer a vine from Egypt.' For when the Messiah is born, **Herod**, who shall reign in Jerusalem, will seek him out to kill him. However, by divine revelation, he will be compelled to flee into Egypt, where he will stay for a while, and afterwards he will return to Jerusalem by the command of God. Therefore the text says: 'You shall transfer a vine from Egypt.' Regarding his mother, however, it says: 'And the pedestal which your right hand has planted.' " Thus spoke that truly holy Rabbenus Haccados. 

But as for why the Mother of God is compared to a pedestal <note>original: "abaco"</note>, enough was said in the third chapter of the seventh book according to the opinion of the same Rabbenus Haccados. Furthermore, according to the traditions mentioned above, which assert that the Messiah was to be called back out of Egypt, that divine saying in Hosea, chapter 11, fits the same Messiah perfectly: "And out of Egypt I called my son." <note>original: וממצרים קראתי לבני / "Et ex Ægypto uocaui filium meum"</note>

Nor does it stand against our purpose that it says "I called" and not "I will call." For as **Rabbi Selomo** <term>Rabbi Selomo: Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</term> says regarding that saying in Isaiah, chapter 42:

> "I have done these words for them,"

every prophetic language speaks of the future as if it were the past. And this is because the word of God is considered as a finished deed, according to the opinion of the ancient **Talmudists**, as has been more broadly declared in the preceding pages.

### Chapter V.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>

Since our Lord Jesus Christ performed many miracles by his own power, therefore, to prove that he was the true Messiah, you ought to show that the Messiah himself was to perform miracles. <margin>GAL.</margin> <note>GAL. refers to Pietro Galatino, the author of this work, who is presented as a character in the dialogue.</note> Isaiah clearly foretold this among others when he says in chapter 35: **"The reward of God, he will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped."** <note>original: "גמול אלהים הוא יבא ויושיעכם : אז תפקחנה עיני עורים ואזני חרשים" - This is Isaiah 35:4-5 translated into English.</note> **"Then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall sing."** From these words it is manifest that the Messiah would not only perform miracles by his own power as God, but that he would even *be* God. Seeing as the ancient Jews handed down the tradition that these words of Isaiah ought to be understood as referring to the Messiah himself. They also openly foretold that the Pharisees—whom they call **parecim** <term>parecim: (פריצים) literally "the violent" or "the lawless," used here to mean scoundrels or those of corrupt character</term>, that is, the wicked, or those corrupt in character, or the reckless—would not believe in the miracles of the Messiah. And Jacob—that is, James of the village of <note>original: "זקיניא"</note> Zaccania—came to heal him in the name of Jesus, the son of Panther. **THE CHAPTER:** Why do they call the Lord Jesus the "son of Panther"?
**GALATINUS:** Because he had no father on earth, some therefore called him the son of Panther, who according to some was the great-great-grandfather of the glorious Virgin, his mother, from the line of Nathan, the son of David. But others called him the son of Joseph, who was indeed the spouse of the same Virgin. # EIGHTH

->Q 3<-

...they create a report <term>fame/reputation: originally *fama*, meaning a widely circulated report or public knowledge</term>, something they themselves have perceived either by sight or by some other sense. A narration of this kind provides true knowledge when two things coincide. The first of these is that the multitude of those narrating reaches such a number that it would be impossible, according to normal human behavior, for that multitude to secretly agree to fabricate a lie. 

For example, if we see people from diverse and distant regions, with different customs and languages, all agreeing that there is a city in the world called Rome, it will be established as a certainty for us that this city exists in the world. 

The second condition is that the thing narrated must be something that can be subjected to the senses. For if everyone in the East and everyone in the West were to narrate that the world had a beginning, or that it was eternal, or were to say that there was one creator of the world or many, their narration would certainly not provide certain knowledge <note>original: *scientia*</note>, but rather faith <note>original: *fides*</note>, since such narrated things cannot be perceived by the senses. 

If, however, for the sake of example, they were to narrate that in some region—say, in Flanders—they use sods <note>peat or turf</note> instead of wood to make a fire, their narration would produce certain knowledge, since what they narrate can be apprehended by the senses. 

Whenever, therefore, these two things coincide—namely, that the narrators are so many and of such a kind that they could not secretly agree to fabricate a lie, and that the thing narrated was perceived by the senses—then, without a doubt, according to the opinion of Avicenna, Algazel, and Ibnazatib <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Algazel (Al-Ghazali) were famous Persian philosophers whose works on logic and soul were widely read in Latin translation. "Ibnazatib" likely refers to another Arabic commentator, possibly Ibn al-Khatib.</note>, it provides certain knowledge. It was in this way that Jacob knew his son Joseph—whom he believed to be dead—was actually alive.

The second kind of things held through frequent report is when the narrators are indeed as we have described, but they say they did not see the thing themselves. They assert, however, that they saw and heard a multitude (such as we have described) who themselves said they had seen and heard what they are narrating. This category provides certain knowledge when those two conditions we mentioned for the first category coincide, along with a third: that if the chain of narrators extends further back in time, it must never be interrupted or entirely thinned out. Instead, the end and the middle must always correspond in quantity and quality to the beginning. 

In this way, some speak of the Law of Moses, saying it came down to Ezra and a few others. In this way, people today know that Alexander existed; in this way, Caesar; in this way, Plato; in this way, Aristotle; and in this way, all the other most excellent men whom ancient antiquity has handed down. 

In this way, if you pay attention, the Jews of our time must know that Moses existed, that he performed wonders, and that he gave the Law. They must also know that the ancient Jews worshipped the calf, killed many prophets, and rejected the Lord Jesus who asserted he was the Messiah, and received two false Messiahs in his place. 

For this reason, Moses directed the Jewish people to this way of knowing when he said in Deuteronomy, chapter 32: *Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will show thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee.* <note>original Hebrew: זכר ימות עולם בינו שנות דר ודור שאל אביך ויגדך זקניך ויאמרו לך — Deuteronomy 32:7</note>. David also used this way of knowing...

# BOOK

...[He] establishes [this], as when Psalm 77 <note>This is Psalm 78 in modern Bibles. The numbering of Psalms often differs between historical Latin versions and modern translations.</note> says: "So that the last generation might know, the children yet to be born, they shall rise up and tell their children, that they may set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep His commandments." <note>original Hebrew: למען ידעו דור אחרון בנים יולדו יקומו ויספרו לבניהם וישימו באלהים כסלם ולא ישכחו מעללי אל ומצותיו ינצורו</note> That is to say: So that the final generation may know; the children who are born shall rise and narrate these things to their own children. And they shall place their trust in God, and shall not forget the works of God, and shall keep His commandments.

<margin>Objection.</margin> CHAPTER. This method of knowing through "frequent report" <term>common report: *crebra fama*, the idea that if a massive number of people across different cultures all report the same event, it must be true</term> seems very weak according to the teaching of Aristotle. First, because we cannot have direct sensation of individual things perceived by the senses that are far removed from us; and consequently, we cannot have certain knowledge of them. Second, because we have not simply experienced these things ourselves, we are only relying on faith and belief. For this reason, there are "probable propositions" set down by Aristotle in his book on *Rhetoric*. Finally, because according to Aristotle, "that which is well-known" is the same as that which is "probable," as is clear in the five modes of probability established by him in the first book of the *Topics*.

<margin>Response of Ibnazatib.</margin> GAL. <note>Likely an abbreviation for a commentator or a specific section of the argument.</note> To this objection, let Ibnazatib <note>A Latinized name for an Arabic philosopher, possibly Ibn al-Khatib or a similar scholar studied by medieval theologians</note>, one of the Arabic philosophers listed above, respond, saying among other things:

> Know that there has been a controversy among the wise. Does the knowledge we hold through frequent report count as "necessary" <term>necessary knowledge: knowledge that is logically certain and cannot be doubted, as opposed to "probable" knowledge</term> or merely "probable"? Regarding this, after many things were said for both sides, the choice of all is finally that it is necessary. For a thing is "necessary" when we are neither willing nor able to make it doubtful to ourselves, even if we try to test our own minds. Furthermore, when we have heard all the objections raised against frequent report and then test ourselves, we find our souls judging with precision that Moses, for example, existed; and that he said he was a messenger of God sent to the faithful of Israel. We do not find anything among the objections that can overturn this. Such is the case with things that are necessary. Therefore, nothing that is argued against frequent report deserves a response. For a response ought to be "probable." But to treat a necessary matter with a probable argument creates circular reasoning, and that is impossible. These are his words, translated word-for-word from the Arabic.

From these words, it is clear that what has been said against frequent report does not deserve an answer.

<margin>What is necessary.</margin> Finally, the miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ are proved to be established through "necessary reason"—that is, through their effects. For the art of reasoning and demonstrating <note>the study of logic</note> teaches that causes are best concluded from their effects. Indeed, no one who possesses reason doubts that a man is "strong" if they see him performing acts of strength. And for whomever "speed" is present, it is obvious that he himself is "fast." For the nature of each thing performs what is characteristic to itself, and does not mix with the effects of contrary things. Therefore, that our Lord Jesus Christ and his followers visibly performed works in his name which exceed the capacity of all nature—in the miraculous healing of illnesses, in the raising of the dead, in the stupendous transformation of the celestial bodies and elements, and (what is more miraculous) in the sudden inspiration of human minds—it is evident that unlearned men <note>original: *idiotę*, used here in the classical sense of laypeople or those without formal education</note> and the ignorant were instantly filled with the Holy Spirit and attained the highest wisdom, an understanding of the scriptures, and the eloquence of various languages. I say that all these things were done by our Lord Jesus Christ, and after him by his followers in his name, as the subsequent effect clearly shows. This is because it was not through the violence of arms...

[...not by] violence, nor by the permission or license of pleasures, but through the unrefined and simple disciples of Christ, who were very few and poor. Against the unheard-of rage and tyranny of the persecutors of the whole world—both Jews and Gentiles—countless crowds, not only of the unrefined and common people but also of the wisest men, spurned the worship of demons. This demonic worship had previously enticed souls so strongly that never before, neither through Moses nor through any other—even when the Jews themselves saw many stupendous miracles—had they been so completely turned away from it. Yet now, they were most affectionately converted to the faith of the Lord Jesus himself. In this faith, they are taught things that transcend all human intellect and reason; they restrain the pleasures of the body which are most desired by mortals, and they are commanded to labor for the sake of invisible things and to despise all worldly things. That the minds of mortals should assent to these things is both the greatest miracle and a manifest work of divine inspiration. Moreover, that this was not done by fortune or chance is especially clear from this: God predicted many centuries beforehand through the oracles of the prophets that He would do all this, even designating the time and the manner of its doing. Therefore, this so wonderful conversion of the world to the faith of Christ is the most certain evidence of the past miracles which are narrated and read in written books. So much so, that it is not necessary for those miracles to be repeated further, since they appear most evidently in their own effect. Although even in our own times, for the preservation of the Christian faith, God does not cease to perform miracles through His saints. It was led to believe such arduous things, to do such difficult things (contrary to flesh and blood), and to hope for such high and hidden things—and it believed them without [new] miracles. Luke 18:31-33.</note> Likewise in Matthew chapter 16: *The Son of Man,* he said, *is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will render to every man according to his works.* <note>Matthew 16:27.</note> Concerning his disciples, he spoke in Matthew chapter 10: *Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. Be therefore wise as serpents, and simple as doves. But beware of men. For they will deliver you up in councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues, and you shall be brought before governors and before kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles,* and so forth. Finally, he prophesied concerning the Jews when, as Luke says in chapter 19: *Seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: If thou also hadst known, and that in this thy day, the things that are to thy peace; but now they are hidden from thy eyes. For the days shall come upon thee, and thy enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and straiten thee on every side, and beat thee flat to the ground, and thy children who are in thee; and they shall not leave in thee a stone upon a stone, because thou hast not known the time of thy visitation.* <note>Luke 19:41-44. This refers to the Roman Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> He said the same in other places as well. Wherefore there is no doubt that he was a true prophet, and none other than that same one of whom Moses spoke, as we have already shown.

### That the Messiah Ought to Preach Repentance. Chapter VIII.

->CAPNIO,<- 
<note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name of Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist and character in this dialogue.</note>

We read in the Gospels that our Lord Jesus Christ taught repentance; indeed, when he first began to preach, he proposed these words: *Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven will draw near to you.* <note>Matthew 4:17. The Latin "Poenitentiam agite" can be translated as "Repent" or "Do penance."</note> It is certain that by preaching repentance—both by himself and through his disciples—he led the entire world to the worship of the one and true God. For this reason, so that you may also be able to show by this mystery that he existed as the true Messiah, [show] that the Messiah himself was going to preach repentance, and through repentance [lead] the whole world...

...will lead the whole world to the goal of salvation, you must show this through the scriptures of the ancient Jews.

**GALATINUS**: Concerning repentance, therefore, which the Messiah was to preach both by himself and through his disciples, it is written in the Jerusalem book of <term>Makkot</term> <note>original: "Maccoth," meaning "Lashes," a tractate of the Talmud dealing with legal punishments</note>, in the chapter that begins *Ellu hen haggolin* <note>Hebrew: אלו הן הגולין</note>, that is, "These are the exiles." There it is said, word for word: 

"Phinehas said, It is written in Psalm 25: *Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he will teach sinners the way.* <note>original: "טוב וישר יהוה על כן יורה חטאים בדרך"</note> But why is He good? Because He is upright. And why is He upright? Because He is good. Therefore, He will teach sinners the way. Indeed, He will teach the way by which they may perform repentance. For it was asked of **Wisdom**: what is the condemnation of the sinner? And she said to those who asked, as it is written in Proverbs chapter 13: *Evil pursues sinners.* <note>original: "חטאים תרדף רעה"</note> They also asked **Prophecy**: what is the condemnation of the sinner? And she said, as in Ezekiel chapter 18: *The soul that sins, it shall die.* <note>original: "הנפש החטאת היא תמות"</note> They also questioned the **Law**, saying: what is the condemnation of the sinner? And it answered them: *Let him offer a sacrifice, and it shall be forgiven him.* As it is written in Leviticus chapter 1: *And it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.* <note>original: "וירצה לו לכפר עליו"</note> Finally, they asked the **Holy and Blessed God**: what is the condemnation of the sinner? And He said to them: *Let him perform repentance, and it shall be forgiven him.* And this is what is written in Psalm 25: *Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he will teach the erring,* or sinners, *the way,* or *in the way.* For He shows sinners the way of performing repentance." 

This is the tradition. It is also found in <term>Yoma</term> <note>original: "יומא," meaning "The Day," referring to the tractate on the Day of Atonement</note>, in the chapter beginning *Yom Ha-Kippurim* <note>Hebrew: יום הכפורים</note>, that is, "The Day of Atonements." There we read: 

"Rabbi Isaac said: Come and see that the way of the Holy and Blessed God is not like the way of flesh and blood. For the way of flesh and blood is that if a man offends his neighbor, sometimes he may appease him with words, but sometimes he cannot appease him with words alone. But the way of the Holy and Blessed God is not so. A man commits a transgression, and yet he appeases Him with words. As Hosea says in chapter 14: *Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity. Take words with you and return to the Lord.* <note>original: "שובה ישראל עד יהוה אלהיך כי כשלת בעוניך קחו עמכם דברים ושובו אל יהוה"</note> And not only this, but He will also bestow goodness upon him. As it is said immediately after: *Say to him, take away all iniquity and receive us graciously* <note>literally: "receive good," original: "כל תשא עון וקח טוב"</note>. And not only this, but the Scripture regards him as if he were offering calves in sacrifice. For it is then said: *So we will render the calves of our lips.* <note>original: "ונשלמה פרים שפתינו"</note> Perhaps you will say: calves for our guilt? He teaches what should be said to this in what follows: *I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.* <note>original: "ארפא משובתם אהבם נדבה"</note>" 

This is the tradition. That

the efficacy and power of repentance is still so great appears most clearly from what is read in the <term>Midrash Shir Ha-Shirim</term> <note>original: "שיר השירים," the Rabbinic commentary on the Song of Songs</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs.

Regarding what is said in the fifth chapter of the same book <note>The Midrash on the Song of Songs</note>, *Open to me, my sister.* For there it is said: Rabbi Joses stated that the holy and blessed God said to Israel: "My children, open for me one opening of repentance as small as the eye of a needle, and I will open for you openings of mercy through which wagons and chariots may enter." Rabbi Levi said: "If the children of Israel had performed repentance for even a single day, they would have been redeemed immediately, and the Son of David—that is, the Messiah—would have come to them immediately." From where does he prove this? From that which is written in Psalm 95: <note>original: "היום אם בקולו תשמעו," Psalm 94 in the Latin Vulgate numbering</note> *Today, if you would hear his voice.* This is the tradition. From these words of the Psalm, cited last regarding the Messiah, and by reason of the preceding words of the same Psalm, it necessarily follows that the Messiah is God. For in the same Psalm, it is first stated: <note>original: "באו נשתחוה ונכרעה נברכה לפני יהוה עושינו כי הוא אלהינו ואנחנו עם מרעיתו וצון ידו"</note> *Come, let us worship, and let us bow down; let us kneel before the face of God our maker. For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand.* And then immediately following is that which was explained as referring to the Messiah: *Today, if you would hear his voice.* From this it is surely consequent that the God who was to teach the way of repentance (as was stated at the beginning of this chapter) is none other than the Messiah himself, who was destined to preach repentance. 

To confirm this matter, it should further be noted what is said in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>The rabbinic commentary on the Song of Songs</note> regarding that verse in Song of Songs 7: *Looking toward Damascus* <note>original: "ציפת פני דמשק"</note> or *toward the face of Damascus.* There it reads: Rabbi Johanan said, "In the future, Jerusalem shall reach as far as the gates of Damascus." What is the proof for this? That which is written in Zechariah 9: <note>original: "משא דבר יהוה בארץ חדרך ודמשק מנוחתו"</note> *The burden* <note>or prophecy</note> *of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be his rest.* What is "Hadrach"? Rabbi Judas and Rabbi Nahmias disagree on this. For Rabbi Judas says that it is a place in Damascus called Hadrach. But Rabbi Nahmias says that this is the King Messiah, who is *had* <note>original Hebrew: "חד," meaning sharp or acute</note> toward the nations of the world, and *rach* <note>original Hebrew: "רך," meaning tender or soft</note> toward Israel. Another explanation says that "Hadrach" is the King Messiah, who is to come *to lead* <note>original Hebrew: "להדריך," lehadrich, meaning to direct or guide</note> or to bring the entire world through repentance to the face of the holy and blessed God. It follows: *And Damascus shall be his rest.* And when Damascus becomes his rest, his rest shall be nowhere but the house of the sanctuary <note>the Temple</note>. Just as it is written in Psalm 132: <note>original: "זאת מנוחתי עדי עד"</note> *This is my rest forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it.* All this is tradition. 

To understand these things, it must be observed that this word *Hadrach* <note>or *Hidrach*</note> is spoken and pronounced by the Hebrews in two ways. For sometimes it is written with the letter *He* <note>ה</note>, which is the fifth in the alphabet, and then it is a single word which signifies "to lead along a way." But sometimes it is written with the letter *Heth* <note>ח</note>, which holds the eighth place in the alphabet, and then it consists of two words: namely, *had* <note>sharp</note> and *rach* <note>tender</note>. These two qualities apply perfectly to Christ, who will be sharp toward the repentant through justice, and tender through mercy. He was also sharp toward Paul when he was a persecutor, near the gates of Damascus, and afterwards tender to the same man when he was repentant.

<summary>Galatinus uses Midrashic and Prophetic texts to argue that the Messiah's role is to lead the world to repentance. He analyzes the name "Hadrach" from Zechariah as a title for the Messiah, representing both his justice (sharpness) and his mercy (tenderness).</summary>

This was not only for that time, but truly for eternity. For Christ as God will never cease to dwell in the minds of the faithful. ### That the Messiah had to be poor and humble. Chapter IX.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>Capnio is the scholar-persona of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist.</note>

Among the other things that the more recent Jews most strongly deny concerning the Messiah is his poverty and humility. For when they hear that the poverty and humility of our Lord Jesus Christ was so great and so wondrous—that he had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8), nor the means to pay the temple tax <note>original: "didragma"</note>, nor the means (as Luke records) to satisfy the hunger of his poor disciples—lest they be forced to confess that He was the true Messiah, they deny that the Messiah himself was to be poor and humble. It is necessary that you show this from their own scriptures to overcome their lack of faith. GALATINUS: <note>Pietro Galatino, the author, acting as the teacher.</note> Although Jewish blindness and pride have erred so greatly in this matter that they decided the Lord was not the Messiah because he was so exceedingly poor and humble, they nevertheless used to read that the King Messiah would be poor; but they did not understand that he would come in such a way because of their own pride. CAPNIO: This, I say, is what you must chiefly prove. GALATINUS: Let them first hear Zechariah saying these things among others in his ninth chapter: <note>original: "גילי מאד בת ציון הריעי בת ירושלם הנה מלכך יבוא לך צדיק ונושע הוא עני ורוכב על חמור ועל עיר בן אתונות"</note> That is: *Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King comes to you; he is just and having salvation; he is poor <note>original: "pauper," translating the Hebrew 'ani'</note> and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass.* And a little later: <note>original: "ודבר שלום לגוים ומשלו מים עד ים ומנהר עד אפסי ארץ"</note> That is: *And he shall speak peace to the nations; and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.* That these things must be understood as referring to the Messiah is clear through the gloss <note>interpretive commentary</note> of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105)</note>. Which says: "Behold, your King comes to you. This cannot be explained except as referring to the King Messiah. Because it is said here, 'And his dominion shall be from sea to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth.' And no such ruler was found in the 'Second House'—that is, during the time of the Second Temple." From which it is clearly evident that the Kingdom of the Messiah is to be understood spiritually, since a temporal kingdom and such poverty cannot exist together. To this also points what Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Moses the Preacher, an 11th-century rabbi from Narbonne</note> says in his exposition of Genesis, upon that passage in the 49th chapter of the same book: *Binding his foal unto the vine...*

Thus it says: When the Messiah comes to Jerusalem, he will be the one binding his donkey, and he will ride, and upon it he will come into Jerusalem, so that he may lead himself in poverty, or humility, just as it is written in Zechariah chapter 9: *The poor and humble one, riding upon a donkey, or a she-ass.* There follows in the book of Genesis in the same place: *And his donkey’s colt to the choice vine.* For when he comes to gather Israel—as is said in Zechariah 10: *I will whistle for them and gather them, for I have redeemed them* <note>original: "אשרקה להם ואקבצם. כי פדיתים"</note>—then he will ride upon the foal of his donkey. And so Zechariah says in chapter 9: *And upon a colt, the foal of donkeys.* This is the tradition.

Likewise, in the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>The "Great Genesis," an ancient collection of Jewish explanations and stories regarding the first book of the Bible.</note> regarding that verse written in Genesis chapter 49, *The scepter shall not depart from Judah*, among other things, it is read: *The scepter shall not depart.* This refers to the King Messiah, the son of David, who is to come to shatter the kingdoms with a rod, or with a staff. Just as it is said in Psalm 2: *You shall break them with a rod of iron; like a potter’s vessel you shall dash them to pieces* <note>original: "תרועם בשבט ברזל ככלי יוצר תנפצם"</note>. It follows: *And a scribe (or a crusher) from between his feet.* This is also the King Messiah, who is to come to crush the nations with his feet. Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 26: *The foot of the poor shall trample it* <note>original: "תרמסנה רגלי עני"</note>. For that poor man is the Messiah, of whom it was said in Zechariah chapter 9: *Poor and riding upon a donkey.* Thus far the tradition. From these things which have been said, therefore, it is clearly evident enough that the Messiah was to be poor and humble, and was to come riding upon a donkey to bring salvation. Therefore, the Jews will be least able to deny that our Savior was the true Messiah simply because he was poor and humble.

### That the Messiah was to undergo many sufferings, and that God too would suffer much. Chapter X.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>Johann Reuchlin's scholar-persona.</note>

Since the Jews of our time—when they hear that our Redeemer was hungry even after a fast of forty days and nights, was tempted in many ways by the devil, was exhausted from his journey while traveling through cities and towns preaching the kingdom of God and leading sinners to repentance, or that he fled like a fearful man from the Jews who wanted to stone him, or that at the approaching hour of his passion he began to fear and be weary and sorrowful so that he might show himself to be a true man—they say that he was neither the true Messiah nor God. For this reason, you would do well to show from their own scriptures that both the Messiah and God himself (for the two were to be the same) were destined to suffer such things, and indeed far more grievous ones. 

GALATINUS: I shall first bring forward Jeremiah, chapter 14, who produces these words among others: *O Hope of Israel, its Savior in time of trouble, why should You be like a stranger in the land, and like a traveler who turns aside to stay for a night? Why should You be like a man astonished, like a warrior who cannot save? Yet You, O Lord, are in our midst, and Your name is called upon us; do not leave us* <note>original: "מקוה ישראל מושיעו בעת צרה למה תהיה כגר בארץ וכארח נטה ללון למה תהיה כאיש נדהם כגבור לא יוכל להושיע ואתה בקרבנו יהוה ושמך עלינו נקרא אל תניחנו"</note>. # BOOK

...[his] Savior in the time of trouble, when you shall be like a stranger in the land, or like a traveler turning aside to stay, or to seek lodging. Why are you like a man who is fearful, or terrified, like a strong man who cannot save? <note>This is a citation of Jeremiah 14:8-9, where the prophet asks God why He behaves like a helpless stranger in His own land.</note> You, however, are in our midst, O God, and your name is invoked upon us: do not forsake us. Regarding the things mentioned above, a passage in the book **Torath Cohanim** <term>Instruction of the Priests; the ancient Rabbinic commentary on Leviticus known as the Sifra</term>, that is, the "Law of the Priests," which is the exposition of the book of Leviticus, serves perfectly. There, regarding the statement in the 25th chapter of that book: <note>original: "וכי גרים ותושבים אתם עמדי"</note> *Since you are strangers and sojourners (or dwellers) with me.* <note>Leviticus 25:23</note> For it is said there: The Holy One, blessed be He, said, "Do not make yourselves into a permanent substance [on earth]," for you are but guests and temporary residents with me. And so David said in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 29: <note>original: "כי אנחנו לפניך גרים ותושבים בכל אבותינו"</note> *Since we are strangers or pilgrims before you, and dwellers, or settlers, like all our fathers. Our days upon the earth are like a shadow, and there is no staying.* <note>1 Chronicles 29:15</note> And so it is also said in Psalm 38: <note>original: "גר אנכי עמך תושב בכל אבותי"</note> *For I am a stranger or a pilgrim with you, a dweller or settler, like all my fathers.* <note>Psalm 39:12 in modern numbering.</note> They are called with me **gherím uetošabím** <note>Hebrew: גרים ותושבים</note>, that is, strangers or pilgrims, as well as dwellers or settlers. It is enough for the servant to be like his Master; when that which is to come for me arrives, behold, it shall be for me just as it was for you. This is the tradition.

Now, the aforementioned words of both Jeremiah and this tradition cannot properly apply to God alone, nor to man alone. Therefore, they apply most excellently to the Messiah alone, who is both God and man. For by reason of his divinity, he is the "Expectation of Israel," and by reason of his humanity, he was in his passion like a stranger, a pilgrim, and a man terrified and fearful—even like a strong man who cannot save.

To the same purpose, according to the Chaldean translation <note>Refers to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, is that which is written in Isaiah chapter 5: <note>original: "לכן גלה עמי מבלי דעת"</note> *Therefore my people are led into captivity without knowledge.* Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: "Because of this, namely because they are without science and knowledge." And the rest follows: <note>original: "כי הרחיבה שאול נפשה ופערה פיה לבלי חק"</note> *Therefore hell has enlarged its soul, and opened its mouth without limit.* Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "Hell has enlarged its soul," that is, itself. "And it opened its mouth without limit." Because there was no **hok** <note>Hebrew: חק</note>, that is, divine precept, in their hand. And afterward: <note>original: "וישח אדם וישפל איש"</note> *And man shall be bowed down, or curved, and man shall be humbled, or made lower.* Regarding this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: Jonathan translated this into Chaldean thus: *And man shall be curved or bowed down, and the high or strong of men shall be humbled.* <note>Refers to the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel.</note> It is clear through this kind of exposition that they themselves were such before the Holy and Blessed God, that He might show Himself as a man **Nidham** <note>Hebrew: נדחם, meaning stunned or terrified, from Jeremiah 14:9.</note>, that is, terrified or fearful. This is what He says in Deuteronomy 32: <note>original: "צור ילדך תשי ותשכח אל מחוללך"</note> *The Rock that begot you, you have forsaken, and you have forgotten the God who gave you birth.*

->**BOOK EIGHT. 571**<-

"The God who made you to be born, or who begot you, you will weaken, or afflict, and you will forget the wounded, or killed, or afflicted, or your sorrowful God." <note>This is an interpretive translation of Deuteronomy 32:18, playing on the Hebrew word *Tzur* (Rock/Creator), which some commentators linked to *Tzar* (suffering or anguish).</note> Thus far, R. Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says. Similar to this is what is held in the book **Siphre**, <margin>Talmudic exposition.</margin> <term>Sifre: An ancient Rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy.</term> in that place where the previously mentioned words, "The God who begot you, you will weaken, or afflict," are explained along with the rest. There it is said word-for-word:

"The Holy and Blessed God said to Israel: You have made me as if I were a male wanting to give birth. For if a woman were in labor, sitting upon her birth-stool, would she not be troubled? As it is said in Isaiah, chapter 37: <note>original: "באו בנים עד משבר וכח אין ללדת"</note> *The children have come to the birth, and there is no power to bring them forth.* <note>Isaiah 37:3</note> And if it were a woman in pain, giving birth for the first time, would she not be even more troubled? As in Jeremiah, chapter 4: <note>original: "קול כחולה שמעתי צרה כמבכירה"</note> *For I heard a voice as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one bringing forth her first child.* <note>Jeremiah 4:31</note> And if there were two in her womb, would she not be in even greater anguish? As it is said in Genesis, chapter 25: <note>original: "ויתרצצו הבנים בקרבה"</note> *And the children struggled together within her.* <note>Genesis 25:22</note> And if it were a male, who has no way of giving birth, who sought to give birth, would not his anguish be doubled? As it is said in Jeremiah, chapter 30: <note>original: "שאלו נא וראו אם יולד זכר"</note> *Ask now, and see, if a male can give birth?*" <note>Jeremiah 30:6. This midrash uses the biological impossibility of a male giving birth to illustrate the "unnatural" and extreme nature of God's suffering due to Israel's actions.</note>

Another exposition: "The God who begot you, you will weaken, or afflict, and you will forget the wounded, or killed, or afflicted, or your sorrowful God." The Holy Blessed God said: "You have forgotten me because of the merit of your fathers." And so He himself says in Isaiah, chapter 51: <note>original: "הביטו אל צור חצבתם"</note> *Look to the rock from which you were hewn, or carved.* <note>Isaiah 51:1</note>

<margin>Another Talmudic exposition.</margin> Yet another exposition: "The God who begot you, you will weaken." The Holy and Blessed God said: "Every time I sought to do good for you, you weakened my celestial power." It follows: "And you will forget your sorrowing God." R. Meir said: "Namely, the God who will be in sorrow for you, or through you. The God, I say, who will be in anguish for you, or through you." As it is said in Psalm 47: <note>original: "שם חיל כיולדה"</note> *There was pain as of a woman in labor.* <note>Psalm 48:6 in modern numbering.</note> All these things are from the book **Siphre**.

It is also read in the book **Sanhedrin** <term>A major volume of the Talmud dealing with law and the Messiah.</term> in the chapter *Helec*, that R. Yehudi said: "The Son of David (that is, the Messiah) will not come until the wicked Kingdom (that is, the Roman Empire, according to the gloss of R. Solomon) has extended itself over Israel." R. Ula said: "Let the Messiah come, but let me not see him." R. Yose said: "Let him come, and would that I be worthy to sit in the shadow of his donkey’s tail." <note>This colorful expression reflects a desire to be near the Messiah's humble arrival, even in the lowliest position.</note>

Abbaye said to Rabba: "What is the reason why you do not wish to see him? Is it because of his passion, or his tribulation?" For there is a tradition: The disciples of Eliezer asked him, saying, "What shall a man do to be delivered from the passion, or the tribulation of the Messiah?" <note>Commonly known as the "Birth Pangs of the Messiah" — a period of global suffering preceding his arrival.</note> He answered them: "Let him occupy himself with the Law <term>Torah</term> and works of mercy." Mor said: "Behold, he practices the Law and works of mercy, yet perhaps sin will make him liable." Just as Jacob objected; for it is written in Genesis, chapter 31: And the Lord said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers, and to the place of your birth, and I [will be with you...]"

"...I will be with you." And yet it is written in Genesis, chapter 32: <note>original: "ויירא יעקב מאוד"</note> *And Jacob was greatly afraid.* <note>Genesis 32:7</note> For he feared lest sin had made him vulnerable. So also said **Rabbi Yohanan**: <note>A leading 3rd-century Palestinian rabbi.</note> "Let the Messiah come, but let me not see him." **Resh Lakish** <note>Simeon ben Lakish, a prominent 3rd-century scholar and contemporary of Yohanan.</note> said to him: "What is the reason? Is it because of what is written in Amos, chapter 5: <margin>Amos 5; Jeremiah 30</margin> *As if a man should flee from the face of a lion*?" <note>Amos 5:19</note> Not at all; rather, it is because of what is written in Jeremiah, chapter 30: *Ask now, and see, whether a male can give birth?* For what reason? Or what does this mean: <margin>H</margin> <note>original: "מדוע ראיתי כל גבר ידיו על חלציו כיולדה ונהפכו כל פנים לירקון"</note> *Why do I see every man with his hands on his loins, like a woman in labor, and all faces are turned to paleness?* <note>Jeremiah 30:6. The Latin uses "ictericiam," referring to a jaundiced or sickly yellow-green color caused by terror.</note> This means: "Because I saw every man with his hands on his loins like one giving birth, and all faces—namely of the angels and of Israel—turned pale," according to the gloss of **Rabbi Solomon**. <note>Rashi (Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac).</note> But what does it mean to have "seen every man"? **Rabba** <note>A common title for a great teacher or specifically referring here to an authority in the Talmud.</note> said: "This refers to the One who possesses all power and authority—namely God," as the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says, "who Himself will be in anguish like one giving birth." And what is meant by *And all faces are turned to paleness*? Rabbi Yohanan said: "Even the faces of the family above [the angels] and the family below [mankind]." For in the hour when the Holy and Blessed God said: "These [the Israelites] are the work of my hands, and those [the Gentiles] are also the work of my hands. How then can I destroy the latter for the sake of the former?" **Rabbi Papa** <note>A 4th-century Babylonian scholar.</note> said: "To this end is what men are accustomed to say: 'The ox ran and fell, so they substituted a horse for it in the stable.'" Thus far the tradition. 

The gloss of Rabbi Solomon, explaining the example brought at the end, says this: "When a certain man's ox was running, it fell. Therefore, they put a horse in its place in the stable. The owner of the ox and horse would not have done this before, for he loved the ox so much. But after the ox was healed, it was difficult for him to drive the horse out of the stable to put the ox back there." <margin>Rabbi Solomon</margin> So does the Holy and Blessed God. For when the fall of Israel occurs, God gives their greatness to the nations of the world. But when Israel later returns to repentance, it is hard for God to destroy them—that is, the Gentiles—for the sake of Israel. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. 

Certainly, several things are to be noted in this tradition. First, that the Messiah was desired with great affection by everyone, even by those who, because of the torments he was to suffer, did not wish to see him. Secondly, that according to that authority of Jeremiah which they bring in there, wishing to give the reason why he did not want to see him—namely, *Ask, I pray, and see if a male gives birth. For what reason? Because I saw every man with his hands on his loins like one giving birth*—God Himself, in the time of the Messiah, was to suffer extreme torments. Thus, the "Christian Talmudists" <note>Hebraist scholars who interpreted Jewish texts through a Christological lens.</note> explain that "every man" there refers to the Holy and Blessed God. Third and finally, that the nations of the world were established by God in the place of the Jews, and the Jews themselves were cast out from their place. This also, as far as it pertains to our purpose, appears more clearly in the **Bereshit Rabbah Ketanna** <margin>Bereshit Rabbah</margin> <term>Bereshit Rabbah: A collection of ancient Rabbinic interpretations (Midrash) on the Book of Genesis.</term> (that is, in the Lesser Exposition of the book of Genesis), where it is written concerning Genesis chapter 36: *And Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom.* <note>Genesis 36:32</note> It says: "This is what is written in Jeremiah chapter 30: *For thus says the Lord: We have heard a voice of terror, or trembling; of fear, and not of peace. Ask now, and see, whether a male gives birth...*"

## That the Messiah must voluntarily undergo the most bitter torments for the human race. Chapter XI.

### CAPNIO,

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'C' containing a figure of a scholar seated at a desk with books.</image-desc>
Since we read that Christ suffered voluntarily for the salvation of the human race, I would like to know whether the ancient Jews predicted that the Messiah would undergo torments voluntarily. **GALATINUS**: Indeed. For, setting aside the prophets for now, it is most clearly shown in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Hadarsan** <note>Moses ha-Darshan of Narbonne (11th century), a famed compiler of Midrashic legends.</note> that the Messiah himself would suffer torments freely and voluntarily out of love for the human race. There, upon that saying in the first chapter of the same book: <note>original: "ויאמר אלהים יהי אור ויהי אור"</note> *And God said: Let there be light, and there was light* <note>Genesis 1:3</note>, it is read as follows: <margin>Psalm 97</margin> This is what is written: <note>original: "אור זרע לצדיק"</note> *Light is sown for the righteous.* <note>Psalm 97:11</note> **Rabbi Abba** said: <margin>Daniel chapter 2</margin> It is also written: <note>original: "ונהורא עמיה שריא"</note> *And the light dwells with him.* <note>Daniel 2:22</note> For this is the light of the King Messiah. <margin>Psalm 36</margin> For thus it was said of him: <note>original: "כי עמך מקור חיים באורך נראה אור"</note> *For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light.* <note>Psalm 36:9</note> This is the light of the King Messiah. Moreover, he teaches that God hid the Messiah and his generation beneath the throne of His glory. Then **Satan** said before God: "Lord of the world, this light hidden beneath the throne of your glory—to whom does it belong?" He answered him: "To the Messiah and his generation." Satan said before Him: "Lord of the world, allow me, and I will oppose the Messiah and his generation." God said to him: "You will not be able to prevail against him." Satan said again before Him: "Allow me, and I will be able." The holy and blessed God said to him: "If you, Satan, are so eager for this, I will destroy him from the world. Nevertheless, I will not destroy even one single soul of that generation." And soon the holy and blessed God began to speak with the Messiah, and said to him: "My righteous Messiah, those who are hidden with you are of such a kind that it shall be that their sins will lead you into a heavy yoke. For your eyes shall not see light, and your ears shall hear great reproach. Your nose shall smell stench, and..."
