<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the characters Capnio (Reuchlin) and Galatinus, specifically quoting a Midrashic account (attributed to Moses ha-Darshan) where God describes the physical suffering the Messiah will endure for the sins of humanity. It establishes the theological argument for the Messiah's pre-existence and voluntary sacrifice.</meta>

**BOOK EIGHT**

[...your] mouth will taste bitterness, and your tongue will cling to the roof of your mouth; your skin will stick to your bones, and your strength will be wasted away by grief and groaning. Is it therefore your will to be among these things? For if you take these upon yourself, it will indeed be well. But if not, behold, I will drive them away from now on." The Messiah answered before Him: "Lord of the world, I indeed joyfully take upon myself these tribulations or torments, yet on this condition: that in my days You bring the dead to life—both those who have died from the first Adam until then, and not only those, but also those who were devoured by wolves and lions, and those who happened to be submerged in the seas and rivers. And not only those, but also the miscarriages. And not only the miscarriages, but also those whom You intended to create according to Your foreknowledge, save them in my days." The holy and blessed God <note>A translation of the Hebrew title "HaKadosh Baruch Hu," a common way to refer to God in Jewish tradition.</note> said to him, "I grant it." Immediately, therefore, out of love, the Messiah took upon himself all torments and tribulations. As it is written in Isaiah, chapter 53: <term>נגש והוא נענה</term> <note>original: "niggas ve-hu na’aneh"</note> That is: **He was oppressed, and he was afflicted.** This entire account is a tradition in which five things especially worthy of note against the Jews of our age are contained.

The first of these is that the Messiah, before he existed according to his humanity, was light and illumination with God and in God, even in the beginning when God created the world. With this, the word of the Lord Jesus himself is in strong agreement, where he says in John, chapter 8: *Before Abraham was, I am.* Likewise in chapter 7 <note>The author likely refers to the themes in John 8:12 or 12:46</note>: *And I have come as a light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in darkness.*

The second point is that by divine permission, Satan was to oppose the Messiah and those believing in him, and was to disturb him with every effort. With this, the saying of the same Lord in Luke, chapter 22, most closely agrees: *Simon, behold, Satan has asked for you, that he might sift you like wheat.* From this it is clear that it does not detract from Christ at all that he was tempted by the devil.

The third point is that the Messiah was to suffer in manifold and most grievous ways because of the sins of the human race. This is noted where it is said that God entered into a pact with the Messiah and said to him: "My righteous Messiah, those who are stored up with you—namely, through predestination—will be of such a kind that their future sins will lead you into a most heavy yoke." From this it is evident that none of those things which our Savior suffered prevents him from having been the Messiah. Since it was necessary for the Messiah himself to suffer for the salvation of men and so that the scriptures might be fulfilled.

The fourth point is that just as through Adam all were dying, so through the Messiah all were to be brought to life. This is noted where the Messiah is introduced speaking with God and saying: "Lord of the world, I indeed joyfully take upon myself these tribulations or torments, on the condition that in my days You bring the dead to life," along with the rest.

The fifth and final point is that the Messiah was to be tortured and suffer torments not unwillingly, but freely and voluntarily out of love, for the sake of the salvation of the human race. From these points, not only is the intended argument clear, but also that the Messiah himself, who was to be affected by torments, is true God.

## That God was to suffer beatings, reproaches, insults, and even death. Chapter XII.

### CAPNIO,

Although in the preceding parts you have shown quite abundantly that the Messiah is both God and man, and that God Himself was to undergo many torments; yet, so that Jewish obstinacy <note>original: "perfidia," a term used in historical polemics to describe a refusal to believe in Christian doctrine</note> may be more and more convinced, you should still more expressly prove through their own scriptures that God Himself was to be afflicted with beatings, reproaches, and even death for the salvation of the human race. 

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> This is clear, first of all, from what is written in the third chapter of Lamentations: <term>יושב בדד וידם כי נטל עליו : יתן בעפר פיהו אולי יש תקוה : יתן למכהו לחי ישבע בחרפה</term> <note>original: Lamentations 3:28–30</note>. That is: **He shall sit alone and keep silent, because he has carried, or borne, it upon himself. He shall put his mouth in the ground, or in the dust. Perhaps there will be hope. He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he shall be filled with reproach, or insult.** 

That these things ought to be understood as referring to God <margin>Lamentations</margin> is clear in the *Midrash Echa* <note>A Rabbinic commentary on the Book of Lamentations</note>, that is, in the exposition of the lamentations of Jeremiah. Where, upon those same words, it is said exactly thus: 

"Rabbi Samuel the son of Nahman <note>A significant 3rd-century teacher in the Land of Israel</note> said: 'The Holy and Blessed God called the ministering angels and said to them: "When a king of flesh and blood <note>A common Hebrew idiom (basar va-dam) referring to a mortal human being, contrasted with the Divine</note> mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He hangs a sackcloth over his door." And He said to them: "I also shall do thus." As it is written in the fiftieth chapter of Isaiah: <term>אלביש שמים קדרות ושק אשים כסותם</term> <note>original: Isaiah 50:3</note>. That is: **I clothe the heavens with darkness, and make sackcloth their covering.** 

Again He said to them: "When a king of flesh and blood mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He extinguishes the lights." And He said to them: "I also shall do thus." And this is what is written in the third chapter of Joel: <term>שמש וירח קדרו וכוכבים אספו נגהם</term> <note>original: Joel 3:15</note>. That is: **The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars have hidden their brightness, and God shall roar from Zion, and utter His voice from Jerusalem.** 

Again He asked them, saying: "When a king of flesh and blood mourns, what does he do?" They answered Him: "He walks barefoot." He said to them: "I too shall act thus." And this is what is written in the first chapter of Nahum: <term>יהוה בסופה ובשערה דרכו וענן אבק רגליו</term> <note>original: Nahum 1:3</note>. That is: **God's way is in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of His feet.** 

Again He asked them, saying: "When a king of flesh and blood mourns, what does he do?" They said to him: "He sits and keeps silent." And He said to them: "I also shall do thus." And this is what is written in the third chapter of Lamentations: **He shall sit alone and keep silent, because he has carried, or borne, it upon himself; he shall put his mouth in the ground, or in the dust. Perhaps there will be hope. He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he shall be filled with reproach.**"' 

For this reason, the Rabbi, explaining this scripture and arriving at these <term>פסוקים</term> *pasukim*, that is, verses, used to weep always. All this is tradition. Micah also spoke in this manner in the fifth chapter regarding the striking of the cheek of God: <term>בשבט יכו על הלחי את שופט ישראל</term> <note>original: Micah 5:1</note>. That is: **They shall strike the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek.**

576 BOOK [VIII]

...upon the cheek of the judge of Israel. <note>Micah 5:1. The author is connecting the "judge of Israel" who is struck on the cheek with God Himself.</note> Who this judge of Israel might be, Isaiah shows when he says in chapter 33: **The LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King; He will save us.** <note>original: יהוה שפטנו יהוה מחקקנו יהוה מלכנו הוא יושיענו</note> Moreover, that God was to suffer the gravest insults from the Jews was foretold through the prophet Hosea, speaking the words of God in chapter 7: **Woe to them! For they have strayed from me. Destruction to them! For they have transgressed against me. And I redeemed them, yet they have spoken lies against me.** <note>original: הוי להם כי נדדו ממני שד להם כי פשעו בי ואנכי אפדם והמה דברו עלי כזבים</note> This means: Woe to them, because they have departed—meaning, they will depart—from me. Visitation <note>The Latin 'Visitatio' here implies a judicial inspection or punishment</note> is for them, because they have blamed—meaning, they will blame—me. "And I redeemed"—meaning, I will redeem—them. "They, however, have spoken"—meaning, they will speak—lies against me.

In these words, God threatened the Jews with two greatest evils: namely, eternal damnation in the world to come, because by denying Him before Pilate, they were to depart from Him. And therefore He says, "Woe to them because they have departed," that is, they will depart from me. And also their final devastation and dispersion throughout the world, when He says, "Destruction to them, because they have sinned," that is, they will sin against me. And wishing to express the cause, He adds, "And I redeemed," that is, I will redeem them. "They, however, have spoken," that is, they will speak lies against me. It is as if He said, "Behold how great their ingratitude shall be. For while I shall redeem them, they themselves will speak lies against me," namely, by falsely accusing me before Pilate and afflicting me with the most serious insults. 

That these things ought to be explained exactly as they have been set forth is clearly evident through their ancient Teachers, and especially through those things said in the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A Rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms, dating from the late Roman to early Medieval periods</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, upon that verse of Psalm 39: **I said, I will guard my ways, from sinning with my tongue.** <note>original: אמרתי אשמרה דרכי מחטוא בלשוני</note> For it is said there: This is what is written in Proverbs chapter 15: **A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.** <note>original: מענה רך ישיב חמה ודבר עצב יעלה אף</note> For an evil tongue—namely, one that speaks against God—is more serious than idolatry. For when the children of Israel finally sinned in the desert, the sentence of judgment was not brought against them until they sinned against God with their mouths. For so the scripture says: **And God heard the sound of their words, and was angry.** And again, it says in Numbers chapter 14: **As I live, says God, if I do not do to you just as you have spoken in my ears.** <note>original: Numbers 14:28</note> And so also Malachi says in chapter 2: **You have wearied the LORD with your words.** <note>original: הוגעתם יהוה בדבריכם</note> He does not say "in your deeds," but "in your words." And so also Isaiah himself says in chapter 3: **For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their tongue and their deeds are against the LORD, defying His glorious presence.** <note>original: Isaiah 3:8. יהוה למרות עיני כבודו</note> Likewise He says through Jeremiah, in the twelfth chapter: **I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.** <note>original: עזבתי את ביתי נטשתי את נחלתי נתתי את ידידות נפשי בכף איביה</note> That is, I have left my house, I have left behind or cast away my inheritance, I have given the love of my soul, or I have given out of the love of my soul into the hand of her enemies. **My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me, therefore...**

[EIGHTH BOOK]

...I hated her. <note>original: "odi eam." This concludes a citation from Jeremiah 12:7, "I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies."</note> Thus far the tradition. From this, the proposition is clear. For when God says that He has given His soul, or Himself, out of love, there is certainly no doubt that He gave it over to passion and death for their redemption. This is noted in that phrase where He says, "Into the hand of her enemies." Furthermore, it is clear through the *Midrash Shir Ha-Shirim* <note>The Midrash on the Song of Songs, a collection of rabbinic allegorical interpretations</note>—that is, through the exposition of the Song of Songs—that God, on account of the love for His people, was to give His soul, that is, Himself. The Midrash explains that saying from the first chapter of the same book: **Tell me, [O thou] whom my soul loveth.** <note>original: הגידה לי את שאהבה נפשי (Higgidah li et she-ahavah naphsi)</note> It explains it thus: "Tell me of the people whom my soul loved; namely, the people for whom I gave <term>my naphsi</term> <note>Hebrew: נפשי. Meaning 'my soul,' but interpreted here as 'my very self' or 'my person'</note>—that is, my soul, or my very self, or my person." 

That God was to undergo death is also clear through what is written in the first chapter of Malachi: **And you said, "Behold, what a weariness!" and you made me expire, says the <margin>LORD of Hosts</margin>** <note>original: יהוה צבאות (Adonai Tzevaot)</note> **God of hosts.** <note>original: ואמרתם הנה מתלאה והפחתם אתי אמר (Ve-amartem hinneh matla'ah ve-hippachtem oti amar). The author argues the original Hebrew text read "made me expire" rather than "sniffed at it."</note> For there it was written, "you made me expire." But the scribes placed "you made him expire" <note>A reference to the *Tiqqune Sopherim*, or "Corrections of the Scribes," where later editors allegedly changed the text to avoid appearing blasphemous toward God</note>, as Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> testifies there in his gloss. Likewise, in the first chapter of Habakkuk: **Are you not from of old, O LORD my God, my Holy One? You shall not die.** <note>original: הלוא אתה מקדם יהוה אלהי קדושי לא תמות (Halo atah mi-qedem Adonai Elohai Kedoshi lo tamut)</note> For so it was written there; but the scribes placed "we shall not die," as is said in the book *Siphre* <note>Sifre, an ancient legalistic and homiletical commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note> regarding that saying in the 10th chapter of Numbers: "Rise up, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee." From these things which have been said, therefore, it is manifest that God was to suffer strikes, insults, and death. Since God in His divine nature cannot suffer these things, it is clearly evident that they must be understood regarding the Messiah, who was to be both God and man. Indeed, the prophets foretold that He Himself would suffer all these same things.

### *That the Messiah in His passion was to be sold, mocked, struck with whips and fists, afflicted with innumerable shames and insults, clothed in purple, and crowned with thorns.* Chapter XIII.

->CAPNIO<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'C' featuring floral and vine scrollwork.</image-desc> Since our Lord Jesus Christ in His passion was sold, mocked, despised, and struck with whips and fists, affected by the most grievous shames and injuries, and clothed in purple and crowned with a crown of thorns; I would like to know, not without reason, whether it can be proven through the writings of the ancient Jews that the Messiah was to undergo all these same things in His passion. 

GALATINUS: It certainly can. For Zechariah foretold in the 11th chapter that the Messiah, God and man, was to be sold for a cheap price—that is, thirty pieces of silver—speaking thus in His person: **And they weighed <margin>The value from upon them</margin> my price at thirty pieces of silver. And God said to me, "Cast it to the potter"—or the statue-maker—"the great value by which I was honored by them."** <note>original: וישקלו את שכרי שלשים כסף ויאמר יהוה אלי השליכהו אל היוצר אדר היקר אשר יקרתי מעליהם. This is Zechariah 11:12-13.</note> Regarding this, Amos also in the 2nd chapter...

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Messiah's suffering was predicted in Hebrew scripture and acknowledged by ancient Jewish authorities. It specifically transitions from the general idea of God's self-sacrifice to the specific indignities of the Messiah's Passion.</meta>

[EIGHTH] BOOK

**"For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him away"** <note>original: שלשה פשעי ישראל ועל ארבעה לא אשיבנו (Shlosha pish’ei Yisrael ve-al arba’ah lo ashivennu). Amos 2:6.</note> — thus it says; that is: **"For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not convert him, or bring him back, or transfer him, because they sold, or allowed to be traded for silver, the righteous one."** The explanation of these words is set forth most extensively in the twenty-fourth chapter of the fourth <meta>catchword: book</meta> book. 

That the Messiah himself was to be scorned in his passion is found in Psalm 89, where it is said: **"With which your enemies have reproached, O LORD; with which they have reproached the <term>heels</term> of your Messiah."** <note>original: אשר חרפו אויביך יהוה אשר חרפו עקבות משיחך (Asher cherpu oyvecha Adonai, asher cherpu ikvot meshichecha). Psalm 89:51–52.</note> <note>The word *ikvot* (עקבות) means footsteps or heels. Galatinus interprets this as the "final things" or the end of the Messiah's life.</note> Here, the <gloss>gloss of Rabbi Solomon</gloss> <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says: **"The heels of your Messiah,"** that is, the final things of King Messiah. For the final things of the Messiah were scorned when he himself, in his passion and death, was held in contempt by all. 

That this interpretation is correct is clear in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Hadarsan** <note>An 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note> regarding what is said in the thirty-ninth chapter concerning Joseph: **"And he fled outside."** For there it is read that Rabbi Yodan said: "David said, 'Just as I did not speak a Song until I was reproached or held in contempt, so the children of Israel are not going to speak a Song when King Messiah comes until he himself has been reproached, or held in contempt, or reviled. Just as it is written: **"Because your enemies have reproached, O God, because they have reproached the heels,"** that is, the extremities or the end of your Messiah.'" <meta>catchword: Messiah</meta>

Concerning the reproach of the Messiah, it is also found in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Book of Psalms, also called Midrash Shocher Tov.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—under the title of Psalm 17, **"The words of this Song."** For it is said there: "When the Messiah comes in haste, they will not speak a Song until the Messiah himself has been reproached. Just as it was said: **'Because your enemies have reproached, O God, because they have reproached the heels,'** that is, the final things of your Messiah." 

In the *Mishnah* also—that is, in the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism. Galatinus uses "Mishnah" and "Talmud" somewhat interchangeably here to refer to the Jewish traditional corpus.</note>—it is written that in the "heels"—that is, against the final things of the Messiah—impudence shall be multiplied. 

Furthermore, that he was to be struck with whips and blows to the cheek, and afflicted with the gravest insults, is most clearly evident through what Isaiah said, speaking in the Messiah's person in the fiftieth chapter: **"I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to those who pluck out the hair"** <note>or "those who tear."</note> **"I did not hide my face from confusion and spitting."** <note>original: גוי נתתי למכים ולחיי למורטים פני לא הסתרתי מכלימות ורוק (Gevi natatti la-makkim u-lechayay la-mortim; panay lo histarti mi-kelimot va-rok). Isaiah 50:6.</note> 

The Psalmist also signified that this was to happen in Psalm 129, saying: **"Upon my back the plowers plowed; they prolonged their furrow."** <note>original: על גבי חרשו חורשים האריכו למעניתם (Al gabbi charshu chorshim; he’erichu le-ma’anitam). Psalm 129:3.</note> Which the <term>Chaldean interpreter</term> <note>Referring to the Targum, the Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> who is at hand translates thus: **"Upon my body the enemies plowed; they prolonged their plowing."** <note>original: על גושמי רארו רארו אויביו למווחרתהון (Al gushmi ar’u ar’u oyvav le-machartahon). Galatinus provides a Latinized Aramaic reading.</note> 

In this passage, the prophet, taking the past tense for the future according to the prophetic custom—in order to show the infallible certainty of the future truth—spoke in the person of the Messiah. Therefore, the "plowers" were to plow upon the body of the Messiah because the Jews were to strike it most cruelly with whips. They were also to "prolong their plowing furrows" upon him because they were to fill his whole body with welts and strikes, according to what was said in Isaiah chapter 1: **"From the sole of the foot even unto the head, there is no soundness <meta>catchword: in it</meta> in it..."**

Galatinus emphasizes that these sufferings were essential precursors to the Messiah's ultimate victory and the "Song" of redemption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the specific details of the Messiah's suffering—specifically the purple robe and the crown of thorns—were prefigured in Hebrew Scripture and interpreted by ancient Jewish scholars.</meta>

[BOOK] EIGHT

...in him there is health. That he was also to be clothed in purple for mockery is found in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses Hadarsan** <note>An 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his midrashic compilations.</note>, regarding that saying from chapter 49 of the same book: <hebrew>כבס ביין לבשו ובדם ענבים סותה</hebrew> (Kivves ba-yayin levusho u-ve-dam anavim suto). That is: **"He shall wash his garment in wine, and his covering or clothing in the blood of grapes."** <note>Genesis 49:11. This verse is part of Jacob’s blessing over the tribe of Judah, which Christians historically interpreted as a prophecy of Christ.</note> There it is read as follows: **"He shall wash,"** he says, **"his garment in wine."** For when the Messiah comes, he is dressed in beautiful-looking purple, which in color will be similar to wine. It follows: **"And in the blood of grapes his clothing."** For the clothing of King Messiah will be silk, red as blood, and it will be embroidered above with other colors. And he himself will be the head of Israel. And this is what was said in Isaiah, chapter 63: <hebrew>מדוע אדום ללבושך</hebrew> (Madua adom li-levushecha). That is, **"Why is your garment red?"** <note>Isaiah 63:2.</note> **"And in the blood of grapes his clothing."** Just as was said by the same prophet in the same place: <hebrew>ובגדיו כדורך בגת</hebrew> (U-ve-gadav ke-dorech be-gat). **"And your garments like those of one treading in the winepress?"** This is the tradition.

While the literal meaning clearly points to both the purple garment with which the Messiah was to be mocked, and his **seamless tunic** <note>A reference to the garment described in John 19:23, woven in one piece from top to bottom.</note> woven from the top throughout, the words of both Isaiah and the patriarch Jacob must be understood mystically. For when he says, **"He shall wash his garment in wine, and his covering in the blood of grapes,"** by repeating the same sentiment with different words, he wished to explain the great mystery of the Messiah’s passion. For this Hebrew word <hebrew>ענבים</hebrew> (*anavim*), meaning **"of grapes,"** which is contained in the second clause, can be interpreted through a Hebrew grammatical rule. By this rule, the letters <hebrew>בומף</hebrew> (*bumaph*) <note>The "Bumaph" letters (Beth, Vav, Mem, Pe) are the labial consonants in Hebrew. Galatinus is explaining a linguistic theory where these letters can be interchanged.</note> are substituted one for another; if the <hebrew>ב</hebrew> (*Beth*) is changed to <hebrew>ו</hebrew> (*Vav*), it becomes the same as the word for **"the humble ones."** And then the sense of this text will be: **"And in the blood of the humble ones his covering,"** with the word "wash" understood.

This was to show that the Messiah, in his humility, would wash his covering or garment—that is, his own body—in his own blood. The words of Isaiah express this even more clearly. That he was also to be crowned with thorns is clearly gathered from the words of the same prophet, where in chapter 5 he says: <hebrew>כרם היה לידידי</hebrew> (Kerem hayah li-yedidi). That is, **"My beloved had a vineyard."** <note>Isaiah 5:1.</note> And a little later: <hebrew>ויקו לעשות ענבים ויעש באשים</hebrew> (Va-yekav la-asot anavim va-ya'as be'ushim). This is: **"And I hoped that it would produce grapes, and it produced thorns."** Here, that Hebrew word <hebrew>באשים</hebrew> (*be'ushim*), although it can mean either "wild grapes" or "thorns," signifies **"thorns"** in this context, not wild grapes. This is clearly indicated by the interpretations of the ancient teachers.

And so **Rabbi Jonah** <note>Likely Jonah ibn Janah (990–1050), a major Hebrew grammarian.</note> explains it this way in this passage when he says: **"And it produced *be'ushim*,"** that is, thorns. As it is said in Job, chapter 31: **"And instead of barley, *ba'ashah*,"** that is, a thorn. <note>Job 31:40.</note> This is hinted at by the preceding clause in Job which says: **"Instead of wheat, the thistle comes forth."** **Rabbi Kimhi** <note>David Kimhi (Radak, 1160–1235), a highly influential medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note> also affirms this, saying that in this text of Isaiah, <hebrew>באשים</hebrew> (*be'ushim*) is a type of thorn. It is certain that all this was fulfilled at that time when, as John relates in chapter 19: **"The soldiers, weaving a crown of thorns, placed it upon his head, and they surrounded him with a purple robe."** <note>John 19:2.</note> From all of this, it is clear that the Messiah, in his passion, was to be sold, reproached, and held in contempt; he was to be beaten with whips and strikes, afflicted with the gravest insults and outrages, and was to be clothed in purple and crowned with thorns. These things, and all the others we have previously mentioned concerning the passion of the Messiah, were announced even more expressly and distinctly by Isaiah himself.

<margin>Sixteen mysteries.</margin>
These are his words. Within these words, many mysteries of the Messiah himself are recorded. The first is that the Messiah, as God’s servant, was to be more excellent in his humanity than all other holy beings existing in either heaven or earth. Concerning this, he says: *He shall be exalted, and raised up, and be exceedingly high.* For this is explained in the book of the **Sanhedrin**, in the chapter **Helek**, in this way: <margin>Talmudic explanation.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "He shall be higher than Abraham, more uplifted than Moses, and more exceedingly high than the ministering angels."</note> This means: "He shall be exalted more than **Abraham**, raised up more than **Moses**, and more highly exalted than the ministering angels" (that is, those who serve God). It follows from this that the Messiah was intended to be God. For since God alone exceeds the nature of angels, and the Messiah was to be higher than the angels who serve God—who, according to the **Talmudists**, are worthier and more sublime than all others—the Jews must necessarily concede, through their own scriptures, that he is indeed God.

The second mystery concerns his exaltation on the **Cross**, through which he was to be exalted, raised up, and greatly elevated; for through his passion and resurrection, he was meant to draw all things to himself. Therefore it follows: *Just as many were astonished at you, and just as his appearance or face was despised—or marred—by men, and his form by the sons of men, so shall he sprinkle many nations,* specifically with the water of **baptism**. Through this, he was to lead those who would receive his law toward eternal salvation. Nor does it matter that the prophet sometimes speaks in the second person and sometimes in the third, as he does this according to the prophetic custom. For this reason, the kings of the nations, marveling at him, were to press their mouths shut, placing their hands over their lips. Because they would see what had not been told to them, and they would contemplate what they had not heard. For it is certain that the mysteries of the Messiah were narrated by the prophets only to the Israelite people. Therefore

# BOOK III

### That the mystery of the Messiah’s passion was expressly and distinctly foretold by Isaiah. Chapter 14.

->CAPNIO,<-
<note>Capnio is the scholar-persona of Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist of the Renaissance.</note>

Tell me, I pray, where Isaiah has recorded the mystery of the Messiah’s passion <note>The "passion" refers to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note> expressly and distinctly. GALATINUS: In the fifty-third chapter. For at the end of the 52nd he begins the discourse on this mystery, and through the whole of the 53rd he pursues it so expressly and so distinctly that he seems not like a prophet predicting future things, but like an Evangelist <note>Isaiah was often called the "Fifth Evangelist" by historical theologians because his descriptions of the suffering servant so closely mirror the Gospel accounts of Jesus.</note> narrating deeds already done. > <note>original Hebrew: Isaiah 52:13–53:12</note>
> Behold, my servant shall deal wisely; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him; for that which had not been told them they shall see, and that which they had not heard they shall understand. Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.

Who has believed our report? And over whom—or to whom—is the arm of God revealed? And he ascended like a sprout before Him, and like a root from dry ground. There was no beauty in him, nor any grace. And we saw him, and there was no appearance, and we did not desire him. He was despised, and the last of men, a man of sorrows, and known for infirmity, and as if his face were veiled from him—or, with a casting down of faces from him. He was vile, and we did not value him. Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he endured our sorrows. And we judged him to be wounded, struck by God, and afflicted. But he himself was wounded—or killed—on account of our faults, and crushed because of our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and in his bruising—or his wound—healing was given to us. <margin>
Sixteen mysteries.

The first indeed is that the Messiah himself, as the servant of God, was to be more excellent in his humanity than all other holy ones existing either in heaven or on earth. Concerning which he says: *He shall be exalted, and lifted up, and shall be very high.* For this is explained thus in the book of *Sanhedrin* <note>The Sanhedrin is a major tractate of the Talmud dealing with law and government; its eleventh chapter, "Helek," contains extensive messianic traditions.</note>, in the chapter *Helek*: "He shall be exalted more than Abraham, lifted up more than Moses, and be very high, more than the ministering angels" <note>original Hebrew: ירום מאברהם ונשא ממשה וגבה מאד יותר ממלאכי השרת</note>—that is, those serving God. 

From which it follows that the Messiah was to be God. For since God alone exceeds the angelic nature, and the Messiah was to be higher than the angels who minister to God—who, according to the *Talmudists* <note>Scholars and redactors of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>, are more worthy and sublime than all others—the Jews certainly ought to concede from their own scriptures that he is God. 

The second mystery concerns his exaltation on the cross, through which he was to be exalted, lifted up, and greatly elevated; for through his passion and resurrection he was to draw all things to himself. Therefore it follows: *As many were amazed at you, and as his appearance was despised—or scattered—by men, or his face and his form by the sons of men, so shall he sprinkle many nations,* namely with the water of baptism. Through this he was to lead those who would receive his law toward eternal salvation. Nor does it hinder the meaning that the prophet sometimes speaks in the second person and sometimes in the third, since he does this in the prophetic manner. For this reason, the kings of the nations, marveling at him, were to shut their mouths, placing their hands over their lips. Because they would see what had not been told to them, and they would contemplate what they had not heard. For it is certain that the mysteries of the Messiah were not told by the prophets except to the Israelite people. Therefore...

# That the mystery of the Messiah’s passion <note>The word "passion" here refers to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note> was expressly and distinctly foretold by Isaiah. Chapter 14.

->CAPNIO<-

Tell me, I pray, where Isaiah mentioned the mystery of the Messiah’s passion expressly and distinctly. **GAL.** In the fifty-third chapter. For at the end of the 52nd he begins the discourse on this mystery, and through the whole of the 53rd he pursues it so expressly and so thoroughly that he seems not like a prophet predicting the future, but like an Evangelist <note>The "Evangelists" are the traditional authors of the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) who recorded the life of Jesus as an eyewitness account.</note> narrating events that have already occurred. For he says thus:

<note>The following is a translation of the Hebrew text of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 provided in the original manuscript.</note>

> Behold, my servant shall deal prudently; he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high. Just as many were astonished at you—so marred was his appearance beyond that of any man, and his form beyond the sons of men—so shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him; for that which had not been told them they shall see, and that which they had not heard they shall consider. Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? For he grew up before him like a tender plant, and like a root out of dry ground. He had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. Yet it was the will of the Lord to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.

This means: Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted, and raised up, and lifted very high. Just as many were astonished at you, and so his appearance or face was rejected, or dispersed <note>Original Latin: "abiectus, uel dissipatus"</note> from men, and his form from the sons of men. So shall he sprinkle many nations; over him kings shall bind their mouths, because they have seen what was not told to them, and they have understood or contemplated what they had not heard. Who has believed our hearing? And over whom, or to whom, has the arm of God been revealed? And he grew up like a sprout before him, and like a root from parched earth. There was no face for him, nor beauty. And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, and we did not desire him. He was despised, and the last of men, a man of sorrows, and known by infirmity, and as if his face were veiled from him, or, with the casting down of faces from him. He was vile, and we did not value him. Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and sustained our sorrows. And we judged him to be leprous, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was wounded, or killed, on account of our faults, bruised because of our sins. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and in his bruise, or wound, we are healed. All of us have wandered like sheep, each one to...

Thus far the prophet. In these words indeed, many mysteries of the Messiah himself are related.
<margin>Sixteen mysteries.</margin>
The first indeed is that the Messiah himself, the servant of God, was to be more excellent in his humanity than the other saints, both those existing in heaven and on earth. Concerning which it says: *He shall be exalted, and extolled, and be very high.* For this is explained in the book of the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The Sanhedrin is a collection of Jewish legal and ethical teachings within the Talmud; the "Helec" chapter often deals with the world to come and the Messiah.</note>, in the chapter *Helec*, in this way:
<margin>Talmudic exposition.</margin>
"He shall be exalted more than Abraham, and lifted up more than Moses, and be very high, more than the <term>ministering angels</term>." <note>original Hebrew: ירום מאברהם ונשא ממשה וגבה מאד יותר ממלאכי השרת</note> <note>The "ministering angels" (Malakhei ha-Sharet) refer to the celestial beings who serve directly in the presence of God.</note> From which it follows that the Messiah was to be God. For since God alone exceeds the angelic nature, and the Messiah was to be higher than the angels who minister to God—who, according to the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>, are more worthy and sublime than all others—the Jews must certainly concede, through their own scriptures, that he is God. 

The second mystery concerns his exaltation on the cross, through which he was to be exalted, lifted up, and greatly extolled, and through his passion and resurrection he was to draw all things to himself. Therefore it follows: *As many were astonished at you, and as his appearance—or his face—was despised, or marred, by men, and his form by the sons of men, so shall he sprinkle many nations,* namely with the water of baptism. Through this, he was to lead those who were to receive his law to eternal salvation. Nor does it stand in the way that the prophet sometimes speaks to the second person, and sometimes to the third, since he does this in the prophetic manner. For which reason the kings of the nations, marvelling at him, were to shut their mouths, placing a hand over their opening. Because they would see what had not been told to them, and they would contemplate what they had not heard. For it is certain that the mysteries of the Messiah were not told by the prophets except to the Israelite people. Therefore

he adds: *Who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?* <note>original: "Quis credidit auditui nostro? & brachiū Domini cui reuelatum est?" — Isaiah 53:1</note> That is: Who ever believed our announcement, so that those to whom a mystery of this kind was never told, or to whom it was never revealed by what means God was to fulfill it, should believe in it most firmly? The third mystery is that the Messiah was to be a small child in our midst, and would have a humble origin. For it says: *He shall grow up as a tender plant before him, and as a root out of dry ground.* <note>Isaiah 53:2</note> In this, both the poverty of the nascent Messiah and the virginity of his mother are expressed. For he himself, on account of his poverty, was rightly to be compared to a slender shoot at his birth; and his mother, because of her virginity, is not unsuitably likened to dry ground, since, being moistened by no human seed at all, she was to conceive and give birth to him. The fourth mystery is that in his progress he was despised, and counted as almost nothing. Concerning which he says: *He has no form nor comeliness; and we saw him, and there was no beauty, and we did not desire him.* For even if the text says *we desired* affirmatively, it must nevertheless be understood negatively. For there, the negative word <note>Hebrew: לא (lo), meaning "not"</note> "not," as Rabbi David <note>original: "R. Dauid" — referring to David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator</note> says, serves two clauses. It is as if he said: "And we saw him, and there was no beauty, nor did we desire him." And wishing to give the reason why they did not desire him, 
<margin>Isaiah 53</margin>
he immediately added: *He was despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity, and as one from whom faces are hidden.* <note>Isaiah 53:3</note> As if to say: we were hiding our faces so that we might not look upon him. And this was because he was despised, which is why we did not value him. The fifth mystery is that he had to suffer for our sins. Therefore he says: *Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows; and we esteemed him as a leper, smitten of God, and afflicted.* <note>Isaiah 53:4</note> Here it is very much to be noted that the Hebrew text has "a smitten God," and not "smitten by God," as our translation says. For the Hebrew text itself says: <note>Hebrew: מכה אלהים (Mucche elohim), literally "Smitten-of-God"</note> *Mucche elohim*, that is, "a smitten or wounded God." For if it were to mean "smitten by God," it would say <note>Hebrew: מכה מאלהים (Mucche meelohim)</note> *Mucche meelohim*, with the preposition <note>the Hebrew letter "mem"</note> which signifies "from," "by," or "out of" among the Hebrews. It follows: *But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the discipline* — that is, the correction — *of our peace was upon him, and with his stripe* — or his wound — *that is, through his stripe and wound, we are healed.* <note>Isaiah 53:5</note> The sixth mystery is that all the righteous, except for him and his mother, wandered from the way of salvation in the common error, and he himself bore the sins of everyone, namely, for punishment. Therefore he says: *All we like sheep have gone astray, every one has turned to his own way; and God made the sin of us all to meet in him,* <note>Isaiah 53:6</note> so that he, of course, might make satisfaction for all of us. The seventh mystery is that he voluntarily and patiently sustained these punishments or sorrows even unto death for us. Therefore he says: *He was offered, and he himself was afflicted* — being voluntary or willing — *and he shall not open his mouth. Like a lamb to the slaughter...* <note>Isaiah 53:7</note>

...will be led, and like a sheep before its shearers, he will be silent, and will not open his mouth. <note>Isaiah 53:7</note> The eighth mystery is that although he would suffer as a man, as God he was to be entirely impassible <term>impassible: a theological term meaning "incapable of suffering or feeling pain," referring to the divine nature of Christ</term>. Therefore he adds: *From anguish and from judgment he was taken away, and who shall declare his generation?* <note>Isaiah 53:8</note> For here, God the Father speaks concerning the Messiah as a man, saying: after he has been "taken away" from those things which could happen to the Messiah according to his humanity—that is, when he is considered with that part removed—who shall declare his generation? This is to say: who will be able to explain the manner and cause of his incarnation? For no one will be granted such a great ability as to be able to explain it fully and perfectly. And giving the reason, he adds: *Because he is cut off*—that is, he will be cut off—*from the land of the living, for the crime of my people, and their sore <note>original: "ulcus" — often translated as wound or plague</note>, or that which was upon them.* This he understands as the "sore" of original sin. For a sore (as physicians agree) is an old wound. The ninth mystery is that just as the prophet described him as the redeemer of the faithful through the merit of his suffering, so he also signaled him as the condemner of the unfaithful through the power of his divinity, where he says: *He will give the wicked into his grave, or into his pit.* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note> This is according to the exposition of Rabbi Jonathan <note>original: "R. Ionathæ" — referring to Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets</note>: "He will deliver the wicked into Gehenna <term>Gehenna: a place of spiritual punishment or purification; here used to mean Hell</term>, and the rich who acted iniquitously with their riches into the death of perdition." The tenth is that he ought to be entirely just and immune from all sin, when he says: *Because he did no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note> And *God willed to crush him with infirmity.* It is as if he were saying: even if he is entirely just and free from all sin, he is nonetheless going to suffer for the sins of others. The eleventh is that because of the merit of his death, he was to have many spiritual sons—that is, disciples—until the end of the world. And this is what he means by: *If he lays down*—that is, because he will lay down—*his soul for sin, he shall see a seed of long days.* <note>Isaiah 53:10</note> This is understood as his faithful followers and his faith, which shall stand forever. There follows: *And the will of God shall prosper in his hand.* And the reason is that, as it is said: *From the labor*—that is, for the labor—*of his soul, which he himself shall see, he shall be satisfied.* <note>Isaiah 53:11</note> The twelfth is that through the wisdom of his teaching, he was to justify many. Wherefore he adds: *In his knowledge my just servant shall justify many, and he himself shall bear their sins.* The thirteenth is that he was to have victory against the devil, and to divide the spoils of the strong, because he was to deliver himself up to death. Therefore he says: *Therefore I will divide for him among the many*—or, *I will make him share with the many*—*and with the strong he shall divide the spoil*—that is, the spoils—*because he exposed or delivered his soul*—that is, himself—*to death.* <note>Isaiah 53:12</note> The fourteenth is that he was to be numbered among the wicked as if he were a guilty man and an evildoer. Therefore he says: *And he was counted with the iniquitous.* The fifteenth is that although his suffering ought to be sufficient to erase the sins of all, it was not nonetheless going to erase the sins of all, but only of those who would believe in him and perform penance. For that reason he adds: *And he himself [bore the] sins...*

...adds: *Who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?* <note>Isaiah 53:1</note> That is: Who has ever believed our announcement, so that those to whom such a mystery was never told, or to whom it was never revealed by what means God was to accomplish it, ought to believe it most firmly? The third point is that the Messiah was to be a small child in his beginning and was to have a humble origin. When it says: *He shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground,* <note>Isaiah 53:2</note> both the poverty of the newborn Messiah is expressed, and the virginity of his mother. For on account of his poverty, he was rightly to be compared to a slender shoot at his birth; and his mother is not ineptly likened to dry ground because of her virginity, since, having been moistened by no human seed whatsoever, she was to conceive and give birth to him. The fourth point is that in his progress he was despised, and regarded as almost nothing. Concerning this he says: *He has no form nor comeliness. And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, and we did not desire him.* <note>Isaiah 53:2</note> For even if the text says "we desired" affirmatively, it is nevertheless to be understood negatively. For the preceding negative word *lo* <note>original Hebrew: לֹא — meaning "not"</note>, as Rabbi David <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, a prominent 12th-century Jewish grammarian and commentator often cited by Christian scholars</note> says, serves two clauses. It is as if he were saying: *And we saw him, and there was no sightly appearance, nor did we desire him.* And wishing to give the reason why they did not desire him, he immediately added: *He was despised, and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity, and as if hiding faces from him.* <note>Isaiah 53:3</note> It is as if he says: we hid our faces so as not to look at him. And this for the reason that he was despised. Whence we did not even esteem him. The fifth point is that he was to suffer because of our sins. Therefore he says: *Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows. And we thought him a leper, a struck God, and afflicted.* <note>Isaiah 53:4</note> Here it is very much to be noted that the Hebrew text has "a struck God," and not "struck by God," as our translation <note>The Latin Vulgate, which was the standard Bible for the author</note> says. For the Hebrew text itself says *Mucche Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: מֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים</note>, that is, a struck or wounded God. For if it were to mean "struck by God," it would say *Mucche me-elohim* <note>original Hebrew: מֻכֵּה מֵאֱלֹהִים</note>, using the preposition *me* <note>original Hebrew: מֵ — meaning "from" or "by"</note> which signifies "from," "by," "of," or "out of" among the Hebrews. It follows: *But he was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities. The discipline*—that is, the correction—*of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise*—that is, through his bruise and his wound—*we are healed.* <note>Isaiah 53:5</note> The sixth point is that all the righteous, except for him and his mother, commonly wandered from the way of salvation, and he carried the sins of all—namely, as to the punishment. Therefore he says: *All we like sheep have gone astray, every one has turned aside into his own way. And God made the sin of us all to meet in him,* <note>Isaiah 53:6</note> so that he might satisfy for us all. The seventh point is that he sustained these punishments or sorrows voluntarily and patiently for us even unto death. Therefore he says: *He was offered, and he was afflicted, being voluntary or willing, and he shall not open his mouth. Like a lamb to the slaughter...* <note>Isaiah 53:7</note>

->### EIGHTH.<-

<note>original: "nem ducetur, & uelut ouis coram tondentibus ſe, obmuteſcet, & non aperiet os ſuum."</note> ...he shall be led to slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearers, he shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth. The eighth point is that although as a man he was to suffer, as God he was to remain entirely <term>impassible<note>In theology, "impassible" means being incapable of suffering or being affected by external pain; the author argues that while Christ's human nature suffered, his divine nature did not.</note></term>. Therefore, the text adds: *He was taken away from distress and from judgment, and who shall tell of his generation?* <note>Isaiah 53:8</note> For here God the Father speaks of the Messiah as a man, saying: "After he has been taken away from those things that could happen to the Messiah regarding his humanity—that is, when he is considered with that human part removed—who shall tell of his generation?" This means: who will be able to explain the manner and cause of his **incarnation**? For to no one will such great power be given that they might be able to explain it fully and perfectly.

And giving the reason, the text adds: *Because he was cut off*, that is, he shall be cut off *from the land of the living, for the wickedness of my people, and for their ulcer* <note>original: "ulcus" — usually translated as "stroke" or "affliction," but interpreted here as a medical sore</note>, or *that which belonged to them*. This is understood as the **ulcer of original sin**. For an ulcer (as physicians agree) is an ancient wound. It is not only that the prophet described him as the **redeemer** of the faithful through the merit of his suffering; he also hinted at him as the condemner of the unfaithfull through the power of his divinity, where he says: *He shall give the wicked into his grave, or into his pit.* According to the exposition of <term>Rabbi Jonathan<note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew prophets</note></term>, this means: *He shall hand over the wicked to **Gehenna** <note>a term for hell or a place of spiritual punishment</note>, and the rich who have acted unjustly into the death of **perdition**.*

The tenth point is that he ought to be entirely just and free from all sin, as it says: *Because he did no iniquity, nor was guile found in his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note> And God willed to crush him with infirmity. It is as if the prophet says: "Even if he will be entirely just and free of all sin, yet for the sins of others he is to suffer."

The eleventh point is that, because of the merit of his death, he was to have many spiritual sons—that is, disciples—until the end of the world. And this is what the text means: *If he shall lay*, that is, because he will lay *his soul as an offering for sin, he shall see a seed of long duration.* <note>Isaiah 53:10</note> This is understood to refer to his faithful followers and his faith, which shall stand forever. It follows: *And the will of God shall prosper in his hand.* And the reason is, as it is said: *From the labor*, that is, because of the labor *of his soul, which he himself shall see, he shall be satisfied.*

The twelfth point is that through the wisdom of his doctrine, he was to **justify** many. Therefore it adds: *By his knowledge my just servant shall justify many, and he himself shall bear their sins.* <note>Isaiah 53:11</note>

The thirteenth point is that he was meant to have victory against the **devil** and to divide the spoils of the strong, because he was to hand himself over to death. Therefore it says: *Therefore I will divide for him among many*, or *I will make him participate with many, and with the strong he shall divide the spoil.* That is, the spoils. Because he exposed or handed over his soul to death—that is, he sacrificed himself.

The fourteenth point is that he was to be numbered among the wicked as if he were a guilty man and an evildoer. Therefore it says: *and he was computed with the iniquitous.* <note>Isaiah 53:12</note>

The fifteenth point is that, although his passion was intended to be sufficient to blot out the sins of everyone, it was not actually going to blot out the sins of everyone, but only those of the people who would believe in him and perform **penance**. For that reason, it adds: *And he...*

The **third point** is that the Messiah was to be a small child in our midst, and would have a humble origin. ### A refutation of the objection of the modern Jews, who falsely interpret the words of Isaiah, through the interpretations of the ancient Talmudists. Chapter 10.

->CAPNIO<- <note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name (meaning "smoky") of the humanist scholar Johannes Reuchlin, the author of this work.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' featuring scrolling foliage or architectural motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc>

Even if all these things are exactly as you have explained, the Jews still rightly object to us that the prophet there [speaks] not of the Messiah (as you have explained) but rather literally of the Jewish people, as if speaking of a single man. Just as it says of the same: *Israel is my firstborn son.* <note>Exodus 4:22</note> For this reason, almost all the more recent commentators, and especially **Rabbi David** <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous medieval grammarian and exegete.</note> and **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), perhaps the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note>, interpret these same words of Isaiah as being about the Jewish people itself. They apply to the same people everything contained in those words: namely the weaknesses, the blows, the contempt, the shame, and other things of that kind.

Therefore, you would also do very well if, in order to convict them of their **faithlessness** <note>original: "perfidiam." In this historical context, "perfidy" specifically referred to a refusal to accept Christian doctrine.</note>, you would refute their false and perverse interpretation by proving through their own scriptures that these same words of the prophet can only be interpreted as referring to the Messiah. It is indeed true that Rabbi Solomon, and Rabbi David, and almost all others of the younger generation, have made a forced interpretation, contrary to the literal sense and the opinion of all the ancient authorities, so that they might hide and obscure the mystery of the Messiah's **passion** <note>The "passion" refers to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note> which is plainly handed down in the aforementioned words of the prophet.

But since the truth is never hidden, it is easy to convict those who speak falsely. I will therefore do two things here. First, I will show that the aforementioned words of Isaiah can in no way be applied to the Jewish people existing in this most recent **captivity** <note>Referring to the Diaspora, the scattering of the Jewish people after the destruction of the Temple.</note>. Then, I will prove through scriptures that are authentic and approved among them that these same words can only be interpreted as referring to the Messiah. 

<margin>The first point.</margin> The first point is evident from this: that many things contained in these words can in no way be applied to the Jewish people. And especially three things. The first of these is: *But he was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities.* <note>Isaiah 53:5</note> For although the Jewish people have been afflicted in many ways in this captivity, they do not suffer this because of the iniquities and crimes of the Gentiles. They do not suffer so that the Gentiles themselves, through the merits of the Jews suffering such things, might be saved by God and receive pardon—as those say who apply these words to the afflicted. For this is not only clearly false, since it is against divine justice (according to which God renders to each according to his works), but also against their own opinion, since almost all of them...

...unanimously <note>original: "nemine discrepante"</note> say that the nations which now suppress and afflict the Jewish people in this captivity <note>The "captivity" refers to the Jewish Diaspora following the destruction of the Second Temple by Rome.</note> are likewise to be punished by God for this reason. To prove this, they bring forward the statement from the last chapter of Joel: *I will gather all nations, and will lead them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will plead with them there over my people.* <note>Joel 3:2</note> Since, therefore, the prophet says that by the bruise or wound of this servant of God of whom he speaks here, others were healed, and that God caused the sin of all other men to meet in him, it follows surely that he is not speaking here of the Jewish people, for whose punishments others are not saved, but rather punished.

<margin>Second.</margin>
The **second point** is when the prophet, speaking of the same servant of God, says: *Because he had done no iniquity, neither was there any deceit in his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note> This is clearly false regarding the Jews, as is perfectly evident from the facts of the matter—for the greater part of them are immersed in usury, iniquities, deceits, sorceries, evil deeds, and other outrages. Furthermore, it is clearly held by the testimony of Holy Scripture that they are in this most recent captivity (as we have proved elsewhere) for nothing other than their own crimes. Indeed, if they wished to perform penance for their sins, they would be immediately redeemed (as will appear in what follows). Moreover, this [interpretation] is against their own explanation. For those who presuppose that they are not in this captivity except on account of a great sin, or great sins, and who ask among themselves what that sin might be, or what those sins might be, hold diverse opinions. Nevertheless, they all agree in this: that the Jewish people are not in this captivity without sin or iniquity, nor because of the sins of other nations, but only because of their own. From this it is clearly evident that this servant of God of whom Isaiah speaks cannot be understood as the Jewish people, but as the Messiah himself, who was to be entirely immune from sin.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Finally, the **third point** is when the prophet at last says of the same servant of God: *And he shall pray for the sinners.* <note>Isaiah 53:12</note> This can in no way be understood regarding the Jewish people existing in this captivity. For they not only do not pray for the salvation of the sinners of other nations, but rather for their destruction, and especially for the ruin and perdition of the Roman Empire <note>The author refers to the Holy Roman Empire, often identified in this era's polemics with the "fourth kingdom" of Daniel.</note> and the Christian Church, thinking that after the fall of the Roman Empire and the destruction of the Church of Christ, they are soon to be liberated from this servitude and captivity, as we have shown elsewhere. From this it is manifest that this saying of the prophet—*And he shall pray for the sinners*—can in no way be verified concerning them. Therefore, from these and many other things contained in this prophecy which can in no way fit the Jewish people existing in this captivity, it is clear and transparent that the servant of God of whom the prophet speaks cannot possibly be the Jewish people themselves. Moreover, that the preceding words of Isaiah can rightly fit no one else but the Messiah himself is clearly evident not only from what has been said and the text itself, but appears even more clearly and evidently from the sayings of the ancient expositors. Indeed, all the ancient expositors—both those who preceded the coming of Christ and those who lived after Christ suffered—held these same views.

### *Refutation of the objection of modern Jews, who falsely interpret the words of Isaiah, through the expositions of the ancient Talmudists. Chapter 10*

->CAPNIO<-

### BOOK EIGHT

...without any disagreement, they say that the nations who now suppress and afflict the Jewish people in this captivity <note>The author refers to the "Galut," or the Jewish diaspora and perceived state of exile.</note> will similarly be punished by God for this. To prove this, they bring forward that saying from the last chapter of Joel: *I will gather all nations, and will lead them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people.* <note>original: "Cōgregabo omnes gentes, & ducam illas in ualle Ioſaphat, & di-ſceptabo cum eis ibi ſuper populo meo." A quote from Joel 3:2.</note> Therefore, since the prophet says that by the stripe or wound of this servant of God—of whom he speaks here—others are healed, and that God has caused the sin of all other men to fall upon him, it surely follows that he is not speaking here of the Jewish people; for because of their punishments, others are not saved, but rather punished.

<margin>Second point.</margin> The second point is when the prophet, speaking of the same servant of God, says: *Because he had done no iniquity, neither was there any deceit in his mouth.* <note>Isaiah 53:9</note> This is clearly false regarding the Jews, as is perfectly evident from the facts themselves. For the most part, they are all immersed in usury, iniquities, deceits, sorceries, evil deeds, and other outrages <note>This reflects the common anti-Jewish polemic of the Renaissance era, where theologians argued that the contemporary Jewish condition was proof of divine disfavor.</note>. Furthermore, it is clearly held from the testimony of Holy Scripture that in this most recent captivity (as we have proved elsewhere) they are there only because of their own crimes. Indeed, if they wished to perform penance for their sins, they would be redeemed immediately (as will be shown in what follows). This is, moreover, contrary to their own exposition. For they presuppose that they themselves are in this captivity for no reason other than a great sin, or great sins; and seeking among themselves what that sin might be, or what those sins are, different men feel differently. Nevertheless, they all agree in this: that the Jewish people are not in this captivity without sin or iniquity, nor because of the sins of other nations, but only because of their own. From this it is clearly evident that this servant of God, of whom Isaiah speaks, cannot be understood as the Jewish people, but the Messiah himself, who was to be entirely free from sin.

<margin>Third point.</margin> Finally, the third point is when the prophet says at last of the same servant of God: *And he shall pray for the sinners.* <note>Isaiah 53:12</note> This can in no way be understood regarding the Jewish people existing in this captivity. For they not only do not pray for the salvation of the sinners of other nations, but rather for their destruction, and especially for the ruin and perdition of the Roman Empire and the Christian Church—thinking that after the fall of the Roman Empire and the destruction of the Church of Christ, they are soon to be liberated from this servitude and captivity, as we have shown elsewhere. From which it is manifest that this saying of the prophet, *And he shall pray for the sinners*, can by no means be verified concerning them. Therefore, from these points and many others contained in this prophecy, which can in no way fit the Jewish people existing in this captivity, it is clear and transparent that the servant of God himself of whom the prophet speaks cannot possibly be the Jewish people. That the aforementioned words of Isaiah can rightly fit no one else than the Messiah himself is clearly evident not only from the things said above and from the text itself, but appears even more clearly and evidently from the sayings of the ancient commentators. For all the ancient commentators, both those who preceded the coming of Christ and those who lived after the passion of Christ, held these same...

### BOOK EIGHT

...interpreted the words of *Isaiah* as being understood only regarding the *Messiah* <term>Messiah: from the Hebrew 'Mashiach', meaning 'Anointed One'; the promised deliverer of the Jewish people</term>. Just as *Solomon* <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> himself openly testifies while explaining that passage, *Behold, my servant shall understand*, along with the rest: he says, "Our masters affirm that this whole section is to be understood as referring to the Messiah." This can also be seen through many others who assert in various places that these words were spoken concerning the Messiah. For in the explanation of the book of *Genesis* by *Rabbi Moses ha-Darshan* <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) commentaries</note>, regarding the verse in chapter 24: <note>original: "ויביאהו יצחק האהלה שרה אמו"</note> That is, *And Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother.* It is said there, word for word: *This is the King Messiah, who lived in a generation of the wicked; he rejected them and chose the holy and blessed God and His holy name, so that he might worship Him with all his heart. And he gave his heart to seek mercy for Israel, and to fast, and to humble himself for them.* As it is said in *Isaiah, chapter 53*: *And he was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our sins. The chastisement of our peace was upon him.* <note>original: "Et ipse uulneratus est propter culpas nostras, cōtritus propter peccata nostra. Disciplina pacis nostræ super eum."</note> And when the children of Israel were sinning, he prayed for them. Just as it is said in the same chapter of *Isaiah*: *And by his stripes we are healed.* And for this reason, God preserves him, so that he may save Israel and rejoice with them in the resurrection of the dead. As it is said in *Deuteronomy, chapter 33*: *Happy are you, O Israel. Who is like you, a people saved by the Lord, the shield of your help?* As *Isaiah* also says in *chapter 45*: *Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation; you shall not be ashamed nor confounded, world without end.* This is the tradition. Furthermore, it is written in the book of the *Sanhedrin* <term>Sanhedrin: a tractate of the Talmud dealing with law and the Messiah</term>, in the chapter titled *Helec*, that it was said by the house of the *Rabbi*—that is, by the disciples of the Rabbi—that "The Sick One" is the name of the *Messiah*, according to what is said in *Isaiah, chapter 53*: *Surely he has borne our sicknesses, and carried our sorrows.* It is also read in the same place that the *Rabbi* <note>Referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, the editor of the Mishnah</note> said: *If the Messiah is among the living, he is like our holy master. But if he is among the dead, he is like Daniel, the man of desires.*

<margin>Messiah</margin>
In the gloss of *Rabbi Solomon* (Rashi), he says: *If the Messiah is among those who still live, in truth he is like our holy master. For he both endured sicknesses and was holy. But if he is among those who are already dead, behold, he is like Daniel, the man of desires, who was sentenced to sufferings in the lions' den, and was holy, and perfect, and a prince.* However, the word "as" <note>original: "כגון"</note> is not taken strictly here. These are the words of *Rabbi Solomon*. From these things, it clearly appears that there was a doubt among the ancient Jews whether the *Messiah* was then living or was dead. For it was established among them that he had already come. Moreover, in the same book and chapter, those words—*Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high* (as we said in the preceding chapter)—are explained this way: *Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper; he shall be exalted more than Abraham, extolled more than Moses, and be higher than the ministering angels* who serve God. From all these things, it is quite clearly evident that all the words of *Isaiah* from the place *Behold, my servant shall understand* until the end of *chapter 53* were understood by the ancient Jews and sages as referring to the *Messiah*.

## Confirmation of the aforesaid confutation through the Aramaic paraphrase of Rabbi Jonathan on the same words of Isaiah. Chapter 16.

### CAPNIO,

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a figure, possibly a scholar or biblical character, seated amidst foliage and classical architectural ruins.</image-desc>
Since the Aramaic translation <term>Aramaic translation: historically referred to as "Chaldean"</term> of Rabbi Jonathan son of Uziel, which they call the *Targum* <term>Targum: an ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible used in synagogues to help the congregation understand the scriptures</term>, carries such great authority among them that none of them dare to contradict it, I wish that, for the confirmation of this refutation, you would show through that same Rabbi’s *Targum* that all the aforementioned words of Isaiah cannot be understood as referring to the people of Israel, nor to any other man, but only to the Messiah himself. **GALATINUS:** It is not without reason, my dear Capnio, that you urge me to do this. For indeed, that same Rabbi in his Aramaic paraphrase explains all those same words—as you know—concerning the Messiah, according to our purpose. For where the Hebrew text says, *Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted, and extolled, and be very high*, he himself says in Aramaic: <note>original: "הא יצלח עבדי משיחא ירם ויסגי ויתקוף לחדא"</note> That is, *Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper, he shall be exalted, and multiplied, and shall be very strong.* But where the Hebrew text has, *So shall he sprinkle many nations, kings shall shut their mouths at him*, he says in Aramaic: <note>original: "כן יבדר עממין סגיאין עלוהי ישתקון מלכין ישוון ידיהון על פומיהון"</note> That is, *So shall he cleanse, or choose, very many nations. Kings shall be silent because of him, and they shall put their hand over their mouth.* From this it is clear that the Hebrew word *yazzeh* <note>original: "יזה"</note> which is placed there, is ambiguous (for it signifies both "to open" and "to shorten" or "to bind"). Here it is taken not for "to open" (as the author of our edition understood it), but for "to shorten" or "to bind." Furthermore, where the Hebrew letter says, *For that which had not been told them they have seen, and that which they had not heard they have understood, or contemplated*, Jonathan himself says thus: <note>original: "ארי דלא אשתעיאו להון חזו ודלא שמעו יסתכלון"</note> That is, *Since those to whom it was not told concerning him have seen, and those who did not hear have contemplated.* And where it says in Hebrew, *Who has believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?*, he says thus in Aramaic: <note>original: "מאן הימין לבסורתנא ודרוע גבורתיה דיהוה ברין על מאן אתגליאת"</note> That is, *Who has believed this announcement of ours? And the strength of the arm of the power of the Lord in this manner, upon whom has it been revealed?* And regarding what is held in the Hebrew, *He has no form nor comeliness*, along with the rest, he explains it thus in Aramaic: <note>original: "לא חיווי חולא חזויה ולא אימתיה אימת הדיוט ויהי זיו קודשא זיויה דלא דיהויה אסתכל ביה"</note> That is, *His appearance will not be a despicable appearance, nor will his reverence or authority be the reverence or authority of a common person <term>common person: the original Latin "idiota" refers to a layperson or someone without official status, rather than a lack of intelligence</term>. But his glory shall be the glory of holiness. And whoever sees him shall contemplate him. Because of this, it shall be for a good announcement.* And regarding what the Hebrew letter has, *And as it were faces hidden from him*, with the rest, he translated it thus in Aramaic: *For the sick, the Presence <term>Presence: the "Shekhinah," the indwelling glory of God</term> withdrew, indeed we were cast away and...*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring an ornamental scene of a figure seated at a desk, possibly a scholar or saint writing.</image-desc>Although the perfidy of the Jews of our time is so thoroughly convinced by what you have said so far regarding the passion of the Messiah that they should not even dare to open their mouths from now on; nevertheless, their impiety should be even more clearly exposed. Rabbi Abhu <note>A prominent 3rd-century Jewish scholar in Caesarea.</note> said: "And his hands were spread toward the heavens, just like **this one**" <note>original Hebrew: "זה" (Ze), meaning "this" or "this one."</note>; that is, he was standing like one crucified, or extended on a cross. This is most clearly proven through what is written in the book *Menahoth* <note>original: "מנחות", meaning "Meal Offerings."</note>, that is, of *oblation*, in the chapter that begins *Hammenahoth* <note>original: "המנחות", meaning "The Offerings."</note>, that is, *The Oblations*.
