According to these two traditions, therefore, God was to carry the cross on his own shoulders, and was to be fixed to the cross with his hands extended. Since God, by His very nature, cannot suffer these things, they must necessarily be understood as referring to the Messiah, who was to be both God and man, and who would die the death of the cross. Furthermore, that his hands and feet were to be pierced <note>term: <term>foderidi</term> (pierced/dug through)</note> on the cross, the Psalmist proclaimed in Psalm 22, saying: "For dogs have surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked has besieged me; they have pierced my hands and my feet" <note>original Hebrew: "כרו ידי ורגלי" (karu yadai v’raglai)</note>. However, the *Sophrim* <note>term: <term>Sophrim</term> (The Scribes), ancient Jewish scholars responsible for transmitting the biblical text.</note>, that is, the Scribes, changed the word **karu** <note>meaning "they pierced"</note> into **ka’ari** <note>original: "כארי", meaning "like a lion"</note>, and by doing so, they perverted both the scripture and its meaning. We have already shown extensively in the first book that they have done this in many other places. Nevertheless, some of our own scholars (albeit out of piety and good zeal) say that when the Hebrew text says here, "Like a lion my hands and my feet," or "my hands and my feet," the construction is defective, and it should be understood as: "The wicked, like a lion, have pierced, bored through, or treated my hands and feet badly." To prove this, they bring forward the Aramaic translation <note>term: <term>Chaldaic</term> (the Aramaic Targum, a Jewish translation and paraphrase of the Bible).</note>, which in this place reads: "For the wicked have surrounded me, who are like many dogs; a congregation of evildoers has besieged me, biting my hands and feet like a lion." From this, they conclude that the Hebrews have not corrupted this passage. But to speak the truth, this argument does not please me at all. First, because even if in nearly infinite manuscripts which the Jews now commonly have in their hands, it is corrupted to **ka’ari** (that is, *like a lion*), nevertheless, in some of the oldest manuscripts, **karu** (that is, *they pierced*) is still found written. Even though the Jews in those cases do not read it as **karu**, as it is written, but as **ka’ari**. For they say in that place, **kethiv** <note>term: <term>Kethiv</term> (what is written), the written form of the Hebrew text.</note>, that is, it is to be written **karu**, but **qere** <note>term: <term>Qere</term> (what is read), the traditional pronunciation that differs from the written text.</note>, that is, it is to be read [as **ka’ari**].

...*caari* <note>original Hebrew: "כארי", meaning "like a lion."</note>. This is the third way of corrupting the scripture, as was shown more extensively in the first book. Then, furthermore, because the Chaldean translation <note>The author refers to the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> which they bring forward is not by Jonathan son of Uzziel—who preceded the birth of Christ by many years—but by Rabbi Joseph the Blind (as they themselves seem to affirm), who flourished nearly three hundred and forty years after the passion of Christ; it should not seem surprising if, following this corruption, it reads this way in this passage. Although that same translation also works greatly against the Jews of our time (which is especially to be noted) both here and in many other places regarding our purpose. Finally, because it was not written here as *caari*—that is, "like a lion"—but *caru* <note>original Hebrew: "כארו", meaning "they dug" or "they pierced."</note>, that is, "they pierced," is clearly evident not only in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Moses Hadarshan, an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic explanations.</note> (as was seen in the eighth chapter of the first book), specifically regarding the verse: *And Abraham still stood before the Lord.* It is also evident through the edition of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, who translated these words thus: *they dug my hands and my feet* <note>original Greek: "ὤρυξαν χεῖράς μου καὶ πόδας μου" (oryxan cheiras mou kai podas mou).</note>. From this it clearly follows that *caru* (they dug) was written in this place, and not *caari* (like a lion). This can also be seen most clearly from that Chaldean translation <note>The author is referring to the Ethiopic/Ge'ez version, which was often confused with or called "Chaldean" or "Indian" in early modern scholarship.</note> used by the Indians and Ethiopians. For it says: **Canauuní oyouíya uaogariya.** <note>original Ge'ez: "ቀነዉኒ ፡ እደውየ ፡ ወእግርየ" (Qanawuni edawya wa-egriya).</note> That is: *They wounded, or pierced, my hands and my feet.* Therefore, David did not speak these words in his own person, as the raving younger Jews say, but in the person of the Messiah, whom he foresaw would suffer such things.

This is also openly suggested from what immediately follows, where it is said: *I will count all my bones*—or *all my adversaries*. *They will consider and look down upon me; they divide my garments among them, and upon my clothing they cast lots.* <note>Psalm 22:17–18. The Hebrew "עצמותי" can mean "my bones" or be related to "my essence/strength."</note> Since David never suffered these things, nor were they ever fulfilled in him, they must be understood as referring to the Messiah, especially since it is written in the book *Sabbath* <note>The Talmudic tractate Shabbat, dealing with laws of the day of rest.</note>, in the chapter beginning *Bamme haishah yotza* <note>original: "במה האשה יוצאת", meaning "With what may a woman go out?" referring to Shabbat 57a.</note>, that Rabbi Hiya had said: "All the prophets did not prophesy except concerning the days of the Messiah." 

The ancient Talmudists also attribute that saying of Zechariah chapter 12—*They shall look upon me whom they pierced* <note>original Hebrew: "והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו" (Ve-hibitu elai et asher dakaru).</note>—to the Messiah son of Joseph <note>In Jewish tradition, "Messiah son of Joseph" is a messianic figure who dies in battle before the arrival of the conquering "Messiah son of David."</note>, as Rabbi David Kimhi reports in the same place. This is also easily proven through what is contained in the book *Succa* <note>The Talmudic tractate Sukkah, regarding the Festival of Booths.</note>, in the chapter *Hahalil hammissa* <note>original: "החליל המשנה" (The Flute), referring to Sukkah 51a.</note>. For there it is read: "It is written in Zechariah chapter 12, *And the land shall mourn, family by family apart.*" For what purpose will this mourning occur? There is a controversy there between Rabbi Dossa and the Masters. For one says that the mourning will be for the Messiah son of Joseph, who will be killed. And the other says that it will be over the evil inclination which will be destroyed. *Bishlama* <note>original Aramaic: "בשלמא," a Talmudic term meaning "it is well" or "it makes sense."</note>, that is, it is well for the one who said that the aforementioned mourning will be over the Messiah son of Joseph. For this is what is written in Zechariah 12: *And they shall look upon me...*

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that ancient Jewish tradition—specifically the Talmudists—recognized the Messiah as both God and man, who would suffer and be pierced, identifying him with Jesus Christ.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>

<note>original Hebrew: "אשר דקרו וספדו עליו כמספד על היחיד והמר עליו כהמר על הבכור"</note>
And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for an only son, and shall be in bitterness for him as one is in bitterness for a firstborn.

That is, **"And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as if mourning for an only son. And there shall be sorrow over him, just as it is customary to grieve for a firstborn."** This is the tradition. Although commentators leave it unexamined whether that Messiah is called the "son of Joseph" because he was to come from the tribe of Joseph, or from a father named Joseph, the saying of the <term>Talmudists</term><note>The ancient Jewish scholars and compilers of the Talmud.</note> is nevertheless understood to refer to Christ our Lord. The reason the Talmudists called him the "son of Joseph" is that he was to have no other father on earth except a putative <note>supposed or legal rather than biological</note> one—namely Joseph, the spouse of his virgin mother—who, as the Evangelists report, was thought to be his father. For this reason, even the glorious Virgin herself said to him in Luke chapter 2: *Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have sought you sorrowing.* From this tradition, therefore, it necessarily follows that God himself was to be wounded and pierced. For since the prophet uttered those words, **"And they shall look upon me whom they have pierced"**—which the ancient Talmudists intended to be understood regarding the Messiah—in the person of God, it is as if God himself were to be crucified. This could not even have been conceived of unless the divinity were to be <term>hypostatically united</term><note>The theological doctrine that the divine and human natures are joined in the one person of Jesus Christ.</note> with humanity in the Messiah himself. It is certainly a consequence, then, that the Messiah who was to be crucified would be both God and man. Furthermore, since it belongs to no one but God alone to pour out the spirit of grace upon men, it is certainly clear that he is entirely God, in whose person the prophet speaks, saying:

<note>original Hebrew: "ושפכתי על בית דויד ועל יושב ירושלם רוח חן ותחנונים והביטו אלי את אשר דקרו"</note>
And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of supplications, and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced.

That is, **"And I will pour out upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of prayers (or supplications). And they shall look upon me whom they have stabbed (or pierced)."**

<margin>Objection of the younger Jews</margin>
**CAP.** The younger Jews <note>A term often used by Christian polemicists to refer to medieval Jewish scholars who disagreed with Christian interpretations of the prophets.</note>, unable to distort such evident testimony of the passion of the God-man, say that in this place it is written among them, "They shall look upon *him*," and not "upon *me*." **GAL.**

<margin>* Refutation.</margin>
The falsehood of these later scholars is evident from the fact that all their ancient books (as you yourself know very well) have it exactly as I have written and translated it. Furthermore, it is proven through the <term>Chaldean translation</term><note>The Aramaic Targum, a translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Rabbi Jonathan, which provides the same words in Aramaic: **"And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of piety and mercy, and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced."** Wherefore the same prophet in chapter 13 says:

<note>original Hebrew: "מה המכות האלה בין ידיך ואמר אשר הכיתי בית מאהבי : חרב עורי על רעי ועל גבר עמיתי נאם יהוה צבאות הך את הרעה ותפוצין הצאן"</note>
What are these wounds between your hands? And he will say, "Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends." Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is my companion (or my equal, or joined to me), says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.

From all of these things, it is established more clearly than light that the Messiah, God and man, was to be hung upon the gibbet of the cross, and was to die by the death of the cross.

### A response to the objection of the Jews, who assert that Christ was not God for the reason that he cried out on the cross that he was forsaken by God. Chapter 18.

->CAPNIO<-
<note>Capnio is the pen name of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and scholar of Hebrew.</note>

On this point, the impious lack of faith of more recent Jews opposes us. They say: "If your Christ was God, why, when he was about to die on the cross, did he cry out that he was forsaken by God, saying: <term>אלי אלי למה עזבתני</term> <note>original Hebrew: Eli, Eli, lama azabtani</note>—that is, 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' For if he had been both God and man, that man could never have been deserted by the God to whom he was <term>hypostatically</term><note>The "hypostatic union" is the theological term for the union of divine and human natures in the single person of Jesus.</note> united (as you claim). Since, as you yourselves assert, what God once assumed, He never set aside. Therefore, when he cried out that he was forsaken by God, he himself openly protested that he was not God."

<margin>HOOGSTRATEN</margin>
<note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican theologian and inquisitor who often debated Reuchlin.</note>
Regarding this, Jerome says that Christ sang <term>Psalm 21</term> <note>Psalm 22 in modern Bibles</note> on the cross, and the others following it, all the way to that verse in <term>Psalm 30</term> <note>Psalm 31 in modern Bibles</note>: "Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit." From this it follows that he did not say those words, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" to show that he was forsaken by God, but because they occurred in the sequence of other words from those same Psalms that he intended to speak.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin>

He did this not as one who was ignorant, nor as one complaining about God or accusing Him, but to lead those Jews who heard him to a most saving consideration of his passion and to faith. The words that immediately follow in that same place clearly suggest this. For when the prophet (speaking in the person of the Messiah, as has been said) had said: <term>אלי אלי למה עזבתני</term>—that is, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—he immediately added: <term>רחוק מישועתי דברי שאגתי</term> <note>original Hebrew: rachoq mi-yshuati divrei sha’agati</note>. That is: "Far from my salvation are the words of my roaring." The words of Christ’s roaring, by which he cried out as a man that he was forsaken by his God, were "far from his salvation" in the hearts of the Jews who desired to kill him—that salvation being his resurrection by God and his elevation into heaven as his disciples watched. ### *That the Messiah was to be given gall and vinegar to drink at his death, and as he died, darkness ought to occur over all the earth. Chapter XIX.*

-> CAPNIO <-
<note>Capnio is the scholarly nickname for Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist and one of the speakers in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'Q' illustrating a scenic landscape with hills and architecture.</image-desc>
Since we read that Christ our Redeemer was given gall and vinegar to drink during his passion, and that darkness occurred over the entire earth as he was dying, it must also be proven through the Jewish scriptures that all these things were destined to happen at the death of the Messiah. This serves to further reproach the impious and obstinate unbelief of the Jews of our time. First, therefore, it should be noted what is read in the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> in the book <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with judicial procedures and the high court.</note>, in the chapter that begins, <note>original Hebrew: נגמר הדין</note> *Nigmar had-din*, that is, "The judgment is finished." There it is said word-for-word: "Rabbi Hasda said: One who was going out to be killed was given a drink of incense powder in a cup of wine, so that his senses would be separated from him [numbed]." Just as it is said in <margin>Proverbs chapter 31</margin> <note>original Hebrew: תנו שכר לאובד ויין למרי נפש</note> This is: "Give an intoxicating drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to the bitter soul." There were, moreover, honorable women in Jerusalem who provided these things voluntarily. Thus says the Talmud. Therefore, the Jews drank the good wine that had been sent for the Lord Jesus Christ and the others to be crucified with him. Because of this, what had been said long before through Amos in chapter 2 was then fulfilled: <note>original Hebrew: ויין ענושים ישתו בית אלהיהם</note> That is: "And they shall drink the wine of the condemned in the house of their God." It is as if he were saying: "The house of Israel shall drink the wine of the condemned," and what will be a greater crime, they shall drink even "the wine of their God." Nor should it seem unfitting to anyone that the prophet attributes the act of a very few Jews to the whole house of Israel. For not only was a huge multitude of people present there, consenting to what was being done, but so were those of whom it is said in Matthew chapter 27: "In the same way the Chief Priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: 'He saved others, himself he cannot [save]...'"

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous chapter regarding the sufferings of the Messiah. ...save himself? If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusts in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him. For he said, "I am the son of God." 

It is also the custom of the divine scripture to sometimes ascribe to a multitude what was done by only one. For it is read in the 7th chapter of Joshua that the Lord said to Joshua himself: "Israel has sinned, and they have transgressed my covenant which I commanded them, and they have also taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen," and so forth. Behold how the Lord attributed to Israel what Achan alone had perpetrated. 

Therefore, in place of incense and good wine and honor, Jewish impiety offered the Lord Jesus myrrh and vinegar mixed with gall. And then that saying of the Psalm was fulfilled: <note>original Hebrew: ויתנו בברותי ראש : ולצמאי ישקוני חמץ</note> "And they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." <note>Psalm 69:21</note> 

That these things were to be understood concerning the Messiah appears more clearly from the *Midrash Ruth* <note>original: "Lidras Ruth." Midrash is a form of rabbinic biblical exegesis. This specific interpretation of Ruth 2:14 is famous in both Jewish and Christian scholarship.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Ruth, where regarding that which Boaz said in the second chapter: "Come here, and eat of the bread, and dip your morsel (or your piece) in the vinegar." For it is said thus: "He speaks concerning the King Messiah. *Come here*, that is, let the Kingdom draw near. *And eat of the bread*, this is the bread of the Kingdom. *And dip your morsel (or your piece) in the vinegar*, these are the sufferings or torments of the Messiah." 

Regarding whom it is said in Isaiah 53: "And he was wounded (or killed) for our faults, bruised for our sins." This is the tradition. From which it is clearly shown that the vinegar of Ruth signified and prefigured the sufferings and torments of the Messiah. 

How much more, therefore, must it be said in the person of the Messiah what was already set forth: "And they shall give gall for my food, and in my thirst they shall give me vinegar to drink." Which points most especially to the just retribution of the Jews, when immediately in the same Psalm it is added: <note>original Hebrew: יהי שלחנם לפניהם לפח ולשלומים למוקש תחשכנה עיניהם מראות ומתניהם תמיד המעד : שפך עליהם זעמך וחרון אפך ישיגם : תהי טירתם נשמה באהליהם אל יהי יושב</note> that is: "Let their table become a snare before them, and that which should be for their welfare, let it become a trap. Let their eyes be darkened from seeing, and make their loins continually to shake. Pour out your indignation upon them, and let the wrath of your anger take hold of them. Let their habitation be desolate; let no one dwell in their tents." 

And immediately after these things it is added: <note>original Hebrew: כי אתה אשר הכית רדפו ואל מכאוב חלליך יספרו : תנה עון על עונם ואל יבאו בצדקתך : ימחו מספר חיים ועם צדיקים אל יכתבו</note> This is: "Because they have persecuted him whom you have struck, and they tell of the grief (or the affliction) of those you have wounded (or killed). That is: "Let their table which they prepared before me, so that I might eat, be a snare, and their sacrifices a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they cannot see, and make their loins tremble continually. Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fierceness of your anger overtake them. To explain these words of the Psalmist <term>Psalmographi; the author of the Psalms, traditionally King David</term>, it must be noted that "table" in Holy Scripture is sometimes called a "kingdom." For this reason, in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: Midras tillim; a traditional Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding the saying in Psalm 23: <note>original Hebrew: תערוך לפני שלחן</note> "You prepare a table before me," it is said: "This table is the Kingdom." 

Sometimes, however, the whole of divine Scripture itself—which is divided into twenty-four books—is called a "table," according to what is said in Deuteronomy chapter 8: <note>original Hebrew: לא על הלחם לבדו יחיה האדם כי על כל מוצא פי יהוה יחיה האדם</note> "Man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord." Both of these "tables" became a snare to the Jews. Because they gave the Messiah wine mixed with myrrh and vinegar mixed with gall to drink, they consequently lost both their kingdom and the true understanding of the Scriptures. 

Therefore, regarding their blindness it is added: "Let their eyes be darkened from vision," that is, so they may not see. Hence even the true Messiah, who should have been their peace (and indeed is called "Peace"), by the just judgment of God became a stumbling block to them, because they embittered his mouth with gall and vinegar. And this is what Jeremiah says in the first chapter of his Lamentations: <note>original Hebrew: צדיק הוא יהוה כי פיהו מריתי</note> "The Lord himself is righteous, for I have made his mouth bitter." <note>The author is playing on the Hebrew word *marithi*, which usually means "I have rebelled," but here he links it to the root *marah*, meaning "bitter."</note> 

For then Jewish wickedness embittered the mouth of God, when they placed a sponge full of vinegar and gall, attached to a reed, to the mouth and nose of our Lord Jesus, the true Messiah. For this reason, that which was said in Ezekiel chapter 8 was also fulfilled: <note>original Hebrew: והנם שולחים את הזמורה אל אפי</note> "And behold, they are sending a stench to my nose." <note>The standard translation of Ezekiel 8:17 is "putting the branch to their nose," but the author uses a polemical interpretation here.</note> Explaining this, Rabbi Kimhi says: "He means to say, a foul odor."

**HOG.** In these places, our own Scripture [the Vulgate] reads quite differently than how you have translated it. For that passage in the Lamentations of Jeremiah reads: "The Lord is righteous, because I have provoked his mouth to anger." And this one from Ezekiel: "And behold, they apply a branch to my nostrils."

For the word *marithi* <note>original: מריתי</note> which is placed in the words of Jeremiah, is derived from the verb *mara* <note>original: מרה</note>, which properly signifies "to make bitter." Therefore *marithi* is the same as "I have made bitter." Furthermore, the saying of Ezekiel has been completely corrupted both among us and among the Hebrews, but much more among us than among them. For they read it as: "And they shall be sending a stench to their own nose." Yet neither reading...

The Messiah, afflicted and humbled by fasting and affected by punishments, will restore merit and reward to all. From this, it is clearly evident that through the death of the Messiah, there was to be a remission of sins. This is seen both from the fact that it says "his land"—that is, his corpse—shall pardon his people, and also because it says that his death (namely, the Messiah’s) ought to pardon the nations in the world to come—that is, in the time of the Messiah. ...daughter of Jerusalem. Therefore, the pronouns situated there refer to the "daughter," that is, the church of Zion and Jerusalem, when it is said: "As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the 
<margin>Interpretation of Rabbi Solomon.</margin> pit in which there is no water." <note>Zechariah 9:11</note> Indeed, Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains these words thus: "As for you also, the church of Zion and Jerusalem, you shall be saved with the Messiah, just as he himself is righteous and saved. By the blood of your covenant, that is, through the merit of the blood of the covenant which was poured out over you at Sinai." Concerning which it is said in Exodus chapter 24: "Behold the blood of the covenant, which the Lord has made." <note>Exodus 24:8</note> "I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit," that is, from captivity. Thus says he. However, when he says "from the pit," meaning from captivity, this cannot be understood as the pit of the Egyptian or Babylonian captivity, since both of those places abound with water, and the prophet says the pit of which he speaks lacks water. Therefore, his words must be understood as referring to the pit of Gehenna <note>A term for hell or a place of spiritual punishment.</note> in which there is no water, but rather fire and sulfur, as is clear in the prologue of <note>original: איכה רבתי</note> *Echa Rabbethi* (that is, the explanation of the Lamentations of Jeremiah). Where it is said: "The Holy and Blessed God promised us that he would deliver us from Gehenna through the merit of circumcision." And where is this said? In Zechariah, who says: "As for you also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water." This is the tradition. However, when he says that salvation was to come through the merit of circumcision, he intended it to be understood as through the merit of the pouring out of the blood of Christ, of which circumcision served as a <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a person, event, or ritual in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note>. For since all the patriarchs and prophets, and all the ancient fathers, however holy they were, who received circumcision, descended into the underworld until the passion of Christ—as is clear in many books of the Talmud, and especially in the book called <note>original: חגיגה</note> *Haghiga* (The Festival Offering), in the chapter which begins <note>original: הכל חייבין</note> *Haccol hayyabin* (that is, "all are obligated"), as we have clearly shown in the preceding pages. It clearly follows, then, that we were to be liberated from the underworld not through the merit of circumcision, but through the merit of the passion of Christ, whose figure circumcision carried. Furthermore, since neither the pardon of sins, nor satisfaction, nor consequently the salvation of souls, ought to occur except through the shedding of blood—as is clear in the book <note>original: יומא</note> *Yoma* (that is, "The Day" of Atonement), in the chapter that begins: "Seven days before the Day of Propitiation." Where it is read word for word: "There is no pardon or remission of sin except through blood." Just as it is written in Leviticus chapter 17: <note>original: דם הוא בנפש יכפר</note> That is: "For the blood itself shall make satisfaction for the soul," or "shall cause the soul to be spared." <note>Leviticus 17:11</note> Since salvation would not have occurred except through the Messiah, as has been proven above, it follows necessarily that God remitted sins neither by the merit of circumcision, nor by the merit of the blood poured out over the sons of Israel on Mount Sinai, but only by the merit of the blood of the Messiah yet to be shed, which the aforementioned bloods prefigured. Without this, there never was, is, nor shall be a perfect remission of sins.

# BOOK EIGHT

### That the Messiah was to descend into the underworld, and lead out all the chosen from there. Chapter 21.

->C A P N I O,<-
<note>This refers to Johannes Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist, who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a landscape or mythological scene within a square border.</image-desc>

Since we believe and confess that Christ our Lord, after his death, descended to the underworld <note>original: "ad inferos"</note> and from there led out the souls of his chosen ones, it is necessary to prove from the Jewish scriptures themselves that the Messiah was to do this very thing. This is done so that the stubbornness <note>original: "perfidia"; in this period, the term was used to describe theological "unbelief" or refusal to accept Christian interpretation.</note> of the younger Jews might be more and more refuted. GALATINUS: That the Messiah was to descend to hell and lead out all the chosen from there is especially clear through what is read in the *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>A significant collection of ancient Jewish interpretations (midrash) on the book of Genesis.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Ha-Darshan. There, upon the words of the 24th chapter of that same book, "And he led me into the tabernacle," it is said word for word: Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said, "I went with the angel of death named <term>קיפור (Kippod)</term> <note>Literally "Hedgehog," but here used as a proper name for an angel of destruction or death.</note> until I reached the gates of Gehenna <note>The place of punishment or purification in Jewish thought; hell.</note>. Immediately I sent the angel Kippod—who is, of course, in charge of Gehenna—to measure Gehenna from the beginning to the end, but he did not have a spare hour to measure it because at that time they killed Rabban Simeon, the son of Gamaliel. I wanted to go, but I could not. After this, however, I went with the angel Kippod, and the Messiah, the son of David, went with me until I reached the gates of Gehenna. When the captives who were in Gehenna saw the light of the Messiah, they rejoiced to receive him, saying: 'This one will lead us out of these shadows.' As it is said in the 13th chapter of Hosea: <term>מיד שאול אפדם ממות אגאלם</term> <note>original: "Mi-yad Sheol efdem, mi-mavet eg’alem"</note>—that is, 'From the hand of hell I will redeem them; from death I will free them.' And thus Isaiah also says in chapter 35: <term>ופדויי יהוה ישבון ובאו ציון</term> <note>original: "U-feduye Adonai yeshuvun u-vau Tziyon"</note>—that is, 'And the redeemed of God shall return, and shall come or enter into Zion.' And the rest, until: <term>ונסו יגון ואנחה</term>—that is, 'And sorrow and sighing shall flee away.' Now, 'Zion' is not mentioned in this place except to signify <term>גן עדן (Gan Eden)</term>, that is, the Garden of Delight, which is Paradise. This concludes the tradition." Although this tradition may seem to present a foolish fiction, nevertheless, because the Talmudists were accustomed to hand down the secrets of the Messiah only in parables, they fashioned that story to suggest the Messiah's descent to the underworld and the joy that the holy fathers existing in Limbo <note>In medieval theology, the "Limbo of the Fathers" was the temporary place of the righteous who died before Christ.</note> were to have because of his arrival and their liberation. This they prove very well with the testimonies of Hosea and Isaiah. This same thing was shown even more openly long before the birth of Christ by that Teacher of theirs whom they call <term>רבינו הקדוש (Rabbenu Ha-Kadosh)</term> <note>Literally "Our Holy Teacher," referring to Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, that is, 'Our Holy Master,' in the book he called <term>גלי רזיא (Gali Razia)</term> <note>Literally "The Revealer of Secrets."</note>. This appears especially in his response to the second petition of Antoninus, the Consul of the city of Rome. "...I am the man who has seen poverty. Likewise, in the same book, at the sixth petition of that same Antoninus <note>Refers to the dialogues between Rabbi Judah the Prince and the Roman Emperor "Antoninus" recorded in Jewish tradition.</note>, the same <term>Rabbenus Haccados</term> <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, the 2nd-century compiler of the Mishnah.</note> says that he found these things among others in the book of Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai titled *Mechkar ha-Kovannot* <note>original: "מחקר הכוונות"; translates to "Investigation of Intentions." Upon hearing these things, Rabbi Hoseas began to speak, saying: "Woe to them, woe to those impious, iniquitous murderers! Woe to them, for on account of their wicked deeds they will be rebels against this Messiah, and will reject the words by which he will command that they be cleansed with the water of purification for the purging of their sins. This is what was said in Hosea chapter 6: *He will visit us after two days; on the third day he will revive us, and we shall live in his presence.*" All these things are said by him whom the Jews themselves call "Our Holy Teacher." From all this, it has been made sufficiently and clearly manifest that the Messiah, being God and man, was to descend into hell immediately after his death and lead out the souls of his chosen ones.

Which Rabbi Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century convert and scholar who translated the Torah into Aramaic.</note> thus translated into Aramaic: <note>original: "ודמות יהוה יחזי"</note> *And he understands the likeness, or the image of the love of God.* Therefore, according to this sense, the aforementioned words of the prophet can be explained: *I shall see your face*, that is, your Messiah. *I shall be satisfied when your form, or figure, or likeness, or image shall rise again*, that is, your son. Although they may explain this in another way, as will be said by us later when we come to speak of the general resurrection, the exposition we have placed here is best confirmed in the *Bereshit Rabbah Ketanna* <note>The "Lesser" Great Genesis, a collection of Rabbinic midrash/interpretation.</note> (that is, in the lesser exposition of the book of Genesis), regarding that which is written in chapter 3 of that same book concerning Adam: *And the Lord sent him out from the garden, or from the paradise of pleasure.* For there it reads literally:

Moreover, this saying of Rabbi Hamias is supported by what is written in Psalm 16 [17:15]: *I, in justice, or through justice, shall contemplate your face; I shall be satisfied when your form, or figure, or image, or likeness shall rise again.* The Holy and Blessed God said: "In that hour I will justify him, namely Adam, from that sentence [of exile]." David said to the Holy and Blessed God: "And in that hour when he shall rise again who is your likeness, I shall be satisfied, and in justice I shall contemplate or see your face." Regarding this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> says: *I shall contemplate your face*, just as it is said in Isaiah 52: <note>original: "כי עין בעין יראו בשוב יהוה ציון"</note> *For eye to eye they shall see when the LORD dwells or inhabits Zion.* Which Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, traditionally the author of the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets.</note> translated into Aramaic thus: <note>original: "ארי בעייניהון יחזון גבורא דיי כד יתיב שכינתיה לציון"</note> *For with their eyes they shall see the power, or the strength that God shall perform when his Divine Presence [Shekhinah] shall sit or dwell in Zion.* 

All of this is tradition. Within these words, three very great mysteries are contained. The first is that God was going to justify Adam, who was once expelled from paradise, by taking away the sentence brought against him. The second is that this was to occur when, according to David’s prophecy, the *temuna* <note>Hebrew for "form" or "likeness."</note> (that is, the form, or figure, or image, or likeness) of God should rise again. The third is that when he who is the likeness of God (that is, he who was like God the Father according to his divinity, but was to rise again according to his humanity), then David knew that he himself was to be healed, and through justice he would see and contemplate the face of God.

<note>original: "ביום ההוא אקים את סכת דוד הנפלת"</note> *On that day I will raise up, or I will lift up, the fallen or prostrate booth of David.* <note>Amos 9:11</note> This is the tradition. Here, a certain ancient Talmudist notes that he called the Messiah *Bar niphli*, that is, "the son of the fallen." For as he proves his statement by the testimony of the prophet, the Messiah—according to his body—was destined to be the "fallen or prostrate booth of David" in his passion and death, but in his resurrection, he was to be raised and lifted up by God.

I also think it should not be passed over in silence what is read in the *Midrash Tehillim* (that is, in the exposition of the Psalms) regarding the title of Psalm 21 <note>Psalm 22 in modern numbering.</note>: <note>original: "על אילת השחר"</note> *Upon the hind of the dawn.* Where it is said: Isaiah <note>Likely a reference to the prophetic voice in the Midrash.</note> wrote, *Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp. I will awake the dawn.* And further below: *Awake in Edom*, that is in Rome, for it is yours to make the King Messiah stand before us. And what does it mean, *I will awake the dawn*? It means the dawn does not awaken me. For from the beginning of the world, the dawn never came upon me and found me sleeping. And this is: *I will awake the dawn.* And so it says in Psalm 117 <note>Psalm 119:62 in modern numbering.</note>: <note>original: "חצות לילה אקום להודות לך"</note> *At midnight I rise to give thanks to you.* Thus far the tradition.

Where it must be noted that the glory of David was in the Messiah, as is held in the *Midrash Tehillim* (the exposition of the Psalms) regarding that verse of Psalm 16: *My heart is glad*, namely in the words of the law, *and my glory rejoices.* Rabbi Abhu said: "That is, in the King Messiah, who is to come forth from me." Just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 4: *For over all the glory shall be a protection.* That is, the Messiah. *My flesh also shall dwell in hope*, namely after death. Rabbi Isaac said: "He teaches by this that decay and worms had no power over him." This is the tradition.

To the aforementioned things it must also be added that in Psalm 16 it is written in this manner: <note>original: "לכן שמח לבי ויגל כבודי אף בשרי ישכן לבטח כי לא תעזב נפשי לשאול ולא תתן חסידך לראות שחת"</note> *Therefore my heart is glad, and my glory rejoices; my flesh also shall dwell in hope. For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you give your holy, or pious one, to see corruption.* Here the prophecy speaks openly concerning the incorruption of Christ's body and his resurrection.

Concerning the same incorruption of the Messiah’s body, we read thus in Isaiah chapter 51: <note>original: "מהר צעה להפתח ולא ימות לשחת ולא יחסר לחמו"</note> *The prisoner hastens to be loosed, and he shall not die in corruption, nor shall his bread fail.* <note>Isaiah 51:14</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, a 12th-13th century grammarian and commentator.</note> says there that *lahmo* (his bread) refers only to the flesh, according to that passage in Leviticus chapter 21: <note>original: "כי אשי יהוה לחם אלהיהם הם מקריבים והיו קדש"</note> *Because the sacrifice of the LORD, the bread of their God, they offer; therefore they shall be holy.*

That the Messiah was to rise on the third day is clear through those things which Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century preacher from Narbonne known for his Midrashic compilations.</note> says in his exposition of the book of Genesis, regarding that statement in chapter 22: <note>original: "ביום השלישי וישא אברהם את עיניו"</note> *On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes.* For there the same Rabbi says literally: "This is what is written in Hosea chapter 6: <note>original: "יחיינו מיומים ביום השלישי יקימנו ונחיה לפניו ונדעה"</note> *He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight, and we shall know...*"

The words of the prophet Hosea are therefore to be understood according to these expositions: *He will revive us*—namely, the Messiah will revive us from the death of sin—*after two days*, during which he will lie in the tomb. *On the third day he will raise us up*, specifically through the hope of the resurrection. ## Chapter XXIII.

<margin>The first testimony.</margin>
The Catholic faith also firmly holds that Christ ascended into heaven. Therefore, it must be proved through the testimonies of the Hebrew Scriptures that the Messiah was to do that very thing after his resurrection.
GALATINUS: We can prove this through seven principal testimonies. The first of these is that which is placed in Deuteronomy, chapter 32: <note>original: "שאת אל שמים ידי"</note> *For I lift up my hand to the heavens.* Which <term>Rabbi Onkelos<note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic (the Targum Onkelos).</note></term>, translating into Aramaic, explained thus: <note>original: "ארי אתקנית בשמיא בית שכינתי"</note> *Because I will ordain, or prepare, in heaven the house of my divinity, and I will say that I remain forever.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> also explained it thus: *I will lift up my hand to the heavens,* that is, to the place of my divinity. Now, the place and house of the divinity is the Messiah according to his humanity. This is shown sufficiently through Isaiah in chapter 57, saying: <note>original: "מרום וקדוש אשכון ואת דכא ושפל רוח להחיות רוח שפלים ולהחיות לב נדכאים"</note> *Thus says the high and lofty one, inhabiting eternity, and whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and with the contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.* Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: *I inhabit the high and holy place,* and from there I am with the contrite and lowly spirit. For I extend my divinity over him. Thus far Rabbi Solomon. Now, no one is more fittingly called "contrite and lowly in spirit"—that is, humble—than the Messiah. Concerning him, Isaiah says in chapter 53: *One struck by God, or of God, and humbled. And he was wounded, or slain, for our transgressions, crushed for our sins.* It seems, therefore, that Rabbi Solomon acted as a prophet in the aforementioned expositions, although he did not know what he prophesied.
<margin>The second testimony.</margin>
The second testimony is from Micah, speaking thus of the Messiah in chapter 2: <note>original: "עלה הפורץ לפניהם פרצו ויעבורו שער ויצאו בו ויעבור מלכם לפניהם ויהוה בראשם"</note> *The breaker <note>Or "the one who breaks through."</note> has gone up before them; they have broken through and passed the gate, and gone out by it; and their King shall pass before them, and the Lord at their head.* That these things are to be understood concerning the Messiah is clearly evident through their own writings. For in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century preacher and scholar from Narbonne.</note> upon that saying in chapter 40 of the same book: <note>original: "בחלומי והנה גפן לפני"</note> *In my dream, behold, a vine was before me.* It is said: This is what is written...

<margin>The sixth testimony.</margin>

### That the Messiah would sit at the right hand of God the Father. Chapter 24.

->CAPNIO,<-

That is also the point which you must especially prove through their own scriptures: namely, that the Messiah was destined to sit at the right hand of God the Father.

->GALATINUS,<-

This we can also prove through many sayings of the ancients. We can do so especially through that same saying of the Psalmist <note>The "Psalmographus" or writer of the Psalms, referring to David.</note> which has now been cited by the one whom they call <term>Rabben Haccados</term> <note>Hebrew: *Rabbeinu HaKadosh*, meaning "Our Holy Rabbi," the title given to Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, that is, our Holy Master. For the Psalmist himself says in Hebrew:

<margin>Psalm 110</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: נְאֻם יְהוָה לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי</note>
"The LORD said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand."

CAPNIO: Even if the proposition is excellently proven by such clear testimony from the Psalmist, the more recent Jews, attempting to extinguish the light of truth, nevertheless assert that David did not speak these words about the Messiah, but about someone else. Indeed, some claim he said these same words about Abraham, whom they assert David called his "Lord" as a display of paternal reverence. Others, however, say that David uttered these words about the angel assigned to him as a guardian. They claim he called the angel "Lord" because, since every person has one of the angels assigned for their protection, the angel is rightly said to be "over" the person he guards. Therefore, the angel can also be rightly called his "Lord" in a certain sense. They throw these and many other such delusions at us so that they might escape the truth.

GALATINUS: They can say such things to those who are ignorant of Hebrew letters, but not to those who are skilled in them. For such scholars (as you well know) easily convict them through their own scriptures. Thus, through the authentic and approved writings of their ancestors, it is most clearly shown that David spoke those words neither about Abraham, nor about the angel assigned as his guardian, nor about anyone else, but about the Messiah, who is both God and man—since it is not fitting for any pure creature to sit at the right hand of God. 

First, this is evident through the <term>Targum</term> <note>The Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of Rabbi Jonathan—that is, through his Aramaic edition—which explains these same words in Aramaic as:

<note>original Aramaic: אֲמַר יְהוָה לְמֵימְרֵיהּ תִּיב לִימִינִי</note>
"The LORD said to his Word: Sit at my right hand." <note>The use of "Word" (Memra in Aramaic) here is a significant theological concept used in the Targums to refer to God's manifestation or agency.</note>

Some, however, say that the Aramaic translation is not as I have related it, but rather: 

<note>original Aramaic: אֲמַר יְהוָה לְמֵימְרֵיהּ לְמִתַּן לִי רַבְּנוּתָא תְּלָת דִּיתֵיבִית לְאוּלְפַן אוֹרָיְיתָא יְמִינִי אוֹחִין</note> 
"The LORD said in his word (or through his word) that he would give me lordship because I sat to learn the law; wait for my right hand." 

To those people, I say it is true...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Capnio (Reuchlin) and Galatinus. Having established the messianic interpretation of Psalm 110, Galatinus now addresses Jewish counter-arguments regarding the authorship and dating of the Aramaic translations (Targums) and cites Midrashic sources to solidify the claim that the "Lord" at God's right hand is indeed the Messiah.</meta>

I say, in the <term>Chaldaic translation</term> <note>Referring to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> of the Psalms, which the Jews now frequently have in their hands, it is just as they say. However, that translation is not by <term>Jonathan</term> <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Targum on the Prophets.</note>, but by Rabbi Akilas, or perhaps by Rabbi Joseph the Blind, who flourished about three hundred years after the destruction of the Second Temple. But the translation of Jonathan, which they themselves have not yet seen, holds exactly as I have reported it. They must deny it for this reason: because they have not seen it themselves. Indeed, Jonathan himself translated the entire Bible into Chaldaic (as we have proven elsewhere), although not all of his books are currently available to us.

Next, it is proven that those words of David, "The LORD said to my Lord, sit at my right hand," were meant to be understood as referring to the Messiah through the <term>Midrash Tehillim</term> <note>A rabbinic commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Psalms.</note>, specifically concerning that verse of the second Psalm: <gloss>I will declare the decree.</gloss> <note>Hebrew: *Asaperah el chok*.</note> Where it is said as follows:

<note>Translation of the Hebrew passage: "I will tell of the decree: in the decree of the Torah, and in the decree of the Prophets and the Writings. In the decree of the Torah: 'Israel is my firstborn son' [Exodus 4]. In the decree of the Prophets: 'Behold, my servant shall prosper, he shall be exalted and lifted up' [Isaiah 52]. In the Writings: 'The LORD said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand' [Psalm 110]."</note>

This means that the mysteries of this King Messiah are recounted in the scriptures of the Law, in the scripture of the Prophets, and in the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>The "Holy Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible known as Ketuvim.</note>. In the scripture of the Law, it is that verse from Exodus 4: "Israel is my firstborn son." In the scripture of the Prophets, it is that verse from Isaiah 52: "Behold, my servant shall understand, he shall be exalted, and he shall be lifted up." In the Hagiographa, it is that verse from Psalm 110: "The LORD said to my Lord, sit at my right hand."

Furthermore, this same point is proven through the *Midrash Tehillim*—that is, through the exposition of the Psalms—concerning the verse in Psalm 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 18:35.</note>: <gloss>And you have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand shall support me.</gloss> <note>Hebrew: *Ve-titten li magen yishekha vi-yminkha tisadeni*.</note> This means: "And you will give me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand will strengthen," or "will receive me." In that same place, it is said:

<note>Translation of the Hebrew passage: "We have learned in the name of Rabbi Hiyya: In the time to come, the Holy One, blessed be He, will seat the King Messiah at His right hand, as it is said: 'The LORD said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand' [Psalm 110]."</note>

This means: Rabbi [Joshua] in the name of Rabbi Hiyya said, "It shall come to pass that God, the Holy and Blessed, will cause the King Messiah to sit at His right hand. Just as it is said in Psalm 110: 'The LORD said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.'" This very thing is also excellently suggested in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses <term>Hadarsan</term> <note>Moses ha-Darshan (the Preacher) of Narbonne, an 11th-century scholar known for his midrashic compilations.</note>, when discussing the verse in chapter 18 of that same book, "And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre." There it is said: "Rabbi Barachias, in the name of Rabbi Levi, explained this through what is written in Psalm 17: 'And you shall give me the shield of your salvation,' and the Blessed One shall cause the Messiah to sit at His right hand. Just as it is said: 'The LORD said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.'" From all these sources, it is clearly shown by tradition that the aforementioned words of David must be understood entirely as referring to the Messiah, and consequently, that the Messiah himself would sit at the right hand of God the Father, which was the point to be proven.

It is necessary that it be proven from the writings of the ancient Jews that the Messiah himself was meant to do this very thing. GALATINUS: That the Holy Spirit was to be sent upon the apostles and other disciples of the Messiah, as well as upon the converts and baptized from the nations, is held most clearly from those things said in the forty-fourth chapter of Isaiah. For there it is read as follows:

<margin>Isaiah 44</margin>

# BOOK EIGHT

He speaks three times concerning the spirit, according to what is said in Zechariah, chapter 12: <note>original Hebrew: *V’shafakti al beit David v’al yoshev Yerushalayim ruach chen v’tachanunim*</note> that is, "And I will pour out upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of prayers." And it is also said in Joel, chapter 3: <note>original Hebrew: *V’hayah acharei chen eshpokh et ruchi al kol basar v’nib’u b’neikhem u-v’noteikhem zikneikhem chalomot yachalumun bachureikhem chezyonot yiru: V’gam al ha-avadim v’al ha-shifachot ba-yamim ha-hemmah eshpokh et ruchi: V’natati moftim ba-shamayim u-va-aretz dam va-esh v’timrot ashan*</note> that is, "And it shall come to pass after these things, I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your old men shall dream dreams. Your young men shall see visions. And even upon the male and female servants in those days I will pour out my spirit. And I will show wonders in heaven and on earth: blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke." 

Regarding this, the <term>gloss</term> <note>A "gloss" is a marginal or interlinear commentary on a text.</note> of **Rabbi Selomon** <note>This refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo itzhaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> says upon the phrase, "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh," that it means: "upon everyone whose heart has become tender, like flesh." Concerning this it is said in Ezekiel 36: "And I will give you a heart of flesh." These are the words of Rabbi Selomon. 

To the preceding points, it is not unfitting to add what is read in the book <term>Tanhuma</term> <note>An ancient collection of Jewish homilies (Midrash) attributed to Rabbi Tanhuma bar Abba.</note> regarding that which is said in Numbers, chapter 15, "And you shall be holy." It reads in this manner: 

> The Lord said to Israel, "In this world, by the hand of the <term>yeezer hara</term> <note>original: *יצר הרע* (yetzer hara). The "evil inclination" or "impulse."</note> (that is, the <term>fomes</term> <note>Latin: *fomitis*. A theological term for the "tinder" or "fuel" of sin, often associated with the inclination toward sin resulting from original sin.</note> or original sin), you are separated from my commandments. But in the future, in the days of the Messiah, I will uproot it from you. Just as it is said in Ezekiel 36: <note>original Hebrew: *V’hasiroti et lev ha-even mi-besarkhem v’natati lakhem lev basar v’et ruchi eten b’kirbekhem*</note> that is, 'And I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will put my spirit in the midst of you.'" And so forth, as above.

This is the tradition. From these things it clearly appears that the Holy Spirit did not come upon the obstinate Jews, nor was it poured out upon them, because they refused to lay aside their heart of stone. The faithful of Christ, however, received it abundantly for this reason: because they possessed a heart of flesh. This can in no way be denied, as experience is the witness. 

Furthermore, that the Messiah himself would send the Holy Spirit upon his disciples was most clearly foretold by **Rabbenus Haccados** <note>Latin for "Our Holy Teacher," referring to Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, who lived long before the birth of Christ. In the book entitled **Gale Razeya** <note>Hebrew: *Gali Razia*, meaning "The Revealer of Secrets." This is a mystical or pseudepigraphal work often cited by Galatinus.</note> (that is, the *Revealer of Secrets*), he replied with these words, among others, to the sixth petition of **Antoninus**, the Consul of the city of Rome: 

> After ten days from his ascension—that is, at the completion of fifty days—he will send the Holy Spirit from the heavens upon the righteous, so that they may be confirmed in his faith. And soon he will command them to go and teach all men his law. Just as it is said in Ezekiel 36: "And I will give my spirit in the midst of you, and I will cause you to walk in my commandments, and you shall keep my judgments and do them." 

The <term>figure</term> <note>A "figure" or "type" is a historical event believed to foreshadow a later spiritual reality.</note> of these fifty days were those fifty days in which Israel killed the paschal lamb and went out from the land of Egypt, during which the Holy and Blessed God sent the Holy Spirit upon them and gave them the holy law, so that they might be firm in his faith. Just as it is written in Exodus 19: "Lo, I will now come to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear me speaking to you, and may believe you forever." These are the word-for-word remarks of the man whom our adversaries themselves call **Rabbenus Haccados** (that is, *Our Holy Teacher*).

# Book Nine

## Concerning the eternal rejection of the Jews and the calling and salvation of the Gentiles.

->That all God’s promises to the Jews were made with a condition: namely, if they would receive the Messiah and obey him.<-

### Chapter 1.

CAPNIO, <note>Johann Reuchlin, the famous German humanist and scholar of Hebrew, who serves as a character in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a child or cherub figure amidst swirling foliage and architectural motifs.</image-desc>
Since, after the unlocking of the mysteries of the Messiah—which the very outcome of events clearly shows were fully accomplished in our Lord Jesus Christ—I believe you are about to speak both of the eternal rejection of the Jews, who refused to receive the true Messiah himself, and of the calling and salvation of the Gentiles, who most devotedly clung to him. Indeed, the very order of the topics to be discussed demands this. For that reason, both as a foundation for what must be said and so that the just and perpetual rejection of the obstinate Jews may appear more clearly and be more easily proven, it is first necessary for you to show through their own scriptures that all God’s promises made to the Jews were made with a condition: namely, if they would receive the Messiah and be obedient to him.

<margin>The erroneous opinion of the more recent Jews.</margin>
GALATINUS. In this the more recent Jews err greatly, firmly asserting that a promise of God regarding good things—even if made to someone who falls from righteousness into wickedness—is never revoked by God, but must always and of necessity be fulfilled. They claim, however, that a threat of evil things, even when made by God with an oath, is often revoked when repentance intervenes.

<margin>The false interpretation of Rabbi Solomon.</margin>
To prove this, they especially bring forward the words of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: "Rabbi Selomo." This refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator on the Tanakh and Talmud.</note> regarding that passage of Jeremiah spoken to the false prophet Hananiah in the twenty-eighth chapter: <note>original: "Propheta qui prophetat ad pacem, cum uenit uerbum prophetæ, scietur esse propheta, quem misit Dominus in ueritate."</note> "The prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of the prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that the Lord has truly sent the prophet." <note>Jeremiah 28:9</note> Upon this, Rabbi Solomon says: "Jeremiah said to Hananiah: I prophesy God’s vengeance. If what I prophesy comes to pass, I shall not be considered a <term>shakran</term> <note>original: שקרן (shakran), a Hebrew term for a liar or deceiver.</note>—that is, a liar or a cheat. For it repents the Holy and Blessed God concerning evil. But the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes, he shall know he is a prophet. If, however, his word does not come to pass, he is a liar."

<summary>This page introduces Book Nine, shifting the focus to the theological rejection of the Jewish people and the salvation of the Gentiles, arguing that God's promises to Israel were always conditional upon their acceptance of the Messiah.</summary>

# BOOK NINE

<header>BOOK [NINE]</header>

Just as it is said in Numbers, chapter 23: <note>original: "Nume. 23. c."</note> "God is not like a man, that he should lie." Indeed, Rabbi Tanhuma <note>A famous 4th-century Jewish sage known for his collections of homilies.</note> explained this, as did Rabbi Selomo <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note>. From these authorities, the Jews infer that God’s promises of good things can never be revoked; however, they believe that God’s threats of punishment very often become void if repentance intervenes. We, for our part, concede the latter part of their opinion—namely, that God's threats and the promises of misfortune made on account of sins can be entirely revoked through repentance. But the first part—that promises of peace or good things made by God can in no way be revoked—we utterly deny as false and heretical.

CAPNIO: I would wish for you to show, through their own scriptures, that they are being untruthful in this.

GALATINUS: First, then, let our contemporary Jews who are entangled in this error hear what they read in 1 Samuel, chapter 2 <note>original: "1. Reg. 2." following the Vulgate numbering</note>, in this manner: "A man of God came to Eli and said to him." <note>original Hebrew: בא איש אלהים אל עלי ויאמר אליו</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Selomo says: "This man of God was Elkanah." And a little later: "Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I said indeed that your house and your father’s house should walk before me forever." <note>original Hebrew: כה אמר יהוה אלהי ישראל אמור אמרתי ביתך ובית אביך יתהלכו לפני עד עולם</note> Which Rabbi Jonathan <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets.</note> interpreted in Aramaic <note>original: "Chaldaice"</note> as: "They shall serve before me forever." <note>original Aramaic: יתשמשו קדמי עד עלמיא</note> And immediately there follows: "But now, says the Lord, far be it from me! For those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed (or made base)." <note>original Hebrew: ועתה נאם יהוה חלילה לי כי מכבדי אכבד ובזי יקלו</note> Behold, he says, "The days are coming when I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father's house." <note>original Hebrew: הנה ימים באים וגדעתי את זרועך ואת זרוע בית אביך</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Selomo says: "This refers to the power you held in my house, and of which you say: Otherwise, I will take it by force."

"Those who honor me"—that is, the sons of Phinehas <note>original: "Pinhas," noting that the Latin edition corruptly calls him "Phinees"</note> who honored me at Shittim <note>Setim</note>—"I will honor." And so it was done in the days of Solomon, when the house of the Sanctuary was built. For then Solomon expelled Abiathar, who was of the house and family of Merari, so that he would no longer be a priest of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke concerning the house of Eli. And Zadok was made High Priest, because he was of the sons of Phinehas. This genealogy is recorded in the book of the Words of Days—that is, in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 6 <note>original: "1. Paralip. 6. cap."</note>. These are the words of Rabbi Selomo, in which he openly contradicts himself and opposes the things you heard him say regarding Jeremiah. Next, I propose to them what they read in Jeremiah, chapter 18, where it is spoken thus: "Can I not..."

> "Thus says the Lord: Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.
> At one moment I may speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to pluck up, to pull down, and to destroy it.
> But if that nation, against which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to it.
> And at another moment I may speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build and to plant it.
> But if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will repent of the good which I said I would do for its benefit."

->This<-

"Can I not do to you as this potter does, house of Israel?" says the Lord. "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel."

<meta>This page continues the argument that God's promises of good are conditional upon the recipient's continued righteousness. It utilizes citations from the prophet Jeremiah and various Rabbinic authorities to demonstrate that even the Patriarchs and Prophets lived in fear of losing God's favor through sin.</meta>

# BOOK NINE

<header>NINTH [BOOK]</header>

"Whenever I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it; if that nation, against whom I have spoken, shall turn from their evil, I will also repent of the evil that I thought to do to them. And whenever I speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; if it shall do evil in my eyes, and not hear my voice, I will also repent of the good which I said I would do for them." <note>original: Jeremiah 18:7–10</note> On this, the gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note> regarding the phrase *I will repent*, says: "that is, I will think another thought." From these testimonies, therefore, it is clear enough (as I judge) that on account of a subsequent fault in one to whom a promise of good was made, God renders that promise void and empty. For even if God is truthful and faithful in all His words, His promise is nevertheless almost always understood to be made with a condition, even if the condition is not explicitly stated. 

This is also elegantly shown by what is said in the exposition of the book of Genesis by Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his Midrashic (interpretive) compilations.</note> regarding that verse in the 32nd chapter of the same book: *And Jacob was greatly afraid, and it was a distress to him.* <note>original Hebrew: ויירא יעקב מאד ויצר לו</note> For there it is read word for word: "This is what is written in Proverbs, chapter 28: *Blessed is the man who is always fearful.* <note>original Hebrew: אשרי אדם מפחד תמיד</note> For such is the custom of the righteous. For though the Holy and Blessed God made them certain and secure, they nonetheless feared. So did he who was chosen among the patriarchs, and he who was chosen among the prophets. Indeed, Jacob is the chosen among the fathers, of whom it is said in Psalm 135: *For the Lord has chosen Jacob for himself.* To him, the Holy and Blessed God had said in Genesis 31: *Return to the land of your fathers, and to the place of your birth, and I will be with you.* And yet, he feared at last, as it is said in Genesis 32: *And Jacob was greatly afraid.* Why did he fear? Because he said: 'Perhaps I have been defiled by something in the house of Laban.' For it is written in Deuteronomy, chapter 23: *And he shall see no uncleanness in you, lest he turn away from you.* 

Now, the chosen among the prophets was Moses, as it is said in Psalm 105: *And he said he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood in the breach.* To him also God had said in Exodus, chapter 3: *Because I will be with you.* And nonetheless, he later feared, just as it is said in Numbers, chapter 21: *And the Lord said to Moses, Do not fear him.* This would by no means have been said unless he had been afraid. Hence it was said: *And Jacob was greatly afraid.* 

We also read there that Rabbi Hillel <note>One of the most important figures in Jewish history, a leader of the Second Temple period.</note> said: 'Do not cease to gather merits, nor be secure in yourself until the day of your death.' How so? In this way: that although a man may be righteous, let him fear sin at all times, and let him not be secure in himself. And thus it is with David, saying in Psalm 27: *Had I not believed to see the goodness of God in the land of the living.* <note>original Hebrew: לולא האמנתי לראות בטוב יהוה בארץ החיים</note> Rabbi Joses said: 'Why is the word *lule* <note>original Hebrew: לולא; meaning "if not" or "unless."</note> marked with points?' <note>Refers to scribal markings (nequdot) in the Hebrew Masoretic text used to draw attention to specific words.</note> Because David said this before the Holy and Blessed God: 'Lord of the world, I trust in You, that You will give a good reward to the righteous in the future; yet I do not know if I will have a portion among them or not.' And behold, David was a <term>hassid</term> <note>original Hebrew: חסיד; meaning a saint, a pious one, or one characterized by loving-kindness.</note>. For so he himself says in Psalm 86: *Keep my soul, for I am holy.* <note>original Hebrew: שמרה נפשי כי חסיד אני</note> And yet...

<meta>This page continues the debate regarding the conditional nature of God’s promises. The previous page established that even the Patriarchs lived in fear that sin might nullify God's favor. Here, the author uses specific scriptural examples from the books of Samuel (referred to here as 1 Kings) and Jeremiah to argue against the Jewish interpretation that God's promises of "good" are irrevocable.</meta>

# BOOK NINE

<header>BOOK</header>

As it is said in Numbers chapter 23: "God is not like a man, that he should lie." <note>original: "Non est ut homo Deus, ut mentiatur"</note> Rabbi Tanhuma <note>A 4th-century Palestinian rabbi famous for his homiletic midrashim (interpretive stories).</note> and Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> explained this. From these sources, the Jews argue that God's good promises can never be revoked; however, God's threats are very often rendered void when repentance intervenes. 

We, however, concede the latter part of their opinion: namely, that God’s threats and promises of punishment made on account of sins can indeed be revoked through repentance. But the first part—that promises of peace, of a covenant, and of good things made by God can in no way be revoked—we utterly reject as false and heretical. 

**CAPNIO:** <note>The persona of Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous Christian Hebraist, in this dialogue.</note> I would wish for you to show them to be liars in this regard, using their own scriptures. 

**GALATINUS:** <note>The persona of the author, Pietro Galatino (1460–1540), a Franciscan friar and theologian.</note> First, therefore, I will enlighten our contemporary Jews who are entangled in this error, so they may hear what they read in 1 Kings chapter 2 <note>In the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings. This refers to 1 Samuel 2:27.</note> in this manner: *And there came a man of God to Eli, and said to him, Thus says the Lord.* <note>original Hebrew: ויבא איש האלהים אל עלי ויאמר אליו כה אמר יהוה</note> Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "This man of God was Elkanah." <note>The father of the prophet Samuel.</note> And a little later: *Therefore the Lord God of Israel says: I said indeed that your house, and the house of your father, should walk before me forever.* <note>original Hebrew: לכן נאם יהוה אלהי ישראל אמר אמרתי ביתך ובית אביך יתהלכו לפני עד עולם</note> Which Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> interpreted thus: *They shall serve before me forever.* <note>original Aramaic: וישתמשון קדמי עד עלמיא</note> And immediately thereafter follows: *But now the Lord says, Far be it from me! For those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed (or rendered vile). Behold, the days come, that I will cut off your arm, and the arm of your father’s house.* <note>original Hebrew: ועתה נאם יהוה חלילה לי כי מכבדי אכבד ובזי יקלו הנה ימים באים וגדעתי את זרעך ואת זרע בית אביך</note>

Where the gloss of Rabbi Solomon says: "that is, the power which you had in my house, and by which you say, 'Otherwise I will take it by force.'" *For those who honor me*—this refers to the sons of Phinehas <note>The Latin text notes "Pinhas," correcting the Vulgate's "Phinees."</note> (whom our edition names corruptly as Phinees), who honored me at Shittim <note>Referring to the event in Numbers 25 where Phinehas killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman to stop a plague.</note>—*I will honor.* And so it was done in the days of Solomon, when the house of the Sanctuary was built. For then Solomon expelled Abiathar, who was of the house and family of Merari, so that he would not be a priest of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord which he spoke concerning the house of Eli. And Zadok was made High Priest because he was of the sons of Phinehas; for so it is recorded in the genealogy in the book of the Words of the Days, that is, in the first book of Chronicles chapter 6. <note>original: "Paralip. 6. cap." *Paralipomenon* is the Greek-derived Latin name for Chronicles.</note> These are the words of Rabbi Solomon, in which he asserts things clearly repugnant to what you heard him say regarding Jeremiah. 

Next, I propose to them what they frequently read in Jeremiah 18, where it is said: *Cannot I do with you as this potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel. At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it; If that nation, against whom I have spoken, shall turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them. And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it; If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them.* <note>original Hebrew: הה כיוצר הזה לא אוכל לעשות לכם בית ישראל נאם יהוה הנה כחמר ביד היוצר כן אתם בידי בית ישראל : רגע אדבר על גוי ועל ממלכה לנתוש ולנתוץ ולהאביד : ושב הגוי ההוא מרעתו אשר דברתי עליו ונחמתי על הרעה אשר חשבתי לעשות לו : ורגע אדבר על גוי ועל ממלכה לבנות ולנטוע : ועשה הרעה בעיני לבלתי שמוע בקולי ונחמתי על הטובה אשר אמרתי להיטיב אותו</note> This means: "Cannot I do to you as this potter, house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel."

"Until this people pass over whom you have possessed" refers to the second arrival in the time of Ezra. For the children of Israel were worthy that a sign or miracle should occur at their second arrival, just as was done in the first; however, sin caused it so that no miracle was performed for them. For this reason, it is found that Jacob feared because of sin. It was also said regarding Jacob, as written in Genesis chapter 28: "And behold, I will be with you, and I will keep you in all places where you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken to you." And yet it is written in chapter 32: "And Jacob feared greatly." He feared indeed lest perhaps sin had invalidated what God had said above and promised to him. All these things are from Rabbi Moses Hadarsan <note>Moshe HaDarshan, an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne known for his midrashic (interpretive) commentaries.</note> from the traditions of the ancients. 

To these must be added what is read in the book of the Sanhedrin, in the chapter *Helek* <note>Chapter 11 of Tractate Sanhedrin in the Talmud, which discusses the afterlife and the Messiah.</note> in this manner: It is written in Exodus: <note>original Hebrew: כל המחלה אשר שמתי במצרים לא אשים עליך כי אני יהוה רפאך</note> "Every exhaustion, or pain which I placed in Egypt, I will not place upon you, for I am God your healer." <note>Exodus 15:26</note> If He will not place exhaustion upon them, why would He be a healer? Rabbi Johanan said: This scripture is explained by itself, when it is immediately said: <note>original Hebrew: ויאמר אם שמוע תשמע לקול יהוה אלהיך והישר בעיניו תעשה</note> "And he said, If listening you will listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is right in His eyes." If you listen (He says), I will not place it. But if you do not listen, I will place every exhaustion upon you, even if I am a healer. This is the tradition.

From all these things it is clearly evident that all of God's promises made of old to the Israelite people were always conditional; that is, if those to whom some good had been promised would withdraw from evil and, persevering in good, would be obedient to Him—even if the scripture sometimes does not explicitly state such a condition. For then the condition itself was to be understood no differently than if it had been explicitly stated. Otherwise, Jacob and Moses—who, after they had received such firm security from God, feared greatly—could in no way be excused from the crime of unfaithfulness and incredulity. To even dream such a thing about men so holy is a sin. 

Since these things are so, it is clearer than the sun that all the promises made to the Jews concerning the Messiah and their salvation were conditional: namely, that they would receive Him and obey Him as God their savior. Therefore, the cause why the Jews were not redeemed and saved through the Messiah is none other than because they did not receive Him, nor did they wish to hear Him; but rather they denied Him and killed Him, according to what was said by the Psalmist <note>literally "Psalm-writer," referring to David.</note> in the Psalm: <note>original Hebrew: לא שמע עמי לקולי וישראל לא אבה לי : ואשלחהו בשרירות לבם במועצותיהם : לו עמי שומע לי ישראל בדרכי יהלכו</note> "My people did not hear my voice, and Israel would have none of me; so I sent them away according to the hardness of their heart in their own counsels. Oh, that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways." <note>Psalm 81:11–13</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion between Capnio (Johann Reuchlin) and Galatinus regarding the nature of divine promises. Galatinus is arguing that the promises made to the Jewish people were not unconditional, but rather dependent on their acceptance of the Messiah. He uses the long duration of the exile—over 1,440 years at the time of writing—as evidence that the literal, earthly kingdom promised to the Davidic line must have been transformed or forfeited due to their rejection of Christ.</meta>
