### That the Messiah was to institute the sacrament of baptism, by which circumcision was to be abolished. Chapter 11.

## CAPNIO <note>The scholar Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), who used the Greek-derived pseudonym "Capnio."</note>

Since Christ commanded the apostles, who were about to proclaim the Gospel law to the nations, that they should baptize the Gentiles—and since he handed down to them the form of baptizing, saying in the last chapter of Matthew: "Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you" <note>Matthew 28:19–20</note>—this sacrament of baptism is the door to the sacraments of this new and evangelical law. Therefore, for a clearer expression of the catholic <note>In the sense of "universal"</note> truth and for the greater confusion of Jewish obstinacy, it is necessary to prove through the Hebrew scriptures that the Messiah himself was intended to institute baptism for the remission of sins.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> <note>Pietro Galatino, the other participant in this dialogue.</note> We have this first from the fact that Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Messiah himself in the 44th chapter, brought forth these words:

> <note>original Hebrew: "Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and Jeshurun whom I have chosen. For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my spirit on your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants. They will spring up like grass in a meadow, like poplar trees by flowing streams. Some will say, 'I belong to the Lord'; others will call themselves by the name of Jacob; still others will write on their hand, 'The Lord's,' and will take the name Israel."</note>

That is: Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and most upright one <note>The Hebrew *Jeshurun*, a poetic name for Israel</note>, whom I have chosen. Because I will pour waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land. I will pour my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your branches. And they shall sprout among the grass, like willows by the watercourses. This one shall say, "I am God's." And that one shall call on the name of Jacob. And another shall write with his hand to God, and shall be addressed by the name of Israel. 

Moreover, Rabbi Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary</note> translated and explained these words—"Because I will pour waters upon the thirsty"—along with the rest, in the Chaldaic <note>A term formerly used for Aramaic</note> language in this way:

> <note>original Aramaic: "For as water is given to a thirsty land and flows over the parched ground, so will I give my Holy Spirit to your children and my blessing to your children's children. And the righteous, the tender, and the delicate shall increase like the blossoms that grow by the streams of water. This one shall say, 'I am a worshiper of the Lord,' and this one shall pray in the name of Jacob, and this one shall offer his sacrifice before the Lord, and be called by the name of Israel.'"</note>

That is (to render it word for word): Because just as waters are given upon the thirsty land, and streams upon the dry, so I will give my Holy Spirit upon your son, and my blessing upon your children's children. And the righteous, the tender, and the delicate shall be anointed (or multiplied), like the blossoms that send their roots over the reaches of the waters. This one shall say, "I am of those who fear God." And this one shall pray in the name of Jacob. And this one shall offer his sacrifice before God, and shall be called by the name of Israel. From these words of the prophet, where he speaks openly of baptism, it is most clearly evident that by the virtue of baptism, those converted from the Gentiles, and all Christians, were to be made children of Israel. For the confirmation of this matter, it should be noted what is found in the Jerusalem book *Yoma* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the Day of Atonement</note>, in the chapter that begins *Yom Ha-Kippurim* <note>The Day of Atonement</note>, in this manner...

### TENTH BOOK

It is written in the 16th chapter of Jeremiah: <note>Jeremiah 17:13 in modern Bibles; the text cites chapter 16.</note> **The hope of Israel is the Lord.** <note>original Hebrew: מקוה ישראל יהוה (Mikveh Yisrael Adonai). To understand these things, it must be noted what is written in the **Lesser Beressith**, <note>original Hebrew: בראשית קטנה (Beressith Ketanna). And he is the one who will plant all Israel like a **choice branch**. <note>original Hebrew: שורקה (Soreca), referring to a high-quality vine.</note> As it is written in the second chapter of Jeremiah: **And I planted you a choice vine, entirely a seed of truth.** <note>original Hebrew: ואנכי נטעתיך שורק כלה זרע אמת</note> That is: "And I planted you as a choice vine, all a seed of truth." 

And how will he act? As it was said in the thirty-sixth chapter of Ezekiel: "And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your impurities," and so forth. This is the tradition. You see how clearly it is said here that the Messiah would be the one to sprinkle these waters of Ezekiel, and by so doing, would plant all Israel—both the literal and the spiritual Israel, of which we spoke shortly before. For the aforementioned words of Zechariah can be understood of no one else but the Messiah. The water of baptism and its power was also prophesied in that place where it was said through Zechariah in the 13th chapter: **In that day there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness: And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they shall be remembered no more.** <note>original Hebrew: ביום ההוא יהיה מקור נפתח לבית דוד וליושבי ירושלם לחטאת ולנדה : והיה ביום ההוא נאם יהוה צבאית אכרית את שמות העצבים מן הארץ ולא יזכרו עוד</note> That is: "In 그날 [that day] there shall be a fountain open to the house of David, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for cleansing, and for sprinkling, or for removing [impurity]. And it shall be in that day, says the God of hosts, I will cut off the names of idols from the earth, and they shall be remembered no more." Which words are most aptly explained thus: "In that day," that is, in the time of the Messiah—just as we have proven the prophet speaks there of the Messiah—there shall be a "fountain," namely of baptism; "open," that is, common to all men; "to the house of David and the inhabi—"

# BOOK

and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, for the Church of Christ gathered from both Jews and Gentiles—specifically to purify souls from original sin and from all other sins, and for sprinkling, which is to say, for washing sinners from every stain of sin, or for distancing, which is to say, for removing the impurity of any sin whatsoever from the soul. Moreover, the time when all this was to be done is shown when it is immediately added: "It shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, and they shall be remembered no more." Since, therefore, this was not done through Abraham, nor through any of the prophets, nor in their days, but was done only in the days of Jesus our Messiah, through himself and through his disciples and others believing in him, it is clearly evident that our Savior himself is the "David"—that is, the Messiah—mentioned in the previous words of Zechariah; and also that his baptism is that fountain open to all, of which it was spoken in the same place. The prophet also gave another most evident sign of this truth when he immediately added these words: **And also the prophets and the unclean spirit I will cause to pass from the land.** <note>original Hebrew: וגם את הנביאים ואת רוח הטומאה אעביר מן הארץ — Zechariah 13:2.</note> This means: "And I will also transfer the prophets and the unclean spirit away from the earth." Rabbi Jonathan explained this in the Aramaic <note>original: Chaldaicè</note> as follows: **And also the false prophets and the unclean spirit I will abolish from the earth.** <note>original Aramaic: ואף ית נבייא שקרא וית רוח מסאבא אבטיל מן ארעא</note> 

If the younger Jews deny that this was fulfilled in the days of our Messiah, let it be brought back to their memory that before the arrival of our Savior, there was such a great abundance of false prophets in the world, not only among the Gentiles but even among themselves, that Elijah the prophet of the Lord said to Ahab, the King of Israel: "Gather to me all Israel at Mount Carmel, and the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and the four hundred prophets of light or of the grove <note>original Latin: prophetas lucis siue nemoris. This refers to the prophets of Asherah, often associated with sacred groves.</note> who eat at Jezebel's table." Besides these, there were many other false prophets among the Jews, whom Ahab later consulted as to whether he should go to Ramoth Gilead. Let them also recall that before the times of our Messiah, in the days of their fathers, unclean spirits were accustomed to give responses through idols. For as we read in the first book of Kings, chapter 1, <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 1:2.</note> Ahaziah the King of Israel said this to his messengers among other things: "Go and inquire of **Baal Zebub** <note>original: בעל זבוב</note>—that is, the **Lord of the Flies**—the god of **Ekron** <note>original: עקרון (Akaron)</note>, whether I shall recover from this my infirmity." Also in the 10th chapter of Zechariah, it is said that the idols spoke fraud. 

Therefore, since in the days of the Jews and before the coming of Christ our Lord, idolatry flourished so greatly not only among the Gentiles but also among the Jews—as well as false prophets and unclean spirits, as has been shown by these few examples out of many—and since it is established that in the days of our Messiah all these things were so utterly destroyed that there is no need for proof, it is undoubtedly consequent that whatever we concluded just before is entirely true. To the preceding points, I think it appropriate to add what is read in the Babylonian book **Yoma** <note>original: יומה (Yoma), meaning "The Day."</note> (that is, the book of "Days"), in the chapter **Yom Kippurim** <note>original: יום הכפורים (Yom akippurim)</note> (that is, the "Day of Atonements"), written in this manner: **Rav** <note>term: Rav (רב). A title for a Babylonian Talmudic sage.</note> said...

# BOOK TEN

Rabbi Akiba says: "Blessed are you, Israel, before Him by whom you shall be cleansed. And who shall cleanse you? Your Father who is in heaven." Regarding this it was said in Ezekiel chapter 36: **And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed.** <note>original: "Et spargã super uos aquas mundas, & mundabimini."</note> And so on as above. And again in Jeremiah 17: <term>מקוה ישראל יהוה</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Mikveh Yisrael Adonai*</note>. This means: "The collection or gathering of waters of Israel is the Lord." For just as a gathering or collection of waters <note>the Hebrew word *mikveh* means both "hope" and a ritual "collection of waters" used for immersion</note> cleanses the impure, so God—the Holy One, blessed be He—will cleanse Israel. This is the tradition. Since, therefore, this act—through the authority of Ezekiel—was attributed a little while ago by the ancient Jewish teachers to the Messiah, it follows necessarily according to their own words that the Messiah is God, who was meant to cleanse all Israel through the waters of baptism by the power of his Holy Spirit, as was explained above. Moreover, that baptism was to be instituted against all sins, and especially against original sin, was specifically foretold through Ezekiel, who says in chapter 36:

-> <term>And I will sprinkle clean water upon you and you shall be clean from all your uncleanness; and from all your idols I will cleanse you.</term> <-
-> <term>And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you; and I will take away the stony heart from your flesh,</term> <-
-> <term>and I will give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my spirit within you, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes,</term> <-
-> <term>and you shall keep my judgments and do them.</term> <-

That is: **And I will pour clean waters upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleanness, and from all your filthiness I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will give in your midst. And I will take away the stony heart from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And my spirit I will give in your midst. And I will act so that you walk in my precepts, and keep my judgments, and do them.** Now, this "stony heart" which he says must be taken away—to be succeeded by a heart of flesh and the Holy Spirit through grace—is understood as original sin, which was to be utterly removed by God through the mediation of baptism. Furthermore, to understand that baptism was meant to make circumcision void, the saying of Rabbi Joshua is especially to be noted, when in the book <term>יבמות</term> *Yevamot* <note>The Talmudic tractate regarding "Levirate Marriages" or brothers-in-law</note>, in the chapter <term>החולץ</term> *Hacholez* <note>meaning "The one who removes the shoe"</note>, he says: <term>Whoever is baptized but not circumcised, behold, he is a proselyte, just as we find with the mothers who were baptized but not circumcised.</term> <note>original Hebrew: מי שהוא טבול ואינו נימול הנה הוא גר כמו שהוא נמצא באמהו' שנטבלו ולא נימולו</note> This means: "He who is baptized and not circumcised, behold, he is a *gher* <note>a convert or proselyte</note>, that is, one converted from the Gentiles to the true faith. For so we find in the mothers—namely Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, and Leah—who were baptized <note>ritually immersed</note> and not circumcised." In this place, it should also be known that circumcision was a figure of the shedding of Christ’s blood. He began to shed it at his own circumcision, and finally, in his passion, he poured it all out for the salvation of the human race. Nor was circumcision ever to be performed again after Christ commanded baptism to take its place, which deletes sins more perfectly, and which both women and men can use. That this sacrament of baptism was also to be proclaimed throughout the whole world can be gathered from what is read in the *Midrash* <term>קהלת</term> *Koheleth* <note>A commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes</note>, when commenting on that verse in the first chapter of the same book: <term>What has been is what shall be.</term> <note>original Hebrew: מה שהיה הוא שיהיה</note> This is...

# BOOK TEN

"What was? It is the very thing that shall be." <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:9</note>. As it is said in the last chapter of Joel: <term>ומעין מבית יהוה יצא והשקה את נחל השטים</term> <note>original Hebrew: *U-mayan mi-beit Adonai yetzei ve-hishka et nachal ha-shittim*</note>. *Regarding the sacrament of penance, and that the Messiah was to institute it through vocal confession for the remission of sins. Chapter III.*

->CAPNIO<-

Since we have correctly established that the Lord instituted not only baptism, but also the sacrament of penance <note>The word *poenitentiæ* can be translated as either "penance" or "repentance"; in this Catholic theological context, it refers to the formal sacrament</note> for the remission of sins. For since baptism is received only once (as it is a sacrament that cannot be repeated), it was necessary for penance to be instituted. This was so that the sacrament of penance might come to the aid of those who happened to sin after receiving baptism. For this reason, some have not inaptly called penance "the second plank after a shipwreck" <note>A classic theological metaphor: if baptism is the ship, penance is the plank one clings to after falling into sin</note>. Therefore, since enough has been said regarding baptism, something must now be said from the Hebrew scriptures regarding the sacrament of penance, specifically concerning vocal confession for the remission of sins, which the Messiah was meant to institute. And because we have already said enough (as I judge) in the eighth book regarding the penance which the Messiah was to preach through himself and his disciples, and regarding its efficacy and power, it should now suffice to reveal only those things from the Hebrew writings which pertain to vocal confession.

First, let us hear what is read in the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient Jewish commentary or "exposition" on the Psalms</note>. There, upon Psalm 100, it is said word for word: <term>מזמור לתודה הריעו ליהוה כל הארץ</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Mizmor l'todah hariu l'Adonai kol ha-aretz*</note>. This means: "A Psalm for confession. Shout joyfully to God, all the earth" <note>The Hebrew *todah* can mean "thanksgiving" or "confession"</note>. The Holy and Blessed God said: "All nations shall confess to me, and I will receive them." As it is said in Isaiah chapter 45: <term>כי לי תכרע כל ברך</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Ki li tichra kol berech*</note>. This means: "For to me every knee shall bow." There is another discourse and another exposition: "A Psalm for confession." This is what is written in Proverbs chapter 28: <term>מכסה פשעיו לא יצליח ומוודה ועזב ירחם</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Michaseh peshav lo yatzliach u-modeh v'ozev yerucham*</note>. This means: "He who conceals his crimes shall not prosper; but he who confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy." "He who conceals his crimes"—such a one was Saul. As it is said in 1 Samuel 15: "What then is this voice of sheep?" But he himself responded—

...from Amalek they brought them. <note>This continues a sentence from the previous page, likely referring to spoils or captives from the Amalekites used as an example of sin or its consequences.</note> "He who confesses and forsakes his sins shall obtain mercy" <note>A quotation of Proverbs 28:13</note>. Such a man was David, of whom it is said in the second book of Kings, chapter 12: "And David said to Nathan, 'I have sinned against the Lord.' And Nathan said to David: 'The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die.'" So ends the tradition. From this, an argument is drawn concerning the efficacy of confession made to another person.

Regarding this, it should also be noted that in the *Bereshith ketanna* <note>original Latin: *Beressith ketanna*, meaning "Little Genesis," a reference to a midrashic or smaller commentary on the Book of Genesis</note>—that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis—it is said regarding the statement in the forty-ninth chapter of that same book: <term>יהודה אתה יודוך אחיך</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Yehuda ata yodu-cha acheicha*</note>. This means: "Judah, your brothers shall confess to you," or "shall praise you." For there it is said: This is the confession of which it was spoken by the Holy Spirit through the hand of Job in chapter 15: <term>אשר חכמים יגידו ולא כחדו מאבותם</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Asher chachamim yaggidu ve-lo kichadu me-avotam*</note>. This means: "Those who are wise confess," or "declare, and do not hide from their fathers"—namely, their sins. Of these it is said: Regarding the righteous who conquer or subdue their <term>fomes</term> <note>A technical theological term meaning the "tinder" or "inclination" toward sin, often associated with sensuality</note> or their sensuality, and confess their acts to their fathers. For everyone who confesses his acts is worthy of the world to come. As it is said in Psalm 50: <term>זובח תודה יכבדנני ושם דרך אראנו בישע אלהים</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Zove'ach todah yechabdan-ni ve-sam derech arenu be-yesha Elohim*</note>. This means: "He who sacrifices confession shall honor me; and to him who sets his way aright, I will show the salvation of God."

And so you find this in the case of Judah. For at the hour when the matter of Tamar <note>Referring to the story in Genesis 38 where Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar traps him into fulfilling his levirate duty; Judah eventually acknowledges his fault publicly</note> was brought before him, he confessed, just as it is said in Genesis, chapter 38: <term>הכר נא את בוראך ואל תקח בושת מבשר ודם</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Haker na et borecha ve-al tikach boshet mi-basar ve-dam*</note>. This means: "Acknowledge, I pray, your Creator, and do not be ashamed before flesh and blood"—that is, before man. Immediately, therefore, he conquered his sensuality, or his emotion, and confessed.

However, the Holy and Blessed God curses everyone who does not confess his works. For so we find in Cain, who denied his deed and said in Genesis, chapter 4: "Am I my brother's keeper?" Therefore he was cursed. As it is said in the same place: "And now you are cursed," and so forth. But when he realized he had sinned, he sought pardon from the Holy and Blessed God and said: "Lord of the whole world, my sin is so great that it cannot be borne or tolerated. My sin, I say, is greater than that of the six hundred thousand <note>A common Rabbinic reference to the number of Israelites who sinned in the wilderness</note> who will sin before you, as in Exodus, chapter 34. And when they say to you, 'Take away the sin,' you will immediately be the one who absolves." Immediately, therefore, He whose name be blessed forever said: "If I do not absolve Cain, I shall close the door to all who repent." And because he did not perform a perfect penance, He spared him by half. And from where is this derived? From what is said in Genesis, chapter four: "You shall be a wanderer and restless on the earth." But after he performed penance, it says: "And he dwelt in the land of Nod"—that is, the land of commotion or shaking. And of him Solomon says in the twenty-eighth chapter of Proverbs: "He who hides his crimes shall not be directed. But he who confesses and leaves them shall obtain mercy." So ends the tradition.

**The judgment is finished** <note>original Hebrew: *Nigmar haddin*</note>, that is, the judgment is finalized. For we find this regarding Achan, to whom Joshua said: "My son, I pray you, give honor to the Lord God of Israel, and make confession, and tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me." And Achan answered Joshua and said: "Truly I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel, and thus and so have I done." <note>A reference to Joshua 7:19-20</note> And from where is it held that his sin was forgiven him? From that which is said in the same place, namely Joshua chapter 7: "And Joshua said, 'As you have troubled us, so the Lord shall trouble you on this day.'" "On this day" (he said) you are troubled, but you shall not be troubled in the future <note>This interpretation suggests that Achan's earthly punishment served as an atonement, sparing him from suffering in the afterlife</note>. All this is from tradition.

Furthermore, that all sins, along with the circumstances aggravating the sin, ought to be declared in confession is held not only from the aforementioned confession of Achan, but also from that which is said in the book **Yoma** <note>original: *yoma*, meaning "The Day," the Talmudic tractate concerning the Day of Atonement</note>, that is, of the Days, in the chapter **Yom Ha-Kippurim** <note>original: *iom hakippurim*</note>, that is, the Day of Propitiations or Indulgences. There it is written: Rab Hunna said, "Everyone who has committed a transgression must express the sin specifically." Just as it was said regarding the thirty-second chapter <note>Exodus 32:31</note>, "And they made for themselves gods of gold," and so forth.

That this repentance, at whatever time it is made, is always acceptable to God is held in the **Midrash Tehillim** <note>original: *Midras tehilim*, an ancient Jewish commentary on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that verse of the sixty-fifth Psalm: **To you silence is praise, O God, in Zion, and to you shall the vow be performed.** <note>Psalm 65:1 in many Hebrew versions; 64:2 in the Vulgate</note> For there we read as follows:

> Rabbi Hanina ben Papa asked Rabbi Samuel bar Nachmani: "What is the meaning of 'placing' <note>referring to a theological support or basis</note> in the matter of 'To You'?" He said to him: "The gates of prayer are sometimes open and sometimes closed, but the gates of repentance are never closed, as it is said: 'The trust of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea.' Just as this sea is never locked, but anyone who seeks to wash in it may do so at any hour, so too whenever a person wishes to perform repentance, at any hour a person wishes to return, they may do so, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, receives them."

This means: Rabbi Hanina ben Papa questioned Rabbi Samuel the son of Nachmani, saying, "What is it that is written in the third chapter of Lamentations: 'You have covered yourself with a cloud, that prayer should not pass through'?" He answered him: "Because the gates of prayer are sometimes open, and sometimes indeed closed. But the gates of repentance are never closed in this world. As it is said in the sixty-fifth Psalm: 'The hope of all the ends of the earth, and of the sea of those afar off'—namely, this is repentance. For just as this sea is never closed, but whoever wishes washes himself there at any hour he wishes, so is repentance itself; at whatever hour a man wishes to perform it, he performs it, and the holy and blessed God receives it." Prayer, however, has set times. As it is said in the sixty-ninth Psalm: "But as for me, my prayer is unto you, O Lord, in a time of favor." All this is tradition, from which the proposed point is made clear.

### That the Messiah was to institute a new sacrifice, in which he himself was to be the bread and food. Chapter 4.

->CAPNIO,<-
<note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pen name of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist.</note>

Having spoken of baptism and of penance regarding vocal confession, we must now speak of the sacrament of the Eucharist. This is the sacrament which the Messiah was to institute in bread and wine—by divine power transubstantiating <note>original: *transubstantiando*; the theological concept of the bread and wine literally becoming the body and blood of Christ</note> the bread into his body and the wine into his blood.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> <note>Galatinus is the primary speaker in this dialogue, representing the author Pietro Galatino.</note> Therefore, it must first be proven through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the Messiah himself was to institute a new sacrifice, of which he himself would be the bread and food. First, it must not be overlooked that Psalm 72, which begins "Give the King your judgment, O God," is said by the ancient Jewish teachers to speak entirely of the Messiah. This is shown most clearly in the **Midrash Tehillim** <note>original: *Midras tehilim*, a traditional Jewish commentary or "homily" on the Psalms</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding the title of this same Psalm, which is: "This is King Solomon" <note>original Hebrew: *zeh melekh Shlomoh*</note>, that is, for Solomon, or "for the peaceful one." For it is said there: "This is the King Messiah, of whom it was said in Isaiah chapter 11: 'A rod shall come forth from the stem of Jesse.'" <note>original Hebrew: *Zeh ha-Mashiach she-ne’emar ve-yatzah choter mi-geza Yishai*</note> Although Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the famous medieval Jewish commentator</note> tries to explain this Psalm as being about King Solomon, he interprets the words of that same Psalm, "In his days the righteous shall flourish, and an abundance of peace until the moon is no more" <note>original Hebrew: *Yifrach be-yamav tzaddik ve-rov shalom ad bli yareach*</note> as follows: "In his days, that is, in the days of Solomon, the righteous shall be multiplied, and there shall be an abundance of peace until the end of the world." Yet, when he reached that place where our edition <note>the Latin Vulgate</note> has, "There shall be a firmament on the earth on the tops of the mountains," the Hebrew truth <note>a common phrase used by scholars for the original Hebrew text</note> says: "There shall be a cake of grain" <note>original Hebrew: *Yehi pissath bar*</note>, which is commonly called a *focaccia* <note>a type of flatbread</note>, or a morsel of grain in the earth, on the peaks of the mountains. Not being able to completely silence the truth, he brought forth these words against his own position, saying: "Our masters of blessed memory explained this to be a type of cake in the days of the Messiah, and they explained the whole Psalm as being about the King Messiah." <note>original Hebrew: *Raboteinu peirshu gloska’ot le-yimot ha-Mashiach ve-kol ha-mizmor be-yimot ha-Mashiach*</note> These are his words. However, how and in what manner the Messiah was to be a "cake of grain" <note>original Hebrew: *Pissath bar*</note> according to the exposition of the wise Jewish Masters, is found in the book they call **Sifrei** <note>original Hebrew: *Siphre*, an early rabbinic commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note>. There, concerning the saying in Deuteronomy chapter 32, "The Lord alone led him, and there was no foreign god with him," it is said: "Another word: 'The Lord alone shall lead him,' etc. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: It is destined that I shall seat you in rest in the world, and there will be no foreign god with him, so that there shall not be among you people who occupy themselves with useless trade, as it is said, 'There shall be a cake of grain in the earth,' etc., so that the wheat shall produce cakes as large as the palm of a hand <note>original Hebrew: *pissath yad*</note>, and his fruit shall rustle like Lebanon, for the wheat shall beat one against the other and drop their fine flour on the ground, and you shall come and take from it the fullness of your palm for your sustenance." <note>original Hebrew: *Davar acher Yahweh badad yanchenu...*</note> This means...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where Galatinus is citing Jewish sources to prove that the Messiah would be associated with a miraculous bread or "cake of wheat," which Christians interpret as the Eucharist. It specifically analyzes Psalm 72 and compares the Messiah to Moses.</meta>

BOOK [TEN] 658

<meta>catchword: וכן (And thus)</meta>

I will turn you to the gentleness of the spirit in this world. And no strange God shall be with him. For the sons of Adam will not be in you, practicing any trade. As it is said in Psalm 72: "There shall be a cake of grain in the earth, on the tops of the mountains." For they shall bring forth grain in the days of the Messiah <gloss>Hebrew: *gheluscaoth* גלוסקאות, that is, fine cakes or rolls</gloss>. The text says "fullness" <gloss>Hebrew: *caph* כף, that is, the hollow or palm of the hand</gloss>. It follows: <gloss>Hebrew: *be-Levanon piryo* בלבנון פריו</gloss> This means, "Its fruit shall shake like Lebanon." Because the stalks of grain shall rub against each other, and shall drop their likeness <note>referring to the refined flour or "simila"</note> onto the earth. And you, coming there, will take a handful of the "piece" <gloss>Hebrew: *pissath* פסת, that is, a small round cake like the palm of a hand</gloss>, according to your refreshment or provision.

This same thing is held in the book **Ketubot** <note>original: *Chethuboth*; a tractate of the Talmud concerning marriage contracts</note>, in the chapter that begins **Shnei Dayyanei** <note>original: *Sene dayyane*; meaning 'Two Judges'</note>, where it is read word-for-word as follows: "Rabbi Yose said, in the future, the land of Israel will produce cakes and ornaments of purple. As it was said: 'There shall be a cake of grain in the earth.'" And note that in the language of the Romans <note>Latin/Italian</note>, a thin, spread-out cake is called **pissa** <note>original: *pissa*; likely an early reference to a flatbread or "pizza-like" dough, which the author links to the Hebrew 'pissath'</note>. The Teachers read that verse of the Psalm: <gloss>Hebrew: *pissath bar* פסת בר, that is, a cake or a fragment of grain in the earth</gloss>. They said: In the future, the wheat will grow like a palm tree and rise up like a palm: just as it says, "There shall be a *pissath bar*," that is, a cake or fragment of grain in the earth. 

But perhaps you will say: there will be labor in gathering it. The text teaches that this is not so by what follows: "Its fruit shall tremble, or be moved, like Lebanon." For the Holy and Blessed God will bring forth wind from His treasures, and it will separate the fine flour from it. Then a man will come and carry back from there a full palm of his hand, and from it he will provide for his own sustenance and that of his family. On this, the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the famous 11th-century Jewish commentator</note> says: "And all this will happen in the days of the Messiah." Moreover, Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, a prominent medieval grammarian and commentator</note> said: "There shall be a *pissath* of grain in the earth." This is the same as if it were said: "There shall be a fragment of bread of wheat in the earth." From all these things, it is clear that this Psalm speaks of the Messiah. 

It is therefore manifest, according to the evidence of the text, that the Messiah was to be a "cake of grain" in the earth. Indeed, it was said of him (as has been established): "There shall be a cake of grain, or a fragment of bread, in the earth." That the Messiah himself was to be this cake of grain is confirmed in the **Midrash Kohelet** <note>original: *Midras coheleth*; a traditional Jewish commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes</note>, in the exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes, when it is said regarding the first chapter: <gloss>Hebrew: *Mah she-hayah hu she-yihyeh* מה שהיה הוא שיהיה, that is, 'What is it that was? It is that which shall be.'</gloss> Rabbi Berachiah said in the name of Rabbi Isaac: "Just as the First Redeemer was—that is, Moses—so shall the Last Redeemer be." And it is added: "For just as the First Redeemer made manna descend—as it is said in Exodus 16: 'Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you'—so too the Last Redeemer, that is the Messiah, will be a cake of grain in the earth. According to that saying: 'And there shall be a cake of grain in the earth.'" For this reason, Rabbi Jonathan ben Uzziel <note>A famous disciple of Hillel, attributed with the Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Prophets</note>, turning this passage into Aramaic, explained it as follows: "And thus it shall come to pass..."

Specifically, in the bonds of love. As it is said in the 1st chapter of *Malachi*: "I have loved you, says God. And I will be to them like those who lift the yoke." Because...

## That the Messiah, in this sacrifice, was to transubstantiate bread into his body, and wine into his blood. Chapter VI.

->CAPNIO,<- <note>"Capnio" is the Greek-style nickname for Johannes Reuchlin, the famous 16th-century Hebraist, who acts as the student/interlocutor in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'F' featuring a floral or architectural pattern within a square border.</image-desc>

The Catholic faith firmly confesses and holds that in this sacrifice, by divine power, the bread is truly and really <term>transubstantiated</term> <note>The transformation of the substance of bread and wine into the substance of the body and blood of Christ.</note> into the true body of Christ, and the wine into his true blood. Therefore, I would like to know whether it can be proven through the scriptures of the ancient Jews that the bread was to be truly and really transubstantiated into the body of the Messiah, and the wine into his blood, in this same sacrifice. <margin>GAL.</margin> Most certainly. For concerning the conversion of bread into the flesh of the Messiah himself, the Son of God, it is found in the commentaries of Rabbi Moses the Preacher <note>Rabbi Moshe ha-Darshan of Narbonne, an 11th-century scholar often cited by Christian Hebraists.</note> on the verse of Psalm 136: "Who gives bread to all flesh" <note>original Hebrew: "נתן לחם לכל בשר" (Natan lechem le-chol basar).</note>. Where it is said: "And he spoke a known word: 'Bread is given to all flesh.' This is what they say: 'Taste and see that the Lord is good' <note>Psalm 34:8</note>, for the bread which he gives to all is his own flesh. And when the bread is tasted, it is converted into flesh." And this is what was said: "And see that the Lord is good," and he shall live, and live greatly. <note>Translating the Hebrew commentary: "ואמר דבר ידוע ניתן לכל בשר... והוא בשרי" (And he said a known thing is given to all flesh... and it is my flesh).</note> This means: "Furthermore, a known word was spoken: 'Who gives bread to all flesh.' This is what was said in Psalm 34: 'Taste and see, because God is good.' Because the bread which he gives to all is his very flesh. And as the bread is tasted, it is converted into flesh. And this is what was said..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the sacrificial nature of the Eucharist, moving from the priesthood of Melchizedek to specific Rabbinic interpretations that Galatinus argues prefigure the conversion of bread and wine into the body and blood of the Messiah (transubstantiation).</meta>

# TENTH BOOK

...see, for God is good. And this will be a great wonder. These words are found there. If these few words are examined well, they are understood to be about the conversion of bread into the body of the Messiah. Truly, concerning his blood, which is sacrificed daily on the altar—invisible to us, that is, hidden under the appearance of wine, but visible to God alone—it is read thus written in the book *Mechilta* <note>The *Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael*, an ancient commentary on Exodus.</note>:

"And you have acted impiously against the blood of the innocent. This is what was said: 'And I will see the blood' <note>original Hebrew: וראיתי את הדם (Exodus 12:13)</note>, which will be seen by me and not by others. These are the words of Rabbi Ishmael. And to this is joined: 'And the blood shall be a sign for you' <note>Exodus 12:13</note>. A sign, I say, for you, but it shall not be a sign for others."

**CAPNIO** <note>The persona of Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist.</note>: I would like you to show more clearly through their scriptures this conversion from both species into the body and blood of the Messiah. 

**GALATINUS**: Rabbi Cahana <note>A name often associated in these texts with the author of the *Pesikta* or Midrashic traditions.</note> clearly declares this concerning both, based on what is said in Genesis chapter 49: 

"Binding his foal to the vine, and his donkey's colt to the choice branch; he washed his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes. His eyes are redder than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk." <note>original Hebrew: אסרי לגפן עירה ולשרקה בני אתנו כבס ביין לבושו ובדם ענבים סותה : חכלילי עינים מיין ולבן שנים מחלב</note>

Where Rabbi Cahana says: "These words, 'binding his foal to the vine,' show that the sacrifice which will be made from wine will not only be changed into the substance of the blood of the Messiah, but will also be converted into the substance of his body." Furthermore, those words, "And his donkey's colt to the choice branch," signify that the divinity and the Son of God will be united to the "donkey"—that is, to his physical matter. For *hamor* <term>hamor: the Hebrew word for donkey</term> is interpreted as "materiality" <note>This is a common Kabbalistic wordplay between *hamor* (donkey) and *homer* (matter/substance).</note>. Just as a donkey carries burdens and the clothes of travelers, so the King Messiah will carry the sins of the whole world upon himself. According to what is said in Isaiah chapter 53: "And God caused the sin of us all to meet in him."

When it is said, "He washed his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes," the same meaning is expressed in different words. For "garment" refers to matter. Just as it is said in Job chapter 10: "You have clothed me with skin and flesh" <note>original Hebrew: עור ובשר תלבישני</note>. "And his cloak in the blood of grapes" refers to his divinity. Because just as a cloak surrounds the whole man, so God fills the whole world. 

"His eyes are redder than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk." This means: in the sacrifice which will be made from bread, notwithstanding that it is white like milk, the substance will be converted into the substance of the body of the Messiah; and in that same sacrifice, the substance of the blood of the Messiah will be present, though red like wine. Likewise, in the sacrifice of wine, there will be the blood and the flesh of the Messiah, and these same things will be in the bread. For the body of the Messiah cannot be divided. 

And reason demands this. For if the flesh and blood were divided, they would be distinguished from one another. But the body of the Messiah cannot be divided. As it is written in Exodus 12: "And you shall not break a bone in it" <note>original Hebrew: ועצם לא תשברו בו. Galatinus interprets "bone" as the underlying "substance" or "essence".</note>. Furthermore, flesh without blood, and vice versa, are dead things. But the body of the Messiah, after the resurrection...

<meta>catchword: because</meta>

# BOOK [X]

...because he will be glorified, he will live forever. And from this comes that saying, <note>original Hebrew: דוד מלך ישראל חי וקיים</note> "David, King of Israel, lives and endures." This means that David the King of Israel lives forever in himself. He mentioned the eyes and the teeth so that the speech would be more elegant, and the sense [clearer]. Rabbi Cahana, who lived long before the birth of Christ, said these things word for word. However, as for his statement that the body of the Messiah will be forever living after the resurrection: this is because (as was proven more extensively above) the ancient Hebrews say that one of the names of the Messiah is David. They prove this most especially by the testimony of the 30th chapter [of Jeremiah], which says, <note>original Hebrew: ועבדו את יהוה אלהיהם ואת דוד מלכם אשר אקים להם</note> "And they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their King, whom I will raise up for them." Since he says "I will raise up," which is in the future tense, they say these words of Jeremiah ought to be understood not of David himself—who had preceded him by a long time—but of the Messiah. For this reason, <term>Jonathan<note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic Targum (translation/paraphrase) of the Prophets.</note></term> translated it into <term>Chaldaic<note>A term historically used by scholars for the Aramaic language.</note></term> thus: <note>original Aramaic: וישתמעון ליהוה אלההון וישמעון לדוד משיחא מלכיהון</note> "And they shall serve before the Lord their God, and obey David the Messiah, their King." For that reason, they asserted that one of the names of the Messiah was to be David. Therefore, Rabbi Cahana said correctly that from this comes that mystery: "David, King of Israel, lives forever."

<margin>The Question.</margin>
**HOGSTRATEN**: Our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> of the words cited from Genesis chapter 49 is different. For it says: "Binding his foal to the vine, and his she-donkey, O my son, to the choice branch. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of grapes. His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk." From this it is clear that where Rabbi Cahana has "his city," our text has "his foal." And where he says, "His eyes are redder than wine," we have, "His eyes are more beautiful than wine." Where you translated "his donkey," our text has "his she-donkey."

<margin>The Answer.</margin>
**GALATINUS**: From where does this discord arise? Surely from the <term>equivocation<note>The quality of a word having multiple meanings.</note></term> of the vocabulary. For that which the author of our edition translates as "his foal," is written in Hebrew as <note>original Hebrew: עירה</note> *iro*. Now, this word among the Hebrews signifies both "city" and "foal," according to the diversity of the <term>vowel points<note>The marks added to Hebrew letters to indicate vowel sounds, which were not part of the original ancient script.</note></term>. For if it is pointed with a single point called <term>Hirik<note>The Hebrew vowel sign for a long or short "i" sound.</note></term>, it sounds like *iro*, which means "his city" among us. But if it is pointed with two points, namely <term>Patah<note>The Hebrew vowel sign for an "a" sound.</note></term> and <term>Shva<note>A Hebrew vowel sign indicating a very short "e" or no vowel sound.</note></term>, in this manner: *airo*, it signifies among them what "his foal" does among us. Since these words could have been read either way before the Holy Scripture was pointed, namely as *iro* and *airo*, it now must be read not as *airo*, but as *iro*, for so it has been pointed. Therefore, the author of our edition should have translated it as "his city," and not "his foal." Regarding the fact that our text says "more beautiful," it is written in Hebrew as <note>original Hebrew: חכלילי</note> *hachlili*, which is equivocal to both "red" and "beautiful." Here, however, it is more in harmony with the letter and the truth to say "redder" than "more beautiful." Finally, our text has "his she-donkey," where you say "his donkey" was translated by me; this is because <note>original Hebrew: חמור</note> *hamor*, that is "donkey," is common among the Hebrews...

# BOOK TEN

...is of [that] gender. And therefore among them, it signifies both a male donkey and a female donkey. HOOGSTRATEN.
<margin>Another inquiry.</margin>
Also that text, which the same Rabbi Cahana brought forward from Exodus to prove that the body of the Messiah cannot be divided, saying: "And you shall not break the substance in it." In our version, it does not have "substance," but "bone." For it says: "Neither shall you break a bone of it." <note>original: "Nec os illius confringetis." See Exodus 12:46.</note> GALATINUS.
<margin>Response.</margin>
In that place, the Hebrew Truth <note>A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Bible.</note> uses the word *etzem* <note>original Hebrew: עצם</note>, which signifies both "substance" and "bone." Therefore, the author of our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate translation.</note>, referring it to the Paschal lamb—of which no bone was to be broken—translated it as "bone" and not "substance." However, Rabbi Cahana referred that same text to the body of the Messiah, of which that lamb was a figure. For that reason, he translated it as "substance" and not "bone." Therefore, it is manifest that the truth was spoken by both; for while one spoke of the figure <note>the symbolic representation</note>, the other spoke of the thing figured <note>the reality represented by the symbol</note>. I think that to the aforementioned points, this most noteworthy thing should be added: that Rabbi Johai <note>Likely referring to the 2nd-century sage Shimon bar Yochai.</note>, writing upon the aforementioned text of Numbers chapter 28, "My offering, my bread," and so forth, says thus: "My offering, my bread; you shall observe to offer to me the fires of my sweet savor in its time, that is, in the time of the Messiah. And you shall say to them: the sacrifices which you ought to offer: the Lamb, with the rest. This is the sacrifice which you make at present. But this shall be the bread of two faces." Concerning which it is written in Exodus chapter 25: <note>original Hebrew: לחם פנים לפני תמיד</note> That is, "The bread of faces before me always." <note>Commonly known as the "Showbread" or "Bread of the Presence" in the Tabernacle.</note> Now, the reason why it is called "bread of faces" is because, as Rabbi Judas <note>Likely Rabbi Judah the Prince, the redactor of the Mishna.</note> says, it will be transmuted from the substance of bread, when it is sacrificed, into the substance of the body of the Messiah, who shall descend from the heavens. And he himself will be the sacrifice. Therefore he says, "You shall observe to offer to me," that is, for me to be offered. And he will be invisible and impalpable. The "seat of Elijah" provides the proof for this matter. And the Teachers say that for this reason it is called the bread of faces: because in that sacrifice there will be two substances, divinity and humanity. These are the words of that Rabbi, who preceded Christ by many years. HOOGSTRATEN.
<margin>Another inquiry.</margin>
How is the saying of Rabbi Judas understood, when, to prove that the body of the Messiah in that sacrifice would be invisible and impalpable, he said the "seat of Elijah" bears witness to this thing? GALATINUS.
<margin>Response.</margin>
The Doctors of the Hebrews report that God gave this prerogative to Elijah: that no circumcision should happen in which he himself did not intervene. Wherefore the Teachers themselves established that as often as a circumcision was to be performed, two very ornate seats should always be prepared. One in which he who was about to circumcise the infant would sit. The other in which no one could sit, but would remain empty, because they said that Elijah would come to sit in it. Therefore, for that reason, Rabbi Judas said that the seat of Elijah provides proof for the body of the Messiah being invisible and impalpable in the future sacrifice of bread and wine; lest the more recent Jews, whose bad faith he himself foresaw, should say that the body of the Messiah is not in this sacrifice because it is neither seen nor felt there. For they both believe and confess that Elijah is invisible and impalpable in that seat, and that the same man can exist in many places at the same hour.

...how the life of a priest should be, as he handles this sacrifice. The Lord himself indicates both the sacrifice of our own time and the quality required of the one consecrating it, <margin>Leviticus, chapter 21, says:</margin> <note>original Hebrew: "וקדשתו כי את לחם אלהיך הוא מקריב קדש יהיה כי קדוש אני יהוה מקדשכם"</note> which means: **And you shall sanctify him, for he offers the flesh of your God; he is or shall be the one sacrificing. **GALATINUS:** Here, our Latin edition has two significant corruptions. The second is that in the second clause, the Hebrew truth <note>The original Hebrew text, often referred to by Christian scholars of this era as the "Hebraica Veritas."</note> reads differently. For this Hebrew word <term>lehem<gloss>bread, food, or flesh</gloss></term> has many meanings. Sometimes it signifies food in general; sometimes specifically bread; and sometimes it signifies flesh. Yet, sometimes it is used for bread alone. As it is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 8: <note>original Hebrew: "לא על הלחם לבדו יחיה האדם"</note> **Man does not live by bread alone.** However, it sometimes refers to flesh, as in Numbers, chapter 28: <note>original Hebrew: "את קרבני לחמי לאשי"</note> **My sacrifice, my flesh for the burning, or for my fire.** And likewise in Leviticus, chapter 21: <note>The OCR says "31," likely a typesetter's error for 21.</note> <note>original Hebrew: "לחם אלהיך הוא מקריב"</note> **He is sacrificing the flesh of your God.** So also in Job, chapter 6: <note>original Hebrew: "המה כדוי לחמי"</note> **They are like the sorrows of my flesh.** Thus says Rabbi Kimhi. # On the cessation of the ancient law.

## That upon the arrival of the Law of the Messiah, the Mosaic Law was to cease in all its ceremonies. Chapter 1.

---

->CAPNIO,<-

<note>Johannes Reuchlin, the famous German Hebraist, who appears as the character "Capnio" in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C (stylized as V) featuring a seated putto or cherub-like figure in a landscape, holding a round object.</image-desc>

Since you have said much in the preceding sections, not only regarding baptism—by which circumcision was to be rendered void—and the sacrifice of bread and wine—by which all sacrifices of the old law were meant to fail—but also regarding the institution of the new divine law itself, which was to be established by the Messiah, through which the entire ancient law was to cease in regard to its ceremonies. Therefore, so that the obstinate <term>perfidia</term> <note>A common polemical term in this period for "faithlessness" or "stubbornness."</note> of the more recent Jews may be further refuted, who assert that the old law is immutable and will last until the end of the world, it is now necessary for you to prove through their own scriptures that it was destined to reach its end (upon the arrival of the Law of the Messiah) in all ceremonial matters. This is so that the law might be kept alongside the Messiah’s law, not according to the letter, but according to its spiritual and mystical sense.

**GALATINUS:** That it was indeed meant to be this way is shown most clearly in the *Midrash Coheleth* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes; "Coheleth" is the Hebrew name for the book.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes, regarding that which is said in the second chapter of the same book: <note>original Hebrew: "אמרתי אני בלבי לכה נא אנסכה בשמחה וראה בטוב והנה גם הוא הבל"</note> That is, **I said in my heart: "Come now, I will test you with joy, and see good." And behold, even this is vanity.** <note>Ecclesiastes 2:1</note> For it is said there: **And see good**, namely the good of the law. **And behold, even this is vanity.** Was it not necessary for the scripture to say, "And behold, even this is joy"? Why, then, did it say, "Behold, this is vanity"? **Rabbi Hezkiya** <note>A scholar mentioned in the Midrash.</note> said: "Because all the law which you learn in this world is **vanity** <note>original Hebrew: "הבלים" (habelim)</note>—that is, vanities—in the presence of the law of the world to come." Now, that this "law of the world to come" is the Law of the Messiah, and the "days of the world to come" are his days, is evident from what is read in the same Midrash regarding that which is said in Ecclesiastes chapter 11: <note>original Hebrew: "אם שנים הרבה יחיה האדם בכלם ישמח ויזכר את ימי החשך"</note> that is, **If a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all. And let him remember the days of darkness.** For there, these things are explained in this way: "If a man lives many years, let him rejoice in all these, namely in the joy of the law. And let him remember the days of darkness." These are the days of malice; how many will they be? For whatever preceded will be... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as a catchword for the next page.</note>

<header>BOOK</header>

...[H]abel, <note>original: "Habel," a Hebrew word meaning breath, vapor, or vanity; also the name Abel.</note> that is, all vanity; <term>Torah</term>, <note>original: תורה (Torah)</note> that is, the law which a person learns in this world, is vanity in the presence of the law of the Messiah. To this, the tradition found in that same *Midrash Coheleth*—that is, in the same exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes—is very much in agreement. It is written there regarding that saying in the first chapter of the same book: *There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to come.* <note>Ecclesiastes 1:11; the Latin text provides the Hebrew: "אין לראשונים וגם לאחרונים שיהיו לא יהיה להם זכרון עם שיהיו לאחרונה".</note> This means: There will be no memory of the former, nor even of the posterior things that shall be. That is, there will be no memory of them alongside those things that shall happen at the very end. For however many signs or miracles were performed for the children of Israel from the time they departed from Egypt, and even while they were not yet out of Egypt, it says of them: There will be no memory of the former and the latter, specifically those that occurred after the exodus from Egypt. For there will be no memory of them in comparison with those things that shall occur at the last, and with the signs or miracles of the world to come. As it is written in Jeremiah 23: *But as the Lord lives, who brought up and led the descendants of the house of Israel out of the north country and from all the countries where I had driven them.* <note>Jeremiah 23:8; the text includes the Hebrew: "כי אם חי יהוה אשר העלה ואשר הביא את זרע בית ישראל מארץ צפונה ומכל הארצות אשר הדחתיס".</note> This means: They shall say no more, "As the Lord lives, who made the children of Israel go up from the land of Egypt." Rather, they will say, "As the Lord lives, who made the house of Israel go up and who made them come from the land of the North, and from all the lands to which He had driven them." Thus far the tradition. Now, the signs and miracles mentioned in this tradition are the miracles that were to be performed in the time of the Messiah. For "the future" or "that which is to come" (as has been said many times) is understood in Hebrew literature to mean the time of the Messiah. This is easily shown through the *Targum Yerushalmi*—that is, through the Aramaic Jerusalem translation. Regarding the aforementioned words, *There will be no memory of former things, and also of the posterior things that are to come,* he translated and explained it thus: "There will be no remembrance of them in the generations that shall be in the days of the Messiah." What is this Jerusalem <margin>What the Vulgate edition is.</margin> translation? Perhaps it is that which (as I personally think) is now called the *Vulgate* <note>Galatinus is here speculating on the identity of the "Vulgate" edition, likely referring to a common Aramaic translation used in his time, rather than the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> edition. Its author is unknown, but he is recognized as having held to the manner of an expositor more than that of a translator. To the same purpose (to return to our subject), much is contributed by what is read in the book *Berakhot* <note>original: ברכות (Berakhot), the first tractate of the Talmud, dealing with blessings and prayers.</note>—that is, of "Blessings"—in the Jerusalem [Talmud], in the chapter that begins *Hayu Korin* ("They were reading"): Ben Zoma said, "It is destined that Israel shall not mention the exodus from Egypt in the future world, nor in the days of the Messiah." And what is the proof of this matter? That which is written in Jeremiah, chapter 23: *Therefore behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when they shall no more say, "As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt,"* and so on. The sages said: "Not that the name of Egypt should be uprooted from its place, but that the wonders which will happen in the days of the kingdoms of the nations will be the <term>iccar</term> <note>original: עיקר (ikkar), meaning the root, essence, or primary substance.</note>—that is, the substance—and Egypt will be the <term>taphla</term> <note>original: טפלה (tafelah), meaning secondary, attachment, or accidental property.</note>—that is, the accident—in such a way that the miracles performed in Egypt and in the departure from Egypt will be regarded in the manner of an accidental property." And in this way it was said in Genesis 35: *Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.* Which...

# BOOK ELEVEN

The remaining Masters said: It is not that "Jacob" shall be uprooted from his place, but that "Israel" shall be the substance, and "Jacob" shall be an adjunct to it, or an accident. <note>In medieval philosophy, "substance" is the core reality of a thing, while an "accident" is a secondary quality that can change without changing the thing's nature. Here, the name "Jacob" represents a lesser state of the nation compared to the higher state of "Israel."</note> And so Isaiah also says in his forty-third chapter: *Do not remember the former things, nor consider the things of old.* <note>Isaiah 43:18; the original Hebrew is provided: אל תזכרו ראשונות וקדמוניות אל תתבוננו.</note> This means: Do not remember the first things, and do not care for the ancient things. *Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it shall spring forth. Shall you not know it?* (Isaiah 43:19). "Do not remember," he says, "the former things"—these are the <term>Mizraim</term>, <note>original: מצרים (Mizraim), the Hebrew name for Egypt.</note> that is, the Egyptian signs. "And do not care for the ancient things"—these are the things that happened after the departure from Egypt. "Behold, I am doing a new thing," and so on—these will be the things concerning <term>Gog</term> <note>The apocalyptic battle of Gog and Magog, often associated with the transition to the Messianic age.</note> in the days of the Messiah. Thus far the tradition.

The Gloss of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> explains it this way: *Do not remember the former things*, that is, the signs and miracles which I mention to you and which I performed in Egypt; do not remember them from now on. For you shall be so eager for this [new] redemption that you will be occupied with confessing and praising it. It follows: *And do not care for the ancient things*, that is, do not pay attention to them, nor set your heart upon them. These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

Almost the same thing as was said in the preceding tradition is also placed in the book <term>Berakhot</term>, <note>original: ברכות (Berachoth), meaning "Blessings," the first tractate of the Talmud.</note> that is, the Babylonian book of blessings, at the end of the chapter "From what time do they read." <note>original: מאימתי קורין (Me-ematai korin), the title of the first chapter of Berakhot.</note> There it is said: There is a tradition that Ben Zoma said to the wise men: "And how shall they be mindful of the departure from Egypt in the days of the Messiah? Is it not already written in Jeremiah, in the twenty-third chapter: *Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and they shall no longer say, 'As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt,'* and the rest?" They answered him: It is not that the departure from Egypt shall be uprooted from its place, but that the event of the Kingdoms—that is, the signs that shall happen in the times of the [Messianic] Kingdoms—shall be the substance. And the departure from Egypt—that is, the signs of the departure from Egypt—shall be an adjunct to it; that is, they will be like an accident, which is present or absent without the destruction of the substance. And so Isaiah says in the forty-third chapter: *Do not remember the former things*, and so forth, as above. This is the tradition.

To this also pertains what the Lord commanded the Jews through Moses in the twenty-sixth chapter of Leviticus, saying: *And you shall clear out the old because of the new.* <note>Leviticus 26:10; the original Hebrew is provided: וישן מפני חדש תוציאו.</note> That this is to be understood in this sense is gathered from what is read in the book called <term>Sifre</term>, <note>original: סיפרי (Siphre), an ancient legal commentary (Midrash) on Numbers and Deuteronomy, though here citing a section on Leviticus.</note> concerning that saying in the twenty-sixth chapter of Leviticus: *And I will look upon you and make you fruitful, and multiply you, and establish my covenant with you; and you shall eat the old store, and you shall clear out the old because of the new.* <note>Leviticus 26:9–10; the text includes the Hebrew: ופניתי אליכם והפריתי אתכם והרביתי אתכם והקימותי את בריתי אתכם ואכלתם ישן נושן וישן מפני חדש תוציאו.</note> For these things are explained there as follows: *And I will look upon you* for good; *and I will make you fruitful* through physical generation; *and I will multiply you*, or make you grow, with an upright stature. *And I will establish my covenant with you*—not like the first covenant which you transgressed, as is said in Jeremiah 31: *Because they transgressed my covenant*; but a new covenant which they shall not transgress thereafter. # BOOK XIV.

<margin>Jeremiah 31</margin> <term>Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah—not like the covenant...</term> <note>original Hebrew: הנה ימים באים נאם יהוה וכרתי את בית ישראל ואת בית יהודה ברית חדשה לא כברית (Jeremiah 31:31)</note> that is: And I shall strike for the house of Israel and for the house of Judah a new covenant. Not like the covenant which I struck with their fathers on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. And therefore He says: *And you shall eat the old store long kept, and clear out the old to make way for the new.* <note>Quoting Leviticus 26:10.</note> This is the tradition. Moreover, that the "covenant" in the aforementioned words is the same thing as the "Law" is clearly shown in the book <term>Mechilta</term> <note>A classic Jewish legal commentary (Midrash) on the Book of Exodus.</note>. Where, upon that which is said in Exodus chapter 12 <note>The OCR says chapter 2, but the quote "In the tenth of this month" refers to the Passover instructions in Exodus 12:3.</note>, "In the tenth of this month," it is said: "There is no covenant but the Law." Just as it is said in Deuteronomy chapter 29: *These are the words of the covenant which God commanded Moses to strike with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which He struck with them in Horeb.* Also in Exodus, namely chapter 34: *And He wrote upon the tablets the ten words of the covenant.* This is in the same book, *Mechilta*. From the preceding tradition, therefore, it is clearly held that with the arrival of the new Law of the Messiah, the old Law ought to cease.

Furthermore, in that book which is called <term>Eruvin</term> <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning Sabbath laws.</note>, in the chapter beginning <term>Osin Passin</term> <note>original Hebrew: עושין פסין (Making Partitions), the second chapter of Tractate Eruvin.</note>, it is read that Rabbi Joshua the son of Levi said: <term>To keep the commandments and the statutes and the judgments which I command you today to do them...</term> <note>original Hebrew: לשמור מצות ואת החקים ואת המשפטים אשר אנכי מצוך היום לעשותם (Deuteronomy 7:11).</note> <term>Today to do them; and today to give their reward.</term> <note>original Hebrew: היום לעשותם ליתן שכרם היום</note> This is to say: What is it that is written in Deuteronomy chapter 7, *And keep the commandment and the decrees and the judgments which I command you today to do them*? "Today," he says, "to do them," and not "tomorrow" to do them. This is the tradition. Therefore, "today"—that is, before the Messiah should come—the ceremonial precepts were to be kept; but not "tomorrow," that is, not after He had already come. From all these things it is sufficiently and openly evident that with the arrival of the Messiah, who was to institute a new Law, the old Law was to cease in all its ceremonies.

Since, therefore, in the preceding parts it has been most extensively proved that the Messiah has come, and that He was our Lord Jesus Christ—who did not cease to write the Law of His Gospel for nearly three and a half years by deeds and words in the hearts of believers, and especially in those of His apostles and disciples—and finally, having sent the Holy Spirit, He rendered so firm whatever He had written by teaching in their hearts that it could be deleted by no persecution and no forgetfulness. On that account, it is certain that what had been prophesied long before through Jeremiah chapter 31 in these words was then fulfilled: <term>I have put my law in their midst, and upon their heart I will write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.</term> <note>original Hebrew: נתתי את תורתי בקרבם ועל לבם אכתבנה והייתי להם לאלהים והמה יהיו לי לעם (Jeremiah 31:33).</note> From all these things, it clearly follows that the old Law in all its ceremonies has now ceased. Wherefore it follows plainly that no one is further bound to perform circumcision according to the letter, no one to keep the Sabbath and other Jewish feasts, and no one to celebrate the annual memorials on account of those miracles of theirs. Because since the Messiah came, who gave the new Law, the old things have passed away, and all are bound to keep the new.

# ELEVENTH BOOK.

### How and why Christ fulfilled the old law.
#### Chapter 11.
## CAPNIO,
<note>Capnio is the Greek-derived pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and scholar who defended Jewish texts.</note>

<margin>The Jews' objection.</margin>
The Jews oppose us in this matter in many ways, wishing to prove that the ancient law was by no means meant to cease upon the arrival of the Messiah. Because we Christians say that Christ our Lord was the Messiah, and yet he himself kept that entire law, and led others to keep it through word and deed. For he says in the fifth chapter of Matthew: *I did not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them.* And again after a few verses: *Whoever* (he says) *breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches men so, shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven. But whoever does them and teaches them, he shall be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven.* Therefore, from the words and deeds (they say) of your Christ, whom you claim to be the Messiah, it is clearly evident that the Mosaic law does not cease at all. Wherefore, you ought not to say that it was meant to cease upon his arrival.

<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>What the old law contained.</margin>
GAL. <note>Galatinus, the narrator of the dialogue.</note> What they say is indeed true, that Christ fulfilled the whole of the old law. However, they can by no means infer from this that it has not ceased in those parts where it was destined to cease. So that it may become known to all how he fulfilled that law and the prophets, it must be noted that in that same law and the prophets, five things were primarily contained: namely, Moral precepts, judgments, ceremonial rites, promises and threats, and sacraments.

<margin>Moral precepts.</margin>
The Moral precepts are indeed the ten commandments, without which salvation cannot exist for adults. These are specifically found in the twentieth chapter of Exodus, where it is said: <note>original Hebrew: לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים על פני : לא תשא את שם יהוה אלהיך לשוא : זכור את יום השבת לקדשו : כבד את אביך ואת אמך : לא תרצח : לא תנאף : לא תגנב : לא תענה ברעך עד שקר : לא תחמד בית רעך : לא תחמד אשת רעך ועבדו ואמתו ושורו וחמורו וכל אשר לרעך :</note> [Which translates as:] *You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Honor your father and your mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor's.* This is [the Latin translation provided in the source]: *There shall be no foreign gods for you in my presence. Do not take the name of the Lord your God in vanity. Observe the Sabbath day, to sanctify it. Honor your father and your mother. Do not kill. Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not answer as a false witness against your neighbor. Do not covet your neighbor's house. Do not covet your neighbor's wife, nor his servant, nor his handmaid, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor all things that are your neighbor's.* Moreover, these were not meant to cease upon the arrival of the Messiah, but to be perfected. Therefore our Savior, the true Messiah, in order to perfect them, prohibited not only the act of murder and other evil works, but even the intent of the mind. Saying (in Matthew, chapter 5): *You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you, that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.* Along with the rest of what follows. For that reason, he both kept them himself and led others to keep them. Hence in Matthew chapter 19: *If you wish* (he says)

# BOOK IV

<margin>Judicial matters.</margin>
"...to enter into life, keep the commandments." <note>Matthew 19:17</note> The judicial laws, however, are such as those about which it is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 25: *An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth*, and so on. Since these were incomplete, and were carried out too rigorously and without mercy, they were to be softened by the sweetness of mercy in the time of the Messiah.

<margin>Ceremonial matters.</margin>
Therefore, they have now been perfectly fulfilled, since they are carried out and tempered, especially with mercy, in the court of the church. The ceremonial laws, moreover, were all the sacrifices and those things done concerning them, such as circumcision, the new moons, the fringes <note>original: *fimbriae*, referring to the *tzitzit* or ritual tassels</note>, and phylacteries <note>original: *phylacteria*, small leather boxes containing scripture worn during prayer</note>, and many other things of that kind. Because these were figures <note>or "types," meaning symbolic foreshadowing</note> of those things which ought to be done in and by the Messiah, they were therefore destined to have an end when the Messiah himself arrived. Yet the Messiah himself, Jesus our Lord, perfectly fulfilled them: first by keeping them to the letter until the determined time of their cessation; then by leading them back, through himself and his followers, to their spiritual and mystical sense.

<margin>Promises.</margin>
The promises, indeed, were the coming of the Messiah, the land of promise, the conversion of the nations, the remission of sins, and eternal salvation. These things also our Savior perfectly fulfilled by taking on flesh from the Virgin, being born, performing miracles possible only for God by his own power, suffering, dying, rising again, ascending into heaven in the sight of many, and by promising far better things than the old law promised. For that law promised its observers only temporal and earthly goods, which nevertheless designated spiritual and eternal things. Our Savior and Messiah, however, promised his followers the spiritual and eternal things which that law prefigured. For he said in Matthew, chapter 19: *Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.* And again in Luke, chapter 6: *Blessed are the poor,* he says, *for yours is the Kingdom of God.* For this reason, as it says in Matthew chapter 4, Jesus began to preach and to say: *Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.*

<margin>Sacramental matters.</margin>
Finally, the sacramental matters were the paschal lamb, the red heifer <note>original: *uitula rufa*, a sacrificial cow used for ritual purification in the Old Testament</note>, and others of this kind. These were figures and shadows of Christ’s passion. Therefore, upon the arrival of him whose type they bore, they had to cease entirely. These things Christ himself fulfilled by suffering and dying. To this the Evangelist bore witness when he said: *These things were done so that the scripture might be fulfilled, which says: You shall not break a bone of it.* From these points, therefore, it is clear how and why Christ fulfilled the law and the prophets. He fulfilled the prophets (as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop and Church Father</note> says) by completing everything they had predicted about him. And he fulfilled the law, first by transgressing nothing of the legal requirements, and finally by justifying through faith that which the law itself was unable to do through the letter. Therefore he said: *I did not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them.* From these things it is also clearly shown that although Christ fulfilled the old law in the manner we have stated, it does not follow from this that the law did not cease—in those parts destined to cease at his coming—once he had arrived.

<summary>This page explains the fourfold fulfillment of the Old Law by Christ—through judicial, ceremonial, promissory, and sacramental categories—arguing that he completed their purpose rather than simply abolishing them. It clarifies that while Christ observed the Law's letter, his arrival transitioned these practices into their intended spiritual and eternal meanings.</summary>
