# BOOK ELEVEN.

# Refutation of Jewish arguments, and that the Mosaic law was mutable. Chapter III.

## CAPNIO,
<note>Capnio is the scholarly pseudonym of Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous German humanist and Hebraist who appears as a character in this dialogue.</note>

<margin>Arguments of the more recent Jews.</margin>
The more recent generations of the Jews, attempting to prove the permanence of their law, put forward several arguments against us which you ought to resolve. This is so that their bad faith <note>original: *perfidia*, often used in a theological sense to mean "unbelief" or "rejection of the faith"</note> may be more forcefully exposed, and the truth of the Catholic faith may shine forth more clearly. <margin>First argument.</margin> Thus, they first argue in this way: As long as the cause of an effect remains, that effect also endures. But the cause of the law always remains; therefore, the entire law will always endure. They prove that the cause of the law always remains in this way: the final cause <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which something exists.</note> of the entire law is the intention of leading men back to their own perfection. This intention always remains. Therefore, the entire law will also always remain. <margin>Second argument.</margin> Next, they argue as follows: The perfection of any power is its own proper action. Of the human powers, some are bodily and others are intellectual. Therefore, human perfection consists in both bodily and intellectual action. The law, being ordained toward human perfection, necessarily leads men back to these two things. From this it follows that whatever the law intends is directed either to the adornment of the body or of the soul. Now, the body is adorned by morals, but the soul by intelligence. The literal and tropological <note>The "tropological" sense is the moral interpretation of scripture, explaining how one should act.</note> interpretations of the law demonstrate the former, while the allegorical and anagogical <note>The "anagogical" sense is the spiritual interpretation that points toward eternal or heavenly realities.</note> understandings suggest the latter. Since a human being in this life always stands in need of both the ordering of morals and the understanding of the intellect, the law which administers all these things must necessarily remain forever. <margin>Third argument.</margin> Finally, they argue thus: While the thing prefigured exists, the figure remains. This is proven because, since the object of faith is uncreated truth (for nothing corruptible can be the perfection of an incorruptible power such as the intellectual soul), if anything concerning the foundations of faith was created in symbols <note>original: *figuris*, meaning types or prefigurations</note>, it is believable because it is traced back to uncreated truth, just as matter is to form. Since the thing prefigured is eternal—because it is eternal truth—therefore the figure is also eternal. Consequently, it follows that the Mosaic law itself, which is full of figures, is eternal. From these points, they infer that the Old Law remains always stable regarding its ceremonial requirements.

## GAL.
<note>Galatinus refers to the author, Pietro Galatino, who defends the Christian position in the dialogue.</note>

These arguments are certainly quite frivolous, and like the chaff of falsehood, they are to be burned by the fire of truth. But first, I will show that their conclusion is entirely false. <margin>Refutation of the Jewish conclusion.</margin> Then, I will respond to the arguments themselves. The conclusion by which they assert the ancient law is binding in the same ritual forever is refuted by this reasoning: Whatever is received by something mutable can itself also be changed. This is proven by the principle that everything received is received according to the manner of the receiver. This can be judged in individual cases and in the powers of our own soul. Now, the Old Law is of this nature because it is received by man, whose nature is driven by constant change; therefore, the law itself can also be changed.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom "Quemad." suggests the next page begins with a word like "Quemadmodum" (Just as).</meta>

<summary>This page presents three Jewish arguments for the eternal nature of the Mosaic Law based on its purpose of human perfection and its symbolic connection to eternal truth, followed by Galatinus’s opening rebuttal that the Law must be mutable because humans themselves are mutable.</summary>
<keywords>Mosaic Law, Jewish-Christian polemics, Scholasticism, Final Cause, Four Senses of Scripture, Tropology, Allegory, Anagogy, Mutability of Law</keywords>

# BOOK

For just as a father educates his son through various laws as an infant, a boy, an adolescent, and a young man, so too is a human congregation guided by one law when it is wise and just, and by another when it is foolish. Moreover, the Jewish race, redeemed from Egyptian servitude through Moses, was foolish and wicked, as the Mosaic scripture itself frequently testifies. For this reason, many of the ceremonial precepts of the law—as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>original: *Rabbi Mose Ægyptio*; this refers to the famous medieval Jewish philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204)</note> testifies in the third treatise of his book called *The Guide* <note>original: *More*, referring to the *Moreh Nevukhim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*</note>—were required more by the dullness of that people and their depraved habit of idolatry than by the inherent value of the laws themselves. This is according to the saying of the Psalmist: *Muzzle their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not come near you.* <note>Psalm 32:9</note> Therefore, because of that same dullness and depraved habit, just as a child’s education changes as they age, it happened that the accepted course—that is, the law—was also changed. The Law, therefore, no longer binds through those same rites. This is confirmed both by the testimony of the Law itself and by the illustrious Talmudists. For the Law itself (excepting the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>) did not bind one to its observation except in the Promised Land, specifically while the Temple stood and the Jewish scepter <note>sovereignty</note> remained. Outside of that Promised Land, it was not binding at all. And the text itself clearly shows this in Deuteronomy, chapter 4, saying: *ראה למדתי אתכם חקים ומשפטים כאשר ציוני יהוה אלהי לעשות כן בקרב הארץ אשר אתם באים שמה לרשתה* <note>original Hebrew: *Re'eh limadti etchem chukim u-mishpatim...*</note> That is: *Behold, I have taught you ceremonies and judgments, just as the Lord my God commanded me, so that you should do them in the land which you are about to possess.* And a little later it says: *ויגד לכם את בריתו אשר צוה אתכם לעשות עשרת הדברים ויכתבם על שני לוחות אבנים : ואתי צוה יהוה בעת ההוא ללמד אתכם חקים ומשפטים לעשתכם אותם בארץ אשר אתם עברים שמה לרשתה* <note>original Hebrew: *Va-yaged lachem et brito...*</note> that is: *And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, the ten words, which he wrote on two tables of stone. And he commanded me at that time to teach you the ceremonies and judgments which you ought to perform in the land which you are about to possess.* Here, two things are especially worth noting. First, that he specifically called the Ten Commandments "His Covenant," in the same way the entire Law is usually called later. This was to make it known that the intention of the entire Law consists in and depends upon these ten precepts. The Doctors of the Jews suggest this more plainly, especially Rabbi Saadia <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942), a prominent Jewish philosopher and exegete</note> in the book *Ha-Emunot* <note>original: *ס' האמונות*, *Sefer Ha-Emunot ve-ha-De'ot*, or *The Book of Beliefs and Opinions*</note>, that is, of things to be believed. There he teaches that all the mandates of the Law can be reduced to the ten precepts of the Decalogue itself. Second, it should be noted that he commanded these ten words to be performed simply, without placing any condition of location. He did this to show that they would never cease to be in effect. Since these ten precepts belong to natural law <term>Natural Law: A philosophy asserting that certain rights or values are inherent by virtue of human nature and universally cognizable through human reason.</term> and are an innate participation in the eternal law within us, they vary by neither place nor time. But speaking of the other mandates of the Law, he immediately added: *Which you should do in the land which you are about to possess.* From this, it is clearly evident that the Jews are not at all bound to them outside the Promised Land. This same sentiment is held in other places, namely in Deuteronomy chapters 5, 6, 11, and 12.

<summary>Galatinus argues that the ceremonial Mosaic laws were temporary measures designed for a specific people and place, whereas only the Ten Commandments (as Natural Law) are eternal and universal. He supports this by citing Maimonides, Saadia Gaon, and specific verses from Deuteronomy that condition the ceremonial law's validity on residence in the Promised Land.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Mosaic Law was not intended to be eternal in its ceremonial form. Galatinus is now citing Jewish authorities—both Talmudic and Kabbalistic—to support his claim that the Law is subject to change or cessation, especially upon the arrival of the Messiah.</meta>

### ELEVENTH ###

<margin>The opinion of the Talmudists on the changeability of the law.</margin>
It is clear that the law itself testifies to its own changeability according to changes in location. This same point is proved by the sayings of the ancient Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>; and although these are numerous, it is enough to cite just one for the sake of brevity, namely from the book *Sanhedrin* <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with judicial procedure</note>, in the chapter beginning *Ellu hahukím* <note>original: אלו הנחנקים; "These are those who are strangled"</note>. There it says: *Rabbi Johanan said: In all things, if a prophet says to you: "Transgress the words of the law," obey him, except in the case of idol worship.* From this they conclude that if the time requires a part of the law to be changed—which they call *Horath saa* <note>original: הוראת שעה; "an instruction of the hour," meaning a temporary legal ruling</note>, that is, an indication of the hour or time—a prophet, or even someone lesser than a prophet (provided they are considered wiser than others in their generation), can change it. If that specific occasion or need persists, then that changed part of the law will also remain changed. Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides</note> clearly shows this same thing in his *Book of Judges*, in the section *Halcoth mamorim* <note>original: הלכות ממרים; "Laws of the Rebellious"</note>, chapter 2. <margin>The opinion of the Kabbalists on the giving and cessation of the old law.</margin> I will say nothing here of the opinion of the Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note>, who say that the law was handed down because of the serpent’s venom injected into Adam, and that when the Messiah comes, this venom will cease. Consequently, they believe the law itself must cease at the arrival of the Messiah. From these points, therefore, the falsehood of the Jews' conclusion regarding the perpetual obligation of legal observance is clearly evident.

<margin>Response to the arguments.</margin>
Now to their arguments. Although the solution to the reasons by which they strive to prove their conclusion can easily be seen from what has already been said, let us nonetheless respond to them so that the falsity of those same reasons may appear more clearly.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding their first argument: "As long as the cause remains, so long does its effect remain." This is granted regarding a cause which an effect follows necessarily and by its own nature; but the "minor premise" must then be denied. That is to say: it is not true that the cause of the *entire* law always remains, if we take "the whole" to mean every individual part. For although the chief intention of the law always remains, this is not true of every small part of the law. Many things in the law are not required by the ultimate goal necessarily or by primary intention, but are instead "removals of obstacles" or intended for "well-being." Examples include sacrifices and many ceremonial rites. As Rabbi Moses the Egyptian also shows in the third treatise of his book *The Guide* <note>The *Guide for the Perplexed*</note>. And according to the opinion of the Talmudists, such things do not bind one to observance outside the Promised Land. This would not be possible if those things pertained to human salvation inherently and necessarily.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
The second reason, which seems more particular to them, proves nothing other than that those things which pertain to knowledge and morals remain. This is a point that Catholic truth does not reject. Indeed, it commands all the moral parts of the law to be kept—not because they are part of the Mosaic law, but because they are part of the *eternal law*, the inscription of which upon our minds is usually called the *law of nature*.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
Finally, they argue as follows: "As long as the thing prefigured stands, the figure [the symbol] stands. But the thing prefigured stands forever, because it is eternal truth. Therefore, the figure also stands forever." That is to...

...then we approve. But from this it does not follow that the outward observance of the law remains obligatory. Because the figures of the law consist chiefly in the literal understanding itself, which leads us to, and stimulates, intellectual allegory <note>The "intellectual allegory" refers to the spiritual or symbolic meaning behind physical laws</note>. Indeed, the outward act of the body, even if it helps as a stimulus, has little power in this regard; rather, it is the conceptual literal interpretation itself that chiefly leads and stimulates us to this, even if we perform nothing outwardly. Truly, how much the secrets of the law exceed the literal understanding was made clear at great length in the first book of this work. Therefore, notwithstanding the aforementioned Jewish arguments, it is clear from what has been said that the law of the Jews was changeable. And indeed, it was frequently changed.

## That the law of the Jews has been changed many times. Chapter 4.

## CAPNIO <note>The name "Capnio" is a Greek-derived nickname for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous scholar of Hebrew and the Kabbalah</note>,

<margin>How many precepts there were in the old law.</margin>
I would like you to prove through their own scriptures that the old law was changed many times. GALATINUS: First, listen to what is read in the book *Maccoth* <note>original: מכות; Makkot, a tractate of the Talmud concerning corporal punishment</note>, that is, of "floggings," in the chapter that begins *Ellu hen hallokin* <note>original: אלו הן הלוקין; "These are those who are to be lashed"</note>. It is read in this way: Rabbi Simlai <note>The text reads "Cumlai," a common variant or misspelling in older Latin editions</note> said: Six hundred and thirteen precepts were given to Moses at Sinai. For three hundred and sixty-five is the number of the days of the sun <note>the solar year</note>. Moreover, two hundred and forty-eight are the number of members <note>limbs or organs</note> in a human being. The Rabbi asked, through which scripture is this proved? Through that which says in the thirty-third chapter of Deuteronomy: *Moses commanded the law to us* <note>original: תורה לנו משה; Torah tziva lanu Mosheh</note>. For the word <term>Torah</term> <note>meaning Law or Instruction</note> arithmetically equates to this; that is, written with such letters that they effect six hundred and eleven. For <term>tau</term> signifies four hundred, <term>vau</term> six, <term>resh</term> two hundred, and <term>he</term> five. <note>This is a practice called Gematria, where Hebrew letters are assigned numerical values</note>. Two others are found in the twentieth chapter of Exodus, where it is said: *You shall have no other gods before my face* and *You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness*, and so forth. These two precepts we heard from the mouth of the Divine—that is, from God. All of these together are six hundred and thirteen. Then David came, and he established those same six hundred and thirteen precepts upon eleven, as it is said in the 15th Psalm: *A Psalm of David. Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? And who shall rest on your holy mountain? He who walks uprightly, and works righteousness, and speaks the truth in his heart. He who does not slander with his tongue*—that is, he did not detract—*nor does evil to his friend*—that is, his companion—*and has not taken up a reproach against his neighbor, in whose eyes a vile person is despised.* Such a one was Hezekiah, King of Judah...

...as it is said in the 2nd chapter of the same prophet: וצדיק באמונתו יחיה <note>original: ve-tzaddik be-emunato yikhyeh</note> That is: **The just shall live by his faith.** <note>Habakkuk 2:4</note> All this comes from the aforementioned tradition, with the exception of the glosses of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, or Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note>. Balaam, <note>The non-Israelite prophet from the Book of Numbers</note> that is, said to the angel: "I did not go until the Holy and Blessed God said to me, 'Arise and go with them.' And now you tell me to return?" The angel said to him: "For such is His office, or His art." Did He not also say to Abraham in the twenty-second chapter of Genesis that he should sacrifice his son? This means the words of the masters possess greater authority than the Law itself. For he who says, "There are no תפילין <note>original: "tephillin"</note> (that is, phylacteries)," thereby transgressing the words of the Law, is פטור <note>original: "Patur"</note> (that is, exempt from punishment). But he who says that there are five טוטפות <note>original: "totaphoth"</note> (that is, compartments in the phylacteries) — which are mentioned in the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy — thereby adding to the words of the *Sophorim* <note>original: "Sophorim" — Scribes</note> (that is, the sages), he is guilty. Likewise in the *Midrash* <note>A collection of rabbinic interpretations</note> אלה הדברים <note>original: "Elle haddebarim" — These are the words</note>, which is an exposition on Deuteronomy regarding the verse: **You shall not deviate or turn aside from the word which they declare to you, to the right hand or to the left.** <note>Deuteronomy 17:11</note> It is said there: "Even if they should show to your eyes that the right is the left, and the left is the right, believe them and obey." <margin>
What the phylacteries were.
</margin>
in the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy, it is read as follows: וקשרתם לאות על ידיך והיו לטטפת בין עיניך <note>original: "u-kshartem l'ot al yadekha v'hayu l'totafot bein eynekha"</note> That is: **And you shall bind them** (namely the commandments) **as a sign upon your hands, and they shall be as frontlets** (that is, in phylacteries) **between your eyes.** <note>Deuteronomy 6:8</note> You should know, therefore, that "phylactery" is a Greek name, derived (as some prefer) ἀπὸ τὸ φυλάσσειν <note>original Greek: "apo to phylassein"</note> from the Greek verb which means "to preserve" or "guard," and תורה <note>original: "tora"</note> in Hebrew, which signifies the Law; hence "phylacteries" are as it were "preservers of the law." This etymology pleases me very little, since the Greek and Hebrew languages can by no means be so mixed. Therefore, I say this word is entirely Greek, and in Greek it is called φυλακτήριον <note>original Greek: "phylaktērion"</note>. For they used to make four such "preservers" in which the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments; though in Jewish practice, the phylacteries contain four specific passages from the Torah, the author here identifies them with the Decalogue</note> was placed. They would bind one on the head, where the skull of small children pulsates. These are called תפילין <note>original: "tephillin"</note> in the Talmud, but in Deuteronomy they are called טוטפות <note>original: "totaphoth"</note>.

<margin>
Conclusion of the aforementioned.

From all these things, therefore, it is clearly evident that the Mosaic Law was not only changeable, but also frequently changed. <margin>Concerning the fifth objection regarding other ceremonial matters.</margin>

"And you shall observe this thing as a statute for you and your sons forever." <note>original Hebrew: *ve-sharnartem et ha-davar ha-zeh le-khoq lekha u-le-vaneykha ad olam* (Exodus 12:24)</note> This means, "And keep this matter as a law, or as a precept for you and your children into eternity." Regarding the offering of the first fruits of the crops, the solemnity of Pentecost, the offerings and other sacrifices, and the Day of Atonement <note>The Latin *in casulis* refers to the "huts" or "booths" associated with the Feast of Tabernacles/Sukkot, though the text links it here to the Day of Atonement ceremonies.</note>, as well as the "bread of proposition"—which they more accurately call the **Bread of the Faces** <note>original: *panibus facierum*; a literal translation of the Hebrew *lechem ha-panim*</note>—they bring against us what is held in the twenty-third chapter of Leviticus: "You shall do no work. By these and similar passages, the most wicked Jews of our time strive to prove that the Mosaic Law, as far as ceremonies are concerned, was by no means intended to cease, but was to endure forever. Therefore, you must refute these arguments to the best of your ability.

<margin>Refutation of the aforementioned objections.</margin>

**GAL.** I shall do so most gladly. Regarding that point from which they conclude that the mandates of the Law must be observed forever: if they refer to the moral precepts, they speak the truth. For whatever pertains to morals remains forever and always ought to be observed. In this way, the Catholic truth (as was said above) commands that the moral aspects of the Law be kept—not because they are precepts of the Mosaic Law, but because they are part of the eternal law. 

However, if their argument is applied to the ceremonial laws, I say that in those cases "eternal" or "everlasting" is understood to mean "perpetual" or "for an age." For wherever we have "eternal" or "everlasting" in our edition <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> in these passages, the Hebrew text <margin>What the Hebrew word *Olam* signifies.</margin> has *olam* <note>עולם</note>, which is understood there as "perpetual" or "for an age." If, therefore, *olam* is taken in these same places to mean "perpetual," then *olam* is the same as "continuous," referring to something that lasts for the "age" or "lifetime" of a specific thing without interruption. 

For "perpetual" is properly the same as "continuous." According to that line of Ovid: "Lead my perpetual song down to my own times." <note>A quote from the opening of Ovid's *Metamorphoses*: *Ad mea perpetuum deducite tempora carmen*.</note> Hence we speak of a "perpetual oration," which is continuous and without interruption. Hence a man is called "Perpetual Consul," "Perpetual Censor," or "Perpetual Emperor" who stood as Censor, Consul, or Emperor always and continuously as long as he lived. Yet, when he died, another was substituted. In this way, circumcision and other ceremonies were given to the Jews to be observed as a "covenant of *olam*," that is, a perpetual covenant: meaning always and continuously for as long as they were meant to be observed, and no further. 

If, however, *olam* is taken to mean "an age," then *olam* implies not eternity, but a determined time. To prove this, I will first bring forward what was said of Samuel by his mother Hannah, in the first chapter of the First Book of Kings <note>Known as 1 Samuel in modern Bibles.</note>...

# BOOK <note>Continued from Book Eleven</note>

...in the same chapter, it is said: "And I will bring him, and he shall appear before the face of the Lord, and abide there *leolam*, that is, forever." <note>original Hebrew: *ve-nir’ah et penei YHVH ve-yashav sham ad olam* (1 Samuel 1:22)</note> That is, "And I will lead him, and he shall appear in the sight of God, and remain there for an age," or forever. Regarding this, the commentary of **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> says: "until the end of the age of the Levites." This matches what is said in the eighth chapter of Numbers: "And from fifty years of age he shall cease the work of service and shall serve no more." <note>original Hebrew: *u-mi-ben hamishim shanah yashuv mi-tzeva ha-avodah ve-lo ya’avod od* (Numbers 8:25)</note> And thus all the days of Samuel were fifty-two years. <note>Samuel was dedicated to the Tabernacle as a Levite; since Levites retired at 50 and he was dedicated after being weaned (around age 2), his "forever" service lasted about 50 years.</note>

Furthermore, it is very important to note what is read in the **Midrash** *Elle Haddebarim* <note>The Midrash Rabbah on the book of Deuteronomy; *Elle Haddebarim* means "These are the words."</note>—that is, in the exposition of the book of Deuteronomy—concerning what is written in its fifteenth chapter: "And you shall take an awl and put it through his ear and into the door, and he shall be your servant *olam*," that is, for an age. <note>original Hebrew: *ve-laqahta et ha-mratze’a ve-natattah ve-ozno u-va-delet ve-hayah lekha eved olam* (Deuteronomy 15:17)</note> For there, *olam* is said to mean "all the days of the age of the Lord until the **Jubilee**," <note>The Jubilee was a year of liberation every 50 years when slaves were freed and land returned to its owners.</note> even if the servant had been bought thirty or forty years before the Jubilee.

Thus far the Midrash—that is, the exposition—from which it is clear that in this place *olam* (the "age" which our translator rendered as "eternal") actually refers to a single year or even less, depending on whether that servant happened to die sooner or later. **Rabbi Solomon**, in his commentary on these same words, proves it this way: "And he shall be your servant *olam*, that is, for an age." He says: "It is possible for this to be as its hearing [the context] shows," because it is written in the twenty-fifth chapter of Leviticus: "And you shall return every man to his possession, and every man to his family." <note>original Hebrew: *ve-shavtem ish el ahuzzato ve-ish el mishpahto tashuvu* (Leviticus 25:10)</note> Behold, from this you are taught that this *olam* refers to nothing other than the "age of the Jubilee." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon.

This is also confirmed in the book *Kiddushin*—that is, **Betrothals**. <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with marriage and legal status.</note> For among other things it is said there: "What is it that is written in the twenty-first chapter of Exodus: 'And his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him *leolam*,' that is, for an age?" <note>original Hebrew: *ve-ra’atza adonav et ozno ba-mratze’a ve-avado le-olam* (Exodus 21:6)</note> Until which age? Until the age of the Jubilee, or until the death of the master, as is written above. "And he shall serve *him*": therefore, he shall not serve the son. This is the tradition.

The same is also clear through **Rabbi David Kimhi** <note>Also known as Radak (1160–1235), a famous grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> in the book *Sefer Shorashim* <note>The "Book of Roots," a Hebrew dictionary; transcribed here as *Serafim* likely due to an OCR or printer error.</note> where he says: "It is written in the twenty-first chapter of Exodus, 'And he shall serve him *leolam*,' that is, for an age. It means to say: all the days until the Jubilee." Likewise, regarding that which is written in the twenty-second chapter of Proverbs: "Do not move the *olam* boundary which your fathers have made." <note>original Hebrew: *al tassig gevul olam asher asu avotekha* (Proverbs 22:28)</note> This means: "Do not push back or neglect the boundary of *olam*, that is, of many days, which your fathers established." And in Jeremiah, the second chapter: "For from *meolam* I have broken your yoke." <note>original Hebrew: *ki me-olam shavarti ullekh* (Jeremiah 2:20)</note> That is, "For from a long time ago you have broken your yoke." And in the Psalms: "Into the age (*leolam*) I will not forget your commandments." <note>original Hebrew: *le-olam lo eshkah piqudeikha* (Psalm 119:93)</note> This means *leolam*, or "into the age," signifying "all the days of my life I will not forget your commandments." These are the words of Rabbi Kimhi. From all these examples, therefore, it is manifest that this word *olam* signifies neither eternity nor perpetuity...

# BOOK ELEVENTH

...but an age, and a determined time, and sometimes very short, as has already been shown. From this it is clear that the author of our edition—both the Greek <note>The Septuagint</note> and the Latin <note>The Vulgate</note>—and whatever other translators rendered this word *olam* <note>original Hebrew: עולם</note> as "eternal" or "everlasting" where the Divine Scripture speaks of circumcision, the Sabbath, the tabernacles, or other ceremonies, have interpreted it far differently than the truth of the matter holds. Because of this, many have fallen into the Jewish error and been irrevocably led away from the Christian faith, as it happened that they heard or read that there was an "eternal covenant" or "everlasting law" concerning circumcision and other ceremonies.

But what "eternal" or "everlasting" actually means among the Hebrews, **Rabbi Kimhi** <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, a famous grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> declares most excellently in his book *Shorashim* <note>The "Book of Roots," a standard Hebrew dictionary of the Middle Ages.</note> when he says: It is written in Psalm 84: "They will praise you *sela*" <note>original Hebrew: יהללוך סלה (*yehalelukha sela*)</note>, that is, "they will praise you forever." For they explained this word *sela* as *olam ad* <note>original Hebrew: עולם ועד</note>, that is, "unto eternity." So also in the words of our Masters, there is a tradition from the house of **Rabbi Elazar**, that every place in which the words *Nezah*, *Sela*, or *Vahed* are placed, there is no intermission, but it signifies "for an age" and "for ages of ages."

For *Nezah* <note>original Hebrew: נצח, often translated as "forever" or "victory"</note> is as it is written in Isaiah 57: "And I will not be angry unto *Nezah*" <note>original Hebrew: ולא לנצח אקצוף (*ve-lo la-nezah ekztoph*)</note>. This means: "And I will not be angry or foam with rage unto eternity," or "forever." 

*Sela* <note>original Hebrew: סלה</note>, indeed, is as it is written in Psalm 48: "He will establish her even unto *olam sela*" <note>original Hebrew: יכוננה עד עולם סלה (*yekoneneha ad olam sela*)</note>. This means: "He will rectify, or compose, or ordain her even unto the eternal age," or "always." 

*Vaed* <note>original Hebrew: ועד</note>, however, is as it is written in Exodus 15: "The Lord shall reign for an *olam* and *vaed*" <note>original Hebrew: יהוה ימלוך לעולם ועד (*Adonai yimlokh le-olam va-ed*)</note>. This means: "God shall reign for an age and beyond," that is, in eternity or forever. These are the words of Rabbi Kimhi.

Since, therefore, none of these specific words are placed in the Law where mention is made of circumcision, the Sabbath, sacrifices, or other ceremonies—but only *olam*—it is, as we have seen, clearly and beyond doubt manifest that those ceremonies were not to be observed eternally according to the letter, but for a determined time: namely, until the coming of the Messiah. Especially since these ceremonies, according to the letter, were "not good," they were only intended to be observed spiritually in the days of the Messiah.

# BOOK [ELEVENTH]

...that I might desolate them, so that they might know that I am God. Where the commentary of **Rabbi Shlomo** <note>original: "Rabbi Selonis" or "Rabbi Selomo," referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note> explains that word *Lemaan ashimem* <note>original Hebrew: למען אשימם</note> as follows: "so that I might desolate them and destroy them." For *ashimem* is a term of desolation—that is, signifying a state of being laid waste. Therefore, anyone who interpreted that word as a term for "sin," saying it meant "because of their sins," is in error. For the letter *Aleph* found there is not part of the root of the word. "So that they may know," or "so that they might know, that I am God"—specifically, when I shall have brought these evils upon them. These are the words of **Rabbi Shlomo**. If, therefore, God Himself called the ceremonial precepts which He gave to the Jews "not good," it should not seem strange to you, nor to anyone else, if I have called them the same.

**CAPNIO** <note>Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist, acting as a character in this dialogue.</note>: For what reason, then, were they called "not good"?

**GALATINUS** <note>Pietro Galatino, the author, acting as the primary teacher in the dialogue.</note>: Because through them, men were not justified. For they were "shadows," prefiguring the grace through which we are now justified. Yet they should not be called "evil," since they were divinely commanded and were appropriate for that specific time and those specific people. And for that reason, perhaps, God did not call them "evil," but only "not good"—that is, not of such a kind that men would become good and righteous through them. Because Abraham and all the other fathers were held guilty and liable before God, to the extent that—notwithstanding the sacrifices and other ceremonies—they descended into the underworld <note>original: "infernum," referring to the Limbo of the Fathers, where the righteous dead waited for Christ.</note>, as we have already proven sufficiently and abundantly in the preceding sections. Hence, not without reason, **Isaiah** said in his 40th chapter: *Ve-levanon ein dei baer ve-hayato ein dei olah* <note>original Hebrew: ואין די בער וחיתו אין די עולה</note>. That is: "And Lebanon is not sufficient for burning, nor its animals sufficient for a burnt offering."

The commentary of **Rabbi Shlomo** explains it thus: it is not sufficient for making satisfaction for the sins of the nations. By "Lebanon" here, nothing is understood except the Temple, as is clearly evident in the *Midrash Shir HaShirim* <note>original: "Midras haſſirim," a traditional Jewish homiletical commentary on the Song of Songs.</note>, that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs. For just as this nose is placed at the highest point of a man, so the house of the Lord—that is, the Temple—was placed at the height of the world. Therefore, when it is said, "Like the tower of Lebanon," Lebanon refers only to the house of the Sanctuary. As it is said in Deuteronomy 3: *Ha-har ha-tov ha-zeh ve-ha-levanon* <note>original Hebrew: ההר הטוב הזה והלבנון</note>, that is, "This good mountain and Lebanon."

This is the tradition: just as Lebanon—that is, the Temple—with all its burnt offerings and its sacrifices, was not sufficient to make satisfaction for the sins of the nations according to **Rabbi Shlomo's** exposition, so too it was not enough to satisfy for the sins of the Jews. Since everyone, both the good and the bad (though in different ways), descended into the underworld. This is also excellently proven by what is written in the exposition of the book of Genesis by **Rabbi Moses the Preacher** <note>original: "Rabbi Moſis Hadaſ." (Moshe Ha-Darshan), an 11th-century scholar from Narbonne.</note>, where he comments on the verse in the twenty-seventh chapter of the same book: *Va-yehi ki zaken Yitzchak* <note>original Hebrew: ויהי כי זקן יצחק</note>, that is, "And it came to pass when Isaac was old." It reads as follows: **Rabbi Nehemiah** said: "Tribulations are more beloved to God than sacrifices. For sacrifices come from a man's wealth, but tribulations come from his very body." As it is said in the second chapter of **Job**: *Or be-ad or ve-khol asher la-ish yitten be-ad nafsho* <note>original Hebrew: עור בעד עור וכל אשר לאיש יתן בעד נפשו</note>. That is: "Skin for..."

# BOOK ELEVENTH

"Skin for skin, and all that a man has, he will give for his soul." <note>original Latin: "Pellem pro pelle, & quicquid habet uir, dabit pro anima sua." A quote from Job 2:4.</note> In this passage, "soul" is used to signify the animated body. From all these examples, my purpose is clear: namely, that the ceremonial laws of the Mosaic Law, while they were not "evil" because they were commanded by God, were nevertheless "not good" because they were not powerful enough to justify men. Therefore, upon the arrival of the Messiah, they were to reach their end in such a way that they should be observed in a spiritual sense only.

### Chapter VII. That circumcision in the time of the Messiah was to be observed not carnally, but spiritually.

->CAPNIO,<-
<note>Johannes Reuchlin, the famous Christian Hebraist, acting as a character in this dialogue.</note>

Therefore, so that the <term>perfidia</term> <note>A common 16th-century polemical term used by Christian authors to describe Jewish "unbelief" or "refusal to accept" Christ; it is best understood here as "stubbornness" or "lack of faith."</note> of the Jews may be more and more convinced, it must now be proven through their own scriptures that in the days of the Messiah, their ceremonies were to be kept spiritually. GALATINUS: First, then, let them hear the voice of Almighty God, speaking thus in the 4th chapter of Jeremiah to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: <note>original Hebrew: נירו לכם ניר ואל תזרעו אל קוצים : המלו ליהוה והסירו ערלת לבבכם איש יהודה וישבי ירושלם פן תצא כאש חמתי ובערה ואין מכבה מפני רוע מעלליכם</note> That is: "Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns. In the <term>Midrash</term> <note>A genre of ancient rabbinic commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> on <term>Shir HaShirim</term> <note>The Song of Songs.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Song of Songs—regarding the verse in the second chapter of that book: <note>original Hebrew: ענה דודי ואמר לי</note> "My beloved answered and said to me," it is read as follows:

"The congregation of Israel said: He answered me by the hand of Elijah; he gave the exposition by the hand of Daniel. And he spoke to me by the hand of the King Messiah. And what did he say to me? <note>original Hebrew: קומי לכי רעיתי יפתי ולכי לך</note> That is: 'Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away. For lo, the winter is past.' And so on, until: <note>original Hebrew: עת הזמיר הגיע</note> 'The time of pruning has arrived.' <note>Song of Songs 2:10-12. The Hebrew word 'zamir' can mean both 'pruning' and 'singing.' The time has arrived for the foreskin to be cut away, of which it was said in the thirtieth chapter of Deuteronomy: <note>original Hebrew: ומל יהוה אלהיך את לבבך ואת לבב זרעך לאהבה את יהוה אלהיך</note> That is: 'And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, to love the Lord your God.' <meta>catchword: Ch</meta>

...and with the house of Judah a new covenant, that is, a new law. Thus far has been treated that in which two things to be noted are clearly evident. The first indeed is that circumcision in the time of the Messiah was to be performed spiritually. This he proves through <term>Deuteronomy</term> <note>Deuteronomy 30:6</note>: "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your offspring." This cannot be understood except spiritually, since according to the literal letter, nothing can be removed from the heart without death. The second point is that the law was to be converted into novelty, namely because of the new law which the Messiah was to give. As proof of this, he brings forward that passage from Jeremiah: "And I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah." <note>Jeremiah 31:31</note> By this "covenant," the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Teachers of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> understand the Law, as was made clear on the preceding page. This is also most powerfully proven from what is read in the *Bereshith Rabba Ketanna* (that is, in the smaller exposition of the book of Genesis), regarding the saying in the 17th chapter of that same book: "And I will give my covenant between me and you." <note>original Hebrew: ונתתה בריתי ביני ובינך (Gen 17:2)</note> 

<margin>A fourfold kind of foreskins.</margin>
Where <term>Rabbi Akiba</term> <note>A leading 1st-century Jewish scholar and sage</note> is said to have spoken thus: "There are four kinds of foreskins. For a foreskin of the ear is mentioned, regarding which it is written in Jeremiah chapter 6: 'Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot listen; behold, the word of the Lord was to them a reproach; they do not desire it.'" <note>original Hebrew: הנה ערלה אזנם ולא יוכלו להקשיב הנה דבר יהוה היה להם לחרפה לא יחפצו בו (Jer 6:10)</note> That is: To whom shall I speak and testify, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, and they will not be able to pay attention. Behold, the word of God was a reproach to them. They do not want it. Mention is also made of a foreskin of the mouth, just as it is written in Exodus chapter 6: "uncircumcised of lips." <note>original Hebrew: ערל שפתים (Exod 6:12)</note> That is: "And I am uncircumcised of lips." And again in the same place: "uncircumcised of lips," <note>Exod 6:30</note> that is, "Behold, I am uncircumcised of lips." Mention is also made of a foreskin in the heart, according to that passage in Jeremiah chapter 9: "And all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart." <note>original Hebrew: וכל בית ישראל ערלי לב (Jer 9:26)</note> And again in Leviticus chapter 26: "And I will lead them into the land of their enemies, so that even then their uncircumcised heart might pray, or be humbled, and then they shall be satisfied for their sin." <note>Lev 26:41</note> And again God says: "And you shall circumcise the foreskin of your heart." <note>Deut 10:16</note> And once more in the same book: "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your offspring." <note>Deut 30:6</note> Finally, a foreskin in the body is mentioned, according to that passage in Genesis chapter 17: "And the uncircumcised male, who has not circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, that soul shall be cut off from his people." <note>Gen 17:14</note> <term>Rabbi Tanhuma</term> <note>An influential 4th-century Jewish sage</note> said: "There is a doubt regarding this scripture, which says, 'And the uncircumcised male.' For is there such a thing as an uncircumcised female? But the meaning is that from whichever place someone becomes estranged from God—whether it be male or female—from there they must be circumcised." Thus far Rabbi Akiba.

<margin>Four kinds of circumcisions.</margin>
From these things it plainly follows that just as there are four foreskins, so also there are four kinds of circumcisions. Three of these—namely of the ear, the mouth, and the heart, which are spiritual—are always necessary for everyone. But the fourth kind, because it is physical and is a shadow or figure of the others, now that our Messiah has come—the Master of spiritual precepts—it is not only useless, but even to all those who practice it, it is extremely destructive. Hence Paul, in whom Christ spoke, writing to the Galatians in chapter 5, says in these words: "I, Paul, say to you, that if you are circumcised..." <note>Galatians 5:2; the passage continues "Christ shall profit you nothing."</note>

<summary>Galatinus uses Jewish authorities like Rabbi Akiba and Rabbi Tanhuma to argue that circumcision has four forms (ear, mouth, heart, and body), and that with the Messiah's arrival, only the spiritual forms remain necessary. He concludes that continuing physical circumcision is now spiritually harmful, citing the Apostle Paul.</summary>

...Christ will profit you nothing <note>original: "Christus uobis nihil proderit"; Galatians 5:2</note>. And again in the 4th chapter of Romans: "For we say," he says, "that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness." <note>Romans 4:9</note> How then was it reckoned? In circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And further on: "For the promise to Abraham, or his seed, that he should be heir of the world, was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith." <note>Romans 4:13</note> Likewise to the Galatians in chapter 1 <note>Actually Galatians 2:16; Galatinus or his source may have a different chapter division or a memory error</note>: "But knowing," he says, "that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ. And we believe in Christ Jesus, so that we may be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law." This man [Paul] was the most excellent of <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of Jewish oral law; Galatinus refers to Paul's background as a Pharisee</note>, and one in whom Christ spoke, as he himself testified in 2 Corinthians, chapter 13. In that which he says—that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness in uncircumcision, and not in circumcision—he clearly implies that Abraham was faithful and righteous before he was circumcised.

Which can be proven in this way. For it is written in Genesis, chapter 17: <gloss>original Hebrew: ואברהם בן תשעים ותשע שנה בהמלו בשר ערלתו</gloss> That is, "And Abraham was a son of 99 years when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin." <note>Genesis 17:24</note> But previously, in the 15th chapter of the same book, it is read thus of him: <gloss>original Hebrew: והאמין ביהוה ויחשבה לו צדקה</gloss> This is: "And he believed in God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness." <note>Genesis 15:6</note> Where the <term>gloss</term> <note>A marginal or interlinear commentary</note> of <term>Rabbi Solomon</term> <note>The famous Jewish commentator Rashi (1040–1105)</note> says thus: "The Holy and Blessed God reckoned it—namely the faith with which Abraham believed in God—as righteousness and justification." From which it is clear that Abraham was faithful and righteous before he was circumcised.

This is also confirmed by what is read in the <term>Bereshith Ketanna</term> <note>original: "Beressith קטנה"; a smaller midrashic commentary on Genesis</note>, when it comments upon that saying in chapter 6 of the same book, "Noah was a righteous man." It is said there: <term>Rabbi Johanan</term> and <term>Rabbi Hanina</term> both said, "At forty-eight years of age, Abraham recognized his creator and believed in him." And what did he establish in him—that is, what did he propose he would do for him? To lead the whole world to repentance. From this it follows that just as Abraham was faithful and righteous before he was circumcised, so too Noah (as the sacred scripture testifies) was righteous, upright, and perfect, yet not circumcised. So also <term>Melchizedek</term>. So also <term>Job</term>. So also many others.

Wherefore that saying of <term>Rabbi Joshua</term> is greatly to be noted in the book <term>Yevamot</term> <note>original: "יבמות"; a tractate of the Talmud concerning family law</note>, that is, *Of the Brothers-in-Law*, in the chapter <term>Hachaluẓ</term> <note>original: "החולץ"; meaning "The one who has the shoe removed"</note>, where he says word for word: "One who is baptized but not circumcised, behold, he is a <term>Ger</term> <note>original: "גר"; a proselyte or convert</note>, that is, one converted to the faith." For so we find in the mothers, namely in Sarah and Rebecca and the rest, who were baptized <note>Refers to the Jewish ritual of immersion (mikveh), which Galatinus interprets as a precursor to Christian baptism</note> but were not circumcised. For which reason the Apostle Paul is to be judged to have spoken most excellently when writing to the Galatians in chapter 5: "In Christ Jesus," he says, "neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith, which works through love." <note>Galatians 5:6</note> And again in the same place he says: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but a new creature"—that is, the regeneration which happens through baptism, and a new life. For when the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish nations</note> worshipped demons in idols, they were nothing before God, according to that saying in Isaiah chapter 40: <gloss>original Hebrew: כל הגוים כאין נגדו מאפס ותהו נחשבו לו</gloss> That is: "All the nations [are as nothing before him; they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness]."

For it is a sign, not of the faithful as it once was, but of the unfaithful and of those whom God has rejected. Since I have already spoken at length about this circumcision in the oration I delivered to <term>Pope Leo X</term> <note>Giovanni de' Medici, Pope from 1513–1521; he was a significant patron of the arts and scholars, including those interested in Hebrew studies.</note> regarding the Circumcision of the Lord, I shall say nothing more about it now. ### *That the Sabbath also, in the days of the Messiah, was to be observed only spiritually. Chapter VIII.*

->CAPNIO,<-
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style nickname for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist scholar who defended Jewish texts.</note>

<margin>GALATINUS. Spiritually</margin>
It must now be explained in what manner the Sabbath was to be observed spiritually in the time of the Messiah. A spiritual Sabbath is nothing other than being without sin. For it was commanded that no **servile work** <note>Traditional Jewish law prohibits "melacha" (work) on the Sabbath; here, the author reinterprets physical labor as the "work" of sin.</note> be done on it, as is clear from Exodus chapter 20. But what else is servile work but sin? For according to the word of the Lord in John chapter 8: "Everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin." <note>John 8:34</note> Therefore, the Sabbath in the days of the Messiah was to be kept spiritually because, with the help of the law of the Gospel, one was then to abstain above all from every servile work—that is, from every vice and sin which makes men slaves to the devil. This observance of the spiritual Sabbath finally leads its observer to the eternal Sabbath. For "Sabbath" is interpreted as rest...

<summary>Pietro Galatinus argues that baptism transforms Gentiles into "new creatures" as prophesied by Jewish commentators like Rashi. He concludes that physical circumcision and the Sabbath were merely temporary signs for the Jews, which in the Messianic age are replaced by spiritual counterparts—primarily the avoidance of sin.</summary>

<sig>dd 2</sig>

...interpreted. For this reason, it signified not only the future rest of the Messiah in the tomb on the seventh <margin>How the Sabbath is interpreted and what it prefigured.</margin> day, but also that seventh rest which those who have spiritually kept the Sabbath—by abstaining from every vice and sin—shall possess in the seventh age of the world after the general resurrection. Regarding this eternal Sabbath, it is written in the **Midrash Tehillim** <note>original: "Midras tehilim"; a rabbinic commentary (midrash) on the Book of Psalms.</note>—that is, in the exposition of the Psalms—concerning that verse of Psalm 89 <note>In modern numbering, this is Psalm 90:15.</note>: **"Make us glad according to the days you have afflicted us."** <note>original Hebrew: "Simchenu ki-mot initanu"</note> This means: "Make us joyful for the days, or according to the days, in which you have afflicted us." For it says there: "According to the days in which you have afflicted us," namely, through Babylon, through Greece, and through the Romans, and also in the days of the Messiah. And how many are the days of the Messiah? **Rabbi Joshua** <note>Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah, a leading scholar of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries AD.</note> said: "They are two thousand years." Just as it is said here, "According to the days in which you have humbled us," that is, according to two days. For one day of the Holy and Blessed God is a thousand years, according to what is said in the same Psalm: **"For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday."** <note>original Hebrew: "Ki elef shanim be-enekha ke-yom etmol"; Psalm 90:4.</note> The Teachers have also said that according to the future, the day of the Messiah shall be one. For the Holy and Blessed God shall make for him one day in the future, of which it is spoken in Zechariah chapter 14: **"And it shall be one day, and it is known to the Lord; not day nor night. And it shall come to pass, that at evening time there shall be light."** <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-hayah yom echad hu yivada l'Adonai lo yom ve-lo laylah ve-hayah le-et erev yihyeh or"; Zechariah 14:7.</note> This day is the **world to come** <note>original Latin: "seculum futurum"; refers to the Messianic age or the afterlife, known in Hebrew as Olam Ha-Ba.</note> and the restoration of the dead to life. And this is the light which the Holy and Blessed God reserved for the righteous at the beginning of the world, namely that of which it is spoken in Genesis 1: **"And he saw the light, that it was good."** And again it is said of it in Psalm 36: **"For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light."** Furthermore, Isaiah says in the last chapter: **"And it shall be that their seed shall be from the sufficiency of the month in its month, and from the sufficiency of the sabbath in its sabbath."** <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-hayah midei chodesh be-chodsho u-midei shabbat be-shabbato"; Isaiah 66:23. The Latin text uses "seed" (semen) where modern translations usually say "all flesh."</note> This "Sabbath" is the world to come, which is entirely a Sabbath, that is, a rest. Thus ends the tradition. From this, the proposed argument is clear. But regarding the understanding of Isaiah's words, which this tradition very appropriately brings up at the end, it must be noted: that "month" in Hebrew is called **hodesh** <note>original: "חרש" (chodesh); the word for month or new moon, derived from the root "to renew."</note>; among them, it is used for the completion of all the days in which the moon finishes its course. For the Jews calculate their times by the moon and not by the sun. Therefore, "month" is used for "perfection," and "Sabbath" for "rest." Thus, according to the aforementioned tradition, the words of Isaiah themselves are to be explained: **"And it shall be their seed"**—that is, the spiritual children of the Apostles and holy teachers—**"from the sufficiency of the month,"**—that is, from the sufficiency of the perfection of the present life—**"in its month,"**—that is, in the perfection of their glory in the future. Likewise, the aforementioned seed, **"from the sufficiency of the Sabbath,"**—that is, from the sufficiency of the rest and cessation from vices and sins in this life—**"shall be in its Sabbath,"**—that is, in its eternal rest in the life of the world to come, which shall be entirely a Sabbath, that is, rest, as the aforementioned tradition says. We have explained the words of Isaiah according to this intention.

It provides an allegorical reading of Isaiah 66:23, equating "months" and "Sabbaths" with the perfection and rest achieved by the faithful in the afterlife.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded a discussion on the spiritual interpretation of circumcision and the Sabbath as prefigurations of eternal rest in the "seventh age" of the world. This page shifts focus to the literal arguments used by Jewish contemporaries to assert that the Sabbath remains a binding obligation for all humanity, not just for the Jewish people.</meta>

BOOK Solution to the Objections of the Jews, by which they attempt to show that the Sabbath ought to be observed literally, not only by Christians and all others, but even more so by the Jews themselves. Chapter 9.

# CAPNIO <note>The Greek-style name used by the humanist scholar Johannes Reuchlin, derived from "Kapnion," meaning "little smoke."</note>

<margin>Objections of the Jews concerning the observation of the Sabbath.</margin>

<margin>First objection.</margin>
The impious bad faith <note>original: "perfidia"; in this historical context, the term was used theologically to mean "lack of faith" or "unbelief."</note> of the Jews of our age opposes this in many ways, wishing to prove with every effort that the Sabbath must be literally observed by law, not only by the Jews themselves, but also by us Christians, and by all others of whatever sect they may be. And first, indeed, because its observation is counted among the ten moral precepts. For it is the third in order among the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>. Since the Lord Himself said thus in Exodus chapter 20: **"Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy."** <note>original Hebrew: "Zakhor et yom ha-shabbat le-kadesho."</note> This means: "Remember the Sabbath day, that you may sanctify it." Wherefore, since the precepts of the Decalogue are to be observed by everyone because they pertain to natural law: <margin>Second objection.</margin> it clearly follows that the Sabbath must be observed by all. Secondly, because the Sabbath regards the benefit of creation, which is common to all. For on the Sabbath God rested from every work that He performed: and therefore He sanctified it and blessed it. For this reason, when He wished it to be venerated, He commanded it, and as if assigning a reason, He immediately added: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall do no work on it: you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your manservant, nor your maidservant, nor your beast, nor the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days God made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it." ...that it ought to have been observed, but also that it must be kept by everyone at all times. Even if these arguments are of little weight, you should first refute them to further confound the obstinacy of those who rely on such a fragile and crumbling foundation. Then, it is necessary that you show through their own scriptures that the Sabbath itself has been dissolved <note>original: "solutum" — meaning its legal obligation has been set aside or fulfilled</note> even among them.

**GALATINUS:** I will certainly take care to satisfy your wishes with every effort.

<margin>*Response to the first objection.*</margin> To their first reason, then, I say briefly: the precept regarding the observation of the Sabbath was partly moral and partly ceremonial. It was moral insofar as it commanded that humans ought to be free for divine matters at some time, according to that saying in *Psalm 45*: **"Be still, and know that I am God."** <note>original: "Cessate & cognoscite, quia ego sum Deus." This is Psalm 46:10 in modern bibles.</note> And according to this, it was counted among the moral precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>. But it was ceremonial regarding the specification of the time on the seventh day. And according to this, it was numbered among the precepts of the Decalogue, but among other ceremonial ones. From this it is that we find that the Sabbath was often set aside in the Old Testament. This would by no means have happened if, regarding the observation of the seventh day, it were numbered among the moral precepts of the Decalogue, since it is never permitted to set those aside at any time, because they are of natural law <note>The author distinguishes between "natural law" (timeless morals) and "ceremonial law" (specific rituals that can change).</note>. Hence also our Lord Jesus, the true Messiah, after he had reached thirty years of age, is read to have set aside the Sabbath itself several times regarding that part. For on that day he both healed the sick, giving them the ability to carry their beds, and he allowed his hungry disciples to pluck and rub ears of grain.

<margin>*To the second objection.*</margin> To the second I say: Just as the Sabbath looks to the benefit of creation, so the Lord's Day <note>Sunday, the "dies dominicus"</note> displays the benefit of redemption. For just as God completed the work of creation on the Sabbath, so on the Lord's Day He perfected the work of redemption through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ himself (as the Apostle <note>Paul</note> says) died for our justification and rose for our glory. Since, therefore, by the opinion of all, the work of redemption is greater than the work of creation—for in creation indeed, God spoke, and the world was made, as the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> say; but in redemption, as these same men say, it was necessary for God himself not only to speak, but also to do and to suffer many things, as we have proved most extensively from their own sayings in the 8th book—therefore the Sabbath, as far as its ceremonial aspect is concerned, had to be changed into the Lord's Day by the very one who instituted it. This day respects the benefit of both creation and redemption. For on that day both the world took its beginning, and through the resurrection of the Lord, death received its destruction, and life took its start.

<margin>*To the third objection regarding the Sabbatic river.*</margin> Finally, I respond to the third, by turning that Jewish fiction about the **Sabbatic river** <note>The Sambation, a legendary river in Jewish lore that was said to flow with stones and sand for six days a week but rest on the Sabbath.</note> back against them. For just as that fictitious river was a sign for observing the Sabbath—since it would flow throughout the whole week by dragging stones and would rest on the Sabbaths, as they fabulate—so too is it now an effective argument against them for *not* observing the Sabbath. Since there is now no river under heaven which [rests] more on Sabbaths than...

# BOOK [XI] Solution to the Objections of the Jews, by which they try to show that the Sabbath ought to be literally observed by Christians and all others, let alone the Jews themselves. Chapter IX.

### CAPNIO,

<margin>Jewish objections regarding the observation of the Sabbath.</margin>
<margin>First objection.</margin>
The impious perfidy of the Jews of our age <note>The author uses "perfidy" in the common 16th-century sense of "unbelief" or "lack of faith" regarding Christian doctrine.</note> opposes this in many ways, wishing to prove with all their might that the Sabbath must be observed literally and by right, not only by the Jews themselves, but also by us Christians and all others of whatever sect they may be. And first, indeed, because its observation is numbered among the ten moral precepts. For it is the third in order among the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments. In many Christian traditions, this is considered the third or fourth commandment.</note>. As the Lord himself said in Exodus, chapter 20: **Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.** <note>original Hebrew: זכור את יום השבת לקדשו (*Zakhor et yom ha-Shabbat le-kadesho*)</note>. Therefore, since the precepts of the Decalogue are to be observed by all because they are of natural law:
<margin>Second objection.</margin>
It clearly follows that the Sabbath ought to be observed by everyone. Secondly, because the Sabbath regards the benefit of creation, which is common to all. For on the Sabbath, God rested from every work that He performed, and therefore He sanctified it and blessed it. For which reason, when He commanded that it be called so, as if assigning a reason, He immediately added: "Six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall not do any work on it—you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant nor your female servant, your cattle, nor the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days God made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them. And He rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it." Since, therefore, everyone is obligated to God by reason of creation, it follows that everyone is held to the observation of the Sabbath.
<margin>Third objection.</margin>
<margin>A fiction regarding the Sabbatic river.</margin>
Third and finally, because a natural example leads everyone to this: the Sabbatic river <note>Historically known as the Sambation, a mythical river in Jewish legend that stopped flowing on the Sabbath.</note>, which (as they say) flows rapidly throughout the whole week, dragging stones along, but rests on the Sabbath. Whence it is read in the <term>Beresith ketanna</term> <note>literally "Small Genesis," likely referring to the *Midrash Bereshit Zuta* or a specific minor midrashic commentary</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, upon that saying of the same book: **And He blessed the seventh day.** <note>original Hebrew: ויברך את יום השביעי (*Va-yevarekh et yom ha-shevi'i*)</note>. It is told there that the Roman Lord Rufus <note>Quintus Tineius Rufus, a Roman governor of Judea, often portrayed as a foil to Rabbi Akiba in the Talmud and Midrash.</note> questioned Rabbi Akiba and said to him, "What is the difference between this day and other days?" Rabbi Akiba answered him, saying, "And what is the difference between one man and other men?" Rufus said to him, "What did I say to you? And what did you say to me?" He replied to him, "You indeed said to me: 'How does the Sabbath differ from all other days?' And I said to you: 'How does Rufus excel all other men?' Just as the King wished to honor you above all others for his own glory, so too God wished this day to be honored above the others." Rufus said to him, "How will you make me know this?" The Rabbi replied, "The Sabbatic river shows this, which drags stones all through the week and rests on the Sabbath." By these arguments, therefore, the more recent Jews try to prove that the Sabbath has not only never ceased...

[not only that they] should have [observed it], but that it must always be observed by everyone. **GALATINUS:** I shall indeed take care to satisfy your wishes with every effort.

<margin>Response to the first objection.</margin> 
Regarding their first argument, then, I say briefly: the precept concerning the observation of the Sabbath was partly **moral** and partly **ceremonial**. It was **moral** insofar as it commanded that men ought to be free at some time for divine matters, according to that word in Psalm 45: *Be still, and know that I am God.* <note>original Latin: "Cessate & cognoscite, quia ego sum Deus." Galatinus argues that the "moral" core of the commandment is simply making time for God, regardless of the specific day.</note> According to this aspect, it was counted among the moral precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>. However, it was **ceremonial** regarding the specific designation of the seventh day. According to this aspect, it was numbered among the precepts of the Decalogue, but alongside other ceremonies. Hence it is that we find in the Old Testament that the Sabbath was frequently "broken." This would never have happened if the observation of the seventh day itself were counted among the moral precepts of the Decalogue, since it is never permitted to set those aside, as they belong to **natural law** <note>Natural law refers to moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, which are seen as unchanging.</note>. 

Hence also our Lord Jesus, the true Messiah, after he reached his thirtieth year, is read to have broken the Sabbath itself several times in regard to this ceremonial part. For on that day he both healed the sick—giving them the power to carry their own beds—and he allowed his hungry disciples to pluck ears of grain and rub them in their hands.

<margin>To the second objection.</margin> 
To the second objection, I say: Just as the Sabbath looks back to the benefit of **Creation**, so the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday.</note> displays the benefit of **Redemption**. For just as God completed the work of creation on the Sabbath, so He perfected the work of redemption on the Lord’s Day through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ himself (as the Apostle says) died for our justification and rose for our glory. Since, therefore, by the judgment of all, the work of redemption is greater than the work of creation—for in creation, indeed, God spoke and the world was made, as the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> say; but in redemption, as these same men say, it was necessary for God not only to speak, but also to do many things and to suffer—as we have proved most extensively from their own sayings in the eighth book. Therefore, the Sabbath, in terms of its ceremonial aspect, had to be changed into the Lord’s Day by the very one who instituted it. This day looks back to the benefit of both creation and redemption. For on this day the world took its beginning, and through the resurrection of the Lord, death received its destruction, and life received its start.

Furthermore, Josephus, in the book titled *The Jewish War*, reports where this river was located. Rather than saying more myself, I shall quote his words. For he says thus in Book 7: 

-> "Now Prince Titus stayed for some time at Berytus <note>Modern-day Beirut.</note>, as we have said. Then departing from there, [he saw] on his journey a river well worth noting. It flows between the cities of Arca and Raphanea in the kingdom of Agrippa. It possesses a certain peculiar miracle. For although it is a very full stream at times, and not sluggish in its flow, yet for an interval of six days it dries up at its source and presents a dry bed to the viewer. Then, as if no change had occurred, it rises again on the seventh day just as before. And it is certain that it always observes this order. From this, it is also called the 'Sabbatic River,' being so named after the sacred seventh day of the Jews." <-

Thus far Josephus. Pliny also mentions this river in Book 31 of his *Natural History*, saying: "In Judea, a river dries up on every Sabbath." <note>original Latin: "In Judæa fluuius sabbatis omnibus siccatur."</note> On this account, the Jews would argue that it is not a fiction but the truth that there was such a river, since both Josephus and Pliny mention it and assign the place where it was. 

**GALATINUS:** I admit that such a river existed at that time. However, there is no one now who can say they have seen it, or who can report it was seen by anyone else. Therefore, to claim that such a river exists now must be judged as both a fiction and a mark of extreme stupidity. Furthermore, neither Josephus nor Pliny says that the river rested on the Sabbath, as these men [the Jewish scholars] assert. Instead, one records that it failed for six days and flowed on the seventh, while the other says it was accustomed to fail on the Sabbath. From this, the future failing of the Sabbath was portended: namely, that on that day, it would no longer be a day of veneration. 

From this, the solution to the Jewish arguments—by which they strive to prove that the Sabbath must be literally observed by the whole world—is clear. Their opinion is best refuted by the ancient writings of their own people. For we read among them in the *Perek Perush* <note>original: "פרק perus," likely referring to a "Chapter of Commentary" or exposition</note> upon that verse of Exodus: *See, for the LORD has given you the Sabbath.* <note>original Hebrew: "ראו כי יהוה נתן לכם את השבת"</note> And what does "He gave you the Sabbath" mean? It means He gave it to you, the Jews, and not to the nations of the world <note>The Gentiles.</note>. 

Also in the book *Beitzah* <note>original: "ביצה Biza," a tractate of the Talmud meaning "The Egg."</note>, in the chapter *Yom Tov* <note>original: "יום טוב yom tob," meaning "Festival" or "Good Day."</note>, it is said: Rabbi Yohanan said: "Every commandment that the Holy and Blessed God gave to Israel, He gave to them publicly, except for the Sabbath, which He gave to them in secret." Just as it is written: *Between me and the children of Israel.* <note>original Hebrew: "ביני ובין בני ישראל" from Exodus 31:17.</note> If this is so, then the *Goyim* <note>original: "גויים goim," meaning the non-Jewish nations.</note> are not bound to the Sabbath. This is the tradition. From this, the falsehood of the aforementioned Jewish conclusion is clearly manifest.

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page that the Sabbath was not an inviolable, eternal law, but a ritual that was frequently suspended for holy purposes, signaling its eventual transition into a spiritual observance in the Messianic age.</meta>

BOOK [XI] 696

In the chapter that begins, "And the people who came up from the Jordan," concerning the statement in the 6th chapter of Joshua, "On the seventh day," along with the rest, it is written: Rabbi Joses said, "It was the Sabbath day when the battle was at Jericho." In the *Small Genesis* <note>original: "Bereshith ketanna"; likely referring to the midrashic work *Bereshit Rabbati* or a smaller collection of Genesis commentaries</note>, that is, in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis, concerning that phrase in the 17th chapter of the same book, "All the men of his house," it is said: "We find that Jericho was not captured except on the Sabbath." Rabbi Rahmon said, "This is what is written in the 6th chapter of Joshua: *On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times.*" <note>original Hebrew: "השביעי תסבו את העיר שבע פעמים"</note> Furthermore, in the book called *Rosh Hashanah* <note>term: "Ros hassana"; literally "Head of the Year," a tractate of the Talmud concerning the Jewish New Year</note>, in the chapter *Arba'ah Rashe Shanim* <note>original Hebrew: "ארבעה ראשי שנים"; translates to "Four New Years"</note>, that is, the four heads of the years, it is read: "For three months they would break the Sabbath: for Nisan <note>The first month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in Spring.</note> (that is, March), and for Tishrei <note>The seventh month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in Autumn.</note> (that is, September)." For in those months they would send messengers out into Syria so that they might buy necessary things there. However, when the house of the sanctuary <note>The Holy Temple in Jerusalem.</note> was in its proper state, they would also break the Sabbath during all the months for the sake of the preparations of those things which were necessary for the sacrifices. Also in the book called *Sabbath* <note>The Talmudic tractate *Shabbat*, which deals with the laws of the day of rest.</note>, it is said that Rabbi Simeon said: "For the sake of a living child of one day, they break the Sabbath; but for the sake of King David when dead, they do not break the Sabbath." <note>This refers to the principle that saving a life (Pikuach Nefesh) overrides Sabbath restrictions, whereas honoring the dead does not.</note> In the *Midrash* <note>term: "Midras"; a Jewish method of biblical exegesis or a collection of such interpretations.</note>, that is, in the final exposition of the book of Numbers, regarding that phrase in the 13th chapter of the same book, "Send men for yourself," it is said: "A messenger of a precept <note>original: "nuncius praecepti," referring to a "Shaliach Mitzvah," or one on a mission to perform a religious commandment.</note> is permitted to depart on whatever day he wishes. For what reason? Every messenger is a messenger of a precept, and a messenger of a precept excludes the Sabbath." From all these things it is now clearly evident that among the Jews, the Sabbath was frequently broken.

To clarify these things, it should be noted that if one reasonably considers the things that were being sacrificed, some would be found to signify the mortification of vices, while others signify virtues, good character, or the Passion of Christ. For the firstborn of the sheep and the lambs, which Abel began to offer to the Lord, as well as the Paschal lamb, prefigured the Passion of the Messiah and His sacrifice for the sins of men. However, the he-goats and she-goats designated nothing other than certain vices and sins, and the mortification of the flesh through penance. In the he-goat and she-goat, the foul-smelling and lustful petulance of every sinner, full of immodest words, was signified. Similarly, pride was signified in the bull, lasciviousness in the calf, and noisy shouting and inconstancy in the young goat and the sparrow. Indeed, when these vices are slaughtered and destroyed in confession through penance, they are sacrifices acceptable and most pleasing to God Himself, which were prefigured in those ancient sacrifices (as we have said). 

On the other hand, the sacrifices that pre-signified virtues and good character were the sheep, the lamb, the ox, the ram, the turtle-dove, the young pigeon, and others of that kind. For in the sheep, simplicity and gentleness were signified; in the lamb, innocence; in the ox, fruitful preaching; and in the ram, useful and mild leadership <note>original: "prelatio"</note>. In the turtle-dove—which, having lost its mate, never joins with another—chastity was signified. In the pigeons, which lack gall and fly in flocks, charity was prefigured. ### BOOK V

[My name is great among the nations, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts.] <note>original: "נש לשמי ומנחה טהורה כי גדול שמי בגוים אמר יהוה צבאות"; Malachi 1:11. The author provides a Latin translation immediately following.</note>
That is: "I have no pleasure in you," says the Lord of hosts, "and an offering will not be pleasing from your hand. How all of this is to be understood, Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auen Hazra"; a major 12th-century Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> elegantly suggests in his exposition, saying: "Why do you despise my name?
