But Rabbi Solomon <note>original: "R. Selomo"; referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator.</note>, explaining this, says: "Our Masters explained this saying: A man says to his companion, 'Close that door for me,' and he does not ask for a reward for this. 'Light a lamp for me,' and he does not seek a prize for this. But who is there among you who would close my doors for free? Nor do you light my altar for free. Therefore it is said that you would do much less for free those things which are customary to be done for a reward. Because of this, I have no pleasure in you. For my name is great among the nations, and in every place there is one who offers incense." Along with the rest: "For even the Gentiles will be spontaneous [in their devotion] to my name." These are the words of Rabbi Solomon. 

But Rabbi Jonathan <note>term: "R. Ionathan"; referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> turned these words into the Chaldean <note>term: "Chaldean"; a common Renaissance term for Aramaic.</note> language thus: [I have no pleasure in you, said the Lord of Hosts, and a voluntary sacrifice I will not receive from your hands.] <note>original: "מן קדמי בבני אמר יהוה צבאות וקורבן לריעא לא אקבל מיידכון"</note> That is: "There is no will before me in you," said the Lord of hosts, "and I will not receive a voluntary sacrifice from your hands." From all of these things it clearly appears that the Jewish sacrifices formerly commanded through Moses were for a fixed time and were to be observed spiritually.

And thus He says in Leviticus, chapter 18: "And you shall not approach a woman in her menstrual uncleanness." And there are those who say that even the service of the bed <note>A euphemism for marital relations.</note> will sometimes be prohibited in the future. Know this, however: that on the day the holy and blessed God was revealed upon Mount Sinai, He prohibited the service of the bed for three days. As it is said in Exodus 19:

<margin>"Be ready for the third day; do not come near a woman." <note>original: "היו נכונים לשלשת ימים אל תגשו אל אשה"; Exodus 19:15.</note></margin>
This means: "Be ready for the third day, do not approach a woman." Why this? Because on the third day the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai. If, therefore, for the one day the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, He prohibited it for three days, then in the age to come—that is, in the days of the Messiah—when the

<margin>Shekhinah</margin> <note>Hebrew: "sechina."</note>
...*Shekhinah* <gloss>the Divine Presence</gloss> will be among them, it will not be at all the same way. But what will it be? Furthermore, that which is said in the same Psalm, "God will release..."

<margin>the bound</margin> <note>Hebrew: "asurim."</note>
...*asurim* <gloss>the bound</gloss>, that is, the captives according to another sense, namely the captives of hell and the captives of death. Thus far the tradition—which should be held as no less than prophecy, since it speaks so clearly. To what has been said, Deuteronomy 12 also fits perfectly, where it is written: "The unclean and the clean alike shall eat it, as of the gazelle and the deer... Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life; you shall not eat the life with the meat." <note>original: "הטמא והטהור יאכלנו בצבי ובאיל הטמא והטהור יחרו יאכלנו רק חזק לבלתי אכל הדם כי הדם הוא הנפש ולא תאכל הנפש עם הבשר"; Deuteronomy 12:22-23.</note> That is: "The unclean and the clean shall eat alike. Only take care that the blood is not eaten. For the blood itself is the soul, and the soul shall not be eaten with the flesh." Rabbi Judas <note>Likely Rabbi Judah bar Ilai, a 2nd-century teacher.</note> said regarding this place: "He announces that the children of Israel were mixing flesh with blood before the giving of the Law." It follows: "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh." That is, to eat a limb from a living animal <note>A reference to the Noahide law prohibiting cruelty to animals.</note>. Thus far the source. Although our Jews of the present time say that in these places "unclean" refers to a blind, weak, or lame animal, and such things that were unclean for sacrifice, nevertheless, according to the aforementioned tradition of the ancients, it should be understood as referring to every unclean thing, which in the days of the Messiah would become clean to eat.

## *Chapter 1. That the second coming of the Messiah will be around the end of the world.*

->CAPNIO,<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' featuring a scholar or biblical figure seated at a desk, surrounded by decorative vines and foliage within a square border.</image-desc>
Since so many and such great secrets regarding the first coming of the Messiah, which have hitherto lain hidden, have been recounted by you in the preceding books from the Talmud <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> and other books of the Hebrews, it is now certainly fitting—indeed, necessary—that, in order to further crush the stiff-necked unbelief of the Jews of our age, those things which lie hidden in the Talmud itself and their other volumes concerning his second coming should also be brought to light. First, therefore, it must be proven through their own scriptures that the second coming of the Messiah will occur around the end of the world, not for the purpose of redeeming them (as the Jews themselves falsely believe), but for the purpose of judging. 

GALATINUS: The wretched Jews do indeed wait; they wait for the coming of the Messiah, not for the purpose of judging, but (as you say) coming to redeem them. But they are certainly very much deceived. For all the prophecies by which they expect him to come do not announce his first coming, but his second, such as that prophecy of Daniel which predicted that he would come in the clouds of heaven (as was shown elsewhere) in the 7th chapter. Also that prophecy in the 3rd chapter of Joel, in which, according to the opinion of all commentators, the coming of the Messiah is described, speaks of his second coming. This he calls <note>original: יום יהוה הגדול והנורא (*yom Adonai ha-gadol ve-ha-nora*)</note> the great and terrible day of the Lord. This is a phrase that the prophets usually reserve for the Day of Judgment. And as for what he adds shortly thereafter, saying, 

<margin>This is: "And I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there." This also is understood only as referring to the Day of Judgment.</margin>

<margin>That is: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes." It cannot be understood as anything other than the second coming of the Messiah. BOOK [XII]

in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis <note>The *Bereshit Rabbati*, a midrashic commentary</note> upon that which is said in the 5th chapter of the same book: **This is the book of the generations of Adam.** It is said there: This is what is written in Isaiah, chapter 57: <note>original: "לא לעולם אריב ולא לנצח אקצוף כי רוח מלפני יעטוף ונשמות אני עשיתי"</note> **For I will not contend forever, nor will I be angry for all eternity: for the spirit shall be clothed (or covered) from my face, and the souls I have made.** That is: "Since I will not struggle in eternity" (supply: "with the first Adam") "nor will I be angry forever" (certainly: "with his generations") "Because the spirit from my face shall clothe, or shall put on, or shall cause distress. Therefore, since this gathering is to occur at the time of the resurrection, and the resurrection is at the time of judgment, it clearly follows that the coming of the Messiah which the Jews expect—according to the opinion of certain ancient Talmudists—will occur at the time of judgment. Or at least (as certain other Talmudists say) very near to the judgment. For as it is held in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helec*, Rabbi Elazar says that <note>original: "ימות המשיח ארבעים שנה"</note> **the Days of the Messiah are forty years.** But another Rabbi Elazar, namely the son of Azaria, says that they will be <note>original: "שבעים שנה"</note> **seventy years.** Although others in the same place assign various spaces of time, they all nevertheless agree in the same opinion. Finally, if all the opinions of the ancient Talmudists are considered, both those recited in the same chapter *Helec* and those in other places, they designate the time of the Messiah as either having already passed (as we have most extensively proved in the 4th book concerning his first coming) or as occurring at the end of the world (as has just been predicted concerning his second coming). From these things, therefore, it is clear, according to the opinions of the ancient Jews, that the second coming of the Messiah will be at the end of the world.

### THE TWELFTH BOOK

it must be proven through the sayings of the ancient Talmudists that both the general resurrection of the dead (which the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect during the Second Temple period that denied the resurrection and the existence of spirits</note> deny) will occur, and that the dead themselves are to be raised by the Messiah—something the younger Jews <note>Galatinus often contrasts "ancient" Jewish authorities, whom he sees as closer to Christian truth, with "modern" or "younger" ones who oppose it</note> dare to call false.

<margin>GALATINUS</margin> My dear Capnio <note>The Greek-derived name for the scholar Johannes Reuchlin, the interlocutor in this dialogue</note>, you urge me here to show through the ancient writings of the Jews these two things: namely, that there will be a general resurrection of the dead, and that it will be accomplished through the Messiah. The first point is clear not only through the testimonies of Holy Scripture, but also through the sayings of the Talmudists. For that saying of Psalm 17: <note>original: "אני בצדק אחזה פניך אשבעה בהקיץ תמונתך"</note> **"As for me, I will behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when your likeness (or form, or image) awakes (or rises)."** This they explain—especially Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra and Rabbi Solomon <note>Also known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note>. Indeed, Rabbi Abraham says: "This vision is not of the eye, but of the intellect. And no one sees these words except he who has learned the wisdom of the soul." But Rabbi Solomon in his gloss <note>interlinear or marginal commentary</note> says: "**I will behold your face**, just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 52: 'Because they shall see eye to eye.' **I shall be satisfied when your likeness (or form, or image) awakes**, that is, when the dead shall awake from their sleep." 

Also in the book *Midrash Tehillim* <note>The Midrashic commentary on the Psalms</note>, upon that verse of Psalm 78: <note>original: "ויזכר כי בשר המה רוח הולך ולא ישוב"</note> **"And he remembered that they were but flesh; a spirit (or wind) that goes and does not return."** Thus it is read: <note>original: "סברי דאמרי דלית מתין חיין דבהי רוח הולך ולא ישוב אלא זה יצר הרע שהולך עמו בשעת מיתה ואינו שב עמו בשעת שיעלי המתי"</note> That is: "Some have dared to say that the dead will not live, because it is said: 'A spirit that goes and does not return.' But this refers to the *yetzer hara* <term>evil inclination: the innate human impulse toward wrongdoing</term>, which goes with a man at the hour of death, but does not return with him at the hour when the dead shall rise." 

Furthermore, in the book *Elle Ha'devarim Rabba* <note>Deuteronomy Rabbah, a homiletic commentary on the Book of Deuteronomy</note>, it says: <note>original: "רבי סימאי אומר כל בריה שנבראו מן השמים נפשם וגופן מן השמים... וכן היה רבי סימאי אומר אין לך פרשה שאין בה תחיית המתים..."</note> That is: "Rabbi Simai said: Of all the creatures that were created from heaven, both their soul and their body belong to heaven. But of the creatures that were created from the earth, both their soul and their body belong to the earth. Therefore, if a man performs the Torah and does the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is made, without doubt, to be of the number of the heavenly creatures. As it is written: 'I said, You are gods.' But if he does not perform the Torah nor the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is made to be of the number of the inferior creatures. As it is written: 'Surely you shall die like Adam.' And so Rabbi Simai was accustomed to say: there is no portion [of the Torah] which does not contain the resurrection of the dead, except that we do not have the power to interpret it. As it is said: 'He shall call to the heavens from above... that he may judge his people.' 'He shall call to the heavens from above'—this is the soul; 'and to the earth'—this is the body, to judge with him. And from where is it shown that this speaks of nothing other than the resurrection of the dead? As it is said: 'From the four winds come, O spirit...' For there I will call upon the name of the Lord. And we find that the name of the Place <note>A common Jewish metonym for God</note> was not mentioned except after twenty-one things. From whom to whom? From the ministering angels, who do not mention the Name except after three 'Holies,' as it is said: 'And one called to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts.'"

BOOK

in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis <note>This likely refers to the Midrash Tanchuma, an ancient collection of homilies on the Torah</note> concerning that saying in the 5th chapter of the same book: **This is the book of the generations of Adam.** It is stated there: This is what is written in Isaiah, chapter 57: <note>original: "לא לעולם אריב ולא לנצח אקצוף כי רוח מלפני יעטוף ונשמות אני עשיתי"</note> **"For I will not contend forever"** (add: with the first Adam) **"nor will I be angry for eternity"** (namely, with his generations). **"For the spirit shall proceed from my face"** (or cover, or wrap, or grow faint), **"and the souls I have made."** Rabbi Tanhum said in the name of the Teachers: The King Messiah will never come until all the souls have been created that ascended into thought to be created—that is, those which God foresaw were to be created. What is the proof of this matter? That verse from Isaiah 57: **"And the souls I have made"**—that is, for the sake of the souls I have made, the Messiah will come. All this is tradition. The same point is clear in the *Midrash Coheleth* <note>The Midrash on the book of Ecclesiastes</note>; that is, in the exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes it is read in this way: <note>original: "תנו רבנן אין מלך המשיח בא עד שיבראו כל הנשמות שעלו במחשבה להבראות"</note> That is, the Teachers said in the name of the Rabbi: The King Messiah shall not come until all the souls that were forethought to be created are created. This, indeed, cannot happen except at the end of the world. Also in the chapters of the great Rabbi Elazar <note>The *Pirké De-Rabbi Eliezer*, an 8th-9th century midrashic work</note>, chapter 34, it is said: <note>original: "חי אני נאם יהוה אם לא מעמיד אתכם לעתיד לבא בתחיית המתים ומקבץ אתכם עם כל ישראל אל ארץ ישראל"</note> This means: **"As I live, says God, I who shall make you rise in the future time of the resurrection of the dead. And I will gather you with all Israel to the land of Israel."** Now, the Jews do not expect the gathering of Israel except at the coming of the Messiah. Since, therefore, this gathering is to be at the time of the resurrection, and the resurrection at the time of judgment, it clearly follows that the coming of the Messiah which the Jews expect—according to the opinion of certain ancient Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>—is to be at the time of judgment. Or at least (as certain other Talmudists say) very near to the judgment. For as it is held in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helek* <note>Chapter 10 (or 11) of the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin, which discusses the afterlife and the world to come</note>, Rabbi Elazar says that <note>original: "ימות המשיח ארבעים שנה"</note> **"The days of the Messiah are 40 years."** But another Rabbi Elazar, namely the son of Azariah, says that they will be <note>original: "שבעים שנה"</note> **"70 years."** Although others in the same place assign different spaces of time, they all nevertheless agree on the same general opinion. Finally, if all the opinions of the ancient Talmudists are considered—both those recited in the same chapter *Helek* and those in other places—they designate the time of the Messiah as either having already passed (as we have most extensively proved in the 4th book concerning his first coming) or as being in the future at the end of the world (as has now been proved concerning his second coming). From these things, therefore, it is clear according to the opinions of the ancient Jews that the second coming of the Messiah will be at the end of the world.

### TWELFTH BOOK

...it must be proved through the sayings of the ancient Talmudists that both the general resurrection of the dead (which the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect from the Second Temple period known for denying the resurrection</note> deny) will occur, and that the dead themselves are to be raised by the Messiah—something the younger Jews <note>Referring to Galatinus's Jewish contemporaries</note> dare to claim is false. 

**GALATINUS:** My dear Capnio, you urge me to show here, through the ancient Jewish scriptures, two things: that a general resurrection of the dead will happen, and that it will be accomplished through the Messiah. First, then, it is evident not only by the testimonies of Holy Scripture but also through the sayings of the Talmudists. For that saying in Psalm 17: <note>original: "אני בצדק אחזה פניך אשבעה בהקיץ תמונתך"</note> **"I shall behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your form"** (or figure, or image, or likeness) **"awakens"** (or rises). They explain it this way, especially Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated 12th-century Spanish rabbi, philosopher, and poet</note> and Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the most influential medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note>. Rabbi Abraham says: "This vision is not of the eye, but of the intellect. And no one sees these words unless he has learned the wisdom of the soul." But Rabbi Solomon, in his gloss, says: "**I shall behold your face.** As it is said in Isaiah 52: 'Because they shall see eye to eye.' **I shall be satisfied when your form awakens**—that is, when the dead awaken from their sleep." 

Furthermore, in the book *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient homiletic commentary on the Psalms</note>, concerning that verse in Psalm 78: <note>original: "מה רב טובך אשר צפנת ליראיך"</note> **"How great is your goodness which you have hidden for those who fear you,"** and: **"And he remembered that they were but flesh, a spirit that passes and does not return,"** it is read as follows: <note>original: "סברי דאמרי דלית מתין חיין דבהי רוחי דהו אזל ולא ישוב אלא זה יצר הרע שהולך עמי בשעה מיתה ואינו שב עמו בשעה שיעלו המתי"</note> That is: "Some have dared to say that the dead do not live because it is said, 'A spirit that passes and does not return.' But this 'spirit' is the <term>Yetzer hara</term> <note>The "evil inclination" or "impulse" toward sin in Jewish thought</note>, the evil spark that goes with a man at the hour of death, but does not return with him at the hour when the dead shall rise."

In the book *Deuteronomy Rabbah* (that is, in the commentaries on the book of Deuteronomy), it says: <note>original: "רבי סימאי אומר כל בריה שנבראו מן השמים..."</note> "Rabbi Simai said: Of all creatures created from heaven, their soul and body belong to heaven. But of all creatures created from the earth, their soul and body belong to the earth. Therefore, if a man performs the Law and does the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is undoubtedly like the creatures above, as it is written: 'I said, you are gods.' But if he does not perform the Law nor the will of his Father in heaven, he is like the creatures below, as it is written: 'Indeed, you shall die like Adam.' 

And so Rabbi Simai used to say: There is no portion of the Law that does not contain the resurrection of the dead, but we simply lack the power to interpret it. For it is said: 'He shall call to the heavens from above... and to the earth, to judge his people.' 'He shall call to the heavens from above' refers to the soul; 'and to the earth' refers to the body. Who then is the judge with Him? And how do we know this speaks only of the resurrection of the dead? Because it is said: 'Come from the four winds, O breath' [Ezekiel 37]. We also find that the Name of the Place <note>A common rabbinic substitute for the name of God</note> was not mentioned by Moses until after twenty-four words. From whom did he learn this? From the ministering angels, who do not mention the Name until after three 'Holies,' as it is said: 'And one called to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts.'"

...in the minor exposition of the book of Genesis <note>referring to *Bereshit Rabbah*, a midrashic collection</note> on that statement in chapter 5: "This is the book of the generations of Adam." This same point is read in the *Midrash Kohelet* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the book of Ecclesiastes</note> in this manner: **"The son of David will not come until all the souls that rose in thought to be created are created."** <note>original Hebrew: אין בן דוד בא עד שיבראו כל הנפשות שעלו במחשבה להבראות</note> This means: The Teachers said in the name of the Rabbi: "The King Messiah will not come until all the souls which were pre-planned to be created are brought into existence." And I will gather you with the whole of Israel into the land of Israel." Now, the Jews do not expect the gathering of Israel except at the coming of the Messiah. Since, therefore, this gathering will happen at the time of the resurrection, and the resurrection occurs at the time of judgment, it clearly follows that the coming of the Messiah which the Jews expect must, according to the opinion of certain ancient Talmudists <note>scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>, happen at the time of judgment. Or at the very least (as some other Talmudists say), very near to the judgment. For as it is held in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the chapter *Helek* <note>The tenth chapter of the tractate Sanhedrin, which discusses who has a share in the world to come</note>, Rabbi Elazar said: **"The days of the Messiah are forty years."** <note>original Hebrew: ימות המשיח ארבעים שנה</note> But another Rabbi Elazar, the son of Azariah, says: **"They will be seventy years."** <note>original Hebrew: שבעים שנה</note> Although others in the same place assign various spans of time, they all agree on the same general conclusion. Finally, if all the opinions of the ancient Talmudists are considered—both those recounted in that chapter *Helek* and those in other places—they indicate that the time of the Messiah has either already passed (as we have proved extensively in the fourth book regarding his first coming) or will occur at the end of the world (as is now promised regarding his second coming). From these things, therefore, it is clear that according to the opinions of the ancient Jews, the second coming of the Messiah will be at the end of the world.

# BOOK TWELVE

...through the sayings of the ancient Talmudists <note>Scholars and authors of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> it must be proven both that the general resurrection of the dead (which the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect during the Second Temple period that denied the resurrection</note> deny) will occur, and that the dead themselves are to be raised by the Messiah—something which the younger Jews <note>Galatinus refers here to his contemporaries who he believes have moved away from ancient traditions</note> dare to claim is false.

**GALATINUS.** You urge me here, my dear Capnio, to show through the ancient scriptures of the Jews both that a general resurrection of the dead will occur, and that it will be accomplished through the Messiah. The first point is evident not only through the testimonies of Holy Scripture, but also through the sayings of the Talmudists. For indeed, that statement in Psalm 17: **"As for me, I will behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your form awakes"** <note>original Hebrew: אני בצדק אחזה פניך אשבעה בהקיץ תמונתך - Psalm 17:15. The word "awakes" is interpreted here as "resurrects."</note>—this is to say: "I, in justice, shall see or contemplate your face; I shall be satisfied when your form, figure, image, or likeness awakes or is resurrected."

They explain it in this way, especially Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A celebrated Spanish rabbi and scholar (1089–1167)</note> and Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent commentator on the Bible and Talmud</note>. Rabbi Abraham says: "This vision is not of the eye, but of the intellect. And no one sees these words unless he has learned the wisdom of the soul." However, Rabbi Solomon, in his gloss <note>An explanatory note or commentary</note>, says: "**I will see your face**, just as it is said in Isaiah chapter 52: 'For they shall see eye to eye.' **I shall be satisfied when your form, or figure, or image, or likeness awakes**, that is, when the dead awake from their sleep."

Furthermore, in the book *Midrash Tehillim* <note>A rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note>, concerning that verse in Psalm 78: **"For the spirit goes and does not return,"** <note>original Hebrew: כי רוח הולך ולא ישוב - Psalm 78:39</note> which means, "And He remembered that they were but flesh, a spirit that passes away and does not return," we read the following: **"Some have dared to say that the dead will not live again because it is said, 'The spirit passes and does not return.' But this refers to the *yetzer hara* <note>The "evil inclination" or the impulse toward sin</note>, which goes with a man at the hour of death and does not return with him at the hour when the dead shall rise."** <note>original Hebrew: סברי דאמרי דלית מתין חיין... אלא זה יצר הרע</note> That is to say: some dared to say the dead do not live because of that verse, but it is actually the "evil inclination" or the "kindling of sin" that leaves at death and does not return at the resurrection.

Moreover, in the book *Elle Hadevarim Rabbah* <note>Deuteronomy Rabbah, a collection of homiletic interpretations of the Book of Deuteronomy</note>, it says: **"Rabbi Simai says: Of all creatures that were created from heaven, their soul and their body are from heaven; and all that were created from the earth, their soul and their body are from the earth. Therefore, if a man performs the Torah and does the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is like the creatures of above, as it is said: 'I said, You are gods.' But if he does not perform the Torah nor the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is like the creatures of below, as it is said: 'But you shall die like Adam.' And so Rabbi Simai lived <note>or taught</note> saying: There is no section of the Torah that does not contain the resurrection of the dead, but we do not have the strength to interpret it all. As it is said: 'He shall call to the heavens from above,' and it continues: 'He shall call to the heavens from above'—this refers to the soul; 'and to the earth to judge his people'—this refers to the body. Who judges with Him? And from where is it known that this speaks only of the resurrection of the dead? As it is said: 'Come from the four winds, O breath' <note>Ezekiel 37:9</note>. And we find that Moses did not mention the name of God until after twenty-one words. From whom did he learn this? From the ministering angels, who do not mention the Name until after three 'Holy's,' as it is said: 'And one called to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Hosts.'"** <note>The Hebrew text provided is a long excerpt from Deuteronomy Rabbah 4:7</note>

This means: Rabbi Simai said that for all creatures created from heaven, the soul and body belong to heaven. For creatures created from the earth, the soul and body belong to the earth. If, therefore, a man observes the law and the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is undoubtedly made of the number of the celestial creatures, just as it is written: "I said, You are gods." But if he does not observe the law and the will of his Father who is in heaven, he is made of the number of the lower creatures, just as it is written: "Truly like Adam [you shall die]..."

# BOOK [TWELVE]

...you shall die. <note>original: "moriemini"</note> For this reason, it was said by Rabbi Simai <note>A famous teacher (Tanna) of the late 2nd century</note> that there is no chapter of the scripture in which mention of the resurrection of the dead is not made, even if our intellect is unable to penetrate it. And this is what is written: **"He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people."** <note>Psalm 50:4</note> **"He shall call to the heavens from above"**—this refers to the soul. **"And to the earth"**—this refers to the body. **"That he may judge him."** <note>Galatinus interprets the "judgment" as the reunion of body and soul during the resurrection.</note> And from where do we hold that there is no word in scripture that does not speak of the resurrection of the dead? Where it is said: **"From the four winds shall the spirit come,"** because the name of God is invoked. 

It is also found in the commentaries of the judges <note>Likely referring to the *Sifre*, an ancient legal commentary on Numbers and Deuteronomy</note> that Moses did not mention the name of the Lord except after twenty-one words. But from whom does he say this? From the ministering angels. For the ministering angels themselves do not mention the name of God except after a threefold sanctification. Just as it is said: **"One called to the other and said: Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts."** <note>Isaiah 6:3</note> From all these sayings of the ancient judges, it is clearly evident that a general resurrection of the dead is to come.

->*Chapter III. That the general resurrection of the dead in the end of the world will be accomplished through the Messiah.*<-

->CAPNIO.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' within a square border featuring floral patterns.</image-desc>

As for the other point, then—namely, that this general resurrection must be performed through the Messiah—you ought now to prove that. 

GALATINUS. That can be proven in many ways. First, indeed, through a gloss on the book of Genesis regarding that passage in the second chapter of the same book: **"And the Lord God made every tree to grow out of the ground."** For thus it is said there word-for-word: **"How great"** <note>original Hebrew: מה רב - "Ma rav"</note> which is written in Psalm 31: **"How great is your goodness, which you have laid up for those who fear you."** <note>original Hebrew: מה רב טובך אשר צפנת ליראך - Psalm 31:19</note> That is to say: "How great is the good that you have hidden away for those who fear you." And further down in the same Hebrew gloss, it says: "All the fathers, and the righteous, the tribes, and Moses, and Aaron, and David, and Solomon, and all the Kings of the house of David, and all the prophets shall say to the Messiah: 'The end is near; it belongs to you to bring us back to life.'" 

Just as it was said in the 6th chapter of Hosea: **"He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight."** <note>original Hebrew: יחיינו מיומים ביום השלישי יקימנו ונחיה לפניו - Hosea 6:2</note> Korah also and his assembly, and Abiram <note>Biblical figures who were swallowed by the earth after rebelling against Moses</note>, shall come to him and say: "How long until the end of these wonders? And when will you come and revive us?" Thus it is said in Psalm 85: **"Will you be angry with us forever, or will you extend your wrath from generation to generation? Will you not turn again and revive us, that your people may rejoice in you?"** <note>original Hebrew: הלעולם תאנף בנו תמשך אפך לדור ודור : הלא אתה תשub תחיינו ועמך ישמחו בך - Psalm 85:5-6</note> This is the tradition. From which it becomes manifest that the reviving and resurrection of the dead belongs to the Messiah, and that he himself will come at the end of the world to judge all men. 

In the *Midrash Tehillim* <note>An ancient rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note> as well, that is, in the exposition of the Psalms, regarding that verse in Psalm 93: **"Your throne is prepared from of old."** <note>original Hebrew: נכון כסאו מאז - Psalm 93:2</note>

### BOOK TWELVE

<header>TWELVE</header>
<sig>ee 4</sig>

Thus it says: the Messiah ascended into the mountain of the Holy and Blessed God before the creation of the world. Just as it is said in Psalm 72: **"Before the sun, his name was Yinnon."** <note>original Hebrew: *liphnê-šemeš yinnôn šəmô*. This is a traditional Jewish interpretation identifying "Yinnon" as one of the names of the Messiah, existing before creation.</note> That is: Before the sun, Yinnon—meaning "begotten," or "he shall produce offspring," or "he shall cause to be born"—was his name. Because it is to be, that he himself *yannin*—that is, he shall produce offspring, or cause all those sleeping in the dust to be born. Rabbi Rahmon said: "Those sleeping in the dust" are the dead. This is according to what is said in Daniel, chapter 12: **"And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, and others to reproach and eternal rot."** <note>original: *vermiculationem*, referring to the state of being eaten by worms or decay.</note> Also, regarding what is said in Psalm 3: **"I laid down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord sustained me."** That is: "I lay down" (in place of "I shall lie down") "and I will sleep," and "I have risen" or "I have awakened" (in place of "I shall rise" or "I shall awake"), because God will receive me—specifically through the hands of the Messiah, as the *Midrash* <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary</note> says on that passage. The Kabbalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism</note> also frequently confess this. For, to remain silent about their other sayings on this matter, I will report only those which are found in the Kabbalistic fragments in this manner:

> **It is known to me by the hand of Metatron** <note>A high-ranking angel in Jewish mystical tradition, often described as the celestial scribe or mediator.</note> **that the resurrection of the dead is established. And so it was said long ago: "And he shall judge the poor with righteousness, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked." This was revealed by the Prophet concerning the Lord, for he shall not wage war with his own hands, but by the power of the Name; and all whom he blesses shall be blessed, and all whom he curses shall be cursed. For there is no restraint for the Lord to save by many or by few, so that he shall not need to gather for war at his beginning, nor shall the Lord save by sword and spear; not in the strength of the horse does he delight, nor in the legs of a man is he pleased. The Lord’s pleasure is in those who fear him, in those who hope for his mercy. Blessed are all who wait for him. And it is found in that which says, "the rod of his mouth," that the mouth is a sign of divine power. In that which says "his mouth and the breath of his lips," it contains the half of the name of God. And it encompasses wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. And as the sages say, these three shall be given to the King Messiah. May he come quickly in our days.**

That is: It is established that the restoration of life to the dead has been placed in the hand of Metatron. Just as it is written in Isaiah, chapter 11: **"And he shall judge the poor in justice, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth, and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked."** The prophet shows in this place that he is not going to wage war with his own physical hands, but by divine power. And that all things which he blesses shall be blessed, and all things which he curses shall be cursed. Because God will not change, whether by increasing or decreasing, the salvation which he himself will work. From this we are also taught that it will not be necessary for him to stir up war. Because God provides salvation not by sword or spear. As it is said in Psalm 147: **"His will is not in the strength of the horse, nor is his pleasure in the legs of a man."** The will of God is toward those who fear him, and those who hope in his mercy. Blessed are all who hope in him. And it was found in that phrase, "the rod of his mouth," that the mouth is a sign of divine power. But in that which says, "of his mouth, and the spirit of his lips," it contains the half of the name of God. And it comprehends wisdom, intelligence, and science. And as the sages say, these three things they shall give to the King Messiah. May he come quickly in our days. Thus it is said there. In which things, among other things worthy of note that they posit concerning the Messiah, he says that the resurrection of the dead has been placed in his power. From all these things, therefore, which have been said, it is openly shown that the general resurrection of the dead at the end of the world will be brought about through the Messiah. From which it is truly said...

## That after the general resurrection all people will speak with one language and idiom, and what that language shall be. Chapter III.

### CAPNIO <note>The speaker in this dialogue, representing the famous Christian Hebraist Johannes Reuchlin.</note>

Zephaniah the prophet, speaking of the coming of the Messiah for judgment—which will occur after the general resurrection—says that an "elected lip" <note>original: *labium electum*, a literal translation of the Hebrew for "pure speech" or "purified language"</note> is to be turned toward and restored to all people. For he says thus in the third chapter: **"Wait for me, says God, on the day of my future resurrection. For my judgment is to gather the nations, to assemble the kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation, all the anger of my nose <note>original: *ira nasi mei*, a Latin rendering of a Hebrew idiom where a "flaring nose" signifies intense fury</note>. For in the fire of my zeal the whole earth shall be devoured: for then I will turn to the peoples an elected lip. That all may call upon the name of the Lord, and serve him with one shoulder."** <note>Zephaniah 3:8-9</note> Thus says the prophet. Where the *Midrash* <note>A Jewish homiletic commentary</note> says in its gloss: **"With one shoulder,"** that is, with "one part." Just as it is said in Genesis 48: **"And I have given to you one shoulder,"** <note>Genesis 48:22; the Hebrew word *shechem* means both "shoulder" and the city of "Shechem," here interpreted as a "portion" or "part" of land.</note> meaning one part. Therefore, when the prophet speaks with the voice of God, "I will turn to the peoples an elected lip," what is understood by this "elected lip"? For is this not that tongue which the Lord chose for the purpose of invoking his name, and so that he might be worshiped by all nations with "one shoulder"—that is, with one mind?

<margin>The opinion of the Greeks.</margin>
In this matter, various people say various things. For some say that this "elected lip" is the Greek language, which the Lord chose so that his name might be invoked through it, and that he himself might be worshiped through it. For the New Testament (except for the Gospel of Matthew) was written entirely in the Greek language, and the entire primitive church was founded in the Greek language. Indeed, the very name of the "Christians" is the greatest proof of this matter. For this name, by which they are called Christians, is a Greek name. Not only this, but also the names of either the dignities or the offices which pertain to the Christian faith and concern the worship of God are almost all Greek, such as *Ecclesia* (Church), *Papa* (Pope), *Patriarcha* (Patriarch), *Archiepiscopus* (Archbishop), *Episcopus* (Bishop), *Presbyter* (Priest), *Diaconus* (Deacon), *Subdiaconus* (Subdeacon), *Acolytus* (Acolyte), *Clericus* (Cleric), *Laicus* (Layman), and others of that kind. For this reason, they say that the Greek language itself was chosen by God, so that peoples everywhere might invoke his name in it, and he might be worshiped by all. Whence also the Messiah, the Son of God, is called by all nations even to this day by the Greek name "Christ."

<margin>The opinion of the Latins.</margin>
Others, however, assert that this "elected lip" is the Latin language. Since the primary regions such as Italy, Germany, Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province comprising parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>, Gaul, and Spain...

This will be fulfilled among the elect after the general resurrection. For just as before the division of languages at the Tower of Babel the whole earth was of one lip, so in the general resurrection all men will speak one language, namely Hebrew, which the first parents spoke in Paradise, and which all the elect would have spoken in a state of innocence if those first parents had remained in the grace of God.

And further below: <note>original Aramaic: ארי באשת פורענותי יסופון כל רשיעי ארעא</note> "Because in the fire of my vengeance all the wicked of the earth shall be consumed." <header>BOOK [TWELVE]: That the general judgment will be performed by the Messiah, who is to judge in a glorious human form. Chapter V</header>

### CAPNIO,

The whole body of Christians acknowledges and believes without any doubt that Christ our Lord will be the judge of the living and the dead, and that he will come to judge in a glorious human form. Therefore, so that the unbelief of the younger Jews <note>The author distinguishes between "ancient" Jews who held "correct" views and "modern" Jews who do not</note> may be further overcome, you ought to prove through their own scriptures that he will perform the universal judgment at the end of the world, and that he will come in human form to judge. 

**GALATINUS:** That the universal judgment must be performed at the end of the world by the Messiah is most clearly evident from the ancient *Bereshit Rabbah* <note>Genesis Rabbah, a collection of ancient Jewish explanations of the book of Genesis</note>, that is, in the exposition of the book of Genesis. For there, commenting upon chapter 49 of that same book, on the phrase **"Until [Shiloh] comes,"** it is said: "This is the Messiah. And to him the nations shall gather themselves together; he himself shall be the judge of the entire world." This is also what is written in the fourth chapter of Micah:
> And he shall judge between many peoples, and shall arbitrate for strong nations <note>original Hebrew: וְשָׁפַט בֵּין עַמִּים רַבִּים וְהוֹכִיחַ לְגוֹיִם עֲצֻמִים</note>
It is also said in the eleventh chapter of Isaiah <note>The text incorrectly cites chapter 9</note>:
> But with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked. <note>original Hebrew: וְשָׁפַט בְּדַלִּים בְּמִישׁוֹר לְעַנְוֵי אָרֶץ וְהִכָּה אֶרֶץ בְּשֵׁבֶט פִּיו וּבְרוּחַ שְׂפָתָיו יָמִית רָשָׁע</note>
This is the tradition of all. 

Furthermore, that he is to judge in a glorious human form is found in the seventh chapter of Daniel, who says:
> I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And to him was given dominion, and glory, and a kingdom. And all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed. <note>original Aramaic: חָזֵה הֲוֵית בְּחֶזְוֵי לֵילְיָא וַאֲרוּ עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ אָתֵה הֲוָא וְעַד עַתִּיק יוֹמַיָּא מְטָה וּקְדָמוֹהִי הַקְרְבוּהִי. וְלֵהּ יְהִב שָׁלְטָן וִיקָר וּמַלְכוּ וְכֹל עַמְמַיָא אֻמַיָּא וְלִשָּׁנַיָּא לֵהּ יִפְלְחוּן שָׁלְטָנֵהּ שָׁלְטָן עָלַם דִּי לָא יֶעְדֵּה וּמַלְכוּתֵהּ דִּי לָא תִתְחַבַּל</note>
Regarding this passage, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A significant medieval Sephardic scholar</note> says on Daniel that Rabbi Joshua said: "This 'one like a son of man' is the Messiah," which he spoke excellently. Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator</note> also confirms this in his gloss upon the words "one like a son of man," stating that it is the King Messiah. 

Moreover, it is most evident that Daniel is speaking in the aforementioned words about the second coming of the Messiah, because in the first coming he was to arrive in humility and poverty, as was made clear in the preceding sections. But in the second, he is to come with majesty and glory, which the words of Daniel themselves clearly suggest. This is also openly shown by what precedes and follows in the same chapter. From the things predicted, it is liquidly clear...

Yet again they will say to them: "Do not fear the judgment. For he is your brother." Just as it is said in Psalm 122: "For the sake of my brothers and my companions, I will now speak peace within you" <note>original Hebrew: למען אחי ורעי אדברה נא שלום בך</note>. This means: For the sake of my brothers, or my associates, or my friends, I will now speak peace in you. "But above all, you ought not to fear, because he is your father." As it is said in Deuteronomy, chapter 32: "Is he not your father, who possessed you?" <note>original Hebrew: הלוא הוא אביך קנך</note>. This means: Is he not your father, your creator, or your purchaser? All of this is from tradition. From all these points, it is clearly evident that the Messiah, as both God and man, will perform the universal judgment at the end of the world, and that he will come in human form with glory and majesty to judge.

From the two traditions already mentioned, it is shown clearly enough what reward the righteous shall have after the universal judgment.

### *That the Messiah himself, after the universal judgment, will be the eternal recompense and reward of the righteous.* Chapter VII.

### CAPNIO,

That is: <note>original: עובדיהון גלו קדמוהי בריא דערויח רעי ברעותיה מינזש אמרין</note> "Their works are revealed before him, the Creator, who grazes his flock in his will, just as they say:

Because all their works are manifest before him. Like a shepherd who feeds his flock, he will gather the lambs in his arm." The gloss of <term>Rabbi Solomon<note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note></term> upon these words of the prophet says this: "Behold, his reward is prepared with him for the righteous. And his work—that is, the reward for the work he is to give them." The ancient <term>Talmudists<note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note></term> also most clearly handed down that the Messiah himself must be the future reward and prize of the righteous. For in the book called <term>Seder Olam<note>Hebrew for "Order of the World," a 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology detailing biblical history.</note></term> (that is, the Order of the World), it is read word for word: It is written in Daniel, chapter 2: <note>original: ונהורא עמיה שריא</note> "And light dwells with him." This means: "He knows what is in the darkness, and the light is with him." He knows (it says) what is in the darkness (this refers to the perpetual punishment of the impious in <term>Gehenna<note>A place of spiritual punishment or purification; often translated as Hell.</note></term>). And the light is with him (this refers to the granting of the reward of the righteous in the world to come). So it is said there. That this light, which is the future prize or reward of the righteous, is the Messiah himself, is clearly held in the <term>Bereshit Ketanna<note>Literally "Little Genesis," a reference here to a specific Midrashic or mystical commentary on the book of Genesis.</note></term> (that is, in the Lesser Exposition of the book of Genesis). When commenting on that saying of the same book, "In the beginning God created heaven and earth," and the rest, it is said: Rabbi Abba said, it is written in Daniel, chapter 2: "And the light is with him." This light is the King Messiah. This is the tradition. From these things it is clearly evident that the Messiah himself will be the eternal reward and prize of the righteous. This opinion of the Talmudists is confirmed also by that saying in Genesis, chapter 15: <note>original: אל תירא אברם אנכי מגן לך שכרך הרבה מאד</note> That is: "Fear not, Abram: I am your shield, and your reward shall be very great." For this reason, He himself said in the tenth chapter of John: "I am the door: if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out, and find pasture." The pastures of eternal happiness, he will find in me (as it were) inside and out. Inside through the clear vision of divinity, with perfect enjoyment of it; outside, through the intuition of his glorious humanity. And this is what he said: "He shall go in and out."

from the foundation of your disputation (with the help of divine aid) I have excerpted and collected into these twelve books, as if into bundles. From these, it might be easily perceived what should be thought of the <term>Talmud<note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, which was the subject of intense controversy and censorship in the early 16th century.</note></term>, about which there has been such long-standing debate among you. Indeed, in another work, which is divided into six distinct books according to the distinction of the articles of <term>Hogostratus<note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican inquisitor and a leading opponent of Johann Reuchlin in the "Battle of the Books."</note></term>, I hope to bring to light shortly (God willing), where a most ample space for disputing will be given to you. Thus, once the articles themselves have been skillfully discussed and the reasons of each of you diligently heard, the truth itself, which you seek with such great zeal, may appear more clearly determined. Now, however, I would wish to request this of you: if anything in this work should seem to you to have been said incorrectly by me, please reveal it to me in a friendly manner. For since only a year and a half was given to me to complete so great a work—for which (to confess the truth) barely a whole human lifetime would have sufficed—I fear greatly that on account of excessive haste, it may have happened that I said many things otherwise than was proper. Therefore, I am prepared, by the judgment of wise friends, to emend all things said poorly by me and, where it is necessary, to retract them.

**HOG.** All the things you have said in this work, Galatinus, seem well-said to me, except for one.

**GAL.** Tell me, I pray, what is that one thing?

**HOG.** That in many instances you have not preserved the common mode of writing and pronouncing. For you have brought forth some things written with <term>aspiration<note>In linguistics, "aspiration" refers to the breathy 'h' sound. Hogostratus is criticizing Galatinus for restoring the 'h' in names where Latin tradition had dropped it.</note></term> that usually reject it; others you have pronounced and written far differently than established usage dictates.

**GAL.** What are those things, I ask? Please explain.

**HOG.** Those things which you have reported written with aspiration, contrary to the customary manner of writing, are indeed many, but especially these: *Heua* <note>Eve</note>, *Habel* <note>Abel</note>, *Hanna* <note>Hannah</note>, *Iohannes* <note>John</note>, and *Halleluia*. For this reason, I have no doubt you will be criticized by many.

**GAL.** I beg and beseech those who you think will criticize me for this reason: that they would not wish to accuse me before they hear the reason why I did it. For that reason, I would wish both you and them to know that the author of our <term>edition<note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate translation of the Bible.</note></term>, imitating the Greek edition, translated almost infinite words in a corrupt and depraved manner, just as in many places he handed down a different sense, utterly abhorrent to the <term>Hebrew truth<note>The concept of "Hebraica Veritas," championed by humanists like Jerome and later Reuchlin, which argued that the Hebrew text of the Old Testament was the ultimate authority over later translations.</note></term>. Since these words are not Greek but Hebrew, we ought to follow the Hebrews in them, and not the Greeks. This is especially true in those cases where a variation in the letters results in a variation of meaning; such are the things I have taken care to correct in this work above all others. Therefore, whatever things are written by the letters *He* or *Heth* <note>The Hebrew letters ה (He) and ח (Het), both of which represent 'h' sounds of varying intensity.</note> among the Hebrews, I have written with aspiration...

<meta>This page continues Pietro Galatinus's technical defense of his work. Here, he moves from justifying his theological sources to a detailed explanation of his orthography—specifically why he chooses to spell Biblical names differently than the traditional Latin Vulgate, based on his understanding of original Hebrew phonetics.</meta>

<margin>First rule.</margin> ...ought to be written among us. For I do not agree with the opinion of those who, comparing the <term>Greek breathings<note>In Greek, these are marks (dasia and psili) placed over vowels to indicate the presence or absence of an 'h' sound.</note></term> (the *dasia* and *psili*) to the Hebrew letters <term>heth<note>The eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ח), representing a strong, throaty 'h' sound.</note></term> and <term>he<note>The fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ה), representing a softer 'h' sound.</note></term>, say that only those words which happen to be written with a *heth* among the Hebrews should be written with an aspiration <note>original: "aspiratione"; referring to the 'h' sound</note> among us. This is partly because in Hebrew words (as I have said), we must preserve Hebrew orthography—as much as our letters allow—rather than Greek. It is also because, even if the *heth* is a strong breathing and the *he* is a light one, both letters are nevertheless breathings among them. For that reason, wherever *heth* or *he* is placed among the Hebrews, an 'h' must be placed among us in the same spot, except at the end of words, since our 'h' can never be a final letter, except in certain <term>interjections<note>Short emotional exclamations, like "Ah!" or "Oh!"</note></term>.

Therefore, those who write *Heua* [Eve], *Habel* [Abel], *Hanna* [Hannah], *Ioannes* [John], and *Halleluia* [Hallelujah] without an 'h' err significantly, since these are customarily written among the Hebrews with either a *heth* or a *he*. For *Heua* is indeed written with a *heth* among them, thus חוה (*hauah*), since it is derived from the verb חיה (*haia*), which signifies "to live," with the letter *yod* changed into a *vau*. Hence *Heua* (as Holy Scripture testifies) is interpreted as "mother of the living." *Hanna* is also written with a *heth*, thus חנה (*Hannah*), since it comes from the noun חן (*hen*), which is the same as "grace." *Ioannes* also is written with a *heth* among them, thus יוחנן (*Iohanan*). For it is composed from the name of God, a "gift of God's grace" <note>original Greek: "θεοχαρισματι" (theochariſmati)</note>, which is יהוה [Yahweh], and from the noun חן (*hen*), which is "grace." Therefore, *Ioannes* is interpreted as "the grace of God."

*Habel*, however, is written with a *he* among them; for it descends from the verb הבל (*habal*), which is the same as "he vanished." *Hallelu ia* is similarly written with a *he* in this manner: הללו יה (*hallelu iah*), for they are two words. The first is הללו (*hallelu*), which is the imperative mood and second person plural of the verb הלל (*hillel*), which is the same as "he praised." The second is יה (*iah*), which is one of the divine names and signifies "God" or "the Lord." Hence *hallelu ia*, which is "Praise God" or "the Lord," is turned into our language. From the aforesaid, therefore, it is clearly evident that not only these, but all other words which are written with either a *heth* or a *he* among the Hebrews, ought to be written with an 'h' among us. For both in these and in all remaining Hebrew words, the Hebrew manner of both writing and pronouncing must always be preserved by us (as far as is possible with our letters).

<margin>Second rule.</margin> Otherwise, the word would not retain the same meaning among us as it has among them. This is why (to cite as examples only those many names which you yourself brought up) we ought to write and pronounce: not *Henoch* [Enoch] but *Henoch* <note>The author likely means to emphasize the specific 'h' sound or a different vowel weight here</note>, not *Mathusalam* but *Methuselas* with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Noe* but *Noas* [Noah], not *Phares* but *Peres*, not *Moyses* but *Moses*, not *Josue* but *Iehoſuas* [Joshua] with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Phinees* but *Pinhas*, not *Samuel* but *Semuel*, not *Salomon* but *Selomo* [Solomon], not *Salathiel* but *Salathiel*, not *Ioakim* but *Iehoiakim*, not *Osee* but *Hoseas* with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Bersabee* but *Bathseba* with the second-to-last syllable lengthened, not *Elisabeth* but *Eliseba* with the second-to-last syllable also lengthened, and not *Gomorra* but *Amorrra* <note>Galatinus is attempting to reflect the Hebrew *Ayin* at the start of Gomorrah, which Latin often rendered as a 'G' but he views as a different sound</note>, since the Hebrews write and [pronounce] them so...

<meta>This page continues Pietro Galatinus's defense of his transliteration methods. Having previously discussed the use of the 'h' sound (aspiration), he now focuses on the rules for modifying the endings of Hebrew names to fit Latin grammatical structures without losing their original meaning.</meta>

...they may pronounce them. However, it is permitted that these letters—<term>he<note>The fifth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ה).</note></term>, <term>heth<note>The eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ח).</note></term>, and <term>ayin<note>The sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ע), a guttural sound often transliterated as a vowel or a catch in the throat.</note></term>—when they are final letters in these <margin>Third rule.</margin> as well as in other masculine names, are very frequently changed by us into the letter 's' for the sake of a better <term>hiatus<note>A break or gap between two vowel sounds; here, changing the ending makes the word flow better into Latin sentences.</note></term>. Yet this change brings no change to the meaning. For to bring forward only two examples for each of these letters: among the Hebrews, משה *Mosheh* and ישעיה *Iesaiah* end in *he*; נח *Noah* and משיח *Massiah* end in *heth*; and יהושע *Iehosua* and מושיע *Mossia* end in *ayin*. Nevertheless, these and others of this kind are very often ended by us in the letter 's' without any variation of meaning. Examples include: *Moses*, *Isaias* or *Esaias* (for it can be said both ways), *Noas*, *Messias*, *Iohosuas*, and *Mossias*, which is interpreted as "savior." The very same thing happens most of the time in proper names of the masculine gender ending in <term>aleph<note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet (א).</note></term>. <margin>Fourth rule.</margin> For example: עזרא *Ezra* becomes *Ezras*; שלמא *Salma* becomes *Salmas* (although it is sometimes found written with a *he*), who was the son of Nahshon and was also called Salmon, just as we read him named in the genealogy of our Savior in Matthew. Furthermore, to those which end in <term>iod<note>The letter Yod (י).</note></term> preceded by a <term>patha<note>The Hebrew vowel 'patach', a short 'a' sound.</note></term> or <term>camez<note>The Hebrew vowel 'qamets', a long 'a' sound.</note></term>, we add the syllable '-us', <margin>Fifth rule.</margin> while the *iod* and the preceding *patha* or *camez* are changed into a long 'e' or the 'ae' diphthong. For example: חגי *Haggai* becomes *Haggeus*; מרדכי *Mordochai* becomes *Mordocheus*; זכאי *Zaccai* becomes *Zacchaeus*. Indeed, in most other cases, the '-us' is joined to the final letter among us in such a way <margin>Sixth rule.</margin> that one syllable is formed from them, while the acute accent—which among the Hebrews was on the last syllable—remains on the second-to-last syllable among us. For example: יעקב *Iaakob* becomes *Iacobus*; יוסף *Ioseph* becomes *Iosephus*. And this indeed is done when we wish to adapt them to the <term>declensions<note>The system of changing word endings in Latin to show their grammatical role (subject, object, etc.).</note></term> of our names.

Since these things are so, no one, <term>Hogostratus<note>Jacob van Hoogstraten (c. 1460–1527), a Dominican Inquisitor and opponent of Hebrew studies, whom Galatinus addresses here in dialogue.</note></term>, ought to criticize me (as you might think), nor ought anyone accuse or argue against me because I have not preserved the customary way of writing and pronouncing in the aforementioned cases and many others. For I did not do this out of ignorance or rash presumption, but so that I might correct those things and render them better. Nevertheless, I by no means deny that many things said in this work could have been said more elegantly and ornately, had it not been necessary to use a humbler style and better-known, more common words. This was done partly so that the mysteries of the Christian faith found in the Hebrew books might become better known to everyone, and partly so that there might be a more faithful interpretation of the Hebrew words; for since I wished to translate them word-for-word, I could hardly preserve the proper flow of the Latin speech in some places.

Certainly, you would not have been able to do this by any means unless you had been inspired by the Holy Spirit. Just as He once pronounced the mysteries of the Messiah through the prophets, that same Spirit now clearly explains those same mysteries through you. From this it is openly shown how useful, how profitable, and how conducive it is for the Christian commonwealth that a Christian theo-

# To the Most Holy Leo X, Supreme Pontiff, Johann Reuchlin 
## humbly commends himself.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial "I" set within a rectangular frame. The letter is entwined with intricate white-line scrolling foliage, vines, and floral motifs. A long-necked bird, likely a crane or heron, is depicted amongst the vines on the right side of the letter.</image-desc>

**Italian Philosophy**, <note>original: "Italica PHILOSOPHIA" — Reuchlin refers to the "Italian School" of philosophy, traditionally said to have been founded by Pythagoras in Southern Italy.</note> O most blessed Leo X, Supreme Pontiff of the Christian religion, was first brought forth by its parent Pythagoras, from whom it was passed down to the greatest men endowed with excellent talent. Yet, for many years, it had perished under the immense barking of the **Sophists**, <note>Reuchlin uses "Sophists" as a derogatory term for the Scholastic theologians of his own day, whom he viewed as obsessed with logic-chopping rather than ancient wisdom.</note> buried for so long in shadows and thick night, until a sun of all kinds of best studies arose: Lorenzo de' Medici, your father, the offspring of Cosimo the Great and prince of the Florentine state. Even if we knew him for his spirit and skill in governing the republic, and for conducting all matters at home and at war with counsel and prudence—to such an extent that no one in his age seemed more worthy of praise in civic exercise—nonetheless, we must confess this: he was born even more advantageously, as if sent down from heaven, so that after the disciplines of eloquence and the arts of fine speaking had been handed down to the Florentine youth by the rhetoricians Petrarch, Filelfo, and Bruni, <note>original: "Aretinisq;" referring to Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo.</note> (by which the citizens could, without controversy, be more adorned than all foreign nations by a more polished pen and purity of language), he himself might finally bring to his fatherland that **wisdom which expels vice** and the **method of investigating secrets**, <note>original: "arcanorū inuestigandi rationem" — This refers to the esoteric and mystical studies, like the Cabala, which Reuchlin champions.</note> which had lain hidden in the books and monuments of the ancients until his own time.

For this task, he diligently summoned from everywhere the most learned men and those most skilled in the ancient authors, who possessed both knowledge of things and sufficient eloquence: Demetrius Chalcondyles, Marsilio Ficino, Giorgio Vespucci, Cristoforo Landino, Valori, Angelo Poliziano, Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola, and the rest of the world's most erudite men. Through them, the ingenuity of the ancients and the secret antiquity that had been obliterated by the malice of chance might return to the light. These great men worked toward this goal with emulation. For while one taught, another wrote commentaries; while this one read, that one interpreted and **translated languages into other languages**. <note>The Renaissance project of translating Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic texts into Latin.</note> Marsilio led Greece into Latium; <note>original: "Marsilius Græciam duxit in Latium" — A poetic way of saying Marsilio Ficino translated the Greek works of Plato and Hermes Trismegistus into Latin.</note> Poliziano brought the Romans back to Greece. All pressed on with the work, everyone offering the highest praise to the Medici family. 

Upon these heroes, O most blessed Leo, your divine birthright (as they say) happily fell, by the grace of the Gods; certainly so that there should remain no kind of more elegant learning in which you did not turn out to be most skilled, so much 
indeed <note>original: "quidem" — This is the catchword, meant to match the first word of the following page.</note>

<summary>In this dedication, Reuchlin praises the Medici family, specifically Lorenzo the Magnificent, for reviving ancient philosophy and Greek studies in Florence. He situates his own work on the Cabala as the next step in this Renaissance project of rediscovering "lost" ancient wisdom.</summary>

### BOOK I.

...indeed as a youth, I embraced the sweetness of the most polished **Poliziano**. <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant humanist poet and scholar who served as the tutor to Lorenzo de' Medici’s children, including the future Pope Leo X.</note> Why say more? Nothing was more flourishing than **Florence** in those days. In that city, the finest arts—which had all previously withered away—were being reborn; nothing in languages and letters remained untouched or unpracticed by the most noble Florentines. At that time, I was powerfully moved by the fame of that place and touched by a longing to see it. This was not only because of the magnificent buildings of your ancestral home—so unusual to us **Hercynians** <note>original: "Hercynijs" — Reuchlin uses this term, referring to the ancient Hercynian Forest, to mean "German."</note>—which they named after **Cosimo the Great**, but also because of my desire to visit your father, from whom so many benefits had come forth in our century.

Therefore, having set out for Italy with the illustrious **Eberhard the Bearded**, <note>original: "Eberhardo Probo" — Eberhard V, Duke of Württemberg (1445–1496), Reuchlin's patron.</note> the first Duke of the **Swabians** in our age, to whom I served as Secretary, I entered Florence around the twelfth day before the Calends of April, in the year of salvation one thousand four hundred and eighty-seven. <note>March 21, 1487.</note> When I had commended the remarkable nobility of the **Medici** family to the Duke—as indeed I was bound to do by the truth of the matter—he desired to have a conversation with that great man. When **Lorenzo** noticed this (revealed by I know not whom), he took the traveler's right hand with great kindness and led us all to his home, showing us every single thing worthy of sight. 

First, the most skillfully built stables for the horses; then the armory, filled with every kind of military equipment; afterwards, the individual bedchambers adorned with the most precious wall-hangings and beautiful tapestries; and on the very high roof of the building, a grove planted with trees, gardens of the **Hesperides** <note>In Greek mythology, the Hesperides tended a garden with trees bearing golden apples.</note> and golden apples. When I began to extol his library to the heavens with my words, that sweetest of men replied with his usual great kindness: that he possessed a greater treasure in his children than in his books.

I beseech you, most holy Pope, allow me to speak with you somewhat more freely as a man from the common people. How much do you think I was seized by wonder, and by a certain remarkable joy, when I heard amidst universal applause that you—the excellent son of that excellent and most wise prince, the divine **Lorenzo de' Medici**—had ascended to the highest summit of affairs? I suddenly remembered, like some **hierophant**, <note>A priest or interpreter of sacred mysteries.</note> that paternal prophecy which equaled a true prediction. What could sprout from this **Laurel** <note>A wordplay on the name Lorenzo (Laurentius) and the laurel tree (Laurus), a symbol of victory and poetry.</note> more precious, not only to the people of Florence, but even to the whole world? What greater treasure could be imagined than that ineffable reign of yours, from which all riches flow to us as if from the abyss of the **Pactolus**, <note>A river in Lydia famous for its gold-bearing sands.</note> all graces, all the ornaments of the finest literature, and every good thing that exists among humans? 

Your father sowed the seeds of all ancient philosophy, which now, in you his son, rise into stalks; thus, under your reign, we are permitted to reap the ears of that grain in all languages: **Greek**, **Latin**, **Hebrew**, **Arabic**, and **Chaldean**, <note>Reuchlin uses "Chaldaica" to refer to Aramaic, the language of the Zohar and other mystical texts.</note> in which books are offered to your Majesty in this time. All things that were most prudently begun by your father reach a more fertile completion under your dominion. Therefore, reflecting that only the **Pythagorean** teachings were missing for scholars—which nevertheless lie hidden here and there in the **Laurentian Academy**—I believed it would not be unwelcome to you if I brought into the public square those things which **Pythagoras** and the noble **Pythagoreans** are said to have felt, so that they might be read under your happy divine favor...

He praises Pope Leo X's reign as the fulfillment of Lorenzo's legacy, particularly in the cultivation of ancient philosophy and multilingual scholarship.</summary>

# CABALA

...which has remained unknown to the Latins until now. **Marsilio** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian priest and scholar who led the revival of Neoplatonism in Florence.</note> produced Plato for Italy; **Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples** <note>A French humanist and theologian (c. 1455–1536) who sought to "restore" the original meaning of Aristotle's works.</note> restored Aristotle for France. I shall complete the number, and I, **Capnion**, <note>Johannes Reuchlin’s own nickname; "Capnion" is a Greek translation of "Reuchlin," which is derived from the German word for "smoke" (Rauch).</note> will exhibit for the Germans a Pythagoras reborn through me and dedicated to your name. However, this could not be done without the Cabala of the Hebrews, because the philosophy of Pythagoras took its beginnings from the precepts of the Cabalists; having departed from Great Greece <note>A term for the Greek-speaking areas of Southern Italy in antiquity.</note> within the memory of our fathers, it settled back into the volumes of the Cabalists. Therefore, almost everything had to be dug out from there. For this reason, I wrote about the Cabalistic art, which is a symbolic philosophy, so that the dogmas of the Pythagoreans might become better known to students. In all of these matters, I affirm nothing; I only recount what is believed by the non-believers, who meet at an inn in Frankfurt from their various journeys to hear **Simon the Jew**, an expert in the Cabala. These travelers are **Philolaus the Younger**, a Pythagorean, and **Marranus**, a Muslim. <note>original: "Mahometista" — Marranus is presented as a traveler from the Islamic world, though the name "Marranus" often referred to Iberian converts; here he represents Arabic learning.</note> Now, having dropped off their little bags at the lodging, the travelers—desiring to ward off hunger—shudder at the rowdy crowd of fellow diners. But once those others had left the tavern after their banquet, Marranus began thus: 

"I have restrained myself from many words amidst such a murmur of needy fellow-diners—those who, having drunk too much at lunch, are now leaving—fearing that I might be heard poorly if I, a stranger, had interrupted the noise of those whom I knew to be burdened by a foul drunkenness. But now that they have departed and we two meet alone in this same lodging—both, as is plain to see, travelers and not a little tired from the road—I pray you, if you agree with me, order the innkeeper to bring the second courses and desserts, not at all like those of luxury-loving Sybaris, <note>Sybaris was an ancient Greek city in Italy famous for its extreme wealth and hedonism.</note> now that we may live and talk with a freer manner." 

And behold, the servers approach, bringing out I know not what treats with nuts and cheese, and a Bithynian bottle and a cup—uncertain whether for beer or wine—even though you had suggested nothing of the sort to them. Then Philolaus, with no small skill, said: 

"This merchant acts like an innkeeper, the kind who is hired for coins everywhere; you might say he even gives his guests 'eared' service <note>A play on words suggesting the innkeeper is eavesdropping or overly attentive to sell more.</note> so that he might sell more wine to those who are eager to settle the bill. For as soon as the talk of desserts fell, the dishes were ready. Now, indeed, amidst these honest cups, I hope there will be more relaxed comforts for us. For in my opinion, my fellow guest, a lively expression must be adopted by both of us, and rest must be provided for our tired limbs—especially for me, after a way too long and rough, and the hard paths I have measured out until now. What your own state is, I do not know, since I have not yet been informed about your pilgrimage—how long it has been, or who you are, or where you come from." 

"From Byzantium," he said, "the city of Constantine, which many call New Rome. For I am a Byzantine by birth, varied in my studies, whether you wish for Greek, or Hebrew, or rather Latin; yet I cultivate the doctrine of the Arabs more. And unless it is a burden, do not refuse to indicate in turn who you are." 

"They call me **Philolaus**," he said, "an **Alan** <note>Reuchlin uses the name of the ancient "Alans" to refer to a German/Teutonic identity.</note> by nation, a Pythagorean by discipline, and perhaps a talkative person not unlike yourself. But what is your one name, I ask?" 

"Those in Constantinople call me **Marranus**," and...
