# BOOK I.

...himself, a name known to scholars through Cerinthus and Ebion <note>Two early heretics who combined Jewish and Christian practices; the speaker, Marranus, is identifying himself as someone of mixed religious heritage</note>, because I am both dipped in water <note>baptized</note> and a circumcised Jew <note>original: *recutitus apella* — a classical Latin slur for a Jew, here used by the character to describe his dual background</note>. In other respects, I have been initiated into both the laws of Moses and the doctrine of the Christians. I hear you mention scholars."

Philolaus replied to this: "I ask you this: are there schools of the humanities in Constantinople now, among those most cruel and savage Turks?"

"A great many," he said, "to which men of the most excellent talents have dedicated themselves. For there are more than ten thousand students there—from Persia, Greece, Italy, and Judaism, all within those same walls. Since I have been a student of many arts among them for twenty-two years now, it finally pleased me to wander elsewhere, to see if perhaps across the Alps I might find men devoted to the study of wisdom who are able to discourse both abundantly and plausibly on the greatest questions."

"Then of which school of philosophy?" Philolaus asked.

And Marranus replied, "Of any school you like, since I am not bound by the rules of any single discipline; indeed, no sect of faith prevents me from freely defending whatever I might think."

"Certainly, as I see it," said Philolaus, "you have a desire for exploration equal to my own. For I joined myself as a companion to merchants traveling from Thrace <note>A region in the Balkans, then part of the Ottoman Empire</note> to this noble German market-town of Frankfurt, because I had heard that there is a Jew here of great fame in Cabalistic works and of vast reputation. This single branch of knowledge—as I have often heard very learned men, who enjoy sweet leisure and abundant counsel, judge in my presence—is more closely related to Pythagorean philosophy than any other; indeed, there is nothing more like it. For they say that Pythagoras fished out nearly all his dogmas from that source. They say that Jew’s name is Simon, son of Eleazar, from the ancient lineage of the Yochaites <note>original: *Iochaiicorum* — referring to the followers of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar</note>, and my mind is made up to approach him now that the dinner tables have been cleared."

"Indeed," said Marranus, "if you allow it, I will go with you to the man myself, even though I am poorly schooled in Pythagorean matters. For I have always held the Arabs in greater veneration: Al-Ghazali, Al-Farabi, Abucaten, Hali, Abumaron, Ibn Sina—whom the Latins call Avicenna—and Ibn Rushd—whom they call Averroes—and other Peripatetics <note>Philosophers of the school of Aristotle</note> of that kind. And yet, in my time, no one in Constantinople has ever been denied the chance to pursue any philosophy of almost every language and sect, especially with teachers from many different nations teaching publicly every day."

Then Philolaus said, "Have confidence; for he easily becomes a Pythagorean who willingly trusts in the word, knows how to remain silent for a time <note>A reference to the legendary five-year silence required of Pythagoras's students</note>, and understands all precepts through the intellect."

And the other replied, "I will at least stand by where you allow me, like some follower of Pythagoras, and listen to the conversation that takes place between you. In this way, you will leave me steeped in unspeakable joy, as I would value it most highly to have been present for a conversation among wise men."

¶ And Alanus said, "Let us go. For he is said to be walking alone just now in the orchard of the house where he stays; certainly this is the place, and the door is open. You see..."

# CABALA

Is that not him walking from the garden toward us? Come, more quickly, let us go in—
"Greetings, Master." To which Simon replied, according to the custom of his people: "The Lord be with you."
"Are you that Simon the Jew?" the newcomers ask. Then he replied: "Both, for I am a Jew and I am Simon <note>The OCR reads 'Lu- sum', but based on the context of the dialogue, Simon is confirming both his identity and his faith</note>. But what names shall I take for the two of you, so that I may address you more correctly?"
Each replied to this: "I am Philolaus," and "I am Marranus." 
They answered that, having taken different routes without knowing one another, they had finally met here after a long pilgrimage. They explained that neither this marketplace <note>The famous Frankfurt Trade Fair</note>, looming so large and celebrated throughout almost all of Europe for such a great supply of goods, nor the fairs distinguished by so many precious wares, nor the beautiful convergence of so many diverse nations drew them for their own sake. Instead, it was your fame alone that brought them here, with the desire that you might briefly and conveniently reveal your meditations on the whole system of the Cabala—which is noble and, as it seems to scholars, greatly to be cultivated and sought after—meditations which have been commended with immense praise both in Scythia <note>A region in Central Eurasia</note> and in Thrace <note>A region in the Balkans</note>.

To this, Simon said: "Is there truly a memory of me even among nations as distant as the Scythians and Thracians?"
"There certainly is," both replied, "and a very great one. For about twenty-three years ago <note>original: 'triennium circiter quatuor lustra' — three years plus four five-year periods</note>, at that time when—according to your reckoning from the beginning of the world—it was the year five thousand two hundred and thirty-eight <note>The speaker is using the Hebrew calendar; 5238 corresponds to approximately 1478 AD, though the text immediately references the 1492 expulsion</note>, one hundred and twenty-four thousand Jews were expelled from Spain. From there, a great many of them traveled separately to our regions. They declare that in you, a man very well-known to them, there exists a great discipline of the arts, much learning, an incredible sharpness of mind, a clear integrity of philosophical speech, and especially a divine expertise in Gnostic speculation <note>Deep spiritual or mystical knowledge</note>, which is marvelous to all listeners. They speak of you so highly that, in the eyes of all who are eager to learn, you shine even beyond the Sarmatians <note>Peoples of the Eurasian steppe</note> and the frozen Ocean."

To this he replied: "Such a great estimation of me by you, men of the Pythagorean school, brings me no small blush of shame. For I fear lest, if I attempt to live up to this judgment of yours based on mere rumor, I might frustrate or fail you. However much I myself, through the fragility of my body, seem to have committed a regrettable injury against such a divine study of the Cabala through my own idleness. Clearly, whatever any man might find in me that is sluggish, broken, or imperfect, it might turn into a kind of disgrace for this expertise which you desire—as if the defect of the craftsman should reflect poorly on the worth of the art itself, which is the last thing I would want. For however small I may be—and I know how insignificant I am—and along with me all other Cabalists, whatever they may be thought to be (whether you wish to speak of them with praise or contempt, I leave aside), nevertheless, there is nothing granted by God to the human race dwelling here on earth—especially to those who excel in talent and flourish in mind—that is more desirable than this art of contemplation. There is nothing more beneficial for the salvation of souls, nothing more suited to attaining immortality, by which the human mind, in harmony with nature, may ascend more closely to happiness; that is, to the height of blessedness, which the Greeks call *agathon*... <note>original: 'ἀγα-' — the beginning of the Greek word for 'the Good'</note>

# BOOK I.

...they say, whether you prefer to call it the extreme, the ultimate, or the end <note>The text likely refers to the "summum bonum" or the highest good of human existence discussed on the previous page</note>, from which it happens that we may live lacking nothing, absolutely, always without hindrance, fortunately, tranquilly, and happily. This occurs when, quite skillfully through certain symbols, we have rejected all earthly things and set aside the matter of things, plucking form from form until we have ascended to the first all-forming and formless **form.** Regarding this, the Cabalists <term>Cabalists: Practitioners of Cabala, a Jewish mystical tradition that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal God and the finite universe</term> understand this divine command from Genesis: *Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind* <note>original: "Producat terra animam uiuentem ad speciem suam" — Genesis 1:24</note>, namely toward the divine Idea, which is itself the land of the living in the power of the living God, who flows that life into it through the name *Adonai* <note>A Hebrew name for God, literally "My Lord," associated here with the earthly manifestation of divine power</note>. This is so that you may know, as Joshua says, that the living God is within you and will destroy the opposing powers in your sight. These things are read in the second chapter of the book titled *Sha'ar Orah*, that is, *The Gate of Light* <term>Gate of Light (Sha'ar Orah): An influential 13th-century work by Joseph Gikatilla that explains the ten Sephirot or divine attributes</term>. From this, it follows that all things possessing life tend upward by their own instinct, and all things that influence life incline downward. 

For in this sensible world, whatever consists of the four elements is "silent" <note>Hebrew: *Domem*</note>, that is, a mixture. Such a thing either lacks a soul to produce diverse and wandering motion—lying immobile and at rest like stone and iron—or it vegetates and grows like a plant and herb, or it moves about in many ways, progressing and living only as *brute animals and shellfish*, or even speaks rationally as a human does. Our youths are accustomed to learning these Hebrew names from the book *Ruach Chen*, that is, *The Spirit of Grace* <term>Spirit of Grace (Ruach Chen): A popular medieval Hebrew introduction to philosophy and science</term>: *Domem*, *Tzomeach*, *Chai*, and *Medaber* <note>original: דומם צומח חי ומדבר — these translate to: Silent (inanimate), Sprouting (vegetative), Living (animal), and Speaking (rational human)</note>, that is: the still, the budding, the living, and the speaking. 

Indeed, there is nothing among these that does not, in a certain way, raise itself intently toward the heavens, as if longing for some use of its own virtue through that sight and shaping its character. Thus we see the highest mountains of the earth rise from the deep valleys toward the sky, according to the Song of the Psalmist: *The mountains ascend and the plains descend* <note>Psalm 104:8</note>. So too we experience the storms of the sea being raised on high, as the surging sea ascends in Ezekiel. For even the Lord of nature in that same Prophet makes the spirit of tempests break out, and finally, we see all fiery things being lifted up. For fire ascended from the rock in the Book of Judges. 

Thus, excellent men, with the power of your intellects, you understand that we are forced by a certain necessity to admit that the more noble a thing’s nature is, the more it rejoices in a higher attainment. Consider a grain of wheat cast into the earth: it does not rest until it breaks through the heart of the soil, looks out beyond the paths of the earth, and enjoys the celestial breeze. The same logic applies to metals as well, when that which is more noble bubbles up into higher spirits, refined <note>original: "sublimatum" — refers to the alchemical process of sublimation, where a substance is purified by being turned into vapor</note> by alchemy, so that those things which are higher always appear purer. In this way, we judge those things said to be in the lower regions to be ghastly, filthy, and weighed down by dross; whereas we marvel at those in the higher regions as white, illustrious, and adorned with incredible beauty, following them with songs of praise. How much more, when by the opinion of everyone, skillful Nature marks inanimate, vegetative, and breathing things with such characters that they seek higher things—surely she does not seem to have neglected man, [the noblest] of all ani... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page</note>

-># CABALAE<-

...the ruler of all that breathes, a beautiful and venerable creature, a most noble being, set in authority over all others. He is not only prudent and wise, but also contemplative and capable of religion. God would not have adorned him with these better and holier gifts, nor granted him this specific condition, unless it were so that from an innate natural desire he might strive toward the highest and best things by whatever powers he can. For God—that higher nature—as the most sacred history declares, composed Man of two elements: the dust of the earth and the breath of life. This was done so that, clothed in dust, he might prudently care for bodily things, and endowed with the breath of life, he might wisely love things divine. Thus the earth "brings forth a living soul" according to its own proper species—namely, that peculiar **Idea** <note>In this context, "Idea" refers to the divine archetype or blueprint of humanity in the mind of God</note>, which is not that of brutes, nor plants, nor stones or wood, but is born from the mouth of God and breathed into his face by the Divine spirit, the very illumination of His own mind. 

This is that process which we recently called **Deification**, wherein the exterior sense passes from a present object, through its own medium, into interior sensation, and then into imagination; imagination into estimation; estimation into reason; reason into intellect; intellect into the mind; and the mind into the light which illuminates man. Once he is illuminated, that light turns him back into itself. 

From this it appears correctly understood that the Cabalists <term>Cabalists: Mystics who study the Cabala, a tradition of Jewish mysticism</term>, in the divine tree of numerations <term>Numerations: A common term for the "Sephirot," the ten attributes or emanations through which God reveals Himself</term>, judged that **Tiferet** <term>Tiferet: The sixth Sephirah, representing "Beauty" or "Harmony," located at the very heart of the Tree of Life</term> should be placed as the **microcosm** <note>original Greek: μικρόκοσμον (microkosmon), meaning "a small world"</note> in the midst of the Sephirot. This is the "Great Adam," like the Tree of Life in the middle of the Ideal Paradise, or like a "straight middle line" (as they say). 

For God made man upright, as the royal Ecclesiastes <note>A reference to King Solomon, the traditional author of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes (see Eccl. 7:29)</note> says, flexible toward both things above and things below. Thus, through the "strife and friendship" of Empedocles <note>Empedocles: An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the universe is governed by the opposing forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion)</note>—noted below in those numerations designated by the name **YHWH** <term>יהוה: The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter sacred name of God in Hebrew</term>—man may recognize through human thought that he is a participant in the elements and in this mundane kingdom. 

Yet, through the **Fear** and **Mercy** of God <term>Pachad and Chesed: "Fear" (also called Gevurah/Strength) and "Mercy" (Loving-kindness), the two Sephirot that flank the central pillar of the Tree</term> which are expanded above him, he is capable, according to his own grasp, of apprehending the three simplest notions of truth: **Keter, Chokmah, and Binah** <term>Keter, Chokmah, Binah: The "Supernal Triad" or the three highest Sephirot—Crown, Wisdom, and Understanding—which represent the highest reaches of the divine mind</term>. 

Therefore, man was born here on earth, and nature brought him forth and formed him for this purpose: so that he may walk with his feet among the beasts upon the earth, yet alone among all living creatures, he may converse with the Angels in heaven with his head held high. His hands are placed between his feet and his head, so that he may fix them upon the earth by working for necessary sustenance, and raise them toward heaven by contemplating for eternal life. To protect these, the orbs of the eyes—the only instruments of all the senses given to man to be moveable—were instilled so that they might look toward the earth for the safety of the body, and toward heaven for the safety of the soul. Such is the aptitude, power, and faculty of man. This potential would never have been implanted by the supreme good of God or nature unless that faculty were eventually brought into use, and the potential reduced to action—especially in a man who is diligent and fortunate in this pursuit.

It outlines the psychological ascent from physical sensation to divine "Deification" and explains how the human body's posture reflects its dual purpose: caring for the physical life while contemplating the eternal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how the human mind ascends from the physical world to the divine. It picks up from the discussion of "Deification" or the process by which a person's soul is drawn back into the divine light through different levels of perception and understanding.</meta>

<page-num>727</page-num>
->### BOOK I. 727<-

...remaining. For if that grasp of divinity were not possible for man, nature would have implanted the desire for it in vain. For man, agile and capable, is never satisfied by the sense of bodily things or the crude touch of the elements; rather, he is carried forward by every thought toward the purity of separated things and the knowledge of the highest matters. This is clearly the restlessness of all seekers, through whom a vehement application of the mind—moving through moral, natural, and mathematical truths—is recognized as leading toward the arrangement of supernatural things, until finally, a faithful ascent to the first entity is granted. 

For example: You see a most bright fire burning in the distance; its form is extended through a clear medium—which the Greeks call <term>diaphanon</term> <note>original: διάφανον; the transparent medium that allows light to pass through</note>—all the way to the physical eye. A spiritual vision waits within and perceives that the form of the object presented is its own; therefore, it gladly receives it as a relative and close neighbor. Through the medium of appearance—which you call in Greek <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: φαντασία; imagination or the faculty of forming mental images</note>—it offers this image spiritually to the "brute" or sensory judgment <note>The basic level of animal instinct that processes sensory data without higher reasoning</note>. This image is then led upward to human judgment, and a little higher, the whole matter is promoted to reason itself. Finally, after an agile mental discourse, the mind transfers that abstraction of the physical fire—now so sublimated and sifted—to the intellect. 

In this ascent, therefore, three regions are found, and in each, there is a specific state of abstraction:
1.  **In the first region:** The object, the transparent medium, and the exterior sense. Here the process rests.
2.  **In the second region:** The interior sense, the imagination, and the "brute" judgment. Here the process rests a second time.
3.  **In the third region:** Human judgment, reason, and the intellect. Here it rests a third time.

The mistress of all these is the **Mind**, which, having received a higher light, illuminates and perfects the human intellect. What else shall we think the Cabalists taught regarding <term>Sechel</term> <note>Hebrew: "Intellect" or "Intelligence"</note>, <term>Sandalphon</term> <note>An archangel in Jewish mysticism often associated with the transmission of prayers and the physical world</note>, and <term>Metattron</term> <note>A supreme archangel, sometimes called the "Prince of the Countenance," who serves as the celestial scribe</note>? 

Every "state" has a double distinction. In the first, the body ends and the soul begins; hence it is called "animal." In the second, the soul ends and reason begins; hence it is called "man." In the third, the intellectual power ends and the Mind begins—which alone, without controversy, comes from the outside—hence it is called "God," according to the divine oracle: 

> I said, you are gods. <note>original: "Ego dixi dij estis." A reference to Psalm 82:6</note>

The names of these states are **sense**, **judgment**, and **intellect**. The intervals between them, which carry the forms of things, are the **transparent medium**, the **imagination**, and **reason**. The Cabalists offer something very similar in the <term>Mercaua</term> <note>original: Mercava; the "Chariot" of Ezekiel's vision, representing the highest mysteries of the divine realm</note> regarding the three fathers: Abraham the higher, Isaac the lower, and Jacob the middle. Since the two intervals of the three regions (sense and judgment) are doubled according to "lower" and "higher," and each is reduced to two boundaries, there remain **ten steps of the ladder**. By these, we are able to ascend from the lowest to the highest in the knowledge of all things that truly exist—whether by sense, by science, or by faith. 

Regarding this, Abraham the Cabalist, in that miraculous book <term>Ietzira</term> <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Formation," one of the foundational texts of Kabbalah</note>, says: **Ten Sephirot of nothingness: ten and not nine, ten and not eleven. Understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding; examine them and investigate them, and set the matter on its foundation, and return the Creator to His place.** <note>The Hebrew text provided is: עשר ספירות בלימה י׳ ולא ט׳ י׳ ולא יא׳ חבן בחכמה וחכם בבינה בחן בהם וחקור מהם והעמד דבר על בוריו והשב יוצר מכונו</note>

<header>CABALA</header>

Ten numerations <note>original: *Decem numerationes*; refers to the Sephiroth, the ten attributes or emanations in Cabala</note> besides "what," ten and not nine, ten and not eleven. Understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding; investigate them and examine from them, and establish the matter upon its own purities, and return the Creator to His throne. So much for that. For the human intellect understands the things that are above through wisdom, and perceives the things that are below through intelligence. The external sense establishes a thing from an object through the "species" <note>In medieval philosophy, "species" refers to the mental image or form of an object presented to the mind</note> offered to it, and the internal sense establishes the thing upon its purities—that is, by the abstraction of images which were previously familiar to the transparent medium <note>original: *diaphano*</note> and finally to the imagination <note>original: *phantasiæ*</note>. Then judgment, mediating between imagination and reason, investigates those same appearances, and reason—through various discourse and conclusion—proves them. Then I return to the beginning and say that the intellect restores the Creator, the first cause of all causes, to His throne. This is the mind itself, the **Active Intellect** <note>original: שכל הפועל; *Sekhel ha-Poel*</note>. You have, therefore, most skillful men, the ten numerations by which the apprehension of things happens to man: the object, the transparent medium, the external sense, the internal sense, the imagination, the lower judgment, the upper judgment, reason, and intellect; and all these are not so much the "what" as the "by which" <note>meaning they are the tools of perception rather than the essence of the thing itself</note>. But the supreme mind in man is the "what." For this reason, just as God is in the world, so the mind in man, among the ten Sephiroth of the kingdom, wears the diadem; and it is rightly named **Keter** <note>original: כתר</note>, that is, the **Crown**, which, as Aristotle asserts in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, is alone divine, and alone comes to man from without; by its received light, the lower powers are directed and governed.

-> **Until the intellect, the one who understands, and the thing understood are one** <-
<note>original: עַד הַשֶּׂכֶל וְהַמַּשְׂכִּיל וְהַמֻּשְׂכָּל אֶחָד; a famous philosophical maxim stating that in the act of high contemplation, the mind and the object of its thought become a single unity</note>

That is, so that both the understanding intellect and the thing understood may be one and the same. The Commentator on the Tree of the ten Sephiroth writes that the masters, regarding the words of the Prophet, *In Your light we shall see light*, judged it thus:

-> **For by the abundance of the intellect which flows from You, we shall understand and be set right** <-
<note>original: כִּי בְשֶׁפַע הַשֶּׂכֶל אֲשֶׁר שׁוֹפֵעַ מִמְּךָ נַשְׂכִּיל וְנִתְיַשֵּׁר</note>

This means that in the influence of the mind, which flows from You, we understand and are rectified. I think this is now made clear to all who have diligently scrutinized the condition of human nature. First, that we are led by a natural desire, or (if I may say more correctly) drawn, to apprehend the highest and divine things. Second, that as far as is sufficient for our nature, we can—by applying ourselves according to our measure and capacity—apprehend them. Nature inclines us to the one, and dignity to the other; both are skillfully demonstrated by the Cabalists through the figure of fire, which tends upward and in a certain way comprehends and licks at all things. Concerning this, Rabbi Joseph of Castile <note>Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla, a 13th-century Spanish Cabalist</note>, in the second book of the *Nut Orchard* <note>original: *Horto nucum*, or *Ginnat Egoz*</note>, says among other things in these words:

-> **Know that the intellectual soul** <-
-> **which is emanated into man and forms [images] within him, is called the fire of the supreme form.** <-
<note>original: דַּע כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הַשִּׂכְלִית הַנֶּאֱצֶלֶת בָּאָדָם וּמְצַיֶּרֶת בּוֹ הִיא נִקְרֵאת אֵשׁ צוּרָה עֶלְיוֹנָה</note>

Know that the intellectual soul infused into man, representing the supreme form within him, is itself called fire. To this they apply that saying of Solomon: *The lamp of God is the spirit of man.* Yet, to speak plainly...

<header>BOOK I. 719</header>

As reason proves and the experience of practice confirms, it is necessary for a man to be first instructed in many arts, in substantial branches of human study, and in significant learning before his industry, readiness, and natural talent can be so tamed for the contemplation of the <term>separated forms<note>In medieval philosophy, "separated forms" refer to purely intellectual or spiritual substances—such as angels or divine attributes—that exist independently of physical matter.</note></term> and the simple substances of the superior and <term>intelligible world<note>The realm of reality that can only be understood by the intellect, as opposed to the "sensible world" perceived by the five senses.</note></term> that he may almost creep into the very inner sanctuaries of God. For before all else, it is fitting that we be educated in the ethics and good character of prudent men, so that we may avoid what is shameful and pursue what is honorable. This is what Ecclesiastes warned: "Guard your foot when you go to the house of God" <note>Ecclesiastes 5:1</note>; for <term>Ethan the Ezrahite<note>A biblical figure traditionally identified as a wise man and the author of Psalm 89.</note></term>, in his instruction, sings: "Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of His throne" <note>Psalm 89:14</note>. In this song, he encompasses not only the works of men, which must be perfected by justice, but also the thoughts of the heart and the words of the mouth, which must be consistent with right judgment. Wherefore, with one voice and a similar sentiment, the **Cabalists** teach:

<note>original Hebrew: כי בהמשך אחר התאוה לבד בבני הסכלים יבטלו התשוקות העיוניות</note>
That is: *By indulging in lust and libido alone, as fools do, the desires for higher contemplation are corrupted.* Therefore, after morals are composed and the soul is purged (I will say nothing for now of the almost infinite rules of speaking correctly, truly, or well <note>Referring to Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric—the Trivium.</note>, which are merely the vestibules and doors of the sciences, but not the sciences themselves), there will then be a need for **Mathematics** and **Physics**. These encompass innumerable things contained everywhere in the volumes of the **Arabs**, **Greeks**, and **Latins**, whether concerning the universal number, weight, and measure, or concerning all motion and rest essentially inherent in things, which they call "nature."

For nature is, as **Rabbi Judah Halevi** writes in the book <term>Alcozer<note>Referring to *The Kuzari*, a foundational 12th-century work of Jewish philosophy.</note></term>:
<note>original Hebrew: התחלה והסבה אשר בה ינוח וינוע הדבר אשר הוא בו בעצם ולא במקרה</note>
That is: *The principle and cause by which a thing, in which it resides essentially and not by accident, rests and moves.* In this definition, you see how many and what kind of specific things are gathered together, so that we who investigate nature must look up to almost everything contained from the highest heaven to the lowest center of the earth—whether things stand by their own strength and substance, or in whatever way they lean upon or happen to things. So great is this that even the names of every individual thing could not be found in a man's whole lifetime (to say nothing of their properties, conditions, powers, behaviors, and operations), because of the near-infinity of those things we desire to know, the limited capacity of our rational power, the difficulty of the things to be investigated, the fragility of human power, and the multifaceted distraction of our desires. 

For what of it? Was it not said to **Abraham**: "Look up at the heavens and count the stars, if you are able"? And he could not do it, even though in his time, according to <term>Rambam<note>An acronym for Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, known as Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note></term>, he was a distinguished **Astrologer**. Whence the **Cabalists** teach:
<note>original Hebrew: כל מה שבשמים לא ידע האדם דבר ממנו אלא כוח השעור הלמודי המעט</note>
*Of everything that is in the heavens, man knows nothing of it except for a tiny bit of the power of mathematical measurement.*

<header>OF THE KABBALAH</header>

That is to say: man knows nothing of all that is in the heavens, except by the method of Mathematics, or the formal disciplines, and even then only a very small amount. By this saying I am reminded that the ancients erred in many things regarding Mathematics, even those matters in which they spent almost their entire lives, as is the custom of such studies. This is recorded in the writings of <term>Abubacher<note>Likely referring to the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Bajjah, known in Latin as Avempace, or potentially Abu Bakr al-Hasan ibn al-Khasib.</note></term>, after he testified to us that the ancients of that age—even up to the times after <term>Aristotle<note>The famous Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose system of logic and physics dominated medieval and Renaissance thought.</note></term>—did not fully understand Mathematics. For he speaks thus: <term>Mathematics was not completed in his time<note>original Hebrew: "הלמודים לא נשלמו בזמנו"</note></term>. That is, that the mathematical sciences were not perfected in the time of Aristotle. Since, therefore, as <term>Solomon<note>Referring to the Book of Ecclesiastes 1:8, traditionally attributed to King Solomon.</note></term> says, all things are difficult, and even in those natural things whose principles at least are known to us, or can be known— <margin>Matter, form, privation,</margin> <term>Matter, Form, and Privation<note>original Hebrew: "החומר הצורה ההעדר". These are the three principles of change in Aristotelian physics: the underlying material, the shape/essence it takes, and the absence of the form it is about to receive.</note></term> —there sits such a slowness of apprehension in men, what must we think will become of us when we seek to gaze upon those supreme types of spiritual causes? For that task, we will need the abstractions of all inferior things, along with discourse, reason, and logical speculations; these could easily occupy a man’s entire life, just as it is no small labor to learn the <term>Categories<note>original Hebrew: "המאמרות" (Ha-Ma'amarot). These are Aristotle's ten classifications of everything that can be expressed in speech or thought.</note></term> which we call the predicaments, and—to speak according to their custom—the "most general genera," which are: <term>Substance, quantity, quality, relation, when, where, position, state, action, and passion<note>original Hebrew: "עצם במה איכות הצטרפות מתי אנה מצב לו יפעל ויתפעל". These constitute the complete list of Aristotelian categories used to describe any object or concept.</note></term>. For by these they think that whatever is contained in this circular globe of the Creator is both constituted and understood. Nevertheless, they find things which are publicized and said concerning these very categories and the things they encompass, and for that reason they are called the <term>Predicables<note>Technical terms in logic for the five ways a predicate can be related to its subject.</note></term>: <term>Genus, species, difference, property, and accident<note>original Hebrew: "סוג מין הבדל סגולה מקרה"</note></term>. Upon all these things men set their traps, nets, and searches day and night. They track the individual causes of any thing, which are: <term>Matter, form, the efficient cause, and the end<note>original Hebrew: "החומר הצורה הפועל והתכלית". These are Aristotle's "Four Causes" explaining why a thing exists.</note></term>. From these, as we softly flatter ourselves, we might be able to hunt down the truth of every matter by a certain "evident demonstration" (as they call it), which they name <term>Proof<note>original Hebrew: "מופת" (Mofet), meaning a logical demonstration or certain proof.</note></term>; namely, running from one extreme to the other, as if from the starting gates to the finish line, in the manner of a certain artifice to which they have given the name <term>Syllogism<note>original Hebrew: "הקש" (Heqqesh). A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note></term>. But truly, our teachers have taught the skill and the winding paths by which the sophisms of those men (who are usually better at showing off these things than performing them) are presented:

> <term>Know that every syllogism and demonstration consists of two premises,</term>
> <term>the major and the minor, in three parts; these are called "terms." One of them is the subject,</term>
> <term>which is called the "minor extreme"; the second is the shared part, which is called</term>
> <term>the "middle term"; and the third is the predicate of the conclusion, which is called the "major extreme." And from these</term>

: <term>The Conclusion<note>original Hebrew: "התולדה" (Ha-Toldah), literally "the offspring" or "result."</note></term>. That is: Every syllogism and demonstration is composed of two propositions, or premises (the major and the minor), according to three small parts which are called terms. One of these is the sub-

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the limits of human logic in the face of divine mystery. Having previously discussed how ancient thinkers recognized the incompleteness of their own mathematical and natural sciences, the author now pivots to a critique of the syllogism—the standard tool of Aristotelian logic—as a "net" or "snare" that is insufficient for reaching the highest theological truths. This builds on the theme that spiritual wisdom requires more than just academic training; it requires maturity and a "cooling" of youthful passions.</meta>

<page-num>731</page-num>
<header>BOOK I.</header>
<sig>gg 4</sig>

...the subject of the inquiry, and it is called the **minor extremity**. And the second part is the participant, and it is called the **middle term**. And the third is the predicate of the inquiry, which is named the **major extremity**, and from these comes the conclusion. <note>The author is describing the three parts of a <term>syllogism</term>, a formal logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> This is that net, this the hook, the birdlime and the snare—this is the chain by which, in their opinion, the free truth is captured. They use it indiscriminately and sometimes in vain, whether concerning things subject to nature (such as **physics**), or things accompanying nature (such as **mathematics**), or things which in a certain way strip away nature (such as **metaphysics**). 

However, those things which are essentially absolute and separated from nature entirely, and from all matter and motion, we call **theological**. Certainly, these are not subject to those wordy "syllogistic whispers," for they are "immediate" truths; properly speaking, they are not the subject of "science" <note>In the medieval sense, *scientia* refers to knowledge gained through logical demonstration.</note> but of a firmer and more powerful form of recognition. 

This is what <term>Aristotle</term> suggests to us more absolutely in the first volume of those *Illustrious Books* <note>Referring to the *Metaphysics*, which in the Aristotelian corpus traditionally follows the *Physics* (hence "After Natural things").</note> which he wrote after his works on nature. He suggests that the possession of such knowledge is not human—both because we see that it happens rarely and hardly to one in a thousand, as if it seems to flow into us rather than being acquired by human effort; and because it is established in the greatest difficulty due to the thin and meager instinct of our intellect from the beginning (as I believe). 

<term>Zophar</term> expressed this with a certain figure of speech in the Book of <term>Job</term>: *Man is born a wild donkey’s colt.* <note>original: "Pullus onagri homo nascitur" from Job 11:12.</note> Furthermore, there is a lack and defect of natural aptitude when it is not aided by proper education. This is because for a long time now, many have been deluded by bad teachers. Even before they are wise, and while still in their tender years, they leave behind the study of the best literature and are driven toward **sordid sophisms**. This happens at the persuasion of those whose ears admit nothing except "whether this or whether that," along with their various propositions and corollaries. 

Another cause is the hasty promotion of students to higher degrees. These students should not yet have been entrusted with such high matters when they have yet consumed so little "oil" in the study of more humane letters. <note>"Consuming oil" is a classical metaphor for staying up late to study by lamplight.</note> Consequently, they grow weary in the midst of so many briars and thickets and recoil after much troublesome and fruitless labor, before they have reached the years of venerable old age—indeed, while they are still flourishing in their manhood. 

But I pray you, hear the words of **Job**: *Wisdom is found among the elderly, and prudence in a long life.* <note>Job 12:12.</note> For this reason, when the master <term>Johanan</term> once kindly said to <term>Rabbi Eleazar</term>, "Come, I will teach you the **Work of the Chariot**" <note>original: "opus de Mercaua." This refers to *Ma'aseh Merkabah*, the highest and most secret form of Jewish mystical contemplation regarding the divine throne.</note>—that is, concerning the most sublime contemplations—Eleazar responded: <gloss>I have not yet grown gray</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: לא קשאי (lo qashai), meaning "I am not yet old enough."</note>, as if to say, "I am not yet an old man." 

For that wise disciple, a youth of precocious talent, knew that for such sublime and high wisdom, none are fit or suitable except those whose fires of desire are already settled and extinguished, and whose youthful heat has cooled. Such men, advanced in years, grow old with a certain natural integrity. For what benefit would old age bring, unless it added integrity and a constant uprightness of life? Therefore, I would wish that no one believe those men to be true theologians—no matter how old they are or how much contentious wordiness they possess—who are still held bound by any kind of vice...

# CABALÆ

...defiled by filth, by pride, hypocrisy, avarice, hatred, envy, and often by a [distorted] religion and luxury; having neglected the light of the mind, they follow animal affections. Solomon leaps to support my opinion, saying: 
> The perverse man himself is an abomination to God, <note>Original: *Abominatio Dei est ipse perversus* (Proverbs 3:32).</note>
this is he who is turned away from the heights and sinks toward the slopes, however much nature may have raised him toward the high things. Your Al-Ghazali <note>Original: *Gazel*. Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (1058–1111) was a famous Persian theologian and philosopher whose works were influential in both the Islamic and Western worlds. The author calls him "your Marrano" or "Mussulman" (*Mahumetista*).</note>, that follower of Muhammad, was not ignorant of these motions—so contrary to one another, upward and downward—which are as unhappy for a learned man as can be. In his book *On Divine Science*, he demonstrates that from the conflict of such pulling impressions, a most bitter and fearful torture is created in the soul. 

Thus, beyond vices, secular business also perverts and turns us away; for perhaps parents, a wife, children, household staff, friends, enemies, accidents, events, and any of the close ties of kinship do not allow the strengths of men to ascend to the highest grades of understanding. 

But suppose that for any of you, there is nothing in us that hinders us; imagine our natural capacity is happy and favorable, and there is not even a shadow of madness or foolishness. Now everything is prepared and ready for undertaking the highest things, so that no one can rightly complain of our fragility. Nevertheless, many will be deterred from contemplation by that divine obscurity—higher than heaven, deeper than <term>Tartarus</term> <note>A classical name for the deep abyss of the underworld; here used for the profound mysteries of God.</note>—which is not searchable by sense or reason. This obscurity does not receive light from our studies like other sciences, but brings light with it and, as if from its own storehouse, radiates and shines upon men who are not unworthy. It does not prostitute itself everywhere of its own accord as something cheap, nor does it offer itself to the unwilling. Rather, once it has been very aptly established by our will through prior human sciences, it is drawn in without great resistance. Is it not just as Solomon says: 
> If the iron is blunt, and it has not been polished before, it is sharpened with much labor, and wisdom follows industry? <note>Original: *Si retunsum ferrum... et non prius politum fuerit...* (Ecclesiastes 10:10).</note>

For indeed, those things which are carried forward from the senses to the intellect are gathered by a certain diligence of studies and by artificial reasoning. But those things which reach beyond the intellect to the **Mind** and to its light, put on a nearly divine persona and lack human counsel, so that nothing can be thought by us more deeply than they. It is for this reason that the same Solomon seems to have groaned when he said: 
> A deep depth, or a profound profound—for so it is read in Hebrew—who shall find it? <note>Original: *Alta funditas seu profunda profunda... quis inveniet eam?* (Ecclesiastes 7:24). The author notes the Hebrew doubling for emphasis.</note>
He did not say, "who shall have it," for some have had it; but "who shall find it," as something difficult, though not in every way impossible. For the Lord gives wisdom, and "blessed are they who find her," as it is in the sacred oracles. 

It is, therefore, for the few to find it, and specifically for those upon whom, not by their own merits but by the gift of God, the splendor of such venerable light flashes. Truly, I think there will be no one who does not know that it is not for the multitude to hear the words of God. For this reason they cried out to Moses: 
> Speak you to us and we will hear; let not God speak to us. <note>Original: *Loquere tu nobis & audiemus, non loquatur nobis deus* (Exodus 20:19).</note>
"To you," I say, "we will listen," which <term>Onkelos</term> <note>The famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> interprets as *Neqabel* <note>Original: *Nezabel* (OCR error for *Neqabel*, meaning "we will receive/accept").</note>. Wherefore in the chapter...

# BOOK I.

...it is read as follows: "Moses received," <note>original: *Moſe kibel*</note> that is, Moses heard and received the law from Sinai. From this, it is called **Kabbalah**, which means a "reception" from hearing. I believe it should be noted and stored in a mindful memory that, out of such a great multitude of men—even among so many holy ones—Moses himself was the only one destined to receive the recognition of truth and equity from the mouth of God, and no other besides him. For thus the Kabbalist **Azriel bar Solomon of Gerona** <note>Azriel of Gerona (c. 1160–1238) was a central figure in the early development of Kabbalah in Spain.</note> writes: "Indeed, not all prophets were able to hear the speech from the mouth of God, except for Moses." <note>original Hebrew: לא כל הנביאים היו יכולים לשמוע הדיבור : השכינה כי אם משה (Not all the prophets were able to hear the speech of the Divine Presence except for Moses).</note>

You, therefore, most excellent men—whose minds are wonderfully bound to my love for you by our shared studies—can easily perceive from these points I have touched upon that the **Cabala** is a most necessary thing granted to the human race from heaven. Without it, no one can attain such a rare and difficult apprehension of divine matters. For these divine things are certainly not subject to the proofs of mortal reasoning, nor the <term>thorny disputes</term> of empty words, nor to human syllogisms, because of their very divinity. Rather, they are so great, so grand, and so infinite that they cannot be mastered in a single human lifetime—or even many—despite any amount of tireless labor. This is especially true for us who are clearly breathing in this mud, in this clay and the mortar of a dense body, and who presume to judge all things by bodily sense.

Indeed, the wise masters of the Hebrews say: "For to explain the power of the <term>Work of Genesis</term> <gloss>Ma'aseh Bereshit</gloss> to flesh and blood is impossible." <note>original Hebrew: כי להגיד כח מעשה בראשית לבשר ודם אי איפשר</note> How much more so is this true regarding the <term>Work of the Chariot</term>? <gloss>Ma'aseh Merkabah</gloss> <note>The "Work of Genesis" refers to the secrets of creation, while the "Work of the Chariot" refers to the even more guarded mystical descriptions of God’s throne and the divine realm.</note>

Therefore, we must act as specialized <term>technical writers</term> and master craftsmen are accustomed to doing in their teaching: let us trust each person who is an expert in their own art. For the logician trusts the part of speech received from the Grammarian; the Rhetorician takes his starting points for arguments from the logician; the Poet and the orator borrow from the musician; and the Geometer borrows proportions from the Arithmetician. Astronomy places its faith in mathematical numbers, figures, and dimensions. Things that are beyond nature <gloss>supernatural</gloss> use the conjectures of natural things. Every "higher" science rightly presumes the truth of the rules established by the "lower" sciences, not attempting to prove those things which it has heard are already confirmed by a prior art, but freely believing what has been said. This is done so that a man's whole life does not fail him before even the smallest principle of a single discipline can be perfectly investigated.

If this is the case in human affairs—and in the somewhat more common or manual crafts—that men receive by hearing and believe those who they judge to be endowed with singular learning, should we then think that in the science of the highest and divine things (which we can scarcely touch even one by one with our own strength) the tradition and reception of holy men—which in Hebrew is called **Cabala**—should be despised? For Kabbalah is the symbolic reception of divine revelation, handed down for the soul-saving contemplation of God and the <term>separate forms</term>, <gloss>angels or pure intellects</gloss> which, for those who possess the heavenly...

# KABBALAH

<warning>Partial loss of text at both left and right margins due to gutter shadow and page cropping.</warning>

...[those who] are endowed with **celestial inspiration** are rightly called **Cabalici** <note>Simon creates a hierarchy here: the "Cabalici" are the divinely inspired masters.</note>; their disciples, however, we shall call by the name **Cabalaei**, and those who attempt to imitate them in other ways are to be named **Cabalistae** <term>Kabbalists: Simon distinguishes between the inspired masters, their true students, and the mere practitioners or imitators of the art.</term>. This is just like those who exhaust themselves with daily labor over the published discourses of these masters.

"Indeed, Philolaus," said Marranus, "if you permit, I believe this Jew [Simon] has gathered whatever could be said about the Kabbalah with **Nestorean eloquence** <note>Nestor was a character in Homer’s Iliad known for his persuasive and "sweet" speech that flowed like honey. Marranus is complimenting Simon’s persuasive skill.</note>, so that we might thoroughly understand what the name itself designates and where it arises; whether there is anything in nature or in human practice of the sort they call Kabbalah; and finally, for what cause or purpose it exists, to what extent and for what it is useful, and how necessary it seems for divine contemplation, as well as how much is possible for a fit person who has prepared himself for it. As for who should be called a *Cabalicus*, who a *Cabalaeus*, and who a *Cabalista*, there is no need for more words: he is to be praised in this from head to heel, for he casts no shadows before our eyes."

Then Philolaus said, "You have loosed the rope, Marranus, entering a great and barely navigable sea; you are not yet sailing into port. What this Simon has depicted as if on a small tablet, you see only through a mist and gaze upon through the middle of a cloud. We have not yet even been led to the doors of this art. Therefore, my Simon, most contemplative of the Hebrews, we would love for you to go further. For thus far, you have benefited us no more than to provide a handle for thinking more broadly about the art of Kabbalah: what that thing is which was revealed, who revealed it, who received it, what advantage that reception brings, and what the method of this art is through which—as the rumor goes—miracles are performed. For it was that last thing that drew me here from afar."

"I shall first take issue," said Simon, "with that mention of 'Nestorian eloquence' of which I am accused by Marranus. In my judgment, that would be a disgrace to me as both a philosopher and a Jew, rather than a compliment for one who loves flattery. Such eloquence—which requires an abundance of both words and matter—cannot be contained in such brevity of speech, and it is not the custom among us Jews to pursue the deceptive colors of oratory. For we have learned to speak properly, not to perform oratory under the schoolmaster's rod, and we seek the truth of the cause more than the ornament of speech. 

But I will finish in a few words what you so strongly desire, so that I do not leave you wearied by so many and such perilous journeys, or hanging in suspense with the winding paths of trifles, as if you were yawning. For after you have listened without any boredom, as it appears, I will show by what tracks and signs—and with how many and what kind of 'hounds'—I have hunted down the definition of Kabbalah, so that you do not happen to err regarding the name itself. Certain Sophists <note>In this context, 'Sophists' refers to pseudo-intellectuals or scholastic critics who Simon believes are willfully ignorant.</note>, worthy of mockery, out of their own rashness or—if you prefer—negligence in learning, have falsely asserted that 'Kabbalah' was a diabolical and heretical man, and that therefore all 'Kabbalists' were heretics. Restrain yourselves from laughter, I beg you, if you can—although it is naturally ridiculous (and I would wish you to stop laughing at these human monsters and portents)—while I bring forth those things about whose certainty you asked me when you were doubting."

# BOOK I.

<meta>catchword: -strorum</meta>

First, I will remind you that the Kabbalah <note>original: "Cabalam"</note> is to be sought neither through the rough touch of the senses nor through the commanding arguments of logical artifice. Its foundation is established in the "third region of knowledge," where no pressing judgment, no evident proof, no demonstrating syllogism holds sway; indeed, where even human reason itself does not rule. Instead, there is a nobler kind of knowledge where the light of the mind, falling upon the intellect, moves the free will of belief. 

For those things perceived by the senses are "below science" and are more certain than reason; however, those things into which the mind flows, we place "above science," as they are more solid than rational discourse. I have paused and lingered here for a moment lest you think such divine matters are subject to the inventions of human fragility and, as they say, the rules of logic. 

Forgive me, friends, I do not bring prepared meditations, but as topics arise, I draw one from another. For now I hasten to what you desire. What is that thing? As for what was revealed, no one will convince me that you asked about every revelation of every belief—which are nearly infinite—but rather, what is that primary, universal, and principal revelation of divinity, into which all individual divine revelations are directed and reduced? 

"Certainly, that is the very thing," said Philolaus. 

Then Simon replied: "Rightly so. It is indeed nothing other than the **universal restoration** of the human race after the primordial fall, which is named *Yeshua* <note>original Hebrew: יושוע (Joshua/Jesus)</note> by us and *Salvation* <note>original Latin: "salus"</note> by the Latins. The very first revelation made to our species concerns this, if I carefully weigh the beginnings of the world, before which there was no other. 

For Adam did not speak about his wife after his sleep through a prophetic inspiration, as if he were divining while seized by a dream, when he said: *This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh* <note>Genesis 2:23</note>. Rather, upon waking, he felt he had fewer ribs on one side. After he had made a circuit of all the living creatures of the earth, sea, and air one by one, he suddenly beheld Eve. He, a robust young man, saw a young woman full of life, with a beautiful appearance, a charming face, and endowed with human energy; he began to burn with mutual desire and be filled with natural longing, which until then had not been stirred by any other animal. 

For so says Eleazar, our Master, and Solomon <note>This refers to Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah.</note>, the ordinary commentator of the Holy Scriptures: *Adam came to every beast and animal, and his mind was not satisfied by them until he came to the woman.* <note>Original Hebrew: שבא אדם על כל בהמה וחיה ולא נתקררה דעתו בהם עד שבא על האשה</note> 

From these words—by the faith of men!—a twisted crime has been committed through the malice of perverse men. (If indeed they are to be called men, and not rather devils incarnate and raging ghosts!) These men are ready to stir up the fury of Christianity against us, though we live innocently and peacefully according to the laws of the emperors. They are prepared to incite any kind of injury against us, as has often happened elsewhere, and recently in this city, regarding the words of the Master...

# ON KABBALAH

...of our teachers, they have falsely interpreted and explained it thus: that Adam shamefully copulated with all the beasts and animals. Good God! What audacity from such foul scoundrels, aided by the favor and assent of childish Sophists. For never does the word *ba* <note>original Hebrew: בא (meaning "to enter" or "to come")</note>, according to the properties of the Hebrew language, signify lewd copulation—even if sometimes, by the necessity of the subject matter, it is understood through a certain metaphor to mean feminine intercourse out of a sense of modest shame. An example is found in the sixteenth chapter of Genesis: "Go in to my maidservant, if perhaps I may have children by her." In that place, *ba* means "Go in to the maidservant"; it does not say "Copulate with the maidservant." This is not an equivalent thing here—so much so that even the most wicked of men could not accept it as similar, because of the impossibility of the business being discussed. For truly, how could it be that so great and so significant a man as Adam should be understood to have shared his seed with a bedbug, a flea, a fly, or a cicada? I have reviewed these things for this reason: so that no one might believe anything against us regarding the Holy Scripture (which they claim to know) based on these sorts of trifles, spoken by such slanderous, cursed, and fickle deserters who deserve no faith in this or any other matter. 

I return to the point from which I digressed. Therefore, by the instigation of being alone while they <note>Adam and his faculties</note> were in the world, the man felt that this alone pertained to himself; thus, this was not yet "Kabbalah." Furthermore, this was a matter for everyone to see: that the first-formed man <term>protoplastus: the first human, Adam</term>, as the Lord of the world, added names to every thing by a spontaneous act of will. By this, we know that naming was a matter of choice, not of nature. Nor was it outside the bounds of reason that, after the transgression of the law, he dreaded the penalty of death threatened in the warning—which, by the guidance of reason, he judged would not be a bodily death, since he did not feel himself die immediately after eating from the tree. Therefore, as **Ramban** <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, or Nachmanides, a major 13th-century Jewish scholar</note> suggests, he understood it as "dying in sin," just as we Kabbalists understand it. 

Now, I ask you, what in all these things was finally a matter of divine revelation? Certainly, up to this point, we have found nothing that did not entirely follow either the counsel of reason or the movement of the senses. On the contrary: that most ruinous transgression of the law—that great insult against God the Best and Greatest, that hostile rashness, that contagious lust, that foul and poisonous plague, that toxic and hideous pestilence, the corrupter of the human race residing in the very channels of the veins and creeping into posterity through the seminal flow itself—no thought of human fragility had the power to presume or conceive by what way or in what manner it could be expiated and turned away. 

Here, I say—here at the point of imminent desperation, than which nothing is more ruinous—there was a need for the effective help of divine revelation. God the Creator <note>original: "fictor Deus," the fashioner</note> did not then entirely desert his own handiwork, but he injected a certain hope that it would not be impossible for this very crime (however immense and committed against infinite majesty) to be abolished, removed, and extinguished in the course of time. He said, therefore, to the angels in the hearing of Adam: "And now, lest he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat..."

Following his defense of Adam’s character, Simon now discusses the moment of Adam's expulsion from Eden and the divine mercy hidden within the sentence of punishment. ### BOOK I.

...may live forever, and the Lord God sent him out of the garden of pleasure <note>Paradise</note>. This was the last voice that the wretched man heard from the mouth of God as he was already being driven from the garden. Yet, amidst such great sorrows and lamentations, he received a firm hope toward his Creator: that such a horrible sentence would, in the course of time, become revocable through the mercy of God. The words of the divine oracle indicated this to him, for He said: *Now, let him be, lest he put forth his hand and take also from the tree of life.* <note>original: "Nunc sine iam, ne mittat manum suam & sumat de ligno uitæ." A reference to Genesis 3:22.</note> Indeed, God did not add the word *now* or *at last* in vain; by it, the present time is designated, suggesting that the sentence would not be perpetual, but that an abolition of it could be obtained in a future time, if ever a man destined to eat from the tree of life should come. This was so even though Adam suspected, while his spirit still ruled his limbs, that he was paying an irrevocable penalty—for God had not been with him the following day, nor had He spoken face to face as was His custom. This was an open sign of indignation and of a mind alienated from Adam; for He who, as the Creator of all, had previously spoken with every living creature and beast, now disdained to speak mouth-to-mouth with a sinful man.

Yet, lest the most merciful Father should leave him entirely destitute of all consolation, He immediately sent an angel, from whom Adam might learn more fully of the future restoration from such a great ruin. For thus the Kabbalists write in their commentaries regarding the *Book of Yezirah* <note>The Sefer Yetzirah or "Book of Formation," a foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note>: *That the fathers had known angels as their teachers; the teacher of Adam was Raziel.* <note>original Hebrew: שהאבות רבותיהם היו מלאכים ידועים רבו של אדם רזיאל</note> This angel, by the will of the most high God, showed him the way of expiation and explained, in the Kabbalistic manner, how the divine speech was to be received through allegory—of which not only is no word placed in vain, but not even a letter, however small or thin, nor even a single stroke <note>apex</note>. 

But I call upon you, Philolaus, and you, Marranus—men who are the most learned of all the learned—grant me this indulgence: perhaps my religion should have prohibited me from betraying such recondite and hidden secrets to those outside our sect and uninitiated in the Jewish rite. Knowledge of these things, as God loves me, is often and greatly denied even to our own disciples, so that it is scarcely possible to find them even in rare books, except when wrapped in coverings and enigmas. For thus it is read in the Talmud: *The secrets of the Law are not transmitted except to a counselor, a craftsman of wisdom, and one skilled in secret speech.* <note>original Hebrew: אין מוסרים סתרי תורה אלא ליועץ וחכם חרשים ונבון לחש. See Isaiah 3:3.</note> Therefore, should I say more, or should I remain silent? I am made to hesitate not a little, both by the prohibitions of the masters and by the immense heat of each of you (as I judge) to scrutinize the highest things, being inflamed by a divine fire. Yet, boldly being more indulgent to myself, I shall temper the harshness of the precepts. I see that the light of the sun is dispersed without discrimination over all who remove the obstacle. I will speak—albeit quite inelegantly according to the custom of our nation—nonetheless as best I can, regarding what most learned and wise men have said and recorded as divinely revealed.

# CABALA

...I have understood he left behind. And I will nonetheless explain the very firm speech held by the Creator of the world with the blessed angels in the inner depths of his divinity. For God said, "Behold, Adam is become as one of us." <note>Genesis 3:22</note> He said "one of us," not "one of you." For in you angels, there is number and alterity <note>the state of being different or "other"</note>; but in us, that is in God, there is infinite, eternal, simple, and most absolute unity. Nor can that "one" found among angels, if such a thing exists, be the same as the "One" in God. Therefore, God did not count the angels with Himself when He spoke of "one," because it is contradictory for the same thing to be "one" in nature for both God and angels, so great is the distance between the Creator and the creature.

What then does He mean when He says, "Behold, Adam is like one of us"? From this we certainly conjecture that there is a certain **Celestial Adam**, shown to the angels in heaven as proceeding from God, whom He had made by the Word; and that there is another, the **Earthly Adam**, presented to God, whom He had fashioned from clay with His own hands and driven from the garden. The former is one with God; the latter is not only other, but truly a different person and a different thing.

Therefore, after the miserable fall of the human race, He taught the angels about the restoration of salvation that would come at some time, and through whom it would come. Indeed, He taught them not as much as He Himself could teach, but as much as the angelic condition was able to grasp, demonstrating in their presence who it was that would redeem the human race. For then the salvation of man had been clearly predestined. Wherefore He said, "Behold, here is that Adam, who not only is essentially the source of the world and of your own origin, but even before every creature, he was one of us in eternity before time began."

<term>Onkelos</term> <note>A famous 2nd-century convert and scholar who translated the Torah into Aramaic</note> interprets this in Aramaic <note>original: Chaldaicè</note> thus: הוה יחידי בעלמא מנית <note>original Aramaic: "He was unique in the world from me."</note>

That is, *Behold, Adam was my only-begotten or my unique one in eternity from myself.* This is the same term God uses to **Abraham**, saying, "Take your only-begotten son." And when He had already indicated the person of the future redeemer, lest they should perhaps think that He Himself would soon turn away the hatred of such a wicked crime by some perfunctory intercession, He immediately moved the doubt and deferred the matter into the future, saying: "And now, in this present time, let not this my one who exists from myself in eternity put forth his hand and take also from the tree of life," implying clearly that what He alone would now prohibit, He would later grant.

By this they wisely understood that although it would not happen now, yet later, in the course of time, through this Celestial and Eternal Adam-God, this ruin would come to be repaired by the fruit of the tree. As the Lord of the universe sat upon His throne, with all the host of heaven standing by Him (as **Micah** <note>The prophet Micaiah in 1 Kings 22:19</note> says) on His right and on His left, they gave thanks for such great mercy toward mortal weakness.

Therefore, the angel **Raziel** <note>In Jewish mysticism, the "Angel of Secrets" who gave Adam a book of wisdom</note> was sent to the fallen Adam, who was full of sorrow, to console him. He spoke thus: "Do not be consumed beyond measure by groaning and distress because the human race has fallen into utter perdition. For this sin will surely be expiated. For from your offspring shall be born..."

### BOOK I

...just and peaceful, a heroic man, whose name will contain mercies, and also these four letters **I.H.V.H.** <note>original: i.h.u.h., the Tetragrammaton or the sacred four-letter name of God</note>; and he, through right faith and a peaceful offering, shall stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and the fruit of that tree shall be the salvation of all who hope. When this speech was finished, that condemned and wretched Adam, amidst all the miseries into which he had fallen—amidst the pain and mourning with which he was afflicted in such great calamity—conceived a hope of changing his transgression, trusting in God. Therefore, touched by an incredible love for his Maker, he gave thanks for the grace of divine mercy. This was the first **Kabbalah** <note>The word means "reception" or "tradition"</note> of all, the primordial messenger of salvation. O welcome thing! O desirable cause! What could be more beneficial? What more acceptable? What more opportune could be brought from the heavens to the lost condition of mortals? What help could be more suitably provided than to announce public salvation to the captives? This is that most holy and supreme revelation into which all divine revelations are led back; this is the most desired tradition, this most soul-healing reception, in which all Kabbalistic receptions are recapitulated. All traditions of divine things, all teachings of celestial matters, the visions of prophets, and the meditations of the blessed are here united and communicated. For this reason, when Adam had openly reported each of these things to his wife, he began—in her presence and for the remembrance of posterity and as an act of thanksgiving—to sacrifice to God upon an erected altar. For so our Masters have handed down: *That the first Adam also offered a young bull.* <note>original Hebrew: שגם אדם הראשון הקריב שור פר</note>

<margin>I have acquired</margin> <note>original Hebrew: קניתי (qanithi)</note> But Eve, now to be the future mother of the living, her despair removed, was finally known by her husband; she conceived and bore her firstborn. Whereupon, overflowing with immense and incredible joy because she thought a savior had soon been born to her, she exclaimed: *I have acquired a man from the Lord.* <note>original Hebrew: איש את יהוה (Ish et YHWH)</note> This referred to those four letters which they had received from the angel long ago, and she named the one she had acquired **Cain**. When the parents recognized that he was, contrary to their hope, perverse in his wicked character, they began a second birth and fathered **Abel**. When both sons were then young men, the parents handed down this **Kabbalah** to them—that is, the reception by hearing concerning the restoration of salvation. This was then ardently loved by Abel, but vilely despised by Cain. Abel, led by the opinion that he himself might be that very same person whose revealed restoration they expected—since he felt himself pleasing to God through right faith and an accepted offering (because the Lord had looked upon him and his gifts, but did not look upon Cain and his gifts)—began to desire the fruit of the tree with all the affection of his heart and mind. He judged this fruit to be established in the offering of life. For that reason, it was called the "tree of life," and so named because life was to be offered to the Creator through the tree by the one who gave it. Wherefore he strove to stretch out his hand there, so that he might receive from the tree, consume it, and take it away <note>The author connects the name Abel to the idea of consuming or taking away</note>; for this is what **Abel** <note>original Hebrew: אבל (Hevel)</note> signifies. From this, he patiently bore his brother's hatred against him, and even when Cain was vehemently angry and seeking an occasion for a quarrel...

# KABBALAH

...he did not protest with smooth words to appease his brother, but remained entirely silent. When he saw Cain threatening him with death—having snatched a branch from a tree or a wooden club—Abel was greatly gladdened. He hoped to be slain by wood, for at that time there was no use of iron before the birth of **Tubal-cain** <note>In Genesis, Tubal-cain is identified as the first blacksmith</note>, who was the first hammer-smith and craftsman in all works of bronze and iron. Armed thus with a massive wooden club, Cain spoke to his brother Abel. *And it happened, when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.* The Romans <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate translation</note> add the reading "Cain said, 'Let us go outside,'" which is not found in the context of the Holy Scriptures. But the unarmed Abel did not resist the armed man; rather, he offered himself to death willingly and gladly. He was prepared not only to satisfy the Creditor (God) on our behalf but even to pay the original debt entirely, if possible, and to be offered as an acceptable, devoted, and appointed sacrifice for that payment.

After Abel had died without children, Adam waited a long time, hoping that perhaps what he had not found in his sons might occur in his grandsons. But what could he hope for in the rejected generation of Cain? All confidence in that line had long since vanished. He saw that they were all occupied with sedentary crafts and manual trades, devoting themselves to servile work and following the pursuit of minor comforts and things necessary for the body. They thought of nothing divine, nothing noble, nothing worthy of a heroic man. For this reason, he sought and obtained another offspring and another seed from God. The most pious father was cheered by this beyond what can be said, saying: "God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed." Therefore, he called his name **Seth** <note>Seth means "appointed" or "placed"</note>, whom he fathered in his own image and likeness. This was not because his other children lacked human form and image—for they were men as well—but because the generation of the others (excepting Abel) should until then have been called a generation of demons rather than men, on account of their cursed malice and detestable vices. It is not that he had fathered actual, substantive demons and devils, as some impious and profane people lie about, but rather that they were "evil by will." Nothing is truly evil except vice and the demonic spirit.

"I shall proceed, therefore, if you wish, continuing through the same door I entered."

"Proceed diligently, we pray," they replied.

Simon said again: "Our father Adam received a grandson through Seth, mindful of that **Kabbalah** which the angel **Raziel** <note>The angel of secrets in Jewish mysticism, said to have given a book of wisdom to Adam</note> had handed down to him: that from his lineage, a man would be born who would be the future Savior. For this reason, he was called **Enos** (which means 'Man'). At that time, it was thought—and indeed greatly hoped—that he should be named according to the angelic Kabbalah by the four-letter name **Y.H.V.H.** <note>The Tetragrammaton, the sacred name of God</note>, or at least more Kabbalistically through 'Mercies,' by placing the letter **Shin** <note>The Hebrew letter ש</note> in the middle of those four letters, **Y.H.S.H.V.H.** <note>This creates the name "Yahshua" or Jesus, a central idea in Christian Kabbalah</note>. For thus it is written in the sacred history: *Az huchal likra be-shem YHWH* <note>Genesis 4:26: "Then he began to call on the name of the LORD"</note>. The Romans read this not very learnedly as 'This man began to call upon the name of the Lord.' But certain rare and most contemplative Kabbalists interpret it more correctly according to the properties of the language and through the art of **Gematria** <note>The system of calculating the numerical value of words</note>. They say he was then expected to be called through the letter **Shin**, which in the Kabbalistic art is the same as *be-rachamim* (meaning 'in mercies'), and the letter **Shin** designates through the art of **Notarikon** <note>A system of using letters as shorthand or acronyms</note> the 'middle' of those four letters..."

**Then it was begun to call upon the name of the Lord:** <note>original Hebrew: "הוחל לקרא בשמו יהוה" (Huchal likro b'shem YHWH) from Genesis 4:26.</note> That is, "Then it was hoped he would be called" by means of the letter *Shin* <note>original: "Sin"; the Hebrew letter ש</note> placed in the middle of I.H.V.H. <note>This refers to the Renaissance Kabbalistic idea that inserting the letter 'Shin' into the name YHWH produces 'Yehoshua' or Jesus.</note> as if, according to the angel's pronouncement, Enos <note>The son of Seth</note> would take from the tree of life and redeem the world; the hero himself being named I.H. in mercies V.H. <note>original: "i.h. in miserationibus u.h."</note> Mark this secret and observe the mystery! However, since he was not actually called in this way by the designation of any angel, they abandoned that hope and placed it in another. For by the warning of angels—that is, the messengers of God—names were bestowed upon the fathers for various events, whether past (as Cain was named because "I have possessed"), <note>Refers to Genesis 4:1, where Eve says "I have gotten/possessed a man from the Lord."</note> or present (as Enos was named because he was a "man"), or future (as Abel was named because he was destined to bring "mourning" to his parents). For Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and he walked with God; he received the commands to make an ark of wood, in which he would save the world. Therefore, in a Kabbalistic sense, he "hoped in the wood," for as Job says, **For there is hope for a tree,** <note>original Hebrew: "כי יש לעץ תקוה" (Ki yesh la-etz tikvah) from Job 14:7. Thus, he blessed Shem, the future servant of God in whom he hoped for salvation above the others: **Blessed be the Lord God of Shem.** <note>original Hebrew: "ברוך יהוה אלהי שם" (Baruch YHWH Elohei Shem) from Genesis 9:26.</note> This is translated Kabbalistically as: "Blessed be the Shem [Name] of the four-letter God"; through this, the Kabbalists say: **He made it known that Shem would be a servant of God,** <note>original Hebrew: "הודיע כי יהיה שם עובד האלהים" (Hodia ki yihyeh Shem oved ha-Elohim)</note> as Rabbi Moses of Girona <note>The famous medieval scholar Nahmanides, also known as Ramban (1194–1270).</note> writes.
