### OF KABBALAH

...they received a son. Concerning him, when God had commanded that he take his only-begotten son Isaac, whom he loved, and sacrifice him upon wood on a certain high mountain of Moriah, it seems incredible with what joy and great gladness Abraham exulted. This was because he was mindful of the divine promise, by which God pledged to him in these words: "I will establish," He said, "my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you; and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed." <note>This is a paraphrase of Genesis 17:7 and 12:3. The author argues Abraham was happy to sacrifice Isaac because he believed it was the mystical mechanism for this universal blessing.</note> Wherefore, he was confident that he was bringing about the salvation of the human universe which we mentioned; he took the boy immediately at the voice of God, and he himself cut all the wood for the sacrifice with his own hands. Indeed, an oracle had taught that the **original fall** through the wood <note>The Tree of Knowledge in Eden.</note> could be repaired through wood. <note>The author is drawing a parallel between the wood carried by Isaac and the wood of the Cross.</note> Hence the Scripture says that Abraham took the wood of the offering and laid it upon Isaac his son, and placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood, and stretched out his hand and took the sword to sacrifice his son. For unless Isaac had received from his father the **Kabbalah** of human salvation—handed down through the **tree of life** and the future offering of a certain **just man**—surely he would not have looked upon his impending death before his eyes with such benevolence, a ready countenance, and cheerfulness of soul, embracing it willingly. As is the condition of mortals, he would have either turned away from the drawn blade, or at least tried to mitigate his father's perceived cruelty with gentle words, or else fled. But suspecting that he himself might be the one through whom the restoration of the primordial ruin would occur, he considered nothing more pleasant than that sacrifice, and nothing sweeter than that death, for the sake of which the entire human race would be redeemed through his participation. This very hope was made even firmer for him because God had destined that same location for sacrifices since the founding of the world. For the land of Moriah was pointed out to Abraham by the finger of God; it was there that the first **Adam** built an altar and offered gifts to God, as did Cain and Abel, and where Noah and his sons also sacrificed. So our Masters dispute in the *Chapters of Rabbi Eliezer*, <note>A famous 8th-century Midrashic work.</note> supported by **Ramban** <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman (Nachmanides), a major medieval Sephardic scholar.</note> and **Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla** <note>original: "R. Ioseph filio Carnitolis." Joseph Gikatilla (1248–1305) was a central figure in Spanish Kabbalah.</note> in the book *The Gates of Justice*, <note>original: "Portarum iustitiæ" referring to Gikatilla's *Sha'are Ora* (Gates of Light).</note> and in that same place the holy city of Jerusalem was built, according to the testimony of **Solomon the Gaul**. <note>Possibly a reference to a specific medieval commentator or traveler.</note> However, when the matter was left unfinished and the father and son departed from Moriah, the voice of **Zadkiel** <note>In Jewish tradition, Zadkiel is the angel of mercy who stayed Abraham's hand.</note> was heard speaking to Abraham: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." By this, he alone was recognized as the protection for all future generations. And the voice of God himself was also heard through the angel **Raphael** over Isaac: "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," lest perhaps he should believe himself to be that very savior. For this also belongs to the Kabbalists who write thus: *The teacher of Isaac was Raphael.* <note>original Hebrew: "רבו של יצחק רפאל" (Rebbo shel Yitzchak Raphael). In Kabbalah, each patriarch is associated with a specific angelic tutor.</note> For that man <note>Isaac</note> there was no hope concerning one of his sons, <note>Esau</note> who had already lost the paternal blessing through the practice of hunting. But regarding the other, <note>Jacob</note> the father promised great things for himself, foretelling what was to come with these words of prophecy: "People shall serve you, and nations shall bow down to you."

### BOOK I.

It was not without reason, therefore, that such a great expectation of universal salvation was placed upon Jacob (for so that son was called) by our ancestors. It was because he was the first of all mortals to see the gate of heaven opened, and a ladder stretching from earth to heaven, and the four letters **I.H.V.H.** <note>original: "i.h.u.h." This refers to the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter sacred name of God.</note> standing upon it, which he desired in his prayers to grasp. He also added to this work the consonant **Shin** <note>original: "Sin"</note> which, through the method of **notariacon** <term>Notariacon: A kabbalistic technique of using letters to represent whole words or forming new words from the initials of others.</term>, signifies **ointment** <note>original: "שמן" (shemen)</note>. By this, he built a certain temple named **Bethel** <note>Meaning "House of God."</note> using an anointed stone. The suspicion was increased by the fact that the angel **Peliel** was an intimate of Jacob; this angel forewarned him of many things through constant report and speech, both that God had chosen Jacob for Himself, and that "blessed shall he be whose help is the God of Jacob." The **Kabbalists** <note>original: "Cabalistæ"</note> write as follows: **The teacher of Jacob was Peliel.** <note>original: "רבי של יעקב פליאל"</note>

But having been instructed by his angel, Jacob learned that he himself would not be that savior whom the heavenly **Kabbalah** had thus far put forward. By divine revelation, he deferred the matter to another age, saying: "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen in the last days. The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until **Shiloh** comes, and the assembly of nations shall be for him." <note>A translation of the prophecy in Genesis 49:10.</note> By this prophecy, it became known that someone would eventually be the savior of the human race, who would be born from Judah in the last days, and would be "Shiloh," and would bear the scepter of the kingdom, and the nations would flock to him.

For this reason, after these Patriarchs, the great Moses did not offer himself to death of his own accord—as Abel once did, or as Isaac did long ago—but he refused and wished to withdraw himself from the care of the people. This was despite the fact that he spoke with God as a friend with a friend, face to face, and used a staff as a scepter, and the entire nation of the Jews flocked to him. He knew, however, that he was not of the family of Judah, but was born of the house of Levi; nor was he born in the last days; nor was he **Shiloh**, which according to the **Syriac translation of Onkelos the Chaldean** <note>Referring to the Targum Onkelos, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Torah.</note> signifies the **Anointed One**, whom we call the **Messiah**. Nevertheless, concerning the whole reason and method of restoring the **original fall** <note>The fall of Adam.</note>, he was sufficiently and more than adequately instructed by his angel **Metatron**. For the Kabbalists write thus: **The teacher of Moses was Metatron** <note>original: "רבי של משה מטטרון"</note>, who is the messenger of **Shaddai** <note>original: "Sadai" – a Hebrew name for God, often translated as "The Almighty."</note>.

Thus, the entire community of prophets received this revelation of the most holy Jacob: that in the last days, one shall be born from the seed of Judah who is to abolish original sin—the Messiah, the King of Peace—at which time the scepter and prefecture of Judah would cease, and the nations would be called together from every side. This tradition has migrated by succession from the fathers to the college of prophets. All of them, individually, conferred among themselves in daily discussion concerning the **Golden Age of the Messiah**, exulting with the greatest joy in that blessed school of the Holy Spirit. They poured forth their joys from the depths of their hearts, joined together by a single bond of fellowship in the Messiah the Savior. Although they spoke of that same coming King at different times and in many and various ways, each of them nevertheless reached a similar and clearly consistent conclusion. This one indeed, in these words: "I beseech you, Lord..."

# KABBALAH

And another thus:
> For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise. <note>Malachi 4:2</note>

Why do I linger with many words? All of them rejoice with one heart and speak all good things with one mouth, praising that day of this savior and longing for that time about which David cried out to God:
> Send out your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and into your dwellings. <note>Psalm 43:3</note>

Regarding this word "light," **Rabbi Solomon the Frenchman** <note>original: "Rabbi Salomon Gallus." This refers to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> said: "Your light," that is, the King Messiah, according to what is written:
> I have prepared a lamp for my Messiah. <note>Psalm 132:17</note>

From this we are made more certain that David held no doubtful opinion of himself—that he himself would be that King Messiah who would reconcile the human race to God—even though a divine oracle had emanated:
> I have found David my servant, I have anointed him with my holy oil <gloss>because one who is anointed is called 'Messiah'</gloss> and I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. I will keep my mercy for him forever, and my covenant shall be faithful to him, and I will establish his seed forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven. <note>Psalm 89:20-29</note>

David therefore placed all his hope in his seed; wherefore he called the son born of **Bathsheba** "Solomon," <note>The name Solomon (Shlomo) is derived from the Hebrew word for peace (Shalom).</note> because he had heard and believed that the Messiah, through whom salvation would come to the world, would certainly be the Prince of Peace, according to the **Kabbalah** revealed to him:
> In his days there shall be an abundance of peace until the moon is taken away. <note>Psalm 72:7</note>

Therefore, it must be understood as referring to another "seed" of his, rather than the son of Bathsheba; for that Solomon loved women, through whom his heart was corrupted so that he followed foreign gods, nor was his heart perfect with the Lord his God, as was the heart of his father David. For this reason, God raised up an **adversary** <note>original: "satan." In the original Hebrew context of the Book of Kings, this refers to a political or military opponent raised by God.</note> against Solomon, so that he did not have full peace, he who possessed only the name of it. # BOOK I.

...they have directed that salvation toward Solomon; however, they intend a different Solomon than the son of Bathsheba, and a different temple than that of the historical Solomon, who subjected the temple he built to the law of destruction. Concerning that historical temple, God foretold: "The temple which I have sanctified for my name, I will cast out from my sight." <note>1 Kings 9:7</note> For this reason, neither this Solomon nor this temple was able to abolish original sin, however much it stands written by the Kabbalist in the **Gate of Light** <note>original: "Porta lucis," referring to Joseph Gikatilla’s *Sha'are Orah*, a foundational 13th-century Kabbalistic text.</note> as follows:

"At the beginning of the world’s creation, the divine indwelling dwelt among the lower beings; and while the divine indwelling was below, the heavens and the earth were found to be united, and the sources and the channels were perfectly active, flowing from the upper to the lower, and the Blessed Name was found to be filling both the upper and the lower. Then the first Adam came and sinned, and the ranks were corrupted, the channels were broken, the pool ceased, the divine indwelling departed, and the bond was severed. Afterward, Solomon came and built the House, and then the channels and the flows returned to their preservation or conduits," and so forth. <note>original Hebrew: בתחלת בריאתו של עולם שכינה חיה שרויה בתחתונים... "At the beginning of the creation of the world, the Shekhinah (Divine Presence) dwelt in the lower realms..."</note>

In this passage, when the Kabbalists speak of Solomon, they seem to be alluding to the reality of the matter rather than the literal name, since they understand it to refer to a certain coming **Prince of Peace** <note>original: "Sar Salom" (שר שלום)</note> according to the words of Isaiah. This figure is the one whom the worker of miracles himself shall name: Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the future age, and **Prince of Peace**. <note>Isaiah 9:6</note> Truly, some have thought that King Hezekiah was designated here; but others, reading the following words, "Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom," understand it to refer to the King Messiah. He is the one who shall take away the sins of all—those daily wars and battles stirred up in the souls of men, which our parents sinned, and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities. <note>Lamentations 5:7</note> So it indeed seemed to **Jonathan the Chaldean** <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, who in the passage above translated "Prince of Peace" as the **Messiah of Peace**. <note>original: "Meſſiha d’ſhalma" (משיחא דשלמא)</note> Concerning him, Isaiah says again: "The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises and wounds we are healed." <note>Isaiah 53:5</note>

This shall be that true Solomon, who will erect a much more sublime Temple, one that is clearly eternal and indissoluble. For thus the Kabbalists write: "The house of the sanctuary which is below is arranged to correspond with the house of the sanctuary which is above." <note>original Hebrew: כי בית המקדש של מטה מכוון כנגד בית המקדש של מעלה</note> From Solomon, the founder of that earthly temple, until King Jehoiachin (the same as Jeconiah—for both names contain the same letters, though transposed), the expectation of universal salvation among the entire assembly of prophets was placed in the coming Messiah, from Isaiah until Ma- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ad Ma-," likely leading to Malachi on the next page.</note>

It explains how the earthly Temple is seen as a reflection of a heavenly reality and identifies the "Prince of Peace" as the redeemer who heals original sin.</summary>

-># THE KABBALAH<-

...to Malachi who said: "The Lord whom you seek shall suddenly come to his temple." <note>Malachi 3:1</note> Concerning this, Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A renowned medieval biblical commentator and grammarian, often known as Radak (1160–1235).</note> writes that the "Lord" here is the Messiah, who will himself be the messenger of the covenant, whom Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Targum (Aramaic translation) of the Prophets.</note> interprets as "the Great Master." After the prophets, however, the expectation of salvation and the arrival of the Messiah—and indeed the entire Kabbalistic practice, of whatever sort it may be—is centered upon and drawn back to the eternal liberation of that same Messiah. All of this descended clearly to the scribes of the Law and the elders who were called the "Heads of the Fathers" (who are hardly numbered because of their great multitude) and to the Men of the Great Assembly. It was received in succession by the scholars from Ezra, who delivered the Kabbalah to Simeon the Just, the High Priest and prefect of the synagogue. From him, in turn, his pupil Antigonus received it along with his colleagues, among whom were Zadok and Boethus, the root of the heretics, from whom they were called Sadducees and Boethusians, as Judah the Levite writes in the third discourse of the book *The Kuzari*. <note>original: "Alcofder," a Latinization of the Arabic title *Al-Khazari*. This 12th-century work by Judah Halevi defends Judaism through a dialogue between a king and a rabbi.</note> Next came Joseph son of Yoezer and Joseph son of Jochanan of Jerusalem; from them Joshua son of Perachiah, who had a certain Nazarene disciple in the time of the Maccabees (not the one belonging to the Christians). <note>A reference to a controversial passage in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 107b) which some historical polemicists used to claim a different chronological origin for the figure of Jesus.</note> And Nittai of Arbela, from whom came Judah son of Tabbai and Simeon son of Shetach, from whom came Shemaiah and Abtalion. From these came Hillel and Shammai, who had many thousands of disciples; from these Rabban Jochanan ben Zakkai, and he fostered the disciples whom he nourished, who were Eliezer (whom they write as Eliezer son of Hyrcanus), Joshua son of Hananiah, Joseph the Priest, Simeon son of Nethanel, and Eleazar son of Arach. Regarding Rabban Jochanan, who lived one hundred and twenty years, it is said that his Kabbalah was received by Rabban Gamaliel, from whom his son Simeon received it, and from him his heir Judah the Prince <note>term: "Nagid" (Prince/Leader). This refers to Judah Ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah.</note>, who is called "Our Holy Teacher"; he followed his father Gamaliel in receiving it. Thus far the Kabbalists, whose sayings and the rest followed the allegorical expositions of the Sacred Scripture: Hananiah son of Akashia, Abba Saul, Rabbi Tarphon, Akavia son of Mahalalel, Hananiah the Chief of Priests, Hanina son of Teradion, Hananiah son of Hachinai, Nechunya son of Ha-Kanah, Halafta, Dusai son of Yannai, Hanina son of Dosa, Dosa son of Harchinas, Rabbi Akiba, Eleazar son of Azariah, and Eleazar Hisma. Then Rab Levita, Rabbi Jochanan son of Beroka, and after him Simeon from the children. Then Zadok, then Yose; him follows Ishmael, and from another lineage Rabbi Meir, from whom Eleazar son of Jacob received it, as well as Jochanan the Shoemaker <note>Jochanan Ha-Sandlar.</note> and Eleazar son of Shammua. Then Nehorai, whom Yannai and Mattathiah and Samuel the Less followed, as well as Elisha son of Abuyah, Eleazar of Kaphar, Judah son of Thema, and Joshua son of Levi; and after them many others. These are sometimes called *Thanaim* <note>term: "Tanaim" (Repeaters/Teachers). The Rabbinic sages whose views are recorded in the Mishnah (c. 10–220 CE).</note> because of their Talmudic disputations—as if they were "dictators"—but because of their meditations on the highest things, led back from individual lower things to the most exalted heights, having been received from their elders and handed down to posterity, they are called *Mekablim* in Hebrew <note>term: "Mekablim" (Receivers). The Hebrew root of Kabbalah (Q-B-L) means "to receive."</note>, and in our age by the Latins, by the authority of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, before whom their name in the Roman tongue...

->### BOOK 1.<-

...was known, they are called Kabbalists or Kabbalics. Then **Marranus** said: "Do you know that man, most learned Simon, who first brought the name of Kabbalah to the Latin people?" 

And **Simon** replied: "Indeed, I know him (as I recall); he was once an exile from his home among the French and the Savoyards <note>The Allobroges were a Celtic tribe of ancient Gaul; here it refers to the region of Savoy.</note>, driven from his fatherland and most bitterly chased by envious men in a certain detestable persecution because of his extraordinary studies in philosophy and his noble character. There is indeed a certain class of men (as **Terence** <note>A famous Roman playwright (c. 185–159 BC) known for his comedies.</note> says) who wish themselves to be the first in all things, yet they are not. They are born, perhaps, from the crow—a bird which, until the years of Coroneus (as it is in the fables), was first dressed in white feathers and later in black. It provides them the color of their clothing, both white and black, from which they are called the 'blackened brothers' <note>original: "fratres atrati." This is a satirical jab at the Dominican friars, who wore black and white habits and were frequent critics of Kabbalistic and Renaissance studies.</note>. Indeed, that bird is always hateful to **Phoebus** <note>The god Apollo.</note> because of its wicked informing. 

But this poetry is known to both of you: these men were the gadflies, the scourges, and the dogs—so noble and so "learned" were these Christians—yet in our century, they have most skillfully shared many secret dogmas of the Hebrews with Roman ears." 

At this, **Philolaus** said: "Leaving these historical deeds behind, I advise that we must return to the Kabbalistic Art (if you trust me), since it will be evening shortly after, and it can hardly be said how much our desires tend elsewhere." 

"I have indeed run through the individual points," said **Simon**, "and you shall expect nothing more false from me." 

And **Marranus** said: "If that is so, I have certainly interrupted your speech very inconveniently. For you were weaving the thread of a discourse most fit for the thing we desire. Nothing was more pleasing than, after a correct definition of Kabbalah, to know what that thing is which has been revealed so excellently to the race of mortals beyond all others—then who revealed what, and who received it. It was at this point that you were led away by my interruption, which I somewhat regret. Therefore, my friend, we pray that you return to it." 

"I shall indeed obey you cheerfully," **Simon** said. "And I will hasten at last to the method of the Art which I noticed you desire, unless evening is already imminent, when perhaps you are weary from hearing and I myself am exhausted from speaking. For quite enough things have slipped from us in these few short hours; and whether it was my rashness (if you like) or (which is truer) my singular affection toward you—which ought not to happen in so great a matter—I have said everything unprepared and off the cuff." 

Then **Philolaus** said: "But we both entreat you to complete the table <note>original: "abacum," referring to a counting board or systematic list.</note> with a reckoning of the authors who both held and handed down the Kabbalah, lest we go away to our inn to dine as we must with this member of our discourse not yet perfected." 

When this was said, **Simon** replied again: "To my judgment, there exist innumerable Kabbalists (for it does not matter to encompass them by number). Some of them are those who only heard, while others were both listeners and writers. Nevertheless, since you urge me so, I will recount them..."

# CABALAH

...I will mention just a few in passing, whose books on Kabbalistic subjects come into daily use, as far as my memory serves me. For they are not all preserved in their entirety; of some, only fragments have surfaced, while others, alas, have been so completely lost that they are now scarcely known even through the records and mentions of the most learned men. For just as the ancient fathers lost many volumes through the unfairness of time and the long passage of years—to the great loss of posterity, though our ancestors still remembered them—so too we, living now in the very sixth millennium of the world <note>The "sixth millenary" refers to the Jewish calendar's calculation of world history, which at the time of writing was in the 5000s (the 6th millennium).</note>, have lost the books of our ancestors. This has happened either through old age, which consumes all things, or through the malice of wars, or by floods and ruin, or by the sudden accident of fire, or sometimes by that shameful and detestable hatred and envy which has incited even lazy and foolish "governors" to become book-burners.

Books of Enoch and of our father Abraham are cited by trustworthy men; even Moses cites the books of the **Wars of the Lord**. Joshua cites the **Book of the Upright** <note>original: "librum iustorum," often known as the Book of Jashar.</note>, and the whole collection of the books of **Kiriath-sepher** <note>original: "Kyriath-sepharim," meaning "City of Books."</note>, which Othniel captured under the leadership of Caleb. Ahasuerus mentions the **Book of Memorable Deeds**. Jonathan, in the Book of Maccabees, mentions the **Holy Books of the Spirit**. The Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomena"</note> commemorate the **Books of Lamentations**, the books of Samuel the Seer, of Nathan the Prophet, of Gad the Seer, of Shemaiah the Prophet, of Iddo the Seer, of Ahijah the Shilonite, and the books of Jehu son of Hanani—all of which are now nowhere to be found. We also lament the loss of the library of Darius, which, as Ezra says, was a precious thing in Ecbatana.

By the same token, countless of our own authors have perished, though we do not doubt that many survive which we have not yet seen. Nor will I boast of the same glory as the **Man from Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who claimed to have bought seventy Kabbalistic volumes once hidden by Ezra.</note>, who claimed that those seventy volumes of Kabbalistic secrets which Ezra once commanded to be written were acquired by him at great expense. I possess nearly nothing of the gold and silver required to bid for such books, should they ever be offered.

However, we do make use of the following books to the best of our ability: 
*   The book of our father Abraham, titled **On Creation** <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah*.</note>, which some quite learned men attribute to **Rabbi Akiba**; it is certainly adorned with noble commentaries, as it is otherwise quite hidden and obscure. 
*   And the book <term>Zohar</term> <note>original: "זוהר" (Hebrew); meaning Splendor</note> of **Splendor**, which **Simeon son of Yohai** composed while he lay hidden in a certain vast and dark cave for twenty-four years. 
*   And the book <term>HaBahir</term> <note>original: "הבהיר" (Hebrew); meaning The Bright</note> of **Brightness**, which your people call the *Lucidarius* <note>A common title for medieval handbooks of general knowledge.</note>. 
*   There are also the works published on Kabbalah by the illustrious **Abraham Abulafia** <note>original: "Abraham Alaphia"</note>, and the excellent commentaries of **Ramban** (for so is **Rabbi Moses son of Nahman** <note>Also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270).</note> called), whom you call the man of Gerona, written upon the secrets of the Law.
*   Also the commentaries of that most learned writer **Rabbi Menahem Recanati** on the secrets of Ramban. 
*   And the **Book of the Perplexed** <note>The *Guide for the Perplexed*.</note> by **Rambam**—ending with the letter "m," that is, **Rabbi Moses son of Maimon**, whom they call Moses the Egyptian. 
*   And the book <term>Sha'arei Tzedek</term> <note>original: "שערי צדק" (Hebrew); meaning Gates of Justice</note> of the **Gates of Justice**, which **Rabbi Joseph son of Gikatilla** <note>original: "Carnitola"</note> wrote.

# BOOK I.

...the book *The Gates of Light* <note>original: "Sha'are Orah"</note>, that is, the gate of light, by Master Joseph of Castile in Spain (as they say). And the book *The Beliefs* <note>original: "Ha-Emunot," referring to Saadia Gaon's "Book of Beliefs and Opinions."</note>, that is, concerning beliefs, whose author was Rabbi Saadia in Asia. And the book *The Secret of the Law* <note>original: "Sod ha-Torah"</note> concerning the mystery of the law, which that wise man Abraham Aben Ezra composed. And the book of Rabbi Hamai, son of Hanina, who is called the head of the most eloquent in Kabbalah, and by the same author, the book *Contemplation* <note>original: "Iyyun"</note>, that is, of speculation. Finally, another book, *The Holy Commentary* <note>original: "Perush Qadosh"</note>, that is, a commentary on holiness, which Rabbi Azriel wrote. And the book *Names* <note>original: "Shemot"</note>, that is, concerning names. And the book *Explanations of the Alphabet*, the title of which is *The Book of the Commentary on the Alphabet* <note>original: "Sefer Perush ha-Aleph-Bet"</note> from Rabbi Akiba. And the book of Rabbi Ama, *The Gate of Secrets* <note>original: "Sha'ar ha-Razim"</note>, concerning the hidden things of the nineteenth Psalm. And the book *Unity* <note>original: "Yihud"</note>, that is, unique, concerning the union or collection, which Rabbi Abraham Aben Ezra mentions in the first chapter of *The Mystery of the Law*. And the book *Visions* <note>original: "Mar'ot"</note>, that is, of mysteries. And the *Book of Abstruse Questions*. And the little book of Kabbalah published by Azriel (others call him Oriel) of Gerona. And the book which is titled *The Way of Faith and the Way of Denial* <note>original: "Derekh ha-Emunah ve-Derekh ha-Kephirah." The Latin "expiatione" suggests Reuchlin may have interpreted "Kephirah" through the lens of atonement/Kippur, or simply the rejection of heresy.</note>. And the *Book of Principles* <note>original: "Sefer ha-Ikkarim," though the text says "radicum" (of roots).</note> by Rabbi Joseph Albo, to which they likewise prefixed the title of Kabbalah, although he comments more on ethics than on <term>anagogical</term> <note>Interpretation that seeks a spiritual or mystical meaning beyond the literal text.</note> matters. Finally, there exists a most elegant book in Kabbalah against the pseudo-philosophers called *The Kuzari* <note>original: "Alkozer"</note> in the Arabic manner, which Rabbi Judah Halevi composed, whose words are these:

> There is no good Kabbalah except with a good heart. <note>original Hebrew: "Kabbalah tovah ela im ha-lev ha-tov."</note>

In this, he seems to me to have very wisely repelled malicious sophists from such holy contemplation—those who, like dying flies, ruin the sweetness of every ointment, no matter how precious. Finally, we use commentaries on the *Book of Formation* <note>original: "Sefer Yetzirah," a foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note> by Master Jacob Cohen, and a composition by Rabbi Isaac on the same book, which he titled *The Explanation of the Holy Name*. There is also a book published by Rabbi Todros <note>original: "Tedacus"</note> Halevi concerning the ten Kabbalistic <term>numerations</term> <note>The Sefirot, or the ten attributes/emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>. I do not wish to add the book attributed to Solomon under the name of Raziel, for it is a magical fiction. Thus far, I have most clearly opened to you strangers the "paper poverty" of my household affairs, which I am certainly not accustomed to reveal to others. Yet in my opinion, no one has ever written more skillfully, more distinctly, or more clearly on this art until recently than Rabbi Joseph son of Abraham of Castile, a citizen of Salamanca. He diligently labored over three volumes of this faculty, through which he made the entire instruction of the Kabbalists clearer: the first on words, the second on letters, and the third volume on vowel points. The title of his book is *The Nut Orchard* <note>original: "Ginat Egoz," a famous work by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>, after the Song of Solomon: "I went down into the nut orchard to see the fruits of the valley." It appears that this "nut" is like a golden apple enclosed in a silver network, as we read in Proverbs: "Golden apples in silver carvings is a word spoken in its proper manner." So too is Kabbalah: that golden and divine apple bound with silver threads—namely, with ingenious instructions and human arts—just as is common in the workmanship of goldsmiths, who with subtle engravings do not entirely hide a golden, sweet-smelling apple...

### OF THE KABBALAH

...they cover or clothe it in silver so that none of it can be seen, but through certain hollow holes and silver lattices, they allow both the color of the fruit and the scent of amber <note>original: "ambræ," likely referring to ambergris or a sweet-smelling resin used in pomanders</note> to breathe forth. To those looking from afar, all that is latticed seems to be solid silver, but those looking more closely, if they search studiously, catch a glimpse of the gold as well. And just as gold differs from silver, by so much more is the Kabbalah proven to differ from the physical <note>original: "C...ca" in OCR; context suggests "physica" or natural science</note> art, even though a single spiritual instinct embraces both types. 

But one precedes the other as a priest <note>original: "Hierophantas," a teacher of sacred mysteries</note> does; just as one type of gold is indeed "good," but another is "the best"—in the same way that it says in the Pentateuch <note>the first five books of the Bible</note> regarding Havilah <note>original: "Heuilan"; see Genesis 2:11-12</note> that "the gold of that land is good" (for it is not written "the best" there, as some read it, but "good"). And in Isaiah regarding Ophir: "I will make a person more precious than fine gold, even a person than the golden wedge of Ophir." 

Thus, whatever men who love the finest arts recognize through the science of nature in scripture is equal to "good gold" and is called the *Work of Genesis* <note>original: "opus de Bresith"; Hebrew: Ma’aseh Bereishit</note>. But what we receive through spiritual science is called the *Work of the Chariot* <note>original: "opus de Mercaua"; Hebrew: Ma’aseh Merkavah</note> and is compared to the "best and purest gold." For the Kabbalists write thus: *Bereishit is the wisdom of nature, and the Work of the Chariot is the wisdom of Divinity* <note>original: בראשית : חכמת הטבע ומעשה מרכבה היא חכמת האלהות</note>. That is to say, that *Bereishit* <note>the Hebrew name for the Book of Genesis</note> is the wisdom of nature, and the *Work of the Chariot* <note>referring to the divine throne-vision of Ezekiel</note> is the wisdom of divine things. 

And since both wisdoms are concerned in some way with the world and those things that exist in the world, it is the unanimous judgment of the Talmudists <note>scholars of Jewish law and tradition</note> and the Kabbalists that there are two worlds. The first is the intellectual world, which is called *the world to come* <note>original: "olam ha-ba" עולם הבא</note>, that is, that future world which is certain. And the second is the sensible world, which is called *this world* <note>original: "olam ha-zeh" עולם הזה</note>, that is, the present world. This we have received from the words of our sages concerning the studious devotee of the forty-two letter Name of God, saying thus: that such a person without a doubt exists as *one beloved above and beloved below, inheriting two worlds: the present world and the future world* <note>original: ועלה ונוחל למטה ונוחל שני עולמים העולם הזה והעולם הבא</note>. 

Therefore, the Talmudists and the Kabbalists are divided into two faculties, even though both arise and emanate from received traditions. For both hold to the traditions of their ancestors, even when no reason is given. But they are distinguished by this arrangement of purpose: that the successful and blessed Kabbalist finally transfers and translates all his study, all his effort, all his labor and diligence, and the entire intention of his mind from the sensible world <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note> to the spiritual world. The Talmudist, however, remains in the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of this universal world; and although he may occasionally go forth freely toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God himself as immanent and absolute, but as the craftsman and cause of things and as one occupied with his creations. Furthermore, he assigns the angels to daily ministries and to the execution of the effects of the divine will...

### BOOK I. 751

...always referring the contemplations of higher things to this lower world. However, one of these faculties often borrows the perceptions of the other and draws them toward its own desire. For indeed, the Talmudists <note>scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> and the Kabbalists <note>practitioners of Jewish mysticism</note> occasionally communicate their studies back and forth, much like the active and contemplative lives. Although they both follow the same context of Holy Scripture, one is usually invited toward "servile fear" <note>fear of punishment</note> and the other toward "filial love" <note>the love of a child for a parent</note>, each using their own style of graceful persuasion. For it will appear that the Talmudist remains with sharp zeal around the precepts and mandates of the law, explaining them, directing them, venerating and kissing them, so that we might correctly define the Talmud as nothing other than an explanation of the law according to the intention of the author. Thus the Talmudists are called *Meforshim* <note>Hebrew: מפורשים, meaning "interpreters"</note> and *Perushim* <note>Hebrew: פרושי</note>, that is, "expositors" and "Pharisees" <note>Reuchlin connects the word "Pharisee" to the Hebrew root meaning "to explain" or "separate"</note>, who always persist in their work from the pulpit and the chair of Moses. They preach and exhort the common people, saying with the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>, "Serve the Lord in fear," and with Joshua, "Fear the Lord and serve Him." Indeed, they say: "Do it this way," and "Omit that that way," with such and such a regulation. From this, they have reduced the six hundred and thirteen precepts—summarized in one word as *Taryag* <note>Hebrew: תריג, the numerical value of 613</note>—into two headings: *Aseh* and *Lo Ta'aseh* <note>Hebrew: עשה לא תעשה</note>, which means "Do" and "Do not do." You are accustomed to calling these affirmative and negative commandments, which are very beneficial to know and quite necessary in practice.

The Kabbalists, however, although (as Truth bears witness) they are men who piously observe the law, nevertheless lean more heavily toward contemplation. Therefore they are called *Anshei ha-Iyyun mi-Ba'alei ha-Torah* <note>Hebrew: אנשי העיון מבעלי התורה</note>, which means "Men of Speculation from among the Masters of the Law." They leave the care of the republic and private matters, the rites of home and war, and customs in judicial and moral affairs (along with their history) to the Talmudists. They reserve for themselves only those things which pertain to the peace and tranquility of the soul and which refer to the love of God. For they say: *Kavvanat klal ha-Torah shene devarim, ve-hem Tikkun ha-Guf ve-Tikkun ha-Nefesh* <note>Hebrew: כוונת כלל התורה שני דברים והם תקון הגוף ותקון הנפש. This is a reference to Maimonides' "Guide for the Perplexed," 3:27</note>. That is: "The intention of the entire Law consists of two things: the good disposition of the soul and the good disposition of the body." For the whole Law tends chiefly toward the perfection of man, and according to it, we attain two perfections: one of the mind and the other of the body. Truly, that which aids the soul and perpetuates life is far worthier and of a higher pre-eminence, even though the suitable condition and proper composition of the body is prior in time and nature. Therefore, the Kabbalists must be held in a higher place and a worthier rank, following that exposition of the law which, through certain symbols, most greatly impels the elevation of the mind toward the heavens and toward divine matters. Your Greeks call this the "anagogical" <note>term: anagogic (from Greek *anagein*, "to lift up"), referring to a mystical or spiritual interpretation of a text</note> institution, which is not only philosophy but is "Sophia" itself—that is, Wisdom. 

Whence they are deservedly named "the Wise," *Le-halokh neged ha-hayyim* <note>Hebrew: להלוך נגד החיים</note>, as the Preacher Solomon says, because they proceed to where life is. According to the capacity of mortals, while still dwelling in their little bodies, they ascend from time to eternity and from the lowest things to the highest. Make a trial of it if you wish, honored guests. "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." To be sure, "heaven" is called by the Talmudists all things of the visible world which are above the moon, and which...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between the "Work of Genesis" (natural science) and the "Work of the Chariot" (metaphysics/Kabbalah). It uses the analogy of a silver-covered golden apple to illustrate how divine truth is veiled by the physical world.</meta>

### OF KABBALAH ###

...they cover or hide with silver, so that none of it can be seen, but through certain holes and silver lattices they allow the color of the apple to shine through and the scent of amber to exhale. To those looking from afar, all that is latticed appears to be solid silver; however, those looking closer, if they search diligently, perceive the gold as well. And just as gold differs from silver, so Kabbalah is found to differ far more from the art of the Talmudists, although a single spiritual instinct embraces both types. 

But one precedes the other, as among the Hierophants <note>ancient priests or explainers of sacred mysteries</note>, just as one type of gold is indeed good, but another is the best. In this manner, it is written in the Pentateuch <note>the first five books of the Bible</note> regarding the land of Havilah <note>original: Heuilan</note> that "the gold of that land is good"; for it is not written there "the best," as some read it, but "good." And in Isaiah regarding Ophir <note>a legendary region famous for its wealth</note>: "I will make a man more precious than the best gold, and the gold of Ophir." 

Thus, whatever men who love the best arts learn through the science of nature from the scriptures is equal to "good gold," and is called the *Work of Bereshit* <note>original: Bresith; Hebrew for 'In the Beginning,' referring to the study of the physical creation</note>. But what we receive through spiritual science is called the *Work of the Chariot* <note>original: Mercaua; referring to Ma'aseh Merkavah, the mystical study of the divine realm</note>, and it is compared to the best and purest gold. For the Kabbalists write: "Bereshit is the wisdom of nature, and the Work of the Chariot is the wisdom of divinity." <note>original: בראשית חכמת הטבע ומעשה מרכבה היא חכמת האלהות</note>

And since both forms of wisdom are concerned in some way with the world and those things that exist in the world, it is the unanimous judgment of both the Talmudists <note>scholars of Jewish law</note> and the Kabbalists that there are two worlds. The first is the intellectual world, which is called *the world to come* <note>original: עולם הבא - Olam Ha-Ba</note>, namely that which is always coming. And the second is the sensible world <note>the world perceived by the senses</note>, which is called *this world* <note>original: עולם הזה - Olam Ha-Zeh</note>. 

This we have received from the words of our sages concerning the devoted student of the Divine Name of forty-two letters, saying that such a person undoubtedly exists as one who: "Ascends and descends, and inherits two worlds: this world and the world to come." <note>original: עולה ויורד למטה ונוחל שני עולמים העולם הזה והעולם הבא</note> Therefore, the Talmudists and the Kabbalists are divided into two faculties, even though both arise and flow from the accepted traditions. For both hold to the traditions of their ancestors, even when no reason is given. 

But they are distinguished by this order of focus: the happy and blessed Kabbalist finally transfers and translates all his study, all his effort, all his labor and diligence, and the entire intention of his mind from the sensible world to the intellectual world. The Talmudist, however, remains in the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of this universal world. Although he may occasionally proceed with permission toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God as an immanent and absolute being, but rather as the Craftsman and cause of things, occupied with His creations. He views the Angels as servants bound to daily ministries and to executing the effects of the divine will.

# BOOK 1. #

...always referring the contemplations of divine matters back to this lower world. However, one of these faculties often borrows the insights of the other and draws them toward its own desire. Indeed, the Talmudists and the Kabbalists share their studies back and forth, much like the active and contemplative lives. # KABBALAH #

->[The sages] cover or shield [the core] with silver, so that nothing of the interior can be seen. And just as gold differs from silver, so too is Kabbalah <note>The Jewish mystical tradition of "receiving" divine secrets</note> proven to differ far more from "Physical Art" <note>Natural science or the study of the physical world</note>, even though one spiritual instinct encompasses both forms. But one precedes the other, as the High Priest precedes the initiates. Just as one kind of gold is good, but another is the very best—in the same way that the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> says of Havilah <note>Genesis 2:11-12, a land near Eden</note> that "the gold of that land is good" (for it does not say "best," as some read it, but "good")—so it is with the words of Isaiah regarding Ophir <note>A legendary region famous for its wealth</note>: "I will make a man more precious than fine gold, even than the gold of Ophir."

Therefore, whatever knowledge of the natural world that lovers of the finest arts learn from the Scriptures is equal to "good gold," and it is called the "Work of the Beginning" <note>original: *opus de Bresith* / *Ma’aseh Bereshit*; the study of the creation of the physical world</note>. But that which we receive through spiritual science is called the "Work of the Chariot" <note>original: *opus de Mercaua* / *Ma’aseh Merkavah*; the study of the divine throne and the mysteries of God</note>, and it is compared to the best and purest gold. For the Kabbalists write thus: <note>original Hebrew: בראשית חכמת הטבע ומעשה מרכבה היא חכמת האלהות</note> "The Beginning is the wisdom of nature, and the Work of the Chariot is the wisdom of divinity."

The first is the **Intellectual World**, which is called the "World to Come" <note>original: עולם הבא / *Olam Ha-Ba*</note>, which is a certain [spiritual state]. The second is the **Sensible World** <note>The world perceived by the five senses</note>, which is called "This World" <note>original: עולם הזה / *Olam Ha-Zeh*</note>. We have received this from the words of our sages concerning the diligent student of the Divine Name of forty-two letters, of whom they say that such a person without a doubt exists as: <note>original Hebrew: נעלה ונחמד למעלה ולמטה ונוחל שני עולמים העולם הזה והעולם הבא</note> "Exalted and delightful above and below, inheriting two worlds: this world and the world to come."

For this reason, the Talmudists and the practicing Kabbalists are divided into two faculties, even though both arise and emanate from the same received traditions. Both hold to the traditions of their ancestors, even when no logical reason is given. But they are distinguished by this order of perception: the "fortunate and blessed" Kabbalist finally transfers and translates all his study, all his effort, all his labor and diligence, and the entire intention of his mind, from the sensible world to the intellectual world.

He does not approach God as the Immanent and Absolute Being, but rather as the Architect and Maker, the cause of things occupied with His own creations. Furthermore, he regards the Angels as daily ministers and servants who carry out the effects of the divine will.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Jewish mystical thought, moving from the general distinction between legalists and mystics to a specific Kabbalistic interpretation of the Creation story in Genesis. It focuses on the symbolic meaning of the "two worlds" and the significance of the first letter of the Bible.</meta>

->### KABBALAH ###<-

...beneath it, they call it "Earth." Furthermore, they also interpret "Heaven" as **form** and "Earth" as **matter**. For this reason, they say that "in the beginning" [God] created form and matter, and then fashioned their composition in each individual thing through a divine oracle <note>referring to the creative speech of God</note>, making all things not so much by turning them with a physical hand as by carving them out with a living Word. For it is read: <note>original Hebrew: ויאמר אלהים / *Vayomer Elohim*</note> **"And God said,"** that is: "Let there be light," and God said, "Let there be a firmament," and God said, "Let the waters be gathered," and God said, "Let the earth sprout," and God said, "Let there be lights," and God said, "Let the waters produce creeping things," and God said, "Let the earth produce," and God said, "Let us make man," and God said, "Behold, I have given you every herb." Therefore, the heavens and the earth were perfected with all their array and their entire "furniture" <note>a term for the contents or inhabitants of the universe</note>, such as the four elements which are called the "first-named shadows": the Spirit of the Lord, the waters beneath the firmament, and so on.

There follow likewise the other mixed things which are commonly called "elementated" <note>things composed of the four elements</note>: birds and flying things, beasts and creeping things, fishes and great whales, and the ruler of them all, **man**. To him alone among all corporeal beings was granted **free will**; so that he would not use it badly, laws were fixed for him, constitutions were promulgated, and punishments for transgression were threatened. Since that which flows in <note>the celestial influence</note> is called "Heaven"—that is, <note>original Hebrew: שמים / *Shamayim*</note> as if it were <note>original Hebrew: אש ומים / *Esh u-Mayim*</note> **"fire and water"**—and since it produces nothing from itself, but only nourishes what has been produced by heavenly, hot, and moist heat, then the sun and moon are recited in that order as the most powerful influences established within it. Under their leadership, all the remaining armies are arranged: the lights and stars, night and day, splendor and darkness, signs and seasons, days and years.

These things, then, concern the corporeal globe and the things mixed within it. But two worlds are accepted by the **Kabbalists**: the corporeal and the incorporeal, the visible and the invisible, the sensible and the mental, the material and the ideal. They believe the "Lower World" and "Upper World" are designated when they read, "In the beginning God created heaven and earth," thus symbolically interpreting "heaven" as the highest things and "earth" as the lowest. They interpret it in this way: <note>original Hebrew: ברא השם העליונים והתחתונים</note> **"In the beginning, the Name [God] created the upper and the lower things."** This is because they judge this simple and immaterial world to be the "highest," while this compact and "cemented" world <note>meaning the physical, solid world</note> is the "lowest."

From this, they also note that the Law of *Bereshit* <note>the Book of Genesis or the "Work of Creation"</note> promulgated concerning creation begins with the letter *Beth* <note>the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet: ב</note>. According to the art of **Arithmetic** <note>referring to Gematria, the mystical study of the numerical value of letters</note>, this letter signifies the number **two** among the numbers. It is as if it were intended to suggest that God principally created two things: the entire "highest" world with all who dwell in it, and the entire "lowest" world and everything pertaining to it. For if it were otherwise, it would have been enough for Moses to have written: <note>original Hebrew: ראשית ברא אלהים שמים וארץ / *Reshit bara Elohim...*</note>, which would be read by the Latins no differently than: "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." Indeed, that summary of creation could have started without the letter *Beth*, just as Solomon says in Proverbs: "The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways," where the word "beginning" is placed without the *Beth* and without any other preposition. However, contrary to custom, by starting with these two created worlds...

<summary>This page explores the Kabbalistic interpretation of Genesis, arguing that the creation of "Heaven and Earth" refers to the duality of the spiritual (ideal) and material (corporeal) worlds. The author highlights the mystical significance of the letter Beth, the first letter of the Bible, as representing the number two and thus the two-fold nature of creation.</summary>

### BOOK I. ###

ii 3

...the twice-two particles *Et* <note>original Hebrew: אֵת</note> and *Te* <note>original Hebrew: תֵּא</note>. One is a particle of "excellent demonstration" which is called *ha* <note>the Hebrew definite article "the," used for emphasis</note>, and the other is of "all-encompassing comprehension," which is composed of *Aleph*, the first element of the alphabet, and *Thau*, the last. This is what the Greeks mean by Alpha and Omega, and the Romans by "stem and stern" <note>original: *prora et puppis*, a Latin idiom meaning from beginning to end</note>. Through these, God is seen throughout the heavens to embrace all things that are excellently simple and spiritual—from *Aleph* to *Thau*, that is, from the first to the last—and likewise through the earth, from "head to heel" <note>meaning from top to bottom</note>, he embraces all things that are excellently corporeal and the contents within them. Nevertheless, each individual thing exists in that one Beginning as a single created entity. Just as Ezekiel’s "wheel within a wheel" <note>referring to the mystical vision in the Book of Ezekiel 1:16</note> was seen to be a single likeness of the glory of the Lord despite all its intricate turnings, so too—to use the very words of **Rabbi Saadia** in his book *Amunoth* <note>Saadia Gaon (882–942); his book *Sefer Emunot ve-De'ot* or *The Book of Beliefs and Opinions*</note>, that is, *Of Beliefs*: "Like the yolk in the middle of the egg" <note>original Hebrew: כחלמון בתוך ביצת / *k’chalmon b’toch beitzah*</note>. Or, as I myself am accustomed to say, it is like the yolk of a single egg, which is gathered together and held by the white, and contained within the firmament of the shell. In this same way, that first "intelligible world" <note>the realm of pure spirit and thought</note> enfolds the second [the sensible world], so that its entire power is governed from there. Thus it happens that both are bound together by the chains of harmony, to such an extent that they often exchange their own natures and the names of their contents with mutual freedom.

For in the second world—that is, the sensible world <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note>—nine spheres are moved by the immobile Empyrean <note>the highest, most spiritual heaven</note>, over which **Metattron** <note>a high-ranking angel in Jewish mysticism who governs the material world</note> presides with constant care; but in the first world [the intelligible], nine choirs of angels are moved by the immobile God. Just as in the immobile silence, the Creator of all things created all things at once, he later set each individual thing into its own distinct form by speaking with a ninefold discourse <note>referring to the nine times "God said" appears in the creation narrative of Genesis</note>. Conversely, the elements are named: fire is called *Seraph*, air is called *Cherub*, water is *Tharsis*, and earth is *Ariel*. Those things that exist in the lower world are found in a much better form in the higher worlds. For this reason, these lower things can be fittingly called the "true examples" and the shadowed images, signs, marks, and symbols of the heavenly things. Through these, we are moved to think about the super-celestial and angelic substances, powers, and operations, following a path of abstraction or imitation, or by some other reason and method possible for us while we are still clothed in flesh.

From this, they establish two Paradises: one celestial and the other terrestrial. In these, both the earthly man and the heavenly man may receive the rewards for their virtues. In the earth of this world, as long as he lives as a guest in the body—as if in some corruptible "garden of pleasure"—he may gain glory, honor, joy, gladness, and every desire for his own delight because of some heroic or pre-eminent virtue praised by the children of this age. Yet these things are but shadows and fleeting things, like smoke. But in the "celestial earth"—and more truly the "super-celestial" land of the living where the unfading paradise of eternal beauty exists—to the soul of the man who once lived rightly according to virtue in his mortal life and is now stripped of the body, that most merciful, greatest, and best God shows "every good." This is something he could not even have seen before, burdened as he was by the heavy and dense corpse of a dark body. In both the **Kabbalah** and the **Talmud**, this is called *Aspaklaria* <note>original Hebrew: איספקלריא, a term derived from the Latin *specularia*, meaning a mirror or lens through which divine light is perceived</note>...

<summary>This page explores the Kabbalistic doctrine of the "Two Worlds," using the Hebrew alphabet and the analogy of an egg to explain how the spiritual realm governs and reflects the physical realm. It describes the hierarchies of angels and spheres, concluding with the distinction between the fleeting rewards of the earthly paradise and the eternal divine vision (Aspaklaria) in the celestial paradise.</summary>

<page-num>754</page-num>
# KABBALAH #

*Ham'irah* <note>original Hebrew: הַמְּאִירָה</note>, that is, the **Illuminating Speculation**, which is to say "making visible." This is what you call the "intuitive knowledge of God," as it is something that happens to the blessed soul through the light of glory. Those who have pondered this most deeply approve of it as the only true state of blessedness. For there is another kind of knowledge that occurs through natural forms, which is not the state of blessedness; this is called *Istakhlarya she-eino Ham'irah* <note>original Hebrew: אסתקל ריא שאינו המאירה</note>, which means **Contemplation that is not illuminating**.

Now indeed, when the clear vision of God and the perpetual enjoyment of divinity are granted to the highest part of man—the intellect and the will—the blessed are gifted with them. Therefore, by the highest right, these things happen to no one except in the supreme world. As the Kabbalists say: "Before he attains this vision, his soul departs from him" <note>original Hebrew: שֶׁיַּשִּׂיג לָרְאִיָּה תִּפָּרֵד נַפְשׁוֹ מֵעָלָיו / *she-yashig la-re'iyah tipared nafsho me-alav*</note>. For this reason, if God is ever said to be seen by a mortal man, it is thought to happen through the agency of an angel, "in the appearances of angels" <note>original Hebrew: בְּמַרְאוֹת הַמַּלְאָכִים / *be-mar'ot ha-malakhim*</note>, as **Nachmanides** <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, a 13th-century Sephardic scholar and mystic; original: *Rabban Gerundensis*</note> writes in his commentary on Exodus.

Wherefore, on account of the double happiness of man—both spiritual and corporal—and for the retribution of a double reward, they assert there is a double Paradise, as you have heard. They say: "And its gardens are twofold <note>original Hebrew: וגנתותיו יומים / *u-ginotav yomayim*</note>, all of which you see in the Work of Creation <note>original: *Beresith*</note>; they are all arranged according to the intellectual and superior forms." I feel this way even regarding the gold of Havilah, the bdellium and the onyx stone <note>referring to the riches of Eden in Genesis 2:11-12</note>, and all other gems of infinite price.

In the same way and for the same reason, the Kabbalists asserted that a double Gehenna—that is, two underworlds—were designated: one for the upper and one for the lower world. These exist to torture wicked bodies in time, and wicked souls in eternity. A common name has been given to this place: *Arka* <note>original Hebrew: אֲרְקָא</note>. This is the place of Tartarean punishment which, among other things, contains seven monstrous receptacles of the harshest punishments, destined for those guilty of crimes by the just judgment of God.

Thus that Kabbalist in the *Garden of the Nut* <note>the *Ginat Egoz*, a foundational Kabbalistic work by Joseph Gikatilla</note>, in his second volume, treats the seven dwellings of the infernal regions in these words: "One: there is both an upper and lower Gehenna; one for the body in this world, and another for the soul in the world to come after this. And the place encompassing all these is called *Arka*, for in it are: Gehenna, the Gates of Death, the Shadow of Death, the Pit of Destruction, the Miry Clay, Perdition, and the Abyss <note>original Hebrew: גיהנם ושערי מות וצלמות ובאר שחת וטיט היון ואבדון ושאול / *Gehinnom, Sha'arei Mavet, Tzalmavet, Be'er Shachat, Tit ha-Yaven, Avaddon, and She'ol*</note>." 

Thus far the words of **Joseph of Castile** <note>Joseph Gikatilla (1248–1305), a major figure in Spanish Kabbalah</note>. Now these chains, this prison, these shackles, this servitude, and this captivity of sinners remain—for bodies in the present world as well as for souls in the future world—so that the just may be accompanied by the fair rewards of virtue, and the wicked may be followed by the deserved torments of vice. For what else is owed to the pious but life and honor? What else to the wicked but death and horror? Yet this is not only to be understood in a temporal sense, but as the Kabbalists intend it, intellectually; for they write: "Even in their death, the righteous are called living" <note>original Hebrew: אֲפִילוּ בְּמִיתָתָן קְרוּאִים חַיִּים / *afilu be-mitatan keru'im chayyim*, a famous Talmudic maxim</note>.

<header>BOOK 1.</header>

**The righteous, even in their death, are called living; and the wicked, even in their life, are called dead.** <note>original Hebrew: צדיקים אפילו במיתתם קרואים חיים ורשעים אפילו בחייהם קרואים מתים / *Tzadikim afilu be-mitatam keruim hayyim ve-reshaim afilu be-hayyehem keruim metim*</note> That is to say, the just are said to be alive even when they die, and the wicked are said to be dead even while they live. To those skilled in the Kabbalah, God’s sentence will not be obscure: *On the day you eat of it, you shall die* <note>Genesis 2:17</note>. Specifically, this refers not to a physical death, but a spiritual one. For Adam lived more than nine hundred years after eating the forbidden fruit; yet, in the very moment he transgressed the law, he died. In his sin, I say, he became a source of contagion to the entire human race and to all future offspring, who were destined for the eternal dwellings of the lower regions.

This remained the case until, by God’s decree, the Messiah should come—that Redeemer who would lead man back into paradise. This paradise is not a terrestrial one, but a heavenly one; he would restore to the children the life which the parent had lost—an eternal life, not a temporary one, belonging to the soul rather than the body. This life is that very intimacy with God and that most joyful sight of divinity, which is filled with every possible delight. 

It is in this Messiah that all true Kabbalists (not the deceptive ones) fix and place all their trust. To him they direct all the saving prophecies of the Holy Scriptures: those concerning the Promised Land, the city of Jerusalem "which is bound firmly together" <note>Psalm 122:3</note>, the mountain of God, His holy place, the holy way, the sanctuary, the courts of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the house of the Lord, the gate of the Lord, and many other similar things. **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Also known as Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> in his *Mishneh* <term>Mishneh Torah: Maimonides' code of Jewish law; the name literally means "Repetition of the Law" or "Deuteronomy"</term> also intended these to be understood as referring to heavenly beatitude.

For this reason, we often and greatly contend with the **Talmudists** <term>Talmudists: Scholars focused on the legal and traditional discussions of the Talmud, often interpreted here as favoring literal/physical meanings over mystical ones</term>, and we frequently split into two opposing opinions. They try to refer the entire liberation of King Messiah to a release from physical captivity—or more accurately, our dispersion. They look for the noise and din of arms, military expeditions, the conquest of regions, the devastation of lands, and the victory of an Israelite army, just as we read happened to our ancestors under the savior Moses against the Canaanites and Palestinians. Or, at the very least, they look for some ingenious means of escape such as they have found in other liberations—though they have now been dispersed and exiled for so many centuries under so many kingdoms: seventy years under the Babylonians, fifty-four under the Persians, one hundred and thirty under the Greeks, and now one thousand four hundred years under the Romans, and yet there is no end in sight.

We, on the contrary, in my judgment, believe more correctly according to the Kabbalah that the Messiah is to come to liberate the wretched mortals of the human race from the chains of original injustice <note>The author is referring to Original Sin</note>, to forgive sins, and to save the souls of those piously serving God. These souls were excluded from eternal life in the person of our father Adam until the satisfaction of the Messiah. In order to fulfill the justice of a merciful and kind God, the Messiah must reach out his hand and take from the Tree of Life and eat of it, so that through him we may live forever. This satisfaction was not meant to occur through royal pomp, nor the boasting of honor and glory, because the original sin to be expiated by the Messiah sprouted from pride and self-exaltation. Instead, it must occur in humility and endurance—not with chariots and horses, but in the name of the Lord our God; and not in victory, nor in human triumph—

...triumph, but in labor, fasting, vigils, strength of soul, contempt for vain glory, compassionate mercy, a special love for God, a right love for fellow men, and finally in that heroic, liberal, and spontaneous death. For vice is fought with virtue alone; no wise man has ever valued highly the power, princely genealogies, or crowns of this world. Indeed, this is what it means to be wise: to despise the glory of this world, since when the glorious rich man dies, he will not take everything with him (as the Psalmist says <note>Psalm 49:17</note>), nor will his glory descend with him. Therefore, whatever is written in the sacred scriptures about trophies and the subjection of peoples—while the history of what took place remains true—is understood by the Kabbalists to refer to the intellectual world and supernal powers. Thus, the future King Messiah will, by the best right, neglect and even despise these light and abject follies of this world—its honors and kingdoms—as vain and foolish. He comes to abolish the guilt of the human species and to open a path for virtue.

Hence, if we are led by right reason, the Messiah himself will be recognized from that noble chapter of Isaiah <note>Isaiah 52:13–53:12</note> alone, which begins <term>Behold, my servant shall understand</term> <note>original Hebrew: הנה ישכיל עבדי / *Hineh yaskil avdi*</note> and ends <term>and he shall intercede for the transgressors</term> <note>original Hebrew: ולפשעים יפגיע / *ve-la-posheim yapgia*</note>. Regarding this, I marvel more than can be said—and not without a unique sense of shame on behalf of men of foreign nations (I speak to you alone in confidence)—that Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, a famous 11th-century French rabbi</note> and David Kimhi <note>Radak, a 12th-13th century grammarian and exegete</note>, and other men who are not at all unlearned in the more recent sect, have out of some faint-heartedness, or perhaps shame before the nations, interpreted that entire context of Isaiah as referring only to the [Jewish] people now scattered everywhere. This is despite the fact that it is most clearly prophesied concerning the Messiah, as the Chaldean translation of Jonathan <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Prophets</note> expresses by name, saying: <term>Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper</term> <note>original Aramaic: הא יצלח עבדי משיחא / *Ha yatzlah avdi Meshicha*</note>. 

This is the one truly seen by Isaiah in the prophetic spirit in that place: a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity, a man with a hidden face, a man of no honest reputation, touched by a divine stroke, despised and shunned, shorn like a lamb, slain like a sheep, cut off from the land of the living, counted among the wicked, and inglorious among the sons of men. But what of him among the sons of God? Clearly, he is greatly exalted, elevated, and shining exceedingly. For who shall tell of his generation? The will of the Lord God is directed by his hand, and the Lord has abolished in him the iniquity of us all, because he struck him for the crime of the people. For he himself was wounded for our crimes and bruised for our iniquities—he who certainly never committed iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. But the Lord willed the crushing of his countenance. Therefore, since he himself is the righteous servant of God, he shall justify many through the knowledge of himself; he shall bear their iniquity, take away the sins of many, and intercede for sinners. Isaiah told all these things about the true Messiah, and truly he did not lie. This is firmly that [congruence]...

Israel, according to the opinion of the Kabbalists, and that salvation of our God so often promised—that we might be justified **by his knowledge** <note>original Hebrew: *be-da’ato* (Isaiah 53:11). The OCR reads *be-ra'ato*, likely a scribal error for "knowledge."</note>, that is, in the knowing of him—not so that we may be saved in tumult or in flight, but standing together under one king and in one army of faith, we may be set free in the death and knowledge of the Messiah. This knowledge ends sin and removes the obstacle to the clear vision of God: that is, the original and contagious guilt of the human race. Concerning this, we read in the book of Kabbalah on faith and expiation: **A way demonstrating the emanated or infused power, which is a created power led by the seven variations, which are the thirteen orders of expiation by which the world is directed, until sin is finished and the Messiah comes, who is the power of God. And in the power of grace, which is the angelic power, and in the power emanated and infused from it, which is the power of the prophet, the spirit of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton <note>The four-letter holy name of God (YHWH), often substituted with "Lord" in English.</note>, shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. Behold the seven variations by which the Messiah conducts himself to do good for the righteous and to destroy the wicked with a blessing: By the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked.** <note>Isaiah 11:2-4. This passage describes the seven-fold spirit of God resting on the Messiah.</note>

That is, a way demonstrating the power that is granted or infused, which as a created power is guided by seven variations. These are the **thirteen orders of expiation** <note>Referring to the *Thirteen Attributes of Mercy* from Exodus 34:6–7, central to Jewish liturgy and Kabbalistic thought.</note> by which the world is governed until sin is ended and the Messiah, who is the power of God, arrives. And by the power of grace (which is the power of angels) and the power emanated and infused from it (which is the power of a prophet), the spirit of the Lord—the Tetragrammaton—shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and intellect, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. Behold the seven variations which the Messiah uses to benefit the good and destroy the evil, according to what is written: *And with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked.* These are the words of the aforementioned Kabbalistic volume, by which we are warned that the King Messiah conquers the adversaries of God's people not by hand but by mouth, not with weapons but with the spirit. He gives the sevenfold grace of God to the pious and slays the wicked—all of this by the "spirit of his mouth," which is his spiritual doctrine. This doctrine he will scatter and sow among all nations through just and chosen men, the righteous disciples. Regarding this, the prophecy of Isaiah referring to the time of the Messiah—*You shall draw waters from the wells of the Savior* <note>Isaiah 12:3</note>—was interpreted into Aramaic by Jonathan son of Uzziel <note>The author of the *Targum Jonathan*, a famous Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets.</note> with these words: **And you shall receive a new doctrine in joy from the chosen ones of the righteous.** <note>original Aramaic: *ve-tekabbelun ulpan hadat be-hedvah mi-behirei tzidkaya*</note> Truly, that is the "new doctrine": that the true light shines, and he who hates is in darkness, while he who loves dwells in the light. Therefore, the end of the commandments is this: that we love one another in the doctrine of the Messiah, **who will teach the peoples to walk in the paths of the Tetragrammaton** <note>original Hebrew: *she-yoreh ha-ammim lalechet be-darchei YHWH*</note>, as Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A medieval biblical scholar known as the Radak (1160–1235).</note> writes concerning that same prophet in the fifty-first chapter on the verse *for a law shall go forth from me*—which, of course, whoever follows shall be saved, and whoever despises shall perish. For the old things are of fear, but the new are of charity—**of upright love from a whole heart** <note>original Hebrew: *shel ahavah yesharah mi-lev shalem*</note>—according to our masters. Therefore, the Messiah shall be an example of life for all who are to be set free. Upon him depends the salvation of the entire world, which is called eternal salvation and is explained by our teachers as lasting "through all the days of the ages," where it is read: *Israel is saved in the Lord with a salvation*
