eternal. Concerning this, something is written in the book *Kabbalah Hakkadmah* <note>The "Ancient Kabbalah," likely referring to a specific foundational text in the Jewish mystical tradition.</note>:

->**This is the secret of the Messiah who shall come quickly in our days, whose entire operation shall be through the name YH; and these are YH which is YHU and the seventh day, and this name is his perfect name, and all the work shall be completed through his hand.**<- <note>Original Hebrew: *Zeh-hu sod ha-Mashiach she-yavo bimherah ve-yamenu...*</note>

That is: And this is the secret of the King Messiah who will come quickly in our days, whose entire operation will begin in the letters *u. h.* and also *i. h.* <note>The author uses Latin letters to represent the Hebrew letters of the Tetragrammaton: Y (i), H (h), W (u), H (h). Thus, *i.h.u.h.* refers to YHWH.</note> which is the mystery of the seventh day; and this name is his integral name, and every work shall be perfected in his hand. Behold, it is defined by the wise Kabbalists that all things are to be perfected through the Messiah, and his entire operation is performed through the most sacred four letters **i. h. u. h.** <term>Tetragrammaton (The four-letter holy name of God, YHWH)</term> in the mystery of the seventh day. This refers not to the literal number of days so named, but to the transition from the active life to the **contemplative life**—that is, in the very quietude of the soul and peaceful tranquility, by withdrawing from the excessive anxieties of this world and from servile labor <note>original: *cementarijs operibus*, literally "masonry works," a metaphor for heavy manual or worldly toil.</note>. For it is written: *And he rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had done.*

However, although many <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> attribute various names to this King—as can be understood from the citations of many doctors in the book *Sanhedrin*, in the section *Helek* <note>A famous portion of the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a-99a) that discusses the Messiah.</note>, cited from the chapter where it is written: *And Rabbi Yohanan said: What is the name of the Messiah?* To which place Rabbi Eliezer responded, saying: *The Days of the Messiah.* And later in many of their writings, such as the commentaries on the Song of the Synagogue <note>Likely referring to the Song of Solomon or liturgical poems.</note>:

->**Shiloh, Yinon, David, Haninah, Sprout, Righteous, Comforter.**<- <note>Original Hebrew: *Shiloh, Yinon, David, Haninah, Tzemach, Tzaddik, Menachem.* These are traditional titles for the Messiah derived from various biblical verses.</note>

These names of the Messiah are explained as Shiloh, Yinon, David, Haninah, Sprout, Righteous, and Comforter; yet these individuals are considered to be descriptive titles or symbolic names, much like the seven examples recounted there, which are: the Ark, the Mercy Seat, the Tables of the Law, the Rod of Aaron, the Jar of Manna, and the Spirit of God.

But according to the Kabbalists, you have heard how this one **ineffable name i. h. u. h.** is proper to the Messiah, which will integrate and perfect his substantive name. For they teach that it must be believed that this is his integral name, which is piously and holily integrated into "mercies." No Talmudist would stealthily deny this, since that great master in the aforementioned place in the Talmud said that the name of the Messiah will come to be called similarly to *Hanina*, that is, **mercy**, citing a verse from Jeremiah 16. However, the Romans <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate translation used by the Catholic Church.</note> read this verse loosely and improperly as: *who will not give you rest.* But that is not an etymological interpretation. For in my judgment it should be read more correctly as: *because I will not give you mercy.* Jonathan the Chaldean <note>Refers to Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated this as *rachamin*, that is, **mercies**. It is as if he wanted to say, according to the Talmudists: because you walk in the depravity of your heart, so that you do not hear God, there will be no Messiah—who is named "Mercies"—for you. By this, it clearly becomes known that **in mercies** <note>Original Hebrew: *be-rachamim*</note> from the midst of **i. h. u. h.**, the name shall be the proper name of the Savior Messiah. His dignity and office, although it consists of rigor and severity according to the prophecy of King David expressed without any controversy regarding the Messiah himself—*He shall judge your people,* he says, *in justice, and your poor in judgment*—nevertheless, because judgment, that is, **in judgment** <note>Original Hebrew: *be-mishpat*</note> according to...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 758 regarding the mystical name of the Messiah. It focuses on how the Messiah reconciles divine justice with mercy, specifically through the integration of the letter "Shin" into the holy four-letter name of God (the Tetragrammaton).</meta>

<page-num>759</page-num>
<header>BOOK I.</header>

All Kabbalists also admit mercy alongside justice. For so it is read in the *Gates of Light* <note>original: *Portæ lucis*, referring to Joseph Gikatilla’s *Sha'arei Orah*, a foundational Kabbalistic text.</note>, chapter 4: <note>original Hebrew: כי המשפט חציו דין וחציו חסד</note> "For judgment is half rigor and half mercy." That is, that judgment is partly rigor and partly mercy, by which means the reconciliation of the first fall—through a renewed union and a certain new betrothal of the people with God—is to occur, as Hosea foretold: *I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in judgment; in mercy and in compassion*, where the word <note>original Hebrew: ברחמים (*be-rachamim*)</note> "in mercies" is placed. Lest anyone think, therefore, that the very arrival of the Messiah is destined by some legal necessity rather than from mere grace and the most liberal gift of God, the illustrious name of "mercy" will be rightly bestowed upon this Savior. This name will be composed of letters—both vowels and a consonant—that signify only mercy and nothing else besides.

And we conjecture this will occur through the holy four letters <term>Tetragrammaton (The four-letter name of God, YHWH)</term> by which the Ineffable is depicted as if by signs and symbols, and through the consonant **Shin**, by which the Ineffable name is spoken <note>Reuchlin argues that adding the letter *Shin* (s) to the silent name *Y-H-W-H* makes it pronounceable as *Ye-h-o-sh-u-ah* (Jesus).</note>. For it is commonplace in Kabbalah that this sign **Shin** is explained as <note>original Hebrew: ש"ץ (*Sh. Tz.*)</note> through <term>Notarikon (A Kabbalistic system of shorthand where letters of a word stand for entire phrases)</term> as <note>original Hebrew: שפתי יחיה בצדק (*Siftei yichyeh be-tzedek*)</note> "My lips shall live in righteousness." That is: the Tetragrammaton name is called out, which is to say, it is pronounced. There are no other letters by which bare mercy alone is designated except these five: **i. h. u. h.** <note>The Latin equivalent of the Hebrew Y-H-W-H.</note> and the consonant **Shin**, which is **s**. Regarding the four vowels <note>In this context, the author treats the letters of the divine name as "vowels" or "soul-letters" that give life to the language.</note> in the book *Gates of Justice* <note>original: *Portarum Iustitiæ*, referring to the *Sha'arei Tzedek*.</note>, it is read: <note>original Hebrew: וזהו סוד שאמזול' כי הנה יהוה יוצא ממקומו יוצא ממדת רחמים</note> "And this is the mystery that our Masters (may their memory be in peace) said: 'For behold, the Lord [YHWH] comes out of His place'—He comes out from the attribute of mercy." That is: And this is the mystery which our Masters spoke of, that behold, the four-lettered name (as Micah says), **i. h. u. h.**, will go forth from its place; it will go forth through the property of compassions.

Regarding the consonant **Shin**, all Kabbalists who are not ignorant of Kabbalistic <term>Gematria (The practice of calculating the numerical value of Hebrew words to find hidden meanings)</term> will not deny that the letter **Shin** contains within itself the ratio of the entire four-lettered name according to arithmetic proportion; they will also agree that the same attribute of clemency and mercy is possessed by it. Therefore, the salvation of all men is to be expected from the mercy of God alone, which Habakkuk openly expressed when addressing God: *When you are angry, you will remember mercy*. Where David Camhi—whom our people call Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical exegete.</note> (just as some pronounce it *Rabbi*, and in Germany they say *Ribi*, through the easy conversion of the vowel *a* into *i*, as a similar judgment exists among the Greeks and Latins; for their grammarians say *logikoi*, we say *logica*, they say *mitir*, we say *mater*, so too *Samson* becomes *Simson*, and *Camhi* becomes *Kimhi*, and many others)—that man, I say, David the Spanish Jew, teaches that through the name <note>original Hebrew: רחם (*rechem*)</note> "mercy" placed there, it must be understood Kabbalistically (that is, symbolically) according to arithmetic proportion as **Abraham**. It is as if Habakkuk were saying: "O God, when you are touched by the anger of our sin, remember the seed of Abraham, to whom you promised that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed." And again: "O God, you spoke to him, saying 'All the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed.'" But so that Habakkuk himself might indicate what that seed would be, he added: *You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Messiah*, where the same Master Kimhi writes: <note>original Hebrew: הוא משיח בן דוד (*Hu Mashiach ben David*)</note> "This is [the Messiah, the son of David]..."

# CABALA

...is the Messiah, son of David. Therefore, I say with the wise Kabbalists that all our true salvation depends on the Messiah, as many of us as reach for it. Hence it happens that we strive to detach ourselves from all created things as much as we can, to ascend through all grades and migrate into him, so that we might at least follow him, or certainly enter through his gate, according to the strength of each individual. For he is our very one, to whose coming the whole law is intellectually referred by us—and not only the scripture of Moses, but also the writings of the prophets and whatever is contained in the <term>Hagiographa (The "Holy Writings," referring to the third section of the Hebrew Bible, including Psalms and Proverbs)</term>. For the entire text which we call the <note>original: *Essrim Varba*, transliterating the Hebrew *Esrim Ve-Arba*</note> **Twenty-Four**, and which you call the **Bible**, we encompass entirely under the name <note>original: תורה (*Torah*)</note> **Torah**, that is, the Law. As it says in Daniel, chapter 9: *By walking in the law of the Lord our God, which he set before us by the hand of his servants the prophets.* 

We have determined this scripture alone to be so stable and so firm that we can safely found all our thoughts upon it, and the most profound contemplations of speculative men may move through it without confusion. This is because it was proclaimed by the voice of the highest God, and because it is accustomed to work with such great energies in the minds of the most contemplative men. Through it, we are able to ascend from any mixture to simple things, from simple things to the simplest, from effects to causes, and finally from the lower world to the higher—from the higher world to the Messiah, who is the highest object of our mind and conceivable in the final degree as the King of the ages. Through him, we may finally pass plainly into the incomprehensible God. 

Furthermore, through these sacred letters—as if by **Jacob's ladder**, whose top touches the heavens and upon which God himself leans—angels ascend and descend. They are the carriers of prayers from here and gifts from there, carrying help back and forth, as certain of your own writers have said. Indeed, I feel there is nothing else that could be imagined to weave our soul more closely to God, like a connecting thread, than this very sacred scripture of which we speak. It leads us first into a divine admiration; then into an acknowledgment of those things according to human capacity; and finally into that most burning love for the divinity known in whatever way, displaying the most certain effect of hope. 

Through this, with **Ezekiel’s** living creatures and wheels, we are lifted from the earth, so that we may go when they go and stand when they stand. This is the only field of true contemplation; its every word is a sacrament, and its every speech, jot, and tittle <note>original: *apices, punctaq;* referring to the minute decorative crowns and vowel points in Hebrew scrolls</note> is full of secret meanings—as not only our own people but even Christians attest. This is the **Kabbalah** which does not allow us to grovel on the ground, but lifts our mind to the highest goal of comprehension. Yet even this cannot rationally transcend the soul of the Messiah, except by a certain incomprehensible intuition, like a momentary rapture. By this, we Kabbalists believe it is not impossible for us to be snatched up in spirit nearly to the third world, where the Messiah is present for all...

# BOOK 1.

...flowing into the lower things. For in the most general numbering of the world, there are three. The first is material, the second is formal, and the third is formless. Or, if you prefer it this way: I say the first is the lowest, which is the sensible world; the second is the supreme and mental, which is the intelligible world; and the third is <note>original: ὑπερώτατος (*hyperōtatos*)</note> **super-supreme**, or if one may say, the most supreme, incomparable, and divine. I have chosen to consider this corporeal world as the first in relation to us, as it stands beneath the others—perhaps in a reversed order, for by right reason in the category of causes it ought to have been last, acting as a receptacle for all higher things. This world is composed first of the heavens and celestial beings, second of the elements and things made of elements, and third of human nature and individual men, who are called in Hebrew <note>original: עוֹלָם הַקָּטָן (*Olam ha-Katan*)</note> **the Small World**, in Greek <note>original: μιϰρόϰοσμος (*mikrokosmos*)</note> **Microcosm**, and in Latin **the little world**. This entire body, as your Aristotle pleases in his book *On the World*, is a globe composed of heaven and earth and the natures contained within them; indeed, it possesses seven celestial dwellings and seven terrestrial dwellings. <term>Rabbi Menahem Recanati (A 14th-century Italian Kabbalist known for his mystical commentary on the Torah)</term> enumerates these in his commentary on the 25th chapter of Leviticus. Those pertaining to the heavens are: <note>original: שָׁמַיִם רָקִיעַ שְׁחָקִים זְבוּל, מָעוֹן מָכוֹן עֲרָבוֹת (*Shamayim, Rakia, Shechakim, Zevul, Maon, Machon, Arabot*)</note> **Sky, Firmament, Clouds, Dwelling, Residence, Foundation, and the Plain**. Second, those pertaining to the earth: <note>original: אֶרֶץ אַרְקָא גֵיָא יַבָּשָׁה תֵּבֵל חֶלֶד (*Eretz, Arka, Geia, Yabbashah, Tebel, Cheled*)</note> **Earth, Ground, Valley, Dry Land, Inhabited World, and the Lowly Place**. <term>Joseph of Salamanca (Likely referring to Joseph Gikatilla, a major Spanish Kabbalist)</term> also recited by name the seven dwellings of the lower regions in his *Garden of Nuts* (as you heard a little earlier). Regarding the **Microcosm**, it is no secret to any of us that seven things pertain to the human condition, in whichever direction you look: these are the body, the soul, and the composite of these which we call <note>original: נֶפֶשׁ (*Nefesh*)</note> **Being** (or Soul), as in the words of the King of Sodom: <note>original: תֶּן לִי הַנֶּפֶשׁ (*Ten li ha-nefesh*)</note> **Give me the person**—that is, the human being composed of the four powers of the soul and the four qualities of the greater world. This world, since it is truly animated, is illuminated by its own mind, which is called **Metattron** <note>Metatron is often described in Kabbalah as the "Prince of the Presence" or the celestial scribe who governs the lower worlds</note>. 

The second world is the supreme world of the "separate intelligences," which are called by the Kabbalists <note>original: שְׂכָלִים נִפְרָרִים (*Sekhalim Nifradim*)</note> **separate intellects**, and by the Hebrew philosophers <note>original: דֵּעוֹת נִפְרָדוֹת (*Deot Nifradot*)</note> **separate minds**. That world is full of species, forms, liberated minds, and angels; it is embraced, surrounded, and governed by the soul of the **Messiah** itself. Among the Kabbalists, this soul is the "idealized Idea" of all lives, to which every individual, specific, and generic vitality is referred. From there, as if from a nursery, all life is drawn, and it is named by the Kabbalists the **Land of the Living**. <note>original: לְפִיכָר דָרְשׁוּ בַּפָּסוּק תּוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה לְמִינָהּ זוֹ נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ (*Lefikhakh darshu ba-pasuk totze ha-aretz nefesh chayah le-minah, zo nefesh shel Mashiach*)</note> **Therefore they comment on the verse: "Let the earth bring forth the living creature [soul] according to its kind"—this is the soul of the Messiah.** These words are read thus in the <term>*Porta Lucis* ("The Gates of Light," or *Sha'are Orah*, a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla)</term> in the second chapter: "Just as in the human world, which is called the Microcosm, the mind rules the soul of man, so **Metattron** rules the celestial world, the soul of the **Messiah** rules the angelic world, and **Adonai** (the Lord) rules the incomparable world." Furthermore, just as the light of the mind is the "active intellect," so the light of Metattron is **Shaddai** (Almighty), the light of the Messiah's soul is **El Chai** (the Living God), and the light of **Adonai** is **En Soph** (the Infinite). And since he is the most expert in the nature of things...

is the Messiah, son of David. I say therefore, with the wise Kabbalists, that the entirety of our true salvation depends upon the Messiah, for as many of us as reach out to him. From this it follows that we should strive to detach ourselves from all created things as much as possible, and attempt to ascend through all grades and migrate into him, so that we may at least follow him, or certainly attain him, according to each man’s strength. For he is the one to whom our every law is intellectually referred—and not only the scripture of Moses, but also the writings of the prophets and whatever is contained in the Hagiographa <note>original: "Hagiographis," referring to the *Ketuvim* or "Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>. Through this Scripture, along with **Ezekiel’s** living creatures and wheels, we are lifted from the earth, so that when they go, we go, and when they stand, we stand. This is the only field of true contemplation, where every single word is a mystery, and every single speech, syllable, tip of a letter, and its points are full of secret meanings—not only according to our traditions, but also by the testimony of Christians. This is the Kabbalah which does not allow us to dwell on the ground, but extols our mind to the highest goal of comprehension; yet it cannot rationally transcend the soul of the Messiah, except by a certain incomprehensible intuition, like a path of momentary rapture. By this rapture, we Kabbalists believe it is not impossible to be caught up in the spirit nearly to the third world, where the Messiah is [flowing into] <note>The Latin "inf[ra]" with catchword "re" forms "influere," meaning to flow in or influence</note> all things.

-># CABALA<-

...is the Messiah, son of David. I say, therefore, along with the wise Kabbalists, that all our true salvation depends on the Messiah, for as many of us as reach out to him. By this, it happens that we should release ourselves as much as possible from all created things and strive to ascend through all degrees and migrate into him, so that we may at least follow him, or certainly attain him, according to each man's manly effort. For he is our very self, toward whose coming every law is intellectually referred by us—and not only the scripture of Moses, but also the books of the Prophets and whatever is contained in the <term>Hagiographa</term> <note>The "Holy Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible, including Psalms, Proverbs, and Daniel.</note>. For that entire text which we call <term>Twenty-Four</term> <note>original: "Esrim Varba" (Esrim Ve-Arba). This refers to the 24 books of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, and which you call the Bible, I say we designate the whole thing by the name of the Law of <term>the Lord</term> <note>original: "יהוה" (YHWH). The author identifies the divine name itself with the Law.</note>. As in Daniel, chapter 9: *By walking in the law of the Lord our God, which he set before us by the hand of his servants the prophets.*

This scripture alone we have determined to be so stable and so firm that we can safely found all our thoughts upon it, and the firm contemplations of speculative men [can be founded] without confusion; partly because it was promulgated by the voice of the highest God, and partly because it is accustomed to work with such energies in the minds of the most contemplative men. Through it, we are able to ascend from whatever mixed things to the simple, from the simple to the most simple, from effects to causes, and finally from the lower world to the higher—from the higher to the Messiah, who becomes the highest object of our mind and is perceivable at the final degree as the King of Ages. Through him, we may finally pass plainly into the incomprehensible God. 

Furthermore, through these sacred letters, as if by <term>Jacob's ladder</term> <note>Referencing Genesis 28:12, a ladder reaching to heaven used by angels.</note>—whose top touches the heavens and upon which God himself rests—the angels ascend and descend. These are the carriers of prayers from here and gifts from there, who carry help back and forth, as some of your own [authors] say. And truly, I feel there is nothing else that could even be imagined to weave our soul more closely to God, like a connecting thread, than this same Sacred Scripture mentioned here. It first leads us into divine admiration; then into an acknowledgment of those things according to human capacity; and finally into that most burning love for the divinity, however it is known, displaying the most certain effect of hope. 

Through this, with <term>Ezekiel’s living creatures and wheels</term> <note>A reference to the "Merkabah" or Chariot vision in Ezekiel 1, central to Jewish mysticism.</note>, we are lifted from the earth, so that we may go when they go and stand when they stand. This is the only field of true contemplation, whose individual words are each sacraments, and whose individual speeches, syllables, flourishes, and points are full of secret meanings—attested not only by our writers, but also by Christians. This is the Kabbalah which does not allow one to dwell on the ground, but extols our mind to the highest goal of understanding. Yet, the mind cannot rationally transcend the soul of the Messiah, except by a certain incomprehensible intuition, like a way of momentary rapture, by which we think it is not impossible for us Kabbalists to be snatched up in spirit near the <term>third world</term> <note>In this context, the world of pure intellect or divinity (Atziluth) above the celestial and material realms.</note>, where the Messiah is in all...

# BOOK 1.

...influences. For there are three worlds in the most general sense. The first is **material**, the second is **formal**, and the third is **formless**. Or, if you prefer it this way: the first I call the lowest, which is also the sensible world <note>The world perceived by the senses.</note>; the second is the supreme and mental world, which is also the intelligible <note>The world perceived by the intellect.</note>; and the third is *hyperousios* <note>original: "ὑπερούσιος" — meaning "beyond essence" or "super-substantial."</note>, that is, the super-supreme, or if I may say, the most supreme, incomparable, and divine.

I have chosen to consider this corporeal world as the "first" in relation to us, as it stands below the others—perhaps in a reversed order, for by right reason in the category of causes it ought to have been the last, serving as a receptacle for all higher things. This world is constituted, first, of the heavens and celestial things; second, of the elements and things made of elements; and third, of human nature and individual men, who are called in Hebrew **the little world** <note>original: "עולם הקטן" (Olam ha-Katan)</note>, in Greek **microcosm** <note>original: "μικρόκοσμος"</note>, and in Latin *parvus mundus*.

This entire body of the universe, as your Aristotle pleases in his book *On the World*, is a globe constituted of heaven and earth and the natures contained within them, indeed with seven celestial habitations and seven terrestrial habitations. Rabbi Menahem Recanati enumerates these in the 25th chapter of Leviticus with these names:

### The Seven Heavens
1. **The Heavens** <note>original: "שמים" (Shamayim)</note>
2. **The Firmament** <note>original: "רקיע" (Rakia)</note>
3. **The Clouds** <note>original: "שחקים" (Shehakim)</note>
4. **The Abode** <note>original: "זבול" (Zevul)</note>
5. **The Dwelling** <note>original: "מעון" (Ma'on)</note>
6. **The Residence** <note>original: "מכון" (Machon)</note>
7. **The Plains** <note>original: "ערבות" (Arabot)</note>

### The Seven Earths
1. **Earth** <note>original: "ארץ" (Eretz)</note>
2. **Arka** <note>original: "ארקא"</note>
3. **Valley** <note>original: "גיא" (Gai)</note>
4. **Dry Land** <note>original: "יבשה" (Yabashah)</note>
5. **Waste** <note>original: "חרבה" (Charabah)</note>
6. **World** <note>original: "תבל" (Tebel)</note>
7. **Duration** <note>original: "חלד" (Cheled)</note>

Joseph of Salem <note>The author is referring to Joseph Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a famous Kabbalist.</note> also recited by name the seven habitations of the lower regions in his *Garden of Nuts* (as you heard a little earlier). Regarding the **Microcosm** <note>Man as a miniature reflection of the universe.</note>, it is not hidden from any of us that seven things pertain to the condition of man, in whichever part you look: these are the body, the soul, and the composite of them which we call <term>Nefesh <note>original: "נפש". While often translated as "soul," here it refers to the "living person" or "vital breath" that combines body and spirit.</note></term>. An example of this is the word of the King of Sodom: **Give me the persons** <note>original: "תן לי נפש" (Ten li nefesh) from Genesis 14:21. The author interprets this as "Give me the human beings."</note>. This is composed of the four powers of the soul and the four qualities of the greater world. Indeed, since this world is animated, it is illuminated by its own mind, which is called **Metattron** <note>Metatron is a high archangel in Kabbalistic tradition, often described as the "Prince of the Countenance" and the celestial mediator.</note>.

The second is the supreme world of the **separate intelligences** <note>Spiritual beings or angels that exist without physical bodies.</note>, which are called by the Kabbalists **separate intellects** <note>original: "שכלים נפרדים" (Sekhalim nifradim)</note>, and by the Hebrew philosophers **separate knowledges** <note>original: "דעות נפרדות" (De'ot nifradot)</note>. This world, full of species, forms, unbound minds, and angels, is embraced, surrounded, and ruled by the **Soul of the Messiah** itself. Among Kabbalists, this soul is the idealized "Idea" of all lives, to which all individual, specific, and generic vitality is referred. From there, as if from a nursery or fishpond, all life is drawn; it is named by the Kabbalists the **Land of the Living**. <note>original: "לפיכר דרשו בפסוק תוצא הארץ נפש חיה למינה זו נפש של משיח!" — "Therefore they commented on the verse: 'Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind' (Genesis 1:24)—this is the Soul of the Messiah!"</note>

These words are read thus in the second chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>The *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>: Just as in the human world, which is called the Microcosm, the mind rules over the soul of man, so **Metattron** rules over the celestial world, the **Soul of the Messiah** rules over the angelic world, and **Adonai** <note>The Lord.</note> rules over the incomparable world. Furthermore, just as the light of the mind is the **active intellect** <note>The "intellectus agens," a philosophical concept of the power that allows the human mind to grasp universal truths.</note>, so the light of Metattron is **Shaddai** <note>original: "Sadai", an Almighty name of God.</note>, and the light of the Soul of the Messiah is **Elhai** (that is, the Living God), and the light of Adonai is **En-soph** <note>original: "En-soph" (Ein Sof), meaning "The Infinite" or "Without End," referring to God's essence before manifestation.</note>. And since he is most learned in the nature of things...

# BOOK 1. 761

...flowing into the others. For there are three most general worlds. The first is material, the second is formal, and the third is formless. Or, if you prefer it this way: I say the first is the lowest, which is also the sensible world <note>The world perceived by the senses.</note>; the second is the highest and mental world, which is also the intelligible <note>The world perceived by the intellect rather than the senses.</note>; and the third is the <note>original: "ὑπερώτατος" (hyperōtatos)</note> most-supreme, or if one may say, the supremest, incomparable and divine. However, I have chosen to consider this corporeal world as the "first" in relation to us, as it stands beneath the others—perhaps in a reversed order, since by the true logic of causes it ought to have been the last, serving as a receptacle for all higher things. This world is composed, first, of the heavens and celestial beings; second, of the elements and things made of elements; third, of human nature and individual men, who are called in Hebrew <note>original: "עולם הקטן" (Olam ha-Katan)</note> "the small world," in Greek <note>original: "μικρόκοσμος" (mikrokosmos)</note> "microcosm," and in Latin *parvus mundus*. This entire body, as your Aristotle pleases to say in his book *On the Universe* <note>original: "de Mundo"</note>, is a globe composed of heaven and earth and the natures contained within them, indeed with seven celestial dwellings and seven terrestrial dwellings. Rabbi Menahem Recanati <note>A 13th-century Italian Kabbalist.</note> enumerates these in the 25th chapter of Leviticus with these names; first, those pertaining to heaven: *Shamayim, Rakia, Shachakim, Zebul* <note>Names for the various layers of the heavens in Hebrew: "Heavens," "Firmament," "Clouds," and "Dwelling."</note>. Second, those pertaining to the earth: *Eretz, Arka, Ge, Yabashah, Charbah, Tebel, Cheled* <note>Hebrew terms for various aspects or regions of the earth: "Land," "Earth," "Valley," "Dry Land," "Desert," "Inhabited World," and "Lifespan/World."</note>. Joseph of Salamanca <note>Referring to Joseph Gikatilla, a Spanish Kabbalist.</note> also recited by name the seven dwellings of the lower regions in his *Garden of the Nut* <note>original: "Horto nucis" (Ginnat Egoz), a famous Kabbalistic work.</note>, as you heard a little earlier. Regarding the Microcosm <note>The human being as a "miniature universe."</note>, it is not hidden from any of us that seven things pertain to the condition of man, whichever part you look at: these are the body, the soul, and the composite of these which we call <note>original: "נפש" (Nephesh)</note> the soul or living being, as in that saying of the King of Sodom: <note>original: "תן לי הנפש" (Ten li ha-nephesh)</note> "Give me the soul" <note>Genesis 14:21.</note>, that is, "Give me the people." This is composed, of course, of the four powers of the soul and the four qualities of the greater world; and since this greater world is surely animated, it is illuminated by its own mind, which is called **Metattron** <note>Metatron is a high archangel in Jewish mystical tradition, often described as the celestial scribe or the "Prince of the Countenance."</note>.

The second is the supreme world of the "separate intelligences" <note>Beings of pure intellect without physical bodies, like angels.</note>, which are called by the Kabbalists <note>original: "שכלים נפרדים" (Sechelim nifradim)</note> "separate intellects," but by the philosophers of the Hebrews <note>original: "דעות נפרדות" (Deot nifradot)</note> "separate minds." The soul of the Messiah himself encompasses, surrounds, and governs that world, which is full of species, forms, and liberated minds and angels. Among the Kabbalists, this soul is the "ideated Idea" of all lives, to which every individual, specific, and generic vitality is referred. From there, as if from a nursery, all life is drawn out; it is named by the Kabbalists the "land of the living," <note>original: "לפיכך דרשו בפסוק תרצא הארץ נפש חיה למינה וגו׳ נפש של משיח"</note> which means: "Therefore they comment on the verse, *Let the earth bring forth the living soul according to its kind,* etc., that this is the soul of the Messiah." These words are read thus in the second chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Portae lucis" (Sha'are Orah), a central text of Kabbalah.</note>: "And just as in the human world, which is called the Microcosm, the mind rules over the soul of man, so **Metattron** rules the celestial world, and the soul of the Messiah rules the angelic world, and **Adonai** <note>The Lord.</note> rules the incomparable world. Furthermore, just as the light of the mind is the active intellect, so the light of Metattron is **Sadai** <note>original: "Shaddai," a name of God meaning "Almighty."</note>, and the light of the soul of the Messiah is **Elhai** <note>original: "El Chai," meaning "The Living God."</note>, and the light of **Adonai** is **Ensoph** <note>original: "Ein Sof," meaning "The Infinite" or "Without End," referring to God in His purest essence.</note>." And since he is most learned in the nature of things...

# KABBALAH

762

<meta>catchword: in the book</meta>

To those who examine the world closely, it easily appears that the lowest part of a higher nature communicates with the highest part of a lower nature. Indeed, they are so closely connected that one might often doubt whether things are merely touching or truly continuous. One might wonder about that point in nature where continuous things are joined—much like where a horse's leg and its hoof meet, where one might ask if the substance is horn or flesh because of the immediate connection of their existences. For this reason, I believe it is said without error that Man is a Microcosm <note>A "little world" or miniature map of the universe.</note> and that the great sensible world communicates through the Mind. Likewise, the corporeal world and the intellectual world communicate through Metatron <note>In Kabbalah, Metatron is often the highest angel, serving as the celestial scribe and the mediator between the divine and the human.</note>, who is the active intellect of the first moved sphere <note>the "primum mobile," the outermost sphere in the geocentric model of the universe.</note>; he is one with the celestial nature as his inferior, and with the angelic nature as his superior. The supreme world, however, communicates with the incomparable and "super-supreme" third world through the soul of the Messiah, which serves as a kind of essence continuous with both the angelic and divine worlds. For there is no gap between the soul of the Messiah and *Elhai* <note>original: "Elhai" (The Living God).</note>. Rather, *Elhai* is the fountain of living waters, and the soul of the Messiah is the stream of life.

The third world is that of the Deity, which consists of that which the Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels, often associated with light and fire.</note> called "Holy, Holy, Holy," the tri-grammatized Lord <note>A reference to the Trisagion (thrice-holy) and perhaps a mystical variation on the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God.</note>. It is said in Deuteronomy: "Great, powerful, and terrible," or rather, "to be revered." <note>Deuteronomy 10:17</note>. He is Great before creation, powerful in creation, and revered after creation. And here He is "One" <note>original Hebrew: "אחד" (Echad)</note>; or more properly, the principle of unity, because the *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note> designates the principle, and *had* means "one"—as if He were the Principle of the One, folding all things into the simplicity of His unity. According to the Kabbalists, His emanation is thus: Spirit, Word, Voice <note>original: "ה-דבר קול" (Ruach, Davar, Kol).</note>. For so wrote Rabbi Azariel <note>Azariel of Gerona, a 13th-century philosopher and Kabbalist.</note> in his *Commentary on Holiness*, after the things I have just recited, in these words:

*From the spirit is produced the word and the voice, not through the opening of lips, and not through the speech of the tongue, nor by the breath of man.* <note>original Hebrew: "מרוח ימצא הדבר והקול בלא פתיחת שפתים ובלא דבור לשון ולא נשמת אדם"</note>

And these three are one spirit, because God is one, as we read in the *Book of Formation* <note>original: "libro Ietzira" (Sefer Yetzirah), one of the earliest extant books on Jewish esotericism.</note> concerning creation, in these words: *One is the spirit of the living God, blessed be He and blessed be His name, who lives forever; Voice, Spirit, and Word; and this is the Holy Spirit, two spirits from the Spirit.* <note>original Hebrew: "רוח אלהים חיים ברוך הוא ומבורך שמו חי העולמים קול ורוח ודבר וזו היא רוח הקדש שתים רוח מרוח"</note> These are the words of Abraham our father. And according to what Rabbi Hamai <note>A legendary figure often cited in early Kabbalistic texts.</note> wrote in the *Book of Speculation* <note>original: "העיון" (Sefer ha-Iyun).</note>: "These three are one, and they have a proportion among themselves as One, Unifying, and Unified." <note>original: "אחד מיוחד יחיד" (Achad, Meyuchad, Yachid).</note> Moreover, a little earlier, the same author says: "They are the Beginning, the Middle, and the End; and these are a single point, and the Lord of the Universe." <note>original: "אדון הכל" (Adon ha-Kol).</note> Thus it is written in the cited volume. Therefore, that third world, which is incomparably the highest, is constituted of these three which are one—as if from the highest essence, power, and operation—extending into eternity and beyond. It is neither concave, nor convex, nor keeled, nor does it have a surface; for as Azariel writes in the book...

# BOOK I.

765

<meta>Catchword: for</meta>

In the previously cited "Book of Holiness," it is written: <note>original: "הוא ראשון בלי תחלה והוא אחרון בלי תכלה"</note> "He is the first without beginning, and He is the last without end." That is to say: He is the first without a commencement, and He is the last without a limit. Indeed, He is one whom our thoughts cannot even reach, and He is named <term>Ein Sof</term> <note>original: "Ensoph"; the Infinite or Boundless nature of God before any self-manifestation.</note>, which means "infinitude." This is a certain supreme reality that is, in itself, incomprehensible and ineffable, withdrawing and concealing itself in the most remote recess of its divinity and in the inaccessible abyss of its foundational light. Thus, nothing is understood to proceed from it; it is as if the most absolute deity remains through its leisure in an all-encompassing enclosure within itself, naked, without clothing, and without any cloak of surrounding circumstances. It is neither poured out from itself, nor is its goodness spread out by its splendor. It is, without distinction, both being and non-being, and all things which seem to our reason to be contrary and contradictory to one another. It is like a segregated and free unity that most simply enfolds all things. For so it is read in the "Book of Faith and Expiation": <note>original: "כבר אמרתי לך כי הממצא יש מאין אינו חסר ובי היש הוא האין באין בענין אין והאין הוא ביש בענין יש ללמוד שהאין הוא היש והיש הוא האין"</note> 

That is: "I have already told you that the one producing being from non-being lacks nothing, and that being is in non-being in respect to the reality of non-being, and non-being is in being in respect to the reality of being." And further down: "By which you may learn that non-being is being, and being is non-being." So it is found written there. This, however, transcends all our intellect, which is unable to combine contradictions in their source through the path of reason. For we walk by those things which are made manifest to us by nature itself; but nature, falling far short of this infinite power, cannot simultaneously connect those contradictions that are separated by an infinite distance—as a certain most philosophical German, the <term>High Priest of Dialectic</term> <note>Likely a reference to Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), who wrote extensively on the "coincidence of opposites" (coincidentia oppositorum) and died roughly 52 years before this text was published.</note>, left to posterity a little more than fifty-two years ago.

Therefore, once the burden of worldly cares has been set aside and the sophistries of old wives' disputes have been despised, the happy <term>Kabbalist</term> <note>A practitioner of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note> breaks through the darkness via <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>Literally "Tradition" or "that which is received."</note>—that is, the path of what is received and believed—and leaps forth into the splendor by which he reaches the light. Thus, he migrates from light into radiance and through that radiance (as much as human nature can grasp) he comprehends that true Luminary under the mode of "being," but not as "non-being," unless this occurs through the abstraction of all things which are not the absolutely first Principle. 

And as the mind of the Kabbalist frequently travels this path through ineffable joy and alacrity of spirit—carrying humble and earthly things within the secret of a profound silence—it is transferred to super-celestial and invisible things that transcend all human sense. Then, even if he is still a guest in mortal skin, he nevertheless becomes a companion of the angels, just like an inhabitant of the super-celestial dwelling. His conversation is known to be so frequent in the heavens that, at times, he walks with them toward higher things as if they were companions on his journey, and he visits the soul of the Messiah. At other times, however, he descends under angelic guidance (yet not without his own reason) to the lower powers, both celestial and the other virtues of nature, and he strives to understand their dignities and operations and to venerate them with singular honor.

From this arises the intimate friendship of the Kabbalist with the angels, through which sometimes...

### KABBALAH

764

...one who correctly knows the divine names performs wondrous things, which the common people call miracles. For instance, Rabbi Meir <note>Rabbi Meir was a famous Jewish sage of the 2nd century. This story refers to a legend where he rescued his sister-in-law from a brothel through miraculous means.</note>, by using a divine name, saved his own wife’s sister from the corruption of a brothel where she was held. No lecher, no matter how strong, was able to violate or defile her once the word was spoken. These accounts are recited in the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Porta lucis"; the *Sha'are Orah* by Joseph Gikatilla, a foundational 13th-century Kabbalistic text.</note> and many other such works along with their authors. 

However, within the memory of our fathers, there was such a dispute regarding the miracle-working of the Kabbalists that they were often ignominiously threatened by the envious and the profane as if they were "shrewd magicians." It was as if those works had not been perfected by the angel <term>Michael</term> <note>The archangel associated with mercy and the defense of Israel.</note>, but much more by <term>Samael</term> <note>The archangel of death and the accuser, often associated with the left side or darkness.</note>—namely, through Egyptian incantations and certain dark secrets. Nevertheless, the "rod of the Kabbalists" always devours the "rods of the tricksters" <note>A reference to Exodus 7:12, where Aaron’s rod devours the rods of Pharaoh's magicians.</note>, and anything divine acts more healthfully than anything demonic. For the artistry of the Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of humanity; by contrast, the poison of magical vanity always turns toward destruction. The latter works through the names of darkness and evil spirits, while the former works through the names of light and the blessed angels. 

Concerning these matters—were it not for the fact that, according to our custom, the festive day of the Sabbath is now pressing upon us at this evening hour—I would certainly have treated more fully whatever I felt on the subject, since it pertains to the fruits of this art which you so greatly desire. But it is nearly nightfall, excellent men, and we must withdraw. This is not only so that I do not get a beating for neglecting the commandment, but also so that I do not fail my Kabbalistic profession if, on this Sabbath, I were to dig out the supreme and hidden secrets with laborious effort beyond what is permitted by <term>Shabbethai</term> <note>original: "Sabbathaí"; refers to the intelligence of the planet Saturn, which corresponds to the seventh day, the Sabbath.</note>. Instead, let me remain in silence and enjoy leisure for a while until the following day has passed. We shall explain the remaining matters here the day after tomorrow, or in whatever place you choose, through the Kabbalistic art.

Then Philolaus <note>A character representing the Pythagorean tradition.</note> said: "You have taken up the most difficult parts of speaking for our sake. Since midday, you have discussed so many wondrous things in such number with a continuous oration, yet you seemed to be moved by no trouble at all."

And he replied: "My love for you, which I hope is mutual, has taken away all the trouble. Indeed, if the holidays were not upon us, I would not think it right to send men of your stature—who have traveled here for the sake of learning—away hungry and unsatisfied by the doctrine of the Kabbalah. But the law must be obeyed."

To this Marranus <note>A character representing a scholar of Jewish heritage.</note> added: "In truth, Simon, I confess that I have never left anyone’s presence feeling more learned. To me—or if you prefer, to both of us, as I speak for him too—it is believed that enough has been done as far as time has permitted."

Philolaus said: "Marranus, I would wish you to plead your own cause alone. For my part, although these matters are great and approach the Pythagorean doctrine most holily, I am still eager to drink more copiously from them. I shall consider myself satisfied only if the day after tomorrow brings an end to the art. Regarding this matter, Simon, we shall return after your Sabbath, since you bear us with such singular kindness."

And he said: "Return then, without fear, and in the meantime, be of good health."

# THE SECOND BOOK OF JOHANN REUCHLIN OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut decorative initial 'A' featuring foliage and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

**A**S BOTH Philolaus the younger and Marranus <note>Philolaus and Marranus are fictionalized characters in Reuchlin’s dialogue; Philolaus represents Pythagorean philosophy, while Marranus represents a traveler seeking wisdom.</note> left for home from that place, the conversation between them as they walked was varied and quite sophisticated, as one would expect from philosophers learned beyond measure. They spoke of this very Hebrew <note>Refers to Simon, the Jewish Kabbalist who serves as the primary teacher in the dialogue.</note>, whose singular kindness toward strangers they commended alongside his profound learning, and his dignity of character which shone in all things and above all men. Everything about the man pleased them, except for this one coming Sabbath which (as they judged) would be full of boredom, because they would be pulled away from the most delightful conversation of such a master and cast aside until the third day. This was a troublesome loss of time, since they did not know what they would do on the morrow. Then, while walking, they ruminated on the "juice" of the doctrine they had received, mutually reviewing brief summaries of what had been said. 

Because they were burning with a fervor for learning, the speech of that admirable Jewish man suddenly returned to their memory—the sharpness of his debating, his grave and erudite instruction which delighted without causing satiety, and which was neither feigned nor colored, but which brought forth the most fruit precisely where it lacked the flowers of rhetoric. When they had hurried from their journey back into their lodging, soon after they had sat down and even before they had caught their breath, Marranus began thus: 

"Of all the wise men whom I have heard since my tender years, I do not know if there has ever been any who seemed to me sharper in speech or more sublime in thought than this one man, Simon. Even now, as I hold him in my memory, his speech—though plain, simple, unaffected, not sought from afar, and not at all smelling of 'Demosthenes' oil' <note>original: "Demosthenis oleum olente"; a classical idiom referring to the smell of the lamp oil used by the Greek orator during his late-night studies, implying speech that is overly labored or artificial.</note> but rather extemporaneous and everyday—has so excited my soul to contemplate arduous things that I have conceived of nothing more pleasing. Good gods! A Jewish man, born of Jews, nourished, educated, and taught by them—a nation which everywhere among peoples is held to be barbaric, superstitious, vile, abject, and alienated from the splendor of all the good arts—believe me, in my eager desire, I would have looked upon this man’s face and heard his speaking words through a perpetual night, if this wretched Sabbath evening had not intervened." 

Then Philolaus said: "Not even all the Greeks—to whom, by universal consent, the discipline of many arts, sharpness of genius, and abundance of speech are attributed—could have ascended so high into the lofty summits of secret things, unless perhaps that one Pythagoras of mine, the father of philosophy, had done so. Yet even he received that excellence of doctrine not from the Greeks, but rather from those very Jews. Therefore, by the best right, he himself should also be called a 'Receiver'—that is, a <term>Cabalista</term> <note>From the Hebrew root 'QBL' (Kibel), meaning to receive. Reuchlin argues that Pythagoras’s philosophy was actually an adaptation of ancient Jewish Kabbalah.</note>—although, so that he might bring back something worthy of admiration to his homeland from a distance after his long pilgrimage, he found it easier...

...it was commonly believed that he himself <note>Referring to Pythagoras.</note> changed that name of "Kabbalah," which was unknown to his own people, into the Greek name of "philosophy." We correctly infer this from the argument that he left his disciples no means of inquiring into the reasons for things, but rather he willed it to be the first principle of his dogma that, to those asking for a cause, they should answer: <note>original Greek: αυτὸς ἔφα (*autos epha*)</note> **"He himself said it,"** which is, **"Ipse dixit."** This follows the custom of the Kabbalists, who cite the reasons for understanding things in almost no other way than by saying: <note>original Hebrew: אמרו חכמים (*Amru Hakhamim*)</note> **"The Sages have spoken."**

Thus our famous phrase, "He himself said it." This "He himself" is Pythagoras, who is said to have given the name to philosophy in this way. Since the highest Hebrew authors were called <term>Hachamim</term> <note>Hebrew for "wise men" or "sages."</note>, and the Greeks before him were once called <term>Sophi</term> <note>Greek for "wise men."</note>, he thus attempted to clothe the ancient discipline with the ornament of a new name.

Nor should those things which Simon the Jew brought forth seem worthy of less praise to you just because they are taken from an ignoble teacher of the Hebrew nation—as if from "barbarian" authors <note>The term "barbarian" here is used in the classical sense to mean "non-Greek." Reuchlin is defending the value of non-Western ancient wisdom.</note> and brought by a barbarian man—given that our Pythagoras, the greatest of all, began his first studies of the sciences together with a barbarian named Zora <note>Likely referring to Zoroaster.</note>. Indeed, it is beyond doubt that during the time he was in Egypt, those who philosophized with him were called "prophets," along with the Chaldeans of the Assyrians, the Druids of the Gauls, the Samanaeans <note>Ancient term for Buddhist or Indian ascetics.</note> among the Bactrians, many of the Celts, the Magi among the Persians, the Gymnosophists <note>The "naked philosophers" of India encountered by Alexander the Great's campaigns.</note> among the Indians, that Anacharsis among the Scythians, and Zamolxis of Thrace (who was formerly the slave of Pythagoras himself). All of this was left in writing by the famous Alexander, surnamed Polyhistor, in his book <note>original Greek: περὶ πυθαγορικῶν συμβόλων (*peri pythagorikōn symbolōn*)</note> *On Pythagorean Symbols*. Finally, among the Indians, there are those they call Brahmins, as Aristobulus the Peripatetic mentions.

Indeed, if one may speak the truth, it is certainly not found anywhere that Pythagoras learned anything of divine or human matters from either the Greeks or the Romans. But as Antiphon stated in his book <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν ἐν ἀρετῇ πρωτευσάντων (*peri tōn en aretē prōteusantōn*)</note> *On Those Who Excelled in Virtue*, Pythagoras went for the sake of learning to the Egyptians, the Arabs, and the Chaldeans, after he had found his teacher and preceptor, Pherecydes, in Syria—which is and is named Judea.

For this reason, he [Pherecydes] was also commonly called a Syrian, whom others called a Tyrian, and others a Tyrrhenian. <note>original Greek: Βάρβαρον ἀλλ' οὐχ Ἕλληνα γεγονέναι ἴστω ὁμολογεῖν τὸν πρῶτον Φιλόσοφον (*Barbaron all' ouch Hellēna gegonenai istō homologein ton prōton philosophon*)</note> **"Let it be acknowledged,"** they say, **"that this first of all philosophers was a barbarian and not a Greek."** I know for certain, my most learned guest Marranus, that you have read these things written by Eusebius Pamphili <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian.</note> in the eleventh volume (if I recall correctly) of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, who also added this: <note>original Greek: μόνη παρὰ τῶν σοφῶν ἑλλήνων ἔχειν οὐδὲν, πενίᾳ σοφίας καὶ ἀρετῆς συνοικούντων (*monē para tōn sophōn ellēnōn echein ouden, penia sophias kai aretēs synoikountōn*)</note> **"that he had nothing from the wise Greeks, who lived in a poverty of wisdom and virtue."** Concerning these matters, as it is in Plato's *Timaeus*, a certain Egyptian barbarian, and a very old one at that, seemed to speak quite truly to Solon [when he] said...

...to have said, "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; you have no ancient belief, no teaching gray with age." <note>A famous quotation from Plato’s *Timaeus*, where an Egyptian priest rebukes the Greek statesman Solon for the Greeks' lack of deep historical memory.</note> Nor will it be anything less than most praiseworthy in Pythagoras—a man of outstanding wisdom and nobility—that on foreign and distant soil, through immense labor, cold, and sweat, and with much study and meditation over many years, he gathered things together. I will not say these things were improved, but they were certainly made more splendid when he carried them back on his own shoulders to his homeland, and even to Italy (which was then called Great Greece <note>Latin: *Magna Graecia*</note>), to the incredible admiration of all for himself and his followers, so much so that everyone who excelled in wisdom and learning was believed to have been a student of Pythagoras. From this, the "Italic philosophy" primarily received its name from him. 

Numenius the Pythagorean supports this praise in the first volume of *On the Good*, when he says that whatever the Brahmans <note>Ancient Indian philosophers.</note>, Magi <note>Persian priests and sages.</note>, Egyptians, and Jews discovered, Plato and Pythagoras themselves set forth in Greek. From this, we strongly suspect that what most learned men and experts in various languages assert is true: that everything the Jews received or discovered is now set forth through the thefts of others—Greeks on one side, Latins on the other—and that nothing in our philosophy is ours which was not previously the Jews'. This is true however much their deserved glory is taken away from them in this century, and though now everything of theirs is held in contempt, because the present age desires a more illustrious and polished explanation of all studies. 

"Then you speak the truth, excellent Philolaus," said Marranus, "which makes me agree all the more with Euripides’ *Hecuba*: <gloss>For a word coming from those without reputation and from those held in honor, though the same, does not have the same power. <note>original Greek: λόγος γαρ ἐκτ’ ἀδοξούντων / ἰὼν κ’ ἀπ’ τῶν δοκούντων αὐτὸς οὐ ταυτὸν σθένει.</note></gloss> That is, a speech proceeding from the inglorious and the glorious is not of equal worth, even if it is the same speech. For if someone like Aristotle or some Theophrastus had brought forth those things which Simon taught us today, in everyone's opinion nothing would be worthier of hearing, nothing weightier, nothing more memorable; he would only have added a more even style of speaking and some veneer of eloquence. 

Now, because he is a Jew, who handled the whole matter a bit more rustically and concisely in his own manner, there is no doubt that these things will be filthy in the ears of the Sophists <note>Here referring to the overly-logical or pedantic university scholars of Reuchlin's own time.</note> of our age—who seem to themselves quite subtle—if any of them hear or are going to hear it. Or rather, to all those now philosophizing either wickedly or foolishly, these things appear tangled, noisy, gaping, meager, and horrid, sounding of rustic harshness and foreign strangeness. Even though (as is their custom) they have not first examined them as much as they ought—as if gold were not gold just because we search for it in the mud. 

But since we have returned by the straight path, with no one showing the way, from this man to our lodging, and since dinner by chance is not yet prepared for us, I suggest that each of us recite our parts among ourselves—especially the worthier things we have heard—and fix them in our memory so they do not slip away while we hold everything fresh." And Philolaus said: "How..."

# OF THE CABALA

It is commonly believed that Pythagoras himself changed the name "Cabala"—which was unknown to his own people—into the Greek name "Philosophy." We correctly infer this by the following argument: he left his disciples no method for seeking the truth other than his first principle of dogma, which was that they should respond to those asking for a reason with "He himself said it" <note>Greek: *autos epha*; Latin: *ipse dixit*</note>. This is exactly the manner of the Cabalists, who cite the reasons for hidden things in almost no other way than by saying, "The sages have said" <note>Hebrew: *imre hachamim*</note>. Thus, our Pythagoras said, "He himself said it." Furthermore, it is Pythagoras who is said to have claimed the name of philosophy in this way because the greatest Hebrew authors, the <term>Hachamim|The Hebrew word for "wise men" or "sages."</term>, were once called <term>Sophi|The Greek word for "sages."</term> by the Greeks before his time; thus, he attempted to dress the ancient discipline in the ornament of a new name.

However, the things that Simon the Jew has brought forward should not seem less worthy of praise to you just because they were taken from an ignoble teacher of the Hebrew nation—as if from "barbarian" authors—or brought by a "barbarian" man. For indeed, our great Pythagoras began his first studies of the sciences together with a certain barbarian named Zora <note>Likely referring to Zoroaster, the Persian prophet.</note>. This is beyond controversy: during that time, he practiced philosophy in Egypt with those then called "prophets," with the Chaldeans of the Assyrians, the Druids of the Gauls, the Samanaeans <note>Ancient Greek term for Indian Buddhist or Jain monks.</note> of the Bactrians, many of the Celts, the Magi among the Persians, and the Gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked wise men," referring to Indian ascetics.</note> among the Indians. Even Anacharsis among the Scythians and Zamolxis in Thrace (who was previously Pythagoras’s own slave) are mentioned. All of this was recorded by Alexander, surnamed Polyhistor, in his book *On Pythagorean Symbols* <note>Greek: *peri pythagorikon symbolon*</note>, and later among those in India called the Brahmans, as Aristobulus the Peripatetic mentions.

Indeed, if we may speak the truth, Pythagoras is certainly not found to have learned anything of things divine or human from the Greeks or the Romans. Rather, as Antiphon published in his book *On Those Who Excelled in Virtue* <note>Greek: *peri ton en arete proteusanton*</note>, Pythagoras went abroad for the sake of learning to the Egyptians, the Arabs, and the Chaldeans, after he had found a master and teacher, Pherecydes, in Syria (which is and is named Judea). For this reason, he was also commonly called a Syrian at that time, though others called him a Tyrian or a Tyrrhenian. They proclaimed that "He was a barbarian and not a Greek, as they admit concerning the first philosopher" <note>Greek: *barbaron all' ouch hellena gegonenai hosper homologousin ton proton philosophon*</note>.

I know for certain, my most learned guest Marranus, that you have read these things written by Eusebius Pamphili <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian.</note>, in the eleventh volume of his *Preparation for the Gospel*, if I remember correctly. He also added this: "He had nothing from the wise Greeks, who lived in a poverty of wisdom and ignorance" <note>Greek: *para ton sophon hellenon eschen ouden, penia sophias kai apeiria synoikounton*</note>. Regarding these Greeks, as it is written in Plato's *Timaeus*, a certain barbarian Egyptian, who was very old, seemed to speak quite truly:

# CABALAH

...it was commonly believed that he himself [Pythagoras] changed that name of Kabbalah—which was unknown to his own people—into the Greek name of "philosophy." # KABBALAH

"You have thought ahead wisely, Marranus," he said, "for in this way we shall approach the man more prepared to listen the day after tomorrow, after this Sabbath <note>original: "Sabbathi"</note> appointed to the Jew, as Ovid says: *the seventh day sacred to the man.* <note>original: "septima sacra viro." A reference to Ovid’s *Ars Amatoria*, where he mentions the Jewish Sabbath as a day of rest.</note> In the meantime, you take this seat, I’ll take the other, and sitting together let us speak quickly of everything that should be prepared for dinner. Furthermore, lest there be room for idle attention while we are alone—for that would be nothing else than wasting time—you go first and speak whatever comes to mind <note>literally "comes into the cheek," a Latin idiom for speaking spontaneously</note>, whether for the sake of remembering things past or present, or for commenting on whatever might happen."

Thus Marranus began his discourse: "And although," he said, "everything we have discussed this afternoon seems to me, upon weighing each point exactly, to be higher than what we, lying on the ground, can look up to, nevertheless, many things which at first glance appear arduous and impossible to men, finally, through constancy, untiring practice, and hard work, become both plain and easy, according to that saying of Maro <note>The poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note>: *Labor conquers all things.* <note>original: "Labor omnia vincit."</note> Therefore, I will gladly bring together what I remember hearing from that man, and I will add what I myself feel. Our Hebrew teacher, being about to treat the Kabbalah for us, showed conveniently what is to be understood by that name.

For **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah|From the Hebrew 'Qabbalah', meaning 'reception' or 'tradition'.</term> signifies *reception*; at the same time, he claimed that it was always implanted in our minds, which by their natural condition tend toward the highest things. Wherefore, it is clear that a desire for it is bred in us; and the more these supreme and divine matters are considered sublime and worthy, the less they can be understood or discerned by human reason. This, however, is a commonplace doctrine among competent <term>Peripatetics|Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</term>. To begin, if I may cite my Arabs, with whom I have a habitual familiarity: **Alfarabi** <note>Al-Farabi (c. 872–950), a renowned philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age who integrated Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note>, in the book he wrote *On the Sciences*, uses this sentiment: that divine things, believable through pious faith, are of a higher order, since they are received from divine inspiration. For in them are divine secrets, from the comprehension of which human reasons are weakened, and they do not attain them.

Thus said that Arab, which our friend Simon also affirmed; he calls those orders 'regions,' and in the third region of our soul he places incorporeal things and substances free and exempt from every weight of matter. Not those 'phantastic' and logical universals which **Antisthenes** <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Socrates; he famously argued against the reality of Plato's universal Forms, saying he could see a horse, but not 'horseness'.</note> thought of, but rather—I say—the real forms, species, ideas, and essences themselves. These are the supreme things, around which the Kabbalists are occupied (as I hear) with nearly inexpressible contemplations. And all those individual things which we think we feel or know, they bring to this point; and finally, they reduce the universe into the One—which is the One itself and the First—through intermediaries, as if to the most healthy end of our mind. This is what **Aristotle**, in the 14th book of those things he wrote *After the Natural* <note>The *Metaphysics*. In Reuchlin’s era, the books were often numbered differently; this refers to the theological climax of the work.</note>, said was *self-sufficiency and salvation* <note>original Greek: "αὐταρκειαν καὶ σωτηρίαν" (autarkeian kai sōtērian)</note>. And Simon named it in Hebrew **Salvation** <note>original Hebrew: "ישועה" (Yeshuah)</note>. Just as the Royal Psalmist <note>King David</note> says: *Salvation belongs to the Lord,* and upon this family of the human race...

### BOOK II.

Simon laid the foundations for all the Kabbalists, which are neither to be investigated by reason nor have they been investigated through reason, since the senses have provided them with no basis <term>hypostasis (foundation or underlying reality)</term>, nor has the intellect provided a formal discipline. For these things are the highest of all, and an adequate cause for them cannot be found. From the knowledge of these things, the most eloquent Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was Aristotle's successor in the Peripatetic school.</note> of the Peripatetic sect removed the very capacity of science, for he wrote thus in his *Metaphysics*: *Up to a certain point, therefore, we are able to hunt for the principles of things through their causes, taking our start from the senses. But when we transition to the very extremes and first things themselves, we are no longer able to do so, whether because they have no cause, or because of our own weakness.* <note>original Greek: "Μέχρι μὲν οὖν τινος δυνάμεθα δι' αἰτίων θηρᾶν τὰς ἀρχὰς ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθήσεων λαμβάνοντες. ὅταν δὲ ἐπ' αὐτὰ τὰ ἄκρα καὶ πρῶτα μεταβαίνωμεν, οὐκ' ἔτι δυνάμεθα. εἴτε διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν αἰτίαν, εἴτε διὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν ἀσθένειαν."</note>

That is to say: *We can indeed speculate through cause up to a certain point, taking principles from the senses; but when we have crossed over to the extremes and the first things themselves, we can do no more, either because we have no cause to follow, or because of our own infirmity.* For concerning the celestial and divine things, to which nothing is prior, from what source, I ask you, could any middle ground for a logical demonstration be taken? For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* that to explain such things is a task greater than our strengths can suffice for; rather, he commands us to believe those who spoke of them in the past, even though they speak without any necessity of logical demonstration. These very words of Plato and the mandates of a truly wise man I value so highly that I consider them to be held in the place of an oracle.

And if there are any settled and established foundations of the Kabbalah, these are they. Wherefore I judge the logical syllogism <note>The primary tool of Aristotelian logic used to derive conclusions from premises.</note> to be the sharpest enemy and ambusher of divine knowledge—which consists of pure and naked faith. For by the daring and foolish habit of those who call themselves "theosophists," the syllogism subjects God, the angels, and the most simple and blessed minds—which exist far beyond the powers of this worldly age and the entire march of eternity—and indeed everything ever recorded concerning supernatural matters, to human mortality. It subjects them to be found, proved, and directed by the wandering discourse of reason. It is just as if one were to try and shut those illustrious substances into some Tullianum <note>The *Tullianum* was the deepest, most dreaded dungeon of the ancient Mamertine Prison in Rome.</note>. This is surely like wanting to bind Jove with a willow branch or tie him with a sailor’s rope. Even Thetis (according to Homer) would not permit that, nor would the hundred-handed Briareus, also known as Aegeon.

For this reason, I shall judge these contentious "theologasters" and trifles-selling sophists to be no less the attackers of the heavenly and super-heavenly beings than were the twin Aloadae <note>Otus and Ephialtes, giants in Greek mythology who tried to storm Mount Olympus by piling mountains on top of each other.</note> of massive body, who, as Virgil says, attempted to tear down the great heaven with their hands. They are no different than the Shinarites and the Babylonians of old, those "sons of Adam"—that is, born of a human weakness which they did not recognize in themselves—who built a towering height whose summit would reach even to heaven. Their leaders were called בלבל <note>original: "Balbel"</note> **Balbel**, that is, the "Authors of Confusion": from which comes Babel, which you call Babylon, where they could not understand one another's language. For through these talkative syllogists, all piety toward the entire divine order is lost in matters of belief, and a brotherly hatred is stirred up by the desire for victory. They are like hunting dogs, ready for sedition, a poison of the highest contemplation that ought to be expelled from the whole world. Let these artifices of syllogisms triumph, if it be right, in the realm of nature and human...

-> OF THE KABBALAH <-

...inventions and fictions. But in the sacred oracles, they would find no place for themselves. For this is the dogma that Parmenides, in Plato’s dialogue, handed down to Socrates concerning substantiated things, saying: *But in the same way that you are under their rule, so we are under our own rule, and we do not know anything of the divine by your science.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ ὁμοίως ὑμᾶς ἐκείνων ὑπ’ ἀρχῇ παρ’ ἡμῖν ἀρχῇ, οὐδὲ γιγνώσκομεν τὰ θεῖα οὐδὲν, τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ ἐπιστήμῃ"</note> That is to say: *But if we do not rule over them with our own authority, neither do we know anything divine through our science.* The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> also agree with this speech, and even Aristotle himself—who was both the craftsman and the "organon" (instrument) of knowing, as they say—when in the first volume of the *Posterior Analytics*, he affirms that the science of immediate principles <note>Principles that are self-evident and cannot be proven by something more basic.</note> is indemonstrable. A little later he says: *And we say that there is not only science, but also some principle of science by which we know the terms.* 

Themistius <note>A 4th-century AD commentator on Aristotle.</note> in that passage calls our mind the "principle of science," and the "terms" are those from which axioms <term>dignitates (self-evident principles or axioms)</term> are composed, namely the subject and the predicate. But Philoponus <note>John Philoponus (c. 490 – c. 570), a Christian philosopher and scientist known as "John the Grammarian."</note>, who is commonly called John the Grammarian, explained these things in a much more sublime and true manner, saying: *The Philosopher [Aristotle] has given the explanation of the preceding statement in this way: for the "principle of knowing," he takes "Mind," not our own, but the divine Mind that is above us. And for the "terms," he means the intelligible and divine forms. They are called "terms" because they are the ends or boundaries of all things.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ μὲν Φιλόσοφος τὴν ἐξήγησιν τοῦ προκειμένου ῥητοῦ οὕτως ἀπέδωκεν· ἀρχὴν μὲν εἰδέναι νοῦν εἰληφὼς οὐ τὸν ἡμέτερον ἀλλὰ τὸν θεῖον καὶ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς. ὅρους δὲ τὰ νοητὰ καὶ θεῖα· δὲ αὐτὰ καλεῖσθαι διὰ τὸ πέρατα εἶναι πάντων."</note> 

That is to say: This Philosopher has handed down the narration of the preceding statement thus: For the "Principle of Science," he accepts "Mind"—not ours, but the divine one above us. For the "Terms," he understands the intellectual and divine forms themselves. They are called "Terms" because they are the limits of all things. Therefore, the knowledge of supernatural beliefs depends on the Mind, not on Reason, which can err through the process of ratiocination. For Aristotle writes the same thing: *It [reasoning] admits of falsehood, such as opinion and calculation.* <note>original Greek: "ἐπιδέχε ψεῦδος οἷον δόξα, καὶ λογισμός"</note> That is: *It admits the false, just as opinion and syllogism do (which is reasoning).* 

Whence he finally concludes the *Posterior Analytics* in this way: *All science,* he says, *is coupled with reason. Of principles, there is indeed no science. Since, however, nothing happens to be truer than science except the Mind, it is the Mind that will be the principle of principles.* Indeed, the "principles" are said to be the prior things, and Hesiod and all the ancient theologians made the gods to be the principles. Therefore, this knowledge is properly named "Divine." And as that same Stagirite <note>A common epithet for Aristotle, born in Stagira.</note> wrote in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, the possession of it *would be justly honored.* <note>original Greek: "δικαίως ἂν τιμῷτο"</note> That is: *Rightly so, it is not human, because either God alone, or God most of all, possesses it; and it is unworthy for a man to seek out any other science.* For God alone has this honor according to Simonides. 

But since nothing is more conducive to our happiness than the knowledge of true and divine things, I ask you, Philolaus, by what other way must one proceed toward them if not by science? In what ways is such great height to be grasped? Then Philolaus replied: By Castor! You yourself have made the path plain and open. For since there are five levels of cognition, according to the testimony of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a 5th-century Neoplatonist commentator.</note> following Aristotle (who mentioned only four of them in the first book *On the Soul*), they are: **Mind**, **Reason**, **Opinion**, **Imagination**...
