<meta>This page continues the argument that divine mysteries exceed the reach of human logic. While the previous page focused on Aristotle’s "immediate principles" being indemonstrable, this page narrows in on the specific mental faculty capable of logic (discursive reasoning) and explains why faith provides a higher form of certainty than scientific demonstration.</meta>

### BOOK II.

That is, Mind, discourse, opinion, imagination, and sense. Indeed, the Mind and the senses do not utilize syllogisms <note>A syllogism is a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises—the basic building block of Aristotelian logic.</note>; the former is far superior to reason, while the latter is much inferior. Nor does imagination syllogize, since it is merely a station for the senses and a reservoir for the appearances that migrate from them. Since the senses themselves do not reason, we must not think that the mere appearances within the senses are capable of reasoning. There remain, therefore, opinion and discourse. However, since opinion is the conclusion of discourse itself, it does not perform the act of syllogizing on its own. Thus, the faculty of syllogizing is left solely to discourse, which is called *dianoia* <note>original: "dianoia" — the Greek term for discursive or step-by-step reasoning.</note>. This is the opinion of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Hermiae (c. 440–520 AD), an influential philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> in the commentaries he published on Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics* <note>original: "prima resolutiva" — the Latin title for the Prior Analytics.</note>.

And since I have briefly touched upon this list of ways we comprehend things and the things we comprehend—lest my speech wander too far—I believe that divine matters are above the syllogism. They cannot be understood by human reason because they do not take their origin of knowing from the senses. Instead, they depend purely on faith, received only out of love for the One revealing them and believed for the sake of human happiness.

There are, to be sure, very many things that often intermingle with divine speculation, just as freedmen and lodgers of a single family are sometimes accustomed to use a common name. Such things (as I confess) frequently allow themselves to be treated by the faculty of theology because they have obtained some kind of order toward God—either through their own nature, through being traced back to Him, or perhaps by some other relation such as creation, preservation, perfection, justification, bliss, salvation, and the like. Regarding these, I do not think at present that they are made naturally known to us; their demonstration of *that they are* is brought forward in metaphysics <note>original: "postnaturalibus" — a literal translation of "metaphysics" (the things after nature).</note>, or in theological studies, *why they are*.

I certainly grant the use of reason to those things that once arose from the senses and are devoted to human discourse; but for those matters whose truth depends solely on the authority of the One revealing them, I do not think there is a "science," nor would I wish the syllogism to dominate them. Rather, I hold that faith is more excellent than all else. He who possesses faith is described by Aristotle in the *Prior Analytics* as: *better disposed than if he happened to know.* <note>original Greek: "βέλτιον διακείμενος ἢ εἰ ἐτύγχανεν εἰδώς"</note> That is, he is in a better state than if he were a man of science. Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian commentator on Aristotle.</note> explained this as: "to know better than through demonstration."

To these things Marranus said: "I agree with you, Philolaus, and I also forbid those things which are of pure faith and purely believable to be subjected to the snares of logic <note>original: "logicis tendiculis" — literally 'logical little traps' or 'nooses'.</note>, which are clearly more of a detriment than a gain to those who contemplate. Our own writers, both Greek and Latin, have equally asserted this. The famous Jerome the Dalmatian <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note>, writing on the hundred and fourth Psalm, compares the art of syllogizing when applied to theology to the plagues of Egypt, and says thus:"

> The "gnats" <note>original: "cyniphes" — refers to the third plague of Egypt in Exodus. Jerome uses them as a metaphor for the annoying, stinging nature of logical hair-splitting.</note> are understood to be the sting of the dialectical art; although it seems to have only a small sting of seduction in reality, it nevertheless most gravely wounds human minds.

Wherefore that most learned man [Jerome] entirely removed and rejected this craft—which he also labels the "vanity of the sense" and "obscurity of the mind"—from Hebrew studies. He did this often elsewhere, but most clearly in his writing to Damasus concerning the questions proposed to him, when in the second book he uses these words: "It is not fitting for one disputing about Hebrew matters to use the arguments of Aristotle..."

That is, the very knowledge concerning divine worship and the truth of the universe does not need internal doctrine from men as much as it possesses its own notoriety from itself. That is, Socrates indeed wondered if it were not manifest that it is not possible for men to find those things. Such has always been the opinion of all ages and nearly all religions: that those things which were not previously in human sensation are not grasped by the human intellect. If the intellect does not grasp them, reason does not discuss them; and what reason does not discuss, that which they call <term>dianoia</term> <note>Discursive or step-by-step reasoning.</note> (the discourse of reasoning) does not investigate. This agrees most of all with divinely revealed truth, even if we occasionally form some imaginary concepts of the mind for ourselves. Provided we have received these things religiously and piously, we do not owe it to the violence of argumentation or to any phantasm set before us. Therefore, imitating our ancestors...

### BOOK II

Gregory Nazianzen, who stands out among all our most illustrious teachers in every branch of theology, possessing both a beauty of expression and a weightiness of thought, supports this teaching in a very similar way. In his second book of *Theology*, he affirms that **the divine is not graspable by human intellect, nor is it possible to imagine it in its entirety, however great it may be.** <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὴ ληπτὸν εἶναι ἀνθρωπίνῃ διανοίᾳ τὸ θεῖον, μηδὲ ὅλον ὅσον ἐστὶ φαντάζεσθαι"</note> That is to say, the divine cannot be comprehended through human reasoning, nor can whatever it happens to be be fully imagined. Do not suspect me, Marranus, <note>Marranus is the interlocutor in this dialogue, likely representing a scholar or a convert from Judaism to Christianity.</note> of being entirely ignorant or negligent of Christian teachings.

Philolaus <note>A character in the dialogue representing the Pythagorean tradition.</note> replied: I remember that Athenagoras, the Athenian philosopher, acting as an envoy for the Christians to the emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, said this: **Since even by the very dogmas we hold, we are not focused on human things, but are persuaded by God-lit and God-taught truths, we are able to convince you not to regard us as atheists.** <note>original Greek: "ἐπεὶ καὶ δι᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν δογμάτων, οἷς προσέχομεν, οὐκ ἀνθρωπικοί ἐσμεν, ἀλλὰ θεοφώτοις καὶ θεοδιδάκτοις πείσαι ὑμᾶς μὴ ὡς περὶ ἀθέων ἔχειν δυνάμεθα"</note> This means that through the very doctrines we rely upon—which are certainly not human but sent from heaven and taught by God—we can persuade you (regarding us not as if we were profane people). Here, he implies that persuasion works one way regarding worldly things, but in another way regarding divine things.

Even so, I have known quite a few among you who throw everything into confusion with <term>logical inventions</term> <note>Referring to "logica adinuentiones," the complex scholastic logic of the late Middle Ages.</note> and attempt to establish and confirm natural things by mathematical principles, and then, in turn, theological things by natural ones. But divine causes are by no means equal to natural ones; natural things are not strong enough to govern the divine, and much less can those things which stand by faith alone be demonstrated by any humanly knowable reason. 

Just as things which are purely believed do not necessarily imply things naturally known, so too your most excellent Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher, traditionally identified with the convert of St. Paul, whose works blended Christian theology with Neoplatonism.</note>—whom I would not unwisely consider to be either a remnant or an image of the Pythagoreans—speaks thus on these theological cognitions in his book *On the Divine Names*: **For there is no exact resemblance between causes and their effects, but while effects possess the received images of their causes, the causes themselves are removed from their effects and reside on high according to the principle of their own origin.** <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀκριβὴς ἐμφέρεια τοῖς αἰτιατοῖς καὶ τοῖς αἰτίοις, ἀλλ᾿ ἔχει μὲν τὰ αἰτιατὰ τὰς τῶν αἰτιῶν δεχομενὰς εἰκόνας, αὐτὰ δὲ αἴτια τῶν αἰτιατῶν ἐξήρηται, καὶ ὑπερίδρυται κατὰ τὸν τῆς οἰκείας ἀρχῆς λόγον"</note> 

This shows how deceptive a snare and how fallacious a dogma it is for some of your people to believe that in matters consisting of revelation by faith alone, one must not only use the tools of the <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed premises.</note> but also believe with equal certainty in whatever follows from the sacred oracles through the artifice of the syllogism, or whatever is inferred by a formal, necessary, and logical consequence. For nothing is as far apart as that which is divinely revealed and that which is humanly discovered. Therefore, in the realm of pure faith and things purely believable, believing and knowing are most widely separated. In such matters, the conclusion of a syllogism can never be more evident than its premises; even if certain evidence is mixed into the premises, the conclusion always follows the "weaker part." <note>A rule in logic stating that a conclusion cannot be stronger or more certain than the least certain of its premises.</note> We are correct, then, to affirm that in the same subject and regarding the same truth, the habit of acquired faith and the habit of knowledge generated through demonstration cannot exist at the same time. ...contradicts the sacred oracles, he execrably contradicts the faith. But he who contradicts any conclusion reached by human ingenuity, through subtle inventions, **Aristotelian tricks**, and the **Eleatic discipline**—of which Zeno was the <term>originator of philosophy</term> <note>original Greek: "τῆς φιλοσοφίας ἀρχηγὸς"</note> as Galen says—or through the traps of **Chrysippus** <note>Chrysippus was a Stoic philosopher famous for his complex and often "trapping" logical puzzles.</note> or syllogisms gathered from the revelations of the sacred oracles, that person does not contradict the faith, but rather human science. He fights not against divine illumination, but against mortal industry. In refusing such things, he does not act execrably, but perhaps erringly, or sometimes stubbornly, yet not shamefully. In what way, then, can anyone affirm that believing in things divinely revealed and things humanly invented is of equal dignity? No one would say this, unless he were one who feeds entirely upon the **syllogism** <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> as an ox feeds upon hay. 

Indeed (I ask you), what equality of dignity exists between the former and the latter? The one is an object of **faith**, the other an object of **science**. The **Mind** <note>Latin: "Mens," here referring to a higher spiritual intellect.</note> is the seat of the former; **Reason** <note>Latin: "Ratio," referring to discursive, logical thought.</note> is the seat of the latter. The former flows down from the divine light; the latter takes its origin from the senses. In the region of the Mind, there are some necessary truths which are impossible in Reason. In the Mind, there is a <term>coincidence of opposites</term> <note>A central concept in Renaissance mysticism where contradictions are resolved in the unity of God.</note> and contradictories, which in Reason are separated by the greatest distance. It is therefore not entirely true that if the premises are of faith, the conclusions will also be of faith. 

For this proposition is execrable: *No world is the creator.* Even more execrable is this: *Every carved image must be adored.* In both of these, the faith is blasphemed. However, the following is not necessarily a "true and faithful" statement simply because it follows: *No carved image is to be adored.* For we can demonstrate this by natural reason; therefore, this truth does not depend solely on the authority of the one revealing it. But its evidence is far more certain than any logic. By similar persuasion, we are deceived into agreeing that because a conclusion follows, one of the premises must necessarily be "of faith." For who would deny that it is believed with the highest faith by **Hebrews, Christians, and Saracens** <note>original: "Agarenis," a term for descendants of Hagar, i.e., Muslims.</note> that no carved image should be adored? Yet, to assert this, I might use the weakest natural premises, such as: *No stone is to be adored; but we see that a carved image is a stone.* 

Then **Marranus** said: By Hercules, Philolaus, you aptly bring to mind certain of our <term>sophistical monks</term> when they say: "The conclusion is heretical, therefore one of the premises must be as well." In this matter, I wonder more than can be said how they find any men who believe such things of them; but why do I try to <term>wash an Ethiopian</term> <note>A common classical proverb for attempting a futile or impossible task.</note>, who will never turn white no matter the effort? 

But furthermore, those things which, although they are revealed, also follow from other revealed truths, even if they are accepted by the believer, will be "faith" because they were revealed rather than "science" because they were inferred. Just as the things which my Church commands to be believed—no matter how they are constructed by human wit—are presumed to be revealed by the **Holy Spirit** rather than found by human reason, however much they are brought forth by syllogistic subtlety. Thus did the **Emperor Constantine** write to the church of Alexandria concerning the **Council of Nicaea**, saying: <note>original Greek: "ὃ γὰρ τοῖς τριακοσίοις ὁμοῦ πρεσβ. ἐπισκόποις, συνδόξαν οὐδέν ἐστιν ἕτερον ἢ τοῦ θεοῦ γνώμη, μάλιστα ὅπου"</note> **"For that which seemed good to the three hundred bishops together is nothing other than the judgment of God, especially where..."**

For there is no equal comparison between a word faithfully believed and a "necessary proposition" <note>In logic, a statement that must be true under all circumstances.</note>, since a necessary one can be doubtful, but nothing is more evident than what is **revealed**. Let such logical mixtures not occupy the inner sanctums of sacred things, nor trouble the <term>hierophants</term> <note>From the Greek, meaning a priest who interprets sacred mysteries.</note>; rather, let them withdraw (if they wish to be capable of anything) to the mechanical arts, or masonry, or mathematical calculations. "Rightly," said **Philolaus**, "you proceed, my friend, to the obscure hiding places of **Pythagoras**—a man surely imbued with a more divine doctrine—which are not to be searched out by any cleverness of human wit, and which strike us with a fear of doubting more than they generate the firmness of adhering. For so great a splendor of divine things cannot be seen so narrowly by our 'owl-like' eyes through such thin and old-womanish cracks of sophistry. But there will be need for the greatest powers of thinking and believing, and especially (as **Terence** says) 'faith and silence.' 

Moved by this, Pythagoras—the first to be entrusted with philosophy after drinking in all the disciplines of the whole world—taught his disciples nothing before (as **Apuleius** wrote) he taught them **to be silent**. For this was the first lesson of contemplative wisdom: to learn how to meditate together, and to unlearn how to chatter. It was as if the Pythagorean sublimity of such august majesty were much more worthy than to be comprehended by childishly tossing about trifles in talking and babbling. 

Indeed, it is clear enough to us from what we have received from **Simon** that even Pythagoras, just like the other things of the **Cabalists**, also brought this kind of doctrine into Greece: namely, that a disciple about to ask about the highest question should remain silent. ...with Greek letters <note>original: "κοντο Θ"</note>, "He himself said" <note>original: "αυτὸς ἔφα"</note>, to which we respond, "Believe us," <note>original: "παρ᾽ ἡμῖν πίστευσον"</note> though in different syllables and words. Thus, as the same point is yielded by that speaker, he said, and "believe among us," although in other syllables and words, so says Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father known for his influential theology.</note>. We now hold in our memory the unanimous method of learning used by those who have handled sacred matters more diligently than all others: namely, the **"They said"** <note>original Hebrew: "אמרו" (amru), referring to the tradition of the sages</note> of the Cabalists, the **"He said"** <note>original Greek: "ἔφα"</note> of the Pythagoreans, and the **"Believe"** <note>original Greek: "πίστευον"</note> of the Christians. 

Furthermore, whatever belongs to others is not divine. For Philolaus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher</note> said, "I thought of those same things much earlier"; I now know with more certainty than certainty itself, for I see clearly that everything Simon has shown us fits precisely with the Italian philosophy—that is, the Pythagorean—so that I would not be wrong to judge that all the matters of the Cabalists and the Pythagoreans are of the same flour <note>A metaphor meaning "of the same nature" or "cut from the same cloth."</note>. For both groups now reduce all studies to the salvation of the human race, and they continually refer all beings that exist or subsist to the **Ideas** which truly are, and to the **Idea of Ideas**. 

Whence both assert that there are three worlds, and that the three-fold is not infinite—or rather, not finite—and that all things consist of three, "just as the Pythagoreans say, the whole and all things are limited by three." <note>original Greek: "καθάπερ φασιν οἱ πυθαγόρειοι τὸ πᾶν καὶ τὰ πάντα τοῖς τρισὶν ὥρισται"</note> And Aristotle wrote this in his books *On the Heavens*. For he says, "Some things are bodies and magnitudes, but others inhabit and observe the bodies and magnitudes, and finally, others are the princedoms, powers, and origins of the inhabitants and guardians." 

I understand it this way: Since the lower world is constituted of individual bodies and magnitudes with their own virtues and <term>intelligences</term> <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, "intelligences" were the non-physical beings (like angels) thought to move the celestial spheres.</note> assigned as movers of the spheres, and as curators and guardians of things that can be born and perish, who are said to "observe" the bodies. This is done providently, as a province is assigned to each, whom antiquity sometimes called **Virtues**, sometimes **Angels**, then sometimes **Gods**, and likewise **Daemons** <note>From the Greek 'daimon,' meaning a spirit or lesser deity, not necessarily an evil 'demon' in the modern sense.</note>—or, because of the care for the anxious matters to which they are bound, it also named them "demons." 

Concerning these, Homer sings: "Gods inhabiting Olympic homes." <note>original Greek: "θεοὶ ὀλύμπια δώματ᾽ ἔχοντες"</note> That is, those who are set over natural things are often disturbed by a complaining affection, and having been banished from the highest to the lowest, they plead the causes of their labors: "For many of us who have Olympic homes suffer at the hands of men, placing heavy pains upon one another," <note>original Greek: "πολλοὶ γὰρ τλήμην ὀλύμπια δώματ᾽ ἔχοντες, ἀνδρῶν, χαλέπ᾽ ἄλγε᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀλλήλοισι τιθέντες"</note> as it is in the fifth book of the *Iliad*. For the ancients understand "Olympus" to be the **fifth essence** <note>Also known as the 'aether,' the substance of the celestial bodies, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> or nature—that is, the heaven. Wherefore, the Olympic homes are the celestial spheres or heavens, called "heavens" from "concealing" just as "roofs" are named from "covering." 

Finally, Hesiod says in his *Theogony* that the celestial virtues, elementary powers, and the properties of natural things are **Gods** born of Heaven and Earth; and Orpheus, the first theologian of the Greeks, writing to Musaeus, calls these same beings **Daemons** in these verses: "Celestial and aerial daemons, aquatic and terrestrial, subterranean and fire-roaming..." <note>original Greek: "Δαίμονας οὐρανίους καὶ ἀερίους ἐνύδρους καὶ χθονίους καὶ ὑποχθονίους ἡδὲ πυριφοίτους"</note>

# BOOK II. #

...standing by. Also in his book *Works and Days*, *Hesiod* says that good **Demons** <note>original: "Dæmones". In ancient Greek philosophy, these are intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not necessarily evil beings.</note> are the earthly guardians of mortal men. Indeed, *Apollo* himself, when asked by a certain *Theophilus*, replied that he and spirits like him were **angels**, according to the administrative duty assigned to them, as recorded in the oracles. For he sang thus, as he almost always does in heroic verse: "A name not even to be separated by reason, dwelling in fire, just as God, but we angels are a small portion of God" <note>original Greek: "ὄνομα μηδὲ λόγῳ χωρισμένον ἐν πυρὶ ναίων, ὥσπερ θεὸς μικρὰ δὲ θεοῦ μορις ἄγγελοι ἡμας"</note>. Let us raise our intellect to higher things if we please, namely to the vital influences of this entire universe. For the higher world encompasses the celestial beings, incorporeal essences, divine patterns, and the seals of this world, in whose likeness the forms of all lower things are made. 

These *Pythagoras* called the **immortal first gods** <note>original Greek: "ἀθανάτους πρῶτα θεούς"</note>, like the principles of things produced from the divine mind as **Ideas**, so that they might be the essential **principles** <note>original Greek: "ἀρχαὶ" (archai), meaning origins or first causes</note> and sources of the bodies they inhabit—that is, the species—shaping the complex things of this world. By this it is clearly understood that there are also other "immortal second gods" there—for the first refer to the second—incorporeal entities, singular and individual, differing among themselves not by material number but by formal distinction. That is, spirits free from all matter, simple and unmixed, dwelling by their own nature beyond the perceptible heavens, and as *Aristotle* says, bound neither by time nor place. Hence they neither grow old nor are they changed; much more, affected by no variation or alteration, and finally by no passion, they lead for themselves a most sufficient and excellent life, and they inhabit eternity, which is called the **age** <note>original Latin: "æuum"</note>, or in Greek **Aion** <note>original Greek: "αἰών"</note>, as if it were **always being** <note>original Greek: "ἀεὶ ὤν"</note>. 

Because that same age always was, is, and shall be, beyond time, in the divine mind; yet it was created outwardly from the power of God and established outside the vault of our heavens as a most splendid home for the blessed spirits. These the *Pythagoreans* consider true gods, located in the sublime heights of the ether, eternal both in their origin and their future, endowed with an immortal and divine age. From this same eternity, existence and life are also dispensed and granted to others—more clearly to some, more obscurely to others—as *Aristotle* likewise said. 

But what this thing is, through which existence itself is dispensed and granted from this divine and immortal age to other things—that is, to lower things—not by chance or in passing, or as a superficial influx, but as something substantial for every similar species, was certainly taught first of all by the Pythagoreans, *Socrates* and *Plato*, following their teacher, to the students of that school. For they had heard *Pythagoras*—who always spoke obscurely of divine matters—frequently say that the **Tetractys** <term>A mystical symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle (1+2+3+4), representing the organization of the universe and the source of all things.</term> provided the fountain of perennial nature to our soul. Then they clearly understood that the **Tetractys** was the Idea in the divine mind that transmits, that the "fountain" was the exemplary Idea transmitted, and that "perennial nature" was the essential Idea of things as received. Therefore, as *Alcinous* <note>A 2nd-century Middle Platonist philosopher who summarized Plato's teachings.</note> testifies, they spoke in this manner:

# CABALA #

...**as in relation to God, it is His own thought; but in relation to the sensible world, it is a pattern; and in relation to itself when examined, it is essence.** <note>original Greek: ὡς μὲν πρὸς θεὸν, νόησις αὐτοῦ, ὡς δὲ πρὸς τὸν αἰσθητὸν κόσμον, παράδειγμα. ὡς δὲ πρὸς διεξεταζομένην, οὐσία</note>. That is, an **Idea** is, in relation to God, His own knowledge; in relation to the sensible world, a pattern; and in relation to itself when considered, it is essence. Just like the voice of one speaking (as is found in the writings of the **Areopagite** <note>Referring to Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher who wrote extensively on divine hierarchies and the nature of God.</note>) which becomes one and the same, and is perceived as one by many ears. For the voice is first in the one who speaks, second in the act of vocalizing, and third in each individual ear. 

Moreover, just as in the sensible world a prior sphere always flows into all those that follow, so in the **intellectual world** <note>The realm of pure thought and spiritual beings, above the physical world.</note> we believe not only that individual higher ranks flow into all the lower ranks, but also that the entire higher world flows into the entire lower world. In this way, all things, according to their capacity—as far as possible—may be led back from the momentary to the eternal, and from the lowest to the highest. However, nothing that is merely created can be led back to the **third world**, for nothing by its own nature is capable of such sublimity except God. Yet this third world, I say—the super-supreme world containing all other worlds—consists of the divine essence and the very depths of the Godhead alone, so that it seems to me to be rightly called the **omnipotent seat** <note>original Greek: παντοκρατορικὴ ἕδρα (pantokratorkikē hedra)</note>. That is, the Omnipotent seat, placed, or rather existing, through every age and above every era. 

For it is the age of ages, **a demonstration of existence, substance, essence, nature, entity, and unity.** <note>original Greek: ὑπάρξεως, ὑποστάσεως, οὐσίας, φύσεως, ὀντότης καὶ ἑνότης πόδειξις</note>. That is, pre-existing existence, substances, essences, natures, entity, and unity. This is what our **Pythagoras** called **union** <note>original Greek: ἑνώσιν (henōsin)</note>, and Parmenides the Pythagorean—both using a similar reasoning—called the **super-essential one, and being, one** <note>original Greek: ὑπερούσιον, ἓν, καὶ τὸ ὂν, ἦν</note>. 

But let no one among the ancients, or any great despiser of our ancestors, wish to think that the great and wise Pythagoras was seized by such senile madness that he thought the numbers on a counting board, or children's dice with which they throw four-sided games, or merchants' tokens and other things of that sort, were the **principles of all things**. Such things do not even govern matters, but rather occur as accidents of things. Instead, he wanted it to be understood that the "One" itself is Thrice and Simply One, from whom, by whom, and in whom all things are, and are ordered, and remain, and are contained, and are filled, and are turned. And this same "One" is the **First One** and the **First Good**, as **Aristotle** testifies in the second book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Postnaturalia," a literal translation of "Metaphysics," the books following his "Physics."</note> with these words: 

**"For the Pythagoreans also do not think that 'being' or 'the one' is something else [distinct from things], but that this is their very nature: that the essence of what exists is to be one and to be a being."** <note>original Greek: οἱ γὰρ καὶ πυθαγόρειοι οὐχ ἕτερόν τι τὸ ὂν, οὐδὲ τὸ ἓν, ἀλλὰ τοῦτο αὐτῶν τὴν φύσιν εἶναι, ὡς οὐσίας τοῦτο, τὸ ἓν εἶναι καὶ ὄν τι</note>. 

Indeed, that famous **Xenophanes**, the teacher of Parmenides and a contemporary of Pythagoras, although it was their custom to hide everything [in mystery], nevertheless seemed to explain most clearly what they understood the "One" itself to be when they spoke of the principles of things. He said that this **One** is **God**. Thus, the secrets of Pythagoras are opened to us when he establishes the infinite and...

...and that number is the first principle of things. By the **infinite**, he signifies nothing other than the "ability" or "potency" <note>original: *posse*</note> itself; for no one could ever even conceive of anything prior to "ability" itself. This is what is most infinite in God—indeed, it is God himself, the infinite God, in whom **being** <note>original: *esse*</note> and **ability** <note>original: *posse*</note> are not separated. He contains the essences, virtues, and operations of each and every producible thing, along with all the connections, differences, and unions of their properties and accidents. 

Moreover, **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who introduced the notion of *Nous* (Mind) as the ordering force of the universe.</note> agrees with **Pythagoras** in this matter. **Eusebius Pamphili** <note>A 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> is the authority who claims that before these men, none of the Greeks had any knowledge of God. For Anaxagoras said: "Since all things were together." And **Democritus** <note>The philosopher famous for the atomic theory of the universe.</note> said: "All things were together in potency," <term>in potency</term> <note>original Greek: δυνάμει (*dynamei*)</note> that is, in the "ability" itself. 

This is also that "mixture" or "mingling of things" described by **Empedocles** and **Anaximander** <note>Early Greek philosophers who sought the primary substance of the world.</note>. However, this is by no means confused within some "chaos," "night," or "darkness" <note>original: *erebus*</note> as described by **Hesiod** or **Aristophanes**. Rather, it is distinct within the full light of the Deity, and ordered within the innermost sanctuary of that infinite light. 

Nevertheless, if Hesiod is understood fairly, he certainly established that chaos, night, and darkness are not the *principles* of things, but rather arose *from* principles. For he declared this in his *Theogony*: "From the beginning, and tell if ever any of them was first born; indeed, first of all Chaos came to be." <note>original Greek: ἐξ ἀρχῆς καὶ εἶποθ' ὅτι πρῶτον γίγνετ' αὐτῶν. ἤτοι μὲν πρώτιστα χάος γένετ'</note>. Then it follows: "And from Chaos, Erebus and black Night were born." <note>original Greek: ἐκ χάεος δ' ἔρεβός τε μέλαινά τε νὺξ ἐγένοντο</note>. That is: From the principle—if indeed anything of theirs was made first—certainly Chaos was made first. And from Chaos, Darkness and black Night were born.

**Aristophanes**, however, wrote differently in *The Birds*: "Chaos was, and Night, and black Erebus first." <note>original Greek: χάος ἦν καὶ νὺξ ἔρεβός τε μέλαν πρῶτον</note>. But he devises this poetically in the manner of the Muses, alluding to his "birds" so that Love might hatch from an egg; at the same time, he plays the sycophant to **Orpheus** in the *Argonautica*, who held a similar view. 

Therefore, let me remember this same point by repeating it again and again: each and every thing exists in that very **ability** <note>original: *posse*</note>—not confusedly, not in chaos, not in darkness, nor in obscure night, but distinctly and orderly in full light. Specifically, they exist in that luminous and most splendid clarity of all the most shining rays, and in the intuition, notice, and knowledge of the illustrious and illuminating **Divine Essence**. This is what is most rightly named **Idea** by the most ancient philosophers, from the word <term>to see</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ ἰδέω (*ek tou ideo*), meaning "from 'to see'"</note>, which is <term>to know</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ γινώσκω (*to ginosko*)</note>. 

Since this "ability to be" embraces all things—mental, rational, intelligible, sensible, vital, substantial, dependent, and independent—not only of those things which are, but also of those which are not, Pythagoras could truly call it **infinite**. This was also called by the wisest men <term>to be infinitely powerful</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπειροδύνασθαι (*apeirodynasthai*)</note>, that is, to be able infinitely. For He himself is infinite, and He embraces infinite things in one and the same infinite and essential Idea. 

For there was nothing, nor is there, nor will there be—in the super-celestial, celestial, or earthly realms; whether corporeal or incorporeal; in angels, in men, in beasts, in plants, in minerals, or in the whole nature of the universe—that is not "able," or (to speak grammatically) is not "possible" <note>original: *potis est*</note>. From this, all things proceed; and this is the <term>infinitely powerful and all-powerful power</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπειροδύναμος καὶ παντοδύναμος δύναμις (*apeirodynamos kai pantodynamos dynamis*)</note>.

# CABALÆ #

**The sole-making power.** <note>original Greek: μονοποιὸς δύναμις (*monopoios dynamis*)</note> That is, the infinitely powerful and almighty power-making potency, which is nothing other than the divine essence. Within this essence, before any number exists, it produces **two**. Here, Marranus, you have the whole of my **Pythagoras** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician who taught that numbers were the ultimate reality.</note>.

**Two** is the first number, while **One** is truly the principle of number. Because, as you heard before regarding **Xenophanes** <note>A Greek philosopher who emphasized the "Oneness" of God.</note>, that One is God; and since the production of the "two" remained within the divine essence (for number is established by itself, according to the Peripatetic author **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose works on logic and music were fundamental to medieval education; "Peripatetic" refers to the school of Aristotle.</note>, and next to one, only the binary exists naturally), then necessarily, those two are also God, since outside of God there is nothing except God. 

Therefore, since these three things—the **principle** and the **two things produced**—exist and do not depart from the one essence of God, then they are clearly one God. For the essence is not split by the fact that two produced things are traced back to the one, just as in physical things it often happens that unity moved toward unity (if I may be pardoned for the comparison) proceeds as far as three, while the substance of things remains—like a trunk and its branches, or more accurately, like a human's body, arm, and finger. 

Thus, from the **One** in the divine producers, and from both produced things, the **Trinity** arises. If we add the divine essence to these things as something formally distinct, it will result in a **formal quaternary** [a group of four]. This is the infinite, the one, and the number of two—the substance, perfection, and boundary of every number.

For one, two, three, and four, in a collective progression, constitute **ten**, and beyond ten there is nothing. Wherefore, by this very fact, Pythagoras understood there to be a certain hidden principle of things, which he named the **Tetraktys** <note>The "Sacred Four," a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows.</note>. This is *tetras* in Greek, meaning "quaternary," and *aktis*, meaning the "form of the sun" or "ray" <note>original Greek: ἀκτὶς</note>; because if by a certain formality (even if it is now super-substantial), God himself, that One and Light, constitutes the quaternary, it is as if there are four things formally distinct among themselves. 

And so that he might separate the sacred from the profane, for the best reason he wrote the holy name with the letter *ypsilon* <note>The Greek "y".</note>, whereas "ray" [*aktis*] is commonly written with the letter *iota* <note>The Greek "i".</note>. Furthermore, he himself also presented the **Tetraktys** as a certain God of chief excellence in the masculine gender—in the manner that the Latins often spoke of **Cupid** or **Venus** in the masculine—whereas otherwise they speak of the fundamental number of the quaternary, the Tetraktys itself, in the feminine gender. 

But he wished to show that he was that God by whom he also swore: **"By the Tetraktys,"** <note>original Greek: μὰ τὸν τετρακτὺν</note> than which nothing ought to be held more worthy of veneration. For as **Aristotle** says: **"An oath is the most honorable thing."** <note>original Greek: ὅρκoς τὸ τιμιώτατόν ἐστιν</note>. Indeed, in this place I will not agree with **Hierocles** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who wrote a famous commentary on the *Golden Verses* of Pythagoras.</note>, who I believe himself composed the *Golden Verses* of Pythagoras. 

But likewise, it is argued that out of reverence for its wonderful holiness, the Tetraktys should not be called in the Roman tongue "quaternary" nor "quaternity," but by a changed word, "**quaternion**" or "**quaternitude**." This is similar to what you Christians observe, separating yourselves from the usage of the profane common people; for while from "three" [*ter*], "ternary" [*ternus*] and "ternity" [*ternitas*] should regularly be read, you call the most holy **subsistence** <note>original Greek: ὑπόστασιν (*hypostasin*), a theological term for the distinct persons of the Trinity.</note> by an altered word, **Trinity** [*Trinitas*], as if it were the "unity of three" [*trium unitatem*]—namely, borrowing a letter from "one" and "one" on account of the united nature of each. But to return to the Tetrac—

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus, Philolaus, and Simon. ### BOOK II. ###

...I shall sing; of all things, I say, there is one supreme reality: the **Tetraktys**, the Pythagorean principle. Then Marranus said, "I recall most beautifully from this example of Philolaus, that mark <note>original: *charagma*</note> of four letters, in which the universal salvation of the human race is present. Which Simon confirmed for us with such an abundance of scriptures, where indeed it seemed to me that **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician.</note> did not do badly in changing the Jewish **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>—or rather the very four letters from which the name of the Savior is composed—into the Greek symbol of the **Tetraktys**."

Soon thereafter, Philolaus said, "As for me, I have clearly not yet departed satisfied with that Tetragrammaton and that salvation to which Simon reduced almost the entire human race. Therefore, when I return to him, if he is willing, I will ask for more detail about those matters, especially about that man who is to bring salvation to each of us as the anointed king of the universe, and is therefore called the **Messiah**. 

But I would like to see now whether he is **Asclepius** <note>The ancient Greek god of medicine and healing.</note> coming into this world again, or through 'transanimation' <note>original: *transanimationem*; a term for the migration of a soul into a new body (reincarnation).</note> as they say. About him, the **Emperor Julian** <note>Known as Julian the Apostate, he was a Roman Emperor who attempted to revive paganism.</note> writes in the second book of his work *Against the Galileans* as follows: 

'For Zeus generated Asclepius from himself in the midst of the intelligible beings, and manifested him to the earth through the life-giving life of the sun. This one, making his progress from heaven to earth, appeared uniformly in human form around **Epidaurus** <note>A small city in ancient Greece, the center of the cult of Asclepius.</note>. Growing from there in his progressions, he stretched out his saving right hand over all the earth, so that he might set right souls that were in a disordered state and bodies that were weak.' <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ ζεὺς ἐν μέσοις τοῖς νοητοῖς... κ.τ.λ.</note>

If he had possessed a name composed of those four letters, even with any other reading character added, he would certainly have to be thought of as the Savior himself. 

Or surely, consider how great was **Hercules**, the son of Alcmena, born of Jove—that divine seed whom the people of Thasos call 'Savior,' and inscribed on their public coinage thus: **Of Hercules the Savior of the Thasians**. <note>original Greek: ἠρακλέος σωτῆρος θασίων (*Herakleos Soteros Thasion*)</note> I recently turned and returned such a silver coin, struck in ancient times, between these fingers of mine with incredible pleasure (as is my custom regarding the most ancient things), reading it over. 

From this, I conjectured—not without reason—that by the voice and consensus of all, Hercules was numbered among the gods and proclaimed to be a savior. That there were otherwise many others who brought help to mortals as 'saviors' is indeed not in doubt; among their number, we remember **King Ptolemy of Egypt**, whose name was **Soter**, that is, 'Savior.' For the Romans as well, **Curtius** himself restored the land to safety by his own death, and the **Decii** <note>Roman heroes who famously sacrificed their lives in battle to ensure victory for the state.</note> bravely devoted their own heads for the preservation of the fatherland—wonderful authors of the common safety."

Then Marranus said, "I would gladly advise you, by interrupting, that you should observe more perceptively and understand a little more justly those things which were handed down to us by Simon."

<header>KABBALAH</header>

After that man [Simon] had discussed many things from every side regarding the **Kabbalah** of his school—what it was exactly, and for what it was useful—and had shown how the revelation was received, and that it would easily open the way for us to the peak of blessedness and the highest happiness: then, having been asked by us what that principal thing was which he thought had been revealed by the Divinity, to which generally all revelations of divine things were reduced, he said:

It is that which is called, after the primordial fall of the human race, the **universal restoration** <note>original: *universalis restauratio*; the concept of *Tikkun* or the returning of the world to its original perfection.</note> which is named salvation. This salvation would be given by a just and peaceful man, a heroic man: whose name would contain **four letters** <note>In Christian Kabbalah, this often refers to the name of Jesus written as IHShVH (Yeheshuah), inserting the letter *Shin* into the four-letter Tetragrammaton (YHVH).</note> in its writing. Toward him we ourselves, releasing ourselves from all secular business, ought freely to strive, to ascend through all suitable steps and migrate into him, each according to his strength. All our actions should be formed toward this, all contemplation directed here, and all the sacred scripture of the Jews looks toward this, which can be for us like **Jacob's ladder** <note>A reference to Genesis 28, symbolizing the connection between the earthly and divine realms.</note> placed upon the earth and touching the heavens with its top. Through it we can transcend this corporeal world even into the other angelic world, even to the very soul of that **Messiah Savior**, which is the rest and fulfillment of all souls to be saved, the final boundary beyond which we can progress nowhere. For it bounds the dwelling of the highest world, and communicates with the supreme world—or if the grammarians allow me to say, the "supremest"—which is incomparable. In short, this is the perpetual salvation of all men, completed by the gathering of all good things.

You will remember that these things were thus proposed by Simon; although he spoke through obscurities, you will not doubt the meaning. Neither those "saviors" of yours, nor even certain of the Jews of whom the **twenty-four books of the Bible** <note>The *Tanakh*, the Hebrew Bible, is traditionally counted as twenty-four books.</note> have often made mention, were ever established in such dignity that they could have brought universal salvation to the human race. Through them, men in all the space of the world, however many there were, might always enjoy the age joyfully, and after the fall be able to return into grace with God.

For what many others may have felt about your **Asclepius** <note>The Greek god of medicine.</note>, you may see for yourself. They assert that he was born of meretricious incest from the lovely girl **Coronis**, about whom it is sung: *“In all Haemonia, no one was more beautiful than Coronis of Larissa,”* <note>original: *Pulchrior in tota quàm Larissa Coronis fuit Æmonia*; a quote from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* II, 542-543.</note> and that often in the temple of **Apollo**, the priests subdued and pressed her; these priests, having fathered Asclepius from their adulterous embraces, feigned that he was the son of the God worshiped in that place. But the Egyptian **Apis**, who first brought the art of medicine to Greece with such a notable miracle as a temple-warden that even when dead he was worshiped in temples as a God, was led by a singular favor toward the priests of Apollo to take the infant to be raised and instructed. He then commended him to his former disciple **Chiron the Centaur**, a most skilled physician, so that he might transfer the art of healing the human body into Asclepius. Which being done, in virtue...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue regarding the "universal restoration" of humanity. Having discussed the coming of a four-lettered savior on the previous page, the speakers now debate whether ancient figures like Asclepius (the Greek god of medicine) can be considered true saviors or if they were merely mortal men driven by greed and pride.</meta>

# BOOK II.

Asclepius <note>original: *Aesculapius*; the Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing.</note> was great in both fame and wealth. However, driven by greed and a desire for honor, he traveled through various regions of the world to scrape together money through the medical art. By now abounding in great riches and endowed with immense fame, he foolishly called himself a God, promising health not only to the sick but even life once more to the dead. For this pride, he paid the penalty to Jupiter; for he perished, struck by a lightning bolt. Thus that Pythagorean, Pindar, sang of Asclepius in his third *Pythian Ode*:

"Jupiter, casting with both hands, took away the breath of his heart suddenly. The blazing thunderbolt inflicted death." <note>original Greek: χερσί θ’ ἄρα κρονίων ῥίψας δι’ ἀμφοῖν, ἀμπνοὰν στέρνων κάθελεν ὠκέως, αἴθων δὲ κεραυνὸς ἐνέσκιψε μόρον.</note>

In this same vein, Euripides depicts a complaining Apollo grieving over the death of his son Asclepius:

"For Zeus, by casting a flame into his breast, is responsible for killing my son Asclepius." <note>original Greek: Ζεὺς γὰρ κατακτὰς παῖδα τὸν ἐμὸν αἴτιος Ἀσκληπιὸν στέρνοισιν ἐμβάλλων φλόγα.</note>

Therefore, unless we are completely dull in divine matters, we will not consider a man so far removed from dignity to be the savior of the human race. Indeed, he was not even a universal healer, as he brought help nowhere else but to Pergamum, Ionia, Taranto, Rome, Cos, and Aegae, and the regions around them.

"Marranus," said Philolaus, "you are overcome by an excessive love for your own people <note>original: *tuorum*; referring here to the Christians or those following the "Galilean" faith.</note> more than by the truth. You hold all men in lower esteem—indeed, you think them as little as possible—who are not **Galileans** <note>A term often used by critics or in ancient contexts to refer to Christians.</note>. This is a perverse habit, in my opinion (if I may say so), not only to refuse praise to others but even to disparage them. It seems it is not enough for you and those like you to contend that the best men—famed for virtue in their own age, whom antiquity counted among the Gods for their outstanding deeds—are not Gods, unless you also turn them into hellish devils. In this, you imitate your friend Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) known as the "Christian Cicero," who frequently attacked pagan mythology.</note>, who wrote thus in the tenth chapter of his first book to the Emperor Constantine:

'Asclepius himself, born not without the disgrace of Apollo, what else did he do worthy of divine honors, except that he healed Hippolytus? He certainly had a more famous death, because he deserved to be struck by lightning by a god.'

So he says. But every tongue that is stained with gall lacks a true sense of taste. Yet even he admits that it is a thing worthy of divine honors to grant health, which all sick people admit along with him. But if Lactantius does not know what else Asclepius did, let him ask Socrates, the wisest of men, who vowed that a cock should be offered to him, as it is written in Plato’s *Phaedo*. He did this not so that Asclepius might heal his body—for Socrates, already condemned to death, had drunk the poison—but so that he might return his soul, as he was dying peacefully with a shout of joy and a **paean** <term>A song of triumph or thanksgiving, originally dedicated to Apollo.</term>, to his father Apollo. That is, to the first and incorporeal Sun, the dispenser of eternal life.

For the cock is sacred to Apollo Phoebus (who is called the Sun), as the joyful herald of the hours and the day. Moreover, Asclepius was called by the ancients the 'jubilation of Apollo,' his victory and triumph, which is named a *paean*, because they named it after the pause, cessation, and rest that follows liberation. For in that age, it was the custom for those about to enter battle to first offer a sacrifice to Mars, and after the battle, the victors would return a *paean* to Apollo. How aptly, therefore, did Socrates, in the name of Asclepius (who is the *paean*), honor the Sun, the giver of life...

# KABBALAH

...having been born, he was soon about to die. When the most learned men saw this, they thought it worthy and dutiful to the best people that, once the **Python** <note>The Python was the monstrous serpent or dragon killed by Apollo at Delphi; here it serves as an allegory for overcoming death or disease.</note>—that greatest serpent—had been conquered and trampled underfoot, a path would be swiftly taken from death toward the true life by **Asclepius**. They thought it right to offer thanks, which is to say, to celebrate a **Paean** <note>original: *Pæana*; a song of praise or triumph, often dedicated to Apollo or Asclepius as healers.</note>.

So sang **Orpheus**, the most ancient of seers and a contemporary of those gods (for he is said to have been a companion of the **Tyndarids** <note>Castor and Pollux.</note> and **Hercules**), in his hymns: *"Healer of all, Lord Asclepius, Paean, come blessed Savior, granting a good end to life."* <note>original Greek: ἰητὴρ πάντων ἀσκλαπιὲ δέσποτα παιὰν καρπῷ σωτῆρι βιοτῆς τέλος ἐσθλὸν ἐπάζων. Latin translation provided in text: *Sanator omnium Escumine Pæan, Veni beate saluator, uitæ finem bonum præbens.*</note>

**Julian the Emperor** <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive polytheism.</note> himself asserted that he had been saved by the help of Asclepius in the greatest dangers, and he confessed that he was often made well by his remedies when he was suffering grievously, citing **Jupiter** as a witness to this.

"But what does this have to do with the universal savior?" responded **Marranus**. "My Messiah is proclaimed as the Savior not only of bodies, but of souls."

To this, **Philolaus** replied: "You see, Marranus, what of Hercules? Was he not a molder of morals and a teacher of all discipline in every place on the face of the earth? From this comes the image of **Hercules among the Celts**, which is indeed very old and resembles the truth: where he draws along countless men, each bound by the ears with little golden chains that hang from his tongue, leading them wherever he wishes. The Celts call him **Ogmios** <note>The Celtic god of eloquence, often depicted as an elderly Hercules.</note> in their native tongue."

**Lucian** <note>A 2nd-century satirist and rhetorician.</note> records this in his discourse on the *Gallic Hercules*, concerning which they say: *"We consider Hercules to have led all things by word and reason, since he was wise."* <note>original Greek: ἡμεῖς τὸν ἡρακλέα λόγῳ τὰ πάντα ἡγούμεθα, σοφὸν γενόμενον.</note>

For to tame vices by virtue and to remove ignorance through teaching is nothing other than to trample on monsters: to kill serpents, to strike the **Nemean lion** with a club, to destroy the **Lernaean hydra**, to kill the **Erymanthian boar**, to capture the **hind on Mount Maenalus** which bore golden horns, to pierce the **Stymphalian birds** in the clouds, to strangle **Antaeus** in one's arms, to fix the **pillars** in the sea, to conquer the three-headed **Geryon**, to drive away the cattle, to tame the bull, to overcome **Achelous** in single combat—I omit **Diomedes** and the others—as well as **Cerberus** and the **golden apples of the Hesperides**. All of these and many other such deeds were the work of total virtue, the duty of right reason, and an example of living well.

Then Marranus said: "I would hardly care for the opinion others hold of him, unless you had first complained about his lot; for I could show in short order that he was a man just as we are, and perhaps even less worthy, though noble in the lineage of **Praetus** and **Agenor**. From Agenor came Praetus, and **Belus** was the brother of Agenor; from him came **Aegyptus**, and from him **Lynceus**, then **Abas**, then **Danae**, whose son was **Perseus**, whose son was **Alcaeus**, whose son was **Amphitryon**, whose son Hercules was thought to be. However, they say he was actually the son of Jupiter—that is, the son of some adulterer. From **Alcmene**, **Iphicles** was born to Amphitryon and **Hercules** to Jupiter, brought into the light in a single birth, as is believed. Hercules, however, set on fire by madness..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Philolaus has been praising ancient "savior" figures like Asclepius. Marranus now counters by critiquing the moral failings and physical deaths of these pagan heroes, arguing that true salvation must come from an eternal, divine source rather than from flawed men or myths.</meta>

# BOOK II.

...perished, because he avenged the attempted assault on his wife **Deianira** by the Centaur **Nessus** with an arrow—a standard of conduct he did not display toward the captive girl **Iole**. He most unfairly avenged a mere suspicion of adultery, though he himself, having been conceived through adultery, committed adultery just the same. Perhaps he was just toward others, but he was certainly most unjust toward himself. Do not believe, Philolaus, that the savior of the world would be such a man as **Hercules** or **Aesculapius** <note>Also known as Asclepius, the god of medicine.</note>, if for no other reason than that both died with a shameful mark. For as **Momus** <note>The personification of mockery and harsh criticism.</note> says of both of them in **Lucian’s** *Assembly of the Gods*: *"They still bear the marks of the fire,"* <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τὰ σημεῖα ἔχουσι τοῦ πυρὸς.</note> because they were both consumed by flames. Others praise **Curtius** and the **Decii** <note>Roman heroes famous for their "devotio," or self-sacrifice in battle to save the state.</note> for their greatness of soul; I accuse them of imprudence. Furthermore, some people, led by flattery and fawning or compelled by the violence of tyrants, have honored with the name of "savior" men who not only failed to heal or save them, but utterly devastated and destroyed them. Thus the Sicilians inscribed a public statue in **Syracuse** to **Verres** <note>A notoriously corrupt Roman governor of Sicily.</note> as their *"Savior,"* <note>original Greek: σωτῆρα.</note> that is, "one who gave safety," according to **Cicero's** testimony in the fourth speech of his prosecution of Verres.

But this is irrelevant to our current topic, where we are discussing the true salvation of mankind, which those figures did not provide. For true salvation is eternal endurance, which exists in God and is granted by God, as **Aristotle** wrote in his book *On the Universe* <note>original title: *De Mundo*; a treatise traditionally attributed to Aristotle, though now often debated by scholars.</note> to Alexander. He says, *"All things consist for us from God and through God, and no nature is self-sufficient if it lacks that salvation which comes from Him."* Then he adds: *"In His very essence, for God is truly the savior of all things."* <note>original Greek: τῇ γε οὐσίᾳ, σωτὴρ μὲν γὰρ ὄντως ἁπάντων θεός.</note> Whence in the fourteenth book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: *post naturalia* (after the Physics).</note>, Aristotle speaks again thus: *"It would be a wonder if, in the first, eternal, and most self-sufficient of all things, this very primacy did not exist as a 'good'—namely, self-sufficiency and salvation itself."* <note>original Greek: θαυμαστὸν δ᾽ εἴ τῷ πρώτῳ καὶ ἀϊδίῳ καὶ αὐταρκεστάτῳ τῶν πάντων τὸ πρῶτον οὐχ ὡς ἀγαθὸν ὑπάρχει τὸ αὔταρκες καὶ ἡ σωτηρία.</note> By this we are reminded that our true salvation consists in the first, eternal, and most sufficient Good, which is God, the Greatest and Best, and it is not to be sought elsewhere. For only that supreme Creator and ruler of the world, out of the most merciful will of His super-eminent generosity, can give incorruption to corruptible things, eternity to those subject to time, and unbreakable permanence to transitory things—even though it is the inherent nature of such things that they die once born and grow old once they have increased. For thus God speaks in **Plato’s** *Timaeus*: *"The things made by me are indissoluble, provided I will it; otherwise, everything that is bound together is capable of being dissolved."*

Behold, we receive testimony not only from the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> but also from Plato himself and the **Platonists** that permanence is granted to any things whatsoever (according to their capacity) by the will of God alone, and this is true salvation. For we say a thing is "saved" when it is preserved from harm so that it may remain in peace. This was explained by the magnificent and most eloquent legates of the Greeks <note>Representatives of the Byzantine Church seeking union with the Roman Church.</note>, by unanimous consent in the year of our Lord 1438, at the **General Council of Basel** in a certain illustrious and most learned oration, using these words: *"For 'to be saved,' 'to be preserved,' and 'salvation' mean simply nothing else among the Greeks..."* <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ σωθῆναι καὶ σῴζεσθαι καὶ ἡ σωτηρία ἁπλῶς οὐδὲν ἄλλο παρὰ τοῖς ἕλλησι.</note>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Marranus and Philolaus. Having previously criticized the false "saviors" of antiquity, Marranus now provides a philosophical and linguistic definition of true salvation, moving from physical safety to eternal immortality.</meta>

# CABALA

...and in our tongue and also in our understanding, it means: <note>original Greek: καὶ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ βόλεται γλῶτῃ, ἤ τε διανοίᾳ καὶ ἔτι.</note> that is, to be saved and "salvation" itself simply means nothing else among the Greeks and in their tongue than to remain and to be. Therefore, men who are subject to death, in order that they might truly *be*, conform themselves to the will of God so that they may become immortal and enjoy a blessed age. These are rightly said to have attained salvation. And he who grants them that blessedness of immortality is rightly called a "savior." This term <term>Salvator</term><note>Latin for "Savior." Reuchlin notes that the word was rare or controversial in classical Latin until popularized in a Christian context.</note> began to be used through the authority of **Cicero**, having been previously unheard of, so that "Savior" can now be spoken in Latin. 

Indeed, other things are called "salvation" improperly and only in an imaginary sense. For what of it? If a doctor today brings health to a brute animal, and the day after tomorrow it is thrown into a plague and dies, never to return—should that be called "salvation"? What of the gardener who helps a wilting flower that is destined to fall the next day and be ground into dust—should this three-day preservation of a completely inconsistent thing be named "salvation"? 

In this way, **Hercules** once helped the people of **Thasos**, whereby he is said to have given them salvation, yet they later perished, and today nothing of them exists but a name. So **Ptolemy** saved Egypt, which was later destroyed by so many wars and enemy incursions. So the **Decii** liberated Rome, which was nevertheless demolished in a subsequent overthrow and fire. Believe me, that salvation is imperfect which is broken by time; perfect salvation is that which makes the perishable eternal. Regarding this, **Apollo** taught in the *Orestes* of **Euripides** <note>A famous Greek tragedy by Euripides.</note> that death was removed from **Helen** when he spoke thus: 

*She whom you see saved in the folds of the air... she was not dead beside you; I saved her.* <note>original Greek: ἣν ὁρᾶτ᾽ ἐν αἰθέρος πτυχαῖς σεσωσμένην π. μ' ἔθαπτον πρὸς σὲ δὴ ἐγὼ μὴν ἐξίωσα.</note>

This is she whom you perceive in the vault of the heavens, truly saved, not dead. I saved her. And let us not be ignorant of the fact that this salvation did not come from Apollo, nor from other gods except as mediators, but rather more truly from the Highest God, to whom she dedicated herself by her remarkable virtue. Then he adds: *For since she was living, it was fitting that she now live an incorruptible age.* <note>original Greek: ζῶσα γὰρ ἔσαν, ζῶ νῦν ἄφθιτον αἰών.</note>

"By the **Cabala**, brother of Helen! Marranus, you speak the truth," said **Philolaus**, "and you seem to have spoken most excellently concerning true salvation. I agree that the Savior—of whom the sacred oracles prophesy so magnificently and perpetually—will be he who is the preserver and restorer not so much of this great world <note>The Macrocosm, or the physical universe.</note>, not of regions and cities, not of the lowest elements and stars, nor of wood and stones, plants and trees, fish, birds, or cattle—for all these things follow nature as their guide and the instinct of their condition properly, and they remain in their appointed end—but rather he is the savior of that 'lesser world,' which is **Man**. 

For Man, falling away from the norm of equity handed down to him and from the judgment of right reason, voluntarily plunges his nobility into a deep pool of evils and the pit of eternal corruption through a heap of vices; from this place, he cannot turn back his step by his own strength or help. Here, Marranus—here, I say—we have need of salvation; here we have need of a Savior. Here...

<summary>Marranus defines true salvation as the transition from mortality to eternal existence, contrasting it with temporary physical "saving." Philolaus agrees, arguing that while the natural world follows its course, humanity (the microcosm) has fallen and requires a divine Savior to be restored.</summary>
<keywords>salvation, savior, immortality, etymology, Cicero, Euripides, Helen of Troy, macrocosm, microcosm, human nature, corruption</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue regarding the nature of salvation and the soul's destiny. The previous page discussed the linguistic roots of "Savior" and contrasted true eternal salvation with temporary physical safety. Here, the speaker invokes Pythagorean and Greek philosophical traditions to explain the human condition and the afterlife.</meta>

# BOOK II.

...this class of creatures, Pythagoras calls <note>original Greek: ἀνθρώπους αὐθαιρέτα πήματ’ ἔχοντας</note> "men who have self-chosen sorrows." Regarding them, he wrote in his **Golden Verses**: <note>original Greek: τλήμονες· οἵτ’ ἀγαθῶν πέλας ὄντων οὐκ ἐσορῶσιν, οὔτε κλύουσ’· λύσιν δὲ κακῶν παῦροι συνίσασιν· τοίη μοῖρα βροτῶν βλάπτει φρένας, οἱ δὲ κυλίνδροις ἄλλοτ’ ἐπ’ ἄλλα φέρονται ἀπείρονα πήματ’ ἔχοντες.</note> that is, "Wretched ones, these indeed do not see nor hear the good things that are near them, and few understand the release from evils; such a fate of mortals harms their minds, and they are carried by rollers from some things to others, having infinite losses." 

Indeed, our very prince of philosophers <note>Referring to Pythagoras.</note> surely took this from the **Hebrew Cabalists**, as we can learn from **Simon**; he perceived that man is a rational being, more noble and as it were more divine than other things. Man is not content with only one operation or a single uniform effect like other creatures, which are led by nature alone acting always in the same way. Instead, man is endowed with various gifts like a **Pandora** <note>In Greek myth, Pandora was "all-gifted." Here, it refers to the multifaceted nature of human talent and potential.</note>, which he may use of his own accord for any outcome according to his free will. 

Because of this freedom he says: <note>original Greek: θεῖον γένος ἐστὶ βροτοῖσιν οἷς ἱερὰ προφέρουσα φύσις δείκνυσιν ἕκαστα.</note> that is, "There is a divine race for mortals, to whom sacred nature, bringing them forward, shows each thing." Truly, that sacred nature is the **intellectual soul**. Therefore, according to the intellect, man approaches God as the pure to the pure, and according to the lower senses, he recedes from God like the impure from the pure. 

Thus it happens that reason, which (as he says) shows us each thing, makes us blessed when it turns itself to the enjoyment of the mind; but conversely, it makes us wretched when it runs down to the lust of the senses. Thus man seems placed in the middle between virtue and vice, like the substituted peak in the **letter of Pythagoras** <note>The letter 'Y', which Pythagoras used to symbolize the diverging paths of life: the narrow path of virtue and the broad path of vice.</note> divided by a two-horned distinction, at which the famous **Hercules of Prodicus** <note>A reference to the "Choice of Hercules," a parable where the young hero must choose between a difficult path of Virtue and an easy path of Vice.</note> sat down, thoughtful in his tender youth. 

Just as **Solon** affirmed to **Croesus** in the writings of **Herodotus**, no one should be called blessed before his death and final funeral; so certainly no one should be thought wretched while he lives this life. But the final day must always be awaited for a man, who, if he remains burdened with vices after casting off the body, then begins to be truly wretched. 

As you heard in the previous discourse, Pythagoras divided that misery into two kinds. For after death, the wretched either have good things nearby—which are the gifts of blessedness—though they neither see nor hear them because they do not yet enjoy the vision of God. These are among the number of those to be saved, not weighed down by extreme misery, so that they may finally escape their appointed punishments. Or finally, good things are very far distant from them, so that their evils will never have any end, and they are called those "having infinite losses." 

Therefore, two dwellings of those below are described here. First, the **Elysian Field**, which is transitory, for those to whom good things are near, so that they may eventually return to the heavens above. Second is **Tartarus**, named from its horrible sound, as if it were called "foul tormenting terror" <note>The author uses a Latin wordplay: Tartarus sounds like *tortor* (tormentor), *teter* (foul), and *terror* (dread).</note>, for those whose losses are infinite. These hang distracted by the rollers and spokes of wheels, where the unhappy **Theseus** sits and will sit eternally, and those like him, <note>original Greek: ὅθεν οὔποτ’ ἐκβαίνουσιν</note> "from which they never emerge," as stated by **Plato** when he was imitating Pythagoras.

# CABALA

...written, that is, "From whence they never depart." <note>This fragment likely refers to the state of those trapped in the cycle of "infinite losses" mentioned on the previous page.</note> At this point, let those mockers approach me who never cease to bark against this same Pythagoras—a man so great and so eminent, whose pronouncements were trusted as if they were oracles. For this reason, he was named the "Dictator of Truth," or even "Apollo," which is what the very name **Pythagoras** signifies. <note>The author derives "Pythagoras" from *Pythios* (Apollo) and *agoreuein* (to speak), suggesting he spoke like the god of the sun and prophecy.</note>

However, people everywhere spread the rumor that his opinion was this: that after death, the human soul enters the bodies of certain beasts. This must seem incredible to men who use their reason, especially concerning such an excellent author of philosophy and a most abundant fountain of the sciences, from whom the knowledge of things divine and human has flowed down to us. Rather, this suspicion of **metempsychosis** <term>metempsychosis: the movement of a soul from one body to another, often called transmigration</term> arose from people who were partly ignorant of the Pythagorean mysteries and partly hateful out of envy. Indeed, the outstanding virtue of that man, his most upright life, his distinguished teaching, and his celebrated fame did not lack the malice of rivals. As usually happens, envious detractors left nothing untouched: **Timon**, **Xenophanes**, **Cratinus**, **Aristophon**, **Hermippus**, and others (of whom there is a great multitude) wrote many lies about Pythagoras in their books. They published things that were never said or written by him, or if he had said anything, they perverted it into a worse sense so that it might be believed that such a great man had wandered into error by teaching thoughtlessly. 

They attacked him regarding his principles, regarding numbers, regarding the **not eating of beans**, <note>Pythagoras famously forbade his followers from eating beans, a rule that sparked much ridicule and symbolic interpretation in antiquity.</note> regarding abstinence from eating animal flesh, regarding the underworld, and regarding that "passage of the soul" or **metempsychosis** of which we are now treating. For if he distinguished the patterns and species of things so clearly that they cannot be mutually transformed or confused, how could he ever communicate the human essence—which is its own unique form—to a beast? 

By his own authority, not even a substantive **unity** <term>unity: a "monad" or the number one, considered the building block of reality in Pythagorean thought</term> of a certain number is, according to nature, the unity of another number. As he says: <note>original Greek: αἱ δὲ μονάδες ἐν τῇ δυάδι, πρὸς τὰς ἐν τῇ τριάδι αὐτῇ ἀσύμβλητοι.</note> that is, "The units in the number two are incomparable to those in the number three." This is established in the study of nature, though things are handled far differently in Mathematics (with which we have no business at the moment). 

The "One" of each thing is a particular essence which will not occupy the essence of another thing, <note>original Greek: ἑκάστη γὰρ οὐσία ἑνὸς εἴδους μετέχει</note> that is, "For every substance participates in one species." Therefore, the human soul cannot pass into the life of another animal or any beast whatsoever, but rather remains in the law of its own nature, holding its own duty, <note>original Greek: ὡς τὰ τῷ εἴδει ἕτερα οὐ συνέχεσθαι</note> that is, "So that things differing in species do not merge." 

Furthermore, although one seal pressed into many pieces of wax forms many identical shapes, the same piece of wax cannot bear the diverse forms of different seals at the same time. In no way is the seal of the **human form**, which is the **image of God**, permitted to mix with an inferior nature. Just as Pythagoras was accustomed to teaching all his ideas enigmatically, he signaled the true meaning of this opinion with his own special mark, celebrating among his other symbols that which was most pleasing to him...

### BOOK II

"Do not carry the image of God in a ring," <note>original Greek: λίην θεοῦ εἰκόνα μὴ ποδιφέρειν; original Latin: *In sigillo Dei imaginem non circumferre*</note> which in my judgment is rightly understood in roughly this way: That the image of God, which is the soul of man, is not able to "seal" <note>To "seal" here means to imprint its specific essence or form onto other types of matter.</note> or give form to other natures all around it. For so says **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary sage of ancient Egypt, traditionally regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, which explores the relationship between the divine, the cosmos, and humanity.</note>, the teacher of the Egyptians, in his book to **Asclepius**: "One part of man," he says, "is simple, which we call the form of the divine likeness." And a little further down: "There are two images of God: namely, the world and man." Therefore, whether out of envy or ignorance, people have unfairly explained his [Pythagoras'] views on the passage of souls after death, as well as their descent before the generation of a man. Surely there is no one now, provided they possess any intellect, who does not agree with me on this.

For when many thought the soul of man was drawn out from the potential of matter, our master himself [Pythagoras] determined that it is more to be believed that it is infused into the body by God Himself. For this reason, he asserted that the soul exists "before" the body—which is not to be understood in terms of time, but in terms of purity and the dignity of its nature. He therefore called this infusion the "descent" of the soul, which his followers later treated in various ways with many twists and turns, each according to his own path, and not always according to the author's intent. Pythagoras commanded that the descent of the human soul into the body should not be understood according to location, nor according to a movement from the intellectual world through individual spheres to the elemental world (as **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who taught that the soul physically descends through the celestial spheres, picking up various planetary qualities along the way.</note> and other supporters claim), but rather according to the sequence of natural forms. In this sequence, the final perfection of the human body is the rational soul, which completes the whole so thoroughly that man is rightly called a "divine animal."

Therefore, Pythagoras wished for only those living beings whose nature is sacred—that is, those whom reason distinguishes individually—to be considered a divine race, namely, those propagated from God, as he published in the **Golden Verses** <note>A famous collection of moral and philosophical exhortations attributed to Pythagoras, though likely written by his later followers.</note>. The species of this race is neither changed nor converted; thus the forms of individual kinds remain permanent, even if they differ within that same form. After the death of a man, however, if he has died a just man, his soul transcends into the pure heavens <note>original Latin: *pura æthera*</note> and spends eternity with the blessed, as a god among the gods. For he says:

->*Setting judgment above as the best charioteer, if you leave the body and come into the free ether, you shall be an immortal god, incorruptible, and no longer mortal.* <note>original Greek: ἡνίοχον γνώμην στήσας...; original Latin: *Aurigam iudicium statuens...*</note><-

But if a man dies unjust and wicked in incurable and deadly sins, then Pythagoras taught that his soul must wash away all its guilt through various punishments. He taught that these punishments would be more or less harsh and long-lasting according to the magnitude and multitude of the crimes. To these souls are assigned these lower places of nature, and bodies that are sometimes imaginary or figural, and sometimes real. The soul does not "form" these bodies as an essential part, but rather inhabits them like a **tenant** <term>inquilinus: a temporary resident or lodger who does not own the property</term> for the purpose of enduring punishments, or stands by them through local proximity, like an internal mover to a mobile object, or is tormented around them, subject to tortures—just as **Tityus** is tormented by vultures, **Ixion** upon the wheels of serpents, **Tantalus** in the river, and **Sisyphus** at the stone, and
