# CABALA

Prometheus with the eagles. Since a demon of the Underworld <note>original: *dæmon Tartaræus*</note> can seize and besiege a body, why could not a foul soul, condemned to the punishments of the lower world <note>original: *inferorum poenas*</note>, enter a true body of any species by some dispensation? Or, clothed in air, why could it not display any form to the sight, just as the dying Dido addresses Aeneas: "I shall follow you with black fires." <note>A quote from Vergil's *Aeneid* (4.384), where Dido threatens to haunt Aeneas as a ghost after her suicide.</note> And Pliny the Younger writes of a matter believed to be true, concerning a house that the philosopher **Athenodorus of Tarsus** had purchased; he says it was infamous for its noise and haunting, because the image of a shaggy old man was seen there. Even in our own age, similar frightful sights <note>original: *terriculamentis*</note> occur daily through thicker remnants of the soul. Then various shapes and sights mock the eyes; for suddenly it will become a bristly boar, a black tiger, a scaly dragon, or a lioness with a golden neck; or it will give off the sharp sound of flame, transforming itself into all sorts of wondrous things: fire, a horrible beast, and flowing water. <note>This sequence of transformations is a classic description of the sea-god Proteus from Vergil's *Georgics* (4.407-410).</note>

These indeed we call "phantastic bodies"—that is, appearances—which the released souls of men as well as demons can assume. We know of this from the story of the bold <note>original: *procacem*</note> beautiful woman at Corinth, a **Lamia** <note>A mythological creature often depicted as a female demon or vampire who preyed on young men.</note> who sought the philosopher **Menippus the Lycian**, whom **Apollonius of Tyana** publicly exposed as a ghost <note>original: *lemurem*</note>. Finally, there was that shaggy and beggarly old man at Ephesus, once the cause of a plague, who was noted for this kind of metamorphosis; they say that after he was crushed by stones, he was seen as a dog, like a Molossian hound. **Philostratus** wrote about both of these in the fourth book of his *Life of Apollonius*.

However, there is another explanation for the claim that **Pythagoras** was once **Euphorbus** <note>Euphorbus was a Trojan hero. Pythagoras famously claimed he remembered being Euphorbus in a past life.</note>. He was not the first to institute such a way of speaking; rather, it had been used long before in common practice among the most ancient people. According to this custom, if someone were endowed with a certain virtue or vice, they were likened to another who had formerly been eminent in that same condition. For example, they called any man they pleased who excelled in strength "Hercules." Thus **Marcus Varro** says, "Rusticellus was called Hercules because he could lift his own mule." And the Pythagorean **Numenius** writes that "**Plato** is nothing other than **Moses** speaking in the Attic language <note>original: *Platonem quàm Moysen Attica lingua loquentem*</note>." 

Often, too, **Cicero** was called the "Latin Demosthenes," and others were named similarly from an equality of virtues and works and a likeness of character, not because of a shared single substance. In the same way, the servant in **Plautus**'s play called a man "Solon" <note>Solon was a famous Athenian lawmaker.</note> who was likewise busy writing laws; of that busy man he says, "For now he is busy during the day, clearly a Solon, so that he may write down laws." Those words of Plautus indicate an ingrained custom of ancient speech: that they would say a man *is* someone else if he were similar in nature, talent, character, love, affection, and work. Whence the Romans used to add the word "Another" <note>original: *Alter*</note> to this adage, as in: "You are another self" <note>original: *alter ego*</note>, and "I am another you." This was said even though they knew and saw that, in truth, I am not you, nor are you me. But in both of us, there is the same feeling, an equal zeal, the same will, and the same agreement...

<summary>The author argues that ghostly apparitions are "phantastic bodies" rather than physical ones and explains that Pythagoras's claim of past lives was a linguistic metaphor for shared character (an "alter ego") rather than literal reincarnation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's re-interpretation of Pythagorean philosophy. Having previously discussed how souls might appear as ghosts or phantoms, the author now argues that "metempsychosis" was originally a metaphor for shared character and passion between generations, rather than a literal rebirth of the soul into new bodies.</meta>

->## BOOK II.<-
->791<-

...spirit and mind <note>original: *spiritum, animum*</note> changing from their very substance <note>original Greek: *ἐξ οὐσίας αὐτῶμ μεταβαλλομένους*</note>. For the ancients defined "souls" as the movements and wills of men. This is why people of the same character, care, and diligence—possessing a similar purpose and equal, balanced movement and feeling—are commonly called **unanimous** <note>literally "of one soul"</note>. It is not at all foreign to the early philosophers to say that the soul is the source of motion and sensation in a human being. Aristotle inquires into this, stating that "the animate <note>Greek: *τὸ ἔμψυχου*</note> seems to differ from the inanimate <note>Greek: *τοῦ ἀψύχου*</note> in two ways: by motion and by sensation <note>Greek: *κινήσει τε καὶ τῷ αἰσθάνεσθαι*</note>."

Therefore, whoever is moved and affected by the same things, and appears to perceive the same things through their senses, are popularly said to be of "one soul" <note>Greek: *ψυχῆς*</note>. From this comes that famous <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>original Greek: *μετεmψύχωσις*, the "migration of souls"</note>. To truly learned men, "transanimation" <note>original: *transanimatio*</note> is actually nothing other than finding the same care, similar movement, and equal passion of a deceased person in a living person some time later.

Using this common and well-worn way of speaking, **Pythagoras**—having returned from the **Magi** of the Persians (for that is what they call their wise men)—would sometimes, for the sake of brightening a banquet among friends, use the manner of the Magi. He would say that he contained within himself the souls of the Trojan soldier **Euphorbus**, and of **Callicles**, **Hermotimus**, **Pyrrhus**, **Pyrander**, **Calidona**, and **Alce**, and finally his own soul as Pythagoras. He said this because he carried an affection, a passion, and a will inclined toward certain noble things found in each of those individuals—things toward which they themselves were most strongly moved during their own lives.

Above all, because the virtue of war had shone brightly in the Trojan Euphorbus, Pythagoras claimed to have obtained the soul of Euphorbus, as if he now possessed Euphorbus's heart. He could certainly boast of this when the practitioners of the "art of war" praised him, seeing the strength of his sides, his arms, and his whole body, and weighing his incredible love for the strongest athletes—an affection he showed them through both costly equipment and magnificent expense. Before this, athletes were nourished on dried figs, soft cheese, and wheat; but our Pythagoras is found to be the first to have nourished them with meat.

When they marveled that such a love for fighting could exist in a philosopher dedicated to letters, it is no wonder if he responded that the "soul of Euphorbus" flourished within him. By this he meant that the talent, passion, movement, and will of Euphorbus resided in him; for although he was a teacher of peace and an author of quiet contemplation, he nevertheless felt within himself a Trojan-like desire for war. Once heard, a rumor soon arose among those who believe too easily, and the story spread—either through ignorance of the Pythagorean mysteries or through the malice of the envious, who always distort the best things and repeat what they have heard quite differently from how it was said—that the soul of Euphorbus, slain in the Trojan war, had migrated into Pythagoras. This opinion was later aided by writers and poets. Hence **Ovid**, in the fifteenth book of his *Metamorphoses* <note>original: *Transfigurationis*</note>, having borrowed these bits of Greek trivia in his usual way, sang thus of Pythagoras: "Souls do not die; always having left their prior seat, they live and dwell received in new homes. I myself (for I remember) in the time of the Trojan war was the son of Panthous..." <note>Referring to Euphorbus, son of Panthous, a Trojan hero.</note>

<summary>The author explains that the Pythagorean concept of metempsychosis was a metaphor for shared personality traits and passions across generations, rather than literal reincarnation. He illustrates this by showing how Pythagoras’s physical strength and interest in athletic training led to the legend that he possessed the soul of the Trojan hero Euphorbus.</summary>

# OF THE KABBALAH #

->792<-

...I was once **Euphorbus**, in whose chest the spear of the younger son of Atreus <note>Menelaus</note> once stuck. I recognized the shield, the burden of my left hand, in the temple of Juno at **Argos**, city of Abas. <note>original Latin quoting Ovid: *des Euphorbus eram, cui pectore quondam hæsit in aduerſo haſta minoris Atridæ. Cognoui clypeum læuæ geſtamina noſtra per Abanteis templo Iunonis in Argis.*</note> 

But do not be amazed, **Marranus**, for you will find none of these things written in the books of Pythagoras himself. He published only three volumes: the first **pedagogical** <note>original Greek: *παιδευτικὸν*, concerning education</note>, the second **political** <note>original Greek: *πολιτικὸν*, concerning the state</note>, and the third **physical** <note>original Greek: *φυσικὸν*, concerning nature</note>, which some ascribe to **Lysis**. Let us also include the *Golden Verses*. Scan every single line, and you will nowhere find anything from that man regarding the "transanimation" <note>the crossing of souls</note> of the soul. Therefore, you may more easily believe the rumor was sown by envious people—whatever is said regarding that <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>original Greek: *μετεμψυχώσεῖ*, the transmigration of souls into new bodies</note>. 

Indeed, the inconsistency of the story clearly indicates this: some say Euphorbus's shield was dedicated in the temple of Juno at Argos, while others affirm it was dedicated to **Pallas Athena**. They even claim the inscription on that very shield was: *To Athena, Menelaus from Euphorbus* <note>original Greek: *Ἀθηνᾷ, μενέλαως ἀπὸ εὐφόρβου*</note>. The authority for this is **Maximus of Tyre** in his sixteenth dissertation. Legal experts may decide how much faith should be placed in such testimony. 

For my part, I cannot be led to believe that **Ovid’s** fable about the transition of souls was taught by such an excellent, serious man, learned in every science. I find it even less believable because so many prominent authors have passed down the opposite. For many assert that Pythagoras was the first among the Greeks to discover that souls are immortal, but they speak a manifest falsehood. **Homer**, by far the most ancient of the Greeks, long preceded this dogma; in his works, the souls of the dead in the underworld discourse on many things and prophesy much. Does the famous name of that admirable man <note>Homer</note> suggest anything else but that the dead entirely persist <note>original Greek: *ὅτι ὅλως οἱ νεκύες*</note>—that our souls remain after death? 

Furthermore, in the story of the companions of **Odysseus**, Homer clearly shows (though the imprudent do not see it) that souls separated from the body do not actually take on the nature of beasts, but only put on the **outward habits of brutes**, and live with such horror as **Circe** commanded. However, those who hold the "root and flower of the Moly" <note>the magical herb given by Hermes to protect Odysseus</note> will find their souls are secure, as is told in the tenth book of the *Odyssey*. 

But let us return to that irony regarding Euphorbus. Whenever the Platonists write about the divine dogmas of Pythagoras, they say everything is **delivered in riddles** <note>original Greek: *αἰνίττεσθαι*, to speak in allegories</note>, that is, handed down through a more obscure allegory. This is confirmed by **Apollonius of Tyana**, that famous Pythagorean, in a discourse held with **Thespesion**, the leader of the **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics</note>, as recorded in the sixth volume of **Philostratus**. Apollonius says: *If I touch upon riddles, the wisdom of Pythagoras allows this; for he prayed to speak in riddles.* <note>original Greek: *εἰ δ’ αἰνιγμάτων ἅπτομαι, σοφία πυθαγόρᾳ ξυγχωρεῖ ταῦτα, ηὔξατο γὰρ τὸ αἰνίττεσθαι.*</note> 

When, however, he was disputing with the **Brahmans** of India in the third book of the same work, inquiring about how the soul is preserved, **Iarchas** said: "Just as Pythagoras told it to you, we told it to the Egyptians." Apollonius replied: "Were you then one of the Trojans, just as Pythagoras was Euphorbus?" Hear now, Marranus, what Thespesion answered after first asking: "Which of the Greek leaders..."

He cites historical discrepancies and earlier precedents in Homer to suggest that Pythagoreanism focuses on the immortality of the soul rather than literal reincarnation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Pythagorean doctrine of reincarnation (metempsychosis) should be understood as a philosophical allegory for the physical transformation of matter rather than the literal travel of a soul from one body to another. It follows a discussion where the author suggests Pythagoras's claim to have been the Trojan hero Euphorbus was an "irony" or a riddle.</meta>

## BOOK II. ##

...army, he considered [Achilles] more worthy of admiration. To him **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a first-century philosopher often compared to Pythagoras</note> replied that Achilles had been granted first place by Homer. Then **Iarchas** <note>A fictionalized Indian sage from the life of Apollonius</note> said: "Why," he asked, "do you not also consider my progenitor, or rather, the progenerating body? For this is what **Pythagoras** also thought of **Euphorbus**." <note>original Greek: πῶς ἔφη ἀλλὰ νὰ καὶ τὸν πρόγονον θεωρεῖ τὸν ἐμὸν, μᾶλλον δὲ, τὸ πρόγονον σῶμα, τοτὶ γὰρ καὶ πυϑαγόρας, εὔφορβον ἡγεῖτο.</note> That is to say: "Regarding this matter, Apollonius, consider also my ancestor, or more accurately the body that produced me; for in this way Pythagoras also believed he was Euphorbus." Then he recounts that **Ganges**, once a king of the Indians and son of the river Ganges, surpassed Achilles in many virtues, and that he himself was that very producing body which he now was.

These words do not indicate the "transmigration of souls," but the "transmutation of bodies," much like any matter that is suited to receive this or that form. It is just as if a Comedy were to say, "I was previously a Tragedy," because tragedy and comedy are born from the same letters and elements, as **Aristotle** says in the first book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Or if a certain dog were to say, "I was previously a horse," because the dog fed upon the body of a certain horse; once that food was converted into the substance of the creature fed, that horse might be called in common speech the dog’s <term>progenerating body</term> <note>original Greek: πρόγονον σῶμα (*progonon soma*), the physical material from which a new thing is generated</note>, namely, that from which he was produced. Yet no one would judge from this speech that the soul of the horse had passed into the dog.

For what reason, then, should I believe that Pythagoras taught that souls pass into other bodies, based only on the fact that he said he was previously Euphorbus? For here it is clearly evident and agreed that it was not the soul, but the body itself that was judged to have been Euphorbus. Nevertheless, this saying of his was not plain, but a pure riddle (*ænigma*), by which he wished to hint at a certain secret unknown to that age: namely, that **Prime Matter** <note>the fundamental, formless substance of the universe</note> is not only capable of taking all forms, but is even greedy for them and, always moved by desire, is never satisfied by any single form.

This was equally apparent to the most philosophical Emperor **Marcus Antoninus** <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, when he wrote in the third book of *To Himself* <note>The *Meditations*</note>: "The nature of the whole so loves this, that it changes all things and makes new things like them. For in a certain way, everything that is to come from it is a riddle." <note>original Greek: ὁπίσϑεν οὕτως φιλείἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις, ὡς τὸ τὰ πάντα μεταβάλλειν καὶ ποιέῖν νέα ὁμοία. αἰνίγμα γὰρ τρόπον τινὰ πᾶν τὸ ὑπ᾽ αὐτὸ ἐσομενον.</note> That is to say, nothing is so desired by the nature of the universe as to transmute existing things and make new, similar things. For in a certain way, every seed is itself the being of that which is to come from it. 

And again in the seventh book: "The nature of the universe, out of the whole of essence as if from wax, has now fashioned a little horse; then, dissolving this into the nature of a tree, it has used its matter. Then into a little man, then into something else." <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις, ἐκ τὶ ὅλης ὐσίας ὡς κηρῶ νῦν μὲν ἱππάριον ἔπλασε, συγχίασε δὲ τοῦτο εἰς δένδρον φύσιῳ, συνεχρήσατο τῆ ὕλη αὐτοῦ. εἶτα εἰς ἀνϑρωπάριον εἶτα εἰς ἄλλόν.</note> Hence nature is named by **Orpheus** with these epithets: "much-devising mother" <note>original Greek: πολυμήχανω μήτηρ (*polymêchanô mêtêr*)</note> and "ordainer of foreign shapes" <note>original Greek: ἀλλοτριομορφοδίαιτοϛ (*allotriomorphodiaitos*)</note>. Whatever the case may be, I for my part will far more readily believe that Pythagoras introduced that riddle for the sake of an example, if he said he was Euphorbus or anyone else. But if it is believed that he was weaving a history, it must certainly be thought that he did so for no other reason than to show—

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue regarding the nature of the soul and the body. # OF THE CABALA #

...[that it is possible] for a soul separated from the body to return, by God's power, back into that very same body which it had entirely left and which had decayed. It returns not into just any other body, for it was one and the same body—no matter how many different names it was called—in which Pythagoras had lived so many times. This we have been able to learn from **Iarchas**, the wisest of the Indians <note>A legendary sage often cited in accounts of the life of Apollonius of Tyana</note>. This identity is found not in size or quantity, but in substance and quality; just as the sea, although it is homogeneous and one, we nevertheless call this part the Aegean, that the Ionian, this the Myrtoan, and another the Crissaean.

In the same way, they first named the one man who was reborn several times **Aethalides**, then **Euphorbus**, later **Hermotimus**, then **Pyrrhus**, and finally our famous **Pythagoras**. He, as a most contemplative and divine philosopher, did not attribute these many **regenerations** <note>The process of being born again</note> to the powers of nature, but to God alone. As **Heraclides Ponticus** <note>A Greek philosopher and disciple of Plato</note> reports regarding this **Palingenesia** <note>original Greek: παλιγγενεσία; meaning 'rebirth' or 're-creation'</note>, he invoked **Mercury** <note>The god Hermes, who traditionally guided souls to and from the underworld</note>, so that he might show that no one returns to life except by divine power.

For as **Justin**, that philosopher and Christian martyr, recounts in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, God is especially honored with a title by Pythagoras: he is called the **Animation of all things** <note>original Greek: ψύχωσις τῶν ὅλων (psychosis tōn holōn)</note>. This is because He infuses the soul into all humans, governs it once infused, and restores it when it has been taken away, as often and whenever He wills. Such a thing has often been seen in other men and discovered through certain experience, as reported by the most noble writers.

For **Aristeas of Proconnesus** once died in a fuller’s workshop. Then, in the seventh year afterward, he appeared alive to the citizens of the city, and he then composed poems about the **Arimaspians** <note>A legendary people of the far north said to war with griffins</note>; **Herodotus** mentions his story in the fourth book of his *Histories*. Furthermore, there lived **Er**, a Pamphylian by race, in Armenia; when he had fallen in battle and the other corpses were picked up on the tenth day already decayed, he was found whole with an uncorrupted body. Having been carried home for the funeral rites, on the twelfth day after his death, while he was placed upon the pyre, he rose again and recounted what he had seen in the meantime. **Plato** wrote about this in the tenth volume of the *Republic*. To this we may also add what we read of a girl who died in Rome; as she was being carried to the tomb, she was restored to life by **Apollonius of Tyana**, as told in the fourth book of **Philostratus**. **Alcestis** is also told to have lived for a long time again after being resuscitated by **Hercules**.

Then **Marranus** <note>A character in this dialogue representing the Jewish perspective</note> said: "How closely you approach our own traditions, Philolaus! For if **Simon** <note>Likely referring to Simon ben Jochai, the traditional figurehead of Kabbalistic wisdom</note> were standing here, he would recount to us from the Hebrew books how God once took from the spirit that was in **Moses** and gave it to the seventy men. After some time, when **Elijah** had been taken from men, his spirit settled upon **Elisha**, and likewise he himself made the son of the **Shunammite** woman return to life from death. I add now **Samuel**, who was dead and whom a certain woman in **Endor** raised, who after his resurrection spoke with King **Saul**. But hear what **Ezekiel** the prophet saw: namely, a field full of the dry bones of the dead..."

It bridges classical Greek accounts of people returning from the dead (like Er and Aristeas) with biblical examples of the spirit being shared or restored (like Moses, Elijah, and Elisha).</summary>

# BOOK II. #

...and bones came together with bones, each to its joint, and behold, nerves and flesh grew upon them, and skin was stretched over them from above, and breath entered into them and they lived again, and they stood upon their feet <note>A reference to the vision of the valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37</note>. These things are contained in the sacred writings of the Hebrews, but many more are read as described in the histories of the Christians. Indeed, on my own part, I would dare to affirm this to you without parable, without riddle, and with all irony removed: that **Jesus the Nazarene** truly and plainly raised **Lazarus**, the brother of Martha, who had been dead for four days. Furthermore, he restored to life the deceased son of a certain widow, and the daughter of **Jairus**, a ruler of the synagogue, and others commemorated in holy scripture. God also raised this same Jesus, and at his death many bodies of those who had passed from life arose, and coming out of their tombs, they entered the holy city and appeared to many. Finally, **Paul of Tarsus** restored **Eutychus**—who had departed from life by an accident—to the light of the living. **Martin** <note>Saint Martin of Tours, a 4th-century bishop</note>, while not yet a bishop, and indeed not yet even baptized, raised three dead men. I could produce a catalog of men recalled from destruction back to their former life, were it not that you are aware it is easy for us Christians to believe that the souls of men return into bodies, we who plainly confess that a general resurrection of all human bodies will occur again for living. 

On this subject, the most eloquent Athenian philosopher **Athenagoras** composed an entire book for the Christians <term>On the Resurrection</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀναστάσεως (peri anastaseōs)</note>, which is certainly worthy of learned ears. Even among the Turks, Moors, and Hagarenes <note>Terms used in the Renaissance to refer to Muslims</note>, **Mahometh** speaks thus in the **Alcoran** <note>The Quran</note>: to those who say, "When we are bones, or reduced to nothing, how shall we be made into new men?" he responds, "Even if you were made of stone or iron, or whatever is harder, He who created you the first time will recall you to be resurrected for life again" (thus far in Sura 26). And again in Sura 45 he says, "He who first fashioned us will give us life a second time." 

For this reason, I would wish us to follow **Pythagoras** with all the greater veneration, as he—more closely than almost all other Greek philosophers in nearly all matters, and not only in this cause—has approached our faith. For we see how **Aristotle** believed in nothing except what he could touch with his hand, or discern with his eyes, or grasp through a formal logic <note>original: syllogismo</note>. Therefore, at the end of his treatise *On Generation and Corruption*, he by no means admitted the return of a dead man, using a very weak argument and agreeing more with **Alcmaeon** than with his own teachers, against the proverb common in his time: <term>human affairs are a circle</term> <note>original Greek: κύκλον εἶναι τὰ ἀνθρώπινα (kyklon einai ta anthrōpina)</note>. Others followed him—indeed, a whole cohort of philosophizers—who are to be rebuked in this: that by presuming they know everything and others know nothing, they mock Pythagoras after the rest, and exclaim that line of **Lucian**: <term>Who will buy? Who wants to be more than human? Who wants to know the harmony of the universe and to live again?</term> <note>original Greek: τίς ὠνήσεται, τίς ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον εἶναι βούλεται, τίς εἰδέναι τὴν τοῦ παντὸς ἁρμονίαν, καὶ ἀναβιῶναι πάλιν</note>. In this way, they ridiculously bid for him at auction <note>original: sub hasta licitantur; literally "bidding under the spear," the Roman custom for public auctions</note>, as if he were a piece of livestock to be despised,

<meta>This page continues the dialogue on the merits and history of Pythagoras, shifting from the theological discussion of the resurrection to a defense of Pythagoras’s personal character and lifestyle against historical detractors.</meta>

### CABALA ###

...or a vile slave. I will gladly allow them to know many things, provided they permit others to have learned a little as well. Indeed, I have now become so stirred up in my stomach against those who are accustomed to detract easily from the most ancient teachers and princes of philosophy, and I have grown hot with anger more at length than was necessary, so that you may know that I—no differently than is right—highly value your **Pythagoras** and vehemently hate his detractors, who are not men but monsters of men. 

Then **Philolaus** said: "There are some who must be forgiven for not knowing such hidden and secret mysteries, for we cannot all do everything. Therefore, it will be a kindness to return to them if they have unwittingly brought infamy upon him. However, those who were once practiced in that silence <note>Pythagorean initiates were famously required to maintain silence for several years as a test of self-control</note>, and yet cast off the white toga of the Pythagoreans and began to harm the majesty of his doctrine through insult and to 'diminish the head' <note>original: "caput minuere" — a Roman legal term referring to the loss of civil rights or status</note> of such a great philosopher—those I would judge not only arrogant but even most impure of men. 

Among their number is **Xenophanes**, who is said to have mocked him in his *Elegy*, playing on the story that once, when Pythagoras saw a dog being beaten, he took pity and said: 'Stop this, for it is the soul of a dear friend which I recognized from its voice.' But that mockery is clearly found in **Diogenes Laertius**, as is the story that in the underworld with **Pluto**, the disciples of Pythagoras feast, while he himself saw the soul of **Hesiod** bound to a column, groaning and gnashing, and also the soul of **Homer** hanging from a tree and surrounded by serpents. These and similar crimes of slander were the calumnies of the most infamous sophists, who defile everything by their touch, polluting feasts with their unclean mouths and leaving foul tracks behind. 

Regarding what they spread abroad about Pythagoras and the eating of all living things—claiming that Pythagoras forbade it—it disturbs me very little, since there are most famous authors who refute those lies. For that distinguished writer **Aristoxenus** says Pythagoras did not abstain from living creatures, but ate meat. **Porphyry** proves this in the first book of <term>On Abstinence from Animal Food <note>original: "περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων" (peri apoches empsychon)</note></term>, because while some were nourished on cheese and others previously on figs, Pythagoras was the first of all to feed athletes on meat, saying that meat has the power to acquire incredible strength; so says Porphyry. 

And **Apollodorus** the mathematician testifies that he sacrificed a hundred oxen when he had discovered <term>that the side subtending the right angle of a right-angled triangle is equal in power to the sides containing it <note>original: "ὅτι τριγώνου ὀρθογ, ὀρθὴν γωνίαν ὑποτείνουσα ἴσον δύναται ταῖς περιεχούσαις." This is the earliest known description of the Pythagorean theorem.</note></term>. That is, that the side lying under the right-angled triangle is worth as much as those which are attached. 

Nevertheless, he was of a most modest life, of moderate nourishment, and of sparing drink, as **Lycon of Iasus** wrote concerning Pythagoras. For this reason, his use of common things was rare when abroad; for he was often fed on thin honey alone, as **Athenaeus** has it in the tenth book of the *Banquets of the Learned*. And for this reason, if he were in the pursuit of letters, he would warn to carefully avoid those things which would be heavy food, lest the brain be harmed by the careless burden of the stomach, so that they might be able to apply themselves more vehemently to contemplation; who would not give praise for this?"

<meta>This page continues the defense of Pythagoras's character and teachings. The text argues that Pythagoras’s "obscurity" was a deliberate choice to protect sacred truths and to engage the minds of serious students.</meta>

<header>BOOK II. 797</header>

to the teacher: that those things which he had learned among the **Hebrews** were of a harsh nourishment and forbidden in their law; likewise, what he had recognized among the **Indians** as things to be avoided, such as sea fish (which are neither useful for the stomach nor accepted in the offerings to the gods, for no one has ever heard of a fish being immolated in sacrifices); and finally, what he had received among the **Egyptians** regarding the **bean**, <note>original: "faba"</note> teaching that it is not a pure legume (as **Herodotus** noted in his *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories*</note>). These things they were clearly not to take as food, seeking tranquility of mind through the perpetual study of letters. However, he did not wish such pious warnings to be observed as exactly and "to the nail" <note>An idiom meaning "with perfect precision"</note> as the Law of the Twelve Tables. For he himself is reported by **Xenophilus**, **Aristoxenus**, and certain others of his older contemporaries to have lived on young piglets and tender kids. In the fourth book of the *Attic Nights* by **Aulus Gellius**, you will find that he used no legume more frequently than the bean, as it gently eased the bowels.

But the matter of beans will be explained later among the other symbols; for now, let those things I have said before and those I am about to say regarding numbers come to your mind. Thus you may recognize how impiously certain foul **buffoons** <note>original: "Sanniones" — mocking jesters</note> of philosophy mock **Pythagoras**, the prince of philosophers, with a "sneer from behind" <note>original: "postica sanna"</note> because he taught that **number** is the principle of all things. They argue that since number is a discrete quantity, it must follow after things rather than precede them—as if he himself understood "numbers" to be merely the pebbles used for counting, from which all things supposedly arose!

I marvel at these critics, not without laughter, because although they have heard frequently from the testimony of the wisest men that almost all **Pythagorean philosophy**—and especially that which concerns divine matters—is **mystical** and proposed through **enigmas**, they nonetheless demand that this most divine part of wisdom concerning numbers be taken plainly and without any metaphor, thereby imitating the folly of the **Tyrrhenians**. <note>A reference to literal-mindedness or perhaps a specific historical reputation for superstition</note> Yet it was the custom of the ancient and most venerable sages of that age to hand down the profound inquiry of wisdom through the allegories of secret letters and the mysteries of the senses. Thus, the works of the most ancient philosophers and poets alike are filled with enigmas, both because of the obscurity of the subject matter and out of a light contempt for the common crowd. For as **Maximus Tyrius** says in his tenth disputation: 

-> "For when things are not clearly seen because of human weakness, the myth is a more graceful interpreter." <- 
<note>original Greek: "πραγμάτων γὰρ ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρωπίνης ἀδυνίας ἢ καθορωμένων σαφῶς, εὐσχημονέστερος ἐρμηνεὺς ὁ μῦθος"</note>

Indeed, on the authority of **Macrobius**, that philosophy is truly fitting which is announced under a pious veil of fictions, covered by honorable things and clothed in names. I believe this most carefully excites and introduces the minds of scholars to the notion of wonderful things. For that which is ready at hand before the doors is sought with less diligence than that which is hidden far away in the abyss of the deep. Thus, ease of apprehension (believe one who has experienced it) breeds negligence of study in disciples, and that which is very easily obtained is only coldly sought. It also happens sometimes that we are unable to express abstruse things with any propriety of words, which instead require long circuits and variously composed speech...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pythagorean discipline and the use of symbols. While the previous page addressed dietary habits and the protection of sacred truths, this page explores the social and mnemonic functions of secret signs and the philosophical significance of the Monad (the One) and the Dyad (the Two).</meta>

# CABALA

...we would be forced to express [our ideas], had it not been conveniently found useful to employ brief enigmas. Indeed, this practice is quite practical, for it is common for opposing military camps to issue certain watchwords which they call **tokens** <note>original: "tesseras" — tablets or passwords used by soldiers to identify allies</note>, so that each leader can distinguish his own soldiers and they can recognize one another. Just as in Caesar’s war the token was "Mother Venus," for Sulla it was "Delphic Apollo," for the Jews "The Lord God" <note>original: "Lar Deus" — using the Roman term for a protective household deity to describe the God of Israel</note>, and for Jephthah "Shibboleth" <note>A biblical password from Judges 12:6 used to identify members of the tribe of Ephraim by their distinct pronunciation</note>.

Thus, it would certainly not be unseemly to hand down peculiar and secret symbols of doctrine to one’s close associates, so that whichever disciples used them more frequently would become dearer to the master and love one another more than the rest. From this, the Pythagoreans fashioned for themselves a kind of unbreakable chain of love and friendship through certain symbols and signs. For Pythagoras was, above all, most eager to foster friendship; if he learned that someone shared his symbols, he immediately accepted him as a comrade and friend, according to the records of **Diogenes Laertius** <note>A 3rd-century biographer of the Greek philosophers</note>.

For this reason, everyone desired more ardently to use the Pythagorean symbols—that is, the marks of the mysteries—both because they would be more pleasing to their teacher and because they would appear to the learned as "noble Pythagoreans." Moved by this, in **Plutarch’s** eighth book of *Table Talk*, **Philinus** was the only one among all the guests of **Sulla the Carthaginian** who abstained from animal meat during the feast, simply so he would be recognized as a Pythagorean.

Because of this, he was rebuked by **Lucius**, a Tyrrhenian by birth and a disciple of **Moderatus the Pythagorean**, for following the "shadow" of that dogma rather than its true meaning. This was a fault also worthy of rebuke in other Pythagoreans, who, affected by an immoderate desire for separate and peculiar customs, did not break bread like others at the dinners of comrades and friends, or did not eat brains, or rolled up their bedding upon rising from a feast, or sacrificed with bare feet, or turned away from the sun when about to speak, or left the public road to travel by side-paths, or when they laughed, laughed never or very little, or strictly abstained from eating beans, and used such things excessively, led more by superstition than by right reason.

Imitating only the **bark** <note>original: "corticem" — the outer shell or literal surface of a teaching</note> of the symbols and neglecting the intent, they sought to become known by these sorts of marks and were believed by the common people to be Pythagoreans of that same order. Therefore, symbols of this kind are signs of a single **college** <note>original: "collegij" — a society, guild, or brotherhood</note>.

Now, let us also add that when we measure the vast spaces of divine and human affairs and handle innumerable topics, enigmatic symbols—that is, marks that represent things—contribute greatly to memory, so that whenever we wish to remember, they are quickly presented to our sight. A symbol concerning the principles of things will therefore be most convenient: **the One and the Two** <note>In Pythagorean thought, these are the Monad (representing unity/the divine) and the Dyad (representing duality/matter)</note>. For the concept occurs more swiftly to those looking at individual things than "one" and "two" when we wish to examine the causes and origin of the universe. For at first glance, that which is "the same" and not "another" is placed before the eyes. From this, we conceive all things in the mind because "the same" and "the other" are **the One and the Two**. **Alcmaeon of Croton**, who lived in the time of Pythagoras, sought "two many things" <note>likely referring to dualities or pairs of opposites</note>, which he said were "contrarieties," much like the "strife" of **Empedocles**.

<summary>This page explains how Pythagoras used secret symbols and lifestyle habits to create a "chain of friendship" among his followers, while cautioning that following these outward signs without understanding their inner meaning is mere superstition. It concludes by introducing the Monad (the One) and the Dyad (the Two) as fundamental mnemonic and philosophical symbols for the origins of the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on Pythagorean philosophy, shifting from their social symbols and dietary laws to their mathematical and metaphysical foundations—specifically the significance of the number ten and the classification of existence.</meta>

### BOOK II.

Aristotle, in the first book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Postnaturalia" — literally 'after the physics,' the common Renaissance title for Aristotle's Metaphysics</note>, testifies that he [Pythagoras] set those opposites as wandering and infinitely diverse, such as white and black, sweet and bitter, good and evil, small and great. But the Pythagoreans, because of their love for the art of arithmetic, confined those diverse things that are mutually and reciprocally contrary—which the followers of **Alcmaeon** <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher from Croton who theorized that human affairs were governed by pairs of opposites</note> called "contrarieties"—to the number ten, that famous and all-encompassing number. These pairs are:

->**The Ten Pythagorean Opposites**<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Finite and Infinite | Odd and Even |
| One and Many | Right and Left |
| Male and Female | Resting and Moving |
| Straight and Curved | Light and Darkness |
| Good and Evil | Square and Oblong |

But these are such that, whichever side they fall on, they are two, and they are diverse precisely because they are two. For if they were one, they would not be contrary. Indeed, they reduced the universe to ten because this number is the most perfect of all, by which all nations and all peoples (except the Thracians)—Greeks and barbarians alike—count individual things, neither stopping short of it nor going beyond it, as if by the natural counters of the ten fingers.

Truly, this most adorned world we see shows the perfection of ten, since, according to the Pythagoreans, it is moved by only ten spheres. The number ten is also more perfect than the others because it contains many kinds of numbering: even, odd, square, cube, long, plane, the first incomposite, and the first composite. Nothing is more absolute than this, for in ten proportions four cubic numbers are consumed, by which the Pythagoreans say the universe is constituted.

**Archytas** <note>A Pythagorean mathematician and friend of Plato</note>, that noble Pythagorean of Tarentum, also embraced everything that exists within the number ten. Aristotle—the **Stagirite** <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, referring to his birthplace, Stagira</note> and leader of the Peripatetic school—imitated him, naming ten kinds of being "the ten Categories." He chose to title his volume with this name, showing philosophically (as **Eustathius** argued) ten <term>πράγματα</term> <note>original: "pragmata" — things or real entities</note>, that is, real beings; or (as **Alexander of Aphrodisias** held) ten <term>φωνάς</term> <note>original: "phonas" — voices or linguistic terms</note>, that is, words; or (as **Porphyry** held) ten <term>νοήματα</term> <note>original: "noemata" — thoughts</note>, that is, intellects or concepts.

Or perhaps **Iamblichus** spoke more correctly: ten simple words, not merely as words, but as signifying the simple things themselves by means of ten simple concepts. **Alexander of Aegeus**, **Ammonius** (son of Hermias), and **Simplicius**—those distinguished lovers of wisdom—agree with this. They even diligently judged that within these ten most general beings, two principal classes can be found into which they are divided, even though they arise from a single essence: such as substance and accident, or corporeal and incorporeal, or material and immaterial, or simple and composite.

For the number ten loves the number two in such a way that, progressing from the one, it is born through the two, and returns to the one through the two. For the first incomposite is the triad, consisting of one and two—not indeed "composed," but "consisting," because the number one has no "position" according to Iamblichus. Therefore, it does not create a "composition" when we wish to follow the proper use of words: <term>ὅτε γὰρ ἡ μονὰς μὲν οὖσα ἔτι μονὰς θέσιν προσλαμβάνῃ ὅτε ἡ στιγμὴ μὲν οὖσα στιγμὴ τὴν θέσιν ἀποβάλλῃ</term> <note>original Greek: "For when the monad, while still being a monad, takes on position; and when the point, while being a point, loses position."</note> as Simplicius says in his commentaries on the category of quantity, that is: For neither...

# BOOK II.

from which the number ten arises, and in which it ends. There exists a Pythagorean symbol for this, namely "one" and "two," which Zaratas <note>likely referring to Zoroaster, whom the Pythagoreans considered a teacher</note>, the teacher of Pythagoras, was accustomed to pronounce through names of propagation, calling "one" the father and "two" the mother, as testified by Plutarch of Chaeronea in *The Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus*. For as you learned previously, "one" and "two" together with the divine essence produce that four-foldness, the Tetractys <note>The sacred Pythagorean symbol of four rows of dots adding up to ten</note>, which is the idea of all things completed in the number ten. Pythagoras affirms it to be the **fount of eternal nature** <note>original Greek: παγὰν ἀενάου φύσεως</note>, which is nothing other than the knowledge of things within the divine mind operating rationally. Indeed, Pythagoras allegorically called the mind of God itself "number," when he said that number was the principle of the universe. For thus Plutarch writes in the fourth book of *The Opinions of the Philosophers*: **"Pythagoras takes number in place of the mind."** <note>original Greek: τὸν δ' ἀριθμὸν πυθαγόρας ἀντὶ τοῦ νοῦ παραλαμβάνει</note> This is clearly no unfair sign, because in bodily things nothing is more divine than the mind, and in separate things nothing is simpler than number. Nor, furthermore, can anything be thought more similar to the mind; and from this fount of eternal nature, through streams and channels, flows the Pythagorean number "one" and "two"—that which from eternity was, will be, or rather always is, gushing forth abundantly in the very fount of the immense Ocean. For this reason, men of the ancient age named that very "One" as *Zena* (as Aristotle wished when citing this line from Homer: **"Let there be one prince"** <note>original Greek: εἰς κοίρανος ἔσω</note>), saying *Zena* instead of *Zeua*, namely from "living" <note>the Greek name for Zeus is linked here to the verb 'to live'</note>. The Romans named him *Jove* [Jupiter] as if *Zeua*; and Cornutus, in his book on Greek theology, asserts him to be the soul of the whole world. "Two," however, was named Hera, both the sister and the wife of that *Zenos* (that is, of Jupiter), about whom Homer says this in the fourteenth book of the *Iliad*: **"Hera of the golden throne saw with her eyes her own brother and brother-in-law Zena—that is, Jupiter—sitting on the highest peak of many-fountained Ida."** <note>original Greek: Ἥρη δ' εἰσεῖδε χρυσόθρονος ὀφθαλμοῖσιν αὐτοκασίγνητον καὶ δαέρᾳ Ζῆνα δ' ἐπ' ἀκροτάτης κορυφῆς πολυπίδακος Ἴδης ἥμενον</note> By this, we can more easily understand the meanings of the most wise poets concerning the origin of things: that on "many-fountained Ida"—a mountain so named from "prospect" or "seeing" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰδεῖν (from seeing) or ἐκ τοῦ ἰδέα (from the idea/to know)</note>—Jupiter and Juno reside, just like "one" and "two" in that flowing idea of the quaternion <note>the four-fold number</note>. From there flow the principles of all things, which philosophers of a later age called "form" and "matter." And it is the same for us: "form" and "primary matter" are what "one" and "two" were to the most ancient philosophers, and what Jupiter and Juno were to the fit and illustrious poets. They come together on Mt. Gargarus in Ida and meet in the "Idea" of the divine mind; both are led by two chariots and both by four horses. But in descending, Jupiter remains in Olympus, while Juno reaches toward the lower things, as Homer testifies, saying: **"For I go to see the ends of the fertile earth... but now for your sake I come here through Olympus."** <note>original Greek: εἶμι γὰρ ὀψομένη πολυφόρβου πείρατα γαίης... νῦν δὲ σὲῦ εἵνεκα δεῦρο κατ' ὀλύμπου τό δ' ἱκάνω</note> Nevertheless, neither completely deserts the other. <meta>This page continues the exploration of the Pythagorean Tetractys, moving from the mathematical relationship of the "One" and "Two" to the geometric manifestation of the universe as a pyramid of light and fire.</meta>

# CABALA

Therefore, in this way, the beginning of the universe proceeds from the divine mind. The <margin>**Tetractys** <note>The sacred Pythagorean symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the organization of the universe.</note></margin> looks back toward its own essence, which is the primary unity, producing all things; at the same time, it remembers its own origin from the first product because it existed prior. Thus, it says "once one, twice two," and immediately the "four-foldness" (the quaternary) stands firm. It holds the highest unity at the peak of its summit, and suddenly it becomes a pyramid, whose base is the "flat four" which mathematicians use to signify a surface. Upon this base, the radiating light of the divine unity already mentioned creates the surface of an incorporeal fire. Because of the descent of Juno <note>Here used as an allegory for physical matter.</note>—that is, of matter—to the lower regions, the nature of essential light immediately arises, not as something new, but as something illuminating. 

And this is the creation of the "middle world," which **Simonides** <note>A Greek lyric poet often cited in philosophical contexts.</note> called the "supreme god," because the world cannot bear a direct comparison to the Deity; therefore, in its own judgment, it is illuminated as "super-supreme" and incomparable. Truly, this middle world is rightly called Olympus, because it is entirely full of light and separated forms <note>Non-material intellects or ideas.</note> "in the seats of the immortals" <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀθανάτων ἕδρῃσι; a reference to Homer’s *Iliad*, book 8.</note>—that is, where the floor or pavement of the immortals is located. For it is named the dwelling of the Gods, or as **Maro** <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note> more correctly says in the tenth book of the *Aeneid*, "the high house of the Gods," whose summit is unity, whose walls are trinity, and whose surface is four-foldness.

This is perceived more clearly when its number, by emanating from its own divinity, declines a little and is derived into the shape of created things. For then, let us place together both the Tetractys and a square, and in any of its angles let us place a point representing unity; and in place of the unity of the summit, which has now begun to take a position, let us raise the heavenly apex as high as possible. Once that is done, the four sides raised upward will be four triangles constructed upon their quadrangular width and drawn together into a single high point—and behold, you have a pyramid! This is the form of fire, according to the testimony of **Timaeus of Locri the Pythagorean** in his book *On the Soul of the World*, writing in the Doric dialect: "From these a pyramid is composed, having four bases and equal angles, which is the most mobile and thinnest form of fire." <note>original Greek: ἐξ ὧν πυραμὶς τέσαρας βάσιας καὶ γωνίας ἔχοισα συντίθεται, εἶδος πυρὸς εὐκινητότατον καὶ λεπτομερέστατον.</note> This fire is surely without matter, essential and separate, closest to God and eternal life, as we read in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Postnaturalia," a common Renaissance title for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note> and in the second book of *On the Heavens*. Life is the handiwork of the Mind, but the operation of God is immortality; life, moreover, is eternal life. **Aristotle** borrowed these ideas from the Pythagoreans.

And yet, God Himself is not a created light, but the "light-able" author of all light. Through the most perfect and remote pyramid, raising itself from a triangular base into the heights—which similarly signifies fiery vigor—the Best and Greatest God, in the divine trinity with Himself, is the founder of the incomparable world. For this reason, both the Chaldeans and the Hebrews assert that God is a fire. Inasmuch as the "number four" produces the pyramid, it is the fiery light of the incorporeal and immortal world of "separated intelligences," outside the visible sky, which is called by the Greeks ***Aion*** <note>original Greek: αἰών; meaning an age, an era, or eternity.</note>, and by us an "age," "eternity," and "ether."

<meta>This page continues the description of the "middle world" (Olympus), moving from its physical location to its metaphysical nature as the "aether," characterized by eternal light and the presence of pure, immaterial forms.</meta>

# BOOK II. 805

The bright sky, or aether, is called the glow of eternity; it is a place where there is no physical body, no location, no vacuum, no time, no old age, and no change. Instead, there are unchangeable and impassive beings who possess the highest form of life, which they enjoy throughout all ages—that is, for eternity. These are nearly the exact words of the Stagirite, **Aristotle**, <note>Aristotle was born in Stagira, hence the title "the Stagirite."</note> which both he and the followers of **Plato** and **Socrates** derived from **Pythagoras**. Pythagoras wrote in his *Golden Verses*: "If, having left the body behind, you reach the free aether, you will be an immortal God." <note>original Latin: "Si relicto corpore in aetherem liberum perveneris, eris immortalis Deus."</note> Having overcome the trials of this life, you will recognize the "cohabitation" of immortal gods and mortal men. He elegantly calls this *systasis* <note>original Greek: σύστασιν, meaning a "standing together" or a constitution.</note>, a word derived from "standing together." 

Through this, he shows us three properties of the middle world, which he names the "free aether." It is called "free" because it is set apart from the power of matter and preserved in liberty to be warmed by the fire of God; by its imperceptible motion, it warms the lower regions. Indeed, "aether" is said to be derived from "always burning" or "always warming." <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰεί θέρεσθαι ἤτοι θερμαίνειν (apo tou aiei theresthai etoi thermainein).</note>

Its properties are these: its **condition**, its **chorus**, and its **order**. The **condition** of this world is that everything within it is pure form. They claim its nature is "Jovial" (pertaining to Jupiter), which gives form to both immortal and mortal things and, through a specific nourishing heat, preserves all things of both worlds in their being. Concerning this, the poet **Virgil** <note>Referred to in the text by his family name, Maro.</note> wrote: "O father, O eternal power of men and gods." Because of this nourishing heat, the "spiritual sun" was called **Jupiter** by the ancients. 

For this reason, the **Salii** (the priests of Mars the Strider) called him *Lucecius* <note>From the Latin "lux," meaning light-bringer.</note> and the Cretans called him *Phosphorus*. From this, the name **Olympus** is derived, because it "shines entirely." In this realm, Jupiter presides over and rules everything; indeed, he is everything that exists there. Hence the line in the ninth book of the *Aeneid*: "He gave the nod and made all Olympus tremble." Its condition, I say, is to receive simple, immaterial, and separate forms that exist by themselves, both universal and individual. 

For it contains all the "ideated ideas" of genera and species, acting as the very models to be imitated by more limited examples. The original model of these signs resides in the divine mind. We wish to name it thus: in the world, it is the **absolute model** of the Deity; in the intelligible world, it is the **abstract example**; and in the sensible (physical) world, it is not the example itself, but a **limited copy**—much like the relationship between a seal, the shape it leaves, and the impressed wax.

To this is added the second property, the **chorus**, named from "joy" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς (apo tes charas).</note>—that is, from the infinite joy of the blessed spirits and the unchanging pleasure of the Gods. The citizens and inhabitants of that heavenly dwelling, celebrating with myrtle crowns, perpetually enjoy the ambrosia and nectar of the divine banquet, laughing with "inextinguishable laughter." Concerning this, the wisest of poets, **Homer** <note>Referred to here as "Melesigenes," a traditional name for Homer suggesting he was born by the river Meles.</note>, wrote: "Inextinguishable laughter certainly was raised among the blessed gods." <note>original Greek: ἄσβεστος δ' ἄρ' ἐνῶρτο γέλως μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν. From the Iliad, Book 1.</note> This clearly demonstrates their everlasting joy, which the famous Homer elegantly expressed in the first book of the *Iliad* through constant harmony with lyres and other instruments of the Muses, through dancing, choruses, banquets, restful beds, and occasionally sweet sleep. Why not, Marranus?

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "middle world" or "free aether." The previous page established the nature of this realm as the "Invisible Olympus," a place of pure forms and eternal light. This page explores the inhabitants of this realm—gods and angels—and the specific etymological and philosophical definitions that distinguish them from the supreme God and from lesser spirits like demons.</meta>

# CABALA

i

What greater pleasure can be imagined than to look upon the Ideas and Forms of all things, with God's permission, following after Him? To see them more purely and transparently than any secondary creature can, and then to reveal one’s visions to those below—this is the unique and proper role of the gods. 

For this reason, they are sometimes called "Gods" in Latin (*Dei*), and in Greek <term>theoi</term> <note>original: thei</note> from <term>theein</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ θέειν</note>, which comes from the sharpening of contemplation; from this, <term>theasthai</term> <note>original: θεᾶσθαι</note> means to look upon or to be seen. They are also sometimes called "angels" when they announce what they have seen to others, just as **Orpheus**, invoking **Mercury**, says: "Hear me, Hermes, messenger of Zeus, son of Maia, interpreter of all things." <note>original Greek: κλῦθι με ἑρμεία Διὸς ἄγγελε Μαίαδος υἱέ, ἐρμηνεῦ πάντων. Hermes is the Greek name for the Roman Mercury.</note> Indeed, we use the word <term>angellein</term> <note>original: ἀγγέλλειν</note> to mean to announce and to explain. Often, however, we use one term for the other without considering their specific duties, so that in common speech we use "gods" and "angels" interchangeably. 

When **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> wrote in his *Isagoge* that both we and "angels" are rational beings, **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher who translated Greek logic into Latin.</note>—translating it into Latin—said, "Both we and the 'gods' are rational." This usage is found in the books of many other authors. 

Therefore, let no one think that when we name them "gods," we are making them equal to the supreme and ineffable God who has no name. For we call that supreme majesty "God" because He penetrates all things infinitely from within Himself and runs through every single thing, derived from <term>theein</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ θέειν</note>, which means "to run." <note>This is a classic ancient etymology, suggesting God is the "runner" who permeates the entire universe.</note> Indeed, God is much more interior and intimate to each thing than the thing is to itself; though He is nowhere, He is everywhere. 

But we do not use the name "gods" in that way for those who only execute a limited province assigned to them and are sent for a specific task. Furthermore, **Pythagoras** and his followers do not admit "demons" <note>original: Dæmones. In Greek philosophy, a 'daemon' was a spirit or guiding power, not necessarily the evil entity of later Christian tradition.</note>—no matter how good they may be—into this "chorus" of the middle world. 

Thus **Plotinus**—who, as **Porphyry** and **Longinus** testify, seemed to follow the Pythagorean mysteries most perfectly—says in his book *On the Nature of the Gods*: "We say and believe that the divine race is entirely free from passion." We attribute passions to demons, even though we say they are eternal, placing them in the rank following the gods. It is certainly better to call no being in the "intelligible world" a demon; rather, if a spirit is placed there, it should be considered a god. 

Thus far Plotinus speaks; he is certainly brief in all his teaching, but he must be weighed with an attentive mind—especially in this passage, as it provides an easy way to read the secrets of the ancient poets speaking of the gods without trouble and without offending many people. 

The third property of the intelligible world was demonstrated by Pythagoras himself when he said: "If you live by right reason, grieving for bad deeds and rejoicing in good ones, and pray to the gods to complete your work, then, having shed your body and been carried into the aether, you will be an immortal God." We must consider the **order** Pythagoras observed here in attaining human happiness. For that incorporeal heaven of the middle world, that invisible Olympus of the blessed, admits nothing impure. Therefore, vices must be fled and virtues embraced. Finally, the salvation of humanity lies in the mercy of God; thus the divinity must be worshipped, and those above must be entreated to complete our work...

Clearly, by the best right, I might call such a man not only yours, but more truly *our* Pythagoras; and I shall indeed call him ours as long as I live, because he alone out of the whole crowd of ancient philosophers tasted our wisdom more aptly, more harmoniously, and more properly. Such a promise indeed announces to them the highest joy. Then in the doctrine of Muhammad it is written: "If any kind of delight were missing there, happiness would be far from full. # CABALA

...of it (he says) whatever can be desired will immediately be present. They will all attain the stature of Adam, but in the form of Jesus Christ <note>Reuchlin is citing a common medieval Latin translation/summary of Islamic belief, which often syncretized various prophetic figures.</note>, suffering neither increase nor decrease. And in the 64th chapter of the **Al-Koran** <term>Al-Koran: The Quran</term>: There indeed the believers will recline on silk carpets and purple bedding, and they will forever possess everything they love. They will marry most beautiful maidens—like hyacinths and pearls—who have never been deflowered by men or devils, nor are they subject to menstruation. There will also be things there shining with a color between green and yellow, and gushing springs, and palms and pomegranates. 

Do you not sense here, **Philolaus**, that the essence of these things is symbolic? In the manner of the **Pythagoreans**, almost everything you have heard is spoken allegorically. This is something **Mahometh** <note>original: "Mahometh"; the Prophet Muhammad</note> openly confesses in the *Book of Doctrine*, when he says: "The other age after this world is one whose likeness can be explained, for its inhabitants are not mortal, nor are its days counted by number." 

By this, he declares that what he wrote concerning divine matters was written allegorically, and not entirely plainly or openly—as when he numbered the days of blessedness as being a thousand years long, and the years as forty thousand. He also taught that Paradise has a golden pavement of emerald, distinct with frequently interspersed hyacinths, filled with every fruit-bearing tree, with rivers flowing through pleasant fields—some pouring milk, others white honey, others the purest wine. These things are found in the *Book of Mahometh's Doctrine*, where he designates that garden of the intelligible world, which reason cannot grasp, through a sensible Paradise. 

For **Mahometh** proposed two Paradises to us in the **Al-Koran**, when in the sixty-fourth **Azoara** <term>Azoara: A chapter or Surah of the Quran</term> he says: "He who has stood in fear before God shall receive two paradises as an inheritance, which are secondary to the many-formed goodness of every kind." He also showed two cities of **Jerusalem**, as in the *Book of Doctrine* where **Abdias** <note>Abdias: Likely referring to Abdullah ibn Salam, a Jewish convert to Islam often featured in medieval "Dialogues" with Muhammad.</note> asks: "Why is Jerusalem called the blessed house?" **Mahometh** responds: "Because it is situated directly across from the heavenly Jerusalem." 

These things allude not a little to our **Cabalistic** tradition, where we have heard concerning the two Paradises—one heavenly and the other earthly—signifying twin worlds: the visible and the invisible. The former is present to us, and the latter is in the future. You have already explained quite a lot about that future world in a few words; therefore, **Philolaus**, I ask you to proceed with the rest concerning this world which we inhabit.

**Philolaus** said: I shall do so diligently, provided I first warn you not to err like those unrefined athletes of the wrestling-schools <note>original: "rudibus palaestris"; a metaphor for those trained only in basic, physical logic</note> who only savor what they can perceive with their eyes. As **Ammonius**, son of **Hermias**, wrote regarding **Antisthenes**: when he had said, "I see a man, but I do not see 'humanity'," he therefore believed that "humanity" was nothing but a figment of thought.

# BOOK II. 807

...they are unable to understand, except as much as the pupil of the eye can grasp or the hands can touch. Whatever they hear concerning celestial life, the high gods, the souls in heaven, or the heavenly beings, they immediately relate to the visible sky, the spheres of the stars, the moving firmament, and those orbs we perceive with our senses. It is as if a blessed life could consist of such a great whirlwind of motions and a restless tumult of changes! 

However, those who follow a spiritual sense and the subtle illumination of the mind understand that there is greater truth in the things that are not seen than in those that are seen. The will of the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers and geometry were the keys to the universe.</note> is inclined toward this: they believe that this world and whatever is placed within it is a shadowed image of that true world which exists outside the heavens—a world comprising only intelligences, forms, and souls that are separated from bodies in their substance, power, and operation. 

From this, they firmly hold that the souls of men, once purified from all foul filth and having cast off the bodily mass, dwell without any doubt beyond this entire visible heaven and beyond any risk of misfortune. They live in the **Olympus of eternity** <note>A metaphorical term for the highest, unchanging spiritual realm, borrowed from Greek mythology.</note>, gifted with all liberty and bound by no necessity. 

For as the famous Pythagorean **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whose work heavily influenced Christian and Jewish mysticism.</note> says in his fourth book *On One's Own Daemon*: "One must consider," he says, "that souls which have set out beyond the sensible world have transcended the demonic nature, every fate of generation, and every necessity of this world, as long as they dwell in the **intelligible world**." <term>Intelligible world: The realm of pure thought and divine forms, accessible to the mind rather than the physical senses.</term> Thus far Plotinus.

Therefore, whenever mention is made of the true gods, the separate intelligences, the purer forms, the divine spirits, the beings above, the angels, and the souls of the blessed, always remember and reflect within your mind upon that world which is supreme, intelligible, immaterial, simple, abstract—an incorporeal heaven, an invisible Olympus, a mental paradise, a supernatural ether, perceivable by neither sense nor reason.

Leaving that aside for now, let us descend to our corporeal and sensible world. Its pattern exists in the incomparable world of the **Deity**, its example exists in the **intelligible world** of formality, and its self-subsisting essence <note>original Greek: "τò αὐθυπόστατον" (to authypostaton)</note> is in itself. 

Just as **One** is the origin of the mental world, so **Two** shall be for us the beginning of the corporeal world. It would not be corporeal unless it consisted of these four things: the point, the line, the surface, and thickness (depth), following the example of the cubic figure which these numbers constitute: **one, two, three, four**. 
- **One**, fixed in position, creates a point. 
- A **line** is made from two, drawn from one point to another. 
- A **surface** arises from three lines. 
- **Thickness** (a solid) is born from four: front, back, up, and down. 

And therefore, just as the number two, when multiplied by itself in counting (two times two), produces the **quaternary** (four), so the number two, folding and twisting itself back into itself by saying "twice two, twice," makes the first **cube** (eight). Therefore, after the number five—which is the tetragonal pyramid and the principle of the intelligible world—comes the six-sided cube of the number eight, which we place as the architect over the sensible world. For among the principles of things, there is no memory of the number **seven**, since it is a virgin that gives birth to nothing,

# CABALA

## 868

...therefore she is named **Pallas** <note>original: "Pallas". In Pythagorean thought, the Monad (the number one) was often associated with Pallas Athena, representing wisdom born from the mind.</note>. We turn, therefore, to the first **cube** <term>cube: in this context, a geometric symbol for the three-dimensional physical world</term> according to number, which is the principle of multitude and variety, as it consists of two and is established through four. Hence, just as **Zaratas** <note>original: "Zaratas". A reference to Zoroaster, whom the Pythagoreans believed was a teacher of Pythagoras.</note>, the teacher of Pythagoras, named "two" the mother, so we call the cube that proceeds from it **matter**, the foundation and basis of all natural things and the seat of substantial forms. 

Regarding this, **Timaeus of Locri** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and character in Plato's dialogues.</note>, in his book *On the Soul of the World*, writes: **"From the three angles is born the equal, most stable, and solid body in every direction, having six sides and eight angles,"** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ δὲ τῶν τριῶν γωνιῶν τὸν ἴσον ἔσθ' αἱότατον καὶ στελάϊον πάντη σῶμα, ἑξῆ μὲν πλευρᾶς, ὀκτὼ δὲ γωνίας"</note> that is, from the square is born the cube, the most solid and stable body of all, having six sides and eight angles. Upon this foundation, let the submerged **form** <term>form: the spiritual "blueprint" or essence of a thing</term> lean; if it falls into this solid receptacle and is placed in this material seat, it is no longer wandering or held in common, but becomes stable, uniquely individual, and incommunicable. It becomes, as it were, "bound to the soil," subject to time and place, and proscribed, moving from freedom into the slavery of matter. 

Therefore, we see two principles of temporal forms flow from the One: the **pyramid** and the **cube**—that is, form and matter—which are found to proceed from the same square. The "idea" of this square, as we showed before, is the **Tetractys** <term>Tetractys: a triangular figure of ten points, the most sacred symbol of the Pythagoreans representing the organization of the universe</term>, the divine exemplar of Pythagoras. I have thus explained these primordial symbols as briefly as I could, which in truth designate nothing other than matter and form. 

For this reason, it is necessary to posit a third something by which they may be united. For they do not flow together of their own accord, nor does a chance meeting of any forms into matter happen by luck, nor does the matter of one thing receive the form of another by accident. For a human body does not generate iron as soon as the soul has departed, nor does wool come from a stone. Since, therefore, it is necessary to posit a third something by which they are united, it will be necessary, I believe, to bring in a principle other than the **Aristotelian** <note>Referring to Aristotle’s triad of principles: Matter, Form, and Privation.</note> one, by which matter is moved toward form and its opposite, so that as this or that form ceases, this or that form may be introduced in turn. 

For "privation" and "potentiality" do nothing substantively, since the act of any real activity is minimal in them, and they possess the least amount of "being"; how much less, then, could they join or unite a specific form to any matter? Hence, there were those who found that, in place of privation, **motion** was the third principle. But since motion is an "accident" <term>accident: a philosophical term for a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</term>, how can it be a principle of substance, or who shall be the mover of that motion? 

Therefore, those two Athenians, **Socrates** son of Sophroniscus and **Plato** son of Ariston, contemplated more wisely. In place of motion and variation, they placed **God**, the most agile of active forces, saying there are three principles of things: **God, Idea, and Matter**. Pythagoras had previously symbolized this elegantly with these secret marks, asserting the principles of the universe to be: **The Infinite, the One, and the Two.** 

By these, he designated God as the author of Infinitude, Form as Unity, and Matter as "Otherness" or Duality. He placed the **Infinite** in the supernal and incomparable world; the **One** (or Identity) in the intelligible world; and the **Two** (or Otherness) in the sensible world. For matter is indeed...

## 809

...mother of generation. God, however, joins matter and form through the law imposed upon nature itself. Therefore, long before the time of Pythagoras, the ancient **Orpheus** <note>A legendary Greek hero and musician, often considered by Renaissance scholars as a source of "pious philosophy" that predated Plato.</note> wrote in his book of *Hymns* that after **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iouem". In this context, Orpheus uses Jupiter to represent Form.</note>—whom he calls the **origin of all things** <note>original Greek: "ἀρχὴ πάντων"</note>, that is, the principle of the universe—and after **Juno** <note>original: "Iunonem". Here representing Matter.</note>—whom he calls the **all-parenting bedfellow of Zeus** <note>original Greek: "Διὸς σύλλεκτρον παντογένεθλον"</note>, for he addresses matter with the title of Juno—he writes these words: **"For without you, nothing at all has known the nature of life; for you share in all things, mingled in a most venerable way."** <note>original Greek: "χωρὶς γὰρ σέθεν οὐδὲν ὅλως ζωῆς φύσιν ἔγνω, κοινωνεῖς γὰρ ἅπασιν λαυρανίηι οἵηι σεμνῶς"</note> 

Therefore, after Jupiter (Form) and Juno (Matter), Orpheus added **Law**, that is, distribution, so that there would be a third principle of nature; he named this the **firmness of nature** <note>original Greek: "φύσεως τὸ βέβαιον"</note>. For the word for Law in Greek is *nomos*, as you know, derived from *nemo* (meaning "I divide" or "I distribute"), as it distributes to all things what is their own or what belongs to them. This, he says, is the **celestial law, the just seal** <note>original Greek: "οὐράνιον νόμον σφραγῖδα δικαίαν"</note> (as he sang in his hymns); for the law of nature seals many pieces of matter with a single form, just as a notary <term>notary: original "tabellio", a scribe who used a signet ring to certify documents</term> stamps many pieces of wax with the single image on his ring. 

Now, indeed, any forms stamped into matter are no longer called "ideas" (that is, universal types), but **eide** <note>original Greek: "τὰ εἴδη". In Platonic thought, "ideas" are the perfect blueprints in the mind of God, while "eide" are those blueprints as they exist physically in objects.</note>, namely, forms that are **like expressions in wax, inseparable from the matter** <note>original Greek: "ὡς τὰ ἐν τοῖς κηροῖς ἐκτυπώματα ἀχώριστα τῆς ὕλης"</note>, as **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a Greek philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> wrote. 

Consequently, the origin of this sensible world now stands open before us, which the marriage of the **pyramid** and the **cube**, celebrated by the law of nature, has brought forth. The square bases of those figures, when joined together, create the **dodecahedron** <term>dodecahedron: a twelve-sided geometric solid</term>—the Pythagorean symbol by which the entire universe is designated, composed of matter and form. **Alcinous** <note>A middle-Platonist philosopher, author of a handbook on Plato's doctrines.</note> rightly mentions this regarding the dogma of Plato, saying: **"God used the dodecahedron for the whole,"** <note>original Greek: "Τῷ δὲ Δωδεκαέδρῳ εἰς τὸ πᾶν ὁ θεὸς κατεχρήσατο"</note> namely, when He was fabricating this world. 

For if you place a pyramid raised from four equal-sided triangles upon an eight-angled cube, you will have skillfully constructed the building of a dodecahedron <note>This reflects a historical geometric theory where the cube acts as the base and the pyramid as the "cap" or activating principle.</note>, where the cube (or die) settles below like a **mother**, and the pyramid rests upon it like a **father**. For so said the noble Pythagorean, **Timaeus of Locri**, in his book *On the Soul of the World*: **"Form indeed holds the ratio of the male and the father, while matter holds that of the female and the mother; the third things are the offspring of these."** <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν εἶδος λόγον ἔχει ἀῤῥηνός τε καὶ πατρὸς, ἃ δ' ὕλα, θήλεός τε καὶ ματέρ'. τρίτα δὲ εἶν’ τὰ τούτων ἔκγονα."</note> 

From these principles, therefore, we correctly affirm that all things in this world are made through certain seeds and a secret faculty. They appear with a truly wondrous variety because of the varying proportions of forms to their matter, and the mixture of almost infinite "accidents"—which **Epicurus** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher known for atomism; here his term for "symptoms" or "accidental properties" is used.</note> calls **symptoms** <note>original Greek: "συμπτώματα"</note>—arising through abundance and deficiency, strife and friendship, motion and rest, force and tranquility, the rare and the dense. From these arise the spheres and the stars, as well as the four elements, from which...
