# BOOK II.

## 810

### CABALA

...they evaporate the hot and the moist, and the cold and the dry, as well as any objects of the senses. From this, one thing happens to some and another to others, and it causes all things to change their forms and alter their colors, according to the testimony of **Lucretius** <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE), a Roman poet and philosopher whose work *On the Nature of Things* explored Epicurean physics and the idea that everything is made of atoms in motion.</note>. You perceive, then, that we are now walking with the common crowd of philosophers and treading a well-worn path when we slip into these physical matters; therefore, since so many have written about nature, we must apply less effort here, so that we may instead show what **Pythagoras** thought about natural things, taking our beginning from more noble and sublime matters. 

There are "natural gods," and then there are "supernatural gods"; the lower world nourishes the former, while the upper world cherishes the latter, who are called the **super-celestials** <note>original: "superi"</note>, about whom we have already discussed at length. These beings are the simplest and purest because they are "nowhere" (and thus are "above"), yet because they are "everywhere," they are therefore with us—natives of that realm, but travelers in this one. For they are never in our world unless they are sent; for this reason, they rejoice in the name of **angels** <note>From the Greek *angelos*, meaning "messenger."</note> when they descend to these lower depths, since they are messengers of the **King of Kings**. They appear to us in whatever habit or face they wish, according to their own free will <note>original: "libertatem arbitrii"</note>, as they are always most loving and desirous of bestowing benefits upon us. 

But the "lower gods" never migrate to the celestial realms; instead, they sometimes take up duties regarding us and our affairs, which is why they are likewise called angels. Regarding **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Deo Opt. Max." (Deo Optimo Maximo), a title traditionally used for Jupiter but adopted by Christian humanists to refer to the triune God.</note>, He penetrates all things—the lowest, the highest, and those in the middle—so deeply that nothing exists without God. 

Furthermore, the "gods" of our sphere are the presiding powers. The "lower gods" within the human body are the **souls**, though the former are above bodies while the latter are within bodies. In the middle of these, the **demons** and **heroes** hold their places. Demons are close to the gods; heroes are close to the souls. Pythagoras mentions these in his ***Golden Verses*** <note>A collection of moral exhortations attributed to Pythagoras, highly regarded in the Renaissance as a manual for spiritual purification.</note> and assigned to each their own proper worship. However, he did not permit altars to be defiled with blood, nor did he allow animals to be slaughtered, except for the sake of public utility; rather, he wished for daily and private sacrifices to be made with incense and grain. From this comes the saying: **"Appease God with an offering, and let the calf grow for the plow."**

And since man is a kind of image of this world, he is called a **Microcosm** <note>Literally "little world." This was a central Renaissance idea that the human being contains within themselves the entire structure of the universe (the Macrocosm).</note>; he receives many world-names **metaphorically** <note>original Greek: "μεταφορικῶς"</note> or by way of translation. For the **Mind** in man is called "God" after the likeness of the Supreme and First Mind, either by shared name or by participation. And the **rational soul**, which through the mind leans toward virtue and the highest will, is called a **good demon** or a **genius** <note>In the classical sense, a *daimon* or *genius* was a guiding spirit or a person's inner character, not an "evil demon" in the modern sense.</note>; but that which, through the imagination and base affections, draws the will toward vice and the worst things, is called an **evil demon**. 

For this reason, Pythagoras prays to God to free man from evil and to show all people which "demon" they are using. Once the body is cast off, if the soul remains defiled by vices, it becomes an evil demon, and its life is led in what is called **misery**. But if it casts off its vices, and even if some mark of its former anxiety remains pressed upon it, and it does not yet entirely lose its human and mortal habits and affections (however much virtue it seeks), it will be for a time a "good demon" in this world...

## 811

### LIBER II.

...will live happily and fortunately in divinity, always with a singular joy, as if revolving in a mindful soul the things she did well, retaining a still-unextinguished will to act rightly; this life is called by the Greeks *eudaemonia*, that is, happiness <note>original: εὐδαιμονία. In Greek philosophy, this refers to a state of flourishing or "good-spiritedness," rather than just a fleeting emotion.</note>. Whence that saying of **Virgil** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BCE). This quote is from the *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the spirits in the Underworld.</note> arose: "The same pride in chariots and arms they had when alive, the same care to pasture their sleek horses, follows them now they are laid in the earth." I have learned that the ancients called that soul a *lemur* <note>original: *lemurem*. In Roman religion, these were the shades or spirits of the dead.</note>. If such a spirit is led by benevolence toward us, taking a stronger care of us and our people, and possesses the home as a peaceful and quiet power, it is called a **household god** <note>original: *lar familiaris*. The Lares were protective Roman deities of the household.</note>. If, however, due to the adverse merits of its life, it is punished with no good dwelling place but with wandering as if in a kind of exile—an empty terror to good men but harmful to the wicked—it is named a **ghost** <note>original: *larva*. These were considered malevolent or frightening spirits of the dead, often depicted as skeletons or masks.</note>. 

When it is uncertain what lot the spirit enjoys, whether it be a *lar* or a *larva*, they call it by the name of a **god of the Shades** <note>original: *Manem deum*. The Manes were the collective spirits of the dead, often honored to ensure their benevolence.</note>, adding the title of "God" as a mark of honor; for they declare those to be gods who, having governed the course of life justly and prudently, have met a holy death. Furthermore, we indiscriminately call those noble spirits "gods," "angels," and "demons" <note>original: *dæmonas*. In the classical sense, a *daemon* was a spirit or divine power, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>. These are assigned as guardians to each individual man; though not at all visible, they are always present not only as witnesses of our deeds, but even of our thoughts. They also follow us after death, all the way to the power, judgment, and tribunal of the **supreme demon** <note>This likely refers to a chief spirit or judge of the afterlife, such as Minos in Greek myth or a similar governing intelligence.</note>. 

All these things flowed to us from **Pythagoras**, who learned them partly from the **Egyptians**, partly from the **Hebrews** and **Chaldeans**, and among the most wise **Magi** of the **Persians**, and then passed them down to posterity, as recorded by the most excellent authors: 
*   **Mercury Termaximus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "thrice-great" Egyptian sage associated with the *Hermetica*.</note>, the illustrious legislator and most contemplative writer of the Egyptians, in his *Perfect Discourse* to Asclepius.
*   **Timaeus of Locri** in his book *On the Soul of the World*. 
*   **Hesiod** in *Works and Days*. 
*   **Plato** through **Diotima** in the *Symposium*; through **Socrates** in the *Phaedrus*, and likewise in the *Philebus*; through the **Athenian Stranger** in the *Laws* and the *Epinomis*, and in other places in his books. 
*   **Porphyry** in *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. 
*   **Iamblichus** in *On the Mysteries*. 
*   **Proclus** in [his commentary on] the *Alcibiades*. 
*   **Plotinus** in his book *On Love* and in the book *On One's Own Proper Demon*. 
*   **Maximus of Tyre** in two disputations on the *Demon of Socrates*.

And many other Greeks, whom among the Latins **Cicero** imitated in his volumes *On the Nature of the Gods*, *On Divination*, and in the sixth book of the *Republic*; as did also **Apuleius of Madaura** in his book *On the God of Socrates*, and the rest who followed them. Nor are there lacking among the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> those who have treated the movers of the celestial spheres and stars, and the governors of the elements—whether they assist those bodies or whether something of them resides within as a soul for each—I pass over for now. Now we will briefly enumerate only what remains concerning the **sensible world** <note>The physical world perceptible by the senses.</note>. Pythagoras therefore said that this world, which is an imitator of eternity, is a "containment of all totals" according to the order which is within it; though it is corporeal, it nevertheless possessed primary principles within its body, though the **Stoics** did not agree on this, for they thought those were...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discourse on the nature of the soul and the universe, transitioning from the classifications of spirits (larva, manes) to the physical and metaphysical theories attributed to Pythagoras and his successors regarding the structure of the cosmos and the composition of living beings.</meta>

# CABALA

## 812

[they are] not corporeal because they are spiritual. He himself asserted that the world was both **created** and **subject to decay**, but by the providence and kindness of God, it is never actually destroyed. He also said that the bodies of the elements are spherical, except for fire, which takes the shape of a **pyramid** <note>Pythagoreans believed the four elements were composed of geometric solids; fire was the tetrahedron or pyramid.</note>. Color is the outward appearance of a body. Time is a vessel, the outermost limit of the world, a motion, a certain difference or "otherness" in matter. He taught that matter is subject to the processes of birth and decay, and that **necessity** weighs upon the world; some things happen by necessity, some by fate, some by choice, some by fortune, and some by chance. He believed the cause of these things is hidden from human reason—an opinion in which **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BCE) who introduced the concept of *Nous* (Mind) as the ordering force of the cosmos.</note> also concurs. 

Our author also thought that the world began from fire. The right side is in the east, and the left is in the west. Then, following **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–545 BCE), often cited as the first Greek philosopher.</note>, he divided the heavens into five zones, and then into the two equinoxes and the two solstices, and into the arctic circle. He divided the globe of the earth in the same way. Furthermore, before all others, he discovered the **obliquity of the zodiac** <note>The angle between the earth's equator and the path of the sun (the ecliptic).</note> following the sun's path. He believed the moon appears to be an ignited terrestrial soil, containing within itself fields, mountains, and valleys. He defined the **soul** in this way: it is a **self-moving number** <note>original: *numerus se mouens*. This is a famous Pythagorean definition, suggesting the soul is a mathematical entity that possesses its own source of motion.</note>. He distributed its parts thus: the Vital faculty is around the heart, while the rational and mental faculties are around the head. He held that the soul cannot perish, for the rational part is the work of the eternal God, though the irrational part is subject to decay. 

To the same author we should attribute a more true distribution regarding sacrifices. He maintained that human seed is the "froth" of the most useful blood, consisting of corporeal matter but endowed with an incorporeal power; he also held that the female likewise emits seed. Furthermore, he believed that not only humans but other living creatures also possess **reason**, though they lack **mind** <note>original: *mens*. In this context, 'reason' (ratio) refers to basic logical processing, while 'mind' (mens) refers to higher spiritual or intellectual intuition.</note>. As for the fact that a great many of these animals do not seem to act rationally, the fault lies in the body's **crasis** <note>term: *crasis* (from Greek *krasis*, "mixture"). The specific balance or temperament of bodily fluids and qualities that determines health and behavior.</note>, because they are not gifted with the necessary physical instruments. Therefore, they do not have words, whether they are tame or wild, but they possess certain symbols and marks of their own, signs by which they express their thoughts among themselves. Thus, in their own way, beasts **speak**, but they do not "talk" <note>The author distinguishes between animal communication and human speech.</note>, which the Greeks express more significantly as
<margin>to babble and to declare <note>original: λαλεῖν & φράζειν (lalein & phrazein). *Lalein* often refers to the sound of talking or birdsong, while *phrazein* implies pointing out or explaining something clearly.</note></margin>
of all these things, I cite the volumes of **Plutarch** <note>Specifically referring to *De Placitis Philosophorum* (On the Opinions of the Philosophers), a work traditionally attributed to Plutarch.</note> on the opinions of the philosophers as very good witnesses. Concerning the rest of this world, whether regarding substances or accidents, there exist almost innumerable writers in every sect of philosophers. Some have spoken generally about the nature of the universe, such as **Aristotle**, **Theophrastus**, and your **Arabs** and **Moors**, nearly all of them. Others have written particularly about every individual thing, such as **Julius Pollux**, **Dioscorides**, **Gaius Plinius**, and those like them. 

Nevertheless, of all the disciplines, every successor has grasped from the treasure-house of **Pythagoras's** philosophy like an heir, and has cultivated that inheritance through literary study. Each has adorned it as much as he was able according to the particular quality of his own genius, and has extended it with all his might. But what does it profit to either know or have opinions on all these things, if they do not take away all sorrow and torment in this noble life, and, in the other life after our vacancy from evils, add the most heaped-up embrace of all good things?

# BOOK II.

## 813

...which we have learned so studiously? What does it profit us, in the end, if by knowing well we do evil, and by doing evil we cannot be entirely free from fear, and thus can enjoy no tranquil state of mind? What again does it profit if, obediently following warnings like beasts of burden, we always carry out orders, yet in all other things we are foolish, dull, fatuous, "mushrooms" <note>original: *fungi* — a Latin idiom for a person who is senseless or a "blockhead"</note>, stupid, dolts, and simpletons, differing nothing from a brute animal? 

Therefore, it seemed fitting to Pythagoras to direct all philosophy toward the height of longed-for happiness <term>beatitudo: a state of supreme blessedness or the ultimate goal of human life</term> and the ready security of eternal joy, which he placed in the contemplation of supreme and divine things. He believed that this fruit, like that of a blessed tree, would undoubtedly follow our tireless pursuit of philosophizing, provided that we first—having purified the soul—vehemently turn away from vices and diligently cultivate virtues. By doing so, with a joyful mind and cheerful zeal, and being conscious of no evil within ourselves, we might apply ourselves to mathematical speculations. 

These mathematical studies are observed by us as intermediaries between natural and divine things; for they are partly inseparable from matter like natural things, and partly separated from it like divine things. For a circle or a harmony, although it does not exist without matter, is nevertheless understood without matter. Indeed, no concern for matter is involved when we deal with any mathematical subject. 

Since, therefore, it was difficult—not to say impossible—for our intellect to leap suddenly from natural to supernatural things and from the entirely material to the completely immaterial, Pythagoras wished to place before his disciples certain things which they could grasp both by sense in some way and by the intellect. For this reason, he called the demonstrations of these things "mathematics" or "matheses" <note>original: *mathemata seu matheseis* — from the Greek word for "things learned"</note>, which means "disciplines" or "teachings." The book he composed on these subjects he titled *On Erudition* or *Foundations*, as if it were a work suitable for youths and boys, for whose sake he also chose the name "pedagogy" <note>original Greek: παιδευτικήν (*paideutikēn*), referring to the art of education</note>. In this work, he explained everything that could be said about numbers, figures, and harmonies. 

From there, as if from one illustrious fountain, four most clear streams flowed forth, which we call the four liberal arts: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy—though he numbered astronomy among natural things for the most part and gathered it into the book he called *Physics*, because it consists in the motion of bodies. 

But since in our age there is such an extensive discourse on these matters among the most learned men of letters—so much so that each of these subjects constitutes a single faculty and each faculty leads its own class—I shall entrust each to its own teachers. And because it is now late in the night and the preparations for our dinner are at hand, I shall make an end of speaking—I, who have dared so immodestly to beat upon your most tolerant ears with so many words. 

Then Marranus said, "I swear by the gods above, you have filled me with such pleasure by your speaking that no Muse could be more pleasing to me. Now, forgetting dinner, I have directed almost all my hunger toward a craving for your teaching. Although I see the innkeeper is being meticulous regarding the magnificence and expense of the feast, I would still wish you to [continue] the rest of Pythagoras's philosophy..."

<page-num>814</page-num>
-> CABALA <-

...explain that which pertains to virtues, character, and the diligence of the state, and do so as briefly as you can, while the builders of the feast <note>original: *structores coenae* — those preparing the meal</note> lay out the dining room for us and prepare the rest. 

Therefore, hear me, Marranus (said Philolaus). Pythagoras desired this part of philosophy to be understood under the name of civility <note>original: *urbanitatis* — literally "urbanity" or "city-manners," referring to the conduct required in a civilized society</note>. Regarding this, he composed one volume among his others which he titled *Politikon*—that is, *The Civil Book*—or, as the Latins have perhaps less properly translated it, *On the Republic*. This is because it concerns not only the matters of the multitude, but also the specific character and virtue of every individual. For he who is placed in charge of a city is clearly chosen under a bad omen if he is not worthy even to rule his own house and his own self. 

As Aristotle says in the book of the *Great Ethics*: <note>original: "μέρος ἔστιν ἄρα ὡς ἔοικε καὶ ἀρχὴ ἡ περὶ τὰ ἤθη πραγματεία τῆς πολιτικῆς."</note> "The treatment concerning character is therefore, as it seems, both a part and a principle of politics." Indeed, this "civility" consists of the whole number of the virtues, the parts of which are men endowed with virtue admitted into a single fellowship. For a conversation of wicked men is not to be considered a city, but a gathering of conspirators, where vices are shared just as virtue is shared among the good—as that famous Theognis of Megara wrote in his books to Cyrnus: <note>Theognis was a 6th-century BCE Greek poet known for his gnomic (proverbial) wisdom.</note> "You will learn rightly from the righteous, but if you associate with the wicked, you will lose even your own mind and soul."

Therefore, having set aside contemplative wisdom—which Pythagoras related to nature and enclosed in his book of physics concerning principles and the modes of causes—we find how from the Monad <term>Monade: The "One" or the primary unity from which all things originate</term> comes the indefinite duality, then from the dual number comes points, from points lines, from lines plane figures, and from planes solid figures. From these, solid bodies and this sensible globe of the world are made and arise, with its orbits and the elements of the mixtures: fire, air, water, and earth. Nearly every one of these things he was accustomed to wrap in allegory. 

Finally, leaving aside likewise the mathematical things which he showed through his book *Paideuticon* <note>original: *Particum* in OCR, likely *Paideuticon* meaning "On Education/Instruction"</note>, I think we should now review even those things which he taught concerning character. He wrote of these more diffusely in the *Politikon*, and more briefly, like a summary, in his *Golden Verses*. Since these are no longer read publicly in our age, I will now pursue only those symbols of this kind that were handed down without writing. This was done so that disciples, relying on the power of memory, would grow accustomed to living by signs directed toward good character, and to affirm their profession of the philosophical order through secret tokens <note>original: *arcanis tesseris* — passwords or signs used to identify members of a specific group</note> among themselves. 

Of this number, quite a few were clearly expressed in his books—which are worthy of the admiration of posterity—namely the *Adages*, by the illustrious Erasmus of Rotterdam. Erasmus is a theologian by profession, easily the prince of the most eloquent men in our century, and a "sweet siren" <note>A classical metaphor for someone with incredibly persuasive or beautiful speech</note> who by his own right deserves the greatest praise from all students of refined letters. Truly, in the pursuit of virtues, Pythagoras attributed no small amount to habit, for it is of great importance to grow accustomed to things in one's tender years. Thus, morals are called *ethe* <note>original Greek: ἤθη</note> as if they were *ethe* <note>original Greek: ἔθη</note>, which is to say, "habits." The Stagirite <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, who was born in Stagira</note> often approves this in his ethics, and our man <note>Likely referring to Pythagoras</note> commanded us to choose the best way of life, for habit would soon make it pleasant...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pythagorean ethics from page 814, specifically focusing on how Pythagoras organized moral philosophy into three primary goals: duty to the Divine, duty to oneself, and duty to others.</meta>

<page-num>815</page-num>
<header>BOOK II.</header>

...custom will restore it. Thus, he organized the whole of moral philosophy into three goals: first, into the worship of God and divine things; second, into the respect each individual man has for himself; and finally, duty toward others. Regarding that which pertains most excellently to divine matters, he taught above all that nothing is pleasing to the powers above unless it is free from filth and clearly purified. For this reason, he handed down a <term>proverb</term>—one that should be held frequently on the lips—**do not pour libations to the gods from an unpruned vine** <note>original: *μὴ σπένδειν θεοῖς ἐξ ἀμπέλου ἀτμήτου* — this Pythagorean "symbol" suggests that one should not offer the fruits of a wild or neglected life to the divine, but rather those of a cultivated and disciplined soul</note>. That is, one must not offer wine to the gods from vines that have not been tended. He also established that sacrifices be made from the purest grain. From this comes his saying, **Do not sacrifice without meal.** This Pythagorean sacrifice is of the greatest antiquity, consisting of wine and bread. 

Furthermore, he warned that those things dedicated to God ought not to be transferred thereafter to human uses, often saying: **Abstain from a white cock.** <note>original: *A gallo candido abstineas* — since the white cock was sacred to the sun or the moon in various traditions, it was "set apart" and not to be eaten</note> He also commanded through this symbol that true worshippers must persevere in humility: **to sit while worshipping.** <note>original: *καθῆσθαι προσκυνουντας*</note> As for the fact that one ought to look around in every direction during adoration—from which arose the saying, **Worship having turned about**—this indicates prudence regarding divine prayers, so that it cannot be rightly thrown back at us: *You know not what you ask.*

As for what concerns ourselves, the rule for living rightly consists in human propriety, which is the middle point between extremes—between abundance and deficiency. For in either extreme, a man is flawed, crippled, or like a hundred-handed monster <note>original: *centimanus* — a reference to the Hecatoncheires of myth, representing chaotic excess</note>. Hence this symbol, **Do not step over the balance**, <note>original: *Stateram ne transilias*</note> commands that moderation be applied to all studies and actions. Even more clearly, he said: **Set out salt.** This applies directly to our affections, which are called the "passions." For salt is a sign of modesty, since it is admitted into human food neither in excess nor in too small a measure; indeed, both are rejected—that which is tasteless and that which is overly salty. Therefore, **Do not overstep the salt** was also a proverb. 

Accordingly, all the affections and passions within us are moved by some appearance of good or evil: we rejoice in good things, we are saddened by present evils; again, we desire future goods and fear future evils. Therefore, joy and sorrow are the elements of the passions from which all the movements of our souls arise; their rectitude is called "virtue," and their deviation is called "vice." However, things that are evil often appear to us as good, and conversely, things that are good seem not to be good. For as Seneca says, there is a great difference between the "truth" and the "verisimilar" (the "truth-like"). Therefore, error easily befalls the unskilled masses, who exist in great abundance. Pythagoras sought to turn his disciples away from this by symbolic warning: **Do not walk on the public highway**, <note>original: *Per uiam publicam ne ambules*</note> which means do not follow the errors of the common people. 

Yet, because he also wished this to be observed—**Do not wander outside the public road**—he had already insinuated that one must speak as the many do; or rather, you should not fight against what is established among all people. From this comes the saying: **Do not speak against the sun**, lest you fall into danger—a point which this rightly advises: **Turn away from a sharp sword.** This is achieved if you employ an honest modesty in public, of which this is the mark...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Pythagorean "Symbols" or moral maxims. The previous page ended while discussing symbols related to divine worship and physical posture during prayer; this page concludes the rules regarding the sun and transitions into the management of internal passions and social ethics.</meta>

<page-num>816</page-num>
<header>CABALÆ</header>

...is: **Do not urinate facing the sun.** <note>original: *Aduersus solem ne meijto* — a Pythagorean maxim suggesting respect for the source of light and divinity in nature.</note> Now, therefore, since the error regarding the divine light has been removed, he determined that one must restrain pleasure and grief, desire and fear. For this reason he said: **Do not give your hand to laughter just as much as to sadness.** For he commanded us to enjoy joys and pleasure according to harmony, with a certain honorable temperance which he called the **lyre**. Hence the symbol: **A seven-stringed lyre** <note>original: *ἑπτὰς χορδὰς λύραν*</note>, which means that one should use songs with the lyre. This was by no means an empty mystery; they always used this practice before the start of sleep, lest they be troubled by disturbed dreams. When these dreams did rush in, he commanded them to shake out and roll up the bed-coverings—that is, to gather the dreams into one and cast them away, so that they might not weigh upon the mind when remembered. 

Concerning grief, he used to say: **Do not wear a tight ring**, by which he excluded all sorrow of the soul, except for that felt over a sin committed. Wherefore in his poems he speaks thus: **If you have done evil things, indeed grieve.** In other matters, Pythagoras commanded **that the heart must not be eaten**; this means: do not torment yourself. Furthermore, when anger has boiled over, **efface the footprint of the pot in the ashes**, which signifies that one must withdraw from anger and that the memory of past evils must be removed. 

Concerning greed, he spoke in this way: **Do not feed animals with hooked claws**, and this is directed against rapacious men. Indeed, do not be overly anxious about your daily food, which is why he says: **Do not sit upon a choenix.** Now, a <term>choenix</term> <note>original: *chœnix* — a Greek unit of measure for grain, representing a single person's daily ration</note> is a daily portion of food, which some call a "prebend" and others call "handouts." Likewise, lest you show any sign of avarice hidden in your soul, he warned: **Do not pick up things that have fallen**, by which he forbade anyone to be an overly passionate lover of their own possessions. 

Concerning fear, he said: **Do not turn back when you reach the borders**, by which symbol he not only prohibits trembling at death, but also at whatever might happen in life, however much it terrifies. For these are fixed and determined boundaries which you will not be able to cross. You fear in vain, therefore, what you cannot avoid or turn back from; indeed, never to shrink back from such a fate is a mark of praised and outstanding greatness of soul. 

We have enumerated these Pythagorean "marks" in a summary fashion: first, those which pertain to the divine, and then those which pertain to individual men. Now listen briefly to how one should behave toward another. Since nothing is more desirable than friendship, the greatest care—second only to the gods—must be taken to acquire friends through virtue, as it says in the *Golden Verses*. Yet, one should not take just anyone in passing. Therefore he himself said: **Do not shake hands with everyone.** <note>original: *Ne inieceris dextrā* — suggesting one should not offer friendship or enter into contracts without careful consideration.</note> And once you have found a friend worthy of your innermost secrets, you should make him a partner in all your affairs. For that reason, Pythagoras himself, before all others, used the adage: **Among friends, all things are common**, as both Terence and Cicero attest. For a friend is a "second self," which is why friendship is <term>isotes</term> <note>original: *ἰσότης* — Greek for equality</note>, that is, equality and the same soul. However, men should by no means be admitted into friendship who are otherwise "white" on the inside but carry a "black tail" on the outside (believe one who knows), for the earth bears nothing more pestilential than these, who are like the **Cyanoleuca** <note>original: *Cyanoleucę* — likely referring to a wagtail or a similar bird; a metaphor for a hypocrite or a double-dealer</note> with a black tail between its shoulder-blades, which simulates all things...

The previous page discussed internal emotional control (grief, anger, and greed); this page moves into social ethics, the choice of companions, and finally, conduct within the Commonwealth or State.</meta>

<page-num>817</page-num>
<header>BOOK II.</header>

...and dissembling hypocrites. Therefore Pythagoras said: **Do not taste of those with black tails.** <note>original Greek: *μὴ γεύεσθαι τῶν μελανούρων* (mē geuesthai tōn melanourōn)</note> That is, do not eat of those things which have a black tail. These represent "false brothers," whom people call "the black-clad," for the *psolios* <note>A type of fish, likely the Saddled Seabream, known for the black spot near its tail.</note> turns black at its extremities, as the grammarian Tryphon wrote—meaning, "That which is false turns black at its edges." As for others of lighter friendship who are of little use, whether they be relatives or friends, you should neither despise them nor accept them beyond measure. This is what this allegory establishes: **Do not mix together or step upon the clippings of nails and hair.** 

Nor is it far from the truth that we are commanded to shrewdly avoid every unpleasant house-guest and those individual whisperers and talkative men among us; hence that saying: **Do not have swallows living with us.** <note>Swallows were ancient symbols of persistent, meaningless chatter.</note> Furthermore, a friend should be received with deliberation, but once received, he is not easily to be cast off. Indeed, to break a friendship is inhuman, which is why he said: **Do not break bread.** 

But you should wish to be a friend in such a way that you care for all your friend's affairs just as if they were your own; you should please him not with flattering words and the dye of speeches, but with a zeal for the truth. For the seat of friendship is truth, not flattery, which is why he said: **Do not wipe the seat with oil.** <note>To "wipe with oil" implies making things "smooth" or slippery through flattery rather than firm through truth.</note> 

And just as the love of good men must be won, so the anger of evil men must not be stirred up; he advises this very thing: **Do not poke the fire with a sword.** It is, moreover, the duty of a good man to be useful to all and to harm no one. For if you approach someone either as the author of a trouble or as a companion in imposing a burden, you will be said not to have helped, but rather to have burdened them further, so that you seem to have given way to vice. You will instead deserve gratitude for your virtue when you help someone who is setting down a burden, so that they may be relieved of the weight more quickly; this is what he meant when he said: **Help to lay down a burden, do not help to impose one.** <note>original Greek: *φορτίον συγκαθαιρεῖν μὴ δὲ συνεπιτιθέναι* (phortion synkathairein mē de synepitithenai)</note> This is as if he were saying: assist in such a way that men may be relieved of trouble, not weighed down. 

However, a man of unworthy and perverse character, just as he should not be cut off suddenly, should by no means be cherished by you. For this reason he forbade: **Do not put food into a chamber pot.** <note>A warning against offering wisdom or deep friendship to those who will only defile it.</note> 

Finally, we ought to set aside that ferocity so that absolutely no one rages against any innocent person. For Pythagoras also commanded: **A mild tree must not be violated nor harmed.** Hence the saying among the symbols: **Do not taste fish.** Truly, the fish is the kind of animal that by its very nature harms man in no way. 

Now, as far as the Commonwealth is concerned, this still remains to be cited, which he himself said: **Do not pluck the crown**, signifying that the law must not be violated. And also: **Do not chop wood on the road**, by which we are warned that public matters, and those belonging to the community, are not to be disturbed. As for how much a sense of pride, the inflation of majesty, or the swelling of public honor is unbecoming to a wise man, this secret symbol exhorts us: **One must abstain from beans.** For magistrates were elected by beans according to the custom of the ancients. <note>In ancient Greek democracy, white and black beans were often used as ballots for voting.</note> However, whoever is anxiously occupied in seeking to lead the Commonwealth desires an innumerable evil. <page-num>818</page-num>
<header>KABBALAH</header>

...lest by discouraging the people he should cause offense, he preferred as a faithful teacher to turn his disciples away from all ambition through this rich mystery, so that they would always keep in memory that, clearly, *friends' things are held in common*. <note>original Greek: ὅτι τὰ τῶν φίλων κοινά (hoti ta tōn philōn koina)</note> There is no doubt that more than these were held in memory by Hipparchus and Lysis, listeners of Pythagoras, who kept the precepts of their teacher—which he had shared with his other schoolmates—not in books but in their own minds. These they eventually brought forth in the lecture hall of Thebes. However, I have not seen all of those things, and hurrying toward the end, I wished only to touch upon them briefly. 

This one thing I wished, lest you be ignorant or commit it to oblivion: that almost all Pythagorean philosophy is full of enigmatic words and veils over things. That manner of teaching, which I mentioned before, it is believed he himself first brought to the Greeks from the Hebrews and Egyptians. For the Egyptians were accustomed to communicate sacred things among the priests by certain fictions, so that they might be kept secret from the common people; thus, they would be admired longer and grasped more attentively. Hence those Colossi, statues, altars, and columns publicly engraved with the sacred letters of the Egyptians stood out to the sight of all, but the hieroglyphs were understood only by the initiates and those entering the mysteries. <note>Hieroglyphs were often viewed by Renaissance scholars as mystical symbols rather than a phonetic writing system.</note> About these, Chæremon and Orus and many of the Egyptians have written. 

Thus my Pythagoras did not think it the part of a wise man to "present a lyre to a donkey," <note>A Greek proverb: *ὄνῳ λύρα* (onō lyra), meaning to offer something beautiful or intellectual to someone incapable of appreciating it.</note> or to reveal mysteries that would be received like "a pig to a trumpet," <note>A proverb for someone totally unsuited to a task.</note> or "a jackdaw to a lute," or "a beetle to perfume." Therefore he commanded silence to his disciples, lest they reveal divine matters to the common crowd, since these are more easily grasped by meditating than by speaking.

Then Marranus said: "Do not, my Philolaus, keep Pythagoras for yourself alone, but allow him to be ours as well, and not yours only. Indeed, I seem to have turned out a Pythagorean myself, hardly deaf or forgetful of your discourse—I who have used the commonplaces of Cicero <note>original: *locis Tullianis*</note> and the Rhetorical Art while listening to you, in order to commit to memory all the mysteries, metaphors, enigmas, maxims, apophthegms, allegories, symbols, signs, and sacraments of such a great man and the first of all philosophers, which you have just now reviewed cursorily in the form of a catalog. Let me make a trial of it. 

For you asserted, if I remember correctly, that Pythagoras encompassed all parts of philosophy in three volumes: the preparatory <term>propaedeutic|Initial learning or training required before higher study</term> and the political—that is: the natural, the mathematical, and the moral. These volumes he is said (as I have heard elsewhere) to have commanded to his daughter in his will, that she should not publish them even outside the family—rather, not publish them at all. But he himself clearly demonstrated everything contained therein to a worthy few while he lived, especially mathematics, using his living voice without any veil; the rest he taught in parables. Therefore, speaking in one way but thinking in another (and yet remaining wise), he imparted his doctrine to his own through certain symbols as reminders, so that in imitation of the ancients, he might speak one thing and convey another meaning. 

To begin from the first principles: the 'Infinite' and the 'One' are used to represent God; numbers represent incorporeal things; figures represent bodies; harmony represents the initiates; and for filth and sins, 'vines not to be planted'..."

<summary>Philolaus explains how Pythagoras adopted the Egyptian and Hebrew method of using symbols and hieroglyphs to hide sacred truths from the unworthy, a practice confirmed by Marranus, who notes that Pythagoras even forbade his daughter from publishing his writings.</summary>

# BOOK II.
<meta>catchword: prior</meta>

...for that which is most pure in life, flour. A white rooster is the mark of those dedicated to God. To sit designates humility. Turning around [indicates] prudence, and these things pertain to divine matters. This [next part] looks toward private matters and virtues. The balance scale is a symbol of justice. Salt denotes moderation. The public road [means] the errors of the common people. The sun stands in place of what is manifest and open. A sharp sword signifies dangers. Urine [represents] immodesty. Song [means] pleasure. The lyre [means] harmony. Bed coverings [mean] sleeplessness. A tight ring [means] pain. Food for the heart [means] torment. A pot [means] the boiling over of anger. Curved nails <note>claws or talons</note> [mean] robbery. A *choenix* <term>choenix: a Greek unit of dry measure for grain, about a quart</term> [means] nourishment. Falling things [mean] fortune. Boundaries [mean] fate; these are for a man in himself, and now follows what relates to others. The right hand denotes friendship. A black tail [means] false brothers. Nails and hair are symbols of relatives. Swallows [mean] talkative people and those who depart ungrateful. Bread is the mystery of true friendship. Oil is a sign of flattery. Fire [is a sign] of wrath. A sword [is a sign] of provocation. A burden suggests annoyance. A chamber pot represents the unworthy. A gentle tree [represents] a useful man. A fish [represents] an innocent man. So much for private matters. Now for the republic. A crown is the sign of law and governance. Wood on the road [means] the affairs of the community, [and] ambition. The bean demonstrates [this]; all things are symbolic, all things figurative and allegorical. 

Unless you thought more could be found in the disciples of Pythagoras, I would certainly reduce all these things to that man’s mathematical proportions, since one and two, in the first progression, become three. Behold the republic: and thrice three are nine. Behold divine matters: and thrice four are twelve. Behold private matters regarding another: and four times four are sixteen. Behold private matters regarding oneself. Therefore the republic is a triangle <term>trigonus: a triangular number</term>, and private matter is a square <term>tetragonus: a square number</term>, and just as sixteen is to twelve, so twelve is to nine, each in a hemiolic <term>hemiolia: a ratio of 3:2, also called a sesquialteral proportion</term> proportion. 

See how teachable I am with you as my teacher, and how excellently I "Pythagorize" <note>original: "Pythagorisso", meaning to act or speak like Pythagoras</note>. But truly, what are you making me into? Then Philolaus said: "Clearly a Pythagorean; for I now permit you to break your silence, you have enough of the disciplines, if you understand all formal things intellectually." To this Marranus [said]: "I certainly do not know what this is." He [Philolaus] said: "I will tell you. If you transfer all things that appear to you from the sense to the mind, that is, if you reject all bodily passions and enjoy the contemplation of the mind. Now, for example, I would want you to see a man far away from you in the widest space of a field; but you, not knowing what the thing is, will think it is either a field marker or a small tree trunk, for it has a straight shape and, in your opinion, immovable matter; as you look closer, you will think it has grown into a small tree. Therefore, having rejected the mass of stone, you think it thrives with the life of a plant; then, if by progressive motion you both approach each other, immediately as the form of the tree vanishes, there occurs to you the image of some animal, while you are unknowing and doubting whether it be a griffin or a stork, or any other huge bird, for it is two-footed. And now, having become closer, you see that it has no tail and no wings, and walks with its head erect; soon you leave behind all previous forms and think of the human form. Therefore, when you have come together, [you offer] a greeting...

It then begins an epistemological allegory about how the mind refines sensory data—mistaking a distant man for a stone, then a plant, then an animal—to reach true understanding.</summary>

# CABALA 13

...you speak first, and that person responds rationally, then no suspicion of a faun or a satyr or any other phantom arises in you. But you clearly recognize a man, either a neighbor or a friend, whom when you ask about his parents and relatives (as is customary), he satisfies your every question and then departs. As he leaves, you reflect alone with yourself that this man was born from parents, and those parents again from parents, and those very ones likewise from human seed, and that seed from some man; finally, since nature rejects the infinite <note>Nature rejects an infinite regress of causes; there must be a starting point</note>, it will perhaps seem not at all impossible to designate some one man who was born without human seed. Thus in the 12th book of the *Postnaturalia* <note>The *Metaphysics*</note> wrote Aristotle, and he called him *to teleion* <note>original: τὸ τέλειον</note>, that is, the "perfect" or "complete" one. 

And when you accept from the philosophers that such a perfect man is given, whose body was not born like those of other men, then you will run through reason to the soul of man, always moving from the perfect toward perfection and the more noble. And by the same possibility, you will judge that a certain soul is also granted, not created like other souls, but perhaps one which co-created itself, and that it is not only perfect and more perfect than others, but even the most perfect of all that were, are, will be, or can be. This soul, in the body of a mortal man, you will mentally separate from the body, and above the rest of the separated souls (since it is the most noble) you will place it in the most noble—not a place, but a dwelling. 

Truly the most noble mansion is closest to God, which the Stagirite <note>Aristotle, born in Stagira</note> pursues at length in the book to Alexander *On the World* <note>De Mundo, a treatise formerly attributed to Aristotle</note>. But we judge that soul to dwell in the horizon of the highest-above world which is called incomparable, where there is the union of God and creature. Just as in the horizon of eternity we place the immobile mover of the first movable <term>Primum Mobile: in the ancient geocentric model, the outermost sphere that moves all others</term>, in which the corporeal and incorporeal worlds meet. 

By this path now, you have intellectually changed the human form into a "separated form," and led the same mentally to the supreme mansion of eternity. From there, the highest blessedness instills itself into all angels and grateful souls, and all soul-saving souls are regulated toward that soul as if toward a certain standard. Which certainly, concerning that most perfect body of which we made mention before, the Pythagoreans do not deny. For Pythagoras himself said that man can become an immortal God, through which power he clearly showed that a single glory can glorify both parts of man, and make the whole man blessed, when most especially God himself either absorbs both and imbibes them into his Divinity, or permits the soul to flow its brightness and glorification into the sublimated body, *as a yoke-mate and companion of the way, co-enrolled and having contended together* <note>original Greek: ὡς ὁμοζύγῳ καὶ ὁμοπορεύτῳ, σωαπογραφέντι τε καὶ συναθλήσαντι</note>. That is to say, as a spouse and companion of the path, and at the same time counted, and that which has lived together. 

This dogma of Pythagoras sprouted again from Orpheus, which is discovered in his hymn to Mercury. Now you see hanging before your eyes the golden chain of Homer in the 8th [book] of the *Iliad*, let down from heaven by Jove <note>Jupiter or Zeus</note> to our fragility on the earth, through which you lift yourself by divine help into the heights...

It links these ideas to Homer's "golden chain" as a metaphor for the soul's ascent from the earthly to the celestial realm.</summary>

<header>BOOK II.</header>

...both by acting and by contemplating. It was necessary first to live according to the mind, and then finally to contemplate with the mind and, as a contemplator, to ascend ardently. For life precedes contemplation; since it is fitting for both to be pure in order to achieve that state than which nothing is purer, certainly life must first be purged, and then contemplation must be illuminated. Therefore, what you saw in that abstraction of things from things which we brought forward, experience it in yourself, so that through reason you may return to the mind and disentangle yourself from all external things. This is what the Emperor Marcus Antoninus commands: *unfold yourself* <note>original Greek: ἄπλασσον σεαυτὸν; Latin: explicato te ipsum. This is a Stoic exhortation to simplify the soul and strip away worldly distractions.</note>.

For one migrating from this life into the next must have stripped off every garment and set forth naked—not only from all matter and bodily attachments, but also as a fugitive and free from the entire mass of perturbations, affections, and passions. Lucian of Samosata taught this most skillfully in his dialogue of Charon and Mercury <note>A reference to Lucian’s *Dialogues of the Dead*, where souls must strip off their titles, wealth, and beauty before crossing the river Styx</note>, the most philosophical of all; if you have not read it, read it and imitate it. 

I ask you, what else did Pythagoras mean when he divided into three parts the things that place us on the tracks of divine virtue, if not purgation, illumination, and perfection? For he says: *Work at these things, meditate on these things, you must love these things; these will place you on the tracks of divine virtue* <note>original Greek: ταῦτα πονεῖ ταῦτ᾽ ἐκμελέτα τούτων χρὴ ἐρᾷν σε, ταῦτα σε τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς εἰς ἴχνια θήσει. These are lines from the "Golden Verses," a famous collection of Pythagorean moral exhortations.</note>. Hierocles <note>A 5th-century philosopher who wrote a famous commentary on the Pythagorean Golden Verses</note> wished this to be understood as applying the powers of our rational soul to the love of divine things; and "these things," he says, "will make us like God." 

Let us consider the words of Pythagoras. For he established three things which, when joined, allow us to reach the highest blessedness in an <term>anagogic</term> <note>A method of spiritual ascent that leads the mind from earthly symbols to divine realities.</note> way: the Labor of virtue which consists in action; Meditation which is nourished by the study of many disciplines; and Love which connects us to God as a necessary bond. Moral philosophy provides the first, natural philosophy combined with mathematics provides the second, and theology provides the third abundantly to the seeker. Nor is one sufficient by itself, but these three must come together. 

Porphyry, that greatest explorer of the Pythagoreans, treats this learnedly (as he does all things) in the first book of *On Abstinence from Animal Food* with these words, which I have chosen to quote because of the great authority of his testimony: "For us," he says, "blessed contemplation is not an accumulation of words or a multitude of disciplines, as someone might perhaps think, nor is it established by such things, nor does it increase based on the quantity of arguments and speeches. For if that were so, nothing would prevent those who collect every branch of knowledge from being blessed." <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν... ἡ εὐδαιμονικὴ ἡμῖν θεωρία...; Latin: Non est beata nobis contemplatio...</note>

And a little later, to omit the rest for the sake of brevity, he says: "And it is necessary for us to say this one thing, if we intend to return to our truly own state: we must set aside everything we took on from this mortal nature. Having remembered the blessed and eternal holiness, and how we must strive to return to the incorporeal and quality-less state, we should make certain practices: one, by which we set aside everything material and mortal; another..."

<page-num>822</page-num>
<header>KABBALAH</header>

...but so that we might return and live again, ascending back to those heights in the opposite way we descended here. <note>original Greek: δὲ, ὅπως ἐπανέλθωμεν καὶ παλινζωήσωμεν ἐναντίως ἐπ' αὐτὰ ἀναβαίνοντες ἢ ἐνταῦθα κατήλθομεν.</note> That is: It behooves us, if we truly wish to return to our own proper home from this place, to cast off all those things we took on from our mortal nature. We must do this with the same intensity of feeling toward those things through which our descent occurred. We must remember the blessed and eternal essence and strive to ascend toward the incorporeal and impassive, performing two meditations: one by which we strip away everything material and mortal, and another by which we turn back and return, ascending to those things differently than we descended here. 

And again, after a short discourse, **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized asceticism and the soul's return to the "One."</note> commands us there to completely separate the soul from sense perception, imagination, and every irrational condition that follows from them, as well as from passions of that kind—at least as far as the necessity of nature permits. We must rightly arrange and systematically compose those things pertaining to the mind, establishing tranquility and peace after the war we have waged against irrationality. In this way, we may not only hear about the intellect and intelligible things, but also, according to our strength, enjoy their contemplation. Then, having been translated into the incorporeal nature and living with the truth through the mind, we will no longer live falsely with the relatives of the body. 

Therefore, we must loosen many garments: both this visible garment of flesh and those "garments of skin" <note>original: pelliceis. A reference to Genesis 3:21, which many mystical traditions interpreted as the physical body or the dense, animalistic nature acquired by the soul after the Fall.</note> that we wear closest to our inner selves. Thus far **Porphyry**, who proceeds by discussing many more things on this subject, all tending toward the idea that we come to the enjoyment of the intelligible and mental good through sensible things by living honorably, contemplating purely, and loving divinely. He drew all these things from our **Pythagoras**, as if from a great river of all disciplines. 

"But I," **Marranus** said, "am clearly moved by those things you have recounted in order to the opinion that **Pythagoras** diverted his stream into the fields of the **Greeks** from the infinite sea of the **Kabbalists**, whose successful voyage **Simon** promises us. From there, we may finally water our own studies. Thus, **Simon's** speeches and sentiments concerning the **Kabbalists** seem to me equal to yours concerning the **Pythagoreans**. For what else does either the **Kabbalist** or **Pythagoras** intend, if not to lead the souls of men back to the Gods—that is, to promote them to perfect happiness? 

And what other way is there than their similar mode of teaching? Both use an equal exercise through symbols and signs, adages and proverbs, through numbers and figures, and through letters, syllables, and words. Thus the *upsilon* <note>The Greek letter Y, which Pythagoras used to symbolize the "fork in the road" of life: the narrow path of virtue and the broad path of vice.</note> of **Pythagoras** stands as a symbol of youth. Thus the first syllable of the ***Iliad*** <note>The first word of the Iliad is 'Menin' (Wrath). In esoteric numerology, the first letters or syllables of Homeric works were sometimes mapped to the total number of books in the epic.</note> is a sign and mark of all the books of **Homer**, indicating how many there are in both works. Thus the word for "white" signifies good, and "black" signifies evil. 

In no different way has our **Simon** transferred the first letter of the **Pentateuch** <note>The letter Beth (ב), the first letter of Genesis, which Kabbalists analyzed for its shape and numerical value.</note> and the middle letter of the *Pentagrammaton* <note>The "five-letter name," usually the name of Jesus (YHShVH) formed by inserting the letter Shin (ש) into the Tetragrammaton (YHVH).</note> to other things. He also borrowed *Raham*, on the authority of **David Kimhi** <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish grammarian and commentator. The reference likely concerns the linguistic roots of names like Abraham.</note>, allegorically for **Abraham**, and the other things which we remember well enough from the speech he gave us. 

But listen to how loudly the innkeeper himself calls us to the dining room: "Hey, to the feast!" 

And **Philolaus** says: "Indeed, I shall eat greedily; why don't we go?"

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN
## OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS
### BOOK THREE

After they had departed and the dark moon in its turn suppressed the light, and the setting stars encouraged sleep, they both surrendered to slumber. But first, they exhorted one another not to sleep past the first light of morning, and they took care that they should be awakened. The next day, while dressing according to their custom, they remembered the innkeeper's long and varied tales. He had told his guests at yesterday's feast that certain "propositions and conclusions" had been sent from the Roman Curia to Frankfurt the previous day. These had been fabricated and composed by a certain **Astaroth** <note>original: "Astaroto." This is a derogatory pseudonym Reuchlin used for his chief rival, the Dominican inquisitor Jacob van Hoogstraten, likening him to a demon.</note> against the Apostolic prohibition and directed against **Johannes Reuchlin**. Reuchlin is a man who, for over five years, has innocently but with a brave and unbroken spirit suffered cruel persecutions for his stand that Jewish books should not be burned. These papers had been fixed to the doors of the wise and the vestibules of temples in Rome, but were soon thrown into the mud, dung, and filth there, and trampled underfoot for just reasons. 

This was done, first, because such an act was attempted against the will of the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope, at this time Leo X.</note> and without the knowledge of the most reverend judges, before whom that lawsuit had been pending in the Curia for three years following Astaroth's appeal. Secondly, it was done because it was obvious to everyone that the writing overflowed with the most blatant lies. For at the beginning, Astaroth promised that these conclusions would be debated in the presence of the Pope; however, the Pope refused and certainly prohibited it, since the cause had already been fully debated and discussed during many public sessions held in Rome the previous summer. These sessions were held before the most learned lights of the world: prelates of the Catholic Church, archbishops, bishops, generals of religious orders and their representatives, penitentiaries, and doctors—a great number of men highly skilled in **Theology** and **Law**, who had decreed that **Capnio** <note>A scholarly nickname for Reuchlin, derived from the Greek word for "smoke" (kapnos), a pun on the German "Rauch."</note> should be acquitted.

Furthermore, [the innkeeper reported] that he [Astaroth] had disgracefully labeled the **Eye-Mirror** <note>original: "Oculare speculum." This refers to Reuchlin's 1511 book *Augenspiegel*, in which he defended Jewish books against the Emperor's decree of destruction.</note> a source of scandal and erroneous contents, even though that book was definitively approved by Apostolic sentence. Then also, he wrote of that same book that it had long ago been consigned to the fire by five Universities. This is certainly mere nonsense and clear, bright lies, because there is not, nor has there ever been, any University in the entire world that condemned the *Eye-Mirror*. Rather, only certain headstrong individuals—men with dizzying brains, irregular characters, and deceived by lazy error—gathered in secret conspiracies against the form of Law and justice. Consumed by envy, they "concocted" (as the saying goes) their own opinions against the *Eye-Mirror*. Finally, they say that those who rolled those "corollaries" around in the mud and filth were heard to affirm that in those writings there was nothing contained from **Alpha to Omega** <note>original Greek: "α ad ω"</note> which...

->**ON THE KABBALAH**<-

...had not previously been justified, settled, and resolved in the public defense of Johannes Reuchlin against his Cologne detractors, such that it became clearer than the stars to every reader. Therefore, Astaroth <note>original: "Astarotum." A derogatory name used by Reuchlin for his rival, the inquisitor Jacob van Hoogstraten.</note> always sings that same song with his foul tongue. The younger Philolaus and Marranus recounted these speeches of the innkeeper with their hosts and fellow guests, thinking it a far too serious matter to fight so fiercely for so many years over a thing so small and childish. As soon as they were dressed, they set out quickly for Simon’s house, as they had planned. When they had greeted one another most amicably, as was their custom, Marranus began thus: 

"Venerable Simon, it is truly incredible and can scarcely be told how much your discussion yesterday delighted us; indeed, in your absence, we were as restless as smoke. Thus, without any embarrassment, we have arrived before dawn as soon as your Sabbath had passed." 

And Simon replied, "Welcome, my friends; do you not also keep a holiday today, the day you call the day of the Sun?" 

Then Philolaus said, "We are a Pythagorean crowd; we consider all days to be feasts when we contemplate with a cheerful mind. Nor do we consider the Sabbath to be anything other than leaving behind secular business to strive to cling to divinity. For thus Pythagoras commanded us, according to Laertius: 'One must converse with the gods' <note>original Greek: "ξυλῶσαι διὰ τοῖς Θεοῖς" (scholazein tois theois). Reuchlin translates this as "conversari oportet cum dijs."</note>. Except that you venerate the pure seventh day, most fit for leisure; even for us Pythagoreans, this number produces nothing <note>Pythagoreans called the number seven "Minerva" because it is a "virgin" number—it is not produced by multiplication within the first ten numbers, nor does it produce any of them.</note>, and it is named Minerva."

Then Simon said, "One must listen to the Law, which distributes to each its own, and provides for nature itself as if for a soul. For it wished to serve the strengths of the body, without which neither reason can exist nor the light of the mind be strongly preserved. Therefore, it established that a portion of the lunar month—that is, a seventh part of life—should be at rest, during which nothing may be done except that which would cause irreparable harm if omitted. These are called, if I remember correctly, by the Romans 'fixed festivals' <term>feriae stativae: holidays that occur on the same date every year</term>, common to all people and consecrated for performing divine rites. Just as Neoptolemus in Ennius's work does not permit one to philosophize always, so it is not permitted for everyone to meditate on all things regarding God at all times. Even among your own writers there are those who understand this; there is a time, a people, and a measure for it, as Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his "Theological Orations."</note> wrote against the Eunomians—a man I once read in Greek, most learned and eloquent, when I was living in Achaia. In this way, that which is best and infinite will not become cheapened when it is conceived finitely according to our own measure. For six days we work, but on every seventh day we rest both bodily—as far as the necessity of living permits—and mentally, after the purification of the will, we are intent upon divine things. Joyfully and with all tranquility, we praise the sacred mysteries and serve God alone. This is the point our Kabbalists make: 'The Sabbath is the mystery of the Living God' <note>original Hebrew: "שבת הוא סוד אלהי" (Shabbat hu sod Elohei Chai)</note>, as found in the second chapter of the *Porta Lucis* <note>The "Gates of Light," a foundational Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>. For it stands as a symbol of the higher world, that is, the Jubilee of eternity, where all labor ceases. For this reason, it is commanded in the laws by the usual way of speaking: Deuteronomy 5, 'Observe the Sabbath day.'"

### BOOK III.

...which he wants to be understood as external actions according to the lower world.
And in Exodus 20: *Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy*, namely by joining the powers of the soul to the mind for the advancement of contemplation according to the higher world. Do you recognize it now? The Sabbath is a sign of divine service, by which the senses and reason are released from material occupations—as far as human weakness permits—and the energy of the mind is bound to formal <note>In a philosophical sense, "formal" refers to the essential or spiritual form of a thing, rather than its physical matter.</note> occupations, to consider those things that are above. The Law intended to hint at this through these two words: *Shamor* and *Zakhor* <note>original Hebrew: שמור וזכור</note>, that is, “Observe” and “Remember.” By these, some of our masters understand the precept of the Sabbath to be both affirmative and negative, saying: “Observe,” that is, “beware” (which for them always signifies avoidance), insofar as it restrains us from everything contrary to holiness. Others explain “Observe” as “guard,” so that they attribute “guarding” to the night and “remembrance” to the day. This is not at all far from the foundation of the Kabbalists, who think that this world is night, and the world to come—that is, the superior and intellectual world—is day. In this world, servants dwell; in that world, the free live. To the former, one must say “beware,” “guard,” and “observe”; to the latter, “reminisce,” “recall,” and “remember.” For this word *Zakhor* <note>original Hebrew: זכור</note>, that is, “remember,” contains the affirmative precept and proceeds from love, while the word “beware” fulfills the negative precept and proceeds from fear. Love belongs to the free, while fear belongs to servants; thus, we consider one of these precepts to be more noble than the other.

Moses of Gerona <note>Also known as Nahmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and Kabbalist.</note> wrote almost this same sentiment in a longer treatise on Exodus, from which we accept that there are two Sabbaths, led by the testimony of the scripture in Ezekiel 20: *I gave them my Sabbaths*. For the plural phrasing is satisfied by the number two, not only because God wished to reproach us generally with a single word for each type of feast day numbered in the law (as David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval biblical grammarian and commentator (c. 1160–1235).</note> and the Talmudists believe), but also so that we might always embrace with a mindful spirit this best gift and perfect boon granted to us by God under this peculiar name, which we called the “Jubilee” above. Concerning this, 

<margin>The Gate of Light <note>original: "Porta lucis." This refers to the *Sha'are Orah*, an influential Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla.</note> says this:</margin>

*This is the Jubilee, it is the supernal seventh which is called Jubilee* <note>original Hebrew: יובל זו היא שביעית עליונה שנקראה יובל</note>. From this, all remission, propitiation, and infusion of grace descends—which no one can sufficiently describe, since *no eye has ever seen it, O God, except yours*. For it is *Shabbat Shabbaton* <note>original Hebrew: שבת שבתון</note>, a Sabbath of rest and a Sabbath of Sabbaths, into which all pure human souls, having finally cast off their stains, will return freely to the inheritance of their fathers. They shall be sent into a possession truly our own and proper, which we acquired and retain through the soul of the Messiah of the tribe of Judah (the seventh from the patriarch Abraham), in his capacity as a representative on the horizon of the highest-supernal world, according to the scripture: *And above the Jubilee he shall send out his roots* (Jeremiah 17). This is interpreted by that most excellent Kabbalist Sopher Aman <note>Likely a reference to a "faithful scribe" or a specific Kabbalistic pseudonym.</note> in the book *Razim* <note>original: "Sepher Razim," the *Book of Secrets*.</note> (that is, of Hidden Things), on the verse of the nineteenth Psalm, *Day unto day*.

<note>original Hebrew: אצילותו שהוא פלג אלהים מלא מים</note> “His emanation, which is the river of God full of water.” That is to say, it means that each person will return to his family and to the inheritance of his fathers, as if to say that they will ascend through angels to the place of their destination, where the river of God is filled with water. These are the words of Rabbi Ammi, and they are the waters which are above the heavens, in the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of pure thought or spirit, beyond the physical senses.</note> <note>original Hebrew: שהוא יצא מרוח הקדוש</note> “which proceeded from the Holy Spirit,” where those observing the Sabbath take pleasure and are fed with the heritage of Jacob their father, as Isaiah said. Indeed, that is the very Sabbath of the Kabbalists, to be sanctified at all times, in which we follow the will not of the flesh, but of the soul, and we meditate on divine things, intending nothing against God. This stands as a law for all nations, because it buds forth from nature itself.

For you, to whom the Law of Moses was not given, the ceremonies of the Jews do not bind you to serve by number <note>The speaker suggests that non-Jews are not bound by the specific legalistic counts or "number" of ritual laws found in the Torah.</note>, which Iarchas <note>A legendary Indian sage mentioned in the life of Apollonius of Tyana.</note> once correctly denied to Apollonius. Then Marranus said: “By all means, let it be completed! For you have begun to treat the Kabbalah quite elegantly. You have already shown more than clearly that we are able today to discuss the highest matters with the same clarity as the ancients. Do you not ask the same with me, Philolaus?”

He replied: “Certainly indeed. Truly, now that we have entered the ship of this discipline, we soon feel at the very prow that Kabbalah is nothing else than (to speak in the manner of Pythagoras) symbolic theology, in which not only letters and names are signs of things, but even things are signs of other things. By this we observe that almost all Pythagorean philosophy arose from the Kabbalists, who in like manner transferred the symbolic way of teaching to the Greeks. Indeed, I too, along with this companion of mine, strongly urge you to continue speaking, or rather, teaching.”

Then Simon said: “I would not take so much boasting upon myself as to dare to teach you; nor would it be quite safe in a matter so perplexed, not yet known to foreigners—especially to those learned in the Roman way—except for the very few things that in recent years Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola, and our former associate Paulus Ricius published, which even to this day are not sufficiently understood by the Latins. For I fear if I were to teach such foreign dogmas, a crowd of envious people might shamelessly roar against me, as has happened to many good men before. Such people disapprove of everything they do not know, and easily, with malicious zeal, twist words into a sense foreign to the speaker’s truth. These people Cicero calls ‘calumniators’; I, if it may be said grammatically, shall call them *Calumnienses*, since you yourselves are accustomed to call <unclear>reos</unclear> <note>Likely "religious" or "rigorous"</note> theologians ‘Phariseenses’ [Pharisees].

But I publicly testify to both of you that I wish to teach nothing, but rather to speak and recount what I have read among the Kabbalists that I think would not displease you. I will therefore pursue first that which they intend as the last; for they take care to spend all their study and their entire effort on this one purpose: that in this life...

...capacity, and of the future, who according to each one's capacity may attain perpetual happiness. They trust that this can be achieved most of all by this means: if they finally, with diligence and vigor, grasp what they perceive to be best for the state of both worlds. The possession of this brings a pleasant and perfect rest to those who attain it, since even brute animals seem to exult in their own happiness when they enjoy what they consider best for themselves and reach those things that satisfy their desires. 

You see an ox grazing in a flowery and green meadow; it does not eat everything, but by deliberate choice seeks now this herb, now that. Suddenly it easily leaves one, and completely passes over another, until it reaches the food that is suitable and nourishing for it, where it stops and rests. In this same way, the Kabbalists—after wandering through the vast fields of science and the meadows of contemplation adorned with every beauty—taste many and various herbs of different scents, so that at last, having surveyed the whole pasture, they may find that divine <term>Moly: a magical herb from Homer’s *Odyssey* given by Hermes to Odysseus to protect him from Circe’s magic</term>. Although its root is black, according to Homer’s <note>original: "Homeri opinione"</note> view, its flower shines white like milk. Once found, they seem to have driven away all miseries, having achieved the happy end of their desire in this world. 

The power of the Moly is its essence: the black root represents difficult works, and the flower represents the tranquility of souls. One could believe this to be nothing other than the true happiness of the present age. But the happiness of the future is the grasping of the Highest Good <note>original Latin: "summi boni"</note>, above which there is no good, and from which all goodness comes—a good that no mere creature can fully comprehend. Yet it is said to be "grasped" when one approaches it as closely as possible according to their capacity, just as if someone were to grab the hem of a garment, they would be said to have "grasped" the person wearing it. 

Toward that Good which is named God, we cannot fully ascend because of the fragility of our condition, except by steps and ladders. These are what you are accustomed to call the "Homeric Chain" <note>In the *Iliad*, Zeus describes a golden chain linking heaven and earth.</note>, but we Jews, according to the divine words, call the "Ladder of Jacob" our father. These are stretched from the super-celestial realms down to the earth, like a golden rope or cord directed to us from heaven, like a visual line penetrating various natures. 

For you behold the sun, whose ray travels to our sight through the sphere of Venus, through the sphere of Mercury, through the sphere of the Moon, through the sphere of fire, and through the sphere of air; it touches the opaque body of a concave mirror and reflects from there onto flax or dry wool, which it sets violently ablaze by its brightness until it turns to ashes. The appearance <note>original: "species"</note> of that same flame reaches our eyes and is received by inner sensation; once received, it is judged by the faculty of estimation <term>estimation: in medieval psychology, the ability to perceive "intentions" or qualities not grasped by the five senses, such as sensing danger</term>, and finally is processed by reason, retracing the path by which this whole operation progressed. Then this prudently shows us how inner forms are carried by the <term>animal spirits: the subtle fluids or vapors then believed to travel through the nerves to carry sensory information to the brain</term> to the imagination and to the judgment of estimation; and likewise how external things are received by internal ones, and how the appearance from the flame in the transparent medium...
