# ON THE KABBALAH

<page-num>828</page-num>

...aiming even at the pupil of the eye, by which way a flame is created from the heat of a concave mirror, and how a ray could ignite something, and finally by what means its splendor is continued through many media not natural to it; how much air is to be compared in proportion to fire, fire to the sphere of the moon, and the other orbs to the rest. Our <term>reason: *ratio*, the discursive faculty of the soul that moves step-by-step</term> disputes each of these things through the paths of composition and resolution, walking back and forth, up and down, now thinking of those things; nor does it cease its reasoning until, through the <term>imagination: *phantasia*, the faculty that forms mental images</term>, it returns to the image, the intentions, the splendor, the light, the glow—namely, to that source of light we are speaking of: the sun. First, it recognizes the image of light; then it judges that image to be the proper characteristic of that flame (it is amazed by what the eyes had seen before); then it sees that its "intention" <note>original: *intentio*, a philosophical term for the mental representation or the "reaching out" of the mind to an object</note> has been led from the seen object through the <term>transparent medium: *diaphanum*</term> to the eye outside and was also received within. It recognizes that it is terrestrial, that the splendor is airy, that the flame is fiery; that it clings to the transparent medium like an accident; that it passes through the clear and through the vacuum, whether that be air or fire or something celestial, according to the energy of the substantial form and its peculiar operation. Then, applying these meditations to each nobler thing, having left matter behind, it begins to dispute with itself concerning forms—not yet the "artificial" form (whose scrutiny does not belong here and which is more correctly called a "figure" than a form), but only the natural or superior form.

And so reason proceeds and finds that some forms are particular—existing "now" and "here"—while others are universal, existing always and everywhere. Among the particulars, it finds some existing in bodies to give them their "being," others as co-assisting forms to provide them their "being such," and others entirely separated from bodies in essence, power, and operation. These latter sometimes lose the name of "form" and are called either gods, or angels, or <term>intelligences: higher spiritual beings that govern the celestial spheres</term>, or blessed spirits, or minds, or by any other such name. Those that are universal are no longer called forms, but **Ideas** or **Species** by many who wish to speak very precisely. In this way, reason will indeed ascend as long as it is able. However, when it has been so thinned out by its discourse that it cannot comprehend forms which neither exist in bodies nor are subjected to nature, it calls upon the subsidiary **intellect**. Just as this intellect clearly abstracts this "matter" from this "form"—such as that of a certain donkey buried in a field, which nature then clothes with a human form <note>The text likely refers to the cycle of nature where the decomposition of one body provides the material for the growth or "flowering" of new life</note> from that flowering corpse—so again it strives to abstract form simply from matter. This, indeed, it finds to be arduous and full of labor. For it is easy to abstract matter from form, but to abstract form from matter is difficult. For this reason, that intellect raises itself more purely so that it may offer the <term>mind: *mens*, the highest divine spark or intuitive faculty</term> an opportunity to flow into it. Relying on the clarity of the mind, it recognizes that some forms are entirely absolute from bodily essence, power, and operation, and because of this, they are enclosed by neither place nor time; thus it is truly necessary to judge them to be above the heavens, where motion and time cease. From here, it instructs our will so that...

...one might believe that beyond the heavens there are beings leading the most excellent life, which they enjoy for all eternity. There, that second world begins, most abundant in living lights and the purest minds, which the human soul can enter through steadfast contemplation—certainly much more effectively than the bodily eye can transcend the sun’s sphere through keen sight. And just as we do not look upon the sun unless the sun looks back at us <note>meaning: the sun must first illuminate the eye for the eye to see it</note>, so we are unable to see the higher world unless it also sees us. For that world is itself an entire eye, even brighter than the sun. Moreover, we comprehend the sun through solar light; likewise, we comprehend divine things through divine light. Since we, with our bodily sight, can grasp not only the sun’s sphere but even the higher stars and the very summit of heaven, why should our mind—which in a certain way infinitely excels bodily power—not be able to look upward more deeply and see the contents of the archetypal world? Especially since the concave and convex of the highest heaven are united with such closeness that the horizon of eternity seems to be at no distance from that convex surface. Let us therefore gaze (believe me) upon the divine things of that other world mutually, and those things will in turn gaze upon us, like two directly opposite eyes moved back and forth reciprocally along a single line of sight.

# KABBALAH #

[He spoke] about the trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that comes out of the wall; and he discussed the beasts and the birds and the creeping things and the fishes. <note>A reference to 1 Kings 4:33, describing the vast botanical and zoological knowledge of King Solomon.</note> Beyond these things, Gerundensis <note>Moses ben Nahman, known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a famous Kabbalist and scholar from Girona</note> confirms our opinion: <note>original Hebrew: "He knew the Torah and found everything in it, in its interpretations, in its grammatical nuances, in its letters, and in its ornaments."</note> that is, he knew all these things through the Law, and he found everything within it through its expositions, through the subtleties of its grammar, through its letters, and through its ornaments <note>original: *calamistrationes*—referring to the decorative "tittles" or crowns on Hebrew letters</note>.

It happened, moreover, that after he had fully attained the logic of the forty-eight gates of understanding <note>The Hebrew tradition typically identifies fifty gates; the author here counts forty-eight as a step toward full comprehension</note>, which open the way to the knowledge of all creatures. For all things are generally distributed into five conditions. For they are either **elements**, or **things composed of elements**, or **souls**, or **celestial bodies**, or **incorporeal beings above the heavens**. Each of these perhaps receives ten considerations, the headings of which are as follows:

*   The most general genera
*   Special genera
*   General species
*   The most special species
*   Individual things (which consist further of matter and form)
*   Those things proportional to both
*   And they are further narrowed down by **differences**, **properties**, and **accidents**.

These ten modes, whether of essences or of intellects, when multiplied by five, open the **fifty gates** through which we enter into the secret chambers of creatures. These are designated by the notes remaining in the works of the six days [of Creation] and have been industriously discovered and received by the Kabbalists. For by this same artifice, the enigmatic writing placed by the Count of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Western thought</note> among his *Nine Hundred Conclusions* will easily be explained like an unraveled knot. For he said: "He who seeks what the <term>denarius</term> <note>the number ten</note> is in formal arithmetic, and has known the nature of the first <term>spherical number</term> <note>A number that, when squared or cubed, ends in itself; here referring to the number five</note>, will know the secret of the **fifty gates of understanding**, and of the **Great Jubilee**, and of the **thousandth generation**, and of the **kingdom of all ages**."

Thus said Mirandola. Therefore, I would like a plane or a circle of ten numerical figures to be drawn around a center which is **five**; for five is the middle of the <term>denarius</term> [ten], and in its circumference let the individual numbers of the decimal count be described in a circle. Let a diameter be made from the smallest to the largest—that is, from one to nine. Its division will create two semicircles. On the right side, after one and before nine, let the previously mentioned **two, three, and four** be placed. On the left side, after one and before nine, let **five, six, seven, and eight** be placed <note>This describes a specific geometric arrangement of the digits 1–9 around the number 5</note>. Then let lines be drawn across: from two to eight, from three to seven, from four to six, and from five to five. Then, if you subtract from each of the largest numbers as much as it exceeds five (which is the center of the decimal sphere), and add to the smallest what it lacks from five, there will always arise from both pairs the equalized numbers **five and five**. ### BOOK III ###

The ten-fold revolution is called **spherical**, because, as you have seen, all spherical numbers are reduced to five. This occurs through five lines drawn in a sphere, each of which contains ten. Therefore, when that spherical number is multiplied by ten, fifty will be born—these are either the **fifty gates of understanding** or the **Jubilee years**. Their double proportion, which is the formality of Arithmetic, multiplied by itself, will procreate the "thousandth generation." If you proceed in this way perpetually, infinity will appear; this is the kingdom of all ages, named by the Kabbalists <term>Ensoph</term> <note>Hebrew for "The Infinite" or "Without End," referring to God in His most hidden, absolute state before any manifestation.</note>, and it is the Deity itself without a garment.

For God produced the rest of existence clothed in light as with a garment, so that there would be "light from light." From that point, with the light of His garment, He created the "intelligible world" of separate and invisible spirits, which the Kabbalists call **heaven**, as you have often heard from me. In this way, I understand the words of the most wise and great Rabbi Eliezer, who, when he proposed the question of where heaven was created from, answered: <note>original Hebrew: מאור לבישו לקח</note> "He took from the light of His garment." These matters are recounted by Moses Maimonides (the "Shower of the Perplexed") in the 26th chapter of his second book, and by the younger Rabbi Joseph of Castile <note>Joseph Gikatilla, a major 13th-century Kabbalist.</note>, a citizen of Medinaceli, in the second volume of his *Garden of the Nut*.

Moses, the servant of God, ascended this far, so that he might know the light of His garment, the Sabbath of Sabbaths, the higher Jubilee, and the thousandth generation—all of which is nothing other than the superior world of **Ideas**, **angels**, and **heavenly souls**. Therefore, since he was unable to transcend the clothing of God or see His face, it is rightly said that he lacked one of the fifty gates of understanding. Some of our thinkers believe this missing gate was <note>original Aramaic: חיותא</note> "vivification" <note>the fundamental force of life itself.</note>, yet I do not agree with them. I believe it is actually the very **essence of God**, which the symbol of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The sacred four-letter Name of God: YHWH.</note> indicates. This is an incomparable world, beyond any comprehensible proportion.

For God said to Moses: "You will not be able to see my face." Or more truly: "And my faces shall not be seen, but I will call the name Tetragrammaton before you" (Exodus 33). The Kabbalists explain this as: <note>original Hebrew: שאקרא לפניך השם הגדול שלא תוכל לראותו</note> "I will call before you that great Name, which you will not be able to see." For so Ramban <note>Nachmanides, a famous medieval scholar.</note> writes. From this, it clearly appears that God, being identical with His own Tetragrammaton, was not seen by Moses. This Name is surely the principle of all the gates, existing above every creature before the beginning of creation, of which we read: "God created heaven and earth." The Chaldean translation of Onkelos <note>The standard Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> sounds like this: "The Tetragrammaton created heaven and earth." 

Therefore, the Tetragrammatus God created all things, whom I have heard you call the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>A Pythagorean symbol of ten dots arranged in a triangle, which the author is linking to the Hebrew four-letter Name.</note>. Moreover, Rabbi Eliezer said, as it stands in his chapters: <note>original Hebrew: עד שלא נברא העולם היה הקבה ושמו בלבד</note> "Until the world was created, there was only the Holy One (Blessed be He) and His Name alone." Other Kabbalists also assert this on the testimony of the "Egyptian Moses" <note>Maimonides.</note> in chapter 29 of the second book of the *Perplexed*: <note>original Hebrew: החלת שלא היה שום דבר נמצא כלל אלא השם וחכמתו</note> "In the beginning, there was nothing found at all except the Name and His wisdom."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Gates of Understanding" (Binah), moving from the mathematical structure of the universe to the hierarchy of prophetic knowledge. # KABBALAH #

Since no thing existed, there was nothing at all except the name of God and His wisdom. Therefore, before there was any created thing, according to the doctrine of the Kabbalah, there was nothing but God, and His name, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter divine name (YHWH), often transliterated as Yahweh or Jehovah.</note>, and His wisdom. These three things alone, our tradition holds, were the first secrets of creation; they were by no means fully revealed by our teacher Moses. For this reason, it is said that he investigated the divine realm only through forty-nine gates. Joshua, however, had one less, namely forty-eight. Indeed, we have received this from the book *Explanations of the Alphabet* by Rabbi Akiba: <note>original Hebrew: של מושה נתעלם מיהושע שער אחד ונשתארו מ"ח שערים ושלמה נתקשה על אותו שער להחזירו ולא היה יכול</note> "One gate from the gates of Moses was hidden from Joshua, and forty-eight gates remained; and Solomon struggled over that same gate to restore it, but he was not able."

The Kabbalists accepted this because it is written of Moses in Deuteronomy 34: *No prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses.* Therefore, Joshua was not strong enough to ascend as high as Moses had ascended; thus, it is affirmed with good reason that he was inferior by one degree. Regarding Solomon, however, we read in Ecclesiastes 12 that he *sought to find words of delight*, but the Kabbalists add that God commanded him: *Write correctly the words of truth.* We say these words were handed down and received through the way of Kabbalah, to the extent that he would not dare to write anything other than what he had received; and that was two degrees lower than the reception of Moses.

After God, the second gate is the **archetypal world**, and it is called "Heaven" created by the Tetragrammaton in wisdom, according to the *Jerusalem Targum* <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, which in the place of **In the beginning** <note>original Hebrew: בראשית (Bereshit)</note> placed the words **In wisdom** <note>original Aramaic: בחכמתא (Be-Chokhmata)</note>. This confirms what we have said: that in wisdom, the Tetragrammaton God created heaven—the chamber of the angels—about which nothing was explained by Moses, lest such things become cheapened by a rude and unrefined people who did not understand them, or provide an occasion for idolatry.

But in this visible world, "Earth" is understood, which we affirm to be the third among the gates. By "the void" <note>original Latin: inane</note>, we shall think of matter noted symbolically, which is the fourth gate of understanding. By "the vacancy" <note>original Latin: vacuum</note>, which is privation, we find the fifth. The sixth of these is the "Abyss," the natural appetite for these things. Thereafter, for the various works of the days, the remaining gates follow.

Indeed, the four seals of the elements now indicate four gates. For the pure element of fire—according to <term>Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note> in the twenty-sixth chapter of the second book of his *Guide for the Perplexed*—is called "darkness." The others are spirit (air), water, and the elemental earth. "Light" is the substantial form; "Day" refers to the accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are properties that do not change the essence of a thing, such as color or weight.</note> which contribute most to knowing what a thing is. "Night" refers to hidden properties. "Evening" is the path of corruption (decay), while "Morning" is the path of generation (birth). It is called "One Day" and not the "First Day" because it signifies a composite brought into the light. On the Second Day, the "waters above the firmament" are the species of universal things; the "firmament" is the horizon of eternity and time. The "waters under the firmament" are...

### BOOK III. ###

...natural qualities of the celestial bodies. On the third day follows another visible and material heaven, namely the nineteenth gate; then the earth we tread upon, then the seas we navigate, as well as herbs, seeds, wood, and fruits. On the fourth day, however, the luminaries, signs, seasons, days, years, splendor, the sun, and the moon, by which planets the others are understood through the sharing of heat and cold, dryness and moisture. Saturn, Mars, and Jupiter with their Sun are hot and dry; Mercury and Venus with their Moon are moist and cold, even if these seven spheres are specifically distinguished. Furthermore, the remaining stars designate the thirty-ninth gate; then on the fifth day come forth living souls, which are the life of mortals: in the waters, creeping things, whales, and fish; and generally winged creatures, and specifically birds. On the sixth, the animal that walks upon the earth, and the terrestrial reptile, and cattle, and beasts. Finally, the fiftieth gate, which is man. These are the forty-nine ways of knowing the creatures **שערי בינה** <gloss>Gates of Understanding</gloss>, and the supreme gate is the one Creator of all, fully known by no man except the Messiah, since he himself is the light of God and the light of the nations; therefore, he both knows God and God is known through him. For the royal prophet David exclaims to God thus:
-> Send out your light <-

which Rabbi Solomon the Frenchman <note>This refers to the famous medieval commentator Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, 1040–1105).</note> interprets as **המשיח שנרמה לאור שנ' ערכתי נר למשיחי** <note>original Hebrew: "The Messiah who is compared to light, as it is said, 'I have prepared a lamp for my Messiah.'"</note> that is, the Messiah who is compared to light, because it is written, *I have prepared a lamp for my Anointed*. And Isaiah says, *I have given you as a covenant for the people, for a light to the nations*. And again, *The nations shall walk in your light*. Moreover, Aristotle wrote what I believe to be true, that vision cannot occur without light, as is read in the book *On the Soul*, **οὐχ’ ὁρᾶται ἄνευ φωτὸς** <note>original Greek: "nothing is seen without light"</note> that is, nothing is visible without light. Therefore, as we walk toward the inspection of all things, it is very helpful to apply light to our journey, so that we may choose with mature providence the way by which we can proceed without injury to our feet. To this end, the Kabbalists received certain luminous paths and illustrious experiences which they named **ל"ב נתיבות החכמה** <gloss>thirty-two paths of wisdom</gloss>, which Abraham mentions in the *Book of Creation* <note>The "Sefer Yetzirah," a foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note>, which begins thus: **בשלשים ושתים נתיבות פלאות חכמה חקק יה יהוה צבאות שמו** <note>original Hebrew: "By thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom, Yah, the Lord of Hosts, carved out His name."</note> that is, By thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom, God—the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter divine name (YHWH).</note> of Hosts—engraved or carved His name. Upon which Rabbi Jacob Cohen wrote that when he says "wondrous," he signifies that these paths are secret, hidden, and occult, confirming this interpretation of his through the <term>Thargum</term> <note>Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. And the commentator Rabbi Isaac, on that same book *Yetzirah* <gloss>Creation</gloss>, testifies that the ancient wise men, men of heart, mild and upright, being most practiced in the <term>Cabala</term> <note>Kabbalah; the tradition of Jewish mysticism.</note> through the foundations of the Law, taught us that our elders and fathers walked through many ways, so that they might finally stand in those paths, which are called the wonders of wisdom, handed down by Zadkiel <note>In mystical tradition, the angel Zadkiel is often cited as the celestial teacher of the patriarch Abraham.</note> to our father Abraham in the tradition of the covenant. Thus he spoke. I shall therefore recount to you, excellent listeners, if only I judge it to be something worthy of your esteem...

# KABBALAH #

Then he said: There are 32 paths, which stretch from the highest summit to the lowest base, to be noted in this way. 

The first is the **Miraculous Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Mufla*</gloss>, so called by some, but it is much more correctly named the **Hidden Intelligence**. For Rabbi Solomon the Frenchman <note>This is Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the famous 11th-century commentator.</note> in the book of Deuteronomy, chapter 30, proves that this word *mufla* <note>original: **מופלא**</note> signifies "hidden" <note>original: **מכוסת**</note> in the verse: *For this commandment which I command you today is not above you.* <note>Deuteronomy 30:11. The Latin text argues that "above you" should be read as "hidden from you."</note> He teaches there that it should be read as "not hidden," according to the Aramaic translations <note>The Targums</note> cited there. It is, moreover, the light that grants the power to understand the preceding things without beginning; it is called the "First Glory," because no created thing is able to approach its pure essence and truth.

The second is the **Sanctifying Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Mekuddash*</gloss>, which is the foundation of eternal wisdom; it is called "Faith" and is named the "Parent of Faith," because from its power, faith is infused.

The third is the **Absolute Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Shalem*</gloss>, which is the intention of the first principles; it has no root by which it might pull anything back into the depths of its majesty, which are infused from that which came before.

The fourth is the **Pure Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Tahor*</gloss>, which purifies the Kabbalistic numbers <note>Referring to the Sephirot, the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah.</note> and corrects their formation; it disposes the earth and its extremities so that they exist without being cut off or scattered.

The fifth is the **Radiant Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Mazhir*</gloss>, which in the Kabbalah is called the "Second Glory."

The sixth is the **Resplendent Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Ha-Nitzotz*</gloss>; it sits upon the throne of splendor, illuminates the brightness of the luminaries, and pours its flow into the ruler of surfaces and eminences.

The seventh is the **Guiding Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Manhig*</gloss>; it is the very Throne of Glory, and it perfects the truth of spiritual communications.

The eighth is the **Rooted Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Nishlam*</gloss>, which is called the "Consummate Union"; it is the property of Prudence itself, which is infused from the higher essence.

The ninth is the **Triumphant or Eternal Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Nitzchi*</gloss>, which is called the Paradise of Delight, prepared for the saints.

The tenth is the **Organizing Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Ha-Mitgashesh*</gloss>; it fits the apparatus of holy faith so that they may be clothed in the Holy Spirit, and it is that which is called *Tiphereth* <note>Hebrew for "Beauty," the sixth Sephirah, here associated with a state of spiritual balance.</note> in the state of the supernal beings.

The eleventh is the **Intelligence of Clarity** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Tzachur*</gloss>; it is called the "Image of Magnificence," a "Vision" <note>original: **חזות** (*chazut*)</note>, because from it arises the vision for the prophets who see visions.

The twelfth is the **Marked Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Kavuah*</gloss>, so called because it is a distinguished branch from which spiritual virtues flow like a single pouring, one from another, according to the energy of the first influencer.

### Thirty-first: שכל דמיוני — Imaginary Intelligence ###
The **Thirty-first** is the **Imaginary Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Dimyoni*</gloss>; through it, all created forms and images are changed and altered according to their surfaces and their natures.

### Thirty-second: שכל מוטבע — Natural Intelligence ###
The **Thirty-second** is the **Natural Intelligence** <gloss>Hebrew: *Sekhel Mutba*</gloss>; through it, the nature of material things beneath the sphere of the moon is completed <note>original: "cmatur," likely *consummatur* or *confirmatur*</note> toward perfection.

I have summarized in a brief catalog the teachings of a man most skilled in foreign doctrines <note>Referring to the author's synthesis of various traditions</note>, which our ancestors treat with great difficulty in many books regarding the **Fifty Gates of Prudence** and the **Thirty-two Paths of Wisdom**. This is a subject truly worthy of a better teacher and of much greater value, having the greatest power to urge us to always dwell with the angels in the contemplation of the highest and divine things. If we begin to be familiar with these things, nothing will be difficult for us to say or do.

That familiarity is provided by the letters [of the alphabet], which are their handiwork. If we apply these to the ten Kabbalistic numerations <note>The *Sephirot*, the ten divine emanations</note>, the number thirty-two immediately arises. As it is written in the *Yetzirah* <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* or "Book of Formation," a foundational Kabbalistic text</note>: "Ten *Sephirot Belima* <note>meaning "without anything" or "ineffable"</note> and twenty-two letters." For this reason, many writers combine these ten properties worthy of silence and these twenty-two letters into this sum of paths, which I have arranged in order, though others may not observe the same sequence.

Furthermore, if we carefully add that collection of letters to the fifty gates, we shall discover there the blessed series of **seventy-two angels**. From these, the **Shem Ha-Mephorash** <note>original: *Semhamaphores*</note>—that is, the "Explanatory Name" of the great and supreme God—is said to consist. For 22 added to 50 will produce 72. These are the "mighty angels of all the earth," whom it is thought that the miracle-worker Moses divided by his hand [the sea] unto the dry land, for they are the "angels of division." And he divided the earth according to the number of his angels. For so we read, among other things, in the book *The Gates of Justice* <note>*Sha'are Orah*, written by Rabbi Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla</note>, written by Rabbi Joseph ben Carnitol <note>Gikatilla</note>, a celebrated master in Kabbalah: "And all the nations were left delivered into the power of the seventy princes <note>original: *septuaginta pr-rum*, likely *principum*</note>." 

This refers to the angelic princes, to whom **Recanati** <note>Menahem ben Benjamin Recanati, a 13th-century Italian Kabbalist</note>, a most skilled Kabbalist, applies the "seventy palm trees" in his commentary on Genesis 48, which surround the twelve tribes you know. Moreover, it is certain that there were two columns there—one of cloud and one of fire—over which two angels were set as leaders. Therefore, we should not think it strange that in such a parting of the sea and the liberation of the children of Israel, seventy angels of the world and two columnar angels came to Moses for the ministry of salvation. This salvation clearly comes to us through the ineffable **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, by way of the seventy-two names which are gathered from the Holy Scripture in the explanation of Exodus 14, from the verse beginning "The angel took up..." until the end, where one reads: "And the water was divided." These are surely sacred seals, stored in a mindful soul in this present age, by which...

**BOOK III**

...by symbols, the angels who are called upon bring aid to men, to the praise and glory of the ineffable God. About this, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> wrote in his exposition of the Talmud, supported by the testimony of the Gerundite <note>Moses ben Nahman, or Nahmanides (1194–1270), a scholar from Gerona, Spain</note>, in the beginning of Genesis. These, then, are the characters of the symbols, which I paint for you here with my finger:

-> VHV  YLY  SIT  ALM  MHS  LLH  AKA  KHT  HZI  ALD  LAV  HHA  YZL  MBA  HRI  HKM <-
-> LAV  KLI  LVV  PHL  NLK  YYD  MLH  HHV  NTH  HAA  IRT  SAH  RYY  AUM  LKB  VSR  YIV <-
-> LHH  KVK  MND  ANI  HAM  RHA  YYZ  HHH  MIK  VVL  YLH  SAL  ARI  ASL  MIH  VHV <-
-> DNY  HHS  AMM  NNA  NYT  MBA  PVI  NMM  YYL  HRH  MZR  VMB  YHH  ANU  MHI  DMB <-
-> MNQ  AYE  HBU  RAH  YBM  HYY  MVM <-
<note>These are the 72 triplets of the *Shem Ha-Mephorash* or the "Explicit Name" of God, derived from Exodus 14:19-21. Each name is believed to govern a specific angelic energy.</note>

All these names flow from the attribute of mercy <note>original: "proprietate clementiae"</note>, as the Kabbalists <term>Kabbalists: Practitioners of Jewish mysticism who seek to understand the hidden nature of God</term> assert. This attribute is one of the ten numerations <note>The *Sephirot*, or divine emanations; Simon is referring to *Chesed* (Mercy/Kindness)</note>, whose "Tree" I will demonstrate to you, if the heavenly powers are willing and if you are prepared to listen to me. "Indeed, we are most prepared," they both say, "for we have faced the great dangers of travel for this very purpose, and spent such great sums of money." "But proceed," they say, "so that we may learn something of these angels, whose names I, Marrano, have never heard before; and I believe the same is true for you, Philolaus." "Certainly," says Philolaus, "just as those angels have never been seen by me, so their names were unknown to me; but we shall be grateful, excellent man, if you continue without ceasing."

Then Simon said: "That there were many angels who converged for that great and wonderful work of Moses, when he divided the waters of the sea so that the Israelites might cross with dry feet, we can learn from the Holy Scripture itself, lest anyone think me a deceiver. For the divine words in that place are these: *Vayissa malakh ha-elohim* <note>original: "ויסע מלאך האלהים"</note>—that is, 'And the angel of the angels moved.' This is not as you pronounce it in Latin: 'And the angel of the Lord <gloss>original: "Adonai"</gloss> taking himself up.' For *Adonai*—which we interpret as 'Lord'—is not placed here. Instead, it says *Elohim*, which you likewise read daily translated as 'angels' in the verses: 'You have made him a little lower than the angels,' and 'In the sight of the angels I will sing to you.'

But here it is not written as it often is elsewhere, 'an angel of *Elohim*.' Instead, notably, it says 'the angel of *the* Elohim' <note>original: "mallach ha elohim"</note>, with the demonstrative article <gloss>the</gloss> intervening. It is as if the sacred history wished to say: 'By this angel of the cloud preceding the camp, know that many other angels are also present here, who are the princes of the world.' The Talmud supports us in the *Mechilta* <note>A collection of legal and homiletic interpretations on the Book of Exodus</note>, where Rabbi Nathan seeks the solution to this question from our Master, Simeon Ben Jochai <note>A 2nd-century sage traditionally credited with the authorship of the *Zohar*, the foundational work of Kabbalah</note>, my kinsman. 

'I ask,' he said, 'why is it written everywhere "the angel of Adonai," but here "the angel of the Elohim"?' To which he replied: 'The word *Elohim* <note>original: "אלהים"</note> does not everywhere signify God, but rather a leader or a prefect.' Therefore, that angel is understood to have been present together with the seventy leaders of the provinces; and for that reason, he is called *Malakh ha-elohim*, the angel of those leaders or prefects. And another companion was the angel of fire, the leader of those same ones, so that they are rightly numbered as 72. You have already seen their signs described by me. If you wish—or rather, because you wish (for I know you do)—I will teach you by what path they are drawn out from the sacred letters. Now, take these three verses: *Vayissa, Vayavo, Vayite* <note>Exodus 14:19, 20, and 21; in the original Hebrew, each of these three verses contains exactly 72 letters</note>, and in an upright manner...

# KABBALAH

<note>The left margin of the original manuscript is tight, obscuring the start of several lines near the binding.</note>

...columns individually in the Kabbalistic manner from right to left, so that the letters of each row follow one another continuously from top to bottom. First, place the first character of the first row, which is named **vau** <note>The Hebrew letter ו (Vav)</note>. Then, take the last character of the second row by reading backward, which is **he** <note>The Hebrew letter ה (He)</note>. Finally, return to the beginning of the third row, where you will again find it to be **vau**. When you have joined these three characters in that order, the memorial name of the first angel is born: **vau, he, vau** <note>VHV, the first of the 72 names</note>. And for the second: **lamed, iod, lamed** <note>YLY; the OCR notes only "lamed, iod" due to the tight binding</note>. And for the third: **samech, iod, teth** <note>SIT</note>. This is done likewise for all the others, always in groups of three. When the three columns have been properly erected in this present manner, every explanatory seal of the **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter Name of God (YHWH), here used to describe the source of these expanded names</term> will be revealed. 

Ah, look! Consider and contemplate well: is this not the height of joy, surpassing all the gladness of this world? To remember the holy signs of God and the divine countenances—those whom the Hebrews call **Malachim** <note>original: "Malachim", meaning messengers or angels</note>, the Greeks call **Angels**, and the Latins call **Gods**. To handle with mind and hands such pure and pious, such consecrated things; to converse studiously with those most brilliant beings whose splendor shines only for the keen eyes of noble minds. To take part in the banquets and conversations of the blessed spirits, who love us fraternally more than is the custom of all mortals—and they do not merely "like" us, they truly love us. The very walls seem to exult and congratulate us noble men that, by God's goodness, it has come to pass that through certain seals of human weakness and skillful engravings <note>original: "charagmata", referring to the written characters of the names</note>, we are admitted into the joyful assemblies of the angels, according to the capacity of our strength. With them, let us enjoy and rejoice in tranquility; let us cherish and venerate them, rendering the honor due to a nature so immortal and so sublime, by whom we are loved, instructed, and guarded in turn.

Then **Marranus** <note>A character in this dialogue, representing a seeker of knowledge</note> said: "I see the characters indeed, but I do not hear the sounds of the names; I do not know with what pronunciation the angels should be invoked."

To this, **Simon** <note>The teacher/sage in the dialogue</note> replied: "As they are seen by the eyes, so they are heard by the ears; and as they see us, so they hear those who call upon them. How that can be, I will say in two words: **In spirit and truth** <note>A reference to John 4:24</note>. Whatever 'tongues' our minds possess, such are the 'ears' the angels have. Just as divine spirits speak with the tongues of angels, so let human spirits listen with the ears of their minds. Therefore, they do not establish names for themselves out of necessity, as if they wished to be named and summoned aloud, but they hand down memorial signs because they desire to be remembered by us, lest you think all divine power lies hidden merely in the voice. These symbols, therefore, demand frequent memory of the angels; diligent remembrance leads us mutually into love, and love, in turn, leads back to remembrance. As the proverb says: *Lovers remember everything* <note>original: "minerunt omnia amantes"</note>.

"For this reason, God granted the name **Tetragrammaton**, not so that we might call Him by it (for it is ineffable, and is called by you **unutterable** <note>original: "anekphoniton", a Greek term for a name that cannot be spoken aloud</note>), but for remembrance. For what did the Creator answer to Moses when he asked, 'What is your name?' Surely He said this..."

# BOOK III.
# qq 4

"This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation." <note>A translation of Exodus 3:15</note> Therefore, the **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter Name of God, YHWH</term> is the name for eternity, but for the generations it is only a "memorial," because no human voice can compose a name that can equal the nature of divinity. We know the angels by their works; for that reason, we likewise pronounce names according to those same works of power: such as **Raphael** from "medicine" <note>original: "à medicína Raphael"</note>, **Gabriel** from "virility" or "strength," and **Michael** from "wonder and admiration," which is interpreted as *Who is so strong?* <note>The Hebrew name Mikhael translates to "Who is like God?"</note> However, because we are ignorant of their true essence, the weakness of our mortality is not able to find their proper names, nor to assign them once found, except insofar as it has been granted to us by divine revelation.

Therefore, from the numbers and figures handed down by divine tradition, the most contemplative men are taught to form names for themselves according to the wills of the angels, just as children are taught to compose sounds from letters—whether Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Arabic, or Egyptian. This is not because the voice to be spoken requires letters of this kind, but for the sake of our weak memory, so that the names may be like marks <note>original: "notamina"</note> which excite our senses either by their shape or sound. In turn, the senses move the **fantasy** <term>fantasy: here meaning the faculty of forming mental images</term>, the fantasy moves the memory, the memory moves reason, reason moves the intellect, the intellect moves the mind, and the mind moves the angel. A certain philosopher among your own people, a man of distinguished name, **Maximus of Tyre**, wrote something of this kind very elegantly in the eighth discussion of his book *The Discourses in Rome during his first visit* <note>original: "τῶν ἐν ῥώμῃ διαλέξεων τῆς πρώτης ἐπιδημίας"</note>.

From this, you can infer that it is sufficient if you read the three verses (which I previously decoded in honor and veneration of the seventy-two angels) in that sequence dictated by the Holy Spirit. If, through love for them, you devote yourselves to the most burning love and ecstatic adoration of the name of the most high God, you must carefully remember that just as the number seventy-two proceeds from the number of the Tetragrammaton by **arithmetic proportion**, so the seventy-two angels are produced from the seal of the Creator by a certain divine outflow. 

For since every Hebrew letter designates a specific number, from **Iod**, **He**, **Vau**, and **He**, the number seventy-two arises in this manner: **Iod** denotes ten, **He** five, **Vau** six, and **He** again five. Let all this be gathered from the art of Arithmetic as follows: 
- **Iod** is ten.
- **Iod, He** is fifteen.
- **Iod, He, Vau** is twenty-one.
- **Iod, He, Vau, He** is twenty-six.

Now combine these individual sums: ten, fifteen, twenty-one, and twenty-six, and seventy-two arises. <note>This is a form of Gematria or number mysticism where the Name is expanded cumulatively: 10 + (10+5) + (10+5+6) + (10+5+6+5) = 72</note> Reflecting on these things, you will clearly understand that to invoke spirits, a spiritual voice is needed, not a loud shout like the priests of **Baal**, to whom it was said by the prophet **Elijah** in the third book of Kings, chapter 18: <note>In the Latin Vulgate, 1 Kings is titled 3 Kings</note> "Cry with a louder voice; perhaps your god is in an inn, or on a journey, or surely he is asleep and must be awakened." But if we use any prayer in our supplications, it is not done so that we might move God or the angels with syllables or words as if they were mortals, but so that we might stir our own powers into a heat for them and fix our trust in them like an anchor. It is much like when sailors are accustomed to bring a ship into port by casting out a rope or extending a cable...

# CABALA

...pulling the earth, although it is immobile, with the same effort they use to draw toward the land. In a similar way, through sensible signs established by any tradition, we seem to draw the invisible divinity to us; yet in truth, we—the mobile ones—are drawn toward the immobile divinity. Upon this secret foundation, all sacraments and ritual ceremonies persist. We use these signs, characters, and the voice; hence hymns and songs, hence the drum and the choir, hence strings, cymbals, and the organ, and other musical instruments of that kind. This is not so that we might soften God as if he were a woman, nor so that the angels might be captured by our flatteries and adulations. Rather, it is so that by honoring God and divine things, we may acknowledge the insignificance of our condition, most humbly profess our subjection and obedience, and turn all human pleasure toward the divine. 

Ultimately, in this way, let us conceive an ardent love for the divinity among ourselves, which more than anything else makes us capable of receiving all graces. For this reason, we stretch out our palms, expand our arms, bend our knees, and pray while standing. We slaughter a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, a turtledove, and a pigeon, dividing them in half; we burn a ram caught by its horns in the thicket, killing it with a sword; we mark the **Tau** <note>The Hebrew letter used as a sign of protection in Ezekiel 9:4</note> on the doorposts of houses with blood; we gaze upon the **Bronze Serpent**; and we fashion the **Cherubim** and other images. We speak and vow established words, we build the Sanctuary, and we look with awe upon the High Priest clothed in his varied and wondrous ornaments. 

All these things and those similar to them are done for our sake, so that they may move us, incite us, attract us, and convert us—namely, from visible things to invisible ones. They increase faith, confirm hope, and transfer a true charity among us, most pleasing to God, into a love for divine things, as if in a **recapitulation** <term>anacephalæosis: a Greek rhetorical term for a summary or gathering together of points</term>. All these doctrines belong to the Kabbalists, who, as the third book of the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "Perplexorum"</note> by **Moses the Arab** <note>This refers to Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher</note> attests, say thus: *And every constant remembrance of the Name, and the fear and love of Him, and the service of God <margin>which is this</margin> and the keeping of all the commandments, and that one should believe in the Name of the Lord—that which is necessary for everyone.* <note>The Hebrew text reads: "And all constant remembrance of the Name and His fear and love and the service of God and the keeping of all the commandments and that he believe in the Name YH [Yah] what is necessary for all."</note> Of such ceremonies, the meaning is: frequent memory of God, fear and love of Him, observance of all the commandments, and that God the Most High be believed in—which is necessary for each person. 

Doubtless, we ourselves, being oppressed by the mass of the body, greatly need things that move us to awaken us from our slumber. Just as a noble horse, already exhausted by a long journey, is roused to strength when the trumpet sounds—unable to stand still, twitching its ears—and as an elephant, sluggish with inactivity, rises again into boldness at the sight of fire; so our virtue, weakened by secular things, needs external and bodily incitements, whether of voices or figures. Thus the vigor of our soul may pursue spiritual work more robustly, and our contemplation may be carried upward all the more sharply the more we were previously struck with awe. For this utility, merciful angels have often discovered and proposed to us mortals figures, characters, and sounding voices that are both unknown and absurd—signifying nothing according to the common use of language, but through themselves...

### BOOK III

...of our highest admiration into the constant investigation of intelligible things <note>Things understood by the intellect rather than the senses</note>, and then into the veneration and love of those very things. For these do not signify according to the customs or whims of man, but according to the will of God. It is from this source that the most learned Count of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Cabala into Christian thought</note>, of your own age and school, brought to you what he says in his *Nine Hundred Conclusions*: "In magic, words that seem to have no meaning <note>original: "Non significativæ uoces"</note> have more power than those that do." For every word has power in magic insofar as it is formed by the voice of God; because that in which nature first exercises magic is the voice of God. This is what Pico says.

Then Philolaus said: "We men, while sleeping and snoring, would be moved by a greater awakening through names of this kind if they moved several senses and not just one; so that they would not only appear to our sight through figures and characters, but would simultaneously strike our ears with an articulate voice. Therefore, I greatly desire, if possible, not only to see these things depicted, but also to hear them spoken."

Then Simon replied: "In my opinion—and if I may say so with your permission—those who require an external movement are to be thought very sluggish, and indeed quite dull. However, we are born such that one thing always affects one person more than another, and the same thing does not affect everyone equally."

To this, the learned Marranus said: "I agree with you, Simon, for you speak the truth. Our own people also affirm that angels appear to men in different ways according to the condition and nature of the one seeing them. On this subject, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note> writes extensively in his commentary on Matthew, finally using these words regarding Joseph: 'An angel appears in a dream. And why did he not come openly, as he did to the shepherds, to Zechariah, and to the Virgin? That man was intensely faithful and did not require such a sight.' <note>original Greek: "κατ᾿ ὄναρ φαίνετ᾿ ἄγγελος. θ᾿ διὰ τί μὴ φανερῶς ἐλθὼς ὡς ποιμέσι καὶ τῷ Ζαχαρίᾳ καὶ τῇ παρθένῳ, σφοδρα πιστὸς ἦν ὁ ἀνὴρ, καὶ οὐκ᾿ ἐδεῖτο θ᾿ ὄψεως ταύτης"</note>"

To which Simon replied: "You are correct, and the Cabalists feel no differently, saying that the power of vision in Abraham was stronger than in Lot; for this reason, men appeared to Abraham, while angels appeared to Lot <note>Refers to Genesis 18 and 19; Abraham’s higher spiritual state allowed him to see the divine guests as "men" (integrated into reality), while Lot saw them as "angels" (supernatural beings)</note>. But perhaps we shall speak of these things in another place. Now, as it pertains to our case, there is a great diversity among men, as you know. Some are grateful enough and perhaps content to have seen angels in human form; others in the form of fire, others in the form of wind and air, others in the form of a river and water, others in the form of birds, others in the form of gems or minerals or precious stones, others in the energy of prophecy, others in a certain spirit dwelling within themselves, others in the shape of letters and characters, others in the sound of a voice—and so it is with many types of visions found in Holy Scripture. 

When these characters of the seventy names <note>Likely referring to the Shem HaMephorash, the 72-fold name of God, though here noted as 70</note> do not seem to satisfy you, I will show you the direct way—not only in the characters already mentioned, but also in those to be mentioned hereafter—how a spoken word can be made from the shape of the letters so that it can be articulately pronounced. We have God himself as the author of this art. For we read in the 23rd chapter of Exodus: 'Behold, I send my angel before you to guard you on the way and to lead you into the place I have prepared. Be attentive to his presence and listen to his voice; do not provoke him, for he will not forgive your crimes, because my name is in him.' By this we know that the name of an angel is understood by the highest rite..."

### CABALA

...ought sometimes [to express] the name of God. Therefore, when the Cabalists <note>Followers of the Cabala (Kabbalah), a school of Jewish mysticism</note> were unable to pronounce an angelic name in a way that carried its full meaning, they became accustomed to uttering the whole thing together with the help of a name of God which they added to it. For they see these three characters, יהו <note>original Hebrew: *YHV* (Yod, He, Vav), a portion of the Tetragrammaton</note> or *Gevur* <note>original: "גבור," meaning Might or Strength</note> or *Refa* <note>original: "רפא," meaning to Heal</note> used improperly to signify an angel's name unless the name of God is added, such as Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.

Thus, they too, in other angelic names, attempting to imitate the Holy Scripture, say Raziel, Jophiel, Zedekiel, Peliel, Malthiel, Uriel, and others in a similar fashion. Indeed, just as the Romans called their Capitoline God "Best and Greatest" <note>original Latin: "Optimum Maximum"</note>—"Best" because of his benefits and "Greatest" because of his power, as evidenced by Cicero's testimony in his speech to the Priests regarding his own house—so the Jewish nation calls God *Iah* <note>original: "יה"</note> because of his benefits, and names him *El* <note>original: "אל"</note> because of his force and virtue. For the Cabalists, commenting on the words of King David when he says, "If you, *Iah*, should mark iniquities, Lord, who could stand?" <note>A reference to Psalm 130:3</note> say: "Adonai which is the world of mercy; Adonai which is the world of judgment" <note>original Hebrew: "אדני שׁהוא עולם הרחמים: אדני שׁהוא עולם הדין"</note>, that is, *Iah* represents the world of clemency, and *Adonai* represents the world of severity, as found in the eighth chapter of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Portæ lucis"; referring to the *Sha'are Orah* by Joseph Gikatilla, a foundational text of Spanish Kabbalah</note>. 

Moreover, you read in the sixteenth chapter of Numbers: "O Most Powerful *El*, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin and will your wrath rage against all?" <note>Numbers 16:22</note> Therefore, to us, God is "Best" because he is most clement, and "Greatest" because he is most powerful. These two divine names, *Iah* and *El*, represent these qualities. If you join either of them to any of the seventy-two names, you will produce a remarkably distinguished word with an oxytone <note>A word with the stress on the last syllable</note> accent. 

This must certainly be done by always pronouncing them so that the words become trisyllabic, and that the aspiration <note>The sound of breathing or air</note>—this unique mark written as an *h*—comes from the depths of the chest with a strong breath, as if it were a double Latin letter *h*, and everywhere *Iah* is pronounced as a single sounding syllable. Similarly with *El*; for both of these are uttered as a single syllable even when composed into names, where the accent falls. 

There are, therefore, seventy-two sacred names, which is called the one *Semmaphores* <note>original: "maphores," a corruption of *Schemhamphorasch*, the "Explicit Name" of God</note>, that is, the explanatory name of the most holy four-lettered name <note>The Tetragrammaton: YHVH</note>. These are the invocations of angels to be spoken by men dedicated and devoted to God, with fear and trembling, in this manner: 

Vehuiah. Ieliel. Sitael. Elemiah. Mahasiah. Lelahel. Achaiah. Cahethel. Haziel. Aladiah. Lauiah. Hahaiah. Iezalel. Mebahel. Hariel. Hakamiah. Leuiah. Caliel. Leuuiah. Pahaliah. Nelchael. Ieiaiel. Habuiah. Rochel. Iabamiah. Haiaiel. Mumiah. 

These most excellent men are now ready at hand, with whom you may not only whisper secret conversations in the innermost parts of the heart, but also—if it is lawful—mingle voices and [address] anyone by their symbolic name...

### BOOK III.

...you might care for them, although they are the governors of individual regions, they nevertheless share everything in common. For even if they dwell in the supercelestial world, they nonetheless look after these lower things. If it happens through natural influences that they remain in the heavens and simultaneously govern earthly affairs, how much more are such magistracies granted to the nobler, subtler, and simpler virtues of the higher world, so that they may penetrate our realm, and in turn be penetrated by ours. 

To this end, I shall use the assertion of your Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of the 3rd century and founder of Neoplatonism</note> in his book *On the Intellect, Ideas, and Being*, who says: "This sensible world is determined in only one place, but the intelligible world is everywhere." It is as if he were saying that the latter surrounds, orders, preserves, and penetrates this world of ours. 

Observe, moreover, what wonders the wise men of the Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Jewish mysticism</note> bring to this discussion, saying: **"There is no herb or plant below that does not have a star in the firmament that strikes it and says to it: 'Grow.'"** <note>original Hebrew: "אין לך כל עשב ועשב מלמטה שאין לו מזל ברקיע שמכה אותו ואומר לו גדל"</note> They found this opinion supported by the Holy Scriptures, as is read in Job, chapter 38: "Do you know the laws of the heavens, or can you establish their rule <note>The text suggests "governor" or "executor" here</note> upon the earth?" 

Therefore, do not let such great anxieties for the globe or the cares of lower things hold you back from assigning those angels into the nine choirs of the supercelestial hierarchies by the dispensation of the Creator. For since an angel is "otherness" <note>The quality of being distinct or different</note>, just as God is "identity" <note>The quality of being one and the same</note>, and the first otherness is the binary <note>The number two, representing the first step away from unity</note>, we shall rightly believe that the number of angels arises from the multiplication of the binary. Now, the cubic multiplication of the binary is done thus: two times two, twice <note>2 x 2 x 2</note>, and the first cube will be eight. If you then distribute eight angels into each of the nine choirs, there will be seventy-two, for nine times eight is seventy-two. 

Return now, if you wish, through the choirs to the cube, and through the cube to your *Tetractys* <note>A Pythagorean symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the organization of the universe</note>, which we call the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note> and the Romans call "four-ness." From that, return to the binary, signifying the angelic nature, and from there to the unity, God the Best and Greatest. You will surely experience that if we apply our study to the angels, we are also joined to God through the angels by the ineffable Tetragrammaton: **Yod, He, Vav, He**, in which the most noble nature of those angels first shines forth. 

For if, from those four letters **יהוה**, you take the letter *Yod* four times, and descending thus, the letter *He* three times, the *Vav* twice, and the *He* once, the sum of seventy-two will soon arise for you <note>This is a Cabalistic calculation: (4x10) + (3x5) + (2x6) + (1x5) = 40+15+12+5 = 72</note>. This is the explanatory number of the unutterable and incomprehensible name of God, to which all sacred names are referred. While there is a vast abundance of names, and each is a descriptive title, this alone is God's own and unique name, which is why it is called *The Unique Name* <note>original Hebrew: "המיוחד" (Ha-Meyuchad)</note>. 

Furthermore, these seventy-two are called a single "symbolic name," because their purpose is to signify the one God, the Best and Greatest, albeit through the many and various accounts of the angels—just as we recognize a prince through his courtiers, or an emperor through his army. And truly, the masters of the Cabala venerate and honor these names greatly, through which devoted men...

# CABALA

...it works wonders and things more marvelous than I am permitted to speak of. I will cite as a witness in this cause a most learned man, **Recanati** <note>Menachem Recanati (1250–1310), an influential Italian rabbi and Kabbalist</note>, in his commentary on Exodus 14, who affirms that these characters and these letters are:

> "Above in the essence of the *Merkabah* <term>Merkabah: literally 'Chariot,' referring to the throne-world of God in Jewish mysticism</term>, and they are appointed to perform every task through them, and their operations are known to the **Cabalists**." <note>original Hebrew: "למעלה בעיקיר המרכבה והם ממונים לעשות כל דבר בהם ופעולותיהם ידועים למקובלים"</note>

Thus far the words of **Rabbi Menachem Recanati**. And according to **Rabbi Akiba** <note>A leading 1st-century Jewish scholar and a foundational figure in rabbinic Judaism</note>, they proceed from the throne of God’s glory. 

But let no one think through vain superstition that all things are conferred upon human mortality from heaven by angels alone; rather, all things are done by the majesty of God himself through the angels, even in the lowest realms. As Nebuchadnezzar testifies in the Aramaic of the Book of Daniel: "And according to His will He acts among the host of heaven and the inhabitants of the earth." <note>Daniel 4:35</note> 

For this reason, the traditions of the **Cabala** have received seventy-two verses of pious prayers to God from the Psalms, which are to be written down. Each one of these contains the name **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter divine name of God, YHWH, often considered too sacred to pronounce</term> along with the name of one of the seventy-two angels—except for one verse which indicates the beginning of the creation. They lift their souls as much as possible through these verses to God, strongly ascending from angel to angel. Indeed, among these praises of God, they are raised from one to the next into the heights. 

To this end, the angels assist them, so that leaving behind worldly anxieties, they may be carried toward God by their own spirit, just as the lightest feather is lifted to the sublime and heavenly heights by the movement of the thinnest breeze. Behold and hear the prayer of the verses with the Tetragrammaton and the angels; for I shall show both to you with my finger as much as with my voice, thus:

> The Lord is a shield for me, my glory, and the lifter of my head.
> But You, Lord, do not be far off; O my strength, hasten to help me.
> The Lord is my refuge and my fortress; my God, in whom I trust.
> Turn, Lord, deliver my soul; save me for the sake of Your mercy.
> I sought the Lord and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears.
> Sing praises to the Lord who dwells in Zion; declare His deeds among the peoples.
> The Lord is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in mercy.
> Come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the Lord our Maker.
> Remember, Lord, Your tender mercies and Your lovingkindness, for they are from of old.
> Let Your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, just as we hope in You.
> The Lord lives! Blessed be my Rock, and let the God of my salvation be exalted.
> Why, Lord, do You stand afar off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?
> Shout joyfully to the Lord, all the earth; break forth in song, rejoice, and sing praises.
> The Lord is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.
> The Lord has become my fortress, and my God the rock of my refuge.
> O Lord, God of my salvation, I have cried out day and night before You.
> O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth!

I have already shown you, excellent men, that in every line there is the Name of four letters <term>Tetragrammaton|The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</term>, and the three letters of the angel, placed either in a direct or transverse order. These are arranged from the three verses of Exodus 14: "And he moved," "And he came," and "And he stretched out," <note>original: ויסע ויבא ויט (Vayissa, Vayavo, Vayet). These are the first words of Exodus 14:19, 20, and 21, which each contain 72 letters and are used to derive the 72 Names of God.</note> which names the Romans until now have not interpreted. Moreover, they read the Psalmody in this way, as perhaps you were able to see previously in *Capnio* <note>"Capnio" was the Greek-style nickname for Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering humanist and scholar of Hebrew and Kabbalah.</note> in his work *On the Wonder-Working Word* <note>original: *De Verbo Mirifico*</note>.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous discussion regarding the mystical names of God. Having just finished reviewing the biblical verses associated with the 72 Names, the characters Marranus, Philolaus, and Simon now transition into a systematic explanation of the ten Sefirot—the divine emanations that form the core structure of Kabbalistic thought.</meta>

<page-num>849</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.</header>

Then Marranus said: "Are we to allow you, who have labored so much on this one matter, to wander so far afield? We hasten with all our desire toward the art of Kabbalah itself, if such a thing exists." And Philolaus replied: "In my opinion, it is not just one thing that Simon has discussed, but three or four times more—and far more numerous things indeed. For he spoke of the **Sabbath of Sabbaths**, which is eternal rest and the goal of Kabbalah <note>The "Sabbath of Sabbaths" refers to the ultimate mystical union or the world to come.</note>; and afterwards, by what steps we may ascend to it, as much through the gates of prudence as the paths of wisdom. He has also instructed us with a clear voice concerning the angels who explain the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God (YHWH), considered too sacred to pronounce.</note> and the *Semhamaphores* <note>original: "Semhamaphores"—the 72-fold Name of God derived from Exodus.</note>."

To this, Simon replied: "If you remember the rest correctly, I indeed previously offered some remarks on that worthy religion of the **ten Kabbalistic numerations**, and perhaps I promised that I would speak of them. I shall do so by way of a catalog, if you will listen to me attentively." "Then we listen eagerly," they both said, "so proceed without hesitation."

Soon Simon said: "The ten numerations, called **Ten Sefirot** <note>original: עשר ספירות (Eser Sefirot). These are the ten attributes through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> by the Kabbalists, are treated in many ways by many of us. Some treat them in the manner of a **tree**, others in the **form of a man**, so that mention is often made of the root, trunk, branches, and bark; or often indeed of the head, shoulders, legs, feet, and the right and left sides. These are the **ten divine names** which we mortals conceive regarding God—whether essential, personal, notional, or common—and they are named thus:

1. **Crown** <note>original: כתר (Keter)</note>, which is the crown.
2. **Wisdom** <note>original: חכמה (Hokhmah)</note>, which is wisdom.
3. **Prudence** or **Intelligence** <note>original: בינה (Binah)</note>, which is understanding.
4. **Clemency** or **Goodness** <note>original: חסד (Hesed)</note>, which is kindness.
5. **Gravity** or **Severity** <note>original: גבורה (Gevurah)</note>, which is power or judgment.
6. **Ornament** <note>original: תפארת (Tiferet)</note>, which is beauty.
7. **Triumph** <note>original: נצח (Netzah)</note>, which is victory or endurance.
8. **Confession of Praise** <note>original: הוד (Hod)</note>, which is majesty or splendor.
9. **Foundation** <note>original: יסוד (Yesod)</note>, which is the basis.
10. **Kingdom** <note>original: מלכות (Malkhut)</note>, which is the realm.

But above the Crown is placed **Infinity** <note>original: אין סוף (Ein Sof)</note>, which is the limitless and the abyss. Shall I speak out, or remain silent? The matter is surely one of profound speculation and a sort of immense sea, into which all our contemplation is submerged, and being submerged, is absorbed by a certain gaping void. Do you not remember how much the modern 'divinely-taught' teachers <note>original: "theodidascali"</note> of almost all nations now toil day and night? They labor almost solely on the concepts of attributes, which some call divine perfections and others call attributes—whether negative, affirmative, absolute, relative, or connotative. 

These things you can now easily learn (in my opinion) from the Kabbalistic book, the compendium **Gates of Light** <note>original: "Porta lucis." This refers to the Latin translation of Joseph Gikatilla’s "Sha'are Orah," a fundamental Kabbalistic text.</note>, which **Paulus Ricius** <note>A famous 16th-century convert from Judaism to Christianity and personal physician to Emperor Maximilian I, who translated Kabbalistic works into Latin.</note>—an extraordinarily learned man, formerly one of ours and now a Christian—collected from a certain Castilian Rabbi. Likewise, you can learn from the *Introductions* he wrote on Kabbalah. On that same subject, that great Master of Kabbalah, **Rabbi Joseph, son of Gikatilla**, wrote the book **Gates of Justice** <note>original: שערי צדק (Sha'are Tzedek). This is another title often associated with Gikatilla’s works explaining the Sefirot.</note>. Many commentators have written many things concerning the tree of the ten numerations, unfolding this involved cause and reducing almost the entire sacred Old Scripture into these ten numerations—and through them into those ten names of God, and through those into the single name of the **Tetragrammaton**. They affirm that the **Infinite** <note>original: "Ensoph"</note> is both the **Alpha and Omega** <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, signifying the beginning and the end.</note>, He who said: 'I am the first, and I am the last.' And they affirm that the **Crown** <note>original: כתר (Keter)</note>, that is, the Crown of the kingdom of all ages, is a fountain without a bottom and the **Father of Mercies** <note>original: אב הרחמים (Av Ha-Rachamim)</note>."

He references contemporary scholars like Paulus Ricius and foundational texts like the Gates of Light to explain how all Scripture points back to these divine names and the infinite Ein Sof.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Simon’s catalog of the Ten Sefirot (divine emanations). Having introduced the first Sefirah on the previous page, he now elaborates on its nature before transitioning to the second, Wisdom, explaining the linguistic and numerical symbolism that defines them.</meta>

<page-num>850</page-num>
<header>KABBALAH</header>

...that is, the father of mercies: whose mystery is this, that he seals by means of **Truth** <note>original: *Emeth*. In Jewish tradition, Truth is considered the "seal" of God because the three letters—Aleph, Mem, Tav—are the first, middle, and last letters of the alphabet, encompassing all reality.</note>, which is to say, essence through truth. Just as the noble poet Eliezer Haklir says, *Truth is his seal* <note>original: אמת חותמו (*Emeth chotamo*)</note>. Arithmetic logic proves this; following this method, if I multiply **I Shall Be** <note>original: *Ehieh* (אהיה). The numerical value is 21.</note> by itself, there arise four hundred and forty-one, which is the value of **Truth** <note>original: אמת (*Emeth*: Aleph=1, Mem=40, Tav=400 = 441).</note>, that is, the true or truth: just as *The Lord is Peace* <note>original: *Adonai Shalom*</note>. Many things are reduced to this point, such as the "Great Aleph," the fear of the Lord, inaccessible light, and the days of eternity: as in that verse, *His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity*. So writes the distinguished Kabbalist Tedacus Levi <note>Todros ben Joseph Abulafia, a 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist.</note> in his work on the ten numerations.

Regarding the second numeration, **Wisdom** <note>The Sefirah of *Chokhmah*.</note>, these things are referred to it from the attributes or properties: first, **Substance** <note>original: *Ies* or *Yesh*, meaning "there is" or "being."</note>, that is, being; the primitive law; the letter **Yod** <note>The first letter of the Tetragrammaton (YHVH).</note>, which is the first letter of the four-letter name; the land of the living; the thirty-two paths; the seventy facets of the law; the Lord of the beginning; **Amen**; the Book; the Holy; the Will; the **Beginning**; and other things of that kind.

Perhaps it is a wonder that the second numeration is called "the Beginning." For in Recanati <note>Menahem Recanati, an influential 14th-century Italian Kabbalist.</note>, that excellent master of Kabbalah, regarding the interpretation of Genesis, it says: *And perhaps you will ask, since Wisdom is the second Sefirah, why is it called "Beginning"?* <note>original Hebrew: ואולי תשאל שחהכמה היא ספירה השנייה למה קראה ראשית</note>. For it is written in the Book Bahir <note>One of the oldest Kabbalistic texts.</note>, *There is no "Beginning" except Wisdom* <note>original Hebrew: ראשית אלא חכמה</note>. To which indeed it seems right to me to respond: because that absolute essence of the three highest Kabbalistic numerations—which you call the three persons in the divine—is infinite; since it remains withdrawn and idle in an abyss of darkness, or (as they say) looking toward nothing, it is therefore called **Nothing** <note>original: *Ayin*.</note>, or non-being, and "No-End": that is, **Infinite** <note>original: *Ein Sof*.</note>. This is because we, being punished by a poverty of intellect regarding divine matters, judge those things which are not manifest just as we judge those things which do not exist.

But when it prepares itself so that it might be something and truly subsist, then the "Dark Aleph" is converted into the "Lucid Aleph": for it is written, *As is its darkness, so is its light*. It is then called the "Great Aleph" when it desires to go forth and appear as the cause of all things through the letter **Beth** which immediately follows it; regarding which Menahem Recanati writes thus: *So you will find this letter, namely Beth, making things* <note>original Hebrew: א האות הזאת פועלת הדברים</note>. For this reason, the Aleph receives the same Beth as its nearest and most fruitful letter, and is named **Father** <note>original: *Ab* (אב), formed from Aleph and Beth.</note>, the father of all generation and perfection. Then, having assumed the Beth, it sends it out again into the beginning of the universe, desiring to achieve its goal from the Infinite; wherefore, by joining the letter **Nun** to the Beth, it generates the **Son** <note>original: *Ben* (בן), formed from Beth and Nun.</note>, which is the production within the Godhead and the principle of "otherness." From this it is called **Beginning** <note>original: *Reshit*.</note>, even though it is the second emanation in order: that is, the second Kabbalistic numeration, through which all things are made. For it is written: *You have made all things in Wisdom*.

<summary>Simon explains the first two Sefirot, showing how the "Nothing" of the Infinite becomes the "Beginning" through Wisdom. He uses linguistic and numerical analysis of the Hebrew letters Aleph and Beth to explain the divine relationship of Father and Son.</summary>

the outflow becomes the second numeration, because the son is the boundary of generation. There remains thirdly the middle between *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note> and *Nun* <note>The fourteenth letter.</note>, which is *Yod* <note>The tenth letter, י.</note>, the mark of the holy name **Yah** <note>original: יה (*Ia*), a shortened form of the divine name.</note>. If you interweave both its characters alternately into the name **Understanding** <note>original: בינה (*Binah*).</note>, it will be Understanding, Prudence, or Providence; namely, the third emanation in divine matters. To this are attributed the name *Adonai* <note>Lord</note>, spirit, soul, a vow, the mystery of faith, the mother of children, the king sitting on the throne of mercies, the great jubilee, the great Sabbath, the foundation of spirits, the wonderful light, the supreme day, the fifty gates, the day of atonement, the inner voice, and the river flowing out of Paradise. It is also the second letter of the **Tetragrammaton** <term>the four-letter name of God, YHWH</term>, repentance, deep waters, "my sister," "the daughter of my father," and other things. Thus far we have noted the three numerations which are called by the Kabbalists—according to the testimony of Rabbi Isaac <note>Likely Isaac the Blind, a foundational figure in 12th-century Kabbalah.</note> in his commentaries on the *Book of Formation* <note>original: *libri Ietzira* (*Sefer Yetzirah*).</note>—**the three highest numerations in one throne** <note>original: ספירות העליונות בכסא אחד (*Sefirot ha-Elyonot be-Kise Echad*)</note>; in which sits the Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of **Sabaoth** <term>Hosts or Armies</term>.

To **Goodness**, or Clemency, which is the fourth numeration, along with the divine name **El**, these things are also appropriated: grace, mercy, the right arm, the innocent, the third day, white fire, the face of a lion, the first foot, Abraham the Elder, the East, the higher waters, the silver of God, Michael <note>The Archangel.</note>, the priest, the angel in the appearance of amber <note>original: *electri*, referring to the *Chasmal* or glowing metal/amber seen in Ezekiel's vision.</note>, *Hasmal*, white garments, the South, and other things.

In the fifth numeration of **Severity**, the divine name is **Elohim**, and to it are applied fear, the property of rigor or gravity, the negative precepts of the law, the left arm, fire proceeding from the waters (as in the *Book of Formation*). Likewise the fourth day, the West, Gabriel, Isaac the Elder, night, strength, the golden altar, the second foot, sanctification, and darkness. **Metatron** <note>The supreme angel or heavenly scribe.</note>, the North, and the dark-colored appearance.

To the sixth is applied **Eloha**: illuminating speculation, the tree of life, pleasure, the middle line, the written law, the high priest, the sunrise, and the purple color. And Tedacus Levi <note>Todros ben Joseph Abulafia, a 13th-century Spanish Kabbalist.</note> writes that from this place the seventy nations on earth are explained; its seal is **The Truth of the Lord** <note>original: *Emeth Adonai*.</note>, and it is called peace, and its form is figured in the moon, and its mystery is the third letter of the Tetragrammaton, and this mystery is "Our Father who is in heaven," the supernal man or celestial Adam, judgment, and sentence. Michael. Israel the Elder. The God of Jacob.

To the seventh are referred **Adonai Sabaoth**, the leg, the foot, the right column, the great wheel, the vision of prophecy, Moses, and the rest.

To the eighth belong **Elohe Sabaoth**: the mystery of the column and the left foot, and **Boaz** <note>One of the two pillars of Solomon’s Temple.</note>; from there is drawn the ancient serpent, the discipline of the Lord, the branch, Aaron, the Cherub, the sons of the King, the grinding mills, and other things.

To the ninth is appropriated **Shaddai** <note>original: *Sadai*, meaning Almighty.</note>, the foundation of the world, Zion, the fountain of pools, the righteous one, the living God. The complete Sabbath. The middle between "Keep" and "Remember" <note>Referring to the two versions of the Sabbath commandment in the Decalogue: *Shamor* (keep) and *Zakhor* (remember).</note>. The fiftieth day of Leviathan, Aries, Joseph the Just, Solomon, justice, strength, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and the covenant of the Lord.
